The Order Service: Java and Spring Boot in depth#

One microservice built with Domain-Driven Design (DDD), every mechanism explained, for C# developers

This book follows one service, the shop's order service, from the reasons for Domain-Driven Design to the team's playbook. Read it in order. Each chapter opens with a table that gives its answers first, so you can come back to one chapter later. The whole book takes about 19 hours 10 minutes.

Preface#

This book explains one service completely.

The service is the order service of the book's online shop. It is built with Domain-Driven Design (DDD) in Spring Boot 4.1, on Java 25, with Amazon DocumentDB as its database. Every Spring feature the service uses is explained in full, in the chapter where the service first needs it. For each feature, the chapter says how it works inside and which settings the service uses. It says which choices were open, what goes wrong, how to test it, and what ASP.NET Core does instead.

The book is a sibling of the handbook Java for C# Developers. The handbook teaches each feature at a first-read level, in a chapter you can read in a few minutes. This book starts where the handbook stops. When a chapter here needs the basics, it links to the handbook instead of repeating them.

Who it is for#

You write C#, and you now build Spring Boot services. You have read the handbook, or you have worked with Spring Boot for a few months. You want to judge design advice, not only follow it. When a colleague or a tool proposes a design, you want to know which rule it bends and what that costs.

How to read it#

Read it in order. Each chapter adds one layer or one concern to the same service, and later chapters build on earlier ones. The book has three parts of work in each chapter:

WhereWhat you findUse it for
the table at the topevery difference the chapter covers, one row each, with the answer in the rowthe first read, and every refresh
the sectionsthe full explanation of each row, with the service's own codethe first read
the pragmatic calloutseach place where the service departs from a strict rule, with the reason and the costjudging a design

Every section of this book is open in every reading mode, because the book is read in order. The book opens in Complete. Essentials and Everyday fold only the asides that are marked as legacy or as deeper notes. The reading time in the sidebar is for the whole book.

Every Java example in this book is copied from one real project. The project is a multi-module Maven build with Spring Boot 4.1.2, a platform library and the order service. Its tests pass, and a script compares each example with its source file. So an example here is not a sketch. It compiles, and it runs.

Four chapters stand apart from the others. Each one follows one run of the service as a story, in scenes, with one protagonist. Every scene ends with what you can see at that moment, and what you can hook or tune there. The chapter Maven in depth: resolution and the lifecycle follows the chapter on the build. The chapter Starting the service: from main() to the first request follows the chapter on the container. Two chapters on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), The JVM under the service: memory and The JVM under the service: code, threads and the compiler, follow the chapter on running and shipping. Their numbers come from runs of the service, and each chapter says on which machine.

The last part, Reasoning from first principles, is for the refresh. It defines every DDD and microservices word in one or two sentences. It gives nineteen principles. Then it answers the questions that experienced teams ask, and each answer names the principle that decides it. Every principle and every question is a card in Review. To drill one topic, choose the part in Review.

The two books#

A link to the handbook opens the handbook's page on the website, at the right place. Such a link needs a network connection. The glossary, Java words in plain English, is included in this book too, so the word tooltips work without a connection. The glossary is shared between the two books, and its heading still carries the handbook's appendix letter.

Review asks you the book's 341 questions one at a time. It asks a question again if you missed it. These questions are a deck of their own. They are not part of the handbook's 90-minute refresh.

To find one fact, press ⌘K or Ctrl+K. Then type a Spring annotation, a setting, a C# name or an error message.

An appendix at the back says what the book targets, how its facts were checked, and what it leaves out. See About this book.

Why DDD, and the service we build#

Why DDD, and how much · Chapter 01· 27 min read

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a way to design software around the business rules. Each rule is written once, in the object it protects. This part builds one service with DDD, the shop's order service. This chapter says what DDD solves, what it costs, and when it is not worth it. Then it shows the service.

KindA usual ASP.NET Core serviceThe order service, with DDDNote

Note

How this part was checked. Every Java, YAML, JSON and shell example of this part is copied from a companion service. The companion builds with Spring Boot 4.1.2 and Java 25, and its tests pass. The C# examples were compiled with the .NET SDK 10.0.300 and C# 12. Nothing was run against Amazon DocumentDB.

The problem DDD solvesnew#

The shop has a rule. An order ships only when it is paid and every line is picked. In a usual ASP.NET Core service, the rule is an if in a service method. Months later, a second team adds a batch job that ships orders. The job sets the status directly, and the rule is skipped. Nothing fails until a customer receives an order that nobody paid for.

DDD solves this problem with one idea. Each business rule is written once, inside the object whose data it protects. The object has no setter for that data. So the only way to change the status is the method that checks the rule.

The code below shows both designs. On the left, the rule is in a service, and the status has a public setter. On the right, the rule is a method of the order, from the companion service of this part.

ASP.NET Core and EF Core
public class OrderService(ShopDb db, TimeProvider clock)
{
    public async Task ShipAsync(long orderId)
    {
        var order = await db.Orders.Include(o => o.Lines).SingleAsync(o => o.Id == orderId);
        if (order.Status != OrderStatus.Paid)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("The order is not paid.");
        if (order.Lines.Any(line => line.PickedAt is null))
            throw new InvalidOperationException("A line is not picked.");

        order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped;
        order.ShippedAt = clock.GetUtcNow();
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
    }
}
The order service
public void ship(Clock clock) {
    requireNotFinished();
    if (status != OrderStatus.PAID) {
        throw new OrderNotPaidException(id());
    }
    if (lines.stream().anyMatch(line -> !line.isPicked())) {
        throw new UnpickedLinesException(id());
    }
    status = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
    shippedAt = clock.instant();
    raise(new OrderShipped(id(), shippedAt));
}
Reading the code
order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped;

In C#, Status has a public setter. Any class can write this line, with or without the two checks above it.

public void ship(Clock clock)

In Java, ship is a method of Order. It receives the clock, so a test can fix the time. Clock is from java.time. It has the same purpose as TimeProvider in .NET.

requireNotFinished();

This private method refuses an order that is already shipped or cancelled. The rule about finished orders is written once, and every state change calls it.

throw new OrderNotPaidException(id());

Each broken rule has its own exception class. The platform turns it into an HTTP 422 response with a stable code, here ORDER_NOT_PAID.

status = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;

The field is private, and the class has no setter for it. So this line inside ship is the only place in the service that can make an order shipped.

raise(new OrderShipped(id(), shippedAt));

The order adds an object that says it shipped. This object is called a domain event. Every use case of the order saves it through one step, which also publishes its events. So a use case cannot save the change and forget the event.

The two designs check the same rule. The difference is who can skip it. In the C# design, the rule protects one entry point. In the Java design, the rule protects the data itself. A batch job, a message listener and a controller all call order.ship(clock), because no other way exists.

In the companion, a test runs on every build. ArchitectureTest fails if an entity has a public setter. For more about these tests, see the section What keeps a DDD service readable.

What DDD is, in this book's wordsnew#

Eric Evans described DDD in his book Domain-Driven Design, with the subtitle Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. Addison-Wesley published it in August 2003. DDD works at two levels. This part uses words from both levels, and each word is introduced where the service first needs it.

The first level is about the business and its boundaries. It is called strategic design.

  • The domain is the business that the software serves. Here it is the shop.
  • The words that the business experts use are called the ubiquitous language. This book calls them the business words. The code uses the same words. An order is placed, paid, shipped or cancelled, and its lines are picked. An order is never "processed" or "updated".
  • A bounded context is a part of the business with its own model and its own meaning for each word. In the shop, the order service is one bounded context. The stock service is another one. Each owns its data.

The second level is about the code inside one bounded context. It is called tactical design. Its building blocks are the aggregate, the entity, the value object, the domain event, the repository and the services. The table shows where each one appears in the order service.

Building blockIn the order serviceTaught in
aggregateOrder, with its lines and its last payment, saved as one documentthe chapter on aggregates
entityOrderLine, which has its own identity inside the orderthe chapter on aggregates
value objectMoney, ProductCode and Payment, which have no identity and never changethe chapter on aggregates
domain eventOrderShipped, which the order records when it shipsthe outbox chapter
repositoryOrderRepository, the interface that loads and saves ordersthe chapter on layers
domain serviceShippingPolicy, a rule that needs an order and its notesthe chapter on rules
application serviceOrderService, which runs the steps of each use casethe use-case chapter

A bounded context has its own words for the things of another context. The stock service has its own model of stock. The order service needs one answer from it, and it keeps that answer in its own words:

/**
 * The stock service's answer, in this service's words: either every product is held for the
 * order, or some are not available.
 *
 * <p>The domain decides what the answer means: an order is placed only if everything is available.
 *
 * @param available           whether every product is held
 * @param unavailableProducts the products that are not available; empty when {@code available}
 */
public record StockAvailability(boolean available, List<ProductCode> unavailableProducts) implements ValueObject {

    public StockAvailability {
        unavailableProducts = List.copyOf(unavailableProducts);
    }

StockAvailability is a record with two components. It says whether the stock service holds every product, and which products it does not have. The order service never sees the stock service's own classes. A class that translates another service's model into this service's words is called an anti-corruption layer. For how the service calls the stock service, see the chapter Calling other services.

What to use, and what to keep lightnew#

DDD has many parts, and a team does not need all of them. This book uses the parts that find the rules and the boundaries. It keeps the rest light, or leaves it out.

Use these parts:

  • Event storming. EventStorming is a workshop format. Its official book is by Alberto Brandolini. Its site describes it as a flexible workshop in which people explore a complex business together. In the workshop, developers and business experts look at what happens in the business together. Then the team looks for the rules, and for the boundaries between the parts of the business.
  • Bounded contexts. Each service owns one part of the business and its data. Other services use its API or its events, never its database.
  • Business words, not jargon. A class, a method and an exception use the word that a business expert would use. A business expert says "ship". Nobody in the warehouse says "update the status to 3".
  • Aggregates as consistency boundaries. An aggregate is the group of data that one rule must see at once, and that is saved together. For how to find one, see the chapter Finding the aggregates.
  • The full model only where there are rules. Lookup data and simple features use simpler code. For the three levels of the order service, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The business words reach every name, even the values of an enum. The companion stores the status of an order as its name, so the names are business words that never change:

/**
 * Where an order is in its life. It is stored as its name, so never rename a value.
 *
 * <p>NEW becomes PAID when the payment arrives, and PAID becomes SHIPPED. NEW or PAID may become
 * CANCELLED. SHIPPED and CANCELLED are final.
 */
public enum OrderStatus {
    NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED
}

The comment above OrderStatus names every allowed change of state. A business expert can read it and correct it.

Leave these parts out, unless one bounded context clearly needs them:

  • Event sourcing. With event sourcing, a service stores the list of events of an aggregate instead of its current state. It is useful when the business needs the full history of every change, as an audit or for replay. The order service stores the current state, and it keeps an audit log beside it.
  • Full CQRS. Command query responsibility segregation (CQRS) uses one model for changes and another model, often another database, for reads. It is useful when reads and changes need very different shapes or scale. The order service reads and changes the same documents. For the choice, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

Do you need DDD? The conditions that make it worth its costnew#

DDD costs time and code. It is worth that cost when the rules are the hard part of the software. Look for these conditions. The more of them a service has, the more DDD is worth.

ConditionIn the shopWhy DDD helps
complex rulesan order ships only when it is paid, picked, and no note needs actioneach rule has one home, and a test that names it
many states and workflowsan order is new, paid, shipped or cancelled, and each state allows other actionsthe methods of the aggregate allow only the changes that the state permits
rules that must never be bypasseda shipped order must never changethe data has no setter, so the only way in is the method that checks
a long lifethe order service will run for years and change many timesa new developer finds each rule in one place, not spread over the code
high stakesshipping an unpaid order loses moneya mistake in a rule is found by a fast unit test, not by a customer
rules to recover from an old systeman old shop system may hold some rules only in its stored procedureseach recovered rule becomes a method and a test with a business name
data that breaks rules during a migrationold orders without a valid e-mail addressthe model refuses bad values, so the migration finds them before customers do
finding service boundariesorders, stock and payments change for different reasonsbounded contexts show where one service should end

Two conditions need a closer look. Both appear when a new service replaces an old system.

Rules to recover from an old system. An old system often holds rules that nobody wrote down. They are in stored procedures, in screens and in the memory of its users. DDD gives each recovered rule a place and a name. Write it as a method of the aggregate. Then write a test whose name a business expert can read. The order tests of the companion read like a list of rules:

@Test
void refusesAnUnpaidOrder() {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> newOrder().ship(CLOCK)).isInstanceOf(OrderNotPaidException.class);
}

@Test
void refusesAnOrderWithAnUnpickedLine() {
    Order order = newOrder();
    order.recordPayment(payment(NOW));

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> order.ship(CLOCK)).isInstanceOf(UnpickedLinesException.class);
}
// ...
@Test
void aRepeatedOrEarlierPaymentChangesNothing() {
    Order order = newOrder();
    order.recordPayment(payment(NOW));
    order.pullEvents();

    assertThat(order.recordPayment(payment(NOW))).isFalse();
    assertThat(order.recordPayment(payment(NOW.minusSeconds(60)))).isFalse();
    assertThat(order.pullEvents()).isEmpty();
}

The tests use plain JUnit, with no Spring and no mocks. Each one runs in a few milliseconds. newOrder(), payment(NOW) and CLOCK come from a shared class of test data. assertThatThrownBy is from AssertJ. It runs the code and checks the exception that it throws. Show the test names to a business expert, and ask which rule is missing.

Data that breaks rules during a migration. Old data was written under old rules, or under no rules. In the order service, loading a stored order applies no business rules. But the loader still builds each value object, and each value object checks its own value:

@Override
public Order toDomain(OrderDocument document) {
    return Order.rehydrate(
            OrderId.of(document.getId()),
            document.getVersion(),
            new CustomerContact(document.customerName, document.customerEmail),
            new DeliveryMethod(document.deliveryMethod),
            document.placedAt,
            document.lines.stream().map(OrderDocumentMapper::line).toList(),
            OrderStatus.valueOf(document.status),
            payment(document.lastPayment),
            document.shippedAt,
            document.cancelledAt);
}

Order.rehydrate rebuilds an order without checking the rules of the order, because loading is not a business action. But new CustomerContact(...) checks the format of the e-mail address. So a migrated order with a broken address fails to load. That is the right result, but the wrong time to find it. Before the new service takes traffic, run a check that loads every migrated document through the mapper. Fix or set aside each document that fails. For how the service runs migrations, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

When DDD is not worth itnew#

DDD is not worth its cost when a service has few rules. Microsoft's guide to .NET microservices says the same. Its page "Designing a microservice domain model" discusses a very simple CRUD service. CRUD means create, read, update and delete. For such a service, the page says, entities that hold only data may be good enough. The guide's sample shop uses DDD for its ordering service, but not for its catalog service.

Do not use DDD in these cases:

  • A service that stores and returns data, with no rules beyond the format of each field.
  • Read-only lookup data, such as the delivery methods of the shop.
  • Reports and search pages, which read data and change nothing.
  • Code that connects two systems, and only translates and forwards messages.
  • A prototype that will be thrown away. Write it simply, and model the rules in the real service.

The choice is made per feature, not per service. The order service itself has a feature with no DDD building blocks. Its package description says why:

/**
 * Lookup values, such as delivery methods and note categories, for drop-down lists and for
 * checking codes. The data changes only with a deployment, through a seed migration.
 *
 * <p>This feature uses the simple level: no aggregate, no domain model and no events. A
 * document record, a Spring Data repository, and the logic in the application service. Read-only
 * lookup data has no business behaviour, so DDD's building blocks would only add files.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.reference;

A file named package-info.java holds the comment and the annotations of a whole package. Here the line package com.acme.orderservice.reference; names the package it describes. The reference feature has a document, a repository and a service, and nothing else. For the three levels side by side, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

What DDD costsnew#

A team that chooses DDD should know the costs before it starts. There are three.

The learning curve. DDD has its own words, and a new developer needs weeks to use them well. A developer from a usual ASP.NET Core service expects public setters, rules in services and one class for each table. Each habit must change. The chapters of this part teach each change with its reason.

More types and more mapping. The full style keeps the model and the stored shape apart. So one order has a domain class, a document class and a mapper between them. A view and two data transfer objects (DTOs), one for the request and one for the response, carry it in and out. In the companion, the delivery method of an order appears in 13 files of the order feature. Here is half of the mapper that copies an order to its stored document:

@Override
public OrderDocument toDocument(Order order) {
    OrderDocument document = new OrderDocument();
    document.customerName = order.customer().name();
    document.customerEmail = order.customer().email();
    document.deliveryMethod = order.deliveryMethod().code();
    document.status = order.status().name();
    document.placedAt = order.placedAt();
    document.shippedAt = order.shippedAt();
    document.cancelledAt = order.cancelledAt();
    document.lines = order.lines().stream().map(OrderDocumentMapper::lineDocument).toList();
    document.lastPayment = paymentDocument(order.lastPayment());
    return document;
}

Each new field of an order needs a line in toDocument, and a line in the method that reads the document. The light style of the note feature has no mapper at all. It has other costs, which the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service explains.

Modelling time with experts. The model is only as good as the team's understanding of the business. That understanding comes from hours with the people who do the work. A team without access to business experts gets the extra types, but not the better model.

Easier to reason about: the questions answered in one placenew#

The value of DDD shows when someone asks a question about the code. In a service where the rules are spread over controllers, services and jobs, each answer needs a search. In the order service, each answer has one place. The table lists the usual questions and where the answer is.

QuestionWhere the answer isWhy it is enough to look there
When can an order ship?Order.ship and ShippingPolicyevery rule about shipping is in these two classes
Can anything bypass that rule?Order has no setter, and ArchitectureTest checks itthe build fails when someone adds a public setter to an entity
What does this use case do?the method in OrderService, such as shipeach use case is a short list of steps, with no rule in it
What happens when an order ships?OrderIntegrationEventMapper and the listeners of OrderShippedevery reaction to the event is a listener of that event type
Is the rule tested?OrderTest, in the nested class Shippingeach rule has a test whose name states the rule
What breaks if storage changes?the persistence package of the featurethe domain package uses no MongoDB class, and a test checks it
Where is the code for notes?the note packageeach business feature is one package, with the same folders inside

Here is the use case that ships an order. It names its steps, and it holds no rule:

/** Ships the order. The rule across the order and its notes is checked by the domain service. */
@Transactional
public void ship(OrderId orderId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);                                         // load
    long notesNeedingAction = notes.countNeedingAction(orderId.value());       // ask the note feature
    shippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction);                   // rule across aggregates
    order.ship(clock);                                                         // rule and change
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_SHIPPED);                         // save, publish, audit
}

@Transactional runs the method in one database transaction. The four steps load the order, ask the note feature for a count, check the rule across the order and its notes, and ship. The last line saves the order, publishes its events and records the audit. A reader learns what shipping does from five lines. For the steps of every use case, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

What gets hardertrap#

DDD does not make everything easier. An honest team says what gets harder, and works against it. Four things get harder.

More indirection. A request passes through a controller, an application service, an aggregate, a repository port, an adapter and a mapper. In a usual ASP.NET Core service, the same request passes through a controller, a service and a DbContext. Each extra layer is one more file to open.

Events hide the flow. When a method raises an event, the code that reacts to it is in another class. The IDE does not lead you there with one click. In the companion, two classes react to OrderShipped. One counts the shipped orders. The other decides which events leave the service:

/**
 * Decides which order events leave the service. Placed, shipped and cancelled orders are
 * published; picked lines and recorded payments stay internal. Every published event is a
 * contract to maintain, so publish only what another service needs.
 */
@Component
class OrderIntegrationEventMapper implements IntegrationEventMapper {

    @Override
    public Optional<IntegrationEvent> toIntegrationEvent(DomainEvent event) {
        return switch (event) {
            case OrderPlaced placed -> Optional.of(new OrderPlacedV1(newEventId(), placed.occurredAt(),
                    placed.orderId().value(), placed.deliveryMethod().code(),
                    placed.items().stream()
                            .map(item -> new OrderPlacedV1.Line(item.product().value(), item.quantity()))
                            .toList()));
            case OrderShipped shipped -> Optional.of(new OrderShippedV1(newEventId(), shipped.occurredAt(),
                    shipped.orderId().value()));
            case OrderCancelled cancelled -> Optional.of(new OrderCancelledV1(newEventId(), cancelled.occurredAt(),
                    cancelled.orderId().value()));
            default -> Optional.empty();
        };
    }

The switch matches the type of the event, as a switch with type patterns does in C#. It turns three domain events into the public events of the service, and keeps the others inside. This one class answers the question "which events leave the order feature?". Without it, the answer would need a search through every listener.

The learning curve. The words and the rules of DDD take time to learn, as the section What DDD costs says. A team of beginners writes DDD slowly at first.

DDD done badly is worse than no DDD. A team can copy the layers without the idea.

Gotcha

The layers of DDD without its rules are the worst of both designs. Aggregates copied from database tables, entities with public setters, and rules in the application services give all the extra files of DDD. They give none of its protection. Watch for three signs. An aggregate method only sets a field. An application service holds an if that a business expert would recognise as a rule. A test of a rule needs mocks. For where each rule belongs, see the chapter Where each rule goes.

What keeps a DDD service readablenew#

The costs of the section What gets harder grow with each developer who does things differently. These practices keep a DDD service readable.

  • The same structure everywhere. Every feature has the same folders, and every service has the same features layout. A developer who knows one feature finds the code of another one at once.
  • Steps-only application services. A use case loads, lets the domain decide, saves, publishes and audits. It holds no rule.
  • Business names. A class is named after the business idea, such as ShippingPolicy. It is never named after a pattern alone, such as OrderDomainService.
  • Simple where simple. A feature with no rules uses the simple level. The full model is only where it protects a rule.
  • Traceable events. One mapper per feature decides which events leave it. Give every log line and message a trace ID, so one request can be followed across services. A flow that spans many steps and days uses a workflow engine or a process manager. Either one keeps the state of the flow in one place. For trace IDs, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.
  • Architecture tests. The rules of the design are tests, so the build fails when someone breaks one.
  • Docs and decision records beside the code. Each service has a README with its rules, its events and its decisions. A decision that a team may question later is written as an architecture decision record (ADR). An ADR is a short file that states a decision, its reason and its consequences.

Here are two of the architecture tests of the companion:

@Test
void entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters() {
    ArchitectureRules.entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters().check(CLASSES);
}

@Test
void featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication() {
    ArchitectureRules.featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication(BASE).check(CLASSES);
}

Each test calls a rule from the platform library, and check fails the test when a compiled class breaks it. The rules use ArchUnit, a Java library that reads the compiled classes and checks their dependencies. ArchUnitNET is a separate library for .NET. Its README calls it the C# fork of ArchUnit. The first rule finds a public setter on an entity. The second one finds a feature that uses the inside of another feature. For all the rules, see the chapter Testing in depth.

An anaemic model with an outbox, compared fairlytwist#

A model whose entities hold data but no rules is called an anaemic domain model. Martin Fowler described it in an article of November 2003. He said that its objects are hardly more than getters and setters. Many good .NET services use this design. With an outbox, they also publish their events reliably. An outbox is a table or collection that stores each event in the same transaction as the change. A background process sends it after the commit. So this design deserves a fair comparison.

Anaemic, with an outbox
public async Task ShipWithOutboxAsync(long orderId)
{
    var order = await db.Orders.Include(o => o.Lines).SingleAsync(o => o.Id == orderId);
    // ... the same two checks as in ShipAsync

    order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped;
    order.ShippedAt = clock.GetUtcNow();
    db.OutboxMessages.Add(OutboxMessage.For(new OrderShippedV1(order.Id, order.ShippedAt.Value)));
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();   // the order and the message, in one transaction
}
The order service
/**
 * Saves the order, publishes its events and records the audit, all in the caller's
 * transaction.
 *
 * <p>The events are pulled before saving, because the saved copy that the repository returns
 * is rebuilt from the database and has none. The caller continues with the returned copy,
 * which holds the new version.
 */
private Order saveAndPublish(Order order, String auditAction) {
    List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();
    Order saved = orders.save(order);
    events.publish(raised);
    audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.ORDER, saved.id().value());
    return saved;
}

In C#, the service sets the fields, writes the outbox row and saves. In Java, the order has already recorded its events, inside ship. saveAndPublish pulls them, saves the order and publishes the events in the same transaction. Every use case of the feature calls this one method. So no use case can save a change and forget its event.

The table compares what the anaemic design keeps and what it loses.

ConcernAnaemic model with an outboxRich model with an outbox
events reach other services after a commityes, the outbox is reliableyes, the same outbox
the change and its event commit togetheryes, if the service adds the rowyes, the save step always publishes
a rule has one homeno, each service method checks it againyes, the method of the aggregate
a caller can skip a ruleyes, any class can set the statusno, the status has no setter
a new developer can learn it quicklyyes, it is the usual designit takes some weeks
proof that a rule always holdsread every class that sets the fieldread one method and its test

The anaemic design breaks down in four ways, and each one grows with the size of the team.

  • The same rule is copied. The controller checks that the order is paid. The batch job checks it too, a little differently. A year later, the two checks disagree.
  • A loader bypasses everything. An import or a data fix writes entities directly. It sets a status that no rule would allow.
  • Events are forgotten. The outbox sends every row that a service writes. It cannot send a row that a new endpoint forgot to write.
  • Proof of correctness is slow. To prove that no order ships unpaid, a reviewer must find every line that sets the status. In the rich model, a reviewer reads Order.ship and its tests.

So the outbox fixes the delivery of events, and only that. It does not fix where the rules are, or who may skip them.

The middle groundnew#

A team does not need the full style to get most of the value. Four practices give most of it, and each one is cheap.

  1. State-change methods with their rules, and no state setters. An entity changes only through methods such as ship and resolveAction.
  2. The entity records its events. The method that changes the state also records what happened. The use case publishes the recorded events when it saves.
  3. Value objects for IDs, money, dates and codes. A value that has a format or a rule is a small type that checks itself, such as Money or ProductCode.
  4. Boundaries decided by the strongest people. The boundaries of the services and of the aggregates are the hardest decisions to change later. A small group of the most experienced developers makes them, with the business experts. The team writes everything else.

The note feature of the companion uses exactly this middle ground. Its entity is also its stored document, and it has no mapper. But it keeps its rules:

public void resolveAction(String actorId, Clock clock) {
    if (!actionRequired) {
        throw new NoteHasNoActionException(id);
    }
    if (actionResolvedAt != null) {
        throw new NoteActionAlreadyResolvedException(id);
    }
    if (actorId.equals(createdBy)) {
        throw new NoteResolvedByItsAuthorException(id);
    }
    actionResolvedAt = clock.instant();
    events.add(new NoteActionResolved(id, orderId, actionResolvedAt));
}

resolveAction checks three rules, changes one field and records the event NoteActionResolved. The third rule depends on who acts, so the use case passes the actor's ID in as a plain value. No setter exists for actionResolvedAt. For what this light style drops and what it keeps, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service. For who decides what in a team, see the chapter DDD for a team: the playbook.

Rules engines and decision tablesnew#

Some rules are calculations with many cases. A delivery charge, for example, can depend on the delivery method, the zone and the weight. Thirty cases written as if statements are hard to read and hard to check. A table of the cases is easier, and a business expert can check it.

Decision Model and Notation (DMN) is a standard for such tables. The Object Management Group (OMG) publishes it. Its page says that DMN lets a team define business rules simply and exactly, in decision tables. Among the Java libraries that evaluate DMN tables are these two, as of October 2026.

  • The Camunda DMN engine is a Java library that evaluates DMN decision tables. Its page for Camunda 7.24 says that it implements DMN 1.3, and that it can be embedded in an application.
  • Drools is a group of projects for decision management, mostly in Java. Its user guide for version 8.44.0.Final lists a decision engine for DMN.

A decision table has one row for each case. Here is an example for the shop. The order service has no delivery charges, so this table is only an illustration:

Delivery methodZoneWeight up toCharge
STANDARDUK2 kg3.95 GBP
STANDARDUK10 kg6.95 GBP
EXPRESSUK10 kg12.50 GBP
STANDARDEU10 kg14.00 GBP

Keep the rule's place in the model, even when an engine calculates it. The domain names the rule as a class, and the class asks a port for the answer. The order service has a rule class of this kind, without a port:

/**
 * The rule that needs two aggregates: an order cannot ship while a note on it needs action.
 *
 * <p>It is a domain service because neither aggregate holds the data alone. It is named after
 * the rule, not {@code OrderDomainService}, so unrelated code does not collect in it. It takes a
 * number, not the notes, so the order feature never sees note objects. It has no state, no
 * repository and no Spring annotation, and the order feature's configuration creates it.
 *
 * <p>The guarantee holds only at the moment of shipping. An agent may add a note that needs
 * action a second after the order shipped. The service accepts that, and the README records the
 * decision.
 */
public class ShippingPolicy {

    public void assertCanShip(Order order, long notesNeedingAction) {
        if (notesNeedingAction > 0) {
            throw new OrderHasOpenActionsException(order.id(), notesNeedingAction);
        }
    }
}

A delivery charge would get a class such as DeliveryChargeCalculator, beside ShippingPolicy. Its port would be an interface in the domain. An adapter outside the domain would implement the port, and evaluate the DMN file with the engine. So the domain stays plain Java, and a unit test can replace the table.

Use an engine when the table is large, or when business experts change it more often than the code is released. Keep the rule in code when it has a few cases. An engine adds a library, a file format and a second kind of test.

The order service: its features and its rulesnew#

The rest of this part builds one service, the shop's order service. It keeps the orders that customers place, the lines that warehouse staff pick, and the payment that the payment service reports. It also keeps the notes that customer-service agents write on orders. The package description of the order feature states its rules:

/**
 * Orders: what a customer bought, the lines that warehouse staff pick, the payment, and shipping.
 *
 * <p>This feature uses the full style. Its {@code domain} package is plain Java with typed IDs.
 * The {@code persistence} package stores the aggregate as a separate document through a mapper,
 * behind the {@code OrderRepository} port. The stock service is called through the
 * {@code StockChecker} port.
 *
 * <p>The rules: an order is placed only if the stock service confirms and holds the products.
 * An order ships only when it is paid, every line is picked, and no note on it needs action. A
 * payment is recorded from the payment service's event, and a repeated or late one changes nothing.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.order;

The comment describes the package com.acme.orderservice.order. The service has five top-level packages. Each of the first four is a business feature.

PackageWhat it holdsLevel of DDD
orderorders, their lines, the last payment, and shippingfull
notethe notes of customer-service agents, some of which need actionlight
referencelookup values, such as delivery methods and note categoriessimple, no DDD building blocks
migrationthe indexes and the seed data of the databasenot a feature with rules
sharedthe permission annotations, the audit names and the OpenAPI descriptionnot a feature

These are the rules that the README of the service lists:

  • An order is placed only if the stock service confirms and holds every product.
  • An order has 1 to 50 lines. A line is picked once.
  • An order ships only when it is paid, every line is picked, and no note on it needs action.
  • A shipped or cancelled order cannot change. A payment for it is still recorded, because the money was received. The payment service handles refunds.
  • A payment is recorded from the event PaymentReceivedV1. A repeated or earlier payment changes nothing.
  • Only a note that needs action can be resolved, and only once. The text of a note never changes.
  • Delivery methods and note categories must be active lookup values.

The packages of each feature follow one layout. Here are the folders of the order service:

com/acme/orderservice/
  order/
    api/            the controller, its DTOs and their mapper
    application/    the use cases, the views, and the port to the stock service
    client/         the HTTP client of the stock service
    domain/         plain Java: the model, events, exceptions, repository port, domain service
    messaging/      the events that leave, and the listener of payments
    persistence/    the stored document, its mapper, and the repository adapter
  note/
    api/
    application/
    model/          the entity that is also its stored document, and its repository
  reference/
    api/
    application/
    persistence/
  migration/
  shared/

Each folder name says what the classes in it do. For example, only the domain/ folder of a feature holds its business rules. In the note feature, the model/ folder holds them. For the reasons behind this layout, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

The earlier chapters of this book give an order a long id. This part gives it a typed OrderId, which holds a universally unique identifier (UUID) as text. The service needs the ID before it saves the order, because it sends the ID to the stock service first. A database cannot generate an ID that the service needs before the first save. For the typed ID in full, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

Its events and the services it talks tonew#

The diagram shows every call and every message of the order service. The service sends and receives messages through Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS).

SNS and SQS are two messaging services of Amazon Web Services (AWS). A topic of SNS sends each message to every subscriber. A queue of SQS holds messages until one consumer takes them. The table lists the events of the service. Each event has a JSON schema in the folder contracts/events.

DirectionEventWhereMeaning
outOrderPlacedV1SNS topic order-eventsan order was placed, with its delivery method and lines
outOrderShippedV1SNS topic order-eventsan order was shipped, and it can no longer change
outOrderCancelledV1SNS topic order-eventsan order was cancelled before it shipped
inPaymentReceivedV1SQS queue order-service-payment-receivedthe payment service received money for an order

A public event is a contract, so its fields change only with care. Here is the schema of OrderShippedV1:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "order-service/OrderShippedV1",
  "title": "OrderShippedV1",
  "description": "An order was shipped. Published to the order-events SNS topic.",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId"],
  "properties": {
    "eventId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },
    "occurredAt": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" },
    "orderId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" }
  },
  "additionalProperties": true
}

The event carries only its own ID, its time and the order ID. A consumer that needs more asks the order service. The suffix V1 is the version of the contract. For event schemas and their versions, see the chapter API and event contracts.

The service depends on five other systems. The README says what happens when each one is down.

DependencyUsed forWhen it is down
DocumentDBall datareadiness is down, so no traffic arrives, but liveness stays up, so instances are not restarted
stock serviceplacing an orderonly POST /orders answers 503, and everything else works
SNSpublishing eventsevents wait in the outbox and are resent
SQSpaymentspayments wait in the queue
token issuerchecking tokens, and the token of the stock callrequests get 401, and placing an order gets 503

For each of these, the part has a chapter. For the outbox, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox. For the payment queue, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

Three repositories: platform, service and local environmentnew#

The companion is in one folder, but in real life it is three repositories. Each one has its own release cycle.

RepositoryWhat it holdsWho uses it
shop-platforma parent POM, and a library of code that every service needs, but no business codeevery shop service, as a versioned dependency
order-servicethe order service, with its tests, its contracts and its Dockerfilethe team of the order service
local-environmenta Docker Compose file with MongoDB, stubs of other services, fake AWS and a token issuerevery developer, and the end-to-end tests of the QA team

A service names the platform's parent and one dependency, with no version. The parent manages every version. Here is the start of the order service's Project Object Model (POM):

<!--
  The platform parent sets Java, the plugins and every dependency version.
  In this service's own repository, remove <relativePath>: the parent then comes from the
  company's artifact repository.
-->
<parent>
    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform-parent</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <relativePath>../shop-platform/shop-platform-parent/pom.xml</relativePath>
</parent>

<groupId>com.acme</groupId>
<artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

<dependencies>
    <!-- Everything cross-cutting. No version: the parent manages it. -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
        <artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>
    </dependency>

The element parent names the platform's parent POM. A POM is the build file of Maven. It has the same purpose as a .csproj file in .NET. The platform holds no domain classes. Services share contracts, such as OpenAPI files and event schemas, but never domain classes. A shared domain library would tie the release of every service to the others. For the parent and the library, see the chapter The build: a parent POM and a platform library. For how to write the library, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

The local environment is started once, and then each service runs from its own repository. The README of the service gives the two commands:

cd ../local-environment && docker compose up -d
cd ../order-service && mvn package && docker compose up --build

The first command, docker compose up -d, starts the shared containers in the background. The second one builds the service and starts it in a container. For the local environment in full, see the chapter Running locally and shipping.

A map of the partnew#

Each chapter of the part adds one layer or one concern to the order service. Read them in order the first time. Later, use this list to find a topic.

  • Design. Finding the aggregates, How much DDD: three levels in one service, Features, layers and the rules.
  • Build. The build: a parent POM and a platform library.

Check yourself
1
Name four conditions that make DDD worth its cost for a service.
Complex rules, many states and workflows, rules that must never be bypassed, and a long life. High stakes, rules to recover from an old system, old data that breaks rules, and unclear service boundaries are signs too.
2
An expert asksA service uses entities with public setters and an outbox. Why can it still lose an event?
The outbox sends only the rows that a service method writes. A new endpoint or a batch job can set the status and forget to write the row. The rich model records the event inside the state-change method, so the change and its event cannot be separated.
3
TranslateIn the order service, write this C# in Java: order.Status = OrderStatus.Cancelled; order.CancelledAt = clock.GetUtcNow();
order.cancel(clock); The order has no setters. cancel refuses a finished order, sets the status and the time, and records OrderCancelled.
4
An expert asksWhat makes a DDD service harder to follow, and what keeps it readable?
More layers, and events whose listeners are in other classes. Several practices keep it readable. Use the same layout in every feature, steps-only use cases and business names. Add one event mapper per feature, trace IDs, architecture tests and decision records.
5
Which feature of the order service uses no DDD building blocks, and why?
The reference feature. It holds read-only lookup values with no business behaviour, so an aggregate and events would only add files.
