Finding the aggregates#

Why DDD, and how much · Chapter 02· 26 min read

An aggregate is a group of data that one rule must see at once, and that is saved together. Outside code changes it only through one object, called its root. Finding the aggregates is the most important design decision of a service built with Domain-Driven Design (DDD). This chapter gives the questions and the tests that guide it, and shows why the order service has the aggregates it has.

KindA usual EF Core modelThe order serviceNote
newDbSet<Order> and DbSet<OrderLine>, each saved on its ownOrder, with its lines inside, saved as one documentan aggregate is the data that one rule must see, saved together in one transaction Why
twistorder.Lines.Single(l => l.Id == lineId).PickedAt = now;order.pickLine(lineId, clock);outside code changes a line only through the order, which is the root of the aggregate Why
newno equivalentseven questions about rules, size, conflicts and lifefinding an aggregate needs judgement, but questions and tests guide each step Why
newan Order class with a property for each columnstatus, delivery method, customer, lines and last paymenteach piece is inside because a rule needs it at every change, or because it has the same life Why
trappublic List<Note> Notes { get; set; } on Ordernotes as an aggregate of their owna list with no limit grows until saves conflict or the document reaches its size limit Why
trapOrderLine as an aggregate of its ownthe lines inside the orderwhen every change must update several aggregates together, they are one aggregate Why
newno equivalentmove the part with no limit out, or move the small part ina split keeps the rule with a count or an event, and a migration moves the data Why
newno equivalentOrder and Note, two aggregatesnotes have no limit, no order rule needs all of them, they conflict less, and they live differently Why
twistpublic Order Order { get; set; } on Noteprivate final String orderId; on Notea reference by ID never loads or saves the other aggregate Why
twistpublic long OrderId { get; set; } on NoteString orderId, checked by OrderService.requireExiststhe strict style gives a foreign ID its own type, but the light style keeps text Why
twistpublic record Payment(PaymentReference Reference, Money Amount, DateTimeOffset PaidAt);record Payment(PaymentReference reference, Money amount, Instant paidAt)an entity has an identity, and a value object is only its values Why
twistpublic readonly record struct OrderId(Guid Value);final class OrderId extends Identifiera typed ID lets the compiler catch an order ID passed where a line ID belongs Why
trapa check of another table in the same service methodShippingPolicy, checked when the order shipsa rule across two aggregates holds at the moment of the check, not forever Why
newno equivalentaccept, refuse, make strict, or repairchoose with the business owner, then record the choice in a decision record and a test Why
newa call to another service inside the database transactionthe stock call before the transaction, with an idempotency keyno transaction spans two services, so each step must be safe to repeat Why
traptwo services that inject each other@Lazy OrderService in NoteServicea two-way dependency between features is a warning sign, and it has three ways out Why

What an aggregate is fornew#

An agent cancels an order. At the same moment, warehouse staff ship it. Each change checks that the order is not finished, and each check passes. If nothing connects the two saves, both succeed, and a cancelled order leaves the warehouse. The rules need the status, the lines and the payment to be checked and saved as one thing.

The answer is to treat the order, its lines and its payment as one unit. The unit is loaded whole, changed by one method that checks the rules, and saved whole in one transaction. It has one version. So when the agent and the warehouse save the same version, the second save fails. This unit is called an aggregate. The object that outside code holds, here Order, is called the root of the aggregate.

So an aggregate is a consistency boundary. Everything inside it is checked and saved together. Everything outside it is checked and saved on its own. Vaughn Vernon wrote a series of three essays, Effective Aggregate Design, in 2011. Part I says that an aggregate and a transactional consistency boundary are the same thing. Microsoft's guide to .NET microservices gives the same advice. It says that the best way to find the aggregates is to think about the transactions.

The platform's base class of every root states the same idea in its comment:

/**
 * The base class of an aggregate root: the only object of an aggregate that outside code may
 * hold. Every change to the aggregate goes through the root, which checks the rules.
 *
 * <p>The root carries two things for the layers around it. The first is the version, which
 * optimistic locking needs: the version comes from storage and goes back to storage unchanged,
 * and no rule ever reads it. The second is the list of domain events the root raised. The
 * application service pulls the events after saving and publishes them in the same transaction.
 *
 * @param <ID> the typed identifier of the aggregate
 */
public abstract class AggregateRoot<ID extends Identifier> extends Entity<ID> {

AggregateRoot is generic in its ID type. <ID extends Identifier> means that the ID must be a typed identifier, such as OrderId. It is like a constraint where TId : Identifier in C#. The class holds only the version and the recorded events. It holds no business idea.

In a document database, an aggregate maps well to one document. The order service stores each order, with its lines and its last payment, as one document in the collection orders. One save writes the whole document, so the lines and the status are stored together. For how the service stores it, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

In a usual EF Core model, each table is an entity, and each entity can be loaded and saved on its own. Nothing in the model says which entities must change together. The aggregate is the decision that the model of EF Core leaves to each service method.

The root is the only way intwist#

EF Core entity
public class Order
{
    public long Id { get; set; }
    public OrderStatus Status { get; set; }
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; set; } = [];
}

// in a service, or in any other class
order.Lines.Single(line => line.Id == lineId).PickedAt = clock.GetUtcNow();
The order service
public void pickLine(LineId lineId, Clock clock) {
    requireNotFinished();
    OrderLine line = lines.stream()
            .filter(candidate -> candidate.id().equals(lineId))
            .findFirst()
            .orElseThrow(() -> new LineNotFoundException(id(), lineId));
    line.pick(clock);
    raise(new LinePicked(id(), lineId, line.pickedAt()));
}

In C#, any class can find a line and set its pick time. Nothing checks that the order is still open, or that the line was not picked before. In Java, pickLine is the only way to pick a line. It refuses a finished order, finds the line by its typed ID, picks it and adds the event LinePicked. An unknown line ID throws LineNotFoundException, which the platform answers with 404.

The line itself cannot be changed from outside its package. Its methods that change it are package-private:

/**
 * One line of an order: a product and a quantity that warehouse staff pick.
 *
 * <p>A line is an entity inside the order aggregate. It has its own identity, so a picker can
 * name it, but only the order may change it. That is why {@link #add} and {@link #pick} are
 * package-private: code outside this package goes through {@link Order}.
 */
public class OrderLine extends Entity<LineId> {
    // ...
    /** Creates a new line for an item. Only {@link Order} calls it. */
    static OrderLine add(OrderItem item) {
        return new OrderLine(LineId.newId(), item.product(), item.quantity(), null);
    }

    /** Rebuilds a stored line. Only persistence calls it. */
    public static OrderLine rehydrate(LineId id, ProductCode product, int quantity, Instant pickedAt) {
        return new OrderLine(id, product, quantity, pickedAt);
    }

    void pick(Clock clock) {
        if (isPicked()) {
            throw new LineAlreadyPickedException(id());
        }
        pickedAt = clock.instant();
    }

add and pick have no access modifier. In Java, no modifier means that only classes of the same package can call the method. Order is in the same package, order.domain.model, so it can call line.pick(clock). A controller or a use case cannot. rehydrate is public, because the mapper in the persistence package rebuilds stored lines. It applies no rule. For the access levels of Java, see the section The mapping.

The getter lines() of the order returns a read-only copy. So outside code cannot add or remove a line either. For the full set of these protections, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

Art or science? Questions you can applynew#

Is finding an aggregate an art or a science? The honest answer is both. It is not a calculation, because it depends on the business. The business decides how long two pieces of data may disagree. Only a business expert can say that. But it is not guessing either. A small set of questions and tests decides most cases. Judgement decides the rest, and the reasons for each judgement can be written down.

Ask these questions about each piece of data, and each rule.

  1. Which rule must hold after every change? Write the rule in business words, such as "an order ships only when every line is picked". A rule of this kind is called an invariant. Vernon's first rule is "Model True Invariants In Consistency Boundaries". A rule that the business can check later is not an invariant.
  2. Does the rule need this data at every change? Shipping needs every line. So the lines are inside. Shipping needs only the number of notes that need action, not the notes. So the notes stay outside.
  3. Is the data small and bounded? An order has at most 50 lines. Notes have no limit. Data inside an aggregate is loaded and saved with every change, so it must have a maximum.
  4. Whose job is it to make the data consistent? Vaughn Vernon gives a guideline that he learned from Eric Evans, in Part II. If it is the job of the user who runs the use case, make the data consistent in the same transaction. If it is the job of another user, or of the system, let the data become consistent later.
  5. Do different people change the parts at the same time? Warehouse staff pick lines while agents write notes. Parts that different people change at once conflict if they are saved together.
  6. Do the parts have the same life? A line is created with its order and never exists without it. A note is written later, by someone else, and is resolved on its own.
  7. What does outside code need to find? The root is the object that the business names, and that outside code refers to by its ID. Nobody refers to a line without its order. So the order is the root, and the line is inside.

Then test the answer. Each test takes a few minutes.

  • Write the rule as a method of the root. If the method needs data that the aggregate does not hold, the boundary is wrong, or the rule belongs to a domain service.
  • Count the maximum size. Multiply the largest list by the size of one item. Compare it with the limit of a document, and with what a save should write.
  • Draw two users at the same moment. Name two use cases that change the aggregate at once. If they are common and unrelated, they will conflict.
  • List the use cases that save it. If most of them also save another aggregate, the two may be one.

The comment of Order writes down the result of these questions, so the next developer can see the reasons:

/**
 * An order: the aggregate root of the order feature.
 *
 * <p>The aggregate holds what its rules need at every change: the status, the lines and the last
 * payment. Notes are a separate aggregate, because no order rule needs every note, and they can
 * grow without limit.
 *
 * <p>The rules on the order's own data:
 * <ul>
 *   <li>An order is placed only if every product is available, with 1 to {@value #MAX_LINES} lines.</li>
 *   <li>A shipped or cancelled order cannot change, except that payments are still recorded.</li>
 *   <li>A line is picked once.</li>
 *   <li>An order ships only when it is paid and every line is picked.</li>
 *   <li>A payment is recorded only if it is later than the last one, so repeated and late
 *       messages change nothing. The first payment makes a new order paid.</li>
 * </ul>
 *
 * <p>The rule that no note may need action is across two aggregates, so it lives in
 * {@code ShippingPolicy}.
 *
 * <p>State changes only through these methods. There are no setters, and the time always comes
 * from the {@link Clock} the caller passes.
 */

The comment names what is inside, what is outside and why. The last paragraph says that every time comes from the Clock that the caller passes. Keep a comment like this on every root. It is the shortest note of the boundary decision.

These questions come from two principles. One principle says that a transaction protects one place. The other principle says that some rules must hold now and others may hold a little later. For both principles in full, see the chapter The principles.

The order aggregate, piece by piecenew#

Here are the fields of the order:

public class Order extends AggregateRoot<OrderId> {

    public static final int MAX_LINES = 50;

    private final CustomerContact customer;
    private final DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod;
    private final Instant placedAt;
    private final List<OrderLine> lines;
    private OrderStatus status;
    private Payment lastPayment;
    private Instant shippedAt;
    private Instant cancelledAt;

extends AggregateRoot<OrderId> makes Order a root with a typed ID. The final fields never change after the order is placed. The other fields change only through the methods of the order. The table says why each piece is inside.

PieceThe rule that needs itWhy it is inside
statusevery method, because a finished order cannot changeevery rule reads it, so it must be saved with every change
linesship needs every line picked, and pickLine needs the lineat most 50, and a line never exists without its order
last paymentrecordPayment ignores a payment that is not later than the last onethe idempotent check needs the last payment at every payment
customerno rule, only the format of the name and the e-mail addressit is part of the order, and it has the same life
delivery methodno rule, only the format, because the reference feature checks the codeit is part of the order, and it never changes
notesthe shipping rule needs only the number that need actionoutside, because notes have no limit and their own life

Two pieces have no rule but are still inside. The customer and the delivery method are part of what an order is. They are created with it, they never change, and they are small. A piece with no rule may be inside when it has the same life as the root.

Signs of an aggregate that is too bigtrap#

The easiest model of an order puts everything about it inside. In EF Core, an order would get a navigation property public List<Note> Notes { get; set; }. In a document database, the notes would be embedded in the order document. It works in the first demo, and it fails a year later.

Gotcha

An aggregate with a list that has no limit grows until its saves fail. Each change loads and saves the whole aggregate. So each new note rewrites the whole order, and two agents who add notes at once conflict with each other and with the warehouse.

Watch for four signs.

  • A list with no limit. Notes, comments, history entries and messages grow for as long as the root exists. Ask for the maximum. If nobody can name one, the list does not belong inside.
  • The size limit of a document. Amazon DocumentDB limits a document to 16 MiB, as of October 2026. A save of a larger document fails. Long before that limit, each save writes a large document. Spring Data MongoDB saves a document with @Version as a full replacement, not as a change of one field.
  • Conflicts on save. The aggregate has one version. Two saves of the same version conflict, and the second one fails. Spring Data throws OptimisticLockingFailureException. Inside a transaction, MongoDB usually reports a write conflict, which Spring turns into DataIntegrityViolationException. The platform answers both with 409. If unrelated work often gets 409, the aggregate is too big.
  • Rules that do not need the data. If shipping loads two thousand notes to count three of them, the notes are inside for no rule.

The stored document of the order says why its lines are inside and its notes are not:

/**
 * How an order is stored: one document per aggregate, with its lines and last payment embedded.
 *
 * <p>The lines are embedded because they are few (at most 50) and every order rule needs them.
 * Notes are not: they have no limit, and embedding them would rewrite the whole order for each
 * new note. A document must stay under 16 MB.
 *
 * <p>Only plain types are stored. Enums and codes are strings, so renaming a Java class never
 * breaks stored data. Money is DECIMAL128, so it is exact. The class and its fields are
 * package-private: nothing outside this package knows the storage shape.
 */
@Document("orders")
class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

@Document("orders") names the collection. BaseDocument is the platform's base class of a stored document, with the ID and the version. For the version and the conflicts in full, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

Signs of an aggregate that is too smalltrap#

The opposite mistake splits data that one rule needs. Suppose that each order line were an aggregate of its own, saved as its own document. Picking a line would then be simple. But shipping must check every line of the order, and these checks would read up to 50 separate documents. A line picked a moment after the check would not be seen.

The rule that the order checks today needs its lines in the same aggregate:

public void ship(Clock clock) {
    requireNotFinished();
    if (status != OrderStatus.PAID) {
        throw new OrderNotPaidException(id());
    }
    if (lines.stream().anyMatch(line -> !line.isPicked())) {
        throw new UnpickedLinesException(id());
    }
    status = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
    shippedAt = clock.instant();
    raise(new OrderShipped(id(), shippedAt));
}

lines.stream().anyMatch(line -> !line.isPicked()) checks every line, inside the same object and the same save. anyMatch does the same as Any in LINQ. If a line were outside, this check would need a query, and it would hold only at the moment of the query.

Watch for these signs of an aggregate that is too small.

  • A rule must change several aggregates together, every time. That is the main sign.
  • Most use cases save the same two aggregates in one transaction.
  • A rule reads many aggregates, and a change between the reads would break it.
  • Someone proposes a lock across two aggregates, to make a rule hold.

One use case that saves two aggregates is not a sign by itself. The order service does it once, for a reason. See the section Why order and note are separate aggregates.

How to split or merge an aggregatenew#

A boundary can be wrong, and it can be changed. To split an aggregate that is too big, follow these steps.

  1. Move the part with no limit into an aggregate of its own, with its own root, its own ID and its own version.
  2. Give the new aggregate the ID of the old root. Remove the list from the old root.
  3. Keep each rule that needed the moved part. Give it a number or a yes or no answer, not the objects. A domain service checks the rule, as ShippingPolicy does.
  4. If a rule can wait, react to an event of the other aggregate instead.
  5. Write a migration that moves the embedded items into the new collection. For migrations, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

In the order service, the shipping rule needs one number from the note feature. The note feature answers with a count, and never returns the notes:

/** For the order feature's shipping rule: a plain number, so no note crosses the boundary. */
public long countNeedingAction(String orderId) {
    return notes.countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull(orderId);
}

countNeedingAction returns a long, so no note crosses into the order feature. The repository method behind it is a derived query:

public interface NoteRepository extends MongoRepository<Note, String> {

    Page<Note> findByOrderId(String orderId, Pageable pageable);

    /** Counts the notes on an order that still need action. Spring Data reads the rule from the name. */
    long countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull(String orderId);
}

Spring Data reads the method name countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull and builds the query from it. It counts the notes of one order that need action and are not resolved. For derived queries, see the section Repositories and derived queries.

To merge two aggregates that are too small, do the opposite. Make one root the owner. Turn the other root into an entity or a value object inside it, and give the owner the methods that change it. Then write a migration that embeds the old documents into their owners.

Why order and note are separate aggregatesnew#

A note is an agent's text about an order, such as "the customer asked us to leave the parcel with a neighbour". Some notes need action. An order cannot ship while one of its notes needs action. So the note and the order are linked by a rule. They are still two aggregates, for four reasons.

  1. Notes have no limit. An order with a problem can collect hundreds of notes. Inside the order, they would grow the document toward the 16 MiB limit.
  2. No order rule needs every note. The shipping rule needs one number, the count of notes that need action.
  3. Fewer conflicts. Each note has its own version. An agent who adds a note does not change the order's version. So the agent never blocks the warehouse, and the warehouse never blocks the agent.
  4. A different life. An order is placed by the customer and finished by the warehouse. A note is written by an agent at any time, and resolved later by another agent.

One use case saves both kinds of aggregate. An agent can place an order together with its first notes, and the agent sees that as one action. So the order service stores the order and its first notes in one transaction:

public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
                         List<NewNote> firstNotes) {
    referenceData.requireActive(ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD, deliveryMethod.code(), "deliveryMethod");
    OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();
    StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items);           // outside the transaction

    return transaction.execute(status -> {
        Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);
        Order saved = saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_PLACED);        // aggregate 1
        List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction
        return new PlacedOrder(saved.id().value(), noteIds);
    });
}

transaction.execute runs the lambda in one transaction. The order is saved first, and then notes.addNotes saves each note in the same transaction. If a note is invalid, the whole transaction rolls back, and the order is not stored either. The test OrderJourneyIT.anOrderAndItsNotesAreStoredTogetherOrNotAtAll shows it against a real MongoDB. For TransactionTemplate and why the stock call is outside it, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

Saving two aggregates in one transaction departs from a strict rule. Vernon's Part I says that a well designed bounded context changes only one aggregate in each transaction. His Part II also names reasons to break the rule. One of them is creating several new aggregates in one request, when that means the same as creating them one by one. The order and its first notes are new aggregates of that kind. For the callout of this choice, see the section One request that saves the order and its first notes.

Refer to another aggregate by its IDtwist#

EF Core entity
public class Note
{
    public long Id { get; set; }
    public long OrderId { get; set; }
    public Order Order { get; set; } = null!;
    public string Text { get; set; } = "";
}
The order service
@Document("notes")
public final class Note {

    public static final int MAX_TEXT_LENGTH = 2000;

    @Id
    private final String id;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    private final String orderId;
    private final String text;
    private final String category;
    private final boolean actionRequired;
    private final Instant createdAt;
    private final String createdBy;
    private Instant actionResolvedAt;

    @Transient
    private final List<DomainEvent> events = new ArrayList<>();

In C#, the note has an Order navigation property, so code can reach the order through the note and change it. In Java, the note holds only orderId. It cannot reach the order. The order holds nothing about its notes. Vernon's Part II names this rule "Reference Other Aggregates By Identity". Microsoft's guide recommends the same for EF Core. It calls it a good practice to keep only the foreign key of the other aggregate, with no navigation property to it.

A reference by ID keeps the boundaries real.

  • Loading a note never loads an order, and loading an order never loads its notes.
  • Saving a note never saves an order. So a change to a note never changes the data of the order.
  • Each aggregate keeps its own version, so a note and its order never conflict.
  • The note feature never sees the Order class. It asks the order feature, which checks its own rules.

The annotations on Note are from Spring Data. @Document("notes") names its collection, @Id marks its ID, and @Version marks the version that detects conflicts. @Transient keeps the list of events out of the stored document. The note is its own stored document, in the light style. For that style, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

A type for a foreign ID, or plain texttwist#

The note holds the ID of its order as a String. The strict full style would give it a type of its own, such as OrderRef. It would not reuse OrderId from the order feature. With its own type, the note's model would depend on nothing in the order feature. The note feature could change, or move to another service, without the order's classes.

The order service keeps the text, and lets the owner of the ID check it. When a note is added, the note feature asks the order feature whether the order exists:

/**
 * For other features: checks that an order exists. IDs cross between features as text, and
 * the owner of the ID checks it, so a bad ID gives the order feature's own 400 or 404.
 */
public void requireExists(String orderId) {
    OrderId id = OrderId.of(orderId);
    if (!orders.exists(id)) {
        throw new OrderNotFoundException(id);
    }
}

OrderId.of(orderId) checks the format of the text. A bad ID gives the order feature's own 400, and an unknown one gives its 404. So the check is in one place, the feature that owns the ID.

Pragmatic choice: A String ID between features

The strict rule. Every ID inside a model has a type. An aggregate that refers to another one has its own type for that ID, such as OrderRef.

What we do. IDs cross between features as text. The note keeps orderId as a String, and the order feature checks it in requireExists.

Why. The note feature uses the light style. A type would add a class and a conversion for a value that the note only stores and compares. Text also keeps the two features apart. The note feature imports no class of the order's domain.

When to stop. Add a type when the note's model starts to use the ID in a rule. Add one when a method takes two IDs that could be swapped, or when the feature moves to the full style.

Inside the aggregate: entities and value objectstwist#

C# 12
public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);
public record PaymentReference(string Value);
public record Payment(PaymentReference Reference, Money Amount, DateTimeOffset PaidAt);
The order service
/**
 * A payment that the payment service received for an order. It is a value object made of value
 * objects.
 *
 * @param reference the payment service's reference
 * @param amount    the amount paid
 * @param paidAt    when it was paid, which decides which payment is the latest
 */
public record Payment(PaymentReference reference, Money amount, Instant paidAt) implements ValueObject {

    public Payment {
        Guard.notNull(reference, "paymentReference");
        Guard.notNull(amount, "amount");
        Guard.notNull(paidAt, "paidAt");
    }
}

Both panes build a payment from other values, and both compare by value. The Java record checks its values in a compact constructor, the block public Payment { ... }. Guard.notNull throws an error that names the field, and the platform answers it with 400. implements ValueObject marks the intent. The C# records check nothing until you add a constructor.

An aggregate holds two kinds of objects besides its root. An object with an identity of its own is called an entity. An object that is only its values is called a value object.

KindEqual whenChangesIn the order aggregate
entityit has the same ID, whatever its other datayes, through the rootOrderLine, which a picker names by its line ID
value objectall its values are equalnever, because a new value replaces itPayment, Money, ProductCode, CustomerContact, DeliveryMethod

To decide, ask whether anyone must name the object. A picker must name the line that was picked, so a line is an entity with a LineId. Nobody names a payment. A newer payment replaces the last one, so a payment is a value object. A payment is built from three values, a reference, an amount and a time. Two of them are value objects too.

The platform's base class of an entity defines equality by identity:

/**
 * The base class of an entity: an object with its own identity.
 *
 * <p>Two entities are equal when they have the same class and the same ID, even if their other
 * data differs. The methods are final, so a subclass cannot change what identity means.
 *
 * @param <ID> the typed identifier of the entity
 */
public abstract class Entity<ID extends Identifier> {
    // ...
    @Override
    public final boolean equals(Object other) {
        if (this == other) {
            return true;
        }
        if (other == null || getClass() != other.getClass()) {
            return false;
        }
        return id.equals(((Entity<?>) other).id);
    }

    @Override
    public final int hashCode() {
        return id.hashCode();
    }

equals is final, so no subclass can change what identity means. Two lines with the same ID are the same line, even if one was loaded before it was picked. The marker of a value object is an empty interface:

/**
 * Marks a class as a value object: it is defined only by its values, it never changes, and it
 * checks its own values when it is created.
 *
 * <p>The interface has no methods. It documents the intent, and it lets architecture tests find
 * value objects. Write value objects as records, so Java generates {@code equals} and
 * {@code hashCode} from the values.
 */
public interface ValueObject {
}

ValueObject has no methods. A record generates equals and hashCode from its values, as a C# record does. For value objects and the Guard checks in full, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

Typed IDs inside the aggregatetwist#

C# 12
public readonly record struct OrderId(Guid Value)
{
    public static OrderId New() => new(Guid.NewGuid());
}

public readonly record struct LineId(Guid Value);
The order service
/** The identity of an order: a UUID that the compiler cannot mix up with another ID. */
public final class OrderId extends Identifier {

    private OrderId(String value) {
        super(value, "orderId");
    }

    public static OrderId of(String value) {
        return new OrderId(value);
    }

    public static OrderId newId() {
        return new OrderId(newValue());
    }
}

Both panes give each ID its own type, so a method that takes an OrderId refuses a LineId. In C#, the call does not compile. The compiler gives error CS1503, and says that it cannot convert from LineId to OrderId. In Java, the compiler gives error: incompatible types: LineId cannot be converted to OrderId. Both messages were produced by compiling the call.

The Java ID is a class, not a record. Its constructor is private, and OrderId.of and OrderId.newId create it. The base class Identifier checks that the text is a universally unique identifier (UUID), so every OrderId is valid. The C# record struct accepts any Guid, including an empty one. For the base class and why the ID holds text, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

What holds between two aggregates, and what does nottrap#

The shipping rule needs an order and its notes. They are two aggregates, so the rule is checked by a domain service, ShippingPolicy, when the order ships:

/**
 * The rule that needs two aggregates: an order cannot ship while a note on it needs action.
 *
 * <p>It is a domain service because neither aggregate holds the data alone. It is named after
 * the rule, not {@code OrderDomainService}, so unrelated code does not collect in it. It takes a
 * number, not the notes, so the order feature never sees note objects. It has no state, no
 * repository and no Spring annotation, and the order feature's configuration creates it.
 *
 * <p>The guarantee holds only at the moment of shipping. An agent may add a note that needs
 * action a second after the order shipped. The service accepts that, and the README records the
 * decision.
 */
public class ShippingPolicy {

    public void assertCanShip(Order order, long notesNeedingAction) {
        if (notesNeedingAction > 0) {
            throw new OrderHasOpenActionsException(order.id(), notesNeedingAction);
        }
    }
}

assertCanShip takes the order and a number, not the notes. Its comment already names the problem. Here is the question that every team must answer. Does the rule still hold a second later?

It does not. Agent A ships an order. At the same moment, agent B adds a note that needs action to the same order. MongoDB detects a write conflict when two transactions write the same document. These two transactions write different documents. So both commit, and a shipped order has a note that needs action.

This is the general rule. Separate aggregates give no lasting guarantee across them. A rule across two aggregates holds at the moment it is checked, and only then. The table lists what the order service guarantees, and what it does not.

StatementGuaranteed?Why
an order and its first notes are stored togetheryesone transaction, shown by OrderJourneyIT.anOrderAndItsNotesAreStoredTogetherOrNotAtAll
a note refers to an order that existsyesthe note feature checks it, and orders are never deleted
an order has every line picked when it shipsyesthe lines are inside the order, and ship checks them in the same save
no note needs action when an order shipsonly at the moment of shippingthe rule is across two aggregates
a note that needs action on a shipped orderit can happenthe note feature checks only that the order exists
Gotcha

A rule checked by a domain service across two aggregates is a rule about one moment. In a usual ASP.NET Core service, a check of another table in the same method looks like a lasting guarantee. The same race exists there too, because the check reads one record and the change writes another. Say in the code and in the README which rules hold only at the moment they are checked.

Four ways to handle the gap, and how to record the choicenew#

The time between the check and a later change is called the gap in this book. A team has four options. Choose with the business owner, because each one changes what users see.

OptionWhat the service doesWhat it costs
A, acceptnothing more, and the note is still seen and handleda shipped order can have a note that needs action
B, refusethe note feature refuses a note that needs action on a shipped orderthe note feature must ask for the order's status, and the race at the same moment remains
C, make strictadding such a note also writes the order document, so the two transactions conflictevery note conflicts with every change of its order, as if the notes were inside
D, repaira listener of OrderShipped looks for notes that need action, and alerts someonemore code, and the problem is fixed after it happens

Option B narrows the gap, but does not close it. Two transactions at the same moment can still both pass. Option C closes the gap, because both transactions write the order. Its cost is the cost of an aggregate that is too big. Option D accepts the gap and adds a safety net.

The companion chose option A. The chance is small, and the result is harmless, because the note is still seen and handled. Closing the gap would need a lock across the two aggregates. The README records the decision:

**The shipping rule holds only at the moment of shipping.** An agent can add a note that needs
action to an order a moment after it shipped. The business owner accepted this: the note is
still seen and handled, and closing the gap would need a lock across the two aggregates.
`NoteServiceTest.aNoteNeedingActionCanStillBeAddedAfterTheOrderShipped` records it. Revisit it
if such notes ever need to stop a shipment.

The record names the decision and its reason. It names the test that shows the behaviour, NoteServiceTest.aNoteNeedingActionCanStillBeAddedAfterTheOrderShipped, and when to look at it again. A test records the decision in code:

/**
 * Records a decision. The shipping rule holds only at the moment of shipping: an agent can
 * still add a note that needs action to an order that has shipped, because the note feature
 * checks only that the order exists. The team accepted this gap; the README explains why and
 * when to close it.
 */
@Test
void aNoteNeedingActionCanStillBeAddedAfterTheOrderShipped() {
    String noteId = service.addNote(ORDER_ID, new NewNote("Customer says the parcel is damaged", "COMPLAINT", true));

    assertThat(noteId).isNotNull();
    verify(orders).requireExists(ORDER_ID);
    verify(notes).save(any(Note.class));
}

The test adds a note that needs action and checks that it is saved. It also checks that the note feature asks only requireExists, whatever the status of the order. The test does not run the race. It records the decision in the code that a change would touch. A developer who adds option B must change this test, and its comment points to the decision and the business owner.

For a bigger decision, write an architecture decision record (ADR) beside the code. An ADR is a short file with a title, the context, the decision, and its consequences. Its test is the same kind of test as above.

Pragmatic choice: A shipping rule that holds only at the moment of shipping

The strict rule. A rule that must always hold belongs inside one aggregate, where one transaction protects it.

What we do. The rule "no note needs action when an order ships" is checked by ShippingPolicy at the moment of shipping. A note that needs action can still be added a moment later.

Why. Putting the notes inside the order would make the order too big. Option C would make every note conflict with its order. The business owner accepted the gap, because the late note is still seen and handled.

When to stop. Revisit the decision when a note that needs action must stop a shipment, or when late notes on shipped orders become common.

Between services: no shared transactionnew#

An aggregate is a boundary inside one service. Between two services, the boundary is wider. No transaction spans two services, because each one has its own database. When the order service places an order, it asks the stock service to hold the products. The two changes cannot commit together.

So each step that crosses services must be safe to repeat, and the flow must end in a known state if a step fails. The order service makes the stock call before its own transaction, and sends the order ID as an idempotency key:

/**
 * The port to the stock service, in this service's types. The use case does not know that the
 * answer comes over HTTP, and a unit test replaces it with a mock.
 *
 * <p>It lives in {@code application/port}, not in the domain: calling another service is a step
 * of the use case, and the domain only judges the answer.
 */
public interface StockChecker {

    /**
     * Asks the stock service to confirm that the items are available, and to hold them for the
     * order. The stock service keeps the hold until it sees {@code OrderPlacedV1}, or releases it
     * after a timeout if the order is never placed.
     *
     * <p>Calling it twice for the same order holds nothing twice, because the order ID is the
     * idempotency key.
     */
    StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);
}

reserve may be called twice for the same order, and the stock service holds the products once. If the order's transaction fails after the call, no OrderPlacedV1 is published. The stock service then releases the hold after its timeout. Each service stays consistent on its own, and the services agree after a while. This is called eventual consistency.

A flow with several such steps, each with its own undo, is called a saga. The order service has none, because one hold with a timeout is enough. Consider a saga, or a workflow engine that runs it, when a flow crosses several services and each failure needs its own undo. For the stock call in full, see the chapter Calling other services.

Two features that call each othertrap#

The shipping rule makes the order feature ask the note feature for a count. Adding a note makes the note feature ask the order feature whether the order exists. So each feature's service needs the other one. With constructor injection alone, Spring cannot create either bean first.

The companion breaks the cycle with @Lazy:

public NoteService(NoteRepository notes, @Lazy OrderService orders, ReferenceDataService referenceData,
                   DomainEventPublisher events, AuditLog audit, CurrentActor currentActor, Clock clock) {
    this.notes = notes;
    this.orders = orders;
    this.referenceData = referenceData;
    this.events = events;
    this.audit = audit;
    this.currentActor = currentActor;
    this.clock = clock;
}

@Lazy on the parameter makes Spring inject a proxy in place of the real OrderService. The proxy finds the real bean at its first call. So Spring can create NoteService before OrderService exists. For how Spring resolves such cycles, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

Gotcha

A two-way dependency between features is a warning sign, even when the service starts without an error. @Lazy hides the cycle at startup. The two features still cannot change, be tested or move to another service apart.

There are three ways out.

  • Make one dependency one-way. The note controller could ask the order feature whether the order exists, before it calls the note service. Then the note service needs nothing from the order feature.
  • React to an event. A feature that only needs to know that something happened can listen to an event, instead of calling.
  • Merge the two features. If the two features always change together, they are one feature.

The companion keeps the cycle, and its README lists these ways out. A test of the architecture fails when a feature uses anything of another feature except its application package. For the rules of the layers, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

Check yourself
1
Which two questions decide whether a piece of data belongs inside an aggregate?
Does a rule need the data at every change? And is the data small and bounded? Data that passes both tests goes inside. Data with no limit stays outside. Data that no rule needs usually stays outside too. Small data that is created with the root may stay inside, such as the customer's contact on an order.
2
An expert asksWhy are notes an aggregate of their own, and not a list inside the order?
Notes have no limit, so they would grow the order document. No order rule needs every note, only a count. Each note has its own version, so agents and warehouse staff do not conflict. And a note has a different life.
3
An expert asksAn order ships after a check that no note needs action. Why can a note that needs action still exist on the shipped order?
The note and the order are separate aggregates in separate documents. A note added at the same moment, or a moment later, writes a different document. So nothing conflicts, and the rule held only at the moment of the check.
4
TranslateIn the order service, write this C# in Java: order.Lines.Single(l => l.Id == lineId).PickedAt = clock.GetUtcNow();
order.pickLine(lineId, clock); The line is changed only through its root. The ID lineId is a LineId. The clock is a java.time.Clock.
5
Name the four options for a rule across two aggregates that holds only at the moment of the check.
Accept the gap, refuse the later change, make it strict so the two transactions conflict, or repair it afterwards. Choose with the business owner, and record the choice with a test.
6
What is the main sign of an aggregate that is too small?
A rule must change several aggregates together every time. Most use cases then save the same aggregates in one transaction, or need a lock across them.

How much DDD: three levels in one service#

Why DDD, and how much · Chapter 03· 18 min read

Not every feature needs the full model of Domain-Driven Design (DDD). The order service uses three levels side by side. The order feature uses the full style, the note feature a light style, and the reference feature the simple level. This chapter shows each level in code, what the light style drops and keeps, and the sign that a feature needs the next level.

KindA usual ASP.NET Core serviceThe order serviceNote
newone style for every featurefull for order, light for note, simple for referenceeach feature gets the least DDD that still protects its rules Why
twistpublic interface IOrderRepositoryinterface OrderRepository extends Repository<Order, OrderId>the full style hides storage behind a port, with a document class and a mapper Why
twistan EF Core entity with private setters and methodsNote, a rich entity that is also its @Documentthe light style keeps the rules of the entity and drops the mapping Why
twistpublic record ReferenceItem(string Id, string Type, string Code, string Label, bool Active);record ReferenceItemDocument(@Id String id, String type, String code, String label, boolean active)data with no rules needs no aggregate, no events and no domain model Why
newno equivalentno mapper, no port, no typed IDs, and domain services only across aggregatesthe light style drops the parts that protect against changes of storage and coupling Why
newpublic setters on the entitystate-change methods, recorded events and checked valuesthe light style keeps every part that protects a rule Why
trapcatch DbUpdateConcurrencyException, then retry with the same entityload the note again after a failed saveSpring Data writes the new version into the object even when the save fails Why
twist[NotMapped] public List<object> Events { get; } = [];@Transient private final List<DomainEvent> eventsthe list of events is never stored, and a test without a database proves it Why
twistan Equals override that compares IdEntity.equals, or Note.equals on its String idthe full style compares class and typed ID in a base class, but the light entity writes equals itself Why
twista private constructor that EF Core bindsa constructor marked @PersistenceCreatorSpring Data loads through a constructor that applies no rules, and create applies them Why
newno equivalentquestions about rules, stored shape and other serviceschoose the level for each feature, and name it where the architecture tests can see it Why
newno equivalenta rule appears, or the stored shape starts to bend the modeleach level has a sign that the feature has outgrown it Why

Three levels in one servicenew#

A team that learns DDD often uses the full model everywhere. It makes every feature an aggregate. A lookup list then gets an aggregate root, a typed ID, a document class, a mapper and a port. That is five files for a list that never changes. The opposite mistake gives the core business object no protection at all.

The answer is to choose the level for each feature. A feature gets the least DDD that still protects its rules. The order service shows three levels side by side, so a reader can compare them in one codebase.

LevelFeatureWhat it hasWhat it protects
fullordera plain-Java domain with base classes, typed IDs, a separate document class and a mapper, a repository port with an adapter, and the stock service behind a portthe rules, and the model against changes of storage and of other services
lightnotea rich entity with its state-change methods, rules and events, which is also the stored document, a Spring Data repository used directly, and String IDsthe rules of the entity
simplereferencea document record, a Spring Data repository with a cache, and the logic in the application servicethe one rule that a code must be active, written once

The architecture tests of the platform know the three levels. The comment of the rules says so:

* <p>The rules allow three styles of feature. A full-style feature has a plain-Java
* {@code domain} package with ports and adapters. A light-style feature keeps a rich entity that
* is also its stored document, in a {@code model} package. A simple feature has no domain model
* at all. Rules about the {@code domain} package therefore affect only full-style features, and
* the rules that keep the application layer free of adapters take the full-style features as a
* parameter.

The package name tells the level. A full-style feature has a domain package. A light-style feature has a model package. A simple feature has no package of either kind. So one rule can check that every domain package is plain Java, and it does not touch the light or simple features.

The full level: the order featuretwist#

C# 12
public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task<Order?> FindAsync(OrderId id);
    Task<Order> SaveAsync(Order order);
    Task<bool> ExistsAsync(OrderId id);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<Order>> FindByStatusAsync(OrderStatus status, int page, int size);
}
The order service
/**
 * The port for storing orders, in the domain's own types. The persistence package implements it.
 * Lists are sorted newest first.
 */
public interface OrderRepository extends Repository<Order, OrderId> {

    /** Loads the order, or throws the 404 exception, so a use case loads in one line. */
    default Order get(OrderId id) {
        return findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
    }

    PageResult<Order> findAll(PageQuery page);

    PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page);
}

Both panes declare a repository in the types of the domain, with no database type. The Java interface extends the platform's Repository<Order, OrderId>. That interface declares the three methods that every aggregate needs, to find, save and check one. The default method get loads an order or throws the 404 exception, so a use case loads in one line.

An interface that the inner code declares, and the outer code implements, is called a port. The class that implements it with a real technology is called an adapter. Here is the adapter of the order repository:

/**
 * Implements the domain's {@link OrderRepository} port with MongoDB. The base class supplies
 * load, save and exists. This class adds only the order's own queries, each backed by an index
 * in migration {@code V001}.
 */
@Component
class OrderPersistenceAdapter extends MongoAggregateRepository<Order, OrderId, OrderDocument> implements OrderRepository {

    private static final Sort NEWEST_FIRST = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "placedAt");

    private final OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments;

    OrderPersistenceAdapter(OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments, OrderDocumentMapper mapper) {
        super(orderDocuments, mapper);
        this.orderDocuments = orderDocuments;
    }

    @Override
    public PageResult<Order> findAll(PageQuery page) {
        return toPageResult(orderDocuments.findAll(pageable(page, NEWEST_FIRST)));
    }

    @Override
    public PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page) {
        return toPageResult(orderDocuments.findByStatus(status.name(), pageable(page, NEWEST_FIRST)));
    }
}

MongoAggregateRepository is the platform's base class of an adapter. It implements findById, save and exists with a Spring Data repository and the mapper. The adapter adds only the order's own queries. It is package-private, so nothing outside the persistence package can use it. The use case sees only OrderRepository.

The full level separates the model from its stored shape. The domain class Order holds the rules. The class OrderDocument holds what is stored, as plain types. The mapper copies one into the other. So each side can change without the other. A field can be renamed in the domain, and the stored name stays. Money can be stored as Decimal128, and the domain keeps its Money type with a currency. For the document and the mapper in full, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

The light level: the note featuretwist#

EF Core entity
public class Note
{
    private Note(Guid id, Guid orderId, string text, bool actionRequired)
    {
        Id = id;
        OrderId = orderId;
        Text = text;
        ActionRequired = actionRequired;
    }

    public Guid Id { get; private set; }
    public Guid OrderId { get; private set; }
    public string Text { get; private set; }
    public bool ActionRequired { get; private set; }
    public DateTimeOffset? ActionResolvedAt { get; private set; }

    [NotMapped]
    public List<object> Events { get; } = [];

    public static Note Create(Guid orderId, string text, bool actionRequired) =>
        new(Guid.NewGuid(), orderId, text, actionRequired);

    public void ResolveAction(TimeProvider clock)
    {
        if (!ActionRequired)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("The note needs no action.");
        if (ActionResolvedAt is not null)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("The action is already resolved.");
        ActionResolvedAt = clock.GetUtcNow();
        Events.Add(new NoteActionResolved(Id, OrderId, ActionResolvedAt.Value));
    }
}
The order service
@Document("notes")
public final class Note {

    public static final int MAX_TEXT_LENGTH = 2000;

    @Id
    private final String id;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    private final String orderId;
    private final String text;
    private final String category;
    private final boolean actionRequired;
    private final Instant createdAt;
    private final String createdBy;
    private Instant actionResolvedAt;

    @Transient
    private final List<DomainEvent> events = new ArrayList<>();

    @PersistenceCreator
    Note(String id, Long version, String orderId, String text, String category, boolean actionRequired,
         Instant createdAt, String createdBy, Instant actionResolvedAt) {
        this.id = id;
        this.version = version;
        this.orderId = orderId;
        this.text = text;
        this.category = category;
        this.actionRequired = actionRequired;
        this.createdAt = createdAt;
        this.createdBy = createdBy;
        this.actionResolvedAt = actionResolvedAt;
    }

    /**
     * Writes a new note on an order. The caller has checked that the order exists and that the
     * category is an active lookup value. {@code createdBy} is the ID of the agent who writes it.
     */
    public static Note create(String orderId, String text, String category, boolean actionRequired,
                              String createdBy, Clock clock) {
        Guard.notBlank(orderId, "orderId");
        Guard.notBlank(text, "text");
        Guard.maxLength(text, MAX_TEXT_LENGTH, "text");
        Guard.matches(category, "[A-Z_]{1,50}", "category");
        Guard.notBlank(createdBy, "createdBy");
        Note note = new Note(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), null, orderId, text, category, actionRequired,
                clock.instant(), createdBy, null);
        note.events.add(new NoteAdded(note.id, orderId, note.createdAt));
        return note;
    }

    /**
     * Resolves the action. The agent who wrote the note may not resolve it, so a second person
     * checks the work. The use case passes the actor's ID in as a plain value, so the note never
     * reads the security context.
     */
    public void resolveAction(String actorId, Clock clock) {
        if (!actionRequired) {
            throw new NoteHasNoActionException(id);
        }
        if (actionResolvedAt != null) {
            throw new NoteActionAlreadyResolvedException(id);
        }
        if (actorId.equals(createdBy)) {
            throw new NoteResolvedByItsAuthorException(id);
        }
        actionResolvedAt = clock.instant();
        events.add(new NoteActionResolved(id, orderId, actionResolvedAt));
    }
Reading the code
@Document("notes")

This Spring Data annotation makes the entity its own stored document, in the collection notes. There is no separate document class and no mapper.

@Version

This field holds the version that detects a conflicting save. It is not final, because Spring Data writes the new version into the object when it saves.

@Transient

Spring Data leaves this field out of the stored document. The list of recorded events is kept only in memory.

@PersistenceCreator

Spring Data calls this constructor when it loads a stored note. The constructor applies no rules, because loading is not a business action.

public static Note create(

New notes come from this factory method. It checks the values with Guard, creates a new ID, and adds the event NoteAdded.

public void resolveAction(String actorId, Clock clock)

The only way to resolve a note. It checks its three rules, sets the time, and adds the event. The third rule compares the agent who acts with the author, so the use case passes the actor's ID in as a plain value. The C# pane does not have this rule.

Both panes are one class that is the model and the stored shape at once. EF Core can do the same, and its documentation says how. EF Core calls a constructor with parameters when their names and types match mapped properties. The page says that the constructor may be private, or have any other access level. It also says that EF Core treats a property with a private setter as one it can write, so the property is still mapped. The code above was run with EF Core 10.0.8. EF Core mapped the five properties with private setters, and left out Events.

So the light style has a close match in .NET. The C# developer who writes entities with private setters and methods already writes it. The Java version marks the constructor with @PersistenceCreator. C# relies on a naming convention. Java also marks each field that is not stored.

The full level keeps the document and the model apart, so storage and domain can change independently. The light level gives that up. It is the right trade when the stored shape and the model are the same, and the rules are few. The note has nine stored fields, all of plain types.

The simple level: the reference featuretwist#

C# 12
public record ReferenceItem(string Id, string Type, string Code, string Label, bool Active);
The order service
/**
 * One lookup value, as stored in {@code reference_data}. A record is enough: the data is
 * read-only, so it needs no version and no behaviour.
 *
 * @param type   the list it belongs to, such as {@code DELIVERY_METHOD}
 * @param code   the value that other data stores, such as {@code EXPRESS}
 * @param label  the text a user sees
 * @param active whether new data may use it; old values stay, because stored orders still use them
 */
@Document("reference_data")
public record ReferenceItemDocument(@Id String id, String type, String code, String label, boolean active) {
}

Both panes are one record with five values. The Java record is the stored document, with @Document and @Id. It has no version, because nothing changes it, and no methods, because it has no behaviour. Lookup values change only with a deployment, through a seed migration.

A feature at this level has no aggregate, no domain model and no events. The repository reads each list and caches it:

/**
 * Reads lookup values, and caches each list by its type.
 *
 * <p>The cache is on the repository, not on the service, for a reason. {@code @Cacheable} works
 * through a proxy around the bean, so only calls from another bean pass through it. The service
 * calls this method from two of its own methods; if the cache were on the service, the call from
 * {@code requireActive} to {@code list} would skip the proxy and the cache.
 *
 * <p>The cached list is shared by every caller, so callers must not change it.
 */
public interface ReferenceItemRepository extends MongoRepository<ReferenceItemDocument, String> {

    @Cacheable("reference-data")
    List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);
}

@Cacheable("reference-data") keeps the result of each call in the cache reference-data, keyed by the type. The comment explains why the cache is on the repository and not on the service. For caching in full, see the chapter Caching and scheduling.

The feature still has one rule. A code that another feature stores must be an active lookup value. The rule is written once, in the application service:

/**
 * Throws a 400 for the field unless the code is an active value of the list.
 *
 * @param field the request field the client must correct, such as {@code deliveryMethod}
 */
public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
    boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
            .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
    if (!known) {
        throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
    }
}

requireActive throws an InvalidValueException that names the field, so the client gets a 400 that says which value to correct. The order and note features call it before they create anything. A rule about input in one place, with no state to protect, needs no aggregate.

Pragmatic choice: One class for read-only lookup data

The strict rule. The stored document and the model are separate classes, so each can change without the other.

What we do. One record, ReferenceItemDocument, is the stored document. The service turns it into a view for callers, and no domain class exists.

Why. Lookup data has no behaviour and no state changes. A domain class and a mapper would copy five fields into five fields, and protect no rule.

When to stop. Add a model when a lookup value gets a rule of its own. An example is "a delivery method can be deactivated only when no open order uses it". Add one too when users start to change the values at run time.

What the light style dropsnew#

The light style drops four parts of the full style. Each part protects against something, so each drop has a cost.

DroppedThe full style hasThe light style doesWhat is lost
separate document and mapperOrderDocument and OrderDocumentMapperannotations on the entity, and @PersistenceCreator for loadingthe model and the stored shape must stay the same
repository portOrderRepository, with an adapterthe Spring Data interface NoteRepository, injected into the servicea test mocks a Spring Data interface, and the service sees Spring types
typed IDsOrderId and LineId, checked at every boundaryString IDs, not checked, so an unknown ID is simply not foundthe compiler cannot catch a swapped ID
domain services, except across aggregatesShippingPolicy, for the rule across order and notesno domain service, because the note's rules need only the notenothing, because the note has no rule across aggregates

A domain service is never a default. The full style also has one only where a rule needs two aggregates. So the fourth row is not a real drop. It shows that the light style does not add a service out of habit.

The use case of the note feature uses the Spring Data repository directly. Its test mocks that interface:

/**
 * The note use cases. In the light style the service uses a Spring Data repository directly,
 * so the test mocks that interface instead of a port.
 */
class NoteServiceTest {

    private static final String ORDER_ID = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    private static final String AUTHOR = "agent-1";

    private final NoteRepository notes = mock(NoteRepository.class);
    private final OrderService orders = mock(OrderService.class);
    private final ReferenceDataService referenceData = mock(ReferenceDataService.class);
    private final DomainEventPublisher events = mock(DomainEventPublisher.class);
    private final AuditLog audit = mock(AuditLog.class);
    private String actingAgent = "agent-2";
    private final CurrentActor currentActor = () -> actingAgent;

    private final NoteService service = new NoteService(notes, orders, referenceData, events, audit, currentActor, CLOCK);

mock(NoteRepository.class) creates a Mockito mock of the Spring Data interface. The test needs no Spring context and no database. So the missing port costs little in testing. The real cost is that the service depends on MongoRepository, a type of Spring Data, and on its paging types.

Pragmatic choice: Spring Data annotations on the note's model

The strict rule. The domain model is plain Java, with no framework type in it.

What we do. Note carries five annotations of Spring Data, such as @Document and @Version. Its package is called model, not domain, so the rule "a domain package is plain Java" does not apply to it.

Why. The note's stored shape and its model are the same. A separate document and a mapper would copy nine fields, and the annotations change nothing in the rules. NoteTest still tests every rule with plain JUnit.

When to stop. Move to the full style when the stored shape starts to bend the model. One sign is a field kept only for storage. Others are a type that Spring Data cannot store as it is, and a rule that has to work around an annotation.

Pragmatic choice: The Spring Data repository used directly

The strict rule. The domain declares a repository port in its own types, and an adapter implements it.

What we do. NoteService receives NoteRepository, a Spring Data interface, and calls it directly.

Why. The note feature has two queries of its own, and Spring Data writes both from their method names. A port and an adapter would add two classes that only forward calls.

When to stop. Add a port when a query needs MongoTemplate, when a second store appears, or when the service starts to build Spring Data queries itself.

Pragmatic choice: Plain String IDs in the note feature

The strict rule. Every ID is a type of its own that checks its format, as OrderId does.

What we do. A note's ID is a String that holds a universally unique identifier (UUID). It is created by UUID.randomUUID() and never checked. An ID in a bad format is simply not found, and the client gets 404.

Why. The methods of Note take at most one ID. NoteService.resolveAction takes two, the order ID and the note ID. If a caller swaps them, the note is not found, and the answer is 404. A 404 for a bad ID is a correct answer.

When to stop. Add a typed ID when a swap of two IDs could change the wrong note. Add one too when a bad ID must give 400, not 404.

What the light style keepsnew#

The light style keeps every part that protects a rule. These parts are cheap, and they are the reason to use DDD at all.

  • State-change methods with their rules. A note is resolved only through resolveAction, which checks that the note needs action and that it is not resolved yet.
  • No state setters. The fields that never change are final. The two that change, the version and the time of resolution, have no setter.
  • The entity records its events. create records NoteAdded. The method resolveAction records NoteActionResolved. The use case publishes them when it saves.
  • Checked values. create checks the text and the category with Guard, so no new note has a blank text or a bad code.

A test of the architecture keeps the second point true. It treats a light-style entity like a domain entity:

/**
 * An entity changes only through methods that apply its rules, so it has no public setter.
 * This covers domain entities and the entities of light-style features, which are documents
 * outside a persistence package. A persistence document, which only holds stored data, may
 * have setters.
 */
public static ArchRule entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters() {
    DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> entities = assignableTo(Entity.class)
            .or(DescribedPredicate.describe("light-style entities",
                    (JavaClass type) -> type.isAnnotatedWith(Document.class)
                            && !type.getPackageName().contains(".persistence")));
    return methods().that().areDeclaredInClassesThat(entities)
            .and().haveNameMatching("set[A-Z].*")
            .should().notBePublic()
            .allowEmptyShould(true)
            .as("Entities have no public setter");
}

The rule finds every class that extends Entity, and every class with @Document outside a persistence package. Then it fails for a public method whose name starts with set. A persistence document such as OrderDocument may have setters, because it holds no rule.

The middle ground of the chapter Why DDD, and the service we build also names value objects for IDs, money, dates and codes. The note keeps only part of that. Its category is a plain String that create checks. Its time is an Instant, which is already a value. A code that is used in one place may stay text with a check. A code that is used in several places becomes a value object, as ProductCode is in the order feature. So does a code with a rule of its own.

Versions after a savetrap#

The light style forces four differences from the full style. The first one is about the version. In the full style, the version of an aggregate is final. A save returns a new object with the new version, and the use case continues with that object. The platform's repository port says so:

/**
 * Saves the aggregate and returns the stored copy, which holds the new version.
 *
 * <p>Continue with the returned instance. The instance you passed in keeps the old version,
 * so saving it a second time fails. For a new aggregate it fails as a duplicate insert, with
 * {@code DuplicateKeyException}; for a loaded one, as a concurrent update. Saving also fails
 * with Spring's {@code OptimisticLockingFailureException} when someone else saved the
 * aggregate after you loaded it; that exception is unchecked, so this plain-Java interface
 * can only name it here.
 * Inside a transaction, MongoDB usually reports the same conflict as a write conflict, which
 * Spring translates to {@code DataIntegrityViolationException}. The platform answers both with 409.
 *
 * <p>Never retry a failed save with the same instance. Load the aggregate again, apply the
 * change again, and save that.
 */
A save(A aggregate);

The comment of A save(A aggregate) says to continue with the returned instance. In the light style, Spring Data saves the note in place. It writes the new version into the same object. The note service relies on that:

/**
 * Saves, publishes and audits. Spring Data saves this mutable object in place and sets its
 * new version, so the same instance stays usable. The events are pulled first, because they
 * are not stored.
 */
private void saveAndPublish(Note note, String auditAction) {
    List<DomainEvent> raised = note.pullEvents();
    notes.save(note);
    events.publish(raised);
    audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.NOTE, note.id());
}

notes.save(note) returns the same object for Note, and sets the new version on it. So the service ignores the result. The test NoteRepositoryIT.saveWritesTheNewVersionIntoTheSameInstance checks this against a real MongoDB.

Gotcha

A failed save of a light-style entity still changes its version. Spring Data increments the version on the object before it sends the update. When the save fails because someone else saved first, the object already holds the version that the other save stored. A C# habit is to catch the concurrency exception and retry with the same object. Here, that retry passes the version check, and it overwrites the other change without an error. Load the note again, apply the change again, and save that.

A test of the companion shows the trap against a real MongoDB:

@Test
void rejectsAStaleCopyAndStillChangesItsVersion() {
    Note saved = notes.save(Note.create(ORDER_ID, "Call back", "DELIVERY", true, "agent-1", CLOCK));
    Note firstCopy = notes.findById(saved.id()).orElseThrow();
    Note secondCopy = notes.findById(saved.id()).orElseThrow();
    firstCopy.resolveAction("agent-2", CLOCK);
    notes.save(firstCopy);
    secondCopy.resolveAction("agent-2", CLOCK);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> notes.save(secondCopy)).isInstanceOf(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class);
    // Spring Data wrote the next version into the object before the update failed, so the
    // failed copy must not be saved again: load the note afresh instead.
    assertThat(secondCopy.version()).isEqualTo(1L);
}

Two copies of the same note are loaded, and the first one is saved. The save of secondCopy fails with OptimisticLockingFailureException. But secondCopy.version() is now 1, the version that the first save stored. A second save of that object would match the stored version. So it would overwrite the first change without an error. The comment of NoteService warns about this too. For versions and conflicts in full, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

Events: a base class or a list that is not storedtwist#

In the full style, the base class AggregateRoot keeps the list of events, with raise and pullEvents. The light entity has no base class. It keeps its own list, marked @Transient, and its own pullEvents. A test checks the stored shape without a database:

@Test
void theRaisedEventsAreNotStored() {
    Note note = Note.create(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), "Call back", "DELIVERY", true, "agent-1", CLOCK);   // has an event

    Document stored = new Document();
    converter.write(note, stored);

    assertThat(stored).containsKeys("_id", "orderId", "text", "category", "actionRequired", "createdAt", "createdBy")
            .doesNotContainKey("events");
}

converter.write(note, stored) runs the same converter that Spring Data uses to store a note. The test then checks the keys of the result. The stored document has _id and the other fields, and no key events. In C#, [NotMapped] has the same purpose for EF Core. The run of the C# example above showed that EF Core left Events out of the model.

Equality: a base class or its own equalstwist#

In the full style, the base class Entity compares the class and the typed ID, and its equals is final. The light entity writes its own:

/** Two notes are the same note when they have the same ID, as for any entity. */
@Override
public boolean equals(Object other) {
    return other instanceof Note note && id.equals(note.id);
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(id);
}

other instanceof Note note checks the type and names the cast value note in one step, as a type pattern does in C#. Two notes with the same ID are the same note. NoteTest.twoNotesWithTheSameIdAreEqual builds a second copy of a note, as loading would, with another version. It checks that the two copies are equal. The class is final, so no subclass can break the comparison.

Creating and loadingtwist#

In the full style, an aggregate has two factory methods. place or create is a business action. It applies the rules and records an event. rehydrate rebuilds a stored aggregate for the mapper. It applies no rules and records nothing.

The light entity has create too. For loading, it has a constructor marked @PersistenceCreator, which Spring Data calls. This test loads a note from a stored document:

@Test
void loadingUsesThePersistenceCreatorAndRaisesNoEvents() {
    String orderId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    Document stored = new Document("_id", "note-1").append("version", 4L).append("orderId", orderId)
            .append("text", "Call back").append("category", "DELIVERY").append("actionRequired", true)
            .append("createdAt", java.util.Date.from(NOW)).append("createdBy", "agent-1");

    Note loaded = converter.read(Note.class, stored);

    assertThat(loaded.id()).isEqualTo("note-1");
    assertThat(loaded.version()).isEqualTo(4L);
    assertThat(loaded.needsAction()).isTrue();
    assertThat(loaded.pullEvents()).isEmpty();
}

converter.read(Note.class, stored) builds a note through the constructor. The loaded note has the stored ID and version, and it has no events. So loading through @PersistenceCreator works like rehydrate. The constructor is package-private, so code outside note.model cannot call it to skip create. EF Core finds such a constructor by convention. Spring Data uses the one that @PersistenceCreator marks.

Choosing the level for each featurenew#

Choose the level when a feature is designed, and write it down. Ask these questions in order.

  1. Does the feature change state under business rules? If not, use the simple level. Lookup lists, reports and read-only views are in this group.
  2. Are its rules about its own data, and is its stored shape the same as its model? If yes, use the light level. In the book's view, many features of a service are here.
  3. Does any of these apply? The stored shape and the model differ. The model needs types that Spring Data cannot store as they are. The feature calls another service, or holds the most important rules of the business. If yes, use the full level.

In the order service, the order is the core of the business. It holds money, it calls the stock service, and its stored shape differs from its model. So it is full. The note has three rules about its own data. So it is light. The reference feature only lists and checks values. So it is simple.

The architecture test names the full-style features, so the build checks the level:

/** The features in the full style, whose application layer must use ports only. */
private static final String ORDER = BASE + ".order";
// ...
@Test
void applicationOfFullStyleFeaturesUsesNoAdapter() {
    ArchitectureRules.applicationDoesNotUseAdapters(ORDER).check(CLASSES);
}

ORDER names the one full-style feature. The rule applicationDoesNotUseAdapters then fails if the order's application package uses an adapter, HTTP or MongoDB. A feature that moves to the full style is added to this list. For who decides the level in a team, see the chapter DDD for a team: the playbook.

The sign that a feature needs the next levelnew#

A level is not chosen forever. Each one has a sign that the feature has outgrown it. The comment of the note package names the sign for the light style:

/**
