 * Notes that customer-service agents keep on an order. Some notes need action, and an order
 * cannot ship until every such note is resolved.
 *
 * <p>This feature uses the light style, to compare with the full style of the order feature.
 * {@code Note} is still a rich entity: it holds its rules, changes only through its methods and
 * raises its events. But it is also the stored document, with Spring Data annotations on it, and
 * the application service uses a Spring Data repository directly. There is no port, no adapter
 * and no mapper, and IDs are plain strings. The package is called {@code model}, not
 * {@code domain}, because it is not plain Java.
 *
 * <p>The light style fits a small aggregate whose stored shape and model are the same, and whose
 * rules are few. Move to the full style when the stored shape starts to bend the model, or the
 * model needs types that Spring Data cannot store as they are.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.note;

The last paragraph of the comment above package com.acme.orderservice.note; names two signs. The table gives the signs for each move.

MoveThe signWhat to add
simple to lighta value gets a rule, or users start to change the dataan entity with state-change methods, rules and events
light to fullthe stored shape starts to bend the modela domain package, a document class and a mapper
light to fullthe model needs types that Spring Data cannot store as they area document of plain types, and a mapper that converts them
light to fullthe feature starts to call another servicea port in the application package, and an adapter
light to fulla rule across aggregates appearsa domain service named after the rule
full to lightthe mapper only copies fields of the same names and typesconsider removing the document class and the mapper

Move a feature to the next level in one change, with its tests. The domain tests stay the same, because the rules do not change. Only the persistence and its tests change. A feature can also move down. If every line of a mapper copies a field to a field of the same name, the separate document protects nothing.

Check yourself
1
What does the light style keep from the full style?
State-change methods with their rules, no setters for state, the events that the entity records, and checks of its values. It keeps every part that protects a rule.
2
What does the light style drop?
The separate document class and its mapper, the repository port and its adapter, and typed IDs. It has a domain service only for a rule across aggregates, as the full style does.
3
An expert asksA save of a light-style note fails with a conflict. Why must the service not retry with the same object?
Spring Data writes the new version into the object before it sends the update. After the failure, the object holds the version that the other save stored. A retry would pass the version check and overwrite the other change. Load the note again, and apply the change again.
4
TranslateWrite the C# property [NotMapped] public List<object> Events { get; } = []; as a field of a Spring Data document in Java.
@Transient private final List<DomainEvent> events = new ArrayList<>(); @Transient is from org.springframework.data.annotation. It keeps the field out of the stored document.
5
What is the sign that a light-style feature needs the full style?
The stored shape starts to bend the model. Other signs are types that Spring Data cannot store as they are, a call to another service, or a rule across aggregates.
Next · Why DDD, and how much04Features, layers and the rules33 min

Features, layers and the rules#

Why DDD, and how much · Chapter 04· 33 min read· Quick reference

The order service puts one folder for each business feature at the top. Every feature has the same layers inside, such as domain, application and api. A short list of rules says which layer may use which. Tests check the rules in every build. This chapter explains the layout, what goes where, why the book prefers it to other layouts, and when another layout is better.

KindC#JavaNote
newno equivalentthe service's folders, from pom.xml to src/testevery service has the same files in the same places, so a developer finds a class without searching Why
twistProgram.csOrderServiceApplication with @SpringBootApplicationthe class must be in the base package, because Spring scans that package and every package below it Why
newfolders by technology, such as Controllers and Servicestop-level packages by feature: order, note, referenceone change touches one folder, and a feature can later move to its own service Why
newno equivalentthe same sub-packages in every featuredomain, application, api, persistence, client and messaging, and a feature leaves out what it does not need Why
newno equivalenta table of what goes whereeach kind of class has one package, and the table says which packages it may use Why
newno equivalentapi and messaging, then application, then domainthe domain depends on nothing, and the adapters implement ports that the inner code declares Why
newno equivalentOrderRepository in domain, StockChecker in applicationstorage belongs to the model, but a call to another service is a step of the use case Why
newno equivalenttwelve rules for every serviceeach rule has a reason, and most are checked by a test that fails the build Why
newno equivalentArchitectureTest, with the platform's ArchitectureRulesthe layering is checked on the compiled classes, so a forbidden import fails the build Why
twistinternal sealed class OrderDocumentclass OrderDocument, with no modifierpackage-private is narrower than internal, so only the persistence package sees the document Why
twista namespace takes no XML comment, and CS1587 warnspackage-info.java with a Javadoc commentthe comment documents a whole package, and javadoc shows it on the package page Why
twist<see cref="Order"/> and <c>code</c>{@link Order}, {@code code} and {@value #MAX_SIZE}Javadoc tags in braces, inside a comment that starts with /** Why
newno equivalentfeatures and layers, not adapter/in and adapter/outthe protection comes from the direction of the dependencies, which a test checks, not from folder names Why
newone folder per use case, such as Features/PlaceOrderone application service per featurea slice per use case is fine for simple features, but the rules of one aggregate must stay in one place Why
newno equivalentone model for reads and writes, with no CQRSa separate read model is worth its cost only when reads need a shape or a scale that the aggregate cannot give Why
newno equivalentOrderService split by area of the businessat about ten use cases, split by area, such as fulfilment, and never into a read side and a write side Why
newno equivalenta small shared packageit holds the permission annotations, the audit names and the OpenAPI description, and no business logic Why
newno equivalentthree repositories: shop-platform, order-service, local-environmentthe root pom.xml of the companion exists only for the book, and real services never build together Why
newno equivalenta README with purpose, rules, endpoints, events, dependencies and configurationthe same headings in every service, so a reader knows where each fact is Why

The service's foldersnew#

A developer moves from the order service to the invoice service. They need the class that stores an invoice. If both services have the same folders, they know where to look before they open the project. So every shop service uses the same layout.

Here is the order service's repository, with the main folders only:

order-service/
├── pom.xml                      ← the build: a parent and one dependency
├── Dockerfile                   ← the image, built from the jar
├── docker-compose.yml           ← runs the service against the local environment
├── README.md                    ← purpose, rules, endpoints, events, dependencies, configuration
├── contracts/
│   ├── openapi.yaml             ← the generated API contract, committed
│   └── events/                  ← one JSON schema per event, sent or consumed
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/com/acme/orderservice/
    │   │   ├── OrderServiceApplication.java
    │   │   ├── order/           ← a feature
    │   │   ├── note/            ← a feature
    │   │   ├── reference/       ← a feature
    │   │   ├── migration/       ← database changes, not a feature
    │   │   └── shared/          ← small helpers for every feature
    │   └── resources/
    │       ├── application.yml
    │       ├── application-local.yml
    │       └── seed/            ← lookup values that a migration loads
    └── test/
        ├── java/com/acme/orderservice/   ← the same packages as main
        └── resources/

The file pom.xml is the service's Project Object Model (POM), the build file of Maven. It names the shop's parent POM, which sets every version. For the standard Maven folders, see the section The standard layout. The folders contracts and seed belong to the shop. For the contracts, see the chapter API and event contracts. For the seed files, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

The base package is com.acme.orderservice. The platform library uses com.acme.platform. Both start with the company's reversed domain, com.acme. The class that starts the service is in the base package:

/**
 * Starts the order service, like {@code Program.cs} in ASP.NET Core.
 *
 * <p>{@code @SpringBootApplication} scans this package and every package below it for
 * components. The platform's beans come from its auto-configuration instead, because the
 * platform's packages are not below this one.
 */
@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderServiceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

The class does what Program.cs does in ASP.NET Core. It starts the application. It registers nothing itself, because component scanning finds the service's own classes. For why the class must be in the base package, see the section Which packages are scanned. The platform's beans come from auto-configuration. For how, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

The test tree has the same packages as the main tree. A test of com.acme.orderservice.order.domain.model.Order is com.acme.orderservice.order.domain.model.OrderTest. So the test sees the package-private members of the class it tests. The name of a test class also decides when it runs:

Test class nameExampleWhen it runs
ends in TestOrderTest, OrderControllerTestin every build, with mvn verify, and it needs no Docker
ends in ITOrderPersistenceAdapterIT, OrderJourneyITonly with mvn verify -Pit, because it starts containers in Docker

For how Maven chooses the tests by name, see the section Fast tests and integration tests.

Features at the top, never technologiesnew#

A product owner asks for a new rule. A note in the category DELIVERY must name a delivery date. In a service organised by technology, the change touches four folders, one for each technology. They are the controllers, the services, the repositories and the data transfer objects (DTOs). Four folders change for one business change. Each of those folders also holds the classes of every other business area.

The rule of the shop is that the top-level packages are features, never technologies. A feature is a business capability that a business user recognises. The order service has three features. Each one uses a different level of Domain-Driven Design (DDD):

PackageWhat a business user calls itIts level of DDD
orderorders, picking, payment and shippingfull
notethe notes that agents keep on an orderlight
referencethe drop-down lists, such as delivery methodssimple

Two packages at the top are not features. migration holds the database changes, and shared holds a few small helpers. For both, see the section The same sub-packages in every feature.

Each package says what it holds in its own documentation. Here is the order feature's:

/**
 * Orders: what a customer bought, the lines that warehouse staff pick, the payment, and shipping.
 *
 * <p>This feature uses the full style. Its {@code domain} package is plain Java with typed IDs.
 * The {@code persistence} package stores the aggregate as a separate document through a mapper,
 * behind the {@code OrderRepository} port. The stock service is called through the
 * {@code StockChecker} port.
 *
 * <p>The rules: an order is placed only if the stock service confirms and holds the products.
 * An order ships only when it is paid, every line is picked, and no note on it needs action. A
 * payment is recorded from the payment service's event, and a repeated or late one changes nothing.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.order;

The comment stands before the line package com.acme.orderservice.order;, so it documents that package. For the file package-info.java, see the section Documenting a package. For the levels, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The shop has three reasons for this rule:

  • One change touches one folder. The new rule about delivery notes changes the note package only. A reviewer quickly sees which business area changed.
  • A feature can become a service. If the notes grow into a product of their own, the note package moves to a new repository as it is. Its dependencies on other features are already few and visible.
  • Engineers move between services. A company with eight or ten services has the same layout in each. A developer who knows one service can work in the next one from the first day.

The rule holds even for a service with one feature. A service that only keeps invoices still has the package com.acme.invoiceservice.invoice. The extra level costs one folder. In return, the second feature has a place to go, and the layout matches every other service.

A layout by technology has a strong version too. Its best argument is that a developer who looks for "the controllers" finds them in one place. Many ASP.NET Core projects start this way, with folders such as Controllers and Services. For a small service with one business area, the layout works well. It stops working when the service has several business areas. Then each technology folder mixes them, and any class can call any other class in the same folder. The shop has many services that grow, so it chooses features from the start.

The same sub-packages in every featurenew#

Inside a feature, the sub-packages are always the same, and each has one job. Here is the order feature, the most complete one:

order/
├── OrderConfig.java          ← the feature's wiring, for beans without @Component
├── package-info.java         ← what the feature is, and its rules
├── domain/                   ← plain Java: the model and its rules
│   ├── model/                ← Order, OrderLine, OrderId, Money and the other value objects
│   ├── event/                ← OrderPlaced, OrderShipped and the other domain events
│   ├── exception/            ← OrderNotPaidException and the other rule violations
│   ├── repository/           ← OrderRepository, the port for storing orders
│   └── service/              ← ShippingPolicy, a rule across two aggregates
├── application/              ← the use cases: OrderService, OrderView, PlacedOrder
│   └── port/                 ← StockChecker, the port to the stock service
├── api/                      ← OrderController, OrderApiMapper
│   └── dto/                  ← PlaceOrderRequest, OrderResponse, OrderPlacedResponse
├── persistence/              ← OrderDocument, OrderDocumentMapper, OrderPersistenceAdapter
├── client/                   ← StockHttpClient, StockAdapter, StockClientConfig
│   └── dto/                  ← ReservationRequest, ReservationResponse
└── messaging/                ← OrderIntegrationEventMapper, PaymentReceivedListener
    └── event/                ← OrderPlacedV1, OrderShippedV1, OrderCancelledV1

The folders inside domain tell quickly what a class is. A class in domain/event is something that happened. A class in domain/exception is a broken rule. Without the folders, the domain package of a large feature holds thirty classes in one list.

A feature leaves out the sub-packages it does not need. The note feature calls no other service and sends no event to other services. So it has no client and no messaging. It also uses the light style, so it has a model package in place of domain and persistence:

note/
├── package-info.java
├── model/          ← Note, which is also the stored document, NoteRepository, its events and exceptions
├── application/    ← NoteService, NoteView, NewNote
└── api/            ← NoteController, NoteApiMapper
    └── dto/        ← AddNoteRequest, NoteResponse, NoteAddedResponse

So NoteRepository is in model/, next to Note, and no mapper exists. The reference feature uses the simple level. It has no domain model at all:

reference/
├── ReferenceConfig.java    ← turns on caching
├── package-info.java
├── application/            ← ReferenceDataService, ReferenceItemView, ReferenceTypes
├── api/                    ← ReferenceDataController
│   └── dto/
└── persistence/            ← ReferenceItemDocument, ReferenceItemRepository

So the three features do not have exactly the same sub-packages. The names are the same wherever a feature has the part. A persistence package always stores data, and an api package always translates HTTP. The rules of the platform rely on the names, so a name that means something else in one feature would break a rule. For why the levels differ, see the section Choosing the level for each feature.

Pragmatic choice: Three shapes of feature under one layout rule

The strict rule. Every feature has the same sub-packages, so every feature looks the same.

What we do. Every feature uses the same names, but only for the parts it has. The light-style note feature has a model package in place of domain and persistence. The simple reference feature has no domain package at all.

Why. A lookup list with a full domain gets five files that protect nothing. A small entity whose stored shape is its model gains little from a separate document and a mapper. The names still tell the level. A domain package means plain Java, and a model package means a rich entity that is also its stored document.

When to stop. Stop when a reader cannot tell a feature's level from its package names, or when a team invents a fourth shape. Then write the shapes down and add a rule for each one.

Two top-level packages are not features. The migration package holds the database changes. It changes the storage of every feature, so it is next to the features:

/**
 * The service's database changes: indexes and seed data, as {@code MongoMigration} beans. The
 * platform's runner applies each one once, in ID order, before the service takes traffic.
 *
 * <p>This is not a feature. It changes the storage of every feature, so it sits beside them.
 * Never edit a migration that has run anywhere; add the next one.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.migration;

Each migration is a MongoMigration bean. For the migrations, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data. The shared package has its own section, The shared package, and what stays out of it.

What goes wherenew#

A developer writes a class that turns a PlaceOrderRequest into domain values. Does it go into api or into application? The shop answers such questions with one table. Each kind of class has one package. The last column says which other packages a class there may use:

PackagePurposeContainsMay use
domain/modelthe business concepts and their rulesaggregate roots, which extend AggregateRoot, entities, which extend Entity, IDs, which extend Identifier, and value objects, records that implement ValueObjectits own domain and the platform's domain package
domain/eventwhat happened in the modelrecords that implement DomainEventits own domain model
domain/exceptionthe broken rulesclasses that extend NotFoundException, InvalidValueException or BusinessRuleViolationExceptionits own domain and the platform's exception kinds
domain/repositorythe port for storing one aggregateone interface per aggregate, which extends Repositoryits own domain
domain/servicea rule that needs more than one aggregateplain classes, such as ShippingPolicyits own domain
applicationthe use casesone service per feature, its views, and records that other features pass in, such as NewNoteits own domain, the application package of other features, DomainEventPublisher and AuditLog
application/portwhat the use cases need from other servicesinterfaces in this service's own typesits own domain only
apiHTTP in and outcontrollers, mappers and DTOs with Bean Validationits own application and its own domain types
persistencehow the aggregate is stored@Document classes, Spring Data repositories, mappers and adaptersits own domain and the platform's mongo package
clientcalls to other services@HttpExchange clients, their DTOs and adaptersits own application ports, its own domain and the platform's HTTP support
messagingevents between servicesintegration events, the event mapper and listenersits own application, its own domain and the platform's messaging package
the feature's rootthe feature's wiringthe OrderConfig classanything in the feature

A DTO is a class that only carries data across a boundary, such as the JSON body of a request. The class that turns a PlaceOrderRequest into domain values reads a DTO, so it belongs in api. In the order service, that class is OrderApiMapper.

The domain model has a base class for each kind of concept. The order is the root of an aggregate, called an aggregate root:

public class Order extends AggregateRoot<OrderId> {

OrderLine extends Entity<LineId>. OrderId and LineId extend Identifier. Money and DeliveryMethod are records that implement ValueObject. For each base class, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

An exception in the domain extends one of three kinds. The kind decides the HTTP status that the platform answers with:

The exception extendsExample in the order featureStatus
NotFoundExceptionOrderNotFoundException, LineNotFoundException404
InvalidValueExceptionthrown by a value object, such as the platform's PageQuery for a page size over 100400
BusinessRuleViolationExceptionOrderNotPaidException, UnpickedLinesException422

For the problem responses, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

The OrderConfig class at the feature's root creates the beans that cannot carry @Component:

/**
 * Creates the order feature's beans that cannot carry {@code @Component}: the domain is plain
 * Java, so its classes have no Spring annotation.
 *
 * <p>{@code proxyBeanMethods = false} tells Spring not to wrap this class in a proxy. The bean
 * methods never call each other, so the proxy would only cost startup time.
 */
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class OrderConfig {

    @Bean
    ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy() {
        return new ShippingPolicy();
    }
}

ShippingPolicy is a domain service, so it may not import Spring. The feature's root package is the one place where Spring meets the domain. For @Bean methods, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

The direction of the dependenciesnew#

The table in the section above has a pattern. The outer packages use the inner ones, and never the other way round. The domain is at the centre, and it depends on nothing. The use cases are in the application package. The integration events are in the messaging package:

Each box holds one kind of building block. The order feature has one of each:

Building blockWhat it isIn the order feature
application servicethe use cases of a feature, which order the steps and contain no ruleOrderService
portan interface that the inner code needs, written in the inner code's own typesOrderRepository, StockChecker
adaptera class that implements a port with real technology, such as MongoDB or HTTPOrderPersistenceAdapter, StockAdapter
anti-corruption layeran adapter that translates another service's model into this service's modelStockAdapter
viewthe plain data that a use case returns, so a caller never holds the aggregateOrderView
repositorythe port for loading and saving one aggregate, one per aggregateOrderRepository

A port points inwards. The domain declares OrderRepository in its own types, such as Order and OrderId. The persistence package implements it with MongoDB. So the domain needs no MongoDB type, and a test of the domain needs no database.

The anti-corruption layer is one adapter with an extra job. The stock service speaks of a sku and an answer INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. Those words stop in StockAdapter:

/**
 * Implements the {@link StockChecker} port over HTTP. It is the anti-corruption layer: the stock
 * service's words, such as {@code sku} and {@code INSUFFICIENT_STOCK}, stop here, and the rest
 * of the service sees only {@link StockAvailability}.

The rest of the service sees only StockAvailability, a value object of the order's domain. For the adapter in full, see the chapter Calling other services.

A view protects the aggregate from its callers:

/**
 * What callers of the order feature see of an order: plain data, never the aggregate. A caller
 * therefore cannot call {@code order.ship()} and skip the use case's steps.
 *
 * <p>The customer's contact is left out. A view carries personal data only when a use case
 * needs it.
 */
public record OrderView(String orderId, String status, String deliveryMethod, Instant placedAt, Instant shippedAt,
                        Instant cancelledAt, List<Line> lines, LastPayment lastPayment) {

If the controller got an Order, it could call order.ship() directly. Then nothing would check the notes, publish an event or write an audit record. A view has no such method. For the steps of a use case, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

The light and simple features have fewer boxes. The note feature has no ports and no adapters. Its application service uses a Spring Data repository directly. So the diagram fits the full style exactly, and the other styles drop the adapter column.

Repositories in the domain, other services in the applicationnew#

Both OrderRepository and StockChecker are ports. Both are interfaces in the service's own types, and both have an adapter. But they are in different packages. The repository is in domain/repository:

/**
 * The port for storing orders, in the domain's own types. The persistence package implements it.
 * Lists are sorted newest first.
 */
public interface OrderRepository extends Repository<Order, OrderId> {

    /** Loads the order, or throws the 404 exception, so a use case loads in one line. */
    default Order get(OrderId id) {
        return findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
    }

The default method get loads an order or throws the 404 exception. The port to the stock service is in application/port:

/**
 * The port to the stock service, in this service's types. The use case does not know that the
 * answer comes over HTTP, and a unit test replaces it with a mock.
 *
 * <p>It lives in {@code application/port}, not in the domain: calling another service is a step
 * of the use case, and the domain only judges the answer.
 */
public interface StockChecker {

Both interfaces, OrderRepository and StockChecker, use only the service's own types. The reason for the two places is what each port means. Storage is part of the model. An order that cannot be stored and loaded again is not a useful order. So the domain declares what it needs from storage, and the persistence package decides how to do it.

A call to another service is a step of a use case. The use case asks the stock service, and then gives the answer to Order.place. The domain judges the answer, a StockAvailability, but never makes the call. So the port belongs to the application.

The placement has a second effect. A domain service such as ShippingPolicy may use only the domain. If StockChecker were in the domain, a domain service could call the stock service in the middle of a rule. A slow HTTP call would then hide inside the model, and perhaps inside a transaction. With the port in the application, only a use case can make the call, and it makes it before the transaction starts.

A careful team often puts every port in one place, either all in the domain or all in the application. Its argument is simple. A port is a port, so one rule should place them all. That works, and it is easier to explain. The shop separates the two kinds because the separation stops domain services from calling other services. If a team has no domain services, the benefit is small, and one place for all ports is a fine choice.

The rules a service followsnew#

The layout is not enough on its own. A developer can put a correct class in the correct package, and still read another feature's repository from it. So the shop writes its design as twelve rules. Each rule has a reason and a home chapter:

#RuleWhyWhere it is taught
1A service owns its data. Other services use its API or its events.Two services that share a collection can never change it apart.Storing aggregates in DocumentDB
2The top-level packages are features, never technologies.One business change touches one folder.this chapter
3Every feature has the same sub-packages, and leaves out the ones it does not need.A developer finds a class without searching.this chapter
4The domain is plain Java. It imports no Spring, no MongoDB and no other layer, but it may use the platform's domain package.The rules can be tested with no framework, and they survive a change of storage.The domain model in plain Java
5Business rules live in the domain. Write them in the aggregate first, and in a domain service only when the rule needs more than one aggregate.Each rule has one home, so it cannot be bypassed.Where each rule goes
6The application package runs the use cases. It orders the steps and holds no business rule.A use case reads as a list of steps.the chapter on use cases
7Features talk to each other only through their application package, and IDs cross as String.A feature's model stays private, so it can change.this chapter
8Outside models stay outside. DTOs stay in api, documents in persistence, the other service's DTOs in client, and integration events in messaging. Map at the edge.A change in another model never reaches the domain.this chapter
9A transaction changes one aggregate, and refers to others by ID, with one named exception.Transactions stay small, and a later split of the service can keep the boundaries.Transactions in depth
10Cross-cutting code comes from the platform library.Every service gets the same errors, security, logging and storage support.Writing the platform library
11Events go out through an outbox and come in through an inbox, even with SNS and SQS.Delivery is at least once in both directions, and nothing is lost.Publishing events, and Consuming events
12Every dependency can run locally, with a WireMock stub for each HTTP service and an emulator for each AWS resource.A developer runs the whole service on a laptop.Running locally and shipping

The last column names the chapter that teaches each rule. For example, rule 9 is taught in the chapter Transactions in depth. Rule 11 needs an outbox and an inbox. It is taught in the chapter Publishing events: the outbox and in the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

Rule 1 is visible in the stored documents. Each collection, such as orders, belongs to this service alone:

@Document("orders")
class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

No other service reads the collection orders. The invoice service learns about an order from OrderPlacedV1, or asks the API. For the events, see the chapter API and event contracts.

A strict form of rule 6 also says that the application layer checks permissions. The order service does not follow that part. It checks permissions on the controllers, where users enter. For the reasons and the measured options, see the section Choosing the place by the shape of the service.

Rule 9 names one exception. Placing an order saves the order and its first notes in one transaction. For that exception, see the chapter Use cases: the application service. For why IDs cross as String in rule 7, see the section A type for a foreign ID, or plain text.

The rules as tests that fail the buildnew#

A rule that only a review checks is broken sooner or later. A reviewer is tired, or does not see an import at the top of a file. So the platform states the rules as ArchUnit rules. ArchUnit is a library that reads the compiled classes and checks their dependencies. Each service calls the rules from one plain JUnit test:

class ArchitectureTest {

    private static final String BASE = "com.acme.orderservice";
    /** The features in the full style, whose application layer must use ports only. */
    private static final String ORDER = BASE + ".order";

    private static final JavaClasses CLASSES = new ClassFileImporter()
            .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
            .importPackages(BASE);

    @Test
    void domainIsPlainJava() {
        ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava().check(CLASSES);
    }

    @Test
    void applicationOfFullStyleFeaturesUsesNoAdapter() {
        ArchitectureRules.applicationDoesNotUseAdapters(ORDER).check(CLASSES);
    }
    // ...
    @Test
    void featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication() {
        ArchitectureRules.featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication(BASE).check(CLASSES);
    }
Reading the code
new ClassFileImporter()

The importer reads the compiled .class files, not the source. So it sees every dependency, including one that the source writes with a full class name and no import.

.withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)

The rules check the production code only. A test may use any class it needs.

ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava().check(CLASSES);

Each rule comes from the platform's class ArchitectureRules. check throws an AssertionError that names every class that breaks the rule. So the test fails, and the build fails with it.

The test has ten rules. Each one guards a rule from the section above:

Test methodWhat it checksRule
domainIsPlainJavano domain package uses Spring, MongoDB, Jackson, AWS or another layer4
applicationOfFullStyleFeaturesUsesNoAdapterthe order feature's application uses ports, never an adapter, HTTP or MongoDB6
apiDoesNotUsePersistenceOrClientsan api package uses no persistence, client or messaging class8
controllersUseNoRepositorya controller calls a service, never a repository6
everyEndpointHasAPermissionevery endpoint carries a permission annotationsecurity
documentsOnlyInPersistenceOrModela stored document lives in persistence, or in a light feature's model8
httpClientsOnlyInClientan HTTP client interface lives in a client package8
entitiesHaveNoPublicSettersan entity changes only through methods that apply its rules5
featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplicationa feature uses another feature only through its application package, and never through its ports7
servicesUseNoRepositoryOrEntityOfAnotherFeaturea service never takes another feature's repository or entity7

The rule for rule 4 lists what a domain package must not use:

/** A {@code domain} package uses no framework, no adapter and no other layer. */
public static ArchRule domainIsPlainJava() {
    return noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage(
                    "org.springframework..", "com.mongodb..", "org.bson..", "jakarta..",
                    "tools.jackson..", "com.fasterxml..", "io.awspring..",
                    "..application..", "..api..", "..persistence..", "..client..", "..messaging..",
                    "com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")
            .as("A domain package is plain Java");
}
Reading the code
noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")

Two dots stand for any number of package levels. So ..domain.. matches com.acme.orderservice.order.domain.model and every other domain package.

"jakarta..",

The list forbids Jakarta too. So a domain class cannot use Bean Validation annotations, such as @NotBlank. A value object checks its own values in its constructor instead.

"com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")

The domain may use the platform's domain package, which is plain Java. It may not use the platform's other packages.

The rule matches packages named domain. Only the order feature has one. The light note feature names its package model, because its entity carries Spring Data annotations. So the rule does not touch it, on purpose.

Rule 7 needs a condition of its own. ArchUnit has no ready rule for "a feature uses another feature only through its application package". So the platform writes it:

for (Dependency dependency : origin.getDirectDependenciesFromSelf()) {
    String target = dependency.getTargetClass().getBaseComponentType().getPackageName();
    String targetFeature = featureOf(basePackage, target);
    if (targetFeature == null || targetFeature.equals(feature) || targetFeature.equals("shared")) {
        continue;
    }
    String inFeature = target.substring((basePackage + "." + targetFeature).length());
    boolean allowed = inFeature.startsWith(".application") && !inFeature.startsWith(".application.port");
    if (!allowed) {
        events.add(SimpleConditionEvent.violated(dependency, dependency.getDescription()));
    }
}
Reading the code
origin.getDirectDependenciesFromSelf()

This method lists every class that the class uses directly. Examples are field types, parameters and method calls.

getBaseComponentType()

For an array type, such as OrderView[], this method returns the element type. So an array of another feature's class counts as a use of that class.

targetFeature.equals("shared")

The shared package is open to every feature.

inFeature.startsWith(".application") && !inFeature.startsWith(".application.port")

A use is allowed only when it ends in the other feature's application package. The other feature's ports are excluded, because they belong to that feature's own use cases.

So the note feature may call OrderService.requireExists. It may not import Order, OrderRepository or OrderDocument. The order feature may pass a NewNote to the note feature, because NewNote is in the note feature's application package:

/**
 * A note to add, in plain values. The order feature passes it when it places an order with its
 * first notes, so no note type crosses into the order feature.
 */
public record NewNote(String text, String category, boolean actionRequired) {
}

NewNote holds plain values, so no type of the note's model reaches the order feature. A rule that never fails proves nothing. So the service also has tests that feed each rule a class that breaks it, and expect the rule to fail. For those tests, for the freezing of old violations, and for the other ArchUnit rules, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Package-private classes hide the adapterstwist#

In the order service, the adapters, the stored documents, the controllers and the configuration classes have no access modifier. Here is the stored document of an order, beside an internal class in C#:

C#
internal sealed class OrderDocument
{
    public string? CustomerName { get; set; }
}
Java 25
/**
 * How an order is stored: one document per aggregate, with its lines and last payment embedded.
 *
 * <p>The lines are embedded because they are few (at most 50) and every order rule needs them.
 * Notes are not: they have no limit, and embedding them would rewrite the whole order for each
 * new note. A document must stay under 16 MB.
 *
 * <p>Only plain types are stored. Enums and codes are strings, so renaming a Java class never
 * breaks stored data. Money is DECIMAL128, so it is exact. The class and its fields are
 * package-private: nothing outside this package knows the storage shape.
 */
@Document("orders")
class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

    String customerName;
    String customerEmail;

A class with no access modifier is package-private in Java. Only classes in the same package can use it. For the access levels, see the section The mapping.

The C# class is internal, so the whole assembly can use it. The Java class is narrower. Only the package com.acme.orderservice.order.persistence can use it. Even the package com.acme.orderservice.order, which looks like its parent, cannot. For that trap, see the section A package inside a package.

The service makes these classes package-private:

ClassPackageWho uses it
OrderDocument, OrderDocumentMapper, OrderMongoRepositoryorder.persistenceonly OrderPersistenceAdapter, in the same package
OrderPersistenceAdapterorder.persistenceSpring, which injects it where OrderRepository is asked for
StockAdapter, StockHttpClient, StockClientConfigorder.clientSpring, which injects StockAdapter where StockChecker is asked for
OrderController, OrderApiMapperorder.apiSpring MVC, which calls the controller
PaymentReceivedListener, OrderIntegrationEventMapperorder.messagingSpring and the platform's messaging
OrderConfig, ReferenceConfigthe feature's rootSpring, which reads their @Bean methods

Spring creates beans of package-private classes. The adapter's class and its constructor are both package-private:

@Component
class OrderPersistenceAdapter extends MongoAggregateRepository<Order, OrderId, OrderDocument> implements OrderRepository {
    // ...
    OrderPersistenceAdapter(OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments, OrderDocumentMapper mapper) {

The use case asks for an OrderRepository. Spring finds the one bean that implements it and injects it. The use case never names the adapter, and the compiler would stop it if it tried. The companion's ApplicationWiringTest starts the whole service, so it shows that Spring builds these beans.

So package-private does a second job. It is a rule that the compiler checks. No class outside order.persistence can depend on the storage shape, because it cannot see it.

Some classes must stay public, because another package uses them:

  • The domain classes, because the application, api, persistence and client packages use them.
  • The ports, OrderRepository and StockChecker, because their adapters are in other packages.
  • The application services and views, because the controllers and other features call them.
  • The DTO records in api.dto, because the controller in api uses them. A sub-package is a different package.
  • In the light note feature, Note and NoteRepository, because NoteService in the application package uses them directly.
  • In the reference feature, ReferenceItemDocument and ReferenceItemRepository, because ReferenceDataService uses them directly.

The last two items are part of what the lighter levels give up. Without a port, the application uses the storage types, so they cannot hide.

Documenting a packagetwist#

A new developer opens the reference package and wonders why it has no domain. The answer is in a file in the package itself:

C#
/// <summary>The building blocks of a domain model.</summary>
namespace Shop.Platform.Domain
{
    /// <summary>A marker for value objects.</summary>
    public interface IValueObject { }
}
package-info.java
/**
 * Lookup values, such as delivery methods and note categories, for drop-down lists and for
 * checking codes. The data changes only with a deployment, through a seed migration.
 *
 * <p>This feature uses the simple level: no aggregate, no domain model and no events. A
 * document record, a Spring Data repository, and the logic in the application service. Read-only
 * lookup data has no business behaviour, so DDD's building blocks would only add files.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.reference;

The C# compiler does not accept an XML comment on a namespace. It warns with CS1587, "XML comment is not placed on a valid language element". In Java, a file named package-info.java holds the package declaration and one documentation comment for the whole package. The javadoc tool shows that comment on the package's page.

The service has a package-info.java in each feature and in shared and migration. The platform has one in its domain package. Each says what the package is for and what it must not hold. A rule such as "this package is plain Java" is then written beside the code it governs.

A documentation comment in Java is called a Javadoc comment. It starts with /**. The comments in the companion use four tags:

TagWhat javadoc showsC# XML comment
{@code text}the text in code font, with no HTML read inside it<c>text</c>
{@link Order}a link to the class Order, and {@link #save} links to a method<see cref="Order"/>
{@value #MAX_SIZE}the value of the constant, such as 100no equivalent
<pre>{@code ... }</pre>a block of code, kept as it is written<code>...</code>

Here {@value} keeps a comment true when the constant changes:

/**
 * Which page of a list to return, without any Spring type. Pages count from zero.
 *
 * @param page the page number, from 0
 * @param size the number of items on a page, from 1 to {@value #MAX_SIZE}
 */
public record PageQuery(int page, int size) implements ValueObject {

    public static final int MAX_SIZE = 100;

javadoc writes "from 1 to 100" on the page of PageQuery. If someone changes MAX_SIZE, the page changes with it. @param documents one parameter. On a record, it documents a component.

A block of example code uses <pre>{@code ... }</pre>:

* <p>A service calls them from a plain JUnit test:
*
* <pre>{@code
* ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava().check(classes);
* }</pre>

{@code} stops javadoc from reading the angle brackets as HTML. The tag <pre> keeps the line breaks. <p> starts a new paragraph, because javadoc joins the lines of a comment into one paragraph otherwise.

Why not adapter/in and adapter/outnew#

Hexagonal architecture is also called ports and adapters. It is a well-known layout for services like this one. A careful hexagonal service has packages such as these:

order/
├── domain/
├── application/
│   └── port/
│       ├── in/       ← the use-case interfaces that the outside calls
│       └── out/      ← the interfaces that the use cases need
└── adapter/
    ├── in/
    │   ├── web/      ← the controllers
    │   └── messaging/
    └── out/
        ├── persistence/
        └── stock/

This layout gets a lot right. It names the direction of every port. It makes the adapters look alike, so a reader quickly sees that the web and the queue both drive the use cases. Each use case also gets an interface of its own, so a controller depends on an interface, not on a class.

The shop has the same ports and adapters, with fewer folders. api and messaging are the driving adapters. persistence and client are the driven adapters. The shop leaves out the extra folders for three reasons:

  • The protection comes from the direction of the dependencies. A folder named adapter/out stops nothing. A test that fails when the domain imports MongoDB stops the mistake. The shop has that test, so the folder names add little.
  • An interface for every use case has a cost and little benefit here. The order service has one implementation of each use case. A controller test mocks the class OrderService as easily as an interface. So port/in would double the files and protect nothing.
  • The names match what developers say. A developer says "the API" and "the persistence". The packages use those words.

The hexagonal layout is the better choice in two cases. One is a team that already knows it well, across many services. Then the familiar names are worth more than the shorter tree. The other is a use case with several implementations, such as a product sold to customers who each add their own storage. Then port/in and port/out carry real meaning.

Why not one folder per use casenew#

Vertical slice architecture is another popular layout, and many .NET teams use it. Each use case gets a folder with everything it needs. A careful version looks like this:

orders/
├── placeorder/      ← the endpoint, the request, the handler, the validator
├── shiporder/       ← the same parts for shipping
├── cancelorder/
└── getorder/

The folder placeorder/ holds every class of one use case. Its best argument is strong. A change to one use case touches one folder, which is even narrower than one feature. Each slice can choose its own way to store and to read. A simple read can query the database directly, and a complex write can use a rich model. There is no shared layer that every change must pass through.

The difficulty is the aggregate. Placing, shipping and cancelling all change an order, and the rules of an order must hold in all three. In a strict slice layout, each slice changes the order in its own code. The rule "a shipped order cannot change" is then written in two slices, and the third slice can forget it. The shop's rule 5 says each business rule has one home. So the shop keeps one domain model per aggregate, shared by all its use cases.

A careful slice team solves this too. It keeps a shared domain folder, and the slices call the aggregate's methods. That is close to the shop's layout, with the application service split into one class per use case. The shop keeps one application service per feature. The steps of every use case are the same, and one class shows them side by side. For when to split that class, see the section Splitting a large application service.

Slices are the better choice for a feature with many independent use cases and few shared rules. Reports and searches are good examples. Each one reads differently, and no rule ties them together. A feature of that kind can use slices inside the shop's layout, under its application package.

One model for reads and writes: CQRS or notnew#

Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) splits a feature into two sides. The write side changes the aggregate and checks its rules. The read side answers queries from a separate model, which is shaped for the screens that read it. An event from the write side usually keeps the read model up to date.

The order service uses one model for both. A read loads the aggregate and turns it into a view. Here are the two read use cases of the order feature:

public OrderView get(OrderId orderId) {
    return OrderView.from(orders.get(orderId));
}

public PageResult<OrderView> list(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page) {
    PageResult<Order> result = status == null ? orders.findAll(page) : orders.findByStatus(status, page);
    return result.map(OrderView::from);
}

get loads one order and returns a view. list loads a page of orders, and map turns each one into a view. The same collection and the same documents serve reads and writes.

A careful CQRS design gets several things right. The read model has exactly the shape a screen needs, so a read is one fast query. Reads and writes can scale apart. And the write model never grows fields that only a screen uses. When those benefits are real, CQRS is worth its cost.

The cost is also real. The read model is a second copy of the data, kept up to date by events. So it is briefly out of date after every change, and every screen must allow for that. The team writes and tests the code that keeps the copy right. A replay is needed when the read model's shape changes. For a feature whose reads look like its aggregate, the team does all of that work and gains nothing.

Pragmatic choice: One model for reads and writes

The strict rule. Commands and queries have different needs, so a design that takes DDD seriously gives each its own model.

What we do. Each feature has one application service. Reads load the aggregate and return a view, from the same collection that the writes use.

Why. The order service's screens show an order, a page of orders, and the notes of an order. Each of those is close to the shape of one aggregate. A second model would add a copy of the data and a delay. No read of today would become faster.

When to stop. Stop when a read needs data from several aggregates or features at once, such as a search across orders and notes. Stop also when reads are many times more frequent than writes, and the aggregate is slow to load. A third sign is a screen that needs a shape the aggregate must bend to give. Then add a read model for that query, and only for that query.

CQRS has a second use, which matters here. The order feature and the note feature call each other. The order service asks the note service how many notes need action. The note service asks the order service whether an order exists. Both services take the other one in their constructors, and the companion breaks the cycle with @Lazy. For the cycle and its first three ways out, see the section Two features that call each other.

A query side gives a fourth way out. The count of notes that need action is a query. A small query class in the note feature could answer it, with no dependency on the order feature. The order feature would call the query class, and the note service would call the order service. Each dependency would then point one way. The companion does not do this, because it has no CQRS. Its README calls the cycle a warning sign, and it lists the other three ways out.

Splitting a large application servicenew#

An application service grows with its feature. OrderService has eight public methods today. A year later it may have fifteen, and its constructor may take twelve dependencies. The class is then hard to read, and every test builds all its dependencies. The class says how to split it:

 * <p>The class has no permission annotation. Permissions are checked on the controllers, where
 * users enter. Every method here can therefore be called by another feature or by a message
 * listener without a second, unprotected copy of the method.
 *
 * <p>With about ten use cases, split the class by area, such as {@code OrderFulfilmentService},
 * not into a read side and a write side.
 */
@Service
public class OrderService {

The name OrderFulfilmentService is an example of a class for one area. An area is a part of the business that the users recognise. The order feature has three. Placing an order is one. Fulfilment, which means picking, shipping and cancelling, is another. Payment is the third. Each area becomes one class in the application package, with the same steps in each method. The companion does not split the class yet, because it has only eight public methods.

A split into a read side and a write side looks tidy, but it is a weaker cut. Every change to fulfilment would touch both classes. It also makes the read class look like a read model, when it is not one. If a real read model is needed, see the section One model for reads and writes: CQRS or not.

Three points keep a split safe:

  • The private helper saveAndPublish saves, publishes the events and records the audit. After a split, each class needs it. Move it to a package-private class in the same package, so no other feature can call it.
  • Other features call the new class that owns the use case. The rule featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication still holds, because every new class is in the application package.
  • A split is not a reason to add a rule to the application service. The rules stay in the domain, whatever the number of application classes.

A split is a sign to check the aggregate too. Fifteen use cases on one aggregate can mean that the aggregate holds two things. For those signs, see the section Signs of an aggregate that is too big.

The shared package, and what stays out of itnew#

Every feature needs the permission annotations @OrdersRead and @OrdersWrite. Every feature writes the same names to the audit log. Those classes belong to no single feature. They are in shared:

/**
 * Small helpers that every feature of this service uses: the permission annotations, the audit
 * names and the OpenAPI description. It holds no business logic. Code that several services
 * need belongs in the platform instead.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.shared;

The comment names the three kinds of helper and says that shared holds no business logic. Here are the audit names:

/** The names this service writes to the audit log, kept in one place so they stay consistent and searchable. */
public final class AuditActions {

    public static final String ORDER = "order";
    public static final String NOTE = "note";

    public static final String ORDER_PLACED = "ORDER_PLACED";

The class is final, so no class can extend it. It holds only constants. A search for ORDER_PLACED then finds every place that writes the action, and the audit log always uses the same spelling.

The package has three parts:

PackageWhat it holdsWhy it is shared
sharedAuditActionsevery feature records audit actions with the same names
shared.securityOrdersRead, OrdersWriteevery controller names one of the two scopes
shared.apiOpenApiConfigthe description of the whole API, written once

A shared package often grows until it holds anything. So it has two limits. It holds no business logic, because a rule belongs in a feature's domain. And it holds nothing that other services need, because that belongs in the platform. For the permission annotations, see the section Permission annotations: each scope string written once.

Pragmatic choice: A shared package inside the service

The strict rule. Features share nothing except their application packages, so each feature can move to its own service.

What we do. The shared package holds the permission annotations, the audit names and the OpenAPI description. The architecture rule lets every feature use it.

Why. These classes are the same for every feature of this service. A copy in each feature would drift. None of them holds a rule, so sharing them couples nothing that matters.

When to stop. Stop when a class in shared starts to make a business decision, or when one feature needs a change that the others do not. Then move it into that feature.

The three repositories in real lifenew#

The companion is one folder with three sub-folders. Its root pom.xml builds the platform and the service together:

<!--
  Builds the platform and the order service together, for the book only.

  In a real company, shop-platform, order-service and local-environment are three separate
  repositories. This file lets one command build and test everything:

      mvn verify           unit, slice, wiring and architecture tests (no Docker needed)
      mvn verify -Pit      also the integration tests (*IT), which start containers in Docker
-->
<!-- ... -->
    <modules>
        <module>shop-platform</module>
        <module>order-service</module>
    </modules>

The two <module> lines name the two folders that Maven builds. mvn verify -Pit also runs the tests that need Docker. In real life, nothing builds the platform and a service together. The platform team releases a version of the library. Each service names that version and builds alone. The local environment is a third repository, with no Java at all. For the repositories and who uses each one, see the section Three repositories: platform, service and local environment. For the POMs, see the chapter The build: a parent POM and a platform library.

The separation has a reason. If the order service built against the platform's source, a change in the platform would reach every service at once, untested. With a released version, each service chooses when to upgrade. For the rules of that upgrade, see the section Versions, and the rules for upgrading.

Rule 12 is kept by the local environment. WireMock answers for each HTTP service, with one folder of stubs per service. Floci emulates the AWS resources. So every dependency runs on a laptop:

# Imitates the HTTP services that shop services call. The stubs are in wiremock/mappings/<service>/.
wiremock:
  image: wiremock/wiremock:3.13.0
  command: ["--global-response-templating", "--verbose"]
  volumes: ["./wiremock:/home/wiremock"]
  ports: ["8089:8080"]

# Local SNS and SQS: Floci, a free emulator with LocalStack's API, on port 4566.
floci:
  image: floci/floci:2.3.0
  ports: ["4566:4566"]

The container wiremock serves the stubs, and the container floci answers the calls to Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). The folder wiremock/mappings/stock-service holds the stubs of the stock service. For the local environment in full, see the chapter Running locally and shipping.

A reader new to the companion can read it in this order. Each step builds on the one before it:

  1. The order service's README.md, for the rules and the decisions.
  2. The package order/domain/model, with Order, and its test OrderTest.
  3. OrderService, for the steps of every use case.
  4. The adapters, OrderPersistenceAdapter and StockAdapter.
  5. The note feature, to compare the light style with the full style.
  6. The platform library, for everything the service gets without writing it.

The service's READMEnew#

An engineer on call is woken at night. The order service answers 503 for new orders. They need to know what the service depends on, and what happens when each dependency is down. That fact must be in a known place in every service. So every shop service has a README with the same headings:

HeadingWhat it holds
the first paragraphthe purpose, in the words of the business
Rulesthe business rules, one line each
Three styles in one servicethe level of each feature, a section that only the companion needs
Endpointsevery path, its scope and its success status
Eventseach event sent or consumed, with its topic or queue and its schema
Dependencieseach dependency, what the service uses it for, and what happens when it is down
Configurationeach environment variable and what it means
Run locallythe commands, and how to call the service
Teststhe kinds of test, with examples and the command that runs them
Decisionseach design choice, with its reason and the sign to change it

Here is the section that the engineer on call needs:

| Dependency | Used for | When it is down |
|---|---|---|
| DocumentDB | all data | readiness is DOWN, so no traffic arrives; liveness stays UP, so instances are not restarted |
| stock service | placing an order | only `POST /orders` answers 503; everything else works |
| SNS | publishing events | events wait in the outbox and are resent |
| SQS | payments | payments wait in the queue |
| token issuer | checking tokens, and the stock call's own token | requests get 401; placing an order gets 503 |

The answer is in the second row. Only POST /orders depends on the stock service. Every other endpoint works, so the incident is smaller than it looks.

The section "Decisions" is the most useful one for a reviewer. Each entry states a choice, such as "Permissions are checked on the controllers", with its reason and its limits. A team that writes architecture decision records can link them from here. The README keeps the short version beside the code.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksBoth StockChecker and OrderRepository are ports. Why is the first one in application/port and the second one in the domain?
Storage is part of the model, so the domain declares what it needs from storage. A call to another service is a step of a use case, and the domain only judges the answer. With the port in the application, a domain service cannot call the stock service in the middle of a rule. So only a use case makes the call, before its transaction starts.
2
An expert asksA team says that folders named adapter/in and adapter/out protect the domain better. What does the book answer?
Folder names stop nothing. A test that fails when the domain imports MongoDB stops the mistake. The shop has the same ports and adapters, and an ArchUnit rule checks the direction of every dependency. The hexagonal names are worth it for a team that already knows them, or where a use case has several implementations.
3
The note feature wants to read an order's status. Which classes of the order feature may it use, and which rule checks that?
Only classes in the order feature's application package, such as OrderService and OrderView, and not the application's ports. The rule featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication fails the build for any other use. Order, OrderRepository and OrderDocument stay private to the order feature.
4
When should the order feature get a separate read model?
When a read needs data from several aggregates or features at once, such as a search across orders and notes. Or when reads are far more frequent than writes and the aggregate is slow to load. Then add a read model for that query only. The screens of today are close to one aggregate each, so one model serves both.
5
TranslateWrite this C# class in Java, so that only its own package can use it. It stores an order in the collection orders: 
internal sealed class OrderDocument
{
    public string? Status { get; set; }
}
@Document("orders")
class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

    String customerName;
    String customerEmail;
    String deliveryMethod;
    String status;

A class and fields with no access modifier are package-private. Only com.acme.orderservice.order.persistence can use them. That is narrower than internal, which opens a type to the whole assembly. @Document("orders") names the collection.

The build: a parent POM and a platform library#

The build and the model · Chapter 05· 21 min read· Quick reference

Every shop service builds the same way. A parent Project Object Model (POM) sets the Java release, the plugins and the version of every library. A platform library brings everything cross-cutting. So a service's own build file names the parent, the library and almost nothing else. This chapter walks through the build files and each Maven setting in them. It shows how one change upgrades Boot everywhere.

KindC#JavaNote
newno equivalentfive POMs: two aggregators, the parent, the library and the servicean aggregator only lists folders to build, and a parent passes its settings on to its children Why
twistDirectory.Build.props, found in a folder above the projectshop-platform-parent, a published POM that a service namesthe service fetches the parent by its coordinates, so it works in a repository of its own Why
twist<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework> in Directory.Build.props<java.version>25</java.version> in the parentBoot's parent turns java.version into maven.compiler.release, so one property sets the release Why
twist<PackageVersion Include="..." Version="..." /> in Directory.Packages.propsdependencyManagement, with BOMs importedone BOM sets the versions of a whole family of libraries, and the first import wins a clash Why
trapa version in Directory.Packages.props is enougha library that no BOM covers needs its own managed entrywithout the entry, a child that leaves out the version fails to build Why

trapdotnet test runs every [Fact], whatever the class is calledsurefire runs only classes named like *Test, *Tests, Test* or *TestCasea test class named OrderCheck never runs, and nothing warns you Why

twistPrivateAssets="all" on a PackageReference<optional>true</optional>the library compiles against the test libraries, but a service that uses it does not get them Why
trapno equivalentspring-boot-configuration-processor in the compiler's annotationProcessorPathsjavac 26 does not run a processor that is only on the class path, so an optional dependency alone writes no metadata Why
twista csproj with one PackageReference and no versionthe service POM: a parent, two dependencies and one pluginevery version and setting comes from the parent Why
twistdotnet publishspring-boot-maven-pluginit repackages the jar into an executable jar, with layers for the Docker image Why
