Five build files, five jobsnew#

A developer opens the companion and finds five files named pom.xml. Some of them build code, and some only list other folders. Each POM has one job:

FilePackagingIts job
pom.xml, at the rootpombuilds the platform and the order service together, for the book only
shop-platform/pom.xmlpombuilds the parent and the library together, and is the root of the platform's repository
shop-platform/shop-platform-parent/pom.xmlpomthe parent of every service and of the library, which sets Java, the plugins and the versions
shop-platform/shop-platform/pom.xmljarthe library that every service adds
order-service/pom.xmljarthe service itself

Two kinds of POM appear here. They are easy to mix up, because both have <packaging>pom</packaging>:

  • An aggregator lists folders in <modules>. Maven builds each folder when the aggregator builds. The children do not inherit anything from the aggregator.
  • A parent is named in a child's <parent> element. The child inherits the parent's properties, dependencies, managed versions and plugins. The parent does not know its children.

The platform's aggregator lists the parent and the library:

<!--
  Builds the parent POM and the platform library together. It is never published.
  In the platform's own repository, this file is the root pom.xml.
-->
<!-- ... -->
    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform-build</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

    <modules>
        <module>shop-platform-parent</module>
        <module>shop-platform</module>
    </modules>

The file is never published, because no project depends on shop-platform-build. It only lets one command build both modules. The parent and the library are published, because services name them. For aggregators in general, see the section Multi-module: your solution file.

The root pom.xml of the companion is an aggregator of the same kind, with the modules shop-platform and order-service. It exists only so that one command builds and tests the book's code. For why real services never build together, see the section The three repositories in real life.

The parent POM, on top of Spring Boot's parenttwist#

The shop's parent has a parent of its own. It is the parent POM of Spring Boot:

<!--
  The parent POM of every shop service and of the platform library.

  It sets the Java release, the build plugins and the version of every dependency.
  A service never writes a version number itself. To upgrade Spring Boot for every service,
  change the parent below and release a new platform version.
-->
<!-- ... -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>4.1.2</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform-parent</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

    <properties>
        <java.version>25</java.version>
        <shop-platform.version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</shop-platform.version>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>

The parent of Spring Boot manages the versions of the libraries that Boot supports. It also configures plugins, such as the compiler. So the shop's parent gets all of that, and every service gets it from the shop's parent. For the basics, see the section A Spring Boot pom.

<relativePath/>

By default, Maven first looks for a parent in the folder above, at ../pom.xml. An empty relativePath switches that search off. Maven then always fetches the parent from a repository. The folder above holds the platform's aggregator, which is not this parent's parent, so the search must be off.

<java.version>25</java.version>

Boot's parent sets maven.compiler.release from java.version. So this one line makes every service compile for Java 25. Boot 4.1.2's own default is 17.

<shop-platform.version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</shop-platform.version>

The version of the platform library, used further down. It is the same as the parent's version, because the parent and the library are released together.

The chain has three levels. A service inherits from shop-platform-parent, which inherits from spring-boot-starter-parent. A setting in a lower level replaces the same setting in a higher level. So a service could set java.version itself. It should leave the setting alone, so that every service runs on the same Java release.

The closest match in .NET is a Directory.Build.props file. MSBuild finds it in a folder above the project and applies it. A run for this book put the target framework in such a file, and the project built with it:

Directory.Build.props
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>12</LangVersion>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
shop-platform-parent/pom.xml
<properties>
    <java.version>25</java.version>

The C# pane sets TargetFramework for every project below the file. The Java pane sets java.version for every child. The two files differ in how a project finds them. Directory.Build.props is found by its folder. So it works only when the project is in a folder below it, in the same repository. The shop's parent is found by its coordinates, a group, an artifact and a version. So a service in a repository of its own still gets it from the company's artifact repository.

One place for every version: managed versions and BOMstwist#

The shop uses libraries that Spring Boot does not manage, such as Spring Modulith and Resilience4j. Their versions are properties in the parent. Each property is used once, in the section dependencyManagement:

Directory.Packages.props
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Shop.Platform" Version="1.0.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
shop-platform-parent/pom.xml
    <!-- Libraries that Spring Boot does not manage -->
    <spring-modulith.version>2.1.2</spring-modulith.version>
    <spring-cloud-aws.version>4.1.0</spring-cloud-aws.version>
    <resilience4j.version>2.4.0</resilience4j.version>
    <shedlock.version>7.10.1</shedlock.version>
    <springdoc.version>3.2.0</springdoc.version>
    <archunit.version>1.5.1</archunit.version>
    // ...
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Each BOM fixes the versions of a family of artifacts, like Directory.Packages.props -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.modulith</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-modulith-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-modulith.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>

The versions are the ones the companion builds with, as of October 2026. Upgrading Resilience4j means changing one property.

A bill of materials (BOM) is a POM that only lists managed versions. The element <scope>import</scope>, on a dependency of type pom, copies the BOM's managed versions into this POM. Spring Modulith publishes a BOM for all its modules. So the platform library can add spring-modulith-events-core and spring-modulith-events-mongodb with no version, and both get 2.1.2. For the basics of BOMs, see the section Profiles and BOMs.

The parent imports four BOMs. They are the BOMs of Spring Modulith, Spring Cloud AWS, Resilience4j and ShedLock. If two imported BOMs manage the same artifact, the BOM declared first wins. An entry written directly in dependencyManagement wins over every import. So the order of the imports matters, and a direct entry is the way to settle a clash.

Both sides of the comparison manage versions in one place. In the run for this book, the project then referenced Shop.Platform with no version, and the build used 1.0.0. A POM's dependencyManagement has the same effect. It adds no dependency by itself. It only gives a version to a dependency that a POM declares without one.

Some artifacts are in no imported BOM. Each of them needs an entry of its own:

<!-- Artifacts that no imported BOM covers, so they are pinned one by one -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-modulith-events-sns</artifactId>
    <version>${spring-cloud-aws.version}</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
    <version>${springdoc.version}</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.tngtech.archunit</groupId>
    <artifactId>archunit</artifactId>
    <version>${archunit.version}</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.networknt</groupId>
    <artifactId>json-schema-validator</artifactId>
    <version>${json-schema-validator.version}</version>
</dependency>

<!-- The platform library itself -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>
    <version>${shop-platform.version}</version>
</dependency>

spring-cloud-aws-modulith-events-sns belongs to Spring Cloud AWS, but the spring-cloud-aws-dependencies BOM does not list it. So the parent pins it with the same version property. springdoc-openapi, ArchUnit and the JSON Schema validator have no BOM that the parent imports. The last entry is the platform library. Because of it, a service names shop-platform with no version.

Gotcha

A dependency without a version needs a managed version from somewhere. If a service adds archunit with no version, and no parent or BOM manages it, the build stops. The POM is invalid, because the dependency's version is missing. Add the library to the parent's dependencyManagement first, and then use it without a version.

Test libraries for every service, from the parentnew#

Every shop service tests with the same libraries. A service that forgets one cannot use the platform's test support. So the parent declares the test libraries as real dependencies, not only as managed versions:

<!--
  Test libraries for every service. Each child inherits them with the test scope,
  so they never reach a production jar, and a service declares only shop-platform.
-->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    // ...
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
        <artifactId>testcontainers-mongodb</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>

A <dependencies> section in a parent is inherited by every child. So each service has these libraries, though its own POM does not name them. The scope test puts a library on the test classpath only. The run for this book listed the order service's dependency tree:

[INFO] com.acme:order-service:jar:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT
[INFO] +- com.acme.platform:shop-platform:jar:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT:compile
[INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-cache:jar:4.1.2:compile
[INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test:jar:4.1.2:test
[INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test:jar:4.1.2:test
[INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb-test:jar:4.1.2:test
[INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-security-test:jar:4.1.2:test
[INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-testcontainers:jar:4.1.2:test
[INFO] +- org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mongodb:jar:2.0.5:test
[INFO] +- com.tngtech.archunit:archunit:jar:1.5.1:test
[INFO] +- org.awaitility:awaitility:jar:4.3.0:test
[INFO] \- com.networknt:json-schema-validator:jar:3.0.8:test

The service's own POM names only the first two. Every line after them ends in test, so none of these libraries is in the executable jar. The same run listed the jar's contents. It held 196 libraries, and none of them was a test library.

The parent has nine test dependencies:

ArtifactWhat a test gets from it
spring-boot-starter-testJUnit, AssertJ, Mockito and Spring's test support
spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test@WebMvcTest and MockMvc for the controller slices
spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb-test@DataMongoTest for the persistence slices
spring-boot-starter-security-testjwt() and the other helpers that put a caller into a test request
spring-boot-testcontainers@ServiceConnection, which points Spring Boot at a container
testcontainers-mongodbthe MongoDB container, in the Testcontainers 2 artifact
archunitthe architecture rules
awaitilitya wait for a result that arrives later, such as a message that a listener handles
json-schema-validatora check of each published event against its JSON schema, version 3.0.8 as of October 2026

The MongoDB artifact has a Testcontainers 2 name, testcontainers-mongodb. Its class is org.testcontainers.mongodb.MongoDBContainer. The old class in org.testcontainers.containers still exists and is deprecated. The new class starts a replica set only after withReplicaSet(), and transactions need a replica set. For the trap in that change, see the chapter Testing in depth.

The name of a test class decides whether it runstrap#

A developer adds a test class for the shipping rules. The name OrderCheck seems clear. The test fails on purpose, to see it fail. The developer runs the build:

PredictA test class whose name does not end in Test#
The test method fails on purpose. Does mvn verify fail?
class OrderCheck {

    @Test
    void anOrderShipsOnlyWhenPaid() {
        fail("this should fail the build");
    }
}
Show the answer
No. The build passes, and the test never runs.

Surefire runs only classes whose names match its patterns. There are four default patterns. A class name starts with Test, or it ends in one of three words. They are Test, Tests and TestCase. A run for this book had four test classes. Three were named OrderTest, OrderTests and TestOrder. The fourth was named OrderCheck. The build ran the first three, and never the fourth.

In .NET, dotnet test runs every [Fact], whatever the class is called. A run with xUnit ran a test in a class named OrderChecks.

Name every test class ...Test, or ...IT when it needs Docker.

The shop names a test by what it tests, plus Test or IT. OrderTest tests Order, and OrderPersistenceAdapterIT tests the adapter against a database. A test class that matches no pattern is the more dangerous mistake, because a green build hides it.

Fast tests and integration testsnew#

The order service has two kinds of test. Most of them need nothing but the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), and they run in seconds. A few start MongoDB or an AWS emulator in Docker, and Docker is not always running. So the build runs the two kinds apart:

CommandPluginRunsNeeds Docker
mvn verifymaven-surefire-pluginevery *Test classno
mvn verify -Pitsurefire, then maven-failsafe-pluginevery *Test class, then every *IT classyes

Surefire is the plugin that runs unit tests in the phase test. Failsafe is the plugin that runs integration tests in the phases integration-test and verify. Failsafe's default patterns are IT*, *IT and *ITCase. For the phases, see the section The lifecycle.

The parent configures both plugins in pluginManagement:

<pluginManagement>
    <plugins>
        <!-- ... -->
        <!-- mvn verify runs the fast tests only: *Test.java. The *IT.java tests need Docker. -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <argLine>@{argLine} -javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}</argLine>
                <excludes>
                    <exclude>**/*IT.java</exclude>
                </excludes>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
Reading the code
<pluginManagement>

This section configures a plugin for this POM and every child. It does not add the plugin to the build. A plugin runs only when a POM names it in <plugins>, or when the lifecycle runs it by default. Surefire runs by default in the phase test, so this configuration always applies.

<exclude>**/*IT.java</exclude>

Surefire's defaults already leave out *IT. The line states the rule anyway, so it still holds if someone adds an include pattern later.

<argLine>@{argLine} -javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}</argLine>

The test JVM starts with Mockito as a Java agent. The property org.mockito:mockito-core:jar holds the path of Mockito's jar. The plugin that sets it is shown below. @{argLine} keeps any argument that another plugin, such as JaCoCo, has set.

The parent's <plugins> section adds the plugin that sets the property. Its comment gives the reason for the agent:

<!--
  Sets the property org.mockito:mockito-core:jar to the jar's path, so the test JVMs
  below can load Mockito as an agent at startup. Loading it later, on first use, prints
  a warning on current JDKs, which will block it in a future release.
-->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-dependency-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>properties</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

The goal properties of maven-dependency-plugin sets one property for each dependency, named by its coordinates, with the path of its jar. This plugin is in <plugins>, not in pluginManagement, so it runs in every child.

A run for this book removed the agent from the test JVM and ran OrderServiceTest on Java Development Kit (JDK) 26.0.1. The tests passed, and the output warned twice:

Mockito is currently self-attaching to enable the inline-mock-maker. This will no longer work in future releases of the JDK.
WARNING: A Java agent has been loaded dynamically (/Users/kodebot/.m2/repository/net/bytebuddy/byte-buddy-agent/1.18.15/byte-buddy-agent-1.18.15.jar)
WARNING: Dynamic loading of agents will be disallowed by default in a future release

So without -javaagent, Mockito loads its agent itself while the tests run, and the JDK warns that a future release will block that. With the agent named at startup, no warning appears.

Failsafe runs only in the profile it:

<profiles>
    <!-- mvn verify -Pit also runs the integration tests (*IT.java) with Testcontainers. -->
    <profile>
        <id>it</id>
        <build>
            <plugins>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                    <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
                    <executions>
                        <execution>
                            <goals>
                                <goal>integration-test</goal>
                                <goal>verify</goal>
                            </goals>
                        </execution>
                    </executions>
                </plugin>
            </plugins>
        </build>
    </profile>

A Maven profile is a named block of the build that -P switches on. This one names failsafe in <plugins> and binds its two goals. The goal integration-test runs the *IT classes. The goal verify fails the build if one of them failed.

The parent has a second profile, contract-first. It runs openapi-generator-maven-plugin 7.26.0, which generates Java interfaces and models from a service's contracts/openapi.yaml before the code compiles. The profile is switched on by a property, not by -P. It needs two conditions. The build must set -Dcontract-first, and the module must have the file contracts/openapi.yaml. Maven 3.9 switches a profile on only when all its conditions hold. So the platform's modules, which have no contract, skip it. A run of mvn verify -Dcontract-first on the companion generated the code, compiled it with the service, and passed. For what the profile is for, and when to choose it, see the section Contract first: openapi-generator.

Boot's parent has failsafe in its own pluginManagement, with the same two goals. That alone runs nothing. The run for this book confirmed it. A plain mvn verify on Boot's parent did not run OrderIT. It ran only in a profile that names the plugin.

The choice of a profile has a reason. A developer without Docker still gets a full, green mvn verify. The build server runs mvn verify -Pit, where Docker is always there. For what each kind of test covers, see the chapter Testing in depth.

What the library brings to every servicenew#

A service adds one dependency, shop-platform. Through it, the service gets every library that the platform uses. The library's POM groups them by concern:

<dependencies>
    <!-- Web, validation and health -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    // ...
    <!-- Security: each service checks JWTs (resource server) and gets tokens for its own calls (client) -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
    </dependency>

The first starter, spring-boot-starter-webmvc, brings Spring model-view-controller (MVC) and the embedded server. Each dependency is a compile dependency with no version. Its version comes from the parent. Every project that uses the library also gets the library's compile dependencies. So each of these reaches the service's classpath, and its auto-configuration runs there:

ConcernArtifacts
web, validation and healthspring-boot-starter-webmvc, spring-boot-starter-validation, spring-boot-starter-actuator
the OpenAPI documentspringdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui
securityspring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server, spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client
tracingspring-boot-starter-opentelemetry
calling other servicesspring-boot-starter-restclient, resilience4j-circuitbreaker, resilience4j-retry
DocumentDBspring-boot-starter-data-mongodb
the outbox and the inboxspring-modulith-events-api, -core and -mongodb, spring-cloud-aws-modulith-events-sns, spring-cloud-aws-starter-sns, spring-cloud-aws-starter-sqs
a lock for the resendershedlock-core, shedlock-provider-mongo

So the order service's POM names none of these. It needs only one extra starter, for its cache. For what each concern adds at run time, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

One library for everything has a cost. A service that sends no events still has the messaging libraries on its classpath. The platform answers with a switch that turns messaging off. For the switch, and for why the shop chose one library over one per concern, see the section One library, not one per concern.

The Boot 4 starter namestwist#

A tutorial for Boot 3 adds spring-boot-starter-web. The shop's library adds spring-boot-starter-webmvc. Spring Boot 4 named its modules after their technology, in the form spring-boot-<technology>. These are the starters that the shop uses:

Boot 4 starterNote
spring-boot-starter-webmvcit was spring-boot-starter-web until Boot 4.0, and this rename is the first one a Boot 3 tutorial meets
spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-serverthe old name spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server still exists in 4.1.2, and is deprecated
spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-clientthe old name spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client still exists in 4.1.2, and is deprecated
spring-boot-starter-restclientwithout it, Boot creates no RestClient.Builder bean, and the platform's HTTP clients need one
spring-boot-starter-opentelemetryit sends traces and metrics with OpenTelemetry, and it has no Boot 3 starter
spring-boot-starter-webmvc-testit holds @WebMvcTest and MockMvc, in the package org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test
spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb-testit holds @DataMongoTest, in the package org.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.test
spring-boot-starter-security-testit holds jwt() and the other helpers of spring-security-test

The library adds the two security starters under their Boot 4 names:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client</artifactId>
</dependency>

The second <artifactId> is the Boot 4 name of the OAuth2 client starter. With the old name spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client, the build would still work in 4.1.2, but the starter is deprecated. For the general renames, see the section Starters. For a whole upgrade from Boot 3, see the chapter Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4.

Optional dependencies: test support without test librariestwist#

The platform ships test support, such as the annotation @PlatformWebMvcTest and ArchitectureRules. That code is in the library's main source, so it must compile against JUnit, Spring's test support and ArchUnit. But a service's production jar must never contain those libraries:

Shop.Platform.csproj
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="xunit.assert" Version="2.9.3" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
shop-platform/pom.xml
<!--
  Needed only by com.acme.platform.test. They are optional, so they never reach a
  service's production classpath. Services get them, test-scoped, from the parent POM.
-->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
// ...
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.tngtech.archunit</groupId>
    <artifactId>archunit</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

<optional>true</optional> marks a dependency that this project needs, but a project that uses it does not. The library compiles against ArchUnit. A service that depends on the library does not get ArchUnit from it. The run for this book showed both sides. In the library, ArchUnit is compile (optional). In the service, ArchUnit is test, because it comes from the parent's test dependencies.

PrivateAssets="all" has the same purpose in .NET. A run for this book packed a library with that attribute on xunit.assert. The dependency list of the packed file held its other reference, and not xunit.assert.

So the two parts work together. The library compiles its test code with optional dependencies. The parent gives each service the same libraries with the test scope. A service's test code can then use @PlatformWebMvcTest, and its production jar holds none of it.

The configuration processor, and the file it did not writetrap#

A developer types platform. in application.yml and expects the IDE to complete the platform's settings. An IDE does that from a file named META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json in the library's jar. The annotation processor spring-boot-configuration-processor writes the file while the library compiles. It reads every @ConfigurationProperties class.

The usual advice is to add the processor to the library as an optional dependency. The companion's library did that first, and the file was missing.

Gotcha

On JDK 26, the optional dependency alone wrote no metadata. A build of the companion's library on JDK 26.0.1, with maven-compiler-plugin 3.15.0, produced no spring-configuration-metadata.json. The build printed no warning about it. The same build with -Dmaven.compiler.proc=full wrote the file, with every platform.* key.

A run of javac 26.0.1 for this book showed the cause. With the processor only on the class path, javac did not run it. With the processor on the processor path, or with the option -proc:full, javac ran it and wrote the file. The research run for this book named the processor in the compiler's annotationProcessorPaths, which is the processor path, and the file appeared.

So the parent names the processor in the compiler's configuration, in its pluginManagement:

<!--
  Runs Spring Boot's configuration processor while the code compiles. It writes
  META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json from each @ConfigurationProperties
  class, so an IDE completes the keys. The processor must be named here: on JDK 26,
  a processor that is only a dependency did not run, and the file was missing.
  Boot manages the processor's version.
-->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <annotationProcessorPaths>
            <path>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
            </path>
        </annotationProcessorPaths>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
Reading the code
<annotationProcessorPaths>

This list names the annotation processors that the compiler runs, and where Maven finds them. A processor in this list is not a dependency of the project. So it never reaches a service, and the library needs no optional dependency for it.

<path>

Each processor is one path, with a group and an artifact. The path has no version, because Boot's parent manages the version of the processor. The build of the companion took that version.

The setting is in pluginManagement, so it applies to every child of the parent. After the change, the build wrote the file into the library's jar. It held 16 keys in 9 groups, from platform.logging to platform.security. The order service's jar got a file too, with the four keys of clients.stock. Without the file, a service still starts and binds every setting. Only the completion in the IDE is missing. Check the library's jar for the file after a change to the build.

The service POM: almost nothingtwist#

With the parent and the library in place, a service's POM is short. Here it is in full, without its header:

Order.Service.csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Shop.Platform" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
order-service/pom.xml
<!--
  The platform parent sets Java, the plugins and every dependency version.
  In this service's own repository, remove <relativePath>: the parent then comes from the
  company's artifact repository.
-->
<parent>
    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform-parent</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <relativePath>../shop-platform/shop-platform-parent/pom.xml</relativePath>
</parent>

<groupId>com.acme</groupId>
<artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

<dependencies>
    <!-- Everything cross-cutting. No version: the parent manages it. -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
        <artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>
    </dependency>

    <!-- Only what this service needs on top. Test libraries come from the parent. -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <!-- Builds the executable jar, with layers for the Docker image -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
Reading the code
<relativePath>../shop-platform/shop-platform-parent/pom.xml</relativePath>

In the companion, the parent is in a sibling folder, so this path points to it. In the service's own repository, the folder does not exist. So the line is removed, and Maven fetches the parent from the company's artifact repository.

<artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>

The one dependency that brings everything cross-cutting. Its version is managed in the parent.

<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>

The only extra starter. The reference feature caches its lookup lists, and no other service needs a cache yet. So the cache is in the service, not in the platform.

<artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>

This plugin repackages the jar in the phase package. The result is a Java archive (JAR) that java -jar starts. It holds the service's classes and every library. The library has no such plugin, because a library is not started on its own.

The C# pane is the project file from the run for this book. Its target framework came from a Directory.Build.props above it, and its version of Shop.Platform from a Directory.Packages.props. The Java pane needs more lines, because Maven names a parent by its coordinates, and the service must declare its own coordinates too.

The executable jar has layers. Libraries change rarely, so they are in their own layers, and Docker reuses them from its cache. The Dockerfile extracts the layers with java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --launcher. For the image, see the chapter Running locally and shipping. For executable jars in general, see the section The fat JAR.

The commandstwist#

The companion builds with Maven 3.9.16, and all its tests pass, the unit tests and the integration tests. These are the commands that it uses:

CommandWhereWhat it does
mvn verifythe companion's rootbuilds the platform and the service, and runs every *Test
mvn verify -Pitthe companion's rootalso runs every *IT, with MongoDB and an AWS emulator in Docker
mvn packageorder-servicebuilds the executable jar that the Dockerfile copies
mvn -pl order-service -am packagethe companion's rootbuilds the service and the modules it depends on, here the parent and the library
mvn installshop-platformputs the parent and the library into the local repository, so a service in another folder finds them

The Dockerfile states the build command in its first line:

# Build the jar first:  mvn package   (from the companion root: mvn -pl order-service -am package)

-pl order-service selects one module, and -am also builds the modules it needs. For both flags, see the section Command mapping.

The first build downloads every library and plugin. So it needs Maven Central, or a company repository that mirrors it. After that, the libraries are in ~/.m2/repository, and mvn -o builds offline. For a company repository, see the section Where artifacts come from.

Upgrading Spring Boot for every servicenew#

A new patch release of Spring Boot comes out. The shop has ten services. Without a shared parent, ten teams would each change a version, and some would forget. With the parent, the upgrade has one place to start. The parent's comment says so:

It sets the Java release, the build plugins and the version of every dependency.
A service never writes a version number itself. To upgrade Spring Boot for every service,
change the parent below and release a new platform version.

The words change the parent below mean the element that names spring-boot-starter-parent, version 4.1.2. The steps are these:

  1. The platform team changes the version of spring-boot-starter-parent in shop-platform-parent. It checks the versions of the libraries that Boot does not manage, such as Spring Modulith and springdoc, against the new Boot release.
  2. It builds the platform with mvn verify -Pit. The platform's own tests, and the wiring test of at least one service, show whether an auto-configuration changed.
  3. It releases a new platform version, such as 1.4.0, with upgrade notes.
  4. Each service changes the version in its <parent> element to 1.4.0. The library's version follows, because the parent manages it.
  5. Each service builds and runs its own tests, then ships.

The parent's version and the library's version are always the same. So a service changes one number, and it gets a matching parent and library. The rule of the shop is that a service stays at most one minor version behind. For the versioning rules, see the section Versions, and the rules for upgrading.

For a patch release of Boot, the change is usually the one version line. A minor release can rename a property or deprecate a class. A major release, such as Boot 3 to Boot 4, renames starters and packages. For that kind of upgrade, see the chapter Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4.

Compared with Directory.Build.props and NuGettwist#

Five .NET mechanisms each have a counterpart in the parent or the library. The match is close, but not exact:

.NETThe shop's buildWhat differs
Directory.Build.propsthe parent's properties and pluginsthe parent is published and named by coordinates, so it works across repositories
Directory.Packages.propsthe parent's dependencyManagementa Maven BOM imports a whole family of versions in one entry
a NuGet packagethe platform librarya library can bring auto-configuration, which runs without a line of startup code
a test project's PackageReference listthe parent's test dependenciesevery child inherits them with the test scope
PrivateAssets="all"<optional>true</optional>both keep a dependency to the project itself

The largest difference is the parent. A shared Directory.Build.props is found by its folder. A Maven parent is found by its version. A NuGet package can also add build settings to the projects that use it. Its files build/<package_id>.props and build/<package_id>.targets are imported into each such project. But NuGet's documentation says that such files must not set the properties and items that affect restore, such as TargetFramework and PackageVersion. A Maven parent may set the Java release and every managed version. So each service chooses the version of its build settings, as it chooses the version of a library. That is why an upgrade of Spring Boot is one release of the platform, and a change of one number in each service.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe parent declares the test libraries in <dependencies> with the test scope, and the library declares the same libraries as optional. Why both?
The library's main source holds test support, such as @PlatformWebMvcTest, so it must compile against the test libraries. The optional flag keeps them from reaching a service through the library. The parent then gives every service the same libraries with the test scope. So a service's tests can use the platform's test support, and its production jar holds no test library.
2
Two imported BOMs in dependencyManagement both manage the same artifact. Which version does a child get, and how do you choose another one?
The version from the BOM that is declared first. An entry written directly in the POM's own dependencyManagement wins over every import, so write one to settle the clash.
3
An expert asksWhy does the parent set <relativePath/> for Spring Boot's parent, when the service sets a real path for the shop's parent?
By default, Maven first looks for a parent at ../pom.xml. The shop's parent is in the platform's folder, whose pom.xml is the aggregator. That file is not the parent of Spring Boot, so the empty element switches the search off. In the companion, the service's parent is in a sibling folder, so the service names that path. In the service's own repository, the line is removed.
4
A developer has no Docker on their laptop. Which command gives them a full, green build, and which tests does it leave out?
mvn verify. It runs every *Test class with surefire. It leaves out the *IT classes, which run only with mvn verify -Pit, because the profile it adds failsafe.
5
TranslateWrite this central version as an entry of the shop's parent POM, so that a service can add the platform library with no version: 
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageVersion Include="Shop.Platform" Version="1.0.0" />
</ItemGroup>
<!-- The platform library itself -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>
    <version>${shop-platform.version}</version>
</dependency>

The entry is inside dependencyManagement, so it adds no dependency. It only gives a version to a shop-platform dependency that a child declares without one. The version is the property shop-platform.version.

Quick reference#

The managed versions of the shop's parent, as of October 2026:

LibraryVersionManaged by
Spring Boot4.1.2the parent's parent, spring-boot-starter-parent
Java release25the property java.version
Spring Modulith2.1.2spring-modulith-bom
Spring Cloud AWS4.1.0spring-cloud-aws-dependencies, plus one pinned artifact
Resilience4j2.4.0resilience4j-bom
ShedLock7.10.1shedlock-bom
springdoc-openapi3.2.0a pinned entry
ArchUnit1.5.1a pinned entry
json-schema-validator3.0.8a pinned entry
openapi-generator-maven-plugin7.26.0the property openapi-generator.version, used in the profile contract-first
Testcontainers2.0.5Spring Boot
the platform librarythe same as the parenta pinned entry, with the property shop-platform.version

Maven in depth: resolution and the lifecycle#

The build and the model · Chapter 06· 19 min read

This chapter follows mvn verify from the shell to the jar, a Java archive (JAR). It shows how Maven turns the command into plugin goals. It shows how Maven builds the Project Object Model (POM) it really uses, and how it chooses one version of each library. Then one added dependency breaks the order service at run time.

KindC#JavaNote
twistdotnet build runs a fixed MSBuild sequencemvn verify runs the phases of the default lifecycle, in order, up to verifyeach phase runs the plugin goals bound to it, and a phase with no goals does nothing Why
twista target in the project file, or in Directory.Build.targetsa plugin execution bound to a phasethe goal runs in that phase of every build, after the goals that the packaging binds Why
twistthe project after the SDK and Directory.Build.props are appliedthe effective POM, printed by help:effective-pomthe parent chain, the imported bills of materials and the active profiles are folded in, and nothing else counts Why
trapNuGet takes the lowest version that satisfies every referenceMaven takes the nearest declaration, and the first one at equal deptha direct dependency on an old version wins over a library's need for a newer one, with no warning Why
twistNuGet warns of a downgrade with NU1605nothing warns, unless an enforcer rule runsthe build is green, the tests may be green, and the mismatch shows at run time Why
twistDirectory.Packages.props, with versions managed centrallydependencyManagement in the parent POMa managed version beats mediation, and a direct version beats the managed one Why
twistthe NuGet global-packages folder and NuGet.Config~/.m2/repository and settings.xmlthe local repository caches every download, and a mirror in settings.xml sends every request to the team's repository manager Why
newno equivalentNoSuchMethodError, at the first callthe compiler checked one version of a class, and the runtime linked another Why
twista .dll in bin/ with its dependencies beside itBOOT-INF/lib inside the repackaged jarthe Spring Boot plugin's repackage goal puts every dependency jar inside the jar, with an index and layers Why
twistpackages.lock.json, checked with restore --locked-modeproject.build.outputTimestamp, and exact versionswith the property set, two builds of one commit give the same bytes, in Maven 3.9 Why

Scene 1: the command becomes goalstwist#

For the basics of a POM against a .csproj, see the chapter Maven vs csproj. That chapter also gives the first look at two versions of one library. The shop's services share a platform library. For the parent POM of the shop, see the chapter The build: a parent POM and a platform library. This chapter starts where those two stop, and it follows a real build. The numbers and the output lines come from one run on 26 October 2026, with Maven 3.9.16, on the author's laptop. Maven ran on Java Development Kit (JDK) 26.0.1. The run script is companion/runs/maven/run.sh.

The service is built with one command. In .NET, three commands do the same work:

C#, the shell
dotnet restore
dotnet build --configuration Release
dotnet test --no-build
Java, the shell
mvn verify

mvn verify names a phase, not a task. Maven has a list of phases called the default lifecycle, and the command runs every phase from the first one up to the named one. The phases that matter for the service are these, in order:

PhaseWhat it means, in Maven's wordsWhat ran in the service's build
validatevalidate the project is correct and all necessary information is availablenothing bound
compilecompile the source code of the projectcompiler:compile
testrun tests using a suitable unit testing frameworksurefire:test, the fast tests
packagetake the compiled code and package it in its distributable format, such as a JARjar:jar, then spring-boot:repackage
integration-testprocess and deploy the package if necessary into an environment where integration tests can be runnothing, unless the profile it is active
verifyrun any checks to verify the package is valid and meets quality criteriafailsafe:verify, with the profile it
installinstall the package into the local repository, for use as a dependency in other projects locallynot reached

A phase does nothing by itself. Each phase runs the plugin goals bound to it, and a phase with no goals does not execute. The packaging decides the first set of bindings. For the packaging jar, Maven 3.9 binds the resources, compiler, surefire, jar, install and deploy plugins to their phases. The POM adds more. The run ran mvn package and printed one line for each goal, and this is the list for the order service, in order:

dependency:3.10.0:properties (default)
resources:3.5.0:resources (default-resources)
compiler:3.15.0:compile (default-compile)
resources:3.5.0:testResources (default-testResources)
compiler:3.15.0:testCompile (default-testCompile)
surefire:3.5.6:test (default-test)
jar:3.5.1:jar (default-jar)
spring-boot:4.1.2:repackage (repackage)

Each line names the plugin, its version, the goal, and the execution id in brackets. An id of the form default-compile means the packaging bound the goal. The first line, dependency:3.10.0:properties, is a goal that the parent POM bound. The last line is the Spring Boot plugin's repackage goal, which the starter parent binds with the execution id repackage. The failsafe plugin does not appear. It runs the integration tests, and the parent binds it only inside a profile:

<!-- mvn verify runs the fast tests only: *Test.java. The *IT.java tests need Docker. -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <argLine>@{argLine} -javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}</argLine>
        <excludes>
            <exclude>**/*IT.java</exclude>
        </excludes>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
Reading the code
maven-surefire-plugin

Surefire is the plugin that runs the unit tests, in the phase test. By default it includes every class whose name starts with Test. It also includes the classes whose names end with Test, Tests or TestCase. The parent excludes the *IT.java classes, which are the integration tests.

${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}

A property that the dependency:properties goal sets. The goal runs before the other goals, as the list above shows. Its value is the path of the jar of Mockito, the library the tests use for their mocks. The test JVM, the Java Virtual Machine that runs the tests, loads Mockito as an agent from that path. This is why that goal is the first line of the list above.

In .NET, the sequence is also fixed, and it is MSBuild's. A target in the project file, or in Directory.Build.targets, adds work to it. In Maven, the matching idea is a plugin execution bound to a phase. The parent binds one this way:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-dependency-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>properties</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

The execution names a goal, properties, and no phase. When the phase is left out, the goal's own default phase is used. The goals of the packaging run first in a phase, and the goals of the POM run after them, in the order of the POM.

What you can see here#

The --- plugin:goal (id) @ module --- lines of any build, which say what ran and in which order. mvn help:describe -Dcmd=verify says which goals a phase would run. And mvn -X, the debug output, prints the configuration of each goal as Maven saw it. It is long. Pipe it to a file.

What you can hook here#

A plugin execution, with a goal and optionally a phase, in the parent POM for every service or in one service's POM. Give every execution an id, because a child POM overrides a parent's execution with the same id and merges one with a different id. And give every plugin a version, in pluginManagement of the parent, so that two machines run the same plugin code. The Spring Boot starter parent already does this for the plugins it knows.

Scene 2: the POM that Maven really usestwist#

Before any goal runs, Maven builds one model of the project. It is called the effective POM. It starts from the Super POM, which Maven ships, and layers each parent on top, then the project's own POM, then the active profiles. Properties are replaced with their values. For the order service the chain has five layers:

LayerWhat it adds
the Super POM, inside Maventhe repository Maven Central, and the standard directories such as src/main/java and target
spring-boot-dependencies 4.1.2, the parent of the starter parent, a bill of materials (BOM)the version of every library that Spring Boot manages, such as commons-lang3 3.20.0
spring-boot-starter-parent 4.1.2the compiler settings, the resource filtering, and the repackage execution
shop-platform-parentthe test libraries, the Mockito agent, the surefire excludes, and the profile it
order-service/pom.xmlthe platform, the cache starter and the Spring Boot plugin

The effective POM is what help:effective-pom prints. The run wrote it to a file and searched it for commons. The property and the managed version both came from the bill of materials (BOM) of Spring Boot, three layers up:

<commons-lang3.version>3.20.0</commons-lang3.version>
...
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
    <artifactId>commons-lang3</artifactId>
    <version>3.20.0</version>
  </dependency>

The first line is the property commons-lang3.version, and the dependency block uses it. The second block is inside dependencyManagement. A managed version is not a dependency. It is the version to use if that library appears, from any direction. The next scene shows how far that reaches.

In .NET, the SDK and Directory.Build.props play the same role as the Super POM and the parent. MSBuild can write its evaluated model to one file, with dotnet msbuild -preprocess:out.xml. Maven writes the whole model on request too. The chapter on the parent POM reads one in the section Compared with Directory.Build.props and NuGet.

What you can see here#

mvn help:effective-pom -Doutput=effective.xml writes the model to a file, and -Dverbose=true adds a comment to each element that says which file it came from. mvn help:active-profiles lists the profiles that are active and where each was defined.

What you can hook here#

A property, which any layer can set and a lower layer can override. The Spring Boot parent exposes most of its versions as properties. So <commons-lang3.version> in the service's POM would change the managed version for the whole tree. And a profile, which adds plugins, dependencies or properties when it is active. The parent's it profile is the model.

Scene 3: the version that got intrap#

Now the story. A developer adds Apache Commons Text to the order service, to escape a string for a log line. The library is not managed by Spring Boot, so the version is written in the POM. They also add Commons Lang, because a colleague once said that Commons Text needs it, and they take the version that another project uses. Two dependencies, both with versions:

<!-- the conflict: commons-text needs a newer commons-lang3 than the one declared below -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
    <artifactId>commons-text</artifactId>
    <version>1.12.0</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
    <artifactId>commons-lang3</artifactId>
    <version>3.9</version>
</dependency>

The first dependency block asks for Commons Text 1.12.0, and the second asks for Commons Lang 3.9. The run added these two blocks to the service's POM on a branch made for the run, and the comment already states the ending. Commons Text 1.12.0 was built against Commons Lang 3.14.0. The service now declares Commons Lang 3.9. Maven must choose one version, because one jar of a library goes on the classpath. Its rule is called dependency mediation, and the guide states it in one sentence. Maven picks the nearest definition, the version closest to the project in the tree of dependencies, and at equal depth the first declaration wins.

The dependency tree shows the choice. The run printed it with -Dverbose=true, which keeps the versions that lost:

[INFO] +- org.apache.commons:commons-text:jar:1.12.0:compile
[INFO] |  \- (org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:jar:3.20.0:compile - version managed from 3.14.0; omitted for conflict with 3.9)
[INFO] +- org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:jar:3.9:compile (scope not updated to compile)

The first line is the commons-text node. Read the middle line slowly, because three rules act in it. Commons Text asked for 3.14.0. The BOM of Spring Boot manages Commons Lang at 3.20.0, and a managed version beats mediation, so the request became 3.20.0. Then the service's own declaration of 3.9 beat the managed version. A direct declaration is nearer than anything, and a direct version beats the managed one. The line is in brackets because the node lost. The last line is the version on the classpath, 3.9.

Here are the three rules, in the order Maven applies them:

RuleWhat it saysIn the run
mediationthe nearest definition wins, and at equal depth the first declaration3.9, declared in the service, is at depth one, and 3.14.0 is at depth two
dependency managementa managed version replaces the version a transitive dependency asked forthe BOM turned 3.14.0 into 3.20.0, which is still at depth two
direct declarationthe current POM's own version beats its parent's managed version3.9 in the service beats 3.20.0 from the BOM

NuGet solves the same problem with other rules, and a C# developer's instinct comes from them. NuGet takes the lowest applicable version, the lowest that satisfies every reference. A direct reference wins over a transitive one too, and NuGet calls that rule direct-dependency-wins. But when that rule lowers a version that a library asked for, NuGet logs the warning NU1605 and says that a version was downgraded. Maven printed no warning about the version, and the compile step was green. One test failed later, in scene 5.

Nothing in the build knew that Commons Text would ask Commons Lang for a method that 3.9 does not have. The compiler checked the service's own code against 3.9, and the service's own code calls nothing that is missing. Commons Text was compiled long ago, against 3.14.0, and Maven does not compile a dependency again. The mismatch is inside a jar that nobody compiled today.

What you can see here#

mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose=true, and the words in brackets. The phrase "omitted for conflict with" names a loser, and the version after it is the winner. The phrase "version managed from" names a request that the BOM changed. A second goal, mvn dependency:analyze, reports the libraries the code uses without declaring them and the ones it declares without using them. On the service it listed 45 used but undeclared libraries, such as spring-web and spring-data-mongodb, because the platform brings them in. That is the design, not a fault, so the goal is for reading and not for failing the build.

What you can hook here#

Three hooks, in order of preference. A version in dependencyManagement of the parent, which is how Spring Boot's own BOM works. The service then declares no version at all, and every service of the shop gets the same one. An <exclusions> block on a dependency, which removes one transitive dependency from under it, when a library drags in a jar you have replaced. And the enforcer plugin, which turns the silent choice into a failed build. Its rule requireUpperBoundDeps fails when the chosen version is lower than another version in the tree, which is exactly this scene. Its rule dependencyConvergence fails when two paths reach different versions at all. The parent POM of the shop has no enforcer rule yet. Add one, and the branch of this chapter fails in the phase validate, before a class is compiled.

Scene 4: where the jars come fromtwist#

When Commons Lang 3.9 is not on the machine yet, Maven downloads it once and keeps it. Every download is saved in the local repository, ~/.m2/repository, in a folder per group, artifact and version. The run listed the laptop's folder for Commons Lang, and it held twelve versions:

~/.m2/repository/org/apache/commons/commons-lang3/
3.7  3.8.1  3.9  3.10  3.11  3.12.0  3.14.0  3.16.0  3.17.0  3.18.0  3.20.0  3.21.0

The path is the group org.apache.commons and the artifact commons-lang3, then one folder for each version. The local repository is a cache of downloads, and it also holds what mvn install built on this machine. Maven downloads an artifact when the local copy is missing. For a release version, that happens once. A release version never changes, so a second download is never needed. For a SNAPSHOT version, Maven also checks the remote repository for a newer copy, by default once a day. The shop's own modules are 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT, which means the moving development version.

Where does a download come from? The Super POM declares one repository, Maven Central, at https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2. A POM can add repositories, and so can settings.xml. Maven queries them in a fixed order. The settings files come first, then the POM and its parents, then the POMs of the dependencies on the path to the artifact. A team with a repository manager sends every request to it with one mirror in ~/.m2/settings.xml:

<settings>
  <mirrors>
    <mirror>
      <id>shop-repository-manager</id>
      <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
      <url>https://repo.shop.example/maven2</url>
    </mirror>
  </mirrors>
</settings>

The mirrorOf value * matches every repository id, so the manager sees every request and forwards each one to Maven Central. The Maven documentation calls a repository manager an essential best practice for any significant use of Maven. The <servers> block of the same file holds the credentials, keyed by the mirror's id.

Beside each cached file, Maven's resolver keeps a small file named _remote.repositories. It says which repository the file came from. If a later build does not know that repository, the resolver treats the cached file as absent and downloads it again. This can cause a download that seems not to be needed.

NuGet has the same shape with other names. The global-packages folder, ~/.nuget/packages, is the cache, with one folder per library and version. NuGet.Config holds the sources, and the files are layered from the machine to the solution folder. A difference is in the project file. A NuGet source list is in the config files only. A Maven repository can be declared in a POM, and then every project that depends on that POM queries that repository too.

What you can see here#

The folder ~/.m2/repository, and the versions in it. mvn -o builds offline and fails if something is missing, which is the quickest test of whether the cache is complete. mvn help:effective-settings prints the merged settings, with the mirrors and the servers.

What you can hook here#

A mirror, as above. A repository policy on a repository, which sets the update policy for snapshots to always, daily, never or an interval in minutes. And the flags -U, which forces a check for updated snapshots, and -nsu, which forbids one.

Scene 5: the method that is not therenew#

The branch compiles. Then the tests run, and one test fails. It is not a test of the log line, and not a test of anything that names Commons Text. It is the contract test of the OpenAPI document, which starts the web layer and fetches /v3/api-docs:

[ERROR] com.acme.orderservice.contracts.OpenApiContractTest.theCommittedContractMatchesTheCode -- Time elapsed: 0.584 s <<< FAILURE!
[ERROR] Tests run: 112, Failures: 1, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD FAILURE

The console names the failed test, theCommittedContractMatchesTheCode. The surefire report of the test has the line that matters, java.lang.AssertionError: Status expected:<200> but was:<500>. The test asked for the document and got a 500. Nothing in the test names the two new libraries. The run built the jar without the tests, started the service, and requested the document with curl. The service's error handler logged the cause:

ERROR [nio-8080-exec-2] c.a.p.core.error.GlobalExceptionHandler  : Unexpected error
jakarta.servlet.ServletException: Handler dispatch failed: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: org/apache/commons/lang3/Strings
Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: org/apache/commons/lang3/Strings
	at org.springdoc.api.AbstractOpenApiResource.calculatePath(AbstractOpenApiResource.java:697) ~[springdoc-openapi-starter-common-3.2.0.jar:3.2.0]

The frame below the Caused by line is inside springdoc, the library that writes the OpenAPI document. Springdoc uses a class called Strings from Commons Lang. The jar of Commons Lang 3.9 has no such class. Springdoc asked for 3.20.0, as the tree shows. The Javadoc of NoClassDefFoundError says that the JVM tried to load the definition of a class and no definition could be found. The developer added a dependency for a log line, and broke a library they never touched. Then the run placed one order. The order was accepted:

POST /orders -> 201

The 201 says that the order was created. The request succeeded because the new line of code is not on the request's path. It is in OrderMetrics, the listener that counts placed orders, and that listener runs after the transaction commits, on another thread. Less than a second later the log held this:

ERROR [task-1] .a.i.SimpleAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler : Unexpected exception occurred invoking async method: void com.acme.orderservice.order.application.OrderMetrics.on(com.acme.orderservice.order.domain.event.OrderPlaced)

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'org.apache.commons.lang3.Range org.apache.commons.lang3.Range.of(java.lang.Comparable, java.lang.Comparable)'
	at org.apache.commons.text.translate.NumericEntityEscaper.<init>(NumericEntityEscaper.java:97) ~[commons-text-1.12.0.jar:1.12.0]
	at org.apache.commons.text.translate.NumericEntityEscaper.between(NumericEntityEscaper.java:59) ~[commons-text-1.12.0.jar:1.12.0]
	at org.apache.commons.text.StringEscapeUtils.<clinit>(StringEscapeUtils.java:270) ~[commons-text-1.12.0.jar:1.12.0]
	at com.acme.orderservice.order.application.OrderMetrics.on(OrderMetrics.java:45) ~[classes/:na]

Read the stack from the bottom. The listener called StringEscapeUtils of Commons Text for the first time. The JVM initialised that class, which is the <clinit> frame, and the class built its escapers. One escaper called Range.of in Commons Lang. The JVM looked for that method in the Commons Lang on the classpath, version 3.9. It found no method with that name and those parameters. So it threw NoSuchMethodError. The Javadoc of that error says it plainly. The error is normally caught by the compiler, and it occurs at run time only if the definition of a class has incompatibly changed. Here the definition changed backwards, from 3.14.0 to 3.9.

javap proves it. The run disassembled the Range class from both jars, with -p so that every member shows, and kept the static factory methods:

== commons-lang3 3.9
  public static <T extends java.lang.Comparable<T>> org.apache.commons.lang3.Range<T> between(T, T);
  public static <T> org.apache.commons.lang3.Range<T> between(T, T, java.util.Comparator<T>);
== commons-lang3 3.20.0
  public static <T extends java.lang.Comparable<? super T>> org.apache.commons.lang3.Range<T> between(T, T);
  public static <T> org.apache.commons.lang3.Range<T> between(T, T, java.util.Comparator<T>);
  public static <T extends java.lang.Comparable<? super T>> org.apache.commons.lang3.Range<T> of(T, T);
  public static <T> org.apache.commons.lang3.Range<T> of(T, T, java.util.Comparator<T>);

Version 3.9 has between. Version 3.20.0 has between and of. Commons Text 1.12.0 calls of, so it needs a Commons Lang from the release that added it. Commons Text 1.12.0 asks for 3.14.0, so 3.14.0 or a newer version should have the method.

Two things make this failure worse than a crash. The order was placed, so nobody saw an error. And the listener that failed was a Spring Modulith listener, part of the outbox that the chapter Publishing events: the outbox explains. Spring Modulith writes down each delivery, and a delivery that fails stays incomplete in the registry. It is retried only if something resubmits it. The run read the registry in MongoDB afterwards, and the publication was still there, with completionAttempts: 1. The counter is never incremented, the registry grows, and the log of a background thread is the only place where the cause is written.

The same conflict, with one class and a main method of about twenty lines, is in the lab project of this chapter's run. Its POM declares the same two dependencies, and its one class calls five methods of Commons Text in turn:

substitute: ok -> the order service
wrap: ok -> a sentence that is\nlong enough to be\nwrapped
json: java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'org.apache.commons.lang3.Range org.apache.commons.lang3.Range.of(java.lang.Comparable, java.lang.Comparable)'
camel: ok -> orderPlaced
levenshtein: ok -> 2

The line that starts with json is the call to StringEscapeUtils. Four of the five calls work. Only the one that touches StringEscapeUtils fails. A test suite that happens to use the other four is green. That is why the rule is not "run the tests". The rule is "read the tree".

What you can see here#

A jar, or JAR, is one file that holds many classes. The first NoSuchMethodError or NoClassDefFoundError in a log is the place to start. Spring Boot adds the jar names in square brackets at the end of each stack frame. The two jars that disagree are usually both in the first ten frames. Then javap -p on the class, from each jar, and jar tf to list what a jar holds. The chapter Two JARs, one class covers the case where two jars hold the same class.

What you can hook here#

Nothing at run time. The fix is in the build, in scene 3. Remove the direct declaration of Commons Lang, so that the managed version 3.20.0 wins, and let the enforcer refuse the next one.

Scene 6: the jartwist#

The last goal of the build was spring-boot:repackage. It takes the jar that jar:jar made, which holds only the service's classes, and builds the jar that java -jar runs. The original is kept beside it with the suffix .original. The run listed the Commons jars inside the result:

BOOT-INF/lib/commons-text-1.12.0.jar
BOOT-INF/lib/commons-lang3-3.9.jar

Every dependency jar is inside the jar, under BOOT-INF/lib. The entries are stored and not compressed, so that the launcher can read a class without unpacking the file. The service's own classes are under BOOT-INF/classes. The manifest names Spring Boot's JarLauncher as the main class, and the service's application class as the start class. Two index files are beside them. classpath.idx gives the order of the jars on the classpath. layers.idx groups the content into layers, so that a container image can keep the dependency layer from one build to the next. The chapter The Dockerfile: a layered jar uses the layers. The chapter Running with -cp or -jar explains the plain classpath that the launcher replaces.

In .NET, dotnet publish writes the assembly and every dependency as separate files in one folder. The Java jar holds the same set in one file, and the version that scene 3 chose is the file in it. There is no second copy of Commons Lang that could serve instead.

What you can see here#

jar tf order-service-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar lists every entry, and java -Djarmode=tools -jar order-service-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar list-layers lists the layers. The jar on the classpath at run time is the one in BOOT-INF/lib. When the tree and the jar disagree, the jar is what ran.

What you can hook here#

The layers configuration of the plugin, which can split the application's own modules into a layer of their own. And the mainClass parameter, when a jar holds two classes with a main method and the plugin's guess is wrong.

Scene 7: the same bytes twicetwist#

A build is reproducible when the same source, the same build environment and the same instructions give the same bytes, every time, for everyone. Maven 3.9 can do this, but it must be asked. One property in the parent POM switches the plugins into reproducible mode:

<properties>
    <project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-10-26T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>
</properties>

The property is project.build.outputTimestamp, and its value is a date and time in UTC. With the property set, the jar plugin and the Spring Boot plugin write that timestamp into every entry instead of the clock. The Spring Boot plugin also sorts the classpath index. Maven 3.10.0 turns this mode on by default, with no property. The guide adds a second condition that belongs to this chapter. A reproducible build uses no version ranges, because a range resolves to whatever is newest on the day.

The test is two builds. mvn clean install, then mvn clean verify artifact:compare, which compares the second build with the first and writes a .buildcompare file. The guide warns that this local test does not yet prove that a third party gets the same bytes. The environment can leak into the build. It proves that the build does not depend on the clock.

NuGet's answer to the version half of this question is packages.lock.json. With the lock file committed and restore --locked-mode, a restore either gets the exact versions in the file or fails. Maven has no lock file. Its exact versions, its managed versions and its ban on ranges do the same work.

Pragmatic choice: No reproducible-build property in the parent yet

The strict rule. A build that ships to production is reproducible, so that a jar can be rebuilt from its commit and compared.

What we do. The shop's parent POM does not set project.build.outputTimestamp, and the enforcer plugin is not in it.

Why. The parent was written for the chapters on the service, and each chapter added only what its story needed. This chapter is the first that needs them.

When to stop. Before the first release that a team must be able to rebuild from a tag. Add the property and the two enforcer rules of scene 3 in one change. Keep the branch of this chapter as the test that the rules work.

What you can see here#

The .buildcompare file after artifact:compare, which lists each artifact as ok or different. And mvn artifact:check-buildplan, which names any plugin in the build that is too old to be reproducible.

What you can hook here#

The property above, in the parent, bumped by the release process. The enforcer rules of scene 3, for the versions. And pluginManagement with a version for every plugin, so that the build plan itself does not drift.

Check yourself
1
A library you add asks for version 3.14.0 of another library. Your POM declares version 3.9 of that library directly. Which version goes on the classpath, and does Maven warn?
Version 3.9. The direct declaration is the nearest definition, and it also beats a version that the parent's dependencyManagement sets. Maven prints no warning. The dependency:tree -Dverbose=true output shows the loser in brackets with "omitted for conflict with 3.9".
2
An expert asksWhy can a build compile and pass its tests, and still throw NoSuchMethodError at run time?
The compiler checks only the project's own source against the jars on the classpath. A dependency jar was compiled earlier, against the versions it declared, and Maven never compiles it again. If mediation puts an older version of one of those jars on the classpath, the call inside the dependency breaks. It links against a class that no longer has the method. The error appears at the first call, and only if a test walks that path.
3
TranslateTranslate this central version and its reference. The version is set once for the repository, and the project names the library without a version. 
<!-- Directory.Packages.props -->
<PackageVersion Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.0.3" />
<!-- the project file -->
<PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" />
A managed version in the parent POM, and a dependency without a version in the project. 
<!-- the parent POM -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>2.21</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
<!-- the service's POM -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
</dependency>
The managed version also replaces the version that any transitive dependency asks for, which Directory.Packages.props does only with transitive-pinning switched on.
4
Which goal turns the plain jar of the service into the jar that java -jar runs, and where do the dependency jars go?
The Spring Boot plugin's repackage goal, which the starter parent binds with the execution id repackage. It runs after jar:jar in the phase package. The dependency jars go inside the jar, under BOOT-INF/lib, stored without compression, and BOOT-INF/classpath.idx gives their order.

The domain model in plain Java#

The build and the model · Chapter 07· 46 min read· Quick reference

The order feature keeps its rules in plain Java classes that import nothing from Spring. A few base classes from the platform library give each aggregate its identity, its version and its list of events. This chapter reads the Order aggregate line by line. It covers value objects, typed IDs, placing and loading, the injected clock, exceptions by kind, and the Java features that the code uses.

The domain package: plain Java, and the base classesnew#

A rule such as "an order ships only when it is paid" should be easy to test. It should also stay the same when the service changes its database or its framework version. So the order feature keeps its rules in classes that depend on no framework at all. This is the full style of Domain-Driven Design (DDD) in the order service. This chapter starts from the code. For why the order is an aggregate, see the chapter Finding the aggregates. For why only the order feature uses this full style, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The domain of the order feature is one package with five sub-packages:

order/domain/
  model/        Order, OrderLine, the typed IDs, the value objects, the two status enums
  event/        OrderPlaced, LinePicked, OrderShipped, OrderCancelled, PaymentRecorded
  exception/    one exception class for each broken rule
  repository/   OrderRepository, the port for storing orders
  service/      ShippingPolicy, the one rule that needs two aggregates

The model package holds the aggregate and its values. Every class in these packages uses only the Java standard library and the platform's own domain package. The platform library describes that package in its package-info.java file. A file of this name holds the documentation of a whole package:

/**
 * The building blocks of a domain model, in plain Java.
 *
 * <p>Nothing in this package imports Spring, MongoDB or Jackson. A service's {@code domain}
 * packages may use these classes and still stay plain Java. The classes hold no business
 * concepts: they remove code that every aggregate would otherwise repeat, such as equality by
 * identity, the version for optimistic locking, the list of raised events and simple checks.
 */
package com.acme.platform.domain;

The comment of com.acme.platform.domain names the contract. The base classes remove code that every aggregate would otherwise repeat. They hold no business concept, such as an order or a payment. An architecture rule of the platform makes the build fail when a domain class imports a framework:

/** A {@code domain} package uses no framework, no adapter and no other layer. */
public static ArchRule domainIsPlainJava() {
    return noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage(
                    "org.springframework..", "com.mongodb..", "org.bson..", "jakarta..",
                    "tools.jackson..", "com.fasterxml..", "io.awspring..",
                    "..application..", "..api..", "..persistence..", "..client..", "..messaging..",
                    "com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")
            .as("A domain package is plain Java");
}
Reading the code
noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")

This is ArchUnit, a test library that reads compiled classes. The pattern ..domain.. matches every package with domain in its name, in every feature.

"org.springframework..", "com.mongodb..", "org.bson..", "jakarta..",

A domain class may not use Spring, the MongoDB driver or any Jakarta API. So a domain class cannot carry @Document, @Component or a validation annotation. No domain class is a Spring bean.

"..application..", "..api..", "..persistence..", "..client..", "..messaging..",

A domain class may not use the layers around it either. The application layer uses the domain, and never the other way round.

"com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")

The platform's other packages hold Spring code, so the domain may not use them. Only com.acme.platform.domain is allowed.

The test ArchitectureTest.domainIsPlainJava calls this rule. For the other rules and how a service runs them, see the chapter Testing in depth.

The platform's domain package holds these building blocks. The sections below show each one where the order uses it:

Building blockJava typeWhat it gives each aggregate
AggregateRoot<ID>abstract classthe version for optimistic locking, and the list of raised events
Entity<ID>abstract classequality by class and ID
Identifierabstract classthe UUID check, equality and toString of a typed ID
ValueObjectinterface with no methodsno code, because it only marks the intent for readers and for architecture tests
DomainEventinterfacea time on every event
DomainEventPublisherinterface, a portthe way events leave the use case, which the outbox implements
Repository<A, ID>interface, a portfindById, save and exists, typed for one aggregate
Guardfinal class with static methodschecks for null, blank text, length, format, range and size
PageQuery and PageResult<T>recordspaging without the Page and Pageable types of Spring Data
DomainException and its three kindsa sealed exception classthe choice of the HTTP status

An interface that the domain declares and an outer layer implements is called a port. The class that implements a port is called an adapter. A design built from ports and adapters is called hexagonal architecture. For ports and adapters, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

Pragmatic choice: Base classes from a shared library in the domain

The strict rule. The domain depends on nothing outside itself. Each service writes its own base classes, or none.

What we do. Every full-style domain extends the classes of com.acme.platform.domain. That package is plain Java, and an architecture rule keeps it plain.
