Why. Equality by ID, the version, the event list and the value checks are the same in every service. Written once, they are tested once, and every service behaves the same way.

When to stop. Stop when the shared package gains a business concept, such as a Money class, or a framework type. Stop also when a change to it forces every service to upgrade at once. Then move the concept into the service that owns it.

Entity: identity, written oncetwist#

C# 12
public abstract class Entity<TId> where TId : Identifier
{
    protected Entity(TId id)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(id);
        Id = id;
    }

    public TId Id { get; }
}
The platform library
public abstract class Entity<ID extends Identifier> {

    private final ID id;

    protected Entity(ID id) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
    }

    public ID id() {
        return id;
    }
Reading the code
public abstract class Entity<ID extends Identifier> {

The type parameter ID must be an Identifier or a subclass of it. The C# form writes this as where TId : Identifier. Java writes the bound inside the angle brackets, with extends. For bounds, see the section Declaration.

protected Entity(ID id) {

Only a subclass can call a protected constructor. Code in the same package can call it too, because protected in Java includes the package. For the access levels, see the section The mapping.

this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");

Objects.requireNonNull is in java.util.Objects. It returns the value, or throws NullPointerException with the message id. So an entity always has an ID.

public ID id() {

The accessor has no get prefix, as in a record. The whole domain uses this style. For the naming rules, see the section The names are the contract.

The class also defines equals and hashCode by class and ID. Each one is a final method, so no subclass can override it. In C#, a method can be overridden only when it is virtual. In Java, every method can be overridden unless it is final. For this rule, see the section Overriding needs no keyword. For the code of equals, see the section Inside the aggregate: entities and value objects.

AggregateRoot: the version and the eventsnew#

Every aggregate needs two things that have nothing to do with its rules. Storage needs the version for optimistic locking. The use case needs the domain events that a change raised. If each aggregate kept these itself, each one could get them slightly wrong. So the platform keeps them in one base class:

/**
 * The base class of an aggregate root: the only object of an aggregate that outside code may
 * hold. Every change to the aggregate goes through the root, which checks the rules.
 *
 * <p>The root carries two things for the layers around it. The first is the version, which
 * optimistic locking needs: the version comes from storage and goes back to storage unchanged,
 * and no rule ever reads it. The second is the list of domain events the root raised. The
 * application service pulls the events after saving and publishes them in the same transaction.
 *
 * @param <ID> the typed identifier of the aggregate
 */
public abstract class AggregateRoot<ID extends Identifier> extends Entity<ID> {

    private final Long version;
    private final List<DomainEvent> events = new ArrayList<>();

    /**
     * Creates the root.
     *
     * @param id      the identity
     * @param version the stored version, or {@code null} for an aggregate that was never saved
     */
    protected AggregateRoot(ID id, Long version) {
        super(id);
        this.version = version;
    }

    /** Records an event. A subclass calls this in the method that changed its state. */
    protected final void raise(DomainEvent event) {
        events.add(event);
    }

    /** Returns the raised events and clears the list, so a second call returns an empty list. */
    public final List<DomainEvent> pullEvents() {
        List<DomainEvent> raised = List.copyOf(events);
        events.clear();
        return raised;
    }

    /**
     * Returns the stored version. Only persistence uses it.
     *
     * <p>The version is final. Saving creates a new instance with the new version (see
     * {@link Repository#save}), so the instance you saved keeps the old one.
     */
    public final Long version() {
        return version;
    }
}
Reading the code
public abstract class AggregateRoot<ID extends Identifier> extends Entity<ID> {

A root is an entity, so it inherits equality by ID. The bound on ID is repeated, because Entity accepts only an Identifier.

private final Long version;

The type is Long, the object form of long, so it can be null. A null version means that the aggregate was never saved. The field is final, so the aggregate never changes its own version.

private final List<DomainEvent> events = new ArrayList<>();

The empty angle brackets are called the diamond. The compiler takes the type argument from the declared type, List<DomainEvent>.

protected final void raise(DomainEvent event) {

protected lets only subclasses record an event. final stops a subclass from replacing the method. So a subclass can add an event, but it cannot hide one.

List<DomainEvent> raised = List.copyOf(events);

List.copyOf returns a copy that nobody can change. The method then clears its own list. So each event leaves the aggregate once.

public final Long version() {

Only the persistence adapter reads the version. No rule reads it.

The test of the base class shows both parts:

@Test
void pullEventsReturnsTheRaisedEventsAndClearsThem() {
    Thing thing = new Thing();
    thing.doSomething();

    assertThat(thing.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new ThingHappened(Instant.EPOCH));
    assertThat(thing.pullEvents()).isEmpty();
}

@Test
void aNewAggregateHasNoVersion() {
    assertThat(new Thing().version()).isNull();
}

The first test raises one event. The first call of pullEvents returns it. The second call returns an empty list. The second test shows that a new aggregate has no version.

Optimistic locking needs the version that was loaded. The adapter sends that version back with the save, and storage refuses the save if the stored version has moved on. So the version goes from storage, through the aggregate, back to storage, and nothing in between reads it. For how storage checks it, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB. For what the use case does with the events, see the section Domain events: collected by the aggregate.

Typed IDs: Identifier and its subclassesnew#

An order ID and a line ID are both universally unique identifiers (UUIDs). A method that takes two strings accepts them in the wrong order, and nothing warns you. A typed ID makes that mistake a compiler error. For the two compiler errors, in C# and in Java, see the section Typed IDs inside the aggregate. This section shows the base class that every typed ID extends:

public abstract class Identifier implements ValueObject {

    private static final Pattern UUID_FORMAT =
            Pattern.compile("^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$");

    private final String value;

    /**
     * Checks and stores the value.
     *
     * @param value     the UUID as text
     * @param fieldName the name a client sees in the error, for example {@code orderId}
     */
    protected Identifier(String value, String fieldName) {
        String normalised = value == null ? null : value.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
        if (normalised == null || !UUID_FORMAT.matcher(normalised).matches()) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(fieldName, "must be a valid identifier");
        }
        this.value = normalised;
    }

    /** Returns a new random value, for the {@code newId()} factory of a subclass. */
    protected static String newValue() {
        return UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    }

    /** Returns the UUID as lower-case text. */
    public String value() {
        return value;
    }

    @Override
    public final boolean equals(Object other) {
        if (this == other) {
            return true;
        }
        if (other == null || getClass() != other.getClass()) {
            return false;
        }
        return value.equals(((Identifier) other).value);
    }

    @Override
    public final int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(getClass(), value);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return value;
    }
}
Reading the code
Pattern.compile("^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$");

Pattern is in java.util.regex. The pattern is compiled once, when the class loads, because the field is static final. It accepts only the standard form of a UUID, in lower case.

String normalised = value == null ? null : value.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);

The text is turned into lower case first. So an upper-case UUID from a client is accepted, and it is stored in lower case. Locale.ROOT applies no language rules. With a Turkish locale, a run for this book turned "I" into the dotless "ı".

throw new InvalidValueException(fieldName, "must be a valid identifier");

The error names the field, such as orderId. The platform answers it with 400. So the client learns which value to correct.

protected static String newValue() {

A subclass uses this method in its factory for a new ID. UUID is in java.util, and randomUUID creates a random UUID.

if (other == null || getClass() != other.getClass()) {

Two identifiers are equal only when they have the same class. So an OrderId is never equal to a LineId, even with the same UUID. A run for this book confirmed it.

return Objects.hash(getClass(), value);

Objects.hash combines several values into one hash code. The class is part of the hash, as it is part of equals.

public String toString() {

The text form is the UUID itself. So a message such as "Order " + id prints the ID, with no class name around it.

Gotcha

UUID.fromString accepts text that is not a UUID in the standard form. A C# developer expects it to check the text, as Guid.TryParse does. In a run for this book, UUID.fromString("1-2-3-4-5") returned 00000001-0002-0003-0004-000000000005. On .NET 10, Guid.TryParse returned false for the same text. So Identifier checks the text against a pattern, and it never calls fromString.

The test IdentifierTest records the rule about case:

@Test
void acceptsUpperCaseAndStoresLowerCase() {
    String value = ParcelId.newId().value();

    ParcelId upper = new ParcelId(value.toUpperCase());

    assertThat(upper.value()).isEqualTo(value);
    assertThat(upper).isEqualTo(new ParcelId(value)).hasToString(value);
}

The test class ParcelId is a typed ID made only for the test. The test makes a new ID, and builds a second ID from its upper-case text. The second ID holds the lower-case text, and it is equal to the first one. In C#, Guid.TryParse accepts both cases too. A run for this book printed a Guid parsed from upper-case text in lower case.

Each typed ID of the order feature is a small class. Here is the ID of a line:

/** The identity of a line within an order. */
public final class LineId extends Identifier {

    private LineId(String value) {
        super(value, "lineId");
    }

    public static LineId of(String value) {
        return new LineId(value);
    }

    public static LineId newId() {
        return new LineId(newValue());
    }
}
Reading the code
public final class LineId extends Identifier {

final means that no class can extend LineId. So nobody can write a subclass that changes how the ID is checked.

private LineId(String value) {

The constructor is private. Code outside the class uses the two factories.

super(value, "lineId");

The second argument is the field name that a client sees in a 400 error.

public static LineId of(String value) {

of wraps text that already exists, such as a path variable or a stored value. A static method that creates an object is called a static factory. Its name says what it does. A constructor cannot have such a name.

public static LineId newId() {

newId creates a new random ID. Only the code that creates a line or an order calls it.

A typed ID is a class and not a record, because a record cannot extend a class. The compiler refuses record RecId(String value) extends Identifier with error: '{' expected. For what a record can and cannot do, see the section Where records fit.

Typed IDs stay inside the feature. Between features, an ID travels as plain text. The note feature stores the order ID as a String, and the order feature checks it with OrderId.of. So the features share no type, and the owner of the ID checks it. For this choice and its callout, see the section A type for a foreign ID, or plain text.

The ID holds the UUID as text, not as a java.util.UUID. The JSON body, the path and the stored document all carry the ID as text. So text needs no conversion at any of those borders, and the pattern still checks the format.

Value objects as recordstwist#

C# 12
public record CustomerContact
{
    public CustomerContact(string name, string email)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name))
            throw new ArgumentException("must not be blank", nameof(name));
        (Name, Email) = (name, email);
    }

    public string Name { get; }
    public string Email { get; }

    public override string ToString() => "CustomerContact[masked]";
}
The order service
public record CustomerContact(String name, String email) implements ValueObject {

    public CustomerContact {
        Guard.notBlank(name, "customer.name");
        Guard.maxLength(name, 200, "customer.name");
        Guard.maxLength(email, 254, "customer.email");
        Guard.matches(email, "[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+", "customer.email");
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "CustomerContact[masked]";
    }
}
Reading the code
public record CustomerContact(String name, String email) implements ValueObject {

The record gets a constructor and the accessors name() and email(). It also gets equals and hashCode, which compare the values. implements ValueObject adds no code. It marks the class for readers and for architecture tests.

public CustomerContact {

A constructor with no parameter list is called a compact constructor. It runs before the fields are set, and it needs no assignments. For the rules, see the section Checking values: the compact constructor.

Guard.notBlank(name, "customer.name");

The field name is customer.name, the path of the value in the JSON body. So the 400 error points at the right place in the request.

Guard.matches(email, "[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+", "customer.email");

This is a simple format check. It expects some text, then @, then text with a dot. The section Guard: checks that name the field shows the method.

return "CustomerContact[masked]";

The text form of the contact hides the name and the e-mail address.

Both panes check the value when it is created, and both hide it in the text form. The Java record needs no assignments and no properties. The overridden toString matters because a log line or an exception message often prints an object. In runs for this book, the default text forms printed every value:

FormWhat it printed
the C# record without the overrideCustomerContact { Name = Jo Bloggs, Email = jo@example.com }
a Java record without the override, named Plain in the runPlain[name=Jo Bloggs, email=jo@example.com]
CustomerContact in the order serviceCustomerContact[masked]

So a value object that holds personal data overrides toString. The test ValueObjectTest.customerContactHidesItsPersonalDataInToString checks the masked text.

The other value objects of the order are smaller. A delivery method is a lookup code:

/**
 * How the order reaches the customer, as a lookup code such as {@code STANDARD}.
 *
 * <p>Only the format is checked here. Whether the code is an active lookup value is checked by
 * the reference feature, which owns the list.
 */
public record DeliveryMethod(String code) implements ValueObject {

    public DeliveryMethod {
        Guard.matches(code, "[A-Z_]{1,50}", "deliveryMethod");
    }
}

The record checks only the format, such as STANDARD. It cannot know whether the code is an active lookup value, because that list is stored data of the reference feature. The use case asks the reference feature. For why that check is in the application service, see the section The lookup rule in an application service.

The stock service's answer is a value object too. It holds a list, so its compact constructor copies the list:

public record StockAvailability(boolean available, List<ProductCode> unavailableProducts) implements ValueObject {

    public StockAvailability {
        unavailableProducts = List.copyOf(unavailableProducts);
    }

    public static StockAvailability allAvailable() {
        return new StockAvailability(true, List.of());
    }

    public static StockAvailability unavailable(List<ProductCode> products) {
        return new StockAvailability(false, products);
    }
}
Reading the code
unavailableProducts = List.copyOf(unavailableProducts);

A compact constructor may assign a parameter. The record then stores the new value. Here the record stores a copy that nobody can change. For why a record that holds a list needs this, see the section A record that holds a list.

public static StockAvailability allAvailable() {

Two static factories name the two answers. A caller reads StockAvailability.allAvailable() more easily than new StockAvailability(true, List.of()).

The other value objects of the order feature follow the same pattern:

Value objectWhat it checksWhy
ProductCodethe format [A-Z0-9-]{1,30}whether the product is in stock is the stock service's answer
OrderItema product, and a quantity from 1 to 999an item becomes an order line when the order is placed
PaymentReferencenot blank, at most 50 charactersthe limit matches the schema of the event that brings it
Paymenta reference, an amount and a time, none of them nulla value object made of value objects, compared as a whole
OrderStatusan enum with NEW, PAID, SHIPPED and CANCELLEDstored as its name, so a value is never renamed
LineStatusan enum with WAITING and PICKEDcomputed from the pick time, and never stored

For why a payment is a value object and a line is an entity, see the section Inside the aggregate: entities and value objects. For why an enum is stored by its name, see the section Storing an enum as a number.

Money: a currency, and no silent roundingtwist#

C# 12
public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)
{
    public decimal Amount { get; } = Math.Round(Amount, 2);
}
The order service
/**
 * An amount of money in one currency, such as 12.50 GBP.
 *
 * <p>The amount may have at most two decimal places. A value such as 12.345 is refused, not
 * rounded: money from another service that has more precision is a mistake to report, and
 * rounding it would silently change the amount. The amount is stored with exactly two places, so
 * {@code 10} and {@code 10.00} are equal.
 *
 * @param amount   zero or more, with at most two decimal places
 * @param currency an ISO 4217 code, such as {@code GBP}
 */
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) implements ValueObject {

    public static final int DECIMAL_PLACES = 2;

    public Money {
        Guard.notNegative(amount, "amount");
        if (amount.stripTrailingZeros().scale() > DECIMAL_PLACES) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("amount", "must have at most " + DECIMAL_PLACES + " decimal places");
        }
        amount = amount.setScale(DECIMAL_PLACES);
        Guard.matches(currency, "[A-Z]{3}", "currency");
        if (Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream().noneMatch(known -> known.getCurrencyCode().equals(currency))) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("currency", "is not a known currency");
        }
    }

    public static Money of(String amount, String currency) {
        return new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), currency);
    }
}
Reading the code
Guard.notNegative(amount, "amount");

The check refuses null and a negative amount. It uses signum(), which returns -1, 0 or 1 for the sign of a BigDecimal.

if (amount.stripTrailingZeros().scale() > DECIMAL_PLACES) {

The scale of a BigDecimal is the number of digits after the point. stripTrailingZeros() removes zeros at the end first. So 12.340 has two real decimal places and is accepted, but 12.345 has three and is refused.

amount = amount.setScale(DECIMAL_PLACES);

The compact constructor replaces the parameter with a value that has exactly two places. The record stores that value. setScale without a rounding mode throws ArithmeticException: Rounding necessary when it would have to round. It never has to here, because of the check before it.

if (Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream().noneMatch(known -> known.getCurrencyCode().equals(currency))) {

Currency is in java.util. The check refuses a code with the right form that is not a real currency, such as XYZ.

public static Money of(String amount, String currency) {

The factory takes the amount as text. new BigDecimal("12.50") keeps the exact value. A double cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly. For more, see the section Money is BigDecimal.

The C# record rounds the amount. A run for this book showed that Math.Round(12.345m, 2) gives 12.34, with no error. The Java value object refuses 12.345 with amount must have at most 2 decimal places. The test ValueObjectTest.moneyRefusesMoreThanTwoDecimalPlacesInsteadOfRounding checks it.

Rounding has a careful version. RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN rounds a half to the even neighbour, so many roundings do not drift upwards. C# Math.Round on a decimal does the same by default. That is the right tool when the service computes an amount itself, such as a share of a total. Then the rounding is a business step, and the code names its mode. But a payment comes from another service. An amount with three decimal places means that the other side made a mistake or uses another unit. Rounding it would change the amount and hide the mistake. So the value object refuses it, and the mistake becomes visible instead of hidden.

The two places also decide equality. A record compares its components with equals, and BigDecimal.equals compares the scale. In a run for this book, new BigDecimal("10").equals(new BigDecimal("10.00")) returned false. In C#, 10m == 10.00m is true. Because Money stores exactly two places, Money.of("10", "GBP") equals Money.of("10.00", "GBP"). The test ValueObjectTest.moneyIsEqualWhateverTheNumberOfTrailingZeros checks it. For the trap in full, see the section BigDecimal inside equals.

The amount always travels with its currency. Money.of("1", "GBP") is not equal to Money.of("1", "EUR"), and the test ValueObjectTest.moneyNeedsAKnownCurrencyAndNoNegativeAmount checks that too. Without a currency, every reader of an amount would have to know its unit from somewhere else.

Guard: checks that name the fieldnew#

Every value object checks its values. Without a helper, each one writes its own if and throw, each with its own wording. A client then gets "name is empty" from one field and "missing value" from another. So the platform has one class of checks, each with one fixed message:

public final class Guard {

    private Guard() {
    }

    public static <T> T notNull(T value, String field) {
        if (value == null) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is required");
        }
        return value;
    }

    public static String notBlank(String value, String field) {
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "must not be blank");
        }
        return value;
    }

    public static String maxLength(String value, int max, String field) {
        if (value != null && value.length() > max) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "must be at most " + max + " characters");
        }
        return value;
    }

    public static String matches(String value, String regex, String field) {
        if (value == null || !value.matches(regex)) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "has an invalid format");
        }
        return value;
    }
    // ...
    public static <C extends Collection<?>> C notEmpty(C values, String field) {
        if (values == null || values.isEmpty()) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "must have at least 1 item");
        }
        return values;
    }

    public static <C extends Collection<?>> C maxSize(C values, int max, String field) {
        if (values != null && values.size() > max) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "must have at most " + max + " items");
        }
        return values;
    }
Reading the code
public final class Guard {

The class only holds static methods. final stops anyone from extending it, and the private constructor stops anyone from creating it. Java has no static classes, so this pair does the same work. For more, see the section No static classes.

public static <T> T notNull(T value, String field) {

A generic method declares its type parameter before the return type. Here it returns the value with its own type, so the check fits in an assignment, such as this.customer = Guard.notNull(customer, "customer").

if (value == null || !value.matches(regex)) {

String.matches checks the whole text against the pattern. So the patterns of the value objects need no ^ and $. For how this differs from Regex.IsMatch, see the section IsMatch in Java.

public static <C extends Collection<?>> C notEmpty(C values, String field) {

The type parameter C is any collection. Collection<?> means a collection of any element type. The question mark is called a wildcard. The method returns the same type it received. So a List<OrderItem> comes back as a List<OrderItem>. For the question mark, see the section Variance is at the use site.

Each check builds its message from the field name and a fixed text:

CheckText after the field nameExample message
notNullis requiredpaidAt is required
notBlankmust not be blankcustomer.name must not be blank
maxLengthmust be at most N characterscustomer.name must be at most 200 characters
matcheshas an invalid formatcustomer.email has an invalid format
betweenmust be between MIN and MAXquantity must be between 1 and 999
notNegativemust not be negativeamount must not be negative
notEmptymust have at least 1 itemlines must have at least 1 item
maxSizemust have at most N itemslines must have at most 50 items

The messages reach the client. The platform's exception handler puts the field and the message into the errors list of a 400 response:

@ExceptionHandler(InvalidValueException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> invalidValue(InvalidValueException ex) {
    ProblemDetail problem = domainProblem(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, INVALID_REQUEST, ex);
    problem.setProperty("errors", List.of(fieldError(ex.field(), ex.getMessage())));
    return respond(problem);
}

fieldError builds a small map with the keys field and message. The tests GuardTest.namesTheFieldInTheError and ValueObjectTest.codesAndQuantitiesAreChecked check the texts. For the whole problem response, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

The request of the API checks most of these values too, with Bean Validation:

/**
 * The JSON body that places an order. The validation annotations give a client a 400 that lists
 * every bad field at once, and springdoc copies them into the OpenAPI document. The domain's
 * value objects check the same values again, and the domain's check is the one that counts.
 */
@Schema(description = "An order to place, with its first notes")
public record PlaceOrderRequest(
        @NotNull @Valid CustomerRequest customer,
        @Schema(description = "A DELIVERY_METHOD code", example = "STANDARD") @NotBlank String deliveryMethod,
        @NotEmpty @Size(max = 50) List<@Valid LineRequest> lines,
        @Schema(description = "Notes saved with the order, in the same transaction")
        @Size(max = 20) List<@Valid NoteRequest> notes) {

    public record CustomerRequest(
            @Schema(example = "Jo Bloggs") @NotBlank @Size(max = 200) String name,
            @Schema(example = "jo@example.com") @NotBlank @Email String email) {
    }

The annotations @NotBlank, @Size and @Email check the JSON body before the controller method runs. When several fields are wrong, the 400 lists them all at once. CustomerContact checks the same values again when the controller builds it. When the two checks disagree, the value object decides, because it is the only check on every path in.

Pragmatic choice: The same check on the request and in the value object

The strict rule. Each rule has one home. A format rule is in its value object.

What we do. The request's data transfer object (DTO) carries Bean Validation annotations. The value object checks the same values again with Guard, and its check counts.

Why. The annotations give the client one 400 that names every bad field, and springdoc copies them into the OpenAPI document. But a message, a test, a migration or another feature builds the value object without the request. Only the value object's check covers those paths.

When to stop. Stop when the two lists drift, so that the request accepts a value that the domain refuses. That is the sign that nobody keeps them in step. Then keep only @NotNull and @Valid on the request, and let the domain answer.

The Order aggregate: its fields and its constructornew#

In an anaemic model, a service sets order.Status directly, and any class can do the same. Such a service often adds an outbox for its events. For that design and a fair comparison, see the section An anaemic model with an outbox, compared fairly. The order aggregate allows no such change. Its class comment lists its rules, and its fields can be changed only from inside the class:

/**
 * An order: the aggregate root of the order feature.
 *
 * <p>The aggregate holds what its rules need at every change: the status, the lines and the last
 * payment. Notes are a separate aggregate, because no order rule needs every note, and they can
 * grow without limit.
 *
 * <p>The rules on the order's own data:
 * <ul>
 *   <li>An order is placed only if every product is available, with 1 to {@value #MAX_LINES} lines.</li>
 *   <li>A shipped or cancelled order cannot change, except that payments are still recorded.</li>
 *   <li>A line is picked once.</li>
 *   <li>An order ships only when it is paid and every line is picked.</li>
 *   <li>A payment is recorded only if it is later than the last one, so repeated and late
 *       messages change nothing. The first payment makes a new order paid.</li>
 * </ul>
 *
 * <p>The rule that no note may need action is across two aggregates, so it lives in
 * {@code ShippingPolicy}.
 *
 * <p>State changes only through these methods. There are no setters, and the time always comes
 * from the {@link Clock} the caller passes.
 */
public class Order extends AggregateRoot<OrderId> {

    public static final int MAX_LINES = 50;

    private final CustomerContact customer;
    private final DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod;
    private final Instant placedAt;
    private final List<OrderLine> lines;
    private OrderStatus status;
    private Payment lastPayment;
    private Instant shippedAt;
    private Instant cancelledAt;

    private Order(OrderId id, Long version, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, Instant placedAt,
                  List<OrderLine> lines, OrderStatus status, Payment lastPayment, Instant shippedAt, Instant cancelledAt) {
        super(id, version);
        this.customer = Guard.notNull(customer, "customer");
        this.deliveryMethod = Guard.notNull(deliveryMethod, "deliveryMethod");
        this.placedAt = placedAt;
        this.lines = new ArrayList<>(lines);
        this.status = status;
        this.lastPayment = lastPayment;
        this.shippedAt = shippedAt;
        this.cancelledAt = cancelledAt;
    }
Reading the code
public class Order extends AggregateRoot<OrderId> {

The type argument fixes the ID type. So order.id() returns an OrderId, and no cast is needed.

public static final int MAX_LINES = 50;

This is a constant of the class. The comment shows its value with {@value #MAX_LINES}, so the documentation never disagrees with the code.

private final CustomerContact customer;

A final field is set once, in the constructor. The customer, the delivery method, the time of placing and the list itself never change.

private OrderStatus status;

The fields that change are private and not final. Only the methods of the class change them, after they check the rules.

private Order(OrderId id, Long version, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, Instant placedAt,

The constructor is private. Code outside the class must use place or rehydrate, which the next section shows.

this.customer = Guard.notNull(customer, "customer");

The constructor checks what must hold for every order, new or loaded. An order without a customer cannot exist.

this.lines = new ArrayList<>(lines);

The order copies the list it receives into a list of its own. So a later change to the caller's list does not reach the order. The order can also add to its own list, even when the caller passed a list that cannot change.

The class has no setters. The accessors have no get prefix, as in a record, for example status() and lastPayment(). An architecture rule makes sure that no entity gets a public setter later:

public static ArchRule entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters() {
    DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> entities = assignableTo(Entity.class)
            .or(DescribedPredicate.describe("light-style entities",
                    (JavaClass type) -> type.isAnnotatedWith(Document.class)
                            && !type.getPackageName().contains(".persistence")));
    return methods().that().areDeclaredInClassesThat(entities)
            .and().haveNameMatching("set[A-Z].*")
            .should().notBePublic()
            .allowEmptyShould(true)
            .as("Entities have no public setter");
}
Reading the code
DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> entities = assignableTo(Entity.class)

The rule finds every subclass of the platform's Entity, and so every aggregate and every inner entity.

(JavaClass type) -> type.isAnnotatedWith(Document.class)

It also finds the light-style entities, which are stored documents outside a persistence package, such as Note.

.and().haveNameMatching("set[A-Z].*")

A method whose name starts with set and a capital letter is a setter. Such a method must not be public.

The test ArchitectureTest.entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters runs the rule. So a change to the state always goes through a method that applies the rule, and nobody can skip it.

Placing versus rehydratingnew#

An order comes into memory in two ways. An agent places a new order, or the adapter loads a stored one. These are different actions. Placing checks the rules and tells other services that something happened. Loading only rebuilds what was already true. So the order has two static factories:

/**
 * Places a new order. This is a business action: it applies the rules and raises
 * {@link OrderPlaced}.
 *
 * <p>The caller chooses the ID first, because it already sent the ID to the stock service as
 * the idempotency key of the reservation.
 *
 * @param stock the stock service's answer for these items
 */
public static Order place(OrderId id, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod,
                          List<OrderItem> items, StockAvailability stock, Clock clock) {
    Guard.notEmpty(items, "lines");
    Guard.maxSize(items, MAX_LINES, "lines");
    if (!stock.available()) {
        throw new ProductsUnavailableException(stock.unavailableProducts());
    }
    List<OrderLine> lines = items.stream().map(OrderLine::add).toList();
    Order order = new Order(id, null, customer, deliveryMethod, clock.instant(), lines, OrderStatus.NEW,
            null, null, null);
    order.raise(new OrderPlaced(id, deliveryMethod, List.copyOf(items), order.placedAt));
    return order;
}

/** Rebuilds a stored order. Loading is not a business action, so it applies no rules and raises no events. */
public static Order rehydrate(OrderId id, Long version, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod,
                              Instant placedAt, List<OrderLine> lines, OrderStatus status, Payment lastPayment,
                              Instant shippedAt, Instant cancelledAt) {
    return new Order(id, version, customer, deliveryMethod, placedAt, lines, status, lastPayment,
            shippedAt, cancelledAt);
}
Reading the code
public static Order place(OrderId id, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod,

The name of the business action is the name of the method. The caller passes the ID, the values, the stock service's answer and the clock.

Guard.maxSize(items, MAX_LINES, "lines");

An order has 1 to 50 lines. Lines are added only when the order is placed, so the limit is checked here, and nowhere else.

if (!stock.available()) {

The use case asked the stock service. The order decides what the answer means. An unavailable product means that no order is placed. For the reason, see the section A decision from another service, a rule in the domain.

List<OrderLine> lines = items.stream().map(OrderLine::add).toList();

Each item becomes a line. OrderLine::add is a method reference to the package-private factory of the line. toList() returns a list that cannot change, and the constructor copies it into the order's own list.

Order order = new Order(id, null, customer, deliveryMethod, clock.instant(), lines, OrderStatus.NEW,

The version is null, because the order was never saved. The time comes from the clock that the caller passed.

order.raise(new OrderPlaced(id, deliveryMethod, List.copyOf(items), order.placedAt));

A static method of the class can call the protected raise on an instance of the same class. The event carries a copy of the items.

public static Order rehydrate(OrderId id, Long version, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod,

Rehydrating means rebuilding an object from stored data. The method takes every field, including the version and the status. It applies no rule and raises no event.

Loading must not apply the rules of placing. Suppose that rehydrate asked the stock service again. A stored order whose mug is now sold out could then not be loaded, and it could not be shipped or cancelled either. Suppose that it raised OrderPlaced. Every load would then tell other services that a new order exists. The constructor still checks what holds for every order, such as a customer, so a broken document fails on load.

The caller chooses the ID before placing, because the use case has already sent it to the stock service. The stock service uses it as the idempotency key of the reservation. For that call, see the chapter Calling other services.

Only the persistence mapper calls rehydrate. For the mapper, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB. The line has the same pair of factories, and its add is package-private. See The root is the only way in. The light-style note loads through a constructor instead. See Creating and loading.

The time comes from an injected Clocktwist#

ASP.NET Core 10
builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
The platform library
/** The clock that the domain reads the time from. Code never calls {@code Instant.now()}. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
Clock clock() {
    return Clock.systemUTC();
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnMissingBean

Spring creates this bean only if the service has no Clock bean of its own. So a test can declare a fixed clock, and the platform then creates none.

return Clock.systemUTC();

Clock is in java.time. systemUTC() reads the system time, in the UTC time zone.

Both panes register one object that tells the time, so tests can replace it. In Java, the application service receives the Clock in its constructor. It passes the clock to each domain method that needs the time, such as order.ship(clock). An aggregate is not a bean, so nothing could inject the clock into it. The aggregate reads the time with clock.instant(), which returns an Instant. No domain code calls Instant.now().

The tests pass a clock that always returns the same time:

public static final Instant NOW = Instant.parse("2026-01-15T09:00:00Z");
public static final Clock CLOCK = Clock.fixed(NOW, ZoneOffset.UTC);

Instant.parse reads an ISO 8601 text. Clock.fixed returns a clock that always gives that instant, and ZoneOffset.UTC is its time zone. So a test can expect shippedAt to be exactly NOW. In C#, a test passes its own subclass of TimeProvider that overrides GetUtcNow. For the classes of java.time, see the section java.time.

Changing an order: pick, ship and cancelnew#

Each change of an order is one method. Each method follows the same three steps. It checks the rule, it changes the state, and it raises the event. Here are shipping and cancelling, and the check that both use first:

public void ship(Clock clock) {
    requireNotFinished();
    if (status != OrderStatus.PAID) {
        throw new OrderNotPaidException(id());
    }
    if (lines.stream().anyMatch(line -> !line.isPicked())) {
        throw new UnpickedLinesException(id());
    }
    status = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
    shippedAt = clock.instant();
    raise(new OrderShipped(id(), shippedAt));
}

public void cancel(Clock clock) {
    requireNotFinished();
    status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED;
    cancelledAt = clock.instant();
    raise(new OrderCancelled(id(), cancelledAt));
}
// ...
private void requireNotFinished() {
    if (status == OrderStatus.SHIPPED || status == OrderStatus.CANCELLED) {
        throw new OrderFinishedException(id(), status);
    }
}
Reading the code
requireNotFinished();

This private method runs first in every change. A shipped or cancelled order cannot change. The method throws OrderFinishedException, which the platform answers with 422.

if (status != OrderStatus.PAID) {

Each enum value is a single object, so != compares enum values safely. For enums, see the chapter Enums.

if (lines.stream().anyMatch(line -> !line.isPicked())) {

anyMatch returns true when at least one element matches, like Any in LINQ. One line that is not picked stops the shipment.

shippedAt = clock.instant();

This line is the change. The state changes only after every check has passed.

raise(new OrderShipped(id(), shippedAt));

The event comes last. If a check throws, the order has no event to publish, because nothing happened.

So one method holds the rule, the change and the event. A reader who asks "when can an order ship?" reads ship and its tests. The test OrderTest.Shipping checks the paid order, the unpaid one and the one with a line that is not picked. One shipping rule is missing here. An order with a note that needs action cannot ship either. That rule needs two aggregates, so it is in a domain service. For the reason, see the section Worked example: no shipping while a note needs action.

pickLine follows the same steps. It finds the line by its ID, or throws LineNotFoundException, which the platform answers with 404. Then it asks the line to pick itself. For its code, see the section The root is the only way in.

Recording a payment, once and in ordernew#

The payment service reports each payment with a message. A queue can deliver a message twice, and two messages can arrive in the wrong order. The order must stay correct in both cases. So the method that records a payment keeps the newest payment, and ignores any other:

/**
 * Records a payment, unless it is not later than the last one.
 *
 * <p>SQS can deliver a message twice, and messages can arrive out of order. Both cases leave
 * the order unchanged. A payment for a shipped or cancelled order is still recorded, on
 * purpose: the money was received, and the payment service handles any refund.
 *
 * @return whether the order changed, so the caller knows whether to save it
 */
public boolean recordPayment(Payment payment) {
    if (lastPayment != null && !payment.paidAt().isAfter(lastPayment.paidAt())) {
        return false;
    }
    lastPayment = payment;
    if (status == OrderStatus.NEW) {
        status = OrderStatus.PAID;
    }
    raise(new PaymentRecorded(id(), payment.reference(), payment.amount(), payment.paidAt()));
    return true;
}
Reading the code
if (lastPayment != null && !payment.paidAt().isAfter(lastPayment.paidAt())) {

isAfter compares two Instant values. A payment at the same time as the last one counts as a repeat. So a second delivery of the same message changes nothing.

return false;

Nothing changed, and no event is raised. The return value tells the caller that there is nothing to save.

if (status == OrderStatus.NEW) {

The first payment makes a new order paid. A later payment replaces the last one, and the status stays as it is.

The method does not call requireNotFinished. That is on purpose. The money was received, even for a cancelled order, and the payment service handles any refund. The comment of the method says so, the README of the service says so, and a test records it:

@Test
void aPaymentForACancelledOrderIsStillRecorded() {
    Order order = newOrder();
    order.cancel(CLOCK);

    assertThatCode(() -> order.recordPayment(payment(NOW))).doesNotThrowAnyException();

    assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
    assertThat(order.lastPayment()).isNotNull();
}

The test cancels an order, then records a payment for it. The call throws nothing, the status stays CANCELLED, and the payment is stored. An exception to a rule such as "a cancelled order cannot change" must be written down in the code, and tested. Otherwise the next developer adds the missing check, and payments start to fail.

The use case saves only when the method returns true:

@Transactional
public void recordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    if (order.recordPayment(payment)) {
        saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PAYMENT_RECORDED);
    }
}

The if here is not a business rule. The domain already decided to ignore the payment. The use case only skips the save. For how the message reaches this method, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

OrderLine: a status that is computedtwist#

C# 12
public DateTimeOffset? PickedAt { get; private set; }

public bool IsPicked => PickedAt is not null;

public LineStatus Status => IsPicked ? LineStatus.Picked : LineStatus.Waiting;
The order service
public boolean isPicked() {
    return pickedAt != null;
}

public LineStatus status() {
    return isPicked() ? LineStatus.PICKED : LineStatus.WAITING;
}

Both panes compute the status from the pick time. The line stores only pickedAt. So the status and the time can never disagree. A line with a pick time is picked, and a line without one is waiting. The C# pane uses properties. The Java pane uses two methods, because Java has no properties. For more, see the section The property gap.

The line is an entity with its own LineId, because a picker names the line that was picked. Its methods that change it are package-private, so only the order can call them. See The root is the only way in.

Collections leave as copiestrap#

The order holds its lines in a list that it can change. Outside code must not change that list. In C#, a class returns such a list as IReadOnlyList<T>. Java has no read-only list interface, so the order returns a copy:

PredictA caller clears the lines of an order#
A caller writes order.lines().clear(). Does it compile, and what happens when it runs?
/** Returns a read-only copy, so outside code cannot add or remove lines. */
public List<OrderLine> lines() {
    return List.copyOf(lines);
}
Show the answer
It compiles. When it runs, it throws UnsupportedOperationException, and the order keeps its lines.

Java has no read-only list interface. List has add and clear, so every call compiles. List.copyOf returns a list that throws when someone tries to change it.

In C#, IReadOnlyList<T> has no Clear. A run for this book gave error CS1061. But a C# caller could cast it back to List<T> and clear the order's own list. A run did that, and the order then had no lines.

In Java, return lines; would return the order's own list. Return a copy.

The test OrderTest records the rule:

@Test
void linesCannotBeChangedFromOutsideTheAggregate() {
    Order order = newOrder();

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> order.lines().clear()).isInstanceOf(UnsupportedOperationException.class);
}

assertThatThrownBy runs the lambda and expects it to throw. So the test fails if someone changes lines() to return the field.

Java has several ways to return a collection. They differ in what a caller can do:

What the method returnsCan the caller change it?Does it see later changes of the order?
the field itselfyes, and the order's own list changesyes
Collections.unmodifiableList(lines)no, it throwsyes, because it is a view of the order's list
List.copyOf(lines)no, it throwsno, because it is a copy made at the call
lines.stream().toList()no, it throws, from Java 16no, because it is a new list

The order uses List.copyOf. The copy also refuses null elements. In a run for this book, List.copyOf of a list that held a null threw NullPointerException. For the other ways to create a list, see the section Creating collections.

The copy holds the same line objects as the order. A run for this book kept the list from order.lines(), then picked the first line through the order. The kept line then reported isPicked() as true. So the copy protects the list, and package-private access protects each line. A caller outside the package that calls pick on a line gets a compiler error:

error: pick(Clock) is not public in OrderLine; cannot be accessed from outside package#
Means
A class outside the order's model package called a method that has no access modifier. Only classes of the same package may call such a method.
Fix
Call the method of the aggregate root instead, such as order.pickLine(lineId, clock). The root checks the rules first.

The use cases go one step further. They never return the aggregate at all. They return a view, a record of plain values:

public record OrderView(String orderId, String status, String deliveryMethod, Instant placedAt, Instant shippedAt,
                        Instant cancelledAt, List<Line> lines, LastPayment lastPayment) {

    public record Line(String lineId, String productCode, int quantity, String status, Instant pickedAt) {

        static Line from(OrderLine line) {
            return new Line(line.id().value(), line.product().value(), line.quantity(), line.status().name(),
                    line.pickedAt());
        }
    }

Line is a record declared inside the record OrderView. A record inside another type is always static, so it needs no instance of the outer record. Its full name is OrderView.Line. A caller who holds a view cannot call ship and skip the steps of the use case. For views, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

Domain events: collected by the aggregatenew#

When an order ships, the shop must tell the warehouse and the customer. The order does not send anything itself. It records what happened, and the use case publishes the records after it saves. A record of something that happened in the domain is called a domain event. Every domain event implements one small interface:

/**
 * Something that happened inside the service, named in the past tense, such as
 * {@code OrderShipped}.
 *
 * <p>A domain event is internal. It may change whenever the model changes. Only the events that
 * an integration-event mapper translates leave the service, as versioned integration events.
 * Write domain events as records.
 */
public interface DomainEvent {

    /** Returns when the event happened, taken from the injected clock. */
    Instant occurredAt();
}

The interface has one method, occurredAt(). An event is named in the past tense, because it already happened. Its time comes from the clock that the method received. The order's events are records:

/** An order was shipped. It leaves the service as {@code OrderShippedV1}. */
public record OrderShipped(OrderId orderId, Instant occurredAt) implements DomainEvent {
}

A record implements occurredAt() through its component of the same name. So OrderShipped needs no body. The order feature has five events:

Domain eventRaised byLeaves the service as
OrderPlacedOrder.placeOrderPlacedV1, on the topic order-events
LinePickedOrder.pickLinenothing, because no other service needs it
OrderShippedOrder.shipOrderShippedV1
OrderCancelledOrder.cancelOrderCancelledV1
PaymentRecordedOrder.recordPaymentnothing, because the payment service already knows

A domain event belongs to the service, and it may change whenever the model changes. Only a mapper turns some of them into versioned integration events for other services. For that step, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

The use case publishes the events through a port:

/**
 * The port that application services use to publish the events an aggregate raised.
 *
 * <p>Call it inside the use case's transaction, after saving. The platform's implementation
 * writes the events to the outbox in that transaction, so an event is stored only with its
 * change.
 */
public interface DomainEventPublisher {

    void publish(List<DomainEvent> events);
}

publish takes the whole list of events of one change. The use case calls it after the save, inside the same transaction.

Every use case of the order feature ends with the same private method:

private Order saveAndPublish(Order order, String auditAction) {
    List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();
    Order saved = orders.save(order);
    events.publish(raised);
    audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.ORDER, saved.id().value());
    return saved;
}
Reading the code
List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();

The events are pulled before the save. The repository returns a copy rebuilt from the database, and a rebuilt copy has no events.

events.publish(raised);

The platform's implementation writes the events to the outbox, in the same transaction as the save. So an event is stored only together with its change.

So no use case can save a change and forget its event. The order raised the event in the method that changed it, and this one method publishes whatever was raised. For the steps of a use case, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

The repository porttwist#

C# 12
public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task<Order?> FindByIdAsync(OrderId id);

    async Task<Order> GetAsync(OrderId id) =>
        await FindByIdAsync(id) ?? throw new OrderNotFoundException(id);
}
The order service
/**
 * The port for storing orders, in the domain's own types. The persistence package implements it.
 * Lists are sorted newest first.
 */
public interface OrderRepository extends Repository<Order, OrderId> {

    /** Loads the order, or throws the 404 exception, so a use case loads in one line. */
    default Order get(OrderId id) {
        return findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
    }

    PageResult<Order> findAll(PageQuery page);

    PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page);
}
Reading the code
public interface OrderRepository extends Repository<Order, OrderId> {

The port extends the platform's base port. It names the aggregate and its ID type once.

default Order get(OrderId id) {

A default method has a body in the interface, like a default interface member in C#. Every adapter gets it with no code. For more, see the section Interfaces.

return findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));

findById returns an Optional. orElseThrow returns the order, or throws the exception that the lambda creates. So a use case loads an order, or answers 404, in one line.

PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page);

The queries take and return the domain's own types. The comment says that lists are sorted newest first. How the adapter does that is not the domain's concern.

Both ports load or fail in one line. The Java port returns Optional<Order>. The C# port returns Order?. For when to use Optional, see the section Optional is for return values. The base port is short:

public interface Repository<A extends AggregateRoot<ID>, ID extends Identifier> {

    Optional<A> findById(ID id);

    /**
     * Saves the aggregate and returns the stored copy, which holds the new version.
     *
     * <p>Continue with the returned instance. The instance you passed in keeps the old version,
     * so saving it a second time fails. For a new aggregate it fails as a duplicate insert, with
     * {@code DuplicateKeyException}; for a loaded one, as a concurrent update. Saving also fails
     * with Spring's {@code OptimisticLockingFailureException} when someone else saved the
     * aggregate after you loaded it; that exception is unchecked, so this plain-Java interface
     * can only name it here.
     * Inside a transaction, MongoDB usually reports the same conflict as a write conflict, which
     * Spring translates to {@code DataIntegrityViolationException}. The platform answers both with 409.
     *
     * <p>Never retry a failed save with the same instance. Load the aggregate again, apply the
     * change again, and save that.
     */
    A save(A aggregate);

    boolean exists(ID id);

The interface has two type parameters. A extends AggregateRoot<ID> says that only an aggregate root can be stored. ID extends Identifier says that its ID is a typed ID. The bound on A uses ID, so the aggregate and its ID type must fit together. A repository of Order with a LineId does not compile.

The comment of save names Spring's OptimisticLockingFailureException. The interface cannot import it, because the domain is plain Java. It does not need to declare it either, because the exception is unchecked. So the comment is the only place where a reader learns about it. For what the comment says about the returned instance, see the section The version, and the save that returns a new instance.

The base port is for aggregates only. The reference feature has no aggregate, so its repository extends Spring Data directly:

public interface ReferenceItemRepository extends MongoRepository<ReferenceItemDocument, String> {

    @Cacheable("reference-data")
    List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);
}

MongoRepository is the Spring Data interface for MongoDB, and @Cacheable keeps each list in a cache. A lookup value has no version and no events, so the base port would give it nothing.

The note feature, in the light style, also injects a Spring Data repository directly. For both styles, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The version, and the save that returns a new instancenew#

The version of an order is final, and no rule reads it. So the save cannot write the new version into the order that the use case passes in. The repository returns a new instance instead, and the use case continues with that one. Placing an order saves it, and then uses the saved order's ID for its notes:

return transaction.execute(status -> {
    Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);
    Order saved = saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_PLACED);        // aggregate 1
    List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction
    return new PlacedOrder(saved.id().value(), noteIds);
});

saveAndPublish returns the saved instance. The lambda keeps it as saved, and passes saved.id() to the note feature. The instance order is not used after the save. What goes wrong when a use case saves the old instance again is a trap of its own. For the run that shows it, see the section The order that was passed to save.

A unit test of the use case must behave like the real repository. A mock that returns the instance it received would hide a use case that keeps the old one. So the test's mock builds a new instance with the next version. The mock comes from Mockito:

/** Makes the mocked repository behave like the real one: save returns a stored copy with the next version. */
private void saveReturnsTheStoredCopy() {
    when(orders.save(any())).thenAnswer(call -> {
        Order order = call.getArgument(0);
        long next = order.version() == null ? 0 : order.version() + 1;
        return Order.rehydrate(order.id(), next, order.customer(), order.deliveryMethod(), order.placedAt(),
                order.lines(), order.status(), order.lastPayment(), order.shippedAt(), order.cancelledAt());
    });
}

thenAnswer runs the lambda for each call, and getArgument(0) is the order that the use case passed. The lambda rebuilds it with Order.rehydrate and the next version, as the real adapter does. A first save gives version 0, because a new order has no version. For more about mocks, see the chapter Testing in depth.

A failed save is never retried with the same instance. The comment of Repository.save says so. The use case loads the order again, applies the change again, and saves that. The light-style note works differently, because Spring Data writes the new version into the same object. See Versions after a save. For the stored version and the conflicts, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

Paging without Spring: PageQuery and PageResulttwist#

/**
 * Which page of a list to return, without any Spring type. Pages count from zero.
 *
 * @param page the page number, from 0
 * @param size the number of items on a page, from 1 to {@value #MAX_SIZE}
 */
public record PageQuery(int page, int size) implements ValueObject {

    public static final int MAX_SIZE = 100;
    public static final int DEFAULT_SIZE = 20;

    public PageQuery {
        if (page < 0) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("page", "must not be negative");
        }
        if (size < 1 || size > MAX_SIZE) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("size", "must be between 1 and " + MAX_SIZE);
        }
    }

    /** Returns the first page with the default size. */
    public static PageQuery first() {
        return new PageQuery(0, DEFAULT_SIZE);
    }
}

A list query takes a PageQuery instead of Spring Data's Pageable, so the port stays plain Java. The compact constructor refuses a negative page and a size outside 1 to 100. {@value #MAX_SIZE} puts the value of the constant into the documentation. first() is a static factory for the first page with 20 items. Pages count from zero, as in Spring Data.

The answer is a PageResult, with the numbers that a client needs to ask for the next page:

public record PageResult<T>(List<T> items, int page, int size, long totalItems) {

    public PageResult {
        items = List.copyOf(items);
    }

    public int totalPages() {
        return size == 0 ? 0 : (int) Math.ceil((double) totalItems / size);
    }

    /** Converts each item and keeps the paging numbers, for example from aggregates to views. */
    public <R> PageResult<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> mapper) {
        return new PageResult<>(items.stream().<R>map(mapper).toList(), page, size, totalItems);
    }
}
Reading the code
items = List.copyOf(items);

The record stores a copy that cannot change, as StockAvailability does.

return size == 0 ? 0 : (int) Math.ceil((double) totalItems / size);

41 items in pages of 20 make 3 pages. The test GuardTest.pageQueryLimitsTheSize checks that number.

public <R> PageResult<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> mapper) {

This generic method converts each item and keeps the paging numbers. The function may take any supertype of T and return any subtype of R. This rule is called PECS, "producer extends, consumer super". See Variance is at the use site.

items.stream().<R>map(mapper).toList()

.<R>map gives the type argument of map explicitly. Without it, the compiler infers a stream of "some subtype of R". A run for this book then failed with error: incompatible types: cannot infer type arguments for PR<>.

The use case turns a page of orders into a page of views in one call, result.map(OrderView::from). The controller turns the result into the JSON of a page. For that step, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

Exceptions by kind, with stable codesnew#

A use case throws "this order is not paid". The client must get the same status for it in every service, and a code that its program can test. If each feature wrote its own exception handler, the statuses would drift. So the platform defines exactly three kinds of domain exception. The kind decides the status, and a feature only chooses the kind:

C# 12
public abstract class DomainException : Exception
{
    private protected DomainException(string code, string message) : base(message) => Code = code;

    public string Code { get; }
}

public abstract class NotFoundException : DomainException
{
    protected NotFoundException(string code, string message) : base(code, message) { }
}
The platform library
/**
 * The base of every exception the domain throws. It has exactly three kinds, and the kind
 * decides the HTTP status, so a feature never writes an exception handler.
 *
 * <ul>
 *   <li>{@link NotFoundException}: the thing does not exist (404).</li>
 *   <li>{@link InvalidValueException}: a value has the wrong format (400).</li>
 *   <li>{@link BusinessRuleViolationException}: the request breaks a business rule (422).</li>
 * </ul>
 *
 * <p>The class is sealed, so no other direct subclass can exist. Extend one of the three kinds.
 * The message is returned to the caller, so it must never hold personal data. IDs are fine.
 */
public abstract sealed class DomainException extends RuntimeException
        permits NotFoundException, InvalidValueException, BusinessRuleViolationException {

    private final String code;

    protected DomainException(String code, String message) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
    }

    /** Returns a stable, machine-readable code, such as {@code ORDER_NOT_PAID}. */
    public String code() {
        return code;
    }
}
Reading the code
public abstract sealed class DomainException extends RuntimeException

A sealed class lists the classes that may extend it. It extends RuntimeException, so it is an unchecked exception, and no method has to declare it. For checked and unchecked exceptions, see the section Checked exceptions.

permits NotFoundException, InvalidValueException, BusinessRuleViolationException {

The keyword permits names the classes that may extend DomainException directly. Only these three may. A run for this book compiled class Oops extends DomainException in another package. The compiler refused it.

public String code() {

Every domain exception carries a code, such as ORDER_NOT_PAID. The platform puts it into the problem response.

The compiler's message names the rule:

error: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: DomainException (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)#
Means
A class extends DomainException directly, but the sealed class allows only its three kinds.
Fix
Extend one of the kinds instead, such as NotFoundException or BusinessRuleViolationException.

The C# pane has no list of permitted classes. The closest match in C# is a private protected constructor. Only a derived class in the same assembly can call it. In a run for this book, a class in another assembly that derived from the C# DomainException failed with error CS1729. A class that derived from NotFoundException compiled. The Java rule works by name, across packages and libraries.

Each kind is non-sealed, so features may extend it. Here is one of them:

/**
 * The thing a request names does not exist. The platform answers 404.
 *
 * <p>Write one subclass per kind of thing, such as {@code OrderNotFoundException}. The class is
 * non-sealed and its constructor is protected, so features can extend it but not throw it bare.
 */
public non-sealed class NotFoundException extends DomainException {

    protected NotFoundException(String code, String message) {
        super(code, message);
    }
}

non-sealed opens this branch again. Any class may extend NotFoundException. The constructor is protected, so a feature cannot throw a bare NotFoundException. In a run for this book, new NotFoundException("X", "y") in another package failed with NotFoundException(String,String) has protected access in NotFoundException. For sealed and non-sealed in general, see the section Sealed types: Java's discriminated unions.

The three kinds differ in their status and in how a feature uses them:

KindStatusConstructorHow a feature uses it
NotFoundException404protected, with a code and a messageone subclass for each kind of thing, such as OrderNotFoundException
InvalidValueException400public, with a field and a problemthrown directly, mostly by Guard, and its code is always INVALID_VALUE
BusinessRuleViolationException422protected, with a code and a messageone subclass for each broken rule, such as OrderNotPaidException

One broken rule of the order looks like this:

public class OrderNotPaidException extends BusinessRuleViolationException {

    public OrderNotPaidException(OrderId id) {
        super("ORDER_NOT_PAID", "Order " + id + " cannot ship before it is paid");
    }
}

The class name says which rule broke. The code ORDER_NOT_PAID is the same name in capitals, and the message explains it for a person. The order feature has one exception class for each rule:

ExceptionKindCodeThrown when
OrderNotFoundExceptionnot foundORDER_NOT_FOUNDno order has the ID
LineNotFoundExceptionnot foundLINE_NOT_FOUNDthe order has no line with the ID
ProductsUnavailableExceptionrulePRODUCTS_UNAVAILABLEthe stock service cannot hold every product
LineAlreadyPickedExceptionruleLINE_ALREADY_PICKEDa line is picked a second time
OrderNotPaidExceptionruleORDER_NOT_PAIDan order ships before it is paid
UnpickedLinesExceptionruleUNPICKED_LINESan order ships with a line that is not picked
OrderHasOpenActionsExceptionruleORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONSan order ships while a note on it needs action
OrderFinishedExceptionruleORDER_FINISHEDa shipped or cancelled order is changed

Clients may rely on a code, so a code never changes. A client program tests code == "ORDER_NOT_PAID", and it never parses the message. The message is returned to the caller too, so it must never hold personal data. IDs and product codes are fine. A customer's name is not.

The platform's exception handler maps each kind to its status:

@ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> notFound(NotFoundException ex) {
    return respond(domainProblem(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Not found", ex));
}
// ...
@ExceptionHandler(BusinessRuleViolationException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> businessRule(BusinessRuleViolationException ex) {
    return respond(domainProblem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Business rule violated", ex));
}

@ExceptionHandler names the exception class that the method handles. The method also handles every subclass of that class. So OrderNotPaidException reaches businessRule and becomes a 422. The test OrderControllerTest.aBrokenBusinessRuleIsA422WithItsCode checks the status and the code in the body. HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT is the name of 422 in Spring Framework 7. No feature writes a handler of its own. For the problem response and its code property, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

The light-style Note, for comparisontwist#

/**
 * Writes a new note on an order. The caller has checked that the order exists and that the
 * category is an active lookup value. {@code createdBy} is the ID of the agent who writes it.
 */
public static Note create(String orderId, String text, String category, boolean actionRequired,
                          String createdBy, Clock clock) {
    Guard.notBlank(orderId, "orderId");
    Guard.notBlank(text, "text");
    Guard.maxLength(text, MAX_TEXT_LENGTH, "text");
    Guard.matches(category, "[A-Z_]{1,50}", "category");
    Guard.notBlank(createdBy, "createdBy");
    Note note = new Note(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), null, orderId, text, category, actionRequired,
            clock.instant(), createdBy, null);
    note.events.add(new NoteAdded(note.id, orderId, note.createdAt));
    return note;
}

The note keeps the same ideas as the order, with fewer types. create is a business action that checks the values with Guard and records NoteAdded. It also records the ID of the agent who writes the note, for the rule that another agent resolves it. Its IDs are plain String values. It has no base class, so it keeps its own event list and its own equals. The table compares the two styles where this chapter used them:

ConcernOrder, the full styleNote, the light style
the ID of the entityOrderId, checked by Identifiera String made from UUID.randomUUID()
a reference to another aggregatenone, because the order refers to no other aggregatea String orderId, with no OrderRef type, checked by the order feature
valuesvalue objects, such as CustomerContactStrings checked in create, such as the category with Guard.matches
personal data in toStringCustomerContact[masked]the text is left out, and only its length is printed
loadingOrder.rehydrate, called by the mappera constructor marked @PersistenceCreator, called by Spring Data
eventsAggregateRoot.raise and pullEventsits own list, marked @Transient, and its own pullEvents
the repositorya port with an adaptera Spring Data repository, injected directly

The note has four rules of its own. Only a note that needs action can be resolved. It is resolved once. The agent who wrote it may not resolve it. Its text never changes. resolveAction checks the first three rules. It throws NoteHasNoActionException, NoteActionAlreadyResolvedException or NoteResolvedByItsAuthorException, which are all business rule violations. When it succeeds, it raises NoteActionResolved. requireBelongsTo answers a note under another order with NoteNotFoundException, a 404. A 403 would tell the caller that the note exists. For that choice, see the section Rules about one record: in the domain, with the actor passed in.

A note's text may hold personal data, so its toString leaves the text out:

/** Leaves the text out: an agent may have written personal data in it. */
@Override
public String toString() {
    return "Note[id=" + id + ", orderId=" + orderId + ", " + text.length() + " chars]";
}

The text form prints text.length(), the number of characters, and never the text itself. The test NoteTest.checksItsValuesAndHidesItsTextInToString writes a phone number into a note. It checks that the text form does not contain it, and contains 36 chars.

The reference feature, at the simple level, has no value object at all. A lookup value is a document record, ReferenceItemDocument, with a type, a code, a label and an active flag. An inactive value stays stored, because old orders still use it. For the three levels side by side, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

Testing the modelnew#

A rule of the domain is plain Java, so its test is plain Java too. The test of the order creates orders, calls their methods and checks the result. It starts no Spring and needs no mocks:

/**
 * The order's rules, in plain JUnit: no Spring, no mocks, a few milliseconds. If a test here
 * needed Spring, the code under test would be in the wrong place.
 */
class OrderTest {

    @Nested
    class Placing {

        @Test
        void placesANewOrderAndRaisesOrderPlaced() {
            OrderId id = OrderId.newId();

            Order order = Order.place(id, CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, StockAvailability.allAvailable(), CLOCK);

            assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.NEW);
            assertThat(order.version()).isNull();
            assertThat(order.lines()).singleElement().satisfies(line -> {
                assertThat(line.product()).isEqualTo(new ProductCode("MUG-001"));
                assertThat(line.status()).isEqualTo(LineStatus.WAITING);
            });
            assertThat(order.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new OrderPlaced(id, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, NOW));
        }
Reading the code
@Nested

JUnit runs the tests of an inner class as a group. The class OrderTest has five such groups, one for each method of the order, such as Placing. The report then reads like the list of rules.

Order order = Order.place(id, CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, StockAvailability.allAvailable(), CLOCK);

The test data comes from TestData, with its fixed clock. The stock answer is a value, so no stock service is needed.

assertThat(order.version()).isNull();

A placed order was never saved.

assertThat(order.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new OrderPlaced(id, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, NOW));

Events are records, so the test compares the whole event by value. The time is exactly NOW, because the clock is fixed.

The comment of the class states a rule for the codebase. If a test here needed Spring, the code under test would be in the wrong place. Other tests start from a ready state with a helper:

/** A new order with no raised events, so each test starts clean. */
public static Order newOrder() {
    Order order = Order.place(OrderId.newId(), CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, StockAvailability.allAvailable(), CLOCK);
    order.pullEvents();
    return order;
}

/** A paid order whose lines are all picked, with no raised events: ready to ship. */
public static Order readyToShip() {
    Order order = newOrder();
    order.recordPayment(payment(NOW));
    order.lines().forEach(line -> order.pickLine(line.id(), CLOCK));
    order.pullEvents();
    return order;
}

newOrder and readyToShip pull the events at the end. So each test sees only the events of the method it tests. In the tests, order.lines().getFirst() returns the first element of the list. getFirst was added in Java 21. See Sequenced collections. For the test kinds of the whole service, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy does Order have two static factories, place and rehydrate, and a private constructor, instead of one public constructor?
Placing is a business action. It checks the stock answer and the number of lines, and it raises OrderPlaced. Loading only rebuilds what was already stored. If loading checked the rules of placing, an order with a sold-out product could not be loaded. If it raised the event, each load would announce a new order. The private constructor checks only what holds for every order.
2
An expert asksMoney receives an amount of 12.345 GBP from the payment service. Why does it refuse the amount, when it could round it to 12.34?
The amount comes from another service. A third decimal place means that the other side made a mistake or uses another unit. Rounding would change the amount and hide the mistake. Refusing makes the mistake visible. Rounding with a named mode is right only where the service computes an amount itself.
3
The unit test of OrderService mocks the repository. Why does the mocked save return a rebuilt order with the next version, and not the order it received?
The real repository returns a new instance, because the version of an order is final. A mock that returned the same object would let a use case that keeps the old instance pass its tests. With a rebuilt copy, the test behaves like storage, and a use case must continue with the returned instance.
4
A feature in the order service needs an exception for "this delivery slot is full". Which class does it extend, and which status does the client get?
