It extends BusinessRuleViolationException, with its own stable code such as DELIVERY_SLOT_FULL. The client gets 422 with that code. It cannot extend DomainException directly, because that class is sealed and permits only its three kinds.
5
TranslateWrite this C# value object in the style of the order service, as a Java record that checks its values with the platform's Guard: 
public record OrderItem(ProductCode Product, int Quantity)
{
    public const int MaxQuantity = 999;

    public ProductCode Product { get; } =
        Product ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(Product));

    public int Quantity { get; } = Quantity is >= 1 and <= MaxQuantity
        ? Quantity
        : throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(Quantity));
}
public record OrderItem(ProductCode product, int quantity) implements ValueObject {

    public static final int MAX_QUANTITY = 999;

    public OrderItem {
        Guard.notNull(product, "productCode");
        Guard.between(quantity, 1, MAX_QUANTITY, "quantity");
    }
}

The compact constructor runs before the fields are set. Guard.notNull and Guard.between throw an error that names the field. So the client gets 400 with quantity must be between 1 and 999.

Quick reference#

The Java features that the domain model uses, where each one appears, and where the book explains it:

  • Records hold every value object and every event. Their accessors have no get prefix, such as amount(). See The basics.
  • Compact constructors check values, and may replace them. Examples are Money and PageResult. See Checking values: the compact constructor.
  • An overridden toString in a record hides personal data, in CustomerContact. See Value objects as records.
  • Static factories name how an object is made, such as of, newId and place. See Typed IDs: Identifier and its subclasses.
  • Nested records group related types, such as OrderView.Line. Settings classes use static nested classes in the same way. See Collections leave as copies.
  • sealed, permits and non-sealed close the hierarchy of DomainException, and open each of its three kinds. See Sealed types: Java's discriminated unions.
  • Generics with bounds tie the base classes to typed IDs, as in AggregateRoot<ID extends Identifier>. Wildcards appear in PageResult.map. See Declaration and Variance is at the use site.
  • Generic static methods return the value they check, such as Guard.notNull. See Guard: checks that name the field.
  • Abstract classes with protected constructors and final methods are the base classes Entity, AggregateRoot and Identifier. See Abstract classes.
  • A final class with a private constructor holds static helpers, in Guard and TestData. See No static classes.
  • Package-private access keeps OrderLine.add and OrderLine.pick inside the model package. See The mapping.
  • Default methods give a port shared code, such as OrderRepository.get. An interface may also hold static methods, such as IntegrationEvent.newEventId(). It may hold constants too, such as CurrentActor.SYSTEM. See Interfaces.
  • A marker interface has no methods, such as ValueObject. See Inside the aggregate: entities and value objects.
  • Streams find and convert the lines of the order, with filter, anyMatch and toList(). The outbox also uses flatMap(Optional::stream) and sorted. See Operator translation.
  • Optional is the return type of findById, and orElseThrow turns it into a 404. See Optional is for return values.
  • Collections that cannot change come from List.copyOf and List.of. Maps have Map.of and Map.copyOf. See Creating collections.
  • getFirst returns the first element of a list, from Java 21. The tests use it. See Sequenced collections.
  • var declares a local variable with an inferred type, in some tests. See var.
  • java.time gives Instant, Clock and ZoneOffset. Other features use LocalDate and Duration. See java.time.
  • BigDecimal holds an amount, with setScale and stripTrailingZeros in Money. See Money is BigDecimal.
  • UUID and Pattern create and check the text of a typed ID, in Identifier. See Typed IDs: Identifier and its subclasses.
  • Objects.requireNonNull and Objects.hash check for null and build hash codes, in Entity and Identifier. See Writing them.

Where each rule goes#

The build and the model · Chapter 08· 19 min read

Each rule of the order service has one home. A rule on the order's own data is a method of the aggregate. A rule that needs two aggregates is a domain service. The application service only runs the steps of a use case. This chapter gives five questions that choose the place, a test for rules that slip into services, and a worked example with the notes.

KindC#JavaNote
newan if in the controller or the service classa method of the aggregate, a domain service, or a step of the application serviceeach place holds one kind of logic, and may use only certain things Why
newno equivalentfive questions, asked in orderthe first yes decides the place, so each rule ends in the most local place that can check it Why
newno equivalentthe business-expert testa line that a business expert would call a rule does not belong in the application service Why
newif (notesNeedingAction > 0) throw ... in ShipAsyncShippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction)the rule needs two aggregates, so a domain service receives a number from the note feature Why
newno equivalentStockChecker in application/port, and the answer judged in Order.placethe use case asks the other service, and the domain decides what the answer means Why
newno equivalenta table of the service's rules, each with its placeeach rule has one home, which a reader finds without a search Why
newno equivalentReferenceDataService.requireActivethe lookup check needs stored data, so it stays in the simple feature's service as a pragmatic choice Why
neworder.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped in a serviceorder.ship(clock)with public setters, any caller can skip the rule, forget the event or read the system time Why
newOrderDomainServiceShippingPolicya name that states the rule keeps unrelated code out of the class Why

Three places for a rulenew#

An agent asks the service to ship an order. Three different kinds of logic decide what happens. The order checks that it is paid and picked. A rule across the order and its notes checks that no note needs action. And the use case loads, saves and publishes. The method that ships an order shows all three, one line each:

/** Ships the order. The rule across the order and its notes is checked by the domain service. */
@Transactional
public void ship(OrderId orderId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);                                         // load
    long notesNeedingAction = notes.countNeedingAction(orderId.value());       // ask the note feature
    shippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction);                   // rule across aggregates
    order.ship(clock);                                                         // rule and change
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_SHIPPED);                         // save, publish, audit
}
Reading the code
Order order = orders.get(orderId);

This is a step of the use case. It loads the aggregate, or answers 404.

long notesNeedingAction = notes.countNeedingAction(orderId.value());

This is a step too. It asks the note feature for one number.

shippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction);

This is the rule that needs two aggregates. A domain service checks it.

order.ship(clock);

Here the aggregate checks the rules on its own data, and then changes itself.

saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_SHIPPED);

These are the last steps. The use case saves the order, publishes the events and writes the audit entry.

So the use case contains no rule of its own. It decides the order of the steps, and the domain decides what is allowed. For that structure in full, see the chapter Use cases: the application service. For the code of order.ship, see the section Changing an order: pick, ship and cancel.

Each place holds one kind of logic. The table also lists a fourth place, the value object, which checks the form of a single value:

PlaceWhat it holdsWhat it may useWhat it must not useDoes it change state?How it is tested
the aggregate, such as Orderrules on its own data, such as "paid and every line picked"its own fields, value objects, and the clock it receivesrepositories, other aggregates, Spring, HTTPyes, its own stateplain JUnit, in milliseconds
a domain service, such as ShippingPolicya rule that needs data from more than one aggregatethe aggregates and values that it receivesrepositories, Spring, and state of its ownnoplain JUnit
the application service, such as OrderServicethe steps of a use caserepositories, ports, other features' services, transactionsbusiness rulesno, because it asks the domain to changeMockito mocks of the ports
a value object, such as Moneythe form of one valueGuard, and its own componentsanything outside itselfno, because it never changesplain JUnit

A domain service receives what it needs, and it never loads anything. Because of that, its test needs no mock. The application service is the only place that touches storage, other services and transactions. Because of that, it is the only place whose test needs mocks.

The decision order: five questionsnew#

A new rule arrives. An order may hold at most 50 lines. A developer could check it in the controller, in the use case or in the order. Each choice compiles, and each passes a first test. But only one place covers every way into the service. The order service checks it here, in the factory that places an order:

public static Order place(OrderId id, CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod,
                          List<OrderItem> items, StockAvailability stock, Clock clock) {
    Guard.notEmpty(items, "lines");
    Guard.maxSize(items, MAX_LINES, "lines");

Guard.maxSize throws a 400 that names the field lines. Lines are added only when an order is placed, so every order passes this check. To find such a place for any rule, ask these questions in order, and stop at the first yes:

Each question, with an answer from the order service:

  1. The form of one value. A quantity from 1 to 999 needs nothing but the quantity. So OrderItem, a record, checks it in its compact constructor. Every path that builds an item meets the check.
  2. One aggregate's data. "At most 50 lines" needs only the order's lines. So Order.place checks it. The rules on one aggregate are the most common kind, so most rules stop here.
  3. Two or more aggregates. "No note needs action" needs the order and its notes. So a domain service checks it, and the use case gives it the data. The section Worked example: no shipping while a note needs action shows why.
  4. Another feature owns the data. "The delivery method is an active lookup value" needs the lookup list of the reference feature. So the order feature calls ReferenceDataService.requireActive, and it never reads the list itself.
  5. Input, output, a transaction or a permission. "Call the stock service before the transaction starts" is about how the work runs, not about what is allowed. So it is a step of OrderService.place. A permission is checked where users enter. See Choosing the place by the shape of the service.

The order of the questions matters. The first questions choose the most local places. A check in a value object runs on every path, and a check in the aggregate runs on every change. A check in a use case runs only in that use case. So a rule that could stop at question 1 or 2, but is written at question 5, is skipped by every other use case.

Prefer the aggregate over a domain service whenever the aggregate's own data is enough. Each rule that moves out of the aggregate leaves the aggregate with less to do. When most rules have moved out, the aggregate only holds data. Such a model is called an anaemic domain model. Every caller must then know the rules again. For that outcome, see the section What an anaemic model looks like, and what goes wrong.

The five questions follow from one principle. The root of an aggregate guards the rules on its own data. For that principle and the others, see the chapter The principles.

The business-expert testnew#

The five questions need some thought. A quicker test works on a single line of a use case. Picture a person who knows the business but no code, such as the head of customer service. Read the line to them in plain words. If they say "yes, that is one of our rules", the line does not belong in the application service. The class comment of the order's use cases states the test:

* <p>Every change follows the same steps: load, let the domain apply its rules and change
* itself, save, publish the events, record the audit. The steps that call other services run
* before the transaction. This class decides the order of the steps and never contains a
* business rule: a line that a business expert would recognise as a rule belongs in the domain.

The comment of OrderService lists the steps of a change. Its last sentence names the test, with the words a business expert would recognise as a rule. Here are lines of the order service, read to a business expert:

Line, in plain wordsWould an expert call it a rule?Where it belongs
an order that is not paid cannot shipyesOrder.ship
an order with a note that needs action cannot shipyesShippingPolicy
a repeated payment changes nothingyesOrder.recordPayment
save the order only if the payment changed itno, this is about storageOrderService.recordPayment
reserve the stock before the transaction startsno, this is about how the work runsOrderService.place
publish the events after the savenoOrderService.saveAndPublish
the delivery method must be an active lookup valueyes, but it needs stored dataReferenceDataService, as a pragmatic choice

The fourth line is the one if in the use cases of the order. Its comment explains why it is not a rule:

/**
 * Records a payment from the payment service. A message starts this use case, so no user
 * acts, and the audit log records the system actor.
 *
 * <p>It joins the transaction of the inbox that called it. The one {@code if} here is not a
 * business rule: the domain decided to ignore the payment, so there is nothing to save.
 */
@Transactional
public void recordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    if (order.recordPayment(payment)) {
        saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PAYMENT_RECORDED);
    }
}

order.recordPayment(payment) applies the rule and returns whether anything changed. The if only skips a save when there is nothing to save. An expert would not recognise it. So the test also tells you which if statements may stay in a use case.

Worked example: no shipping while a note needs actionnew#

A customer-service agent writes a note on an order, "call the customer before shipping". The note needs action. Until an agent resolves it, the order must not ship. The rule needs the order, which knows whether it can ship, and the notes, which know whether any needs action. Order and note are two aggregates. For why they are separate, see the section Why order and note are separate aggregates.

The service checks the rule in a domain service:

public class ShippingPolicy {

    public void assertCanShip(Order order, long notesNeedingAction) {
        if (notesNeedingAction > 0) {
            throw new OrderHasOpenActionsException(order.id(), notesNeedingAction);
        }
    }
}

assertCanShip receives the order and a number. It throws OrderHasOpenActionsException when the number is above zero, and the platform answers 422 with the code ORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONS. The class has no field, no repository and no Spring annotation.

Four other designs look possible. Each one is tempting, so each one deserves a fair look.

Why not inside Order, with the notes loaded. The order could hold its notes, and ship could check them. But notes have no limit, and no other rule of the order needs them. Every load of an order would then load every note, and every new note would change the order's document. For the full reasons, see the section Why order and note are separate aggregates.

Why not inside Order, with a repository. The order could ask a note repository in ship. Then the aggregate would do input and output. The domain would no longer be plain Java, and every test of ship would need a mock. The architecture rule domainIsPlainJava forbids it anyway.

Why not inside Order, with the number passed in. This is the strongest alternative. order.ship(clock, notesNeedingAction) keeps every shipping rule in one method, and its test needs no mock either. It is a good design, and a small service may choose it. The service still prefers the policy for three reasons. The number is a fact of the note feature, not of the order. A class of its own shows a reader that this rule spans two aggregates. And a rule across two aggregates holds only at the moment it is checked, so it helps to see such a rule apart. Choose the parameter instead when the cross-aggregate rule is the only one, and the team prefers fewer classes.

Why not in the application service. The use case could write if (notesNeedingAction > 0) throw ... itself. A business expert would recognise that line as a rule. And a rule in one use case is missing from the next one. Suppose that the warehouse later ships orders from a message. Its listener would call another method, and that method must copy the check or forget it. A test of the rule would also need the mocks of the whole use case.

The guarantee holds only at the moment of shipping. An agent may add a note that needs action a second after the order shipped. The business owner accepted that, and the README writes the decision down. For the gap between two aggregates and the ways to close it, see the section What holds between two aggregates, and what does not.

The policy receives a number, not a list of notes. The note feature counts the notes, and gives the order feature only the count:

/** For the order feature's shipping rule: a plain number, so no note crosses the boundary. */
public long countNeedingAction(String orderId) {
    return notes.countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull(orderId);
}

countNeedingAction returns a long. So no note object crosses from the note feature into the order feature. The order feature may not even hold one. An architecture rule makes the build fail when an application service takes another feature's entity or repository:

/**
 * A service never takes another feature's repository or entity. It asks that feature's
 * service, which checks that feature's rules. This is a narrower, clearer form of the rule
 * above for the most common mistake.
 */
public static ArchRule servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities(String basePackage) {

ArchitectureTest runs servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities for the order service. A note is a stored document, so it counts as an entity here. For the rules between features, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

Because the policy receives plain values, its test is plain JUnit:

class ShippingPolicyTest {

    private final ShippingPolicy policy = new ShippingPolicy();
    private final Order order = readyToShip();

    @Test
    void allowsShippingWhenNoNoteNeedsAction() {
        assertThatCode(() -> policy.assertCanShip(order, 0)).doesNotThrowAnyException();
    }

    @Test
    void refusesShippingWhileANoteNeedsAction() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> policy.assertCanShip(order, 2))
                .isInstanceOf(OrderHasOpenActionsException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("2 note(s) need action");
    }
}

The test creates the policy with new, and passes 0 and then 2. No note, no repository and no Spring are involved. The test of the use case only checks that the steps run in order, and that nothing is saved when the rule fails:

@Test
void isRefusedWhileANoteNeedsAction() {
    Order order = readyToShip();
    when(orders.get(order.id())).thenReturn(order);
    when(notes.countNeedingAction(order.id().value())).thenReturn(1L);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.ship(order.id())).isInstanceOf(OrderHasOpenActionsException.class);
    verify(orders, never()).save(any());
    verify(audit, never()).record(anyString(), anyString(), anyString());
}

The mocked note feature returns 1L, the number of notes that need action. The test expects the exception, and verify(orders, never()).save(any()) checks that nothing was saved. The policy's own test covers the values of the rule. The use case's test covers only its place in the steps.

The policy has no Spring annotation, because it is in the domain. The order feature creates it in a configuration class:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class OrderConfig {

    @Bean
    ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy() {
        return new ShippingPolicy();
    }
}

@Bean tells Spring to call the method and keep the result as a bean. Spring then injects it into OrderService. For @Bean and proxyBeanMethods, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

A decision from another service, a rule in the domainnew#

An order is placed only if the stock service can hold every product. The answer comes over HTTP, from another service. The rule "no stock, no order" belongs to this service. So the work is split in two. The use case asks, and the domain decides. The question goes through a port in the application layer:

/**
 * The port to the stock service, in this service's types. The use case does not know that the
 * answer comes over HTTP, and a unit test replaces it with a mock.
 *
 * <p>It lives in {@code application/port}, not in the domain: calling another service is a step
 * of the use case, and the domain only judges the answer.
 */
public interface StockChecker {

    /**
     * Asks the stock service to confirm that the items are available, and to hold them for the
     * order. The stock service keeps the hold until it sees {@code OrderPlacedV1}, or releases it
     * after a timeout if the order is never placed.
     *
     * <p>Calling it twice for the same order holds nothing twice, because the order ID is the
     * idempotency key.
     */
    StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);
}

The comment of StockChecker says why the port is in application/port and not in the domain. Calling another service is a step of the use case. The domain only judges the answer. The answer is StockAvailability, a value object in this service's own words. For that value object, see the section Value objects as records.

The use case asks first, and then hands the answer to the order:

public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
                         List<NewNote> firstNotes) {
    referenceData.requireActive(ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD, deliveryMethod.code(), "deliveryMethod");
    OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();
    StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items);           // outside the transaction

    return transaction.execute(status -> {
        Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);

stock.reserve(orderId, items) runs before the transaction starts, because a slow HTTP call would hold the transaction open. Order.place then receives availability, and throws ProductsUnavailableException when a product is missing. For the code of place, see the section Placing versus rehydrating.

Each half has its own test. OrderTest.refusesProductsTheStockServiceCannotHold checks the rule with a value, and no stock service. The test of the use case checks the steps:

@Test
void savesNothingWhenTheStockIsNotAvailable() {
    when(stock.reserve(any(), any())).thenReturn(StockAvailability.unavailable(List.of(new ProductCode("MUG-001"))));

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.place(CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, firstNotes))
            .isInstanceOf(ProductsUnavailableException.class);
    verify(orders, never()).save(any());
    verifyNoInteractions(notes, events, audit);
}

The mocked port answers that the mug is not available. The test expects the domain's exception, and verifyNoInteractions(notes, events, audit) checks that no note, no event and no audit record was written. For the client behind the port, see the chapter Calling other services.

The same split works for any decision from outside. Another service, a rules engine or a person gives an answer. The use case fetches it and turns it into a value object. The domain says what the answer means for the aggregate.

The rules of the order service, and where each one isnew#

A new developer asks "where is the rule that an order cannot ship unpaid?". The answer should take one look, not a search. This table lists the rules of the service, with the place of each one:

RuleWhere it isWhy there
an order is placed only if the stock service holds every productOrder.place, with the answer from the StockChecker portthe answer comes from outside, but its meaning is a rule of the order
an order has 1 to 50 linesOrder.place, with Guard.notEmpty and Guard.maxSizelines are added only when the order is placed
a quantity is from 1 to 999OrderItem, with Guard.betweenthe form of one value
a product code, a delivery method code and a currency have a fixed formProductCode, DeliveryMethod and Moneythe form of one value
an amount has at most two decimal placesMoneythe form of one value, refused rather than rounded
the delivery method is an active lookup valueReferenceDataService.requireActive, called by OrderService.placethe list is stored data of another feature
a line is picked onceOrderLine.pick, called by Order.pickLinethe line's own data, changed only through the root
a shipped or cancelled order cannot changeOrder.requireNotFinishedthe order's own status
an order ships only when it is paid and every line is pickedOrder.shipthe order's own data
an order cannot ship while a note needs actionShippingPolicy.assertCanShipthe rule needs the order and its notes
a repeated or earlier payment changes nothingOrder.recordPaymentthe order's own last payment
a payment for a finished order is still recordedOrder.recordPayment, on purpose and testedthe money was received, and refunds belong to the payment service
a note that needs action is resolved onceNote.resolveActionthe note's own data
the agent who wrote a note does not resolve its actionNote.resolveAction, with the actor's ID passed inthe note's own author, compared with a plain value
a note under another order is not foundNote.requireBelongsTothe note's own data, answered with 404
a note is added only to an order that existsOrderService.requireExists, called by NoteServicethe order feature owns its IDs
a caller needs a scope to change an orderthe @OrdersWrite annotation on each controller methoda permission, checked where users enter

Most rules are in the aggregate or in a value object. One is in a domain service. Two are in application services, and each of those has a reason in the last column. The check that an order exists is one of them. The order feature owns its IDs, so it checks them for the note feature:

/**
 * For other features: checks that an order exists. IDs cross between features as text, and
 * the owner of the ID checks it, so a bad ID gives the order feature's own 400 or 404.
 */
public void requireExists(String orderId) {
    OrderId id = OrderId.of(orderId);
    if (!orders.exists(id)) {
        throw new OrderNotFoundException(id);
    }
}

OrderId.of(orderId) checks the format and answers 400 for a bad ID. orders.exists(id) asks storage, which is why the check is in the application service. So the note feature gets the order feature's own 400 or 404. The README of the service lists the same rules in plain words, so the business can check them.

The lookup rule in an application servicenew#

A client sends an order with the delivery method DRONE. The format is valid, but the shop has no such method. The list of delivery methods is stored data. A seed migration can add a method, or switch one off. So the domain value object cannot know the list. The check is in the reference feature's service:

/**
 * Lists lookup values, and checks codes against them for the other features.
 *
 * <p>The rule "a code must be an active lookup value" is written once, here. Every feature asks
 * this service instead of reading the collection. An unknown or inactive code is a 400 that names
 * the field, because the client sent a value that is not allowed; it breaks no business rule
 * about the order itself.
 */
@Service
public class ReferenceDataService {
    // ...
    /**
     * Throws a 400 for the field unless the code is an active value of the list.
     *
     * @param field the request field the client must correct, such as {@code deliveryMethod}
     */
    public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
        boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
                .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
        if (!known) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
        }
    }
Reading the code
.anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());

The code must be in the list, and it must be active. An inactive code stays stored, because old orders still use it, but new data may not.

throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");

The answer is 400, and it names the field. The client sent a value that is not allowed. No rule about the order itself broke, so the answer is not 422.

The order feature calls the check as the first step of placing an order. A test checks that the stock service is never called for an unknown delivery method:

@Test
void checksTheDeliveryMethodBeforeCallingTheStockService() {
    doThrow(new InvalidValueException("deliveryMethod", "is not a known value"))
            .when(referenceData).requireActive("DELIVERY_METHOD", "STANDARD", "deliveryMethod");

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.place(CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, firstNotes))
            .isInstanceOf(InvalidValueException.class);
    verifyNoInteractions(stock);
}

doThrow makes the mocked reference feature refuse STANDARD. verifyNoInteractions(stock) then checks that no reservation was made for an order that can never be placed.

Pragmatic choice: A lookup rule in an application service

The strict rule. Business rules are in the domain. An application service has no business if.

What we do. "A code must be an active lookup value" is an if in ReferenceDataService.requireActive. It throws a domain exception kind, InvalidValueException, from the application layer, so the client gets a 400 that names the field. The order feature checks the delivery method, and the note feature checks the category. Each one calls the method before it builds an aggregate.

Why. The rule checks a value of the input against stored data. It does not check the state of an aggregate. The reference feature is at the simple level, so it has no domain model to put the rule in. The rule is written once, and every feature asks the same method, so every code is checked in the same way. Passing the whole list into the aggregate would add a parameter to each factory, only to test one membership. The list is cached on the repository, so the check does not read the database for every order.

When to stop. Stop when the rule gains a condition about the order, such as "express delivery only for orders under 10 kilograms". Stop also when a lookup value gets rules of its own. Then the rule needs the order's data, so it belongs in the domain of the feature that uses the value. The use case loads what the rule needs, and passes it in as a value, as it passes the count to ShippingPolicy. The reference list then only supplies data.

The exception kind is allowed here, because the platform's exception kinds are plain Java. An application service may throw them, and the platform answers each kind with its status. For the three kinds, see the section Exceptions by kind, with stable codes. For the simple level of the reference feature, see the section The simple level: the reference feature.

What an anaemic model looks like, and what goes wrongnew#

A model whose entities hold data, with the rules in service classes, is called an anaemic model. For a fair comparison of that design with an outbox, see the section An anaemic model with an outbox, compared fairly. This section shows what the design does to the place of each rule:

Anaemic, C# 12
public class OrderService(ShopDb db)
{
    public async Task ShipAsync(Guid orderId)
    {
        var order = await db.Orders.FindAsync(orderId) ?? throw new OrderNotFound(orderId);
        if (order.Status != OrderStatus.Paid)
            throw new OrderNotPaid(orderId);

        order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped;
        order.ShippedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
    }
}
The order service
public void ship(Clock clock) {
    requireNotFinished();
    if (status != OrderStatus.PAID) {
        throw new OrderNotPaidException(id());
    }
    if (lines.stream().anyMatch(line -> !line.isPicked())) {
        throw new UnpickedLinesException(id());
    }
    status = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
    shippedAt = clock.instant();
    raise(new OrderShipped(id(), shippedAt));
}

Both panes refuse an unpaid order. In the C# pane, the check is in a service, and the entity has public setters. In the Java pane, the check, the change and the event are one method of the order. Three things go wrong with the anaemic form, and each one grows with the number of callers:

  • Anyone can skip the rule. A batch job, an import or a second endpoint can write order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped. The compiler allows it, because the setter is public. In the order service, no setter exists, and ArchitectureTest.entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters keeps it that way.
  • The event is forgotten. Each service method that ships must also add the event. A new method can forget it, and no test fails. In the order service, ship raises OrderShipped itself.
  • The time is hidden. DateTime.UtcNow inside the service reads the system clock. A test cannot fix the time, so it cannot check ShippedAt exactly. In the order service, ship receives a Clock.

These signs in a pull request show that a model is turning anaemic:

  • A new public setter appears, or a setter becomes public so that a service can set a value.
  • An application service tests an entity's fields with an if, and then changes that entity.
  • Code calls Instant.now() or LocalDate.now() instead of a Clock.
  • A test of a rule needs mocks of repositories.
  • The same check appears in two use cases.

Each sign has the same fix. Move the check and the change into a method of the aggregate, and let the use case call that method.

Name a domain service after its rulenew#

A class called OrderDomainService sounds like the right place for any logic about orders. So it collects all the logic that has no obvious home. After a year, it holds a discount calculation, a date helper and three rules that belong in the aggregate. The order service names its domain service after the one rule that it checks:

/**
 * The rule that needs two aggregates: an order cannot ship while a note on it needs action.
 *
 * <p>It is a domain service because neither aggregate holds the data alone. It is named after
 * the rule, not {@code OrderDomainService}, so unrelated code does not collect in it. It takes a
 * number, not the notes, so the order feature never sees note objects. It has no state, no
 * repository and no Spring annotation, and the order feature's configuration creates it.
 *
 * <p>The guarantee holds only at the moment of shipping. An agent may add a note that needs
 * action a second after the order shipped. The service accepts that, and the README records the
 * decision.
 */

The comment of ShippingPolicy gives each choice and its reason. It names OrderDomainService as the name to avoid. The name of the class states the rule, so unrelated code has no reason to go there. It takes a number, so the order feature never sees note objects. It has no state, no repository and no Spring annotation, so it stays plain Java.

A name says what the class decides or computes. These forms keep the class small:

NameWhat it says
ShippingPolicyit decides whether something is allowed, here shipping
a name ending in Calculator, such as a delivery charge calculatorit computes a value from the values it receives
a name ending in Checker or Validatoravoid it for a domain service, because it hides which rule is checked
OrderDomainService, OrderHelper or OrderManageravoid it, because it names no rule and attracts any code about orders

When a second rule across aggregates appears, write a second class with its own name. Two small policies are easier to find and to test than one service with two unrelated methods.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy does ShippingPolicy.assertCanShip take the number of notes that need action, and not the list of notes?
A number is all the rule needs. With a count, no note object crosses into the order feature, which may not hold another feature's entities. The note feature keeps its own model private, and counts with one query. The policy's test passes 0 or 2, with no note, no repository and no mock.
2
An expert asksWhy is "no note needs action" not an if in OrderService.ship?
A business expert would recognise the line as a rule. A rule in one use case is missing from the next use case that ships, such as a listener for a warehouse message. That use case must copy the check, or it forgets it. Its test would also need the mocks of the whole use case. In a domain service, every caller uses one check, tested with plain values.
3
A new rule says that an order may hold at most 50 lines. Lines are added only when the order is placed. Where does the check go, and why there?
In Order.place, with Guard.maxSize. The rule needs only the order's own data, so it belongs in the aggregate. Every path that creates an order meets it. A check in the controller or in one use case would miss every other path.
4
What is the business-expert test for a line in an application service?
Read the line in plain words to a person who knows the business but no code. If they would call it one of their rules, the line does not belong in the application service. It moves into the aggregate, a value object or a domain service.
5
TranslateWrite this C# exception for the shipping rule in the style of the order service. It extends the platform's kind for broken rules: 
public class OrderHasOpenActionsException(OrderId id, long notesNeedingAction)
    : BusinessRuleViolationException("ORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONS",
        $"Order {id} cannot ship while {notesNeedingAction} note(s) need action");
public class OrderHasOpenActionsException extends BusinessRuleViolationException {

    public OrderHasOpenActionsException(OrderId id, long notesNeedingAction) {
        super("ORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONS", "Order " + id + " cannot ship while " + notesNeedingAction
                + " note(s) need action");
    }
}

The Java class declares its constructor in its body, and the constructor calls super. The code is a stable text that clients may test, and the platform answers the exception with 422.

Wiring the service: the container in depth#

Wiring, configuration and use cases · Chapter 09· 29 min read· Quick reference

At startup, Spring creates every object of the order service and connects each one to the objects it needs. These objects are called beans. This chapter follows how the service uses the container. It covers where the beans come from and how they are injected. It also covers missing beans, a cycle between two features, work at startup, and proxies.

KindC#JavaNote
twistIServiceProvider, built from the IServiceCollectionApplicationContextthe object that creates and holds every bean, and that a test can ask for a bean Why
twistbuilder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>() for each class@Service on the class, found by scanning from OrderServiceApplicationSpring searches the package of the application class and every package below it Why
twistbuilder.Services.AddShopPlatform() from a NuGet packageauto-configuration in shop-platformthe platform's packages are not below com.acme.orderservice, so scanning never finds them Why
twista primary constructor with nine parametersone constructor with nine parameters, and no annotationSpring passes a bean for each parameter, and a unit test passes mocks with new Why
twistAddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderPersistenceAdapter>()@Component on OrderPersistenceAdapter, which implements OrderRepositorySpring finds the one bean that implements the interface, so no line maps one to the other Why
twistAddSingleton(sp => new ShippingPolicy())a @Bean method in OrderConfigthe domain class carries no Spring annotation, so a configuration class of the feature creates it Why
newno equivalent@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)Spring does not subclass the class, so a call from one @Bean method to another creates a second object Why
twista private nested class that implements the interfacenew WebMvcConfigurer() { ... } in a @Bean methoda Java anonymous class implements an interface inline, and C# has no such expression Why
twistTryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System) in the library@Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean Clock clock()the platform's bean backs off when the service or a test declares its own Why
twistsp.GetService<T>() returns null when nothing is registeredObjectProvider<T>.getIfAvailable()it returns null when no bean exists, and getObject() throws instead Why
trapGetRequiredService<T>() with two registrations returns the last oneObjectProvider<T>.getObject() with two beans throwsSpring refuses to choose between two candidates, so a second bean breaks the lookup Why
twistIEnumerable<IIntegrationEventMapper>ObjectProvider<IntegrationEventMapper>.orderedStream().toList()every bean of the type, in the order of @Order, and an empty list when there is none Why
twistnew TransactionScope() around the codean injected TransactionTemplateBoot adds the bean once a transaction manager exists, and the platform provides that manager Why
twistno equivalent built into the containerApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(event)the application context itself is the publisher, and Spring Modulith listens to it Why
twistInvalidOperationException: A circular dependency was detected, at the first resolvethe cycle report at startupboth containers refuse two classes whose constructors need each other Why
newLazy<OrderService>, which needs a registration of its own@Lazy on the constructor parameterSpring injects a proxy that finds the real bean at its first call Why
