newa decorator class that you register yourselfthe proxies of @Transactional, @PreAuthorize and @CacheableSpring wraps the bean, and every other bean receives the wrapper Why
trapa call to this.Method() inside a decorated classa call to this.method() inside a proxied beanthe call skips the proxy, so the service puts the cache on the repository that it calls Why
newno equivalentApplicationWiringTestthe whole container starts with every setting, and nothing connects to anything Why

The container and the beans of the order servicetwist#

For the order of these steps in a real start, with the time each one took, see the chapter Starting the service: from main() to the first request.

For the basics of beans and injection, see the chapter Dependency injection and configuration. This chapter starts where that chapter stops. It shows the container as the order service uses it.

An object that Spring creates and connects to other objects is called a bean. The object that creates and holds the beans is called the application context. Its interface is ApplicationContext, in the package org.springframework.context. It has the same purpose as the IServiceProvider of ASP.NET Core.

The beans of the order service come from three places. Component scanning finds the classes that carry an annotation such as @Service. The @Bean methods of a feature create the objects that carry no annotation. And auto-configuration adds the beans of the libraries:

A test can ask the context for a bean. The wiring test of the service does this to check two beans that the platform provides:

@Autowired
ApplicationContext context;

@Test
void theContextStartsWithThePlatformsBeans() {
    assertThat(context.getBean(PlatformTransactionManager.class)).isInstanceOf(MongoTransactionManager.class);
    assertThat(context.getBeansOfType(SecurityFilterChain.class)).containsOnlyKeys("platformSecurityFilterChain");
}
Reading the code
@Autowired

A test class has no constructor that Spring calls. So the test asks for the context with @Autowired on a field. Production code takes its beans through the constructor instead.

context.getBean(PlatformTransactionManager.class)

getBean returns the one bean of a type, like GetRequiredService<T>() in ASP.NET Core. Production code never calls it. Only a test or the container itself looks up beans by type.

context.getBeansOfType(SecurityFilterChain.class)

This method returns every bean of a type, in a map from bean name to bean. The test checks that only the platform's filter chain exists.

Every bean that the order service declares is a singleton, which is the default in Spring. One object serves every request, so no bean keeps the data of a request in a field. For the scopes, see the section Lifetimes. The quick reference at the end of this chapter maps each container idea to its ASP.NET Core match.

Where the beans come from: scanning and auto-configurationtwist#

The service starts from one class:

/**
 * Starts the order service, like {@code Program.cs} in ASP.NET Core.
 *
 * <p>{@code @SpringBootApplication} scans this package and every package below it for
 * components. The platform's beans come from its auto-configuration instead, because the
 * platform's packages are not below this one.
 */
@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderServiceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@SpringBootApplication combines three annotations. One of them is @ComponentScan, which starts component scanning in the package com.acme.orderservice. Spring then finds every class below that package that carries a stereotype. A stereotype is an annotation that marks a class as a bean. The order service uses these stereotypes:

StereotypeClasses in the order serviceWhy this one
@ServiceOrderService, NoteService, ReferenceDataServicethe use cases of each feature
@ComponentOrderPersistenceAdapter, StockAdapter, PaymentReceivedListener, OrderMetricsan adapter or a listener, which is neither a use case nor a controller
@RestControllerOrderController, NoteController, ReferenceDataControllerSpring MVC sends HTTP requests to these classes
@ConfigurationOrderConfig, StockClientConfig, ReferenceConfig, OpenApiConfiga class that holds @Bean methods or switches a feature on

Several of these classes are package-private, such as class OrderPersistenceAdapter with no public. Spring creates them all the same. Code in another package cannot use a package-private class. So the compiler also checks some of the layer rules. For those rules, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

The other annotation that matters here is @EnableAutoConfiguration. It makes Boot read the auto-configuration classes that each library lists in its Java archive (JAR). The platform library lists eight classes:

com.acme.platform.core.PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.core.PlatformWebAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.core.PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.core.openapi.PlatformOpenApiAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.mongo.PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.mongo.PlatformMongoAuditAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.mongo.PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.messaging.PlatformMessagingAutoConfiguration

The platform's classes are in com.acme.platform. That package is not below com.acme.orderservice, so scanning never finds them. The file above is the only way in. This is deliberate. Spring checks a condition such as "only if the service has no such bean" against the beans that it has processed so far. Boot guarantees that auto-configuration is processed after every bean definition of the service. So the Boot reference recommends bean conditions only on auto-configuration classes. For how the platform writes these classes, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

Each way to register a bean has its place:

WayUse it forIn the order service
a stereotype on the classyour own classesthe services, adapters, controllers and listeners
a @Bean method in a @Configuration classa class that must not carry a Spring annotation, or that needs settings to buildShippingPolicy, the stock HTTP client
auto-configurationa library that adds beans to every service, with conditionsthe clock, the filter chain, the transaction manager, the outbox

In ASP.NET Core, a library usually offers an extension method such as AddShopPlatform(), and Program.cs calls it. A Spring service writes no such line. Adding the library to the Project Object Model (POM) file is enough. For the first scanning trap, a class in a sibling package, see the section Which packages are scanned.

Constructor injection, with nine dependenciestwist#

C#
public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository orders, NoteService notes,
    ReferenceDataService referenceData, IStockChecker stock,
    ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy, IDomainEventPublisher events,
    IAuditLog audit, ITransactionRunner transaction,
    TimeProvider clock)
{
}
Java 25
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final NoteService notes;
    private final ReferenceDataService referenceData;
    private final StockChecker stock;
    private final ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy;
    private final DomainEventPublisher events;
    private final AuditLog audit;
    private final TransactionTemplate transaction;
    private final Clock clock;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, NoteService notes, ReferenceDataService referenceData,
                        StockChecker stock, ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy, DomainEventPublisher events,
                        AuditLog audit, TransactionTemplate transaction, Clock clock) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.notes = notes;
        this.referenceData = referenceData;
        this.stock = stock;
        this.shippingPolicy = shippingPolicy;
        this.events = events;
        this.audit = audit;
        this.transaction = transaction;
        this.clock = clock;
    }
Reading the code
public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, NoteService notes, ReferenceDataService referenceData,

The class has one constructor, so Spring uses it with no annotation. Spring finds a bean for each of the nine parameters, creates those beans first, and then calls the constructor.

private final OrderRepository orders;

Each dependency is a final field, set once in the constructor. Java has no primary constructors, so each field is written out.

AuditLog audit, TransactionTemplate transaction, Clock clock) {

Four of the nine beans come from the platform or from Boot. They are the event publisher, the audit log, the transaction template and the clock. The other five belong to the service.

The C# pane names its own interfaces, such as ITransactionRunner, because .NET has no matching built-in types. Each one has the role of the Java type at the same place in the list.

The unit test builds the same object with new, and no Spring context starts:

private final OrderService service = new OrderService(orders, notes, referenceData, stock, new ShippingPolicy(),
        events, audit, new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager()), CLOCK);

Each argument except two is a Mockito mock. new ShippingPolicy() is the real domain service, and the transaction template runs on a manager that does nothing. For this test in full, with the tests of every other use case, see the section How each use case is tested.

Nine parameters is a lot. A long constructor is a useful signal, because it shows every dependency in one place. When a service needs more, it usually holds too many use cases. For how to split it, see the section Splitting a large service.

Injecting an interface: the port and its adaptertwist#

OrderService asks for an OrderRepository. That type is an interface of the domain, and the persistence package implements it:

C#
builder.Services
    .AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderPersistenceAdapter>();

internal class OrderPersistenceAdapter : IOrderRepository
{
}
Java 25
@Component
class OrderPersistenceAdapter extends MongoAggregateRepository<Order, OrderId, OrderDocument> implements OrderRepository {

    private static final Sort NEWEST_FIRST = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "placedAt");

    private final OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments;

    OrderPersistenceAdapter(OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments, OrderDocumentMapper mapper) {
        super(orderDocuments, mapper);
        this.orderDocuments = orderDocuments;
    }
Reading the code
@Component

The adapter is a bean. Spring registers it under all its types, so a request for OrderRepository finds it. No line maps the interface to the class, as AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderPersistenceAdapter>() does in C#.

class OrderPersistenceAdapter extends MongoAggregateRepository<Order, OrderId, OrderDocument> implements OrderRepository {

The class extends the platform's base class for stored aggregates, and implements the domain's port. For the base class, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

OrderPersistenceAdapter(OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments, OrderDocumentMapper mapper) {

The constructor is package-private too. Spring can still call it.

The same happens for the port StockChecker. StockAdapter implements it, and the use case never knows that the answer comes over HTTP.

The rule is one bean for each port. If a second class implemented OrderRepository, Spring would stop at startup with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. ASP.NET Core would inject the last registration, with no error. For the ways to choose between two beans, see the section Multiple implementations.

A configuration class for the plain-Java domaintwist#

C#
builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp => new ShippingPolicy());
Java 25
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class OrderConfig {

    @Bean
    ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy() {
        return new ShippingPolicy();
    }
}

ShippingPolicy is the domain service that checks the rule across an order and its notes. The order feature keeps its domain in plain Java, with no Spring annotation. An architecture rule, ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava(), fails the build if a domain class imports Spring. So ShippingPolicy cannot carry @Component, and the feature declares it in OrderConfig instead. The @Bean method returns the object, and Spring makes it a bean named shippingPolicy.

The stock client needs settings to build, so it comes from a configuration class too:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class StockClientConfig {

    /** Binds the platform's reusable properties class to this client's prefix. */
    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")
    HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties() {
        return new HttpClientProperties();
    }

    @Bean
    StockHttpClient stockHttpClient(HttpClientFactory clients, HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties) {
        return clients.create(StockHttpClient.class, stockClientProperties);
    }
}
Reading the code
@ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")

On a @Bean method, this annotation fills the returned object from the settings under clients.stock. For this binding, see the section One properties class, bound once for each client.

StockHttpClient stockHttpClient(HttpClientFactory clients, HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties) {

Spring injects the parameters of a @Bean method, as it does for a constructor. HttpClientFactory comes from the platform. The second parameter is the bean that the method above creates, which Spring finds by its type.

return clients.create(StockHttpClient.class, stockClientProperties);

The factory builds a declarative HTTP client for the interface StockHttpClient. For the client, see the chapter Calling other services.

The two ways to make a domain class a bean, side by side:

WayWhat it costsWhen it is the better choice
@Bean in the feature's configuration classone more class, and a reader must look in two placesthe full style, where the domain stays plain Java and is tested with new
@Component on the domain classthe domain imports Spring, and the architecture rule must allow itthe light style, where the note entity already carries Spring Data annotations

The second way is simpler, and a careful team can use it well. One annotation is easy to read, and Spring does nothing else to the class. The order feature still uses @Bean, because its domain must compile and test with no framework. That keeps the rules of the business apart from the rules of the framework. For the levels of Domain-Driven Design (DDD) in this service, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

proxyBeanMethods = falsenew#

Every configuration class of the order service writes @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false). The setting changes how Spring treats the class itself, so it is worth knowing what it switches off.

By default, Spring does not use a @Configuration class as it is. It creates a subclass at runtime, with the Code Generation Library (CGLIB). The subclass intercepts each @Bean method. When one @Bean method calls another one directly, the subclass returns the bean that already exists. So a direct call still gives the one shared singleton.

proxyBeanMethods = false switches the subclass off. Spring then calls each @Bean method as a plain factory method. The Spring javadoc calls this "@Bean Lite Mode". It says that the mode works as if the class had no @Configuration at all.

A run for this book on Spring Framework 7.0.10 showed the difference. A configuration class had two @Bean methods, and the second one called the first one directly:

SettingThe class Spring usedThe object that the direct call returned
proxyBeanMethods = true, the defaultRun$FullConfig$$SpringCGLIB$$0, a subclassthe same bean that the context holds
proxyBeanMethods = falseRun$LiteConfig, the class itselfa second object, which the context does not hold
Gotcha

In lite mode, a call from one @Bean method to another creates a second object. The code compiles, and nothing warns you. Take the other bean as a parameter instead, as stockHttpClient does with stockClientProperties. A parameter works in both modes.

The order service turns the subclass off for two reasons. No @Bean method of the service calls another one, so the subclass would do nothing useful. And without the subclass, Spring does less work at startup. The class comment of OrderConfig says the same.

Every auto-configuration of the platform is in lite mode too. The annotation @AutoConfiguration is itself marked with @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false), and its javadoc says that the setting is always false. The nested configuration inside the messaging auto-configuration writes the setting again, because it is a plain @Configuration:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableScheduling
static class OutboxResendConfiguration {

A nested configuration class must be static, as the javadoc of @Configuration requires.

Keep the default only when your @Bean methods call each other on purpose. Older code does this often, and it is correct there. A factory lambda in ASP.NET Core has no such mechanism. It is always a plain call.

A bean written inline: an anonymous classtwist#

C#
// C# has no anonymous class that implements an interface,
// so the implementation needs a named class.
internal sealed class MdcMvcOptions(PathVariableMdcFilter filter)
    : IConfigureOptions<MvcOptions>
{
    public void Configure(MvcOptions options) =>
        options.Filters.Add(filter);
}

builder.Services
    .AddSingleton<IConfigureOptions<MvcOptions>, MdcMvcOptions>();
Java 25
@Bean
WebMvcConfigurer platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer(PlatformLoggingProperties properties) {
    PathVariableMdcInterceptor interceptor = new PathVariableMdcInterceptor(properties.getMdcPathVariables());
    return new WebMvcConfigurer() {
        @Override
        public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
            registry.addInterceptor(interceptor);
        }
    };
}
Reading the code
return new WebMvcConfigurer() {

This expression creates an object of a class that has no name. The class implements WebMvcConfigurer, and its body follows in the braces. Such a class is called an anonymous class. In C#, new IDisposable { } does not compile, with error CS0144.

public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {

WebMvcConfigurer is the hook of Spring model-view-controller (MVC) for code that changes its setup. It has many methods, each with a default body. The anonymous class overrides only the one it needs. Spring MVC calls every WebMvcConfigurer bean at startup, and this one adds the interceptor that puts path variables into the mapped diagnostic context (MDC).

registry.addInterceptor(interceptor);

The anonymous class reads interceptor, a local variable of the method. Java allows this only for a variable that never changes after it is set.

The C# pane shows the closest shape, a named class that adds an MVC filter. The point is that C# needs a named class where Java writes the class inline.

The companion uses anonymous classes in two more places. ArchitectureRules writes each custom rule as new ArchCondition<>(...) { ... }. And a test creates an exception whose constructor is protected, in one line:

// NotFoundException is non-sealed with a protected constructor, so a test can subclass it.
doThrow(new NotFoundException("ORDER_NOT_FOUND", "Order not found") {
}).when(orders).requireExists(ORDER_ID);

The empty braces after the constructor call make an anonymous subclass of NotFoundException. Its constructor is protected, so a test in another package cannot call new NotFoundException(...) alone. An anonymous subclass can call it. Use an anonymous class for a short implementation that one place needs. When the body grows past a few lines, give it a name. A lambda is shorter still, but only for an interface with one abstract method. For lambdas, see the section Lambdas and method references.

Defaults that a service can replace: the clocktwist#

C#
// in the library's AddShopPlatform()
services.TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
Java 25
/** The clock that the domain reads the time from. Code never calls {@code Instant.now()}. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
Clock clock() {
    return Clock.systemUTC();
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnMissingBean

Spring creates this bean only if no other bean of the type Clock exists. With no type in the brackets, the condition uses the return type of the method.

return Clock.systemUTC();

java.time.Clock gives the current time. systemUTC() reads the system clock in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). The type has the same purpose as TimeProvider in .NET 8.

The order domain never reads the time by itself. Each method that needs the time takes the clock as a parameter, as in order.ship(clock). A test passes a fixed clock, so the times in its events are known in advance. For Clock in the domain, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

The condition is how a service or a test replaces a platform bean. Every bean of PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration carries it. A service that declares its own Clock bean gets that one, and the platform's method never runs.

TryAddSingleton is like @ConditionalOnMissingBean, but it depends on the order of the registrations. A run on .NET 10 showed both orders:

Registrations, in orderWhat GetRequiredService<TimeProvider>() returned
the service's AddSingleton, then the library's TryAddSingletonthe service's clock, and TryAdd added nothing
the library's TryAddSingleton, then the service's AddSingletonthe service's clock, but both registrations stay in the collection

In Spring, the order of your own code does not matter. Auto-configuration always runs after the service's own beans are known, so the condition sees them. The order between two auto-configurations does matter. For that, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

ObjectProvider: a bean that may be missing, or new each timenew#

The platform builds clients for other services with an HttpClientFactory. The factory needs two things that a plain constructor parameter cannot give. It needs a new Boot RestClient.Builder for each client. And it needs the client registrations of Spring Security, but only if the service has any.

A parameter of type ObjectProvider<T> solves both. An ObjectProvider does not hold a bean. It finds the bean when the code asks, and the code decides what to do when there is none:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
HttpClientFactory httpClientFactory(ObjectProvider<RestClient.Builder> restClientBuilders,
                                    ObjectProvider<ClientRegistrationRepository> registrations,
                                    ObjectProvider<OAuth2AuthorizedClientService> authorizedClients) {
    Supplier<OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager> tokenManager = () -> {
        ClientRegistrationRepository repository = registrations.getIfAvailable();
        if (repository == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("A client asks for a token, but no "
                    + "spring.security.oauth2.client.registration is configured");
        }
        return new AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(repository, authorizedClients.getObject());
    };
    return new HttpClientFactory(restClientBuilders::getObject, tokenManager);
}
Reading the code
ObjectProvider<RestClient.Builder> restClientBuilders,

ObjectProvider is in the package org.springframework.beans.factory. The type argument is the bean it finds. Spring injects the provider at once, even when no such bean exists.

Supplier<OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager> tokenManager = () -> {

A Supplier<T> is a function with no parameters that returns a value, like Func<T> in C#. The lambda runs only when a client asks for tokens. So a service with no client registrations still starts.

ClientRegistrationRepository repository = registrations.getIfAvailable();

getIfAvailable() returns the bean, or null when there is none. The factory then throws an error with a clear message, at the moment a client needs a token.

authorizedClients.getObject()

getObject() returns the bean, and throws when there is none. Here the bean must exist, because Boot creates it together with the registrations.

restClientBuilders::getObject

This is a method reference. It turns the method getObject of this provider into a Supplier, which the factory calls once for each client. Boot's RestClient.Builder bean is a prototype, so each call returns a new builder. One client's settings then never leak into another client.

A run for this book recorded what each method of ObjectProvider does:

MethodNo beanOne beanTwo beans
getObject()throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionExceptionthe beanthrows NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
getIfAvailable()nullthe beanthrows NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
getIfAvailable(supplier)the supplier's valuethe beanthrows NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
getIfUnique()nullthe beannull
orderedStream()an empty streamthe beanboth, in the order of @Order
stream()an empty streamthe beanboth, in the order of registration

The closest match in ASP.NET Core is to inject IServiceProvider and call GetService<T>(). It also returns null when nothing is registered. GetRequiredService<T>() throws InvalidOperationException: No service for type ... has been registered. The two containers differ when there are two candidates.

Gotcha

Spring refuses to choose between two beans. In a run on .NET 10, two registrations of one interface made GetRequiredService return the last one. In Spring, getObject() and a constructor parameter both throw NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. So a second bean of a type that the platform looks up breaks the lookup. Mark one bean @Primary, or ask for all of them, as the next section does.

Use ObjectProvider only where its extra behaviour is needed. An ordinary dependency is a constructor parameter, which shows the dependency and fails at startup when it is missing. An ObjectProvider fails later, at the call, and only if the code asks for a bean that is not there.

Every implementation of an interfacetwist#

C#
public class OutboxDomainEventPublisher(
    IEnumerable<IIntegrationEventMapper> mappers)
{
    private readonly List<IIntegrationEventMapper> _mappers =
        mappers.ToList();
}
Java 25
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DomainEventPublisher.class)
OutboxDomainEventPublisher domainEventPublisher(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher,
                                                ObjectProvider<IntegrationEventMapper> mappers) {
    return new OutboxDomainEventPublisher(publisher, mappers.orderedStream().toList());
}
Reading the code
ObjectProvider<IntegrationEventMapper> mappers) {

Each feature that publishes events to other services has one IntegrationEventMapper. The order feature has OrderIntegrationEventMapper, and the note feature has none.

mappers.orderedStream().toList()

orderedStream() returns every mapper bean, sorted by @Order when a bean has one. toList() collects them into a list that cannot change. A service with no mapper gets an empty list.

The migration runner collects its migrations the same way:

MongoMigrationRunner mongoMigrationRunner(MongoTemplate mongo, ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations, Clock clock,
                                          @Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl) {
    return new MongoMigrationRunner(mongo, migrations.orderedStream().toList(), clock, lockTtl);
}

Each migration of the service, such as V001CreateIndexes, is a @Component that implements MongoMigration. The runner sorts them by their ID itself, so the order of the stream does not matter there. For the runner, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

A List<IntegrationEventMapper> parameter would also work. A run on Spring Framework 7.0.10 checked the case with no bean. The List parameter received an empty list, and orderedStream() gave an empty stream. Both follow @Order. The platform uses the provider, as its other lookups do. In your own code, prefer the plain List parameter. It is shorter, and a reader sees the dependency at once. For List and Map parameters, see the section Injecting every implementation: List and Map.

IEnumerable<T> in ASP.NET Core gives the registrations in registration order. Spring sorts a List parameter and orderedStream() by @Order. So give the beans an @Order when their order matters.

The TransactionTemplate beantwist#

C#
using var scope = new TransactionScope(
    TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled);
var saved = SaveAndPublish(order);
var noteIds = notes.AddNotes(saved.Id, firstNotes);
scope.Complete();
Java 25
return transaction.execute(status -> {
    Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);
    Order saved = saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_PLACED);        // aggregate 1
    List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction
    return new PlacedOrder(saved.id().value(), noteIds);
});
Reading the code
return transaction.execute(status -> {

transaction is the injected TransactionTemplate, from the package org.springframework.transaction.support. execute starts a transaction, runs the lambda, and commits. It returns the value of the lambda.

List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction

addNotes is a @Transactional method of another bean. It joins the transaction that the template started.

Nobody in the order service declares a TransactionTemplate. Boot adds a bean named transactionTemplate as soon as a transaction manager exists. A run for this book showed it. Without a manager, the context held no template at all.

Boot creates no transaction manager for MongoDB. The platform declares one, before Boot's transaction setup runs:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(TransactionManager.class)
MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory databaseFactory) {
    return new MongoTransactionManager(databaseFactory);
}

So the template and every @Transactional method use the same MongoTransactionManager. The wiring test checks that this manager is the one in the context. A run for this book read the settings of Boot's template. They are the defaults, with propagation REQUIRED, the default isolation and no timeout.

One difference from @Transactional matters. The template rolls back on any exception that leaves the lambda, also a checked one. @Transactional commits on a checked exception by default. For both, see the chapter Transactions in depth. For why place uses the template, see the section Placing an order: the stock call before the transaction.

ApplicationEventPublisher: the container as an event bustwist#

The platform's outbox publishes each domain event through Spring's in-process event bus. Spring Modulith listens on that bus and stores each event with the change. The publisher is a plain constructor parameter:

private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;
private final List<IntegrationEventMapper> mappers;

public OutboxDomainEventPublisher(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher, List<IntegrationEventMapper> mappers) {
    this.publisher = publisher;
    this.mappers = List.copyOf(mappers);
}

@Override
public void publish(List<DomainEvent> events) {
    if (events.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }
    if (!TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Publish domain events inside the use case's transaction, so they are stored with the change");
    }
    for (DomainEvent event : events) {
        publisher.publishEvent(event);
        mappers.stream()
                .map(mapper -> mapper.toIntegrationEvent(event))
                .flatMap(Optional::stream)
                .forEach(publisher::publishEvent);
    }
}
Reading the code
private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;

ApplicationEventPublisher is in the package org.springframework.context. Any bean can ask for it. In a run on Spring Framework 7.0.10, the injected publisher was the application context itself.

publisher.publishEvent(event);

publishEvent(Object) gives the event to every listener of its type. The event can be any object, here a domain event record of the order feature.

.flatMap(Optional::stream)

Each mapper returns an Optional, which is empty for an event that the mapper does not publish. Optional::stream is a method reference. It turns each optional into a stream of zero or one element, so flatMap keeps only the integration events.

.forEach(publisher::publishEvent);

Another method reference, this time to a method of one object. It means the same as e -> publisher.publishEvent(e).

The class is plain Java with no annotation, and the platform's @Bean method creates it. Its constructor takes a List, so a unit test passes a list and a mock publisher. The bean method converts the provider to that list.

The domain itself never sees ApplicationEventPublisher. Use cases call the platform's port DomainEventPublisher, and only this adapter knows Spring.

ASP.NET Core has no event bus in its container. The closest match is the library MediatR. A run for this book showed that its Publish runs the handlers on the caller's thread. A failing handler fails the caller, as with publishEvent. For the listeners, the outbox and the transaction check, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox. For plain application events, see the section Application events.

The cycle between the order and note featurestwist#

Two use cases make the order and note features call each other. To ship an order, OrderService asks NoteService how many notes need action. To add a note, NoteService asks OrderService whether the order exists. So each constructor needs the other bean:

C#
public class OrderService(NoteService notes) { }
public class NoteService(OrderService orders) { }

// At the first GetRequiredService<OrderService>():
// InvalidOperationException: A circular dependency
// was detected for the service of type 'OrderService'.
Java 25
public NoteService(NoteRepository notes, @Lazy OrderService orders, ReferenceDataService referenceData,
                   DomainEventPublisher events, AuditLog audit, CurrentActor currentActor, Clock clock) {
    this.notes = notes;
    this.orders = orders;
    this.referenceData = referenceData;
    this.events = events;
    this.audit = audit;
    this.currentActor = currentActor;
    this.clock = clock;
}

Without @Lazy, Spring cannot create either bean first. Boot refuses such a cycle by default and stops at startup with a report that starts with this line:

The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:

A box diagram follows the words form a cycle:, and it names each bean in the loop. In a run for this book, a cycle of constructors, a cycle of setters and a bean that injected itself all failed this way. The setting spring.main.allow-circular-references is false by default.

The two containers fail at different times. In a run on .NET 10, building the provider worked, and the first resolve threw. With ValidateOnBuild set, the build failed instead. Spring creates every singleton at startup, so the cycle always shows when the service starts. For the full report and the old behaviour, see the section Circular dependencies.

@Lazy: a proxy that breaks the cycle, and the other ways outnew#

The note service marks its OrderService parameter with @Lazy, from the package org.springframework.context.annotation. On a parameter, the annotation does not delay the bean. It makes Spring inject a stand-in object. Such an object is called a proxy.

The javadoc of @Lazy calls it a lazy-resolution proxy. It finds the real bean at the first call, and keeps it for a singleton. In a run on Spring Framework 7.0.10, a test class Orders was injected as Run$Orders$$SpringCGLIB$$0, and a call through it reached the real bean.

The javadoc also names the cost. The proxy is always injected, even if the real bean does not exist. So a missing bean shows only as an exception at the first call, not at startup. In the order service the bean always exists, and the wiring test starts the context with both services.

ASP.NET Core has no built-in form. A run on .NET 10 showed that a constructor parameter of type Lazy<OrderService> fails with Unable to resolve service for type 'System.Lazy`1[OrderService]'. It works only after you register Lazy<T> yourself.

A cycle is a warning about the design, not about the container. Two features that call each other cannot change, be tested or move to another service apart. These are the ways out, from the container's side:

Way outWhat it gets rightWhat it costs
@Lazy on one parameterone annotation, and the constructor still lists the dependencythe cycle stays, and a missing bean fails only at the first call
ObjectProvider<OrderService> in NoteServicethe code says plainly that it looks the bean up laterthe same cycle, with more code at each call
one dependency made one-way: the note controller calls requireExistsno cycle, and the note service needs nothing from ordersa caller of NoteService.addNote must remember the check
a third bean that both features useno cycle, if the shared question has its own nameone more class, and here the questions belong to their features
an event in place of one callno compile-time dependency at allonly for "something happened", never for a check that must answer now
spring.main.allow-circular-references=truenothing in new codeit allows cycles of setters and fields again, and hides every new cycle

The book recommends the one-way dependency for a new service. It removes the cycle at the cost of one line in a controller. The note feature's check that the order exists then moves to each entry point, which is a risk when a second entry point arrives. For the design side of these ways out, see the section Two features that call each other.

Pragmatic choice: A cycle between two features, broken with @Lazy

The strict rule. Dependencies between features go one way. A cycle means that the two features are one feature, or that a third concept is missing.

What we do. OrderService and NoteService depend on each other, and @Lazy on one constructor parameter lets the container create them. The README records the cycle and the ways out.

Why. Each call asks the owner of the data. The note service checks the order through the order feature, and the order feature counts notes through the note feature. Each check stays in one place, and the architecture rule still allows only calls through the application package.

When to stop. Stop when a third feature joins the loop. Stop also when one of the two features must move to its own service. Then make one dependency one-way.

The class comment of NoteService records the reason, next to the code:

/**
 * The use cases of the note feature, with the same steps as every change: load, apply the
 * rule, save, publish, audit.
 *
 * <p>The order feature calls {@link #addNotes} and {@link #countNeedingAction}, and this class
 * calls {@code OrderService.requireExists}. The two features depend on each other, which Spring
 * cannot build with constructor injection alone. {@link Lazy} injects a proxy for the order
 * service, which finds the real bean at the first call. A two-way dependency is a warning sign;
 * the README lists the ways out.

A comment like this one belongs on every @Lazy that breaks a cycle. Without it, the next developer removes the annotation and the service stops at startup.

The unit test is not affected. NoteServiceTest passes a Mockito mock of OrderService to the constructor, and no proxy is involved.

Work at startup: migrations before trafficnew#

The service must not answer a request or take a message before its indexes and seed data exist. The platform's migration runner therefore runs at a precise moment of startup. The class implements one interface:

public class MongoMigrationRunner implements SmartInitializingSingleton {
// ...
    @Override
    public void afterSingletonsInstantiated() {
        acquireLock();
        try {
            Set<String> applied = appliedIds();
            for (MongoMigration migration : migrations) {
                if (!applied.contains(migration.id())) {
                    run(migration);
                }
            }
        } finally {
            releaseLock();
        }
    }
Reading the code
public class MongoMigrationRunner implements SmartInitializingSingleton {

SmartInitializingSingleton is in the package org.springframework.beans.factory. Its javadoc says that Spring calls the method "right at the end of the singleton pre-instantiation phase". At that point every singleton bean exists.

acquireLock();

Several instances may start at once, and only one may migrate. For the lock, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

Spring starts a context in steps. The source of Spring Framework 7.0.10 and Boot 4.1.2 gives their order:

Steps 2 and 3 come from the method refresh of AbstractApplicationContext. It creates the singletons, which ends with the call to afterSingletonsInstantiated. Only then does it start the lifecycle beans. Boot starts the web server in such a bean, WebServerStartStopLifecycle. The listener containers of Spring Cloud AWS are SmartLifecycle beans too. A run for this book also showed the order, with a SmartInitializingSingleton that printed before a SmartLifecycle started.

Three places could run the migrations:

PlaceWhat it gets rightWhat it costs
afterSingletonsInstantiated, the platform's choiceno request and no message can arrive before the data is readyno port is open while it waits, so a probe gets no answer
an ApplicationRunnerthe web server answers probes, and readiness stays OUT_OF_SERVICE meanwhilethe SQS listeners have already started, so a message can arrive before the indexes exist
a separate job before the deploymentthe service starts fast, and one job migrates onceone more thing to deploy, and the code and the data can be out of step

The ApplicationRunner is the careful choice for many services. Readiness keeps the orchestrator's traffic away while it runs, and the probes answer. It is the wrong choice here only because of the queue listener. For the readiness run, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

The platform's choice has one cost to plan for. An instance that waits for another's migration lock has no open port, so the orchestrator's startup probe must allow for that wait. The local compose file allows 60 seconds:

# Migrations run before the web server starts, and an instance may wait for another's
# migration lock. Allow for that before failed checks count.
start_period: 60s

The setting start_period: 60s gives the container a minute before a failed check counts. A production orchestrator needs the same allowance, as long as the lock can last.

ASP.NET Core runs each IHostedService.StartAsync before the server listens. A run on .NET 10 showed it. Inside StartAsync, a connection to the service's own port was refused. After StartAsync of the host, the same connection worked. So StartAsync is the closest match to step 2. For ApplicationRunner, @PostConstruct and the bean lifecycle, see the section Work at startup.

Where the service relies on proxiesnew#

Several annotations in the order service do nothing by themselves. Spring reads them and wraps the bean in a proxy. Every other bean then receives the proxy, not the object. For how a proxy works, see the section What a proxy actually is. These are the places where the service needs one:

AnnotationOnWhat the proxy does
@Transactionalthe methods of OrderService and NoteService that change datastarts a transaction, or joins one, and commits or rolls back
@OrdersRead and @OrdersWriteeach controller methodchecks the scope before the method runs, because each carries @PreAuthorize
@Cacheable("reference-data")ReferenceItemRepository.findByTypeOrderByCodeAscreturns the cached list for the same type, and calls the method only on a miss
@Lazythe OrderService parameter of NoteServicefinds the real OrderService at the first call

A run for this book showed the class of such a bean. A @Transactional service was injected as OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0, a subclass made at runtime. A subclass cannot override a final method. So the service classes and their public methods are never final. For that trap, see the section Two kinds of proxy.

A typical use case shows the annotation that the proxy reads:

@Transactional
public void cancel(OrderId orderId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    order.cancel(clock);
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_CANCELLED);
}

The controller calls cancel on the proxy. The proxy starts the transaction, calls the method of the real object, and commits when the method returns.

The place method has no @Transactional. It calls the TransactionTemplate instead, which is an ordinary object with no proxy. The template can make only part of the method transactional, and a proxy always wraps the whole method.

For the method security interceptor and its order against the transaction, see the section How method security works. For the cache, see the chapter Caching and scheduling.

Self-invocation: why the cache is on the repositorytrap#

The reference service has two methods that read a lookup list. list returns it to the API, and requireActive checks a code against it. Both read the list through the repository:

    public List<ReferenceItemView> list(String type) {
        if (!ReferenceTypes.ALL.contains(type)) {
            throw new UnknownReferenceTypeException(type);
        }
        return items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream().map(ReferenceItemView::from).toList();
    }
// ...
    public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
        boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
                .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
        if (!known) {
            throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
        }
    }

A natural first design puts @Cacheable on list. Then requireActive would call list. That call would go to this, the object inside the proxy. It would skip the proxy and the cache, and every order would read the database.

Gotcha

A call from one method of a bean to another method of the same bean skips the proxy. The annotation on the called method then does nothing, with no warning. A hand-written decorator in C# is skipped in the same way. But in C# you wrote the decorator yourself, so you can see it. Spring creates the proxy for you, so the skipped call is harder to see. For the prediction and the fixes, see the section Self-invocation: a call from inside the class.

The companion puts the cache where every call passes through a proxy, on the repository:

/**
 * Reads lookup values, and caches each list by its type.
 *
 * <p>The cache is on the repository, not on the service, for a reason. {@code @Cacheable} works
 * through a proxy around the bean, so only calls from another bean pass through it. The service
 * calls this method from two of its own methods; if the cache were on the service, the call from
 * {@code requireActive} to {@code list} would skip the proxy and the cache.
 *
 * <p>The cached list is shared by every caller, so callers must not change it.
 */
public interface ReferenceItemRepository extends MongoRepository<ReferenceItemDocument, String> {

    @Cacheable("reference-data")
    List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);
}

@Cacheable("reference-data") keeps one list for each type. Both methods of the service call another bean, the repository, so both calls pass through its proxy. The journey test OrderJourneyIT.lookupValuesAreSeededAndCached checks that the lists are cached.

The same rule explains two choices in the use cases. OrderService.place calls notes.addNotes on another bean, so its @Transactional joins the transaction. And the private helper saveAndPublish carries no annotation, because a call to it never passes a proxy.

A test that starts the whole containernew#

Most mistakes of wiring show only when the context starts. A missing bean, a cycle, a property that does not bind or a wrong order of auto-configurations all stop the startup. Unit tests never start the context, so they cannot catch them. The order service has one test that starts it with every setting, while nothing connects to anything:

/**
 * Starts the whole service with every setting, while nothing connects to anything. It catches a
 * missing bean, a cycle, a bad property or a wrong auto-configuration order in seconds, without
 * Docker. The settings are in {@code application-wiring.yml}.
 */
@SpringBootTest
@org.springframework.test.context.ActiveProfiles("wiring")
class ApplicationWiringTest {
Reading the code
@SpringBootTest

The test starts the whole application context, as main would.

@org.springframework.test.context.ActiveProfiles("wiring")

The test switches on the profile wiring, so Boot also reads application-wiring.yml. That file points every connection at port 1, where nothing listens, and turns the migrations and the outbox resender off.

The MongoDB client does not need a server when Spring creates it. Only a database operation waits for a server, and the wiring profile limits that wait to 100 milliseconds. So the context starts without a database. The test then asserts a few beans, as the first section of this chapter showed. For the profile file, see the section The settings files and the profiles. For the other kinds of test, see the chapter Testing in depth.

ASP.NET Core has ValidateOnBuild. In a run on .NET 10, it found the cycle when the provider was built. The wiring test goes further, because it starts the real context and binds every setting.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksEvery configuration class of the order service writes @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false). Why is that safe here, and when would it break?
The setting stops Spring from subclassing the class with CGLIB. Without the subclass, a direct call from one @Bean method to another creates a second object. No @Bean method of the service calls another one. Each one takes the beans it needs as parameters, which works in both modes. It would break if someone added a direct call, such as new Uses(policy()).
2
An expert asksWhy does the platform run the migrations in afterSingletonsInstantiated, and not in an ApplicationRunner?
Spring calls afterSingletonsInstantiated after every singleton exists and before the lifecycle beans start. Those beans include the web server and the SQS listener containers. So no request and no message can arrive before the indexes and seed data exist. An ApplicationRunner runs after the listeners have started, so a message could arrive first. The cost is that no port is open while the runner waits for a lock.
3
The note service takes @Lazy OrderService orders in its constructor. What does Spring inject, and when does it find the real bean?
Spring injects a lazy-resolution proxy, a subclass made with CGLIB. The proxy finds the real OrderService bean at the first call, and keeps it, because the bean is a singleton. So Spring can create the note service before the order service exists. A missing bean would show only at that first call.
4
TranslateThe order domain is plain Java, and its class ShippingPolicy carries no annotation. Write this registration as the order feature's configuration class: 
builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp => new ShippingPolicy());
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class OrderConfig {

    @Bean
    ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy() {
        return new ShippingPolicy();
    }
}

The @Bean method returns the object, and Spring makes it a singleton bean named shippingPolicy. Component scanning finds OrderConfig, because its package is under the package of the application class. proxyBeanMethods = false is safe, because no @Bean method calls another one.

Each container idea of the order service, next to its ASP.NET Core match:
