Starting the service: from main() to the first request#

Wiring, configuration and use cases · Chapter 10· 29 min read

The order service starts in sixteen seconds on the author's laptop. In that time Spring reads the settings and writes a recipe for every bean. It builds 658 objects in dependency order and wraps fourteen of them in proxies. Then it runs the migrations and starts Tomcat. This chapter follows that start as one story. One bean, OrderService, is in every scene.

KindC#JavaNote
twistWebApplication.CreateBuilder(args), Build(), then Run()SpringApplication.run(OrderServiceApplication.class, args)one call does all three steps, and nine events mark its phases Why
twistbuilder.Configuration, read when Build() runsthe Environment, assembled before the context existsthe settings are complete before any bean is defined, and an EnvironmentPostProcessor can still add to them Why
newno equivalentApplicationContextInitializer, and the four early eventscode that runs before any bean definition exists, registered in spring.factories and never as a bean Why
twistbuilder.Services, a list of ServiceDescriptorthe bean definitions, written by ConfigurationClassPostProcessora recipe for each bean, with its class, its scope and its constructor, and no object yet Why
twistservices.AddShopPlatform(), which every app must callthe imports file, read by a DeferredImportSelectorauto-configuration is registered after the service's own definitions, so its conditions can see them Why
newno equivalentBeanFactoryPostProcessora hook that edits the recipes before the first object exists, and the step that took six of the sixteen seconds Why
trapa wiring error appears at the first resolve, unless ValidateOnBuild is onevery singleton is created at startup, dependency firsta bean that cannot be built stops the start, so a broken wiring never reaches a request Why
twistthe container calls the constructor, and then nothing morethe constructor, then the Aware callbacks, then the post-processors, which also run @PostConstructa fixed order of fourteen callbacks, and the proxy is made in the last one Why
newa decorator class that you registerthe auto-proxy creator, a BeanPostProcessorit wraps the bean in postProcessAfterInitialization, so the object other beans receive is the wrapper Why
twistIHostedService.StartAsync, before Kestrel listensSmartInitializingSingleton, then SmartLifecycle.start() in phase orderthe migrations run when every singleton exists, and Tomcat starts in a later phase Why
twistthe ApplicationStarted tokenApplicationRunner, then ApplicationReadyEventthe runners run after the server listens, and readiness changes to accepting traffic after them Why
twistSIGTERM, then StopAsync in reverse order, with 30 secondsthe shutdown hook closes the context: Lifecycle stop in reverse phase order, then @PreDestroythe same shape as .NET, but Spring gives each phase 30 seconds and .NET gives the whole stop 30 seconds Why
newno equivalent/actuator/startup, /actuator/conditions, /actuator/beans and /actuator/proxiesfour reports of one start, three from Spring Boot and one from the platform Why

Scene 1: the clock startstwist#

For the container itself, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth. That chapter shows what the container holds. This chapter shows the order in which the container fills, with the time each step took. The times come from one start of the order service in Docker, on 26 October 2026. The laptop had an Intel i9-8950HK, and the container ran Java 25.0.4.1. Your numbers will differ. The order will not.

In ASP.NET Core, three lines start a service. In Spring Boot, one line does the same work:

C#, Program.cs
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddShopPlatform();
var app = builder.Build();
app.Run();
Java, OrderServiceApplication
SpringApplication application = new SpringApplication(OrderServiceApplication.class);
if (Boolean.getBoolean("shop.startup.trace")) {
    application.setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(4096));
}
application.run(args);

The C# side calls app.Run() on an object that Build() made. The Java side calls application.run(args) on the application itself. The platform needs no line of its own, because scene 4 shows how Spring finds it. SpringApplication.run does four things, in this order. It creates the application context. It turns the command line into property sources. It refreshes the context, which creates every singleton bean. And it calls the runner beans. Spring Boot publishes an event at each phase of that work. Nine events mark the whole start, and two of them change the liveness probe and the readiness probe:

EventWhen Spring Boot publishes itWhat exists at that moment
ApplicationStartingEventat the start of run(), before any worknothing, apart from the listeners
ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEventwhen the Environment is known, before the context is createdevery setting
ApplicationContextInitializedEventwhen the context exists and the initializers have run, before any bean definition is loadedan empty context
ApplicationPreparedEventjust before the refresh starts, after the bean definitions are loadedthe recipe of every bean, and no object
ApplicationStartedEventafter the refresh, before the runnersevery bean, and a listening server
AvailabilityChangeEvent, LivenessState.CORRECTright after ApplicationStartedEventthe liveness probe says live
ApplicationReadyEventafter the runnerseverything
AvailabilityChangeEvent, ReadinessState.ACCEPTING_TRAFFICright after ApplicationReadyEventthe readiness probe says ready
ApplicationFailedEventif any step throwsa failed start

Four events come before the refresh. Four come after it. The refresh is where the time goes. The startup report of the run, which the last scene explains, gives these times for the top-level steps:

StepTookWhat happened
spring.boot.application.starting194 msthe listeners were found and told
spring.boot.application.environment-prepared975 msthe settings were read, from every source
spring.boot.application.context-prepared5 msthe context was created and initialised
spring.boot.application.context-loaded13 msthe application class was registered as the first bean definition
spring.context.refresh14,152 msevery bean was defined, created and started
spring.boot.application.started227 msthe started event was published, after the Started line
spring.boot.application.ready2 msthe ready event was published, after the runners

The line that a reader looks for first is the last one Spring Boot logs. The run printed this line. The two numbers differ because the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) was running for three seconds before main started:

c.a.o.OrderServiceApplication : Started OrderServiceApplication in 16.207 seconds (process running for 19.106)

The Started line names the class that holds main. Spring Boot logs it under that class's logger. The first number is the time from the start of run(). The second number is the time since the JVM started. The three seconds between them belong to the JVM. Two chapters after the chapter Running locally and shipping explain them, one on memory and one on code.

Pragmatic choice: A trace switch in main()

The strict rule. The main method of a service does nothing but call SpringApplication.run. Everything else is configuration.

What we do. When the system property shop.startup.trace is true, main gives the application a BufferingApplicationStartup. That object keeps every startup step with its timing, and the Actuator startup endpoint reports them.

Why. The buffer can only be set before run(), so no bean and no setting can do it. And the buffer holds up to 4,096 steps in memory that a running service never reads, so it is off by default.

When to stop. If a team wants the trace on in every environment, move the decision to a SpringApplicationBuilder in the platform, and keep main to one line.

What you can see here#

The Started line, and the two numbers in it. With the trace switch on, the report at /actuator/startup gives every step. The last scene shows how to read it.

What you can hook here#

A listener for the four early events cannot be a bean, because no bean exists yet. Spring Boot finds such a listener in two ways. The application can call SpringApplication.addListeners(...) before run(). Or a library lists the listener in its META-INF/spring.factories file under the key org.springframework.context.ApplicationListener. The platform uses the second way for the next scene's hook.

Scene 2: the settings, before anything elsetwist#

The first second of the start assembles the Environment. It is the object that holds every setting, as one ordered list of property sources. Spring Boot reads fifteen kinds of source, and a later source wins over an earlier one. The chapter Configuration in depth covers the list and the rules. For this scene, four facts matter:

  • The settings files, application.yml and the profile files, are loaded by a class called ConfigDataEnvironmentPostProcessor.
  • That class is an EnvironmentPostProcessor, one among several that Spring Boot ships.
  • Every EnvironmentPostProcessor runs when Spring Boot publishes ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent, before the context exists.
  • The ones that implement Ordered run in their order. The config data one has the order HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10, so it runs early.

The platform adds its defaults in the same phase. Its post-processor reads every META-INF/platform-defaults/*.properties file on the classpath and adds each one last, so a service's own settings always win:

public class PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor implements EnvironmentPostProcessor, Ordered {

    private static final String DEFAULTS = "classpath*:META-INF/platform-defaults/*.properties";

    @Override
    public void postProcessEnvironment(ConfigurableEnvironment environment, SpringApplication application) {
        try {
            Resource[] files = new PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver().getResources(DEFAULTS);
            Arrays.sort(files, Comparator.comparing(Resource::getFilename));
            for (Resource file : files) {
                environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new PropertiesPropertySource(
                        "platform-defaults:" + file.getFilename(), PropertiesLoaderUtils.loadProperties(file)));
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not load the platform defaults", e);
        }

        if (environment.getProperty("platform.logging.structured", Boolean.class, true)) {
            environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new MapPropertySource("platform-defaults:structured-logging",
                    Map.of("logging.structured.format.console", "ecs")));
        }
    }

    @Override
    public int getOrder() {
        // Run after Spring Boot has loaded application.yml, so the check above can read it.
        return Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE;
    }
}
Reading the code
implements EnvironmentPostProcessor, Ordered

The class is not a bean. Spring Boot creates it with reflection, before the context exists. So it has no constructor dependencies, and it cannot inject anything.

environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new PropertiesPropertySource(

A property source added last has the lowest precedence. The service's application.yml, its environment variables and its command line were all added before this one. So each of them wins over a platform default.

return Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE;

The lowest precedence runs last. So this class runs after the config data post-processor, and it can read a setting from application.yml to decide whether to switch on JSON logs.

Spring Boot finds this class through a file in the platform jar. The file is not the auto-configuration imports file. It is the older spring.factories file, which Spring Boot still reads for the hooks that run before the context exists:

# EnvironmentPostProcessor is still registered here, not in the AutoConfiguration.imports file.
org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor=\
com.acme.platform.core.config.PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor

The key of the line is the full name of the interface, org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor. In Spring Boot 3 the interface was in the package org.springframework.boot.env. Spring Boot 4 moved it, and the key moved with it.

ASP.NET Core has the same idea in a different shape. builder.Configuration is a list of configuration providers, and a later provider wins. The difference is when the list is complete. In ASP.NET Core, code can add providers until Build(). In Spring Boot, the Environment is complete when ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent has been handled, one second into the start, and no bean can change which source wins.

What you can see here#

The endpoint /actuator/env lists every property source in order, with each value and the source it came from. The chapter Which source wins reads one. In the startup report, the step spring.boot.application.environment-prepared took 975 ms in the run. The report does not split that time. It shows only the total for the step.

What you can hook here#

An EnvironmentPostProcessor, registered in spring.factories. Use one when a library must set defaults for every service, as the platform does, or when a setting must be computed from another. Do not use one to read a secret from a vault at startup. Spring Boot's own config data loaders exist for that, and they handle the order and the failure cases.

Scene 3: the context exists, and nothing is in itnew#

About a third of a second after the Environment is ready, the context exists, and preparing it takes 5 ms. Spring Boot picks the context class from the classpath. The order service has Spring MVC on its classpath, so it gets a web context. MVC is short for model-view-controller, the name of Spring's web framework. The context class is an AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext. The name is long because it says three things. The context reads annotations. It is a servlet web application. And it owns its web server.

Three things happen before the first bean definition is loaded. Spring Boot applies the spring.main.* settings to the bean factory, such as spring.main.allow-circular-references, which is false by default. Then it runs every ApplicationContextInitializer. Then it publishes ApplicationContextInitializedEvent. Spring Boot's own initializers come from its spring.factories. One of them, ConditionEvaluationReportLoggingListener, is the class that writes the conditions report to the log in the last scene.

Then Spring Boot loads the sources. For the order service there is one source, OrderServiceApplication, which becomes the first bean definition. Spring Boot logs the Starting line at this point, and publishes ApplicationPreparedEvent. The run logged these two lines, 1.8 seconds into the start:

c.a.o.OrderServiceApplication : Starting OrderServiceApplication using Java 25.0.4.1 with PID 1 (/app/BOOT-INF/classes started by app in /app)
c.a.o.OrderServiceApplication : The following 1 profile is active: "local"

The Starting line says four useful things. It names the Java version. It gives the process id, which is 1 in a container. It names the directory the classes were loaded from. And it names the user, which is app and not root. The second line names the active profile, so a wrong profile shows at the top of the log.

Gotcha
A bean cannot listen for an event that was published before the bean existed. A @Component with an @EventListener method for ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent never runs. The event is published during the first second, and the component is created during the refresh, ten seconds later. Register such a listener with SpringApplication.addListeners(...), or in spring.factories. A bean can listen for the four late events, from ApplicationStartedEvent on.

What you can see here#

The Starting line and the profile line. If the profile line names the wrong profile, nothing after it is worth reading. The steps spring.boot.application.context-prepared and spring.boot.application.context-loaded took 18 ms together.

What you can hook here#

An ApplicationContextInitializer, registered with SpringApplication.addInitializers(...) or in spring.factories. It receives the empty context, and it can add property sources or bean definitions in code. Spring Boot's test support uses initializers to add the settings of a test. Application code rarely needs one.

Scene 4: definitions, not objectstwist#

Now the refresh begins. Its first half writes a recipe for every bean, and creates no bean. A recipe is called a bean definition. It holds the bean's class, its scope, its constructor, the beans it depends on, and whether it is lazy. After the start, /actuator/beans listed 625 beans, and OrderService is one of them. At this moment it is only a definition. The definition says that the class is com.acme.orderservice.order.application.OrderService, that the scope is singleton, and that the one constructor takes nine parameters. No OrderService object exists.

The definitions come from one BeanFactoryPostProcessor, called ConfigurationClassPostProcessor. It runs before every other post-processor, because the @Bean methods must be registered before anything else looks at them. It starts from the one definition the previous scene loaded, OrderServiceApplication, and reads its annotation. @SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one:

Annotation inside @SpringBootApplicationWhat ConfigurationClassPostProcessor does with it
@SpringBootConfigurationtreats the class as a @Configuration class, so its @Bean methods and its imports count
@ComponentScanscans the package of the class and every package below it for stereotypes, and writes a definition for each class found
@EnableAutoConfigurationimports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, which reads the imports file of every jar on the classpath

The scan comes first. It finds OrderService through its @Service annotation, and the other 22 or so classes of the service that carry a stereotype. The chapter Where the beans come from: scanning and auto-configuration lists them. Each @Configuration class found is read in turn. So OrderConfig adds a definition for each of its @Bean methods. An @Import annotation on such a class adds more classes to read.

The auto-configuration comes last, on purpose. AutoConfigurationImportSelector is a DeferredImportSelector. A deferred selector runs after every @Configuration class of the application has been read. So when the selector reads the platform's nine auto-configurations from the imports file, the service's own definitions already exist. That is why a condition such as @ConditionalOnMissingBean is safe on an auto-configuration and unsafe on an application class. On the application class the condition runs before the service's other definitions exist, and the answer depends on the order of the scan.

The conditions are evaluated here, while the definitions are written. For the platform's clock bean, the report of the run says why the bean was defined:

"PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration#clock": [
  {
    "condition": "OnBeanCondition",
    "message": "@ConditionalOnMissingBean (types: java.time.Clock; SearchStrategy: all) did not find any beans"
  }
]

The message says that no definition of a Clock existed when the condition ran. A test that declares its own Clock bean makes the same condition fail, and the platform's bean is never defined. For the conditions of the platform, see the chapter Conditions: when a bean or a class applies.

Spring Boot's own auto-configurations go through the same gate, and most of them fail it. The run evaluated 362 positive matches, 194 negative matches and 22 classes with no condition. A negative match looks like this:

"ShutdownEndpointAutoConfiguration": {
  "notMatched": [
    {
      "condition": "OnAvailableEndpointCondition",
      "message": "@ConditionalOnAvailableEndpoint the configured access for endpoint 'shutdown' is NONE"
    }
  ],
  "matched": []
}

The notMatched list names the condition that failed and gives its message. Here the OnAvailableEndpointCondition found that the shutdown endpoint is not enabled, so the auto-configuration for it was skipped. The matched list is empty because no other condition was evaluated on that class.

In ASP.NET Core, the matching idea is builder.Services, a list of ServiceDescriptor objects. Each descriptor holds a service type, an implementation and a lifetime, and no object. The list is complete when Build() runs. The difference is who writes the list. In ASP.NET Core, the application writes every entry, and a library adds entries only when the application calls its extension method. In Spring Boot, the scan and the imports file write the entries, and the application never names the platform.

What you can see here#

Three reports show the definitions. The conditions report, at /actuator/conditions or in the log with --debug, says for every auto-configuration why it was or was not applied. The endpoint /actuator/beans lists every definition with its type, its scope and the names of the beans it depends on. The entry for orderService names nine dependencies, which are the nine constructor parameters. And the startup report has one step for the whole phase, spring.context.beans.post-process, which took 6,538 ms in the run. That is about 40 percent of the start, and ConfigurationClassPostProcessor took 5.6 seconds of it.

What you can hook here#

Three hooks add definitions, and you already use the first two. @Import on a configuration class adds the classes it names. An ImportSelector adds classes by name, and AutoConfigurationImportSelector is the one that imports every auto-configuration. An ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar writes definitions directly, and Spring Data uses one to define a bean for each repository interface. Write your own selector only for a library that must choose its configuration classes at startup. For an application, a @Conditional annotation on a @Bean method does the same with less code.

Scene 5: the recipes are edited, and the post-processors are bornnew#

The definitions exist. Before the first object is created, two kinds of post-processor get their turn. The names are alike, so here they are side by side:

KindWorks onRunsExamples in the order service
BeanFactoryPostProcessorthe definitions, before any bean existsonce, in this sceneConfigurationClassPostProcessor, and the one Spring Boot adds for spring.main.lazy-initialization
BeanPostProcessoreach bean object, as it is createdonce for every bean, in the next scenesthe one for @Autowired, the one for @PostConstruct, the auto-proxy creator, the platform's proxy report

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor may change any definition. The lazy-initialization one marks every definition lazy when spring.main.lazy-initialization is true, so the beans are created at their first use instead of at startup. The order service does not set it. Spring Boot's reference says why. Lazy initialization delays the discovery of a problem, from the start to the first request.

Then Spring creates every BeanPostProcessor, before any other bean. They are beans themselves, so they are the first objects of the refresh. The platform's proxy report is one of them, and its @Bean method is static for exactly this reason:

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.diagnostics.proxies.enabled", havingValue = "true")
public class PlatformDiagnosticsAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    static ProxyReport proxyReport() {
        return new ProxyReport();
    }
Reading the code
static ProxyReport proxyReport()

Spring must create a post-processor before any other bean. If the method were not static, Spring would first have to create the configuration class. That class could in turn need beans that are not yet processed. A static method avoids the whole question, and the Spring Javadoc asks for it.

@ConditionalOnProperty

The report is off unless a service sets the property. A post-processor runs for every one of the 658 beans, so a diagnostic that nobody reads should not exist.

A bean that a post-processor depends on is created early too. Spring then logs a warning that the bean "is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors". That warning means a @Transactional annotation on such a bean does nothing, because the proxy creator was not yet there when the bean was made. The proxy report has no dependencies, so no bean is pulled forward by it.

Pragmatic choice: A diagnostic post-processor in the platform jar

The strict rule. The platform ships only what every service needs in production. A diagnostic belongs in a test, or in a tool.

What we do. The platform ships a BeanPostProcessor that lists every proxied bean, and an Actuator endpoint that shows the list. Both exist only when platform.diagnostics.proxies.enabled is true.

Why. The question "is my bean proxied, and by what?" comes up in every team, and the usual answer is a debugger session. The report answers it with one request, in any environment, and it has no cost when it is off.

When to stop. If the platform gains a second diagnostic, move them both to a separate shop-platform-diagnostics jar that a service adds only when it wants them.

What you can see here#

The startup report has a step for each post-processor: spring.context.beandef-registry.post-process and spring.context.bean-factory.post-process, each tagged with the class that ran. The run had three of the first kind and twelve of the second. And the warning about a bean that is "not eligible" for every post-processor, when it appears, names the bean to look at.

What you can hook here#

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor of your own, when a rule applies to every definition at once. Spring Boot's lazy-initialization processor is the model. It is rare in application code. A BeanPostProcessor of your own is less rare, and the two scenes after the next one show the rules for writing one.

Scene 6: objects, one at a timetrap#

Now Spring creates the singletons, in the order of the definitions, and dependency first. When it reaches a definition, it looks at the constructor parameters. For each parameter it finds the one bean of that type, and creates it first if it does not exist yet. So a bean is often created inside the creation of another. The startup report of the run shows exactly this for the protagonist. The step that created orderService is inside the step that created orderController, because the controller's constructor takes the service.

The chain went deeper. The service's constructor takes a StockChecker, the port to the stock service. Its adapter, stockAdapter, needed the HTTP client stockHttpClient, which needed the restClientBuilder. The adapter is the class that implements the port with a real HTTP call. The report gives the time of each step, and each time includes its children:

Bean being createdTookWhat is inside the time
orderController1,030 msorderService and everything below it, then the controller itself
orderService1,007 msits nine dependencies, created first
stockAdapter927 msstockHttpClient, and the client's builder
stockHttpClient903 msthe HTTP interface proxy, and restClientBuilder
restClientBuilder489 msthe builder of the HTTP client, with its codecs

Most of the controller's second went to the HTTP client of the stock adapter, and building restClientBuilder alone took 489 ms. This is the general shape of a slow start. The first bean to touch a library pays for the library, and the report shows which bean that was.

This is where the constructor of OrderService runs. Its nine parameters arrive as objects that Spring has already finished, with one exception that the next paragraph explains:

public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, NoteService notes, ReferenceDataService referenceData,
                    StockChecker stock, ShippingPolicy shippingPolicy, DomainEventPublisher events,
                    AuditLog audit, TransactionTemplate transaction, Clock clock) {

The exception is the cycle between the order and note features. The order service needs the note service, and the note service needs the order service. Spring Boot refuses such a cycle by default, with a report at startup. The note service breaks it with @Lazy on its constructor parameter. So when NoteService is created, the parameter it receives for the order service is not the order service. It is a small proxy that finds the real bean at its first call. The chapter @Lazy: a proxy that breaks the cycle, and the other ways out explains the choice. For this scene, the point is the order. NoteService was finished before OrderService existed, and the lazy proxy made that possible.

After the constructor, Spring runs a fixed list of callbacks on the new object. The Spring Javadoc gives fourteen, and the order service uses four of them:

OrderCallbackWhat it is forIn the order service
1 to 10the Aware interfaces, such as BeanNameAware and ApplicationContextAwarethe bean learns its name, or gets the contextnot used
11BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitializationa post-processor sees the populated bean, before its init methodsCommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor calls the @PostConstruct method here, as in the leak experiment of the memory chapter
12InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()the bean's own setup, with every dependency presentnot used
13a custom init-methodthe same, named in the definitionnot used
14BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitializationa post-processor may replace the bean with a wrapperthe auto-proxy creator, and the platform's proxy report

The fourteenth callback is the twist of the next scene. Before that, the trap of this scene. In ASP.NET Core, the container builds in Build(). The handbook's run in the chapter on wiring shows when it creates each singleton. A wiring mistake, such as a cycle, can appear at the first resolve, in the middle of a request. Only ValidateOnBuild, which the generic host turns on in the Development environment, moves the error to the build. In Spring, every singleton is created in this scene, and a bean that cannot be created stops the start. The refresh() Javadoc promises this. After the refresh, either every singleton exists or none does.

Gotcha
A proxied method called from @PostConstruct runs without its proxy. The @PostConstruct method runs at callback 11. The proxy that gives a method its transaction, its cache or its permission check is created at callback 14. So a call from @PostConstruct to the bean's own @Transactional method runs with no transaction. Spring's reference says not to rely on the proxy in initialization code. Do the work in a SmartInitializingSingleton, or in an ApplicationRunner, when every bean is complete.

What you can see here#

Each spring.beans.instantiate step in the startup report, with its bean name, its parent step and its time. The run has 690 of them. Sort them by time to find the bean that paid for a library. The endpoint /actuator/beans gives the dependencies of each bean by name. And when a cycle exists, the start fails with a report that draws the cycle as a box. The report names the setting that would allow the cycle, as a last resort.

What you can hook here#

@PostConstruct, for setup that needs the bean's own dependencies and nothing else. @Lazy on a parameter, to break a cycle or to delay an expensive bean. @DependsOn, to force an order between two beans that share no dependency. And SmartInitializingSingleton, for work that needs every bean, which scene 8 shows.

Scene 7: the twistnew#

The constructor of OrderService has run. The object exists. And the object that Spring hands to OrderController is a different object.

Callback 14 is postProcessAfterInitialization, and one of the post-processors that run there is the auto-proxy creator. Its Javadoc says what it does. It wraps each eligible bean with an AOP proxy. AOP is short for aspect-oriented programming. It is the mechanism behind the annotations that need a proxy, such as @Transactional and @Cacheable. The glossary entry AOP gives the words of that mechanism. The creator looks at the bean's class and finds the advisors whose pointcuts match a method of it. If any match, it returns a proxy instead of the bean. Spring stores the returned object as the singleton. So every other bean receives the proxy, and the original object is inside it.

The proxy report sees this happen, because it runs in the same callback, after the creator. It declares no order, and Spring registers unordered post-processors after the ordered ones. So by the time the report sees a bean, the creator has already decided:

@Override
public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
    seen.incrementAndGet();
    if (AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean) && bean instanceof Advised advised) {
        String kind = AopUtils.isCglibProxy(bean) ? "class (CGLIB subclass)" : "interface (JDK dynamic proxy)";
        List<String> advice = Arrays.stream(advised.getAdvisors())
                .map(Advisor::getAdvice)
                .map(Advice::getClass)
                .map(Class::getSimpleName)
                .toList();
        proxied.add(new ProxiedBean(beanName, AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(bean).getName(), kind, advice));
    }
    return bean;
}
Reading the code
AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean)

Spring's own check for a proxy. It returns true for a class-based proxy and for an interface-based one, and false for a plain object.

bean instanceof Advised advised

Every proxy that Spring creates implements Advised. The interface gives the list of advisors, and each advisor gives its advice, which is the interceptor that runs around the method. The simple class name of the interceptor says what the proxy adds.

AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(bean)

The class behind the proxy, through any number of nested proxies. For a class-based proxy the proxy's own class is a generated subclass, so this call is the way to the real one.

return bean;

A post-processor may return a different object, and the creator does. The report only looks, so it returns what it was given.

In the run, the creator wrapped fourteen of the 658 beans. The report at /actuator/proxies listed them. Here they are, with what each interceptor stands for:

BeanProxyInterceptors on itWhat put them there
orderServiceclassTransactionInterceptor@Transactional on its methods
noteServiceclassTransactionInterceptor@Transactional on its methods
eventPublicationRegistry, mongoDbEventPublicationRepositoryclassTransactionInterceptor@Transactional inside Spring Modulith
orderController, noteController, referenceDataControllerclassDeferringMethodInterceptorthe method security of @OrdersRead and @OrdersWrite
orderMetrics, snsEventExternalizerclassAnnotationAsyncExecutionInterceptor, CompletionRegisteringMethodInterceptor, TransactionInterceptor@ApplicationModuleListener, which is @Async, @Transactional and a completion record in one
referenceItemRepositoryinterfaceCacheInterceptor@Cacheable on the repository, as the chapter on wiring explains
noteRepository, orderMongoRepositoryinterfacefour Spring Data interceptorsa Spring Data repository is a proxy of your interface, with SimpleMongoRepository behind it
stockHttpClientinterfaceHttpServiceMethodInterceptoran HTTP interface client, which is a proxy that sends requests
stockClientPropertiesclassMethodValidationInterceptor@Validated on the settings class

The table shows two kinds of proxy. A class-based proxy is a subclass of the bean's class, generated at startup by a library called CGLIB, the Code Generation Library. Spring Boot makes this the default with the setting spring.aop.proxy-target-class, which is true. An interface-based proxy is a dynamic proxy of the Java Development Kit (JDK), which implements the bean's interfaces. For a repository, the class behind the proxy is SimpleMongoRepository, which Spring Data supplies. The HTTP interface client has no class of its own behind its proxy. A repository and an HTTP interface client are interfaces that Spring implements for you, and a proxy is how it implements them.

A class-based proxy has two limits that matter in the service. It cannot override a final method, so a @Transactional method must not be final. And a call from inside the class, through this, reaches the original object and not the proxy. Such a call is called self-invocation. The chapter Self-invocation: why the cache is on the repository shows the second limit on a real method. The Spring source logs a warning for a public final method on a proxied class. The reference documentation only says that such a method "cannot be advised".

The platform's test proves the twist in six lines. The bean the context returns is not an Orders, and its superclass is:

@Test
void theProxyIsWhatOtherBeansReceive() {
    try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Config.class)) {
        Orders orders = context.getBean(Orders.class);

        assertThat(orders.getClass()).isNotEqualTo(Orders.class);
        assertThat(orders.getClass().getSuperclass()).isEqualTo(Orders.class);
    }
}

The test asks the context for an Orders bean, whose one method is @Transactional. The class of the object it gets back is a generated subclass. Every bean that takes an Orders in its constructor receives that subclass.

ASP.NET Core has no auto-proxy creator. A decorator is a class you write and register, and the container passes it to the beans that ask for the interface. Spring does the same wrapping for you, from an annotation, and the price is that the wrapping is invisible until you ask the report.

What you can see here#

Three things. The report at /actuator/proxies, and the one line it writes at startup, which counts the proxied beans. The check AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean), in any test that holds a bean. And the Spring warning about a final method, at WARN level in the log of a start.

What you can hook here#

A BeanPostProcessor. You already use three. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor applies @Autowired and @Value. CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor applies @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy. And the auto-proxy creator applies the annotations that need a proxy. The platform's report is a fourth. The rules for one of your own are short. Declare it in a static @Bean method with no dependencies. Return the bean you were given unless you mean to replace it. Declare no order unless you must run before the creator, and then implement Ordered and expect to see beans before they are proxied.

Scene 8: every singleton exists, and the service wakes uptwist#

The last singleton is created. Nothing listens yet. Two mechanisms now run in order, and the order is the point of this scene.

The first is SmartInitializingSingleton. Spring calls afterSingletonsInstantiated() on every bean that implements it, right after the last singleton exists and before any lifecycle bean starts. The platform's migration runner is one, and the run shows the order it needs. The proxy report logged its summary, and the next line is Tomcat's:

c.a.p.core.diagnostics.ProxyReport       : Proxied beans: 14 of 658 (10 class-based, 4 interface-based); the list is at /actuator/proxies
o.s.boot.tomcat.TomcatWebServer          : Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'

The ProxyReport line is directly followed by Tomcat started. The runner logged nothing in this run, because every migration had been applied in an earlier run. The startup report shows its place. The step of the proxy report came first, then the runner's step, and then Tomcat started. The runner implements the interface and does its work in the one callback:

@Override
public void afterSingletonsInstantiated() {
    acquireLock();
    try {
        Set<String> applied = appliedIds();
        for (MongoMigration migration : migrations) {
            if (!applied.contains(migration.id())) {
                run(migration);
            }
        }
    } finally {
        releaseLock();
    }
}

The callback first calls acquireLock(), so that two instances of the service never run a migration at the same time. Then it runs each migration whose id is not in applied, and releases the lock. The callback runs on the main thread, and the start waits for it. That is what the migrations want. No request and no message can arrive before the indexes exist. The chapter The runner: each migration once, before traffic covers the lock and the history. In the startup report the step is spring.beans.smart-initialize, and the runner's step took 159 ms.

The second mechanism is SmartLifecycle. Spring's lifecycle processor starts every SmartLifecycle bean, lowest phase first, and the web server is one of them. Spring Boot gives its web server the phase DEFAULT_PHASE - 2048, and the graceful-shutdown bean the phase DEFAULT_PHASE - 1024. DEFAULT_PHASE is Integer.MAX_VALUE. So Tomcat starts before a lifecycle bean with the default phase, and stops after it. The inbox of the service reads a queue of Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). The listener containers for that queue started after Tomcat in the run, on a thread of their own:

19:17:41.960Z  [main]              o.s.boot.tomcat.TomcatWebServer          : Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
19:17:42.575Z  [ecycle-thread-1]   a.c.s.l.AbstractMessageListenerContainer : Container io.awspring.cloud.sqs.sqsListenerEndpointContainer#0 started

The first line is on the main thread. The second is on ecycle-thread-1, whose name the log cut short. Spring Cloud AWS made this thread to start its container, and the line came 0.6 seconds after Tomcat.

Tomcat was created much earlier, in the refresh step onRefresh(), before the singletons. The run logged "Tomcat initialized with port 8080" about six seconds before "Tomcat started". Created means the server object exists and the port is known. Started means the port is open. Between the two lines, every bean was built.

ASP.NET Core has one mechanism here, IHostedService, and its StartAsync runs before the server listens, in registration order. The handbook's chapter on wiring maps the migrations to it. Spring has two mechanisms because they answer two questions. "Every bean exists" is the question of SmartInitializingSingleton. "Start, and later stop, in this order" is the question of SmartLifecycle.

What you can see here#

The two Tomcat lines and the time between them. The thread name in square brackets, which is main for the migrations and a lifecycle thread for a listener container. And the spring.beans.smart-initialize steps of the startup report, one for each bean that implements the interface, in the order Spring called them.

What you can hook here#

SmartInitializingSingleton, for work that must finish before the server listens and needs every bean. SmartLifecycle, for a thing that starts and stops, such as a poller or a consumer. Its getPhase() decides the order against Tomcat. A phase above the web server's starts after the port is open. Its stop(Runnable) is called with a callback, so a slow stop can finish on its own thread and then call back. And isAutoStartup(), which is true by default, decides whether Spring starts the bean at all.

Scene 9: started, then readytwist#

The refresh is over. Spring Boot logs the Started line, publishes ApplicationStartedEvent, and sets the liveness state to CORRECT. Then it calls the runners. An ApplicationRunner or a CommandLineRunner is a bean with one run method. Spring Boot calls each one here, after the server listens and before the ready event. The order service has none. Then Spring Boot publishes ApplicationReadyEvent, and sets the readiness state to ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC. The chapter The health probes: liveness without the database shows what the two states mean to Kubernetes.

The conditions report was logged just before the Started line, at DEBUG, because the run set DEBUG=true. It took about 2,130 of the 2,230 lines in the log. Without the setting, those lines do not exist.

Then the first request of the script came. It took 0.31 seconds. The second took 0.04 seconds. The log explains part of the difference. During the first request only, the service fetched the token-signing keys from the OAuth2 server. The rest is the first-run cost in the JVM and in Spring, because the request's code ran for the first time. The chapter The JVM under the service: code, threads and the compiler follows that first run.

Spring MVC created its DispatcherServlet earlier, during the very first HTTP request. In this run that was the readiness poll of the run script. It logged two lines:

o.a.c.c.C.[Tomcat].[localhost].[/]       : Initializing Spring DispatcherServlet 'dispatcherServlet'
o.s.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet        : Completed initialization in 9 ms

The DispatcherServlet is the servlet that receives every request and finds the controller for it. Tomcat creates it when the first request arrives. Here that was the readiness poll, so the 9 ms are not part of the 0.31 seconds.

ASP.NET Core's ApplicationStarted token fires after the server starts, and callbacks registered on it run then. Spring Boot's ready event plays the same role, and the translate question at the end of the chapter writes it.

What you can see here#

The Started line, then the probes. The readiness probe at /actuator/health/readiness answers UP only after the ready event. The run script of this chapter waited for that answer before it sent the first request.

What you can hook here#

An ApplicationRunner, for work that may run after the server listens, such as a warm-up request to the service's own endpoints. An @EventListener for ApplicationReadyEvent, for the same moment without the extra interface. Spring Boot's reference prefers a runner over @PostConstruct for startup work, because the runner sees a complete application.

Scene 10: the stoptwist#

Spring Boot registers a shutdown hook with the JVM. When the container sends SIGTERM, the hook closes the context on a thread named SpringContextShutdownHook. The run stopped the container with docker stop, and the log shows the order. First the readiness state changed, so a load balancer would stop sending requests. Then the context began to close:

19:17:44.483Z  [ionShutdownHook]  o.s.b.a.ApplicationAvailabilityBean      : Application availability state ReadinessState changed from ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC to REFUSING_TRAFFIC
19:17:44.483Z  [ionShutdownHook]  ConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext : Closing org.springframework.boot.web.server.servlet.context.AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext
19:17:52.613Z  [ecycle-thread-3]  a.c.s.l.AbstractMessageListenerContainer : Container io.awspring.cloud.sqs.sqsListenerEndpointContainer#0 stopped
19:17:52.614Z  [ionShutdownHook]  o.s.boot.tomcat.GracefulShutdown         : Commencing graceful shutdown. Waiting for active requests to complete
19:17:52.652Z  [tomcat-shutdown]  o.s.boot.tomcat.GracefulShutdown         : Graceful shutdown complete
19:17:52.681Z  [ionShutdownHook]  .s.m.e.c.DefaultEventPublicationRegistry : No publications outstanding!

Closing the context does three things in order. It publishes ContextClosedEvent. It stops the lifecycle beans, highest phase first, which is the reverse of the start. And it destroys the singletons, which calls each @PreDestroy method. The log shows the lifecycle part. The SQS listener container stopped first. The awspring source gives it the default phase, Integer.MAX_VALUE, and the Spring documentation does not state it. It stopped first, and it took eight seconds to report that it had stopped. Then the graceful-shutdown bean ran, waited for active requests, and found none. Then Spring Modulith's registry logged that no event publication was outstanding.

Graceful shutdown is on by default since Spring Boot 3.4. The setting server.shutdown is graceful, and the setting spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase gives each phase 30 seconds. ASP.NET Core has the same shape. SIGTERM calls StopApplication, the hosted services stop in the reverse order of their registration, and HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout gives them 30 seconds in total. For the setting on the service's side, see the section Graceful shutdown.

What you can see here#

The lines between "Closing" and the end of the log, with their thread names and their times. A gap between two lines is a bean that took that long to stop. In the run, the gap was the listener container.

What you can hook here#

@PreDestroy, for releasing what the bean opened. SmartLifecycle.stop() and its phase, for the order. The two settings above, for the kind of shutdown and the time each phase gets. And an @EventListener for ContextClosedEvent, which runs first, before any bean stops.

Scene 11: the four reports, in one placenew#

Every number in this chapter came from one of four reports, and each one is a setting away:

ReportWhereHow to turn it onWhat it answers
the startup steps/actuator/startupthe trace switch in main(), and startup in management.endpoints.web.exposure.includewhich step, and which bean, took the time
the conditions/actuator/conditions, or the log with DEBUG=trueconditions in the exposure list, or the environment variablewhy an auto-configuration was or was not applied
the beans/actuator/beansbeans in the exposure listevery bean's type, scope and dependencies
the proxies/actuator/proxies, and one log lineplatform.diagnostics.proxies.enabled=true, and proxies in the exposure listwhich beans are wrapped, and by what

The run script that captured them is companion/runs/startup/run.sh, and its output folder holds the four reports of the run this chapter quotes. The endpoints need a token like any other request of the service, or a public path for the actuator in the local profile. The run used the second. Nothing in the four reports is a secret. The endpoint /actuator/env is another matter, and the chapter Secrets never in a file says why it stays closed.

A fifth report is Java Flight Recorder. It captures the same startup steps when main gives the application a FlightRecorderApplicationStartup. It also captures what the JVM did at the same time. The two JVM chapters that follow the chapter on running the service use it.

Check yourself
1
Spring Boot publishes ApplicationStartedEvent and then ApplicationReadyEvent. What runs between the two?
The runner beans. Spring Boot calls every ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner after the started event, when the server already listens, and publishes the ready event after them. The readiness probe answers UP only after the ready event.
2
A bean has a @PostConstruct method that calls the bean's own @Transactional method. Does the call run in a transaction?
No. The proxy that opens the transaction is created in the last callback of the bean's initialisation, after @PostConstruct has run. And a call through this never reaches the proxy anyway. Do the work in a SmartInitializingSingleton or an ApplicationRunner.
3
An expert asksWhy can a @Component never receive ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent, and what receives it instead?
The event is published while the settings are assembled, before the application context exists. A component is created during the refresh, seconds later, so it cannot be a listener yet. A listener for the early events is given to SpringApplication.addListeners, or listed in META-INF/spring.factories under the ApplicationListener key.
4
TranslateTranslate this registration of startup work. In ASP.NET Core the callback runs once the server has started. 
var app = builder.Build();
app.Lifetime.ApplicationStarted.Register(() => Console.WriteLine("listening"));
app.Run();
A bean with a listener for the ready event. Spring Boot publishes it after the server listens and after the runners. 
@Component
class Listening {

    @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)
    void onReady() {
        System.out.println("listening");
    }
}

Configuration in depth#

Wiring, configuration and use cases · Chapter 11· 29 min read· Quick reference

The order service reads its settings from application.yml, from a profile file and from environment variables. Typed classes receive the settings, and a missing value stops the service at startup. The platform library adds its own defaults below everything else. This chapter explains each layer, every key the service and the platform set, the Boot 4 names that changed, and where secrets come from.
