The settings files and the profilestwist#

For the basics of application.yml, profiles and typed settings, see the chapter Dependency injection and configuration. This chapter shows the files of the order service, and the layers around them.

appsettings.Development.json
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Acme": "Debug" }
  }
}
application-local.yml
logging:
  level:
    com.acme: DEBUG

Both files hold the settings of one environment, here the developer's machine. The line com.acme: DEBUG sets the log level for every class under com.acme, which includes the platform. In .NET, the category under LogLevel takes that place.

The service has three files of settings, and each one has a job:

FileWhen Boot reads itWhat it holds
src/main/resources/application.ymlalwaysevery key that every environment needs, with placeholders for the values that differ
src/main/resources/application-local.ymlwhen the profile local is activethe addresses of the local containers, and fake secrets
src/test/resources/application-wiring.ymlwhen a test activates the profile wiringvalues that connect to nothing, for the wiring test
src/test/resources/application.propertiesin every testone key, readable console logs

A Spring profile is a named set of settings that you switch on at startup. The local compose file of the service switches on the profile local with an environment variable:

services:
  order-service:
    build: .
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: local

With SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: local, Boot also reads application-local.yml, after application.yml. A key in the profile file overrides the same key in the main file. This works as appsettings.Development.json does with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT. Production needs no profile. It reads application.yml, the environment variables and the platform's defaults.

The service has no file for production. Every value that differs between environments comes from an environment variable. So a deployment to a new environment changes no file, and every environment runs the same application.yml.

The first key of application.yml is spring.application.name, which is order-service. Boot writes it into every JSON log line. For the log fields, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

A new service needs few keys of its own. The minimum is the name, the database, the token issuer and the path variables for the logs. Everything else has a default in Boot or in the platform.

Placeholders, defaults and the environmenttwist#

C#
var mongoUri = builder.Configuration["MONGO_URI"]
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("MONGO_URI");
var region = builder.Configuration["AWS_REGION"]
    ?? "eu-west-2";
Java 25
mongodb:
  # The Spring Boot 4 key. Boot 4 ignores the old spring.data.mongodb.uri without a warning.
  # DocumentDB: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<cluster>:27017/orders?tls=true&replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=primary
  # The platform forces retryWrites=false, which DocumentDB needs.
  uri: ${MONGO_URI}
Reading the code
uri: ${MONGO_URI}

${MONGO_URI} is a placeholder. Spring replaces it with the value of MONGO_URI, which the deployment sets as an environment variable. The value is the whole connection string, including the user and the password.

tls=true&replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=primary

These options of the connection string are what Amazon DocumentDB needs. For each one, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

A placeholder can carry a default after a colon. The region of the service uses one:

cloud:
  aws:
    # Credentials come from the task's or pod's IAM role, never from configuration.
    region:
      static: ${AWS_REGION:eu-west-2}

${AWS_REGION:eu-west-2} takes the value of AWS_REGION, or eu-west-2 when the variable is not set. The queue name works the same way. Use a default only for a value that is right in most environments. A connection string or a URL of another service has no safe default, so its placeholder has none.

The README of the service lists every variable that a deployment must set:

Environment variableThe key it fillsWhat it is
MONGO_URIspring.mongodb.urithe DocumentDB connection string, with its user and password
PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLEplatform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundlethe path of the mounted AWS certificate bundle
OAUTH_ISSUER_URIspring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-urithe token issuer whose tokens the service accepts
OAUTH_TOKEN_URI...client.provider.shop-identity.token-uriwhere the service gets its own client-credentials token
STOCK_CLIENT_ID, STOCK_CLIENT_SECRET...client.registration.stock-service.client-id and client-secretthe service's own credentials for the stock service
STOCK_SERVICE_URLclients.stock.base-urlthe base URL of the stock service
PAYMENT_RECEIVED_QUEUEmessaging.queues.payment-receivedthe Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) queue, if it is not order-service-payment-received
AWS_REGIONspring.cloud.aws.region.staticthe region, and the credentials come from the Identity and Access Management (IAM) role

One of these variables is not a placeholder. PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLE sets its key by relaxed binding, which the next section explains. Spring would read any key from the environment in that way. The placeholders are there to make the dependency visible in application.yml, and to give a short name to a long key.

In ASP.NET Core, the same values are environment variables too, and the configuration reads them with no placeholder. The C# pane above reads them in code. A Spring service writes no such code, because the placeholder in the file does the work.

Environment variables and relaxed bindingtwist#

C#
// ASP.NET Core: a double underscore separates the levels
// Platform__Mongo__DocumentDb__CaBundle=/certs/global-bundle.pem
Java 25
# Settings for every environment. Secrets and environment-specific values come from environment
# variables, which the deployment sets from the secrets manager. Never put a secret in this file.
# The platform's defaults (health probes, JSON logs, graceful shutdown and more) apply already;
# see META-INF/platform-defaults/ in the platform jar. Anything here overrides them.
# Spring Boot binds an environment variable to a key by relaxed binding: for example
# PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLE sets platform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundle.

The top of application.yml states the rule. The variable PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLE sets a key with no placeholder in the file. This is called relaxed binding. The Boot reference gives the rules for the name of the variable:

StepFrom the key platform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundle
Replace each dot with an underscoreplatform_mongo_documentdb_ca-bundle
Remove each dashplatform_mongo_documentdb_cabundle
Convert to upper casePLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CABUNDLE

The service's comment writes CA_BUNDLE, with an underscore where the dash was. That form binds too. A run for this book showed that both RATES_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and RATES_TIMEOUTSECONDS set rates.timeout-seconds. A second run, with real environment variables in a child process, bound these names:

Environment variableBound to
CLIENTS_STOCK_BASEURLclients.stock.base-url
CLIENTS_STOCK_READTIMEOUT=250msclients.stock.read-timeout
CLIENTS_STOCK_MDCPATHVARIABLES_0_ and _1_the first and second element of a list

An element of a list takes its index between underscores. The Boot reference shows the form MY_SERVICE_0_OTHER. ASP.NET Core writes __0 for the same thing.

Gotcha

A double underscore in the .NET style does not map to a level in Spring. In ASP.NET Core, Platform__Mongo__DocumentDb__CaBundle marks each level with a double underscore. Spring needs one underscore for each dot. For the basic form, see the section Single values and precedence.

The Spring keys that the service setstwist#

Boot reads the settings of each starter from fixed keys. So application.yml holds the setup that Program.cs would hold in code. The security keys of the service are an example:

security:
  oauth2:
    resourceserver:
      jwt:
        # Spring Security downloads the issuer's signing keys and checks the "iss" claim.
        # It also checks the token's "typ" header: "JWT", or no typ header, passes. "at+jwt" is refused.
        issuer-uri: ${OAUTH_ISSUER_URI}
        # Tokens must be issued for this service.
        audiences: order-service
Reading the code
issuer-uri: ${OAUTH_ISSUER_URI}

The token issuer. Spring finds its signing keys from this address, at the first token. For the details, see the section Where the signing keys come from.

audiences: order-service

A token must name this service in its aud claim. Spring checks the claim only when this key lists an audience. For the claims, see the section What Spring checks in each token.

Each Spring key of application.yml has one job. The table names its home, where it is explained in full:

KeyWhat it does in the order serviceExplained in
spring.application.namethe name in every log line and tracedd-obs
spring.mongodb.urithe connection string of DocumentDB, from MONGO_URIdd-sto
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-urithe issuer whose tokens the service acceptsdd-sec-keys
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiencesthe audience a token must name, order-servicedd-sec-claims
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.stock-service.*the service's own client-credentials login for the stock servicedd-sec-s2s
spring.security.oauth2.client.provider.shop-identity.token-uriwhere that token comes fromdd-sec-s2s
spring.cloud.aws.region.staticthe AWS region, and credentials come from the IAM roledd-sec-aws

The local profile replaces the addresses with the container names of the local environment. It also adds keys that production never sets:

cloud:
  aws:
    endpoint: http://floci:4566
    credentials:
      access-key: local
      secret-key: local
Reading the code
endpoint: http://floci:4566

This key points every AWS client at Floci, the local container that provides Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). In production the key is not set, so the clients use the real AWS addresses.

access-key: local

The local profile gives fixed credentials for Floci. Production has no such key, because the credentials come from the Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.

The local profile also sets spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri. The key tells Spring where to fetch the signing keys inside the Docker network. For why it differs from the issuer, see the section A local token issuer, and the issuer-versus-keys trick.

Boot 4 keys that changed their namestrap#

Boot 4 renamed many keys. The metadata of Boot gives each old key a level. At level warning, the IDE marks the key. At level error, Boot no longer reads the key, and the service can start with the wrong value and no error. The MongoDB key is the worst case:

Gotcha

Boot 4 ignores spring.data.mongodb.uri. In a run for this book, only the old key was set. The client went to localhost:27017, failed with MongoTimeoutException, and nothing was logged about the old key. The Boot 4 key is spring.mongodb.uri. For the basic trap, see the section The MongoDB setting changed its name.

The order service guards against it with a test. The wiring test asks Boot which address it really uses:

/** Spring Boot 4 reads spring.mongodb.uri; the old spring.data.mongodb.uri would be ignored silently. */
@Test
void usesTheConfiguredMongoUri() {
    ConnectionString used = context.getBean(MongoConnectionDetails.class).getConnectionString();

    assertThat(used.getHosts()).containsExactly("localhost:1");
    assertThat(used.getDatabase()).isEqualTo("wiring-test");
}
Reading the code
context.getBean(MongoConnectionDetails.class).getConnectionString()

MongoConnectionDetails is the bean from which Boot builds the MongoDB client. Its connection string is the one that Boot really took from the settings.

assertThat(used.getHosts()).containsExactly("localhost:1");

The wiring profile sets localhost:1. If someone renamed the key back to the Boot 3 form, Boot would use its default host, and this line would fail.

The metadata of Boot 4.1.2 marks each old key as deprecated, with its replacement. A run for this book read it. These renames matter for a service like this one:

Boot 3 keyBoot 4 keyWhat happens to the old key in Boot 4.1.2
spring.data.mongodb.uri, and the other driver keysspring.mongodb.urideprecated at level error, and the run showed that it is ignored
spring.data.mongodb.uuid-representationspring.mongodb.representation.uuiddeprecated at level error
management.metrics.mongo.*management.metrics.mongodb.*deprecated at level error
management.otlp.tracing.endpointmanagement.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpointdeprecated at level error
server.error.include-message, include-stacktracespring.web.error.include-message, include-stacktracedeprecated at level error
spring.http.client.read-timeout, connect-timeoutspring.http.clients.read-timeout, connect-timeoutdeprecated at level warning

A key at level error is not a warning to fix later. The old MongoDB key has that level, and the run shows that Boot does not read it. Treat every key at level error as gone. The plural spring.http.clients is easy to miss, because the singular is only a warning.

A run for this book checked the error keys on Boot 4.1.2. A controller threw a ResponseStatusException with the status 400 and the message "secret detail", and Boot's own error response answered it:

SettingThe body of the 400 response
nonetimestamp, status, error and path, with no message
server.error.include-message=always, the Boot 3 keythe same, with no message
spring.web.error.include-message=always, the Boot 4 keythe same, plus "message":"secret detail"

So Boot 4.1.2 ignores the old key. The platform's defaults file sets the new keys:

# Boot's own error responses never contain a stack trace or an exception message. Both values
# are Boot's defaults, restated. Boot 4 renamed the keys, and it ignores the old server.error.* keys.
spring.web.error.include-stacktrace=never
spring.web.error.include-message=never

Both values, never, are the defaults, so the lines change no behaviour today. They state the choice in the platform's one file of defaults, as the file's other restated keys do. For the error settings, see the section What a problem never contains.

The IDE marks a deprecated key, because it reads the same metadata. That is the cheapest check of a Boot upgrade. For the other changes of Boot 4, see the chapter Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4.

Typed settings in the platformtwist#

C#
public class PlatformLoggingOptions
{
    public bool Structured { get; set; } = true;
    public List<string> MdcPathVariables { get; set; } = [];
}

services.Configure<PlatformLoggingOptions>(
    configuration.GetSection("Platform:Logging"));
Java 25
/** Logging settings, bound from {@code platform.logging.*}. */
@ConfigurationProperties("platform.logging")
public class PlatformLoggingProperties {

    /** Write JSON (ECS) logs. Set it to false locally for readable console logs. */
    private boolean structured = true;

    /** Path variables to copy into the MDC for each request, such as {@code orderId}. */
    private List<String> mdcPathVariables = new ArrayList<>();

    public boolean isStructured() {
        return structured;
    }

    public void setStructured(boolean structured) {
        this.structured = structured;
    }
Reading the code
@ConfigurationProperties("platform.logging")

The class receives every key under platform.logging. The field mdcPathVariables takes platform.logging.mdc-path-variables. For @ConfigurationProperties, see the section IOptions becomes @ConfigurationProperties.

private boolean structured = true;

The default is in the field. A service that sets no key gets JSON logs.

public void setStructured(boolean structured) {

This class is a JavaBean. Spring creates it with its constructor, then calls a setter for each key it finds. The setters are what makes binding work for a class.

The platform has five such classes. Each auto-configuration names the classes it needs with @EnableConfigurationProperties, which makes each one a bean:

@AutoConfiguration(afterName = "org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.client.autoconfigure.OAuth2ClientAutoConfiguration")
@EnableConfigurationProperties({PlatformLoggingProperties.class, ResilienceProperties.class})
public class PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration {

Here PlatformLoggingProperties and ResilienceProperties become beans. A library must register its classes this way. The service's scanning never reaches the platform's packages, so @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the service would not find them. The five classes and their prefixes:

ClassPrefixHolds
PlatformLoggingPropertiesplatform.loggingJSON logs on or off, and the path variables for the mapped diagnostic context (MDC)
PlatformSecurityPropertiesplatform.securitythe paths that need no token
ResiliencePropertiesplatform.resiliencethe retry and circuit breaker settings, in two nested classes
DocumentDbPropertiesplatform.mongo.documentdbthe path of the certificate bundle
MessagingPropertiesplatform.messagingthe outbox resender and the inbox, in two nested classes

A record is the other way to write such a class. For the record form, see the section IOptions becomes @ConfigurationProperties. The two ways compare like this:

FormWhat it gets rightWhat it costs
a record, bound through its constructorit cannot change after binding, and it is shorteach default needs the annotation @DefaultValue, and a record has no setters for a @Bean method to fill
a class with setters, as in the platformdefaults are plain field initialisers, and one class can be bound under several prefixesit can change after binding, and the getters and setters are long

The platform uses classes for two reasons. The defaults read as plain Java, and the HTTP client settings are bound once for each client. For a settings type that a single service owns, a record is the better choice.

One properties class, bound once for each clientnew#

A service may call several other services. Each client needs a base URL, two timeouts and maybe a token. If each client had its own properties class, every service would repeat the same fields. So the platform has one class, and each client binds it under its own prefix.

The settings of the stock client, in application.yml:

clients:
  stock:
    base-url: ${STOCK_SERVICE_URL}
    read-timeout: 3s
    # Each call carries a token from this client registration
    token-registration-id: stock-service

The key token-registration-id names the client registration of Spring Security, so each call carries the service's own token. The client's configuration class binds the keys. @ConfigurationProperties on a @Bean method fills the object that the method returns:

/** Binds the platform's reusable properties class to this client's prefix. */
@Bean
@ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")
HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties() {
    return new HttpClientProperties();
}
Reading the code
@ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")

Spring binds the keys under clients.stock into the returned object, by calling its setters. A second client, say clients.payment, would have a second method with the other prefix.

return new HttpClientProperties();

The object starts with the defaults of the class, a connect timeout of 2 seconds and a read timeout of 5 seconds. The settings then override what they set. Here the read timeout becomes 3 seconds, and the connect timeout stays 2 seconds.

The class is not on @EnableConfigurationProperties, because the method makes it a bean already. The keys of the platform's client class:

Key under clients.<name>DefaultWhat it does
base-urlnone, and it is requiredthe root URL of the other service
connect-timeout2show long to wait for a connection
read-timeout5show long to wait for the response once connected
token-registration-idnonethe client registration whose token each call carries

The closest match in ASP.NET Core is a named options instance, configured once for each client from its own section. For the client that uses these settings, see the chapter Calling other services.

Fail at startup: validated settingstwist#

C#
public class StockOptions
{
    [Required] public Uri? BaseUrl { get; set; }
}

builder.Services.AddOptions<StockOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Clients:Stock")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();
Java 25
@Validated
public class HttpClientProperties {

    /** The root URL of the other service, such as {@code https://stock.internal}. */
    @NotNull
    private URI baseUrl;
Reading the code
@Validated

@Validated, from org.springframework.validation.annotation, tells Boot to validate the object after it binds the settings. Validation runs at startup, when Spring creates the bean.

@NotNull

A constraint of Bean Validation, from jakarta.validation.constraints. A missing base-url leaves the field null, and validation fails.

So a deployment that forgets STOCK_SERVICE_URL never starts. Without the check, the service would start, pass its probes and fail at the first order. The class comment says the same. In ASP.NET Core, ValidateOnStart() moves the same check to startup.

A run for this book bound a copy of this class from a @Bean method, on Boot 4.1.2, with no base URL. The startup failed with this chain of causes:

ConfigurationPropertiesBindException: Error creating bean with name 'stockClientProperties': Could not bind properties to 'Props.HttpClientProperties' : prefix=clients.stock ... BindValidationException: Binding validation errors on clients.stock - Field error in object 'clients.stock' on field 'baseUrl': rejected value [null]; ... default message [must not be null]#
Means
A validated properties class did not get a required value. The message names the bean, the prefix, the field and the constraint.
Fix
Set the key, here clients.stock.base-url, or its environment variable. Do not remove the constraint to make the service start.
What triggers it
clients:
  stock:
    read-timeout: 3s        # base-url is missing

The same run on .NET 10 failed in StartAsync with OptionsValidationException: DataAnnotation validation failed for 'StockOptions' members: 'BaseUrl' with the error: 'The BaseUrl field is required.'

Validate every setting whose absence would break a request, such as a URL or a queue name. Leave a setting without a constraint when its default is right. The timeouts carry @NotNull too, so a service cannot set one to an empty value.

Nested settings with defaults in codetwist#

C#
public class ResilienceOptions
{
    public RetryOptions Retry { get; } = new();

    public class RetryOptions
    {
        public int MaxAttempts { get; set; } = 3;
        public TimeSpan InitialInterval { get; set; }
            = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200);
    }
}
Java 25
@ConfigurationProperties("platform.resilience")
public class ResilienceProperties {

    private final Retry retry = new Retry();
    private final CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker = new CircuitBreaker();

    public Retry getRetry() {
        return retry;
    }

    public CircuitBreaker getCircuitBreaker() {
        return circuitBreaker;
    }

    /** How often to try an idempotent call. */
    public static class Retry {

        /** The number of attempts in total, including the first one. 3 means up to 2 retries. */
        private int maxAttempts = 3;
Reading the code
private final Retry retry = new Retry();

The nested object exists from the start, and the field is final. There is no setter for it. Spring calls getRetry() and then binds the keys under platform.resilience.retry into that object.

public static class Retry {

A static nested class does not belong to an instance of the outer class. It is like a nested class in C#, which is always independent of the outer instance.

private int maxAttempts = 3;

The key is platform.resilience.retry.max-attempts. The comment states what the number means. It counts every attempt, so 3 means one call and up to two retries.

The defaults are in the code, beside the field they belong to. A service that sets nothing gets them all. The keys of this class, with their defaults:

KeyDefaultWhat it does
platform.resilience.retry.max-attempts3the attempts in total, so up to 2 retries
platform.resilience.retry.initial-interval200msthe wait before the first retry
platform.resilience.retry.multiplier2.0how much each later wait grows
platform.resilience.circuit-breaker.failure-rate-threshold50the failure rate, in percent, that opens the breaker
platform.resilience.circuit-breaker.sliding-window-size20the number of recent calls the rate is computed over
platform.resilience.circuit-breaker.minimum-number-of-calls10the breaker computes no rate before this many calls
platform.resilience.circuit-breaker.wait-duration-in-open-state30show long the breaker stays open

Two facts here are easy to state wrongly. max-attempts of 3 is two retries, not three. And the breaker does not open at "50 percent of 20 calls" alone. It computes no rate at all before 10 calls. For how the calls use these values, see the chapter Calling other services.

MessagingProperties has the same shape, with two nested classes, Outbox and Inbox. Its keys are in the quick reference at the end of this chapter.

Durations and lists from texttrap#

A setting in YAML is text, and Spring converts it to the type of the field. Two conversions surprise a C# developer.

PredictA read timeout without a unit#
A developer changes read-timeout: 3s to read-timeout: 3, to mean three seconds. What read timeout does the stock client get?
clients:
  stock:
    base-url: ${STOCK_SERVICE_URL}
    read-timeout: 3s
Show the answer
3 milliseconds, which is far too short for an HTTP call.

A number with no unit is milliseconds for a Duration. The Boot reference says that the default unit is milliseconds, unless @DurationUnit says otherwise. A run for this book bound 3 to PT0.003S. The field readTimeout is a java.time.Duration.

.NET reads the same text differently. In a run on .NET 10, "3" bound to a TimeSpan gave 3 days, and "3s" failed to convert. Always write the unit, as in 3s or 250ms.

Spring accepts two forms of a duration. The table shows what a run for this book bound:

Text in the settingsDuration
3sPT3S, 3 seconds
250msPT0.25S, 250 milliseconds
PT15MPT15M, the ISO-8601 form, 15 minutes
3PT0.003S, 3 milliseconds

A list is the other surprise. The service lists its path variables on one line:

platform:
  logging:
    # Added to every log line of a request, next to traceId
    mdc-path-variables: orderId, lineId, noteId

The key mdc-path-variables fills the field mdcPathVariables, a List<String>. Spring splits the text at each comma and trims the spaces. A run for this book gave the list [orderId, lineId, noteId]. A YAML list, with one - orderId per line, binds to the same list.

.NET behaves differently. A run on .NET 10 bound the text orderId, lineId, noteId to a List<string>. The list was empty, and there was no error. .NET needs one key for each element, as in MdcPathVariables:0. So keep the habit of one key for each element when you write settings for both platforms.

One value with a default: @Valuetwist#

C#
var lockTtl = configuration.GetValue(
    "Platform:Mongo:Migrations:LockTtl",
    TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15));
Java 25
MongoMigrationRunner mongoMigrationRunner(MongoTemplate mongo, ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations, Clock clock,
                                          @Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl) {
    return new MongoMigrationRunner(mongo, migrations.orderedStream().toList(), clock, lockTtl);
}
Reading the code
@Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl

@Value injects one setting into a parameter. After the colon is the default, 15 minutes in the ISO-8601 form. Spring converts the text to a Duration, as it does for a properties class.

A placeholder works in an annotation too. The queue listener takes its queue name from the settings, so each environment can name its own queue:

/** The queue name comes from configuration, so each environment can name its own queue. */
@SqsListener("${messaging.queues.payment-received}")
void on(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    process(event);
}

@SqsListener resolves ${messaging.queues.payment-received} at startup. The key is set in application.yml, with the default order-service-payment-received. For the listener, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

Prefer a properties class for a setting that belongs to a group. The lock time to live (TTL) is the one platform setting outside a class. So the IDE has no description for it, and its default is in an annotation, not beside the other migration keys. A field in a properties class, such as platform.mongo.migrations, would fix both. @Value is right for a single value that one method needs, such as the queue name of one listener.

Switches: @ConditionalOnPropertynew#

A wiring test must not run the migrations, and a service with no events must not start the outbox. The platform lets a property switch such a part off. The switch is an annotation on the bean or on the whole auto-configuration:

/** Runs the migrations at startup. Slice and wiring tests turn it off with the property. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
MongoMigrationRunner mongoMigrationRunner(MongoTemplate mongo, ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations, Clock clock,
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)

Spring creates the bean only when the property has the value true. matchIfMissing = true also creates it when the property is not set at all. So the runner is on by default, and a test turns it off with enabled: false.

A run for this book checked the three cases of this condition:

platform.messaging.enabledThe bean
not setpresent, because of matchIfMissing
falseabsent
TRUE, in upper casepresent, because the value is compared without case

On a whole class, the condition switches every bean of that class. The messaging auto-configuration carries it, so one property removes the outbox and the inbox:

/**
 * The outbox and the inbox. A service that sends and receives no events turns all of it off
 * with {@code platform.messaging.enabled=false}, together with Spring Cloud AWS's
 * {@code spring.cloud.aws.sns.enabled=false} and {@code spring.cloud.aws.sqs.enabled=false}.
 *
 * <p>The resender is in its own nested configuration, which also turns on scheduling. So
 * scheduling is on only when the resender is on, and a service sees it in one property:
 * {@code platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled}.
 */
@AutoConfiguration(after = PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.messaging.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(MessagingProperties.class)
public class PlatformMessagingAutoConfiguration {

The @ConditionalOnProperty on the class switches off every bean of the class, including the nested resender configuration. A service with no events also sets three properties of Spring Cloud AWS and Spring Modulith. For the four properties, see the section Switching a whole area off.

The wiring test sets only spring.cloud.aws.sqs.enabled: false and the two platform switches for the migrations and the resender. It keeps the outbox, so the test checks its wiring too.

In ASP.NET Core, the same switch is an if around the registrations in Program.cs. Spring keeps the switch on the bean itself, so the library decides it and the service only sets the property.

The platform's defaults, below everything elsenew#

Every service of the shop needs the same health probes, JSON logs and safe error responses. The platform could ask each service to copy twenty keys into its application.yml. Copies drift. So the platform adds the keys itself, at the lowest precedence. Any service can still override any of them.

A class that changes the settings before the application context exists is called an environment post-processor. The platform has one:

public class PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor implements EnvironmentPostProcessor, Ordered {

    private static final String DEFAULTS = "classpath*:META-INF/platform-defaults/*.properties";

    @Override
    public void postProcessEnvironment(ConfigurableEnvironment environment, SpringApplication application) {
        try {
            Resource[] files = new PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver().getResources(DEFAULTS);
            Arrays.sort(files, Comparator.comparing(Resource::getFilename));
            for (Resource file : files) {
                environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new PropertiesPropertySource(
                        "platform-defaults:" + file.getFilename(), PropertiesLoaderUtils.loadProperties(file)));
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not load the platform defaults", e);
        }

        if (environment.getProperty("platform.logging.structured", Boolean.class, true)) {
            environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new MapPropertySource("platform-defaults:structured-logging",
                    Map.of("logging.structured.format.console", "ecs")));
        }
    }

    @Override
    public int getOrder() {
        // Run after Spring Boot has loaded application.yml, so the check above can read it.
        return Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE;
    }
}
Reading the code
implements EnvironmentPostProcessor, Ordered {

In Boot 4, the interface is org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor. The Boot 3 type org.springframework.boot.env.EnvironmentPostProcessor still exists, and is deprecated since 4.0.0. Ordered lets the class say when it runs among the other post-processors.

"classpath*:META-INF/platform-defaults/*.properties"

The prefix classpath*: finds the matching files in every Java archive (JAR) on the classpath, not only in the first one. The platform has three files, one for each of its packages.

new PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver().getResources(DEFAULTS)

This Spring class turns the pattern into a list of Resource objects. A Resource is a file that Spring can read, from a JAR or from a folder.

Arrays.sort(files, Comparator.comparing(Resource::getFilename));

The files are sorted by name: core.properties, messaging.properties, mongo.properties. A sorted order is the same on every machine.

environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new PropertiesPropertySource(

The environment holds an ordered list of property sources. For each key, Spring takes the value from the first source that has it. addLast puts the file at the end, below every other source. PropertiesLoaderUtils.loadProperties reads the file into a Properties object.

if (environment.getProperty("platform.logging.structured", Boolean.class, true)) {

This condition reads the settings that exist already, with true as the default. A properties file cannot say "only if another key is not false". So this one default is code.

Map.of("logging.structured.format.console", "ecs")

This key makes Boot write each console log line as JSON in the Elastic Common Schema (ECS). A MapPropertySource holds keys from a map in code.

return Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE;

The order of the post-processor, not of its keys. Boot's own post-processor that loads application.yml has the order HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10. This one runs after it, so the condition above can read the service's setting.

Boot finds the class through one line in the platform's JAR:

# EnvironmentPostProcessor is still registered here, not in the AutoConfiguration.imports file.
org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor=\
com.acme.platform.core.config.PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor

The key of the line, org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor, is the Boot 4 interface. A run for this book registered one processor under this key and one under the deprecated Boot 3 key. Both ran on Boot 4.1.2. So an old registration still works, but it is deprecated. The post-processors run before logging starts. In Boot 4.1.2, the listener that runs them has the order HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10, and the logging listener HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 20. So the platform's logging defaults reach the logging system in time.

The platform's files come below every other source. The diagram shows the order, from command-line arguments and Java system properties down to the platform's files:

Two tests of the platform check the behaviour:

@Test
void addsTheDefaultsWithTheLowestPrecedence() {
    StandardEnvironment environment = new StandardEnvironment();
    environment.getPropertySources().addFirst(new MapPropertySource("application.yml",
            Map.of("server.shutdown", "immediate")));

    postProcessor.postProcessEnvironment(environment, new SpringApplication());

    assertThat(environment.getProperty("server.shutdown")).isEqualTo("immediate");
    assertThat(environment.getProperty("spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation")).isEqualTo("false");
    assertThat(environment.getProperty("logging.structured.format.console")).isEqualTo("ecs");
}
Reading the code
environment.getPropertySources().addFirst(new MapPropertySource("application.yml",

The test replaces the service's file with a map source. It sets server.shutdown, which core.properties also sets.

assertThat(environment.getProperty("server.shutdown")).isEqualTo("immediate");

The service's value wins over the platform's graceful.

assertThat(environment.getProperty("spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation")).isEqualTo("false");

A key that only the platform sets comes through.

The second test, leavesStructuredLoggingOffWhenTheServiceAsks, sets platform.logging.structured to false and checks that the ECS key is absent.

.NET has no post-processor. A library that wants the same effect inserts its source at the start of the list, because in .NET a source added later wins. A run on .NET 10 did this with builder.Configuration.Sources.Insert(0, ...). A command-line argument then won over the library, and a key that only the library set came through.

The alternative is a defaults file that each service copies, or a profile in the platform JAR that each service activates. Both are simple. A copied file goes stale in every service at a different time, and a profile can be forgotten. A post-processor needs no step in the service, and it cannot be skipped. Use it for defaults that every service must have.

What the platform sets, and whynew#

Each package of the platform has its own file of defaults. Every key in them is a decision, and the comment beside it gives the reason. Some keys restate a Boot default on purpose, as the top of the core file explains:

# Defaults that every service gets from the platform's core package.
# They have the LOWEST precedence: a service's application.yml overrides any of them.
# Some keys restate a Spring Boot 4.1 default. They stay here on purpose: the platform's
# behaviour is visible in one file, and a Boot upgrade that changes a default cannot change it.

# Health probes for the orchestrator (a Boot default, restated):
#   /actuator/health/liveness  - is the process alive? Never include other services or the database.
#   /actuator/health/readiness - can it take traffic? The mongo defaults add the database.
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=never

# Tracing. Every request gets a traceId in the MDC, even when it is not sampled.
# Lower the sampling rate in production if volumes are high.
management.tracing.sampling.probability=1.0
# Traces are exported only when management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint is set.
# Metrics would be exported to localhost:4318 by default, so they are off until a service
# sets management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled=true and management.otlp.metrics.export.url.
management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled=false

# Finish the requests in flight when the service is stopped (graceful is a Boot default, restated).
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s

The comments give the reason next to each key. For example, management.tracing.sampling.probability=1.0 keeps every trace. Each key of core.properties, with the Boot 4.1.2 default and the reason for the platform's value:

KeyPlatform valueBoot 4.1.2 defaultWhy
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabledtruetruerestated, so the probes stay on even if a Boot release changes the default
management.endpoints.web.exposure.includehealth,infohealthinfo is added, which the platform's security also leaves public
management.endpoint.health.show-detailsneverneverrestated, so a probe shows the status and no details
management.tracing.sampling.probability1.00.1every trace is kept, and a busy service lowers the rate
management.otlp.metrics.export.enabledfalsetruewith no collector, Boot would push metrics to localhost:4318 and log failures
server.shutdowngracefulgracefulrestated, so requests in flight finish when an instance stops
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase20s30sa real change, so each phase of the shutdown waits at most 20 seconds
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-null-for-primitivesfalsetrue in Jackson 3an omitted boolean means false again, as the next section shows
spring.web.error.include-stacktrace and include-messageneverneverBoot's own error page shows no stack trace and no message, and Boot 4 ignores the old server.error names
logging.structured.json.customizerPersonalDataMaskingCustomizernoneJSON logs mask e-mail addresses and other personal data
springdoc.writer-with-order-by-keystruefalsethe generated OpenAPI file lists keys in a fixed order, so it changes only with the API
springdoc.default-produces-media-typeapplication/jsonnot checkedthe document says JSON instead of */*
springdoc.api-docs.enabled and swagger-ui.enabledtrue and falsenot checked, and falsethe document stays on for the drift check, and the local profile turns Swagger UI on

The trace ID is in the mapped diagnostic context (MDC) and in each log line even when a trace is not sampled. A run for this book showed it with the default rate of 0.1. So a lower rate in production loses traces, but never the IDs in the logs. For tracing, probes and shutdown, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health. For the OpenAPI keys, see the chapter API and event contracts.

The mongo package adds four keys:

# Indexes are created by migrations (MongoMigration), never by Spring at startup.
# Startup index creation is invisible, nobody reviews it, and it can block on a large collection.
spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation=false

# The service is ready for traffic only when the database is reachable.
# Liveness deliberately leaves the database out: a database outage must not restart every instance.
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,mongo

The excerpt shows two of the four keys. auto-index-creation=false leaves every index to the migrations. The table gives all four:

KeyPlatform valueDefaultWhy
spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creationfalseoff in Spring Datarestated, because every index comes from a reviewed migration
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.includereadinessState,mongoreadinessState onlyreadiness fails when the database is down, and liveness does not
spring.mongodb.representation.uuidstandardunspecifiedBoot 4 expects an explicit choice, and the outbox stores UUIDs
spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimaldecimal128unspecifiedmoney stays exact even in a field with no type mapping, such as an event in the outbox

The Boot 4 migration guide says that "An explicit configuration is expected" for the two representations. For the stored types, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

The messaging package sets the outbox and the queues:

KeyPlatform valueDefaultWhy
spring.modulith.events.completion-modedeleteupdatea sent event is removed, so the collection stays small
spring.modulith.events.mongodb.transaction-management.enabledfalsetruethe platform's mongo package already declares the transaction manager
spring.modulith.events.republish-outstanding-events-on-restartfalsefalserestated, because the resender sends unsent events on a schedule
spring.modulith.events.externalization.enabledtruetruerestated, so the events reach SNS
spring.cloud.aws.sqs.queue-not-found-strategyfailcreate, in the codea missing queue stops the startup, instead of a new queue with no dead-letter queue
spring.modulith.events.staleness.resubmittedPT15Mnot set, so the monitor is offa row that stays RESUBMITTED for 15 minutes goes back to FAILED, and the resender takes it again

For each of these, see the chapters Publishing events: the outbox and Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

Jackson 3 and a body that leaves out a booleantrap#

A note can need action, or not. The request to add a note has a boolean for that, and a client may leave it out when it is false. Jackson, the JSON library of Spring, reads the body:

public record AddNoteRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 2000) String text,
        @Schema(description = "A NOTE_CATEGORY code", example = "DELIVERY") @NotBlank String category,
        @Schema(description = "Whether an agent must act on the note before the order ships") boolean actionRequired) {
}

The last component, boolean actionRequired, is a primitive. A primitive cannot be null, so a body without the field gives Jackson no value to put there.

Gotcha

Jackson 3 refuses a body that leaves out a primitive. In Jackson 3.1.7, FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES is on, also in the mapper that Boot 4.1.2 builds. A body without actionRequired fails with MismatchedInputException, and Spring model-view-controller (MVC) answers 400 with the detail "Failed to read request". Jackson 2 had the feature off, so the same request worked on Boot 3. In a run on .NET 10, System.Text.Json with the web defaults read the same body as ActionRequired = False. For the prediction, see the section Jackson 3: what changed for request bodies.

The platform restores the old behaviour with one key, in core.properties:

# Jackson 3 rejects a JSON body that leaves out a primitive field (boolean, int). Treat a missing
# primitive as its default value instead, so an omitted "actionRequired" means false.
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-null-for-primitives=false

spring.jackson.deserialization is a map from a feature of Jackson to on or off. The key after it is the name of the feature in lower case with dashes. A run for this book showed that the key works. The body then gave actionRequired=false, and so did an explicit null. System.Text.Json still rejected an explicit null for a bool in the .NET run.

A slice test of the service records the behaviour, so a change of the platform would fail the build:

/** Jackson 3 would reject the missing primitive; the platform's default makes it false. */
@Test
void anOmittedFlagMeansFalse() throws Exception {
    when(notes.addNote(ORDER_ID, new NewNote("FYI", "GENERAL", false))).thenReturn("note-2");

    mvc.perform(post("/orders/" + ORDER_ID + "/notes").with(AGENT).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                    .content("""
                            { "text": "FYI", "category": "GENERAL" }
                            """))
            .andExpect(status().isCreated());
    verify(notes).addNote(eq(ORDER_ID), eq(new NewNote("FYI", "GENERAL", false)));
}

The test posts the body without the flag and expects 201. It then checks that the service received false. There is a careful alternative. A Boolean wrapper with @NotNull would force every client to send the flag, and the contract would say so. The platform chose the default, so a client that worked against a Boot 3 service keeps working. For the other Jackson 3 defaults, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

Which source winstwist#

For the moment in a start when Spring reads every source, see the chapter Starting the service: from main() to the first request.

The same key can come from several sources. Spring takes the first source in its list that has the key. A run for this book printed that list for an application with a post-processor like the platform's. The order, first wins, for the order service:

PositionSourceIn the order service
1command-line arguments, such as --clients.stock.base-url=...the README uses them to run the service from an IDE
2Java system properties, set with -Dnot used
3OS environment variablesevery value that differs between environments
4application-{profile}.ymlapplication-local.yml, and application-wiring.yml in a test
5application.ymlevery key that every environment needs
6the platform defaults, added lastcore.properties, then messaging.properties, mongo.properties and the ECS switch
7the defaults in codethe field initialisers of the properties classes, and the default of a @Value

The README shows position 1. To run the service from an IDE, it overrides the container names with arguments:

--spring.mongodb.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/orders?directConnection=true
--spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=http://localhost:8090/default/jwks
--spring.security.oauth2.client.provider.shop-identity.token-uri=http://localhost:8090/default/token
--spring.cloud.aws.endpoint=http://localhost:4566
--clients.stock.base-url=http://localhost:8089

Each argument, such as --clients.stock.base-url, wins over application-local.yml, which is still active. So only the addresses change, and every other local setting stays.

A test can set keys above all of these, with @SpringBootTest(properties = ...). The journey test does this. The full list of the Boot reference has more sources, such as SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON. For that list, see the section Single values and precedence.

Between the platform's own files, the order of the file names decides. core.properties is added first, so it wins over messaging.properties for a key that both set. No key is in two files today.

The order in ASP.NET Core has the same idea, with the opposite rule. A source added later wins, so a library's defaults go at index 0.

Secrets never in a filenew#

A committed password stays in the history of the repository for ever. So no file of the order service holds a secret. Each secret reaches the service as an environment variable, which the deployment sets from the secrets manager. The client secret for the stock service is an example:

registration:
  stock-service:
    provider: shop-identity
    client-id: ${STOCK_CLIENT_ID:order-service}
    client-secret: ${STOCK_CLIENT_SECRET}
    authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
    scope: stock.reserve
Reading the code
client-id: ${STOCK_CLIENT_ID:order-service}

The client ID is not a secret, so it has a default.

client-secret: ${STOCK_CLIENT_SECRET}

The secret has no default in application.yml. Only the local profile sets a fake one.

The secrets of the service, and where each one comes from:

SecretIn productionLocally
the database user and passwordinside MONGO_URI, from the secrets managerno password, the local MongoDB has none
the client secret for the stock serviceSTOCK_CLIENT_SECRET, from the secrets managerlocal, in application-local.yml, which the mock issuer accepts
AWS credentialsnone, the IAM role of the task or podthe fixed access-key local, for Floci

The local profile is committed, because its values are not secret. They work only against the containers of the local environment. For a real password on a developer's machine, see the section Secrets. It uses a local file that git ignores. The shop needs no such file, because nothing local is real.

A library such as Spring Cloud AWS can also read the secrets manager at startup. The service then writes spring.config.import=aws-secretsmanager: with the names of its secrets. That removes the step in the deployment. It also ties the startup to AWS, and the service then needs the permission to read secrets. The shop keeps the environment variables, so the service reads its settings in one way in every environment.

Two more rules keep secrets out of the logs. Boot's own error responses contain no exception message, by default. And the JSON logs mask personal data. For both, see the chapters The web layer in depth and Logging, tracing and health.

Completion in the IDE: the configuration metadatanew#

A developer types platform.resilience. in application.yml and expects the IDE to list the keys. The IDE needs a description of the keys for that. Boot's own keys have one in each Boot JAR. The platform's keys need one too.

The description is a file, META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json. The Spring Boot configuration processor writes it at compile time, from the @ConfigurationProperties classes. The parent Project Object Model (POM) runs the processor for every project. For that setting and its trap, see the section The configuration processor, and the file it did not write.

A build of the companion wrote the file into the platform's jar. It held 16 keys in 9 groups. Each key had its type, its default and a description. The description is the /** ... */ comment on the field:

/** The number of attempts in total, including the first one. 3 means up to 2 retries. */
private int maxAttempts = 3;

The file lists the field maxAttempts as platform.resilience.retry.max-attempts, of type java.lang.Integer, with the default 3 and the comment as its description. The first build showed one key without a description, platform.resilience.retry.multiplier. Its field had no comment, so the platform added one. A key with no comment still completes in the IDE, but the IDE cannot explain it.

The order service's jar got a file too, with the four keys of clients.stock. The service binds them with @ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock") on a @Bean method, to the platform's class HttpClientProperties. The fields of that class have comments and initial values. Yet the service's file listed the four keys with their types only, with no description and no default. The class comes compiled, in the platform's jar, and the service's build did not find its comments or its defaults there. So the IDE completes these keys, but cannot explain them. The platform's own keys, compiled from source, have both.

The metadata also lists deprecated keys with their replacement. That is how the IDE marks a Boot 3 key in a Boot 4 service. A key that is not in any metadata, such as platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl from a @Value, gets no completion and no warning.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe platform's post-processor adds its files with addLast, and its getOrder() returns LOWEST_PRECEDENCE. What does each method do?
addLast places the defaults at the end of the list of property sources. Spring takes a key from the first source that has it, so every setting of the service wins. getOrder() decides when the post-processor runs. It runs after Boot's post-processor that loads application.yml, so it can read platform.logging.structured before it adds the ECS switch.
2
An expert asksWhy does the platform validate base-url with @Validated and @NotNull, instead of letting the first call fail?
The check runs when Spring creates the bean, at startup. A deployment that forgets the URL never starts, and it fails with an error that names the prefix and the field. Without the check, the service would start and pass its probes. It would then fail at the first order, far from the cause.
3
TranslateWrite this options setup in the style of the order service. The stock client's settings are bound from clients.stock, and a missing base URL stops the startup: 
builder.Services.AddOptions<StockOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Clients:Stock")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();
/** Binds the platform's reusable properties class to this client's prefix. */
@Bean
@ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")
HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties() {
    return new HttpClientProperties();
}

The validation is on the class. HttpClientProperties carries @Validated. Its field baseUrl carries @NotNull. Spring validates when it creates the bean, so no extra call is needed.

platform.messaging.inbox.retentionP14Dhow long processed event IDs are kept, by a TTL index

Use cases: the application service#

Wiring, configuration and use cases · Chapter 12· 27 min read

Each feature of the order service has one application service. Its public methods are the use cases, such as placing or shipping an order. A use case follows the same steps every time. It loads, lets the domain apply its rules, saves, publishes the events and writes an audit entry. It holds no business rule. This chapter covers each use case, the calls between features, and the tests.

KindC#JavaNote
twistone handler class per command, as with MediatRone application service per feature, such as OrderServicereads and changes of a feature are on one class, until it grows past about ten use cases Why
newno equivalentload, rule and change, save, publish, auditevery use case that changes data has the same steps, so a reader finds each step in the same place Why
twistan action that takes a DTO and returns the entityparameters are value objects, results are IDs or viewsa caller cannot skip a rule, because no aggregate leaves the service Why
newno equivalentOrderView leaves out the customer's contacta view carries personal data only when a use case needs it Why
twistan interface in the application projectStockChecker in order/application/portcalling another service is a step of the use case, so its port belongs to the application layer Why
newno equivalentthe stock call before TransactionTemplate.executea slow HTTP call never holds a DocumentDB transaction open, and the order ID is the idempotency key Why
trapcontext.SaveChanges(), then keep using the same entityOrder saved = orders.save(order)the instance passed in keeps the old version, so the use case continues with the returned copy Why
newno equivalentthe order and its first notes in one transactionone request saves two aggregates, because the agent sees it as one action Why
newno equivalentNoteService.addNotes(orderId, List<NewNote>)features call each other only through the application service, with plain values Why
twista second service class in the same styleNoteService, with String IDs and a Spring Data repositorythe light style has the same steps, with fewer types Why
twista validation attribute that reads a lookup tableReferenceDataService.requireActive(type, code, field)the rule "a code must be an active lookup value" is written once, and every feature asks it Why
newno equivalentif (order.recordPayment(payment))the only if in a use case decides the next step, and never a business rule Why
twistan action per verb on the same servicepickLine, cancel, get and listthe short use cases have the same steps, and the reads return views Why
newno equivalentthe journeys of a request, a message and an eventeach step of a journey has one home, so a bug is found by its step Why
