twista unit test of the service with MoqOrderServiceTest with Mockito and a real TransactionTemplatethe test checks the order of the steps, with the real domain and mocked ports Why

One application service per featuretwist#

A use case is one thing that a user or another system wants to do, such as placing an order. The class that holds the use cases of a feature is called its application service. The order service has three features, so it has three application services:

FeatureApplication serviceIts public methods
orderOrderServiceplace, pickLine, ship, cancel, recordPayment, get, list, requireExists
noteNoteServiceaddNote, addNotes, resolveAction, list, countNeedingAction
referenceReferenceDataServicelist, requireActive

Every caller goes through these classes. The controllers call them for HTTP requests. The message listener calls OrderService.recordPayment for a payment. And the features call each other through them. The class comment of OrderService states the role:

/**
 * The use cases of the order feature. This is the one entry point for the controller, the
 * message listener and other features.
 *
 * <p>Every change follows the same steps: load, let the domain apply its rules and change
 * itself, save, publish the events, record the audit. The steps that call other services run
 * before the transaction. This class decides the order of the steps and never contains a
 * business rule: a line that a business expert would recognise as a rule belongs in the domain.
 *
 * <p>Methods take value objects, which are valid already, and return IDs or views, never an
 * aggregate.

The reads are on the same class as the changes. The reads get and list need no class of their own. The service does not separate commands from queries, which is called command query responsibility segregation (CQRS). For why the service has no CQRS, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

Older designs, and many examples on the web, use one class for each use case. You may meet classes such as PlaceOrder and OrderQueries. Each command then has a record, such as PlaceOrderCommand. The two styles compare like this:

StyleWhat it gets rightWhat it costs
one service per feature, as herea reader finds every use case of a feature in one file, and shared steps stay privatethe class grows with the feature, and must be split by hand
one class per use case, with a command recordeach class is small, and a pipeline can wrap every command the same waymany small files, and the shared steps move to a base class or a helper

In .NET, the second style often goes with MediatR, with one handler for each request. It works well when every command needs the same steps around it, such as validation and logging. The book still recommends one service per feature for a service of this size. Ten use cases fit in one file, and the private helper saveAndPublish keeps the steps the same. Choose one class per use case when a feature has many use cases that share nothing, or when a team already runs a command pipeline.

The steps of a use casenew#

A new developer must add a use case to cancel a line. Where does the rule go? Where is the event published? If every use case had its own shape, each answer would need a search. So every use case that changes data follows the same steps, in the same order.

The use case ship shows every step:

C#
public async Task Ship(OrderId orderId)
{
    var order = await orders.Get(orderId);
    var notesNeedingAction =
        await notes.CountNeedingAction(orderId.Value);
    shippingPolicy.AssertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction);
    order.Ship(clock);
    await SaveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.OrderShipped);
}
Java 25
/** Ships the order. The rule across the order and its notes is checked by the domain service. */
@Transactional
public void ship(OrderId orderId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);                                         // load
    long notesNeedingAction = notes.countNeedingAction(orderId.value());       // ask the note feature
    shippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction);                   // rule across aggregates
    order.ship(clock);                                                         // rule and change
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_SHIPPED);                         // save, publish, audit
}
Reading the code
@Transactional

The whole use case runs in one transaction. The proxy of the bean starts it before the first line, and commits after the last one. For the proxy, see the section Where the service relies on proxies.

Order order = orders.get(orderId); // load

get is a default method of the repository port. It throws OrderNotFoundException when no order has the ID. So the use case loads the order in one line, and the platform answers 404.

long notesNeedingAction = notes.countNeedingAction(orderId.value()); // ask the note feature

The order feature does not read notes. It asks the note feature for a number, and passes the ID as plain text.

shippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction); // rule across aggregates

A rule that needs data from two aggregates is in a domain service, ShippingPolicy. For where each rule goes, see the chapter Where each rule goes.

order.ship(clock); // rule and change

The aggregate checks its own rules, paid and every line picked, and changes its status. It raises the event OrderShipped and keeps it until it is pulled.

saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_SHIPPED); // save, publish, audit

One private helper does the last three steps. See the section Continue with the saved copy.

The method has no permission annotation. The controller checks the scope before it calls the method. So the payment listener and other features call the same method with no identity. For why, see the section Choosing the place by the shape of the service.

Two agents can change the same order at the same time. Both agents load the order, and both ship it. The second save fails, because its version is old. The comment of the repository port names the two ways in which a save fails. The platform answers both with 409:

/**
 * Saves the aggregate and returns the stored copy, which holds the new version.
 *
 * <p>Continue with the returned instance. The instance you passed in keeps the old version,
 * so saving it a second time fails. For a new aggregate it fails as a duplicate insert, with
 * {@code DuplicateKeyException}; for a loaded one, as a concurrent update. Saving also fails
 * with Spring's {@code OptimisticLockingFailureException} when someone else saved the
 * aggregate after you loaded it; that exception is unchecked, so this plain-Java interface
 * can only name it here.
 * Inside a transaction, MongoDB usually reports the same conflict as a write conflict, which
 * Spring translates to {@code DataIntegrityViolationException}. The platform answers both with 409.

The use case catches no exception. When OptimisticLockingFailureException leaves the method, the transaction rolls back. So the event and the audit record of the failed attempt are never stored. The audit log writes with MongoTemplate, which joins the running transaction. The agent gets 409 with the code CONCURRENT_UPDATE and loads the order again. For versions and write conflicts, see the chapters Storing aggregates in DocumentDB and Transactions in depth.

Parameters are value objects, results are IDs or viewstwist#

C#
public PlacedOrder Place(CustomerContact customer,
    DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
    List<NewNote> firstNotes)
{
    throw new NotImplementedException();
}
Java 25
public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
                         List<NewNote> firstNotes) {

Each parameter of place is a value object of the domain, except the notes. A value object checks itself when it is created. new DeliveryMethod("") throws, and the platform answers 400 with the field. So the use case never checks a parameter. The controller builds the value objects from the request, as the section One request through the checks shows.

The result is a small record with the new IDs:

/**
 * The result of placing an order: only the new IDs. The caller reads the order again if it
 * needs more.
 */
public record PlacedOrder(String orderId, List<String> noteIds) {

    public PlacedOrder {
        noteIds = List.copyOf(noteIds);
    }
}
Reading the code
public PlacedOrder {

This is a compact constructor. It runs before the fields are set, and can replace a parameter.

noteIds = List.copyOf(noteIds);

The record keeps a copy that cannot change. A caller that changes its own list later does not change the result.

A use case returns one of three things. A change that creates something returns the new IDs. A read returns a view. Any other change returns nothing, and the controller answers 204. No use case returns an aggregate:

Use caseReturnsWhy
placePlacedOrder, with the IDsthe controller needs the ID for the Location header
ship, cancel, pickLine, recordPaymentnothingthe caller knows the ID already, and reads again if it needs more
get, listOrderView, or a PageResult of themthe data of the order, with no method that changes it
NoteService.addNotethe note's ID, as a Stringthe light style uses plain IDs

Returning the aggregate would make the view record unnecessary. A careful team can return it and agree that callers never call its methods. Nothing enforces that agreement, though. A caller with an Order can call order.ship(clock) and skip the shipping policy, the save and the event. A view cannot be used that way. So the book recommends views for every service, and the cost is one record and one mapping method.

Views that leave out personal datanew#

A view is the data that callers see of an aggregate. The order view holds the status, the lines and the last payment. It does not hold the customer's name or e-mail address:

/**
 * What callers of the order feature see of an order: plain data, never the aggregate. A caller
 * therefore cannot call {@code order.ship()} and skip the use case's steps.
 *
 * <p>The customer's contact is left out. A view carries personal data only when a use case
 * needs it.
 */
public record OrderView(String orderId, String status, String deliveryMethod, Instant placedAt, Instant shippedAt,
                        Instant cancelledAt, List<Line> lines, LastPayment lastPayment) {

    public record Line(String lineId, String productCode, int quantity, String status, Instant pickedAt) {

        static Line from(OrderLine line) {
            return new Line(line.id().value(), line.product().value(), line.quantity(), line.status().name(),
                    line.pickedAt());
        }
    }
// ...
    static OrderView from(Order order) {
        return new OrderView(order.id().value(), order.status().name(), order.deliveryMethod().code(),
                order.placedAt(), order.shippedAt(), order.cancelledAt(),
                order.lines().stream().map(Line::from).toList(),
                LastPayment.from(order.lastPayment()));
    }
}
Reading the code
public record OrderView(String orderId, String status, String deliveryMethod, Instant placedAt, Instant shippedAt,

Every component is plain data, such as a String or an Instant. The typed IDs and the enums of the domain do not leave the feature.

public record Line(String lineId, String productCode, int quantity, String status, Instant pickedAt) {

A record can contain records. OrderView.Line is the view of one line, and OrderView.LastPayment the view of the payment.

static OrderView from(Order order) {

The mapping method has no access modifier, so it is package-private. Only the application package can build a view from an aggregate. A controller in the api package reads views, but cannot build them.

The view leaves the customer out on purpose. The service keeps the contact for the delivery, and no use case of the API needs to return it. Data that is never returned cannot leak in a response, a log line or a cache. The events leave the customer out too. If a screen needs the contact later, a new use case returns it, and the review of that use case asks who may see it.

The note feature has a view of the same kind:

/** What callers see of a note. */
public record NoteView(String noteId, String orderId, String text, String category, boolean actionRequired,
                       boolean needsAction, Instant createdAt, Instant actionResolvedAt) {

    static NoteView from(Note note) {
        return new NoteView(note.id(), note.orderId(), note.text(), note.category(), note.actionRequired(),
                note.needsAction(), note.createdAt(), note.actionResolvedAt());
    }
}

needsAction is computed by the entity. It is true when the note needs action and no one has resolved it yet. The view carries the answer, so no caller repeats the rule.

The controller then maps a view to a response data transfer object (DTO). That second mapping looks like a copy. It lets the API change its JSON without touching the use case. For the DTOs and the mappers, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

Ports in the application layertwist#

C#
// in the application project
public interface IStockChecker
{
    StockAvailability Reserve(
        OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);
}
Java 25
/**
 * The port to the stock service, in this service's types. The use case does not know that the
 * answer comes over HTTP, and a unit test replaces it with a mock.
 *
 * <p>It lives in {@code application/port}, not in the domain: calling another service is a step
 * of the use case, and the domain only judges the answer.
 */
public interface StockChecker {

    /**
     * Asks the stock service to confirm that the items are available, and to hold them for the
     * order. The stock service keeps the hold until it sees {@code OrderPlacedV1}, or releases it
     * after a timeout if the order is never placed.
     *
     * <p>Calling it twice for the same order holds nothing twice, because the order ID is the
     * idempotency key.
     */
    StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);
}

A port is an interface that the inside of the service declares. An adapter outside the domain and the application layer implements it. StockChecker is such a port. The order feature has two kinds of port, in two places:

PortPackageWhy there
OrderRepositoryorder/domain/repositorythe domain says what it needs to load and save an aggregate
StockCheckerorder/application/portcalling another service is a step of the use case, and the domain only judges the answer

The domain receives the answer as a value, StockAvailability. Order.place takes it as a parameter and refuses the order when a product is missing. So the domain has the rule, and it never calls the stock service. The adapter StockAdapter implements the port over HTTP. An architecture rule checks that the application layer of the order feature uses no adapter.

For the adapter, retries and the anti-corruption layer, see the chapter Calling other services.

Placing an order: the stock call before the transactionnew#

Placing an order calls the stock service over HTTP. That call can take seconds. A DocumentDB transaction has a limit of one minute, and its log must stay under 32 MB, as of October 2026. A slow call inside the transaction would hold it open. So place makes the call first, and starts the transaction after it:

public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
                         List<NewNote> firstNotes) {
    referenceData.requireActive(ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD, deliveryMethod.code(), "deliveryMethod");
    OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();
    StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items);           // outside the transaction

    return transaction.execute(status -> {
        Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);
        Order saved = saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_PLACED);        // aggregate 1
        List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction
        return new PlacedOrder(saved.id().value(), noteIds);
    });
}
Reading the code
referenceData.requireActive(ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD, deliveryMethod.code(), "deliveryMethod");

The cheap check runs first. An inactive delivery method is a 400, and the stock service is never called.

OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();

The ID is chosen before the order exists. The stock call sends it as the idempotency key, so a retried call holds the products once.

StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items); // outside the transaction

This is the call to the other service. No transaction is open yet.

return transaction.execute(status -> {

The field transaction is a TransactionTemplate. Only the lambda is transactional. execute returns what the lambda returns, here the PlacedOrder. The parameter status can mark the transaction for rollback. This code does not use it.

Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);

The domain decides. It refuses the order when the stock service reported a missing product.

The method uses the template, because @Transactional would wrap the whole method. The stock call would then run inside the transaction. For the template bean, see the section The TransactionTemplate bean.

The order of the steps has a cost. The stock service may hold the products, and the transaction may then fail. No order is stored, so no OrderPlacedV1 is published. The stock service releases the hold after its timeout, as the comment of the port says. The other order of the steps puts the call inside the transaction. That order avoids the hold with no order. But it holds a transaction open for the length of an HTTP call, and a retry of the call holds it open longer still. The book recommends the call first, with an idempotency key, for any call that can be slow.

Two tests of the service record the order of the steps:

TestWhat it checks
OrderServiceTest.Place.checksTheDeliveryMethodBeforeCallingTheStockServicean inactive delivery method throws, and the stock port is never called
OrderServiceTest.Place.savesNothingWhenTheStockIsNotAvailablea missing product throws, and nothing is saved, published or audited

Continue with the saved copytrap#

The last three steps of every change are in one private helper:

/**
 * Saves the order, publishes its events and records the audit, all in the caller's
 * transaction.
 *
 * <p>The events are pulled before saving, because the saved copy that the repository returns
 * is rebuilt from the database and has none. The caller continues with the returned copy,
 * which holds the new version.
 */
private Order saveAndPublish(Order order, String auditAction) {
    List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();
    Order saved = orders.save(order);
    events.publish(raised);
    audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.ORDER, saved.id().value());
    return saved;
}
Reading the code
List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();

The events are taken from the aggregate first. The copy that save returns is built from the stored document, and has no events.

Order saved = orders.save(order);

The repository returns a new object with the new version. The object passed in keeps the old version, because the version of the full-style aggregate is final.

events.publish(raised);

The events go to the outbox, in the same transaction as the save. For the outbox, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.ORDER, saved.id().value());

The audit record names the action, the kind of resource and its ID. The platform adds who acted and when. For the audit, see the section The current actor, and the audit record.

return saved;

The helper returns the saved copy. place continues with it, as in saved.id().value().

Gotcha

After a save, the object you passed in is stale. With EF Core, a C# developer changes a tracked entity, calls SaveChanges, and keeps using the same object. SaveChanges returns only the number of entries it wrote. In the full style, only the returned copy holds the new version. A second save of the old object fails as a concurrent update. So a use case that saves twice must continue with the returned copy. For the light style, where Spring Data writes the version into the same object, see the section Versions after a save.

No use case of the service saves an aggregate twice today. The helper returns the copy anyway, so a later use case that saves twice is safe. The unit test makes the mock behave like the real repository, and returns a new copy with the next version:

/** Makes the mocked repository behave like the real one: save returns a stored copy with the next version. */
private void saveReturnsTheStoredCopy() {
    when(orders.save(any())).thenAnswer(call -> {
        Order order = call.getArgument(0);
        long next = order.version() == null ? 0 : order.version() + 1;
        return Order.rehydrate(order.id(), next, order.customer(), order.deliveryMethod(), order.placedAt(),
                order.lines(), order.status(), order.lastPayment(), order.shippedAt(), order.cancelledAt());
    });
}

thenAnswer runs the lambda for each call of save. Order.rehydrate builds a new aggregate from stored values, as the mapper does when it loads a document. A mock that returned the same object would hide a use case that ignores the result.

One request that saves the order and its first notesnew#

An agent places an order and writes a note in the same form, "Leave with a neighbour". For the agent, this is one action. If the note failed after the order was stored, the agent would see an error and find an order without the note. So place saves the order and its first notes in one transaction. Inside the lambda, the order feature calls the note feature:

/**
 * For the order feature: adds the first notes of a new order. It joins the caller's
 * transaction (propagation REQUIRED), so the order and its notes are stored together.
 */
@Transactional
public List<String> addNotes(String orderId, List<NewNote> newNotes) {
    return newNotes.stream().map(newNote -> add(orderId, newNote)).toList();
}

@Transactional with the default propagation REQUIRED joins a transaction that is already open. A run for this book showed it on MongoDB. Both inserts carried the same transaction number, and an exception in the inner method rolled back both. The journey test shows the effect on the whole service:

@Test
void anOrderAndItsNotesAreStoredTogetherOrNotAtAll() throws Exception {
    when(stock.reserve(any(), any())).thenReturn(StockAvailability.allAvailable());
    long ordersBefore = mongo.getCollection("orders").countDocuments();

    mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(agent).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("""
                    { %s, "deliveryMethod": "STANDARD", %s,
                      "notes": [ { "text": "Called the customer", "category": "PHONE_CALL", "actionRequired": false } ] }
                    """.formatted(CUSTOMER, VALID_LINES)))
            .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[0].field").value("category"));

    // The order was saved before its note failed, and the rollback removed it again.
    assertThat(mongo.getCollection("orders").countDocuments()).isEqualTo(ordersBefore);
}
Reading the code
"notes": [ { "text": "Called the customer", "category": "PHONE_CALL", "actionRequired": false } ] }

The category PHONE_CALL is not an active lookup value. The order is valid, so the order is saved first, and then the note fails.

.andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[0].field").value("category"));

The agent gets 400, which names the field of the note.

assertThat(mongo.getCollection("orders").countDocuments()).isEqualTo(ordersBefore);

The rollback removed the order again. Nothing of the failed request is stored.

Pragmatic choice: One transaction for an order and its first notes

The strict rule. One transaction changes one aggregate. Vaughn Vernon gives this rule in Part I of his essays "Effective Aggregate Design" (2011). Other aggregates follow by events, in their own transactions, and are consistent a moment later.

What we do. place stores the new order and its first notes in one transaction. The note feature joins the transaction of the order feature. Every other use case of the service changes one aggregate.

Why. The agent submits one form, and expects all of it or nothing. Each of the three other designs has a cost:

DesignWhat it gets rightWhy the service does not use it
an event from the order adds the notesthe strict rule holds, and the order commits alonea note that fails validation fails after the order exists, and the agent does not see the error
two requests from the user interfaceeach request changes one aggregatethe second request can fail after the first one succeeded, so the user interface needs code to repair half an action
the first notes embedded in the orderone document, so one write and no transactionthe notes share the order's version and size, and the note feature loses its own aggregate

Vernon accepts this case. In Part II, he names user interface convenience as a reason to change several aggregates in one transaction. It is safe when creating new aggregates together means the same as creating them one at a time, because each one keeps its own rules. The order and its first notes are new aggregates of that kind. No other writer can conflict with an aggregate that does not exist yet. The transaction holds a few documents in one database, and it calls no other service. So it stays far inside the limits of a DocumentDB transaction, one minute and a 32 MB log, as of October 2026.

When to stop. Stop when the transaction would change an existing aggregate instead of creating a new one. Stop when it grows past a few documents, for example when one request can carry many notes. Stop when it would need a call to another service, or when the notes move to another service. Stop also when a third aggregate wants to join. Then save the order alone. Add the notes with an event, or in a second step that the client can retry. Show the agent a state such as "notes pending".

The transaction never spans services. The stock call is outside it, as the section Placing an order: the stock call before the transaction shows. For what holds between aggregates in general, see the section What holds between two aggregates, and what does not.

Calls between featuresnew#

The order and note features need each other four times. Each call goes through the other feature's application service, with plain values:

InteractionCaller and calleeWhat crossesTransaction
place an order with its first notesOrderService.place calls NoteService.addNotesthe order ID as text, and a list of NewNotethe caller's, joined
ship an orderOrderService.ship calls NoteService.countNeedingActionthe order ID as text, and a long backthe caller's
add a noteNoteService.addNote calls OrderService.requireExiststhe order ID as textthe note's
list the notes of an orderNoteService.list calls OrderService.requireExiststhe order ID as textnone, a read

The rules for such calls follow from the table:

RuleWhy
call the other feature's application service, never its repositorythe owner checks its own rules, and its data is stored as it decides
pass plain values, such as a String ID or a NewNoteno type of one feature's domain enters the other feature
never pass or return an aggregatethe caller could change it and skip the owner's steps
let the owner check its own IDsa bad ID gets the owner's own 400 or 404

The note to add is a record of plain values, in the note feature's application package:

/**
 * A note to add, in plain values. The order feature passes it when it places an order with its
 * first notes, so no note type crosses into the order feature.
 */
public record NewNote(String text, String category, boolean actionRequired) {
}

NewNote holds the category as a String. The note feature checks the category against the lookup list when it creates the note. The order feature checks an order ID for the note feature:

/**
 * For other features: checks that an order exists. IDs cross between features as text, and
 * the owner of the ID checks it, so a bad ID gives the order feature's own 400 or 404.
 */
public void requireExists(String orderId) {
    OrderId id = OrderId.of(orderId);
    if (!orders.exists(id)) {
        throw new OrderNotFoundException(id);
    }
}
Reading the code
OrderId id = OrderId.of(orderId);

The text becomes a typed ID here, inside the order feature. A text that is not a universally unique identifier (UUID) throws, and the platform answers 400.

throw new OrderNotFoundException(id);

The order feature's own exception, which the platform answers with 404 and the code ORDER_NOT_FOUND.

Two architecture rules of the platform enforce the rules in the build. The first rule fails when a feature uses a class of another feature outside that feature's application package. The ports in application/port count as outside. The second rule fails when an application service uses another feature's repository or entity:

/**
 * A service never takes another feature's repository or entity. It asks that feature's
 * service, which checks that feature's rules. This is a narrower, clearer form of the rule
 * above for the most common mistake.
 */
public static ArchRule servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities(String basePackage) {

The name servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities states the rule. ArchitectureTest of the service calls both rules on the compiled classes. For the rules and the packages, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules. The two features depend on each other, which the container must allow. For that, see the section @Lazy: a proxy that breaks the cycle, and the other ways out.

The note feature's use casestwist#

C#
public async Task ResolveAction(string orderId, string noteId)
{
    var note = await notes.FindById(noteId)
        ?? throw new NoteNotFoundException(noteId);
    note.RequireBelongsTo(orderId);
    note.ResolveAction(currentActor.Id, clock);
    await SaveAndPublish(note, AuditActions.NoteActionResolved);
}
Java 25
@Transactional
public void resolveAction(String orderId, String noteId) {
    Note note = notes.findById(noteId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoteNotFoundException(noteId));
    note.requireBelongsTo(orderId);
    note.resolveAction(currentActor.id(), clock);
    saveAndPublish(note, AuditActions.NOTE_ACTION_RESOLVED);
}
Reading the code
notes.findById(noteId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoteNotFoundException(noteId));

The light style injects the Spring Data repository directly. findById returns an Optional, and orElseThrow throws the note feature's 404 when it is empty.

note.requireBelongsTo(orderId);

A note under another order is not found either. The entity checks it. For why it answers 404 and not 403, see the section Rules about one record: in the domain, with the actor passed in.

note.resolveAction(currentActor.id(), clock);

The use case reads the actor, and passes the actor's ID to the note as a plain value. The note refuses an agent who wrote it, so a second agent checks the work.

The steps are the same as in the full style, with fewer types. The IDs are String, the repository is the Spring Data interface, and the entity is its own stored document. The private helper saveAndPublish ignores the result of save, because Spring Data writes the new version into the same object. For the light style, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The other use cases of the note feature:

MethodWho calls itWhat it does
addNote(orderId, newNote)the note controllerchecks that the order exists, then adds one note, in its own transaction
addNotes(orderId, newNotes)OrderService.placeadds the first notes, in the caller's transaction
list(orderId, page)the note controllera page of NoteView, newest first, and 404 for an unknown order
countNeedingAction(orderId)OrderService.shipa plain number, so no note crosses the boundary

list checks the order first, so an unknown order is a 404, not an empty page. An empty page would hide a wrong ID in the URL.

The reference feature: one rule, written oncetwist#

C#
public void RequireActive(string type, string code, string field)
{
    var known = items.FindByType(type)
        .Any(item => item.Code == code && item.Active);
    if (!known)
        throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
}
Java 25
public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
    boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
            .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
    if (!known) {
        throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
    }
}

The reference feature has no aggregate. It lists lookup values, such as the delivery methods, and checks a code against them for the other features. InvalidValueException names the field, so the client gets 400 for deliveryMethod or category.

The names of the lists are constants, which every feature uses:

public final class ReferenceTypes {

    public static final String DELIVERY_METHOD = "DELIVERY_METHOD";
    public static final String NOTE_CATEGORY = "NOTE_CATEGORY";

    static final Set<String> ALL = Set.of(DELIVERY_METHOD, NOTE_CATEGORY);

    private ReferenceTypes() {
    }
}

ALL is package-private. Only the reference feature needs the full set, to answer 404 for an unknown list. The private constructor stops anyone from creating the class. The list method returns ReferenceItemView, a record with the code, the label and the active flag.

The rule "a code must be an active lookup value" is an if in an application service. That is a departure from the rule that business rules are in the domain, and it is made on purpose. For the reasons and for the sign that the rule must move, see the section The lookup rule in an application service.

The list is cached, so the check does not read the database for every order. The cache must avoid self-invocation. For why the cache is on the repository, see the section Self-invocation: why the cache is on the repository.

The only kind of if in a use casenew#

A payment arrives twice, because a queue delivers at least once. The second one must change nothing. Where does that check go? It is a rule about payments, so the aggregate decides. The use case only reacts to the answer:

/**
 * Records a payment from the payment service. A message starts this use case, so no user
 * acts, and the audit log records the system actor.
 *
 * <p>It joins the transaction of the inbox that called it. The one {@code if} here is not a
 * business rule: the domain decided to ignore the payment, so there is nothing to save.
 */
@Transactional
public void recordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    if (order.recordPayment(payment)) {
        saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PAYMENT_RECORDED);
    }
}
Reading the code
if (order.recordPayment(payment)) {

recordPayment returns true when it recorded the payment. It returns false for a payment that is not newer than the last one, such as the same payment delivered twice. The rule is inside the aggregate.

saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PAYMENT_RECORDED);

Only a recorded payment is saved, published and audited.

The test for this if is simple. Does the line decide what the use case does next, or does it decide what the business allows? This one only decides whether there is anything to save. The two kinds, side by side:

DecisionWhere it belongsIn the order service
save only when the domain recorded the paymentthe use casethe if in OrderService.recordPayment
list every order when no status is giventhe use casethe choice of query in OrderService.list
ignore a payment that is not newer than the last onethe domainthe first if in Order.recordPayment
refuse to ship an order that is not paidthe domainOrder.ship, which throws OrderNotPaidException
refuse an order when a product is missingthe domainOrder.place, which judges StockAvailability

If a business expert would recognise the line as a rule, it belongs in the domain. The class comment of OrderService says the same. For the decision order of rules, see the chapter Where each rule goes.

Two tests record both outcomes. OrderServiceTest.RecordPayment.savesTheOrderWhenThePaymentIsNew checks the save and the audit. savesNothingWhenTheDomainIgnoresARepeatedPayment checks that nothing is saved, published or audited.

The short use cases and the readstwist#

C#
public async Task PickLine(OrderId orderId, LineId lineId)
{
    var order = await orders.Get(orderId);
    order.PickLine(lineId, clock);
    await SaveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.LinePicked);
}
Java 25
@Transactional
public void pickLine(OrderId orderId, LineId lineId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    order.pickLine(lineId, clock);
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.LINE_PICKED);
}

Warehouse staff pick each line. pickLine has three of the steps, because it asks no other feature. order.pickLine refuses a line that is picked already, and an order that is finished. cancel has the same shape, with order.cancel(clock).

The reads need no transaction:

public OrderView get(OrderId orderId) {
    return OrderView.from(orders.get(orderId));
}

public PageResult<OrderView> list(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page) {
    PageResult<Order> result = status == null ? orders.findAll(page) : orders.findByStatus(status, page);
    return result.map(OrderView::from);
}
Reading the code
PageResult<Order> result = status == null ? orders.findAll(page) : orders.findByStatus(status, page);

A missing status lists every order. This choice of query is not a business rule.

return result.map(OrderView::from);

PageResult is the platform's page type, in plain Java. map converts each order to a view, and keeps the page number and the total.

The reads have no @Transactional. A read-only transaction would still open a server transaction on MongoDB, and one read gains nothing from it. For that, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

The journeys through the servicenew#

A bug report says "the order was placed, but the warehouse never heard of it". Where do you look? Each step of a journey has one home, so the search starts from the step. These are the main journeys of the order service.

A request to place an order passes the filter chain first. Then an interceptor fills the mapped diagnostic context (MDC) of the logs, and Spring model-view-controller (MVC) reads the body. Next, method security checks the scope. Only then does the request reach the use case. After the commit, the event goes to Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS). The journey of POST /orders:

Each step, with the chapter that explains it:

StepWhat happensExplained in
1the bearer token is checked, or the request gets 401dd-sec-path
2the interceptor copies orderId and the other path IDs into the MDCdd-obs
3Jackson reads the body, and @Valid checks itdd-web
4@OrdersWrite checks the scope orders.writedd-sec-method
5the controller builds CustomerContact, DeliveryMethod and the itemsdd-web
6requireActive, then the stock call outside the transactiondd-uc-place
7the order, its outbox rows, its audit record and its notes, in one transactiondd-uc-two
8Spring Modulith sends OrderPlacedV1 to SNS, on another threaddd-out

Step 8 is outside the request. A run for this book showed that the SNS send happens after the commit, on an executor thread, outside any transaction. So the answer 201 does not wait for SNS, and a failed send is retried by the outbox resender. In the bug report above, look at step 8 first.

A payment enters through the queue listener instead. The listener only translates the message into value objects and calls the use case:

@Override
protected void handle(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    Payment payment = new Payment(new PaymentReference(event.paymentReference()),
            new Money(event.amount(), event.currency()), event.paidAt());
    orders.recordPayment(OrderId.of(event.orderId()), payment);
}

The platform's base class calls handle once for each event, through the inbox, as the system actor. So the same use case serves a message and could serve a request, with no second copy. The other journeys, in short:

JourneyIts stepsExplained in
ship an orderthe same as place up to step 5, then load, ask the notes, check the policy, ship and save, with 409 when another agent saved firstdd-uc-steps
a payment messageSQS delivers it, the inbox records its ID, recordPayment runs as the system actor, in the inbox's transactiondd-inb
an event outthe use case publishes, the outbox stores a row in the transaction, Spring Modulith sends it after the commitdd-out
the stock callthe port, the adapter, the client with its token, retries, the circuit breaker, a 503 when the stock service is downdd-cli

The journey test OrderJourneyIT.anOrderShipsOnlyWhenPaidPickedAndNoNoteNeedsAction runs placing, paying and shipping end to end, with the events. It places an order with a note, ships it after each condition is met, and checks the audit records and the events on the queue. StockAdapterTest runs the stock call against a local HTTP server.

Splitting a large servicenew#

OrderService has eight public methods. A year from now it may have twenty, with returns, refunds, address changes and split deliveries. A class of twenty use cases is hard to read, and its constructor grows with every one. The class comment gives the rule:

* <p>With about ten use cases, split the class by area, such as {@code OrderFulfilmentService},
* not into a read side and a write side.

Split by an area of the business. Picking and shipping could move to an OrderFulfilmentService. Returns and refunds would then be an OrderReturnsService. Each class keeps the same steps, and each one shares the repository port and the helpers it needs. The ways to split, compared:

SplitWhat it gets rightWhat it costs
by area, as recommendedeach class is a part of the business that a team member can namethe shared helper must move to a small class that both use
into a read side and a write sidereads can change faster, and use other storage laterthe two halves of one feature change together, and the reads still need the same views
one class per use caseeach class is tinythe steps and helpers move to a base class, and a reader opens many files

The read and write split is the first step of CQRS. It is worth it when the reads need another shape of storage, such as a search index. The order service has no such need, so it splits by area. With constructor injection, a constructor with more than about ten parameters is a sign that the split is due. For that signal, see the section Constructor injection, with nine dependencies.

How each use case is testedtwist#

C#
var stock = new Mock<IStockChecker>();
var service = new OrderService(orders.Object, notes.Object,
    referenceData.Object, stock.Object, new ShippingPolicy(),
    events.Object, audit.Object, transactions, clock);
Java 25
private final OrderRepository orders = mock(OrderRepository.class);
private final NoteService notes = mock(NoteService.class);
private final ReferenceDataService referenceData = mock(ReferenceDataService.class);
private final StockChecker stock = mock(StockChecker.class);
private final DomainEventPublisher events = mock(DomainEventPublisher.class);
private final AuditLog audit = mock(AuditLog.class);

private final OrderService service = new OrderService(orders, notes, referenceData, stock, new ShippingPolicy(),
        events, audit, new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager()), CLOCK);
Reading the code
private final StockChecker stock = mock(StockChecker.class);

mock is the static method of Mockito that creates a stand-in object for an interface or a class. Moq in .NET has the same purpose.

new ShippingPolicy()

The domain service is real. A unit test of a use case uses the real domain, and mocks only the ports and the other features.

new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager())

A real template, on a transaction manager of the platform that does nothing. So the lambda of place runs, and no database is needed.

The test of place checks the order of the steps with InOrder:

InOrder order = inOrder(referenceData, stock, orders, events, audit, notes);
order.verify(referenceData).requireActive("DELIVERY_METHOD", "STANDARD", "deliveryMethod");
order.verify(stock).reserve(reservedFor.capture(), eq(TWO_MUGS));          // the other service first
order.verify(orders).save(saved.capture());                                // then the order
order.verify(events).publish(List.of(new OrderPlaced(reservedFor.getValue(), STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, NOW)));
order.verify(audit).record("ORDER_PLACED", "order", reservedFor.getValue().value());
order.verify(notes).addNotes(reservedFor.getValue().value(), firstNotes);  // then its notes
Reading the code
InOrder order = inOrder(referenceData, stock, orders, events, audit, notes);

InOrder checks that the calls on these mocks happened in this order, and not only that they happened.

order.verify(stock).reserve(reservedFor.capture(), eq(TWO_MUGS)); // the other service first

An ArgumentCaptor keeps the order ID that the use case sent to the stock service. A later line checks that the saved order has the same ID.

Each use case has a test at the level that suits it:

What is testedTestNeeds
the order of the steps, the event, the audit, a refusalOrderServiceTest and NoteServiceTest, with mocksnothing, it runs in milliseconds
the HTTP status, the scope, the JSONOrderControllerTest and NoteControllerTest, with the service mockeda slice of Spring, no database
the order and its notes in one transaction, the rollbackOrderJourneyITMongoDB and the AWS emulator in Docker
the stock call, its token, its retriesStockAdapterTesta local HTTP server

One rule decides which test proves what. A unit test proves the steps, and only the journey test proves the transaction. The no-op manager cannot roll anything back, so a unit test never shows a rollback. For each kind of test, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy does place call the stock service before it starts the transaction, and what does that order cost?
A DocumentDB transaction has a limit of one minute, and a slow HTTP call inside it would hold it open. So the call runs first, and only the lambda of the template is transactional. The cost is a hold on the stock with no order, when the transaction fails afterwards. The stock service releases the hold after its timeout. The order ID is sent as the idempotency key, so a retried call is safe.
2
An expert asksAn application service could return the aggregate, which saves a view type. Why does the order service return OrderView instead?
A caller with an Order could call order.ship(clock) directly. It would skip the shipping policy, the save, the event and the audit. A view has no method that changes anything. The view also leaves out the customer's contact, so personal data leaves the feature only when a use case needs it.
3
OrderService.recordPayment contains an if. Why is it not a business rule in the wrong layer?
The aggregate decides whether to record the payment, and returns true or false. The if only decides whether there is anything to save. A line that a business expert would recognise as a rule, such as "ignore an older payment", is inside Order.recordPayment.
4
The note feature needs to know whether an order exists. Which call does it make, and what crosses between the features?
It calls OrderService.requireExists(orderId), with the order ID as plain text. The order feature turns the text into an OrderId and checks it. A bad ID gets the order feature's own 400, and an unknown one its 404. No type of the order domain enters the note feature.
5
TranslateA message starts this use case, inside the transaction of the inbox. Write it as a method of OrderService: 
public async Task RecordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment)
{
    var order = await orders.Get(orderId);
    if (order.RecordPayment(payment))
        await SaveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PaymentRecorded);
}
@Transactional
public void recordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    if (order.recordPayment(payment)) {
        saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PAYMENT_RECORDED);
    }
}

@Transactional with the default propagation joins the transaction of the inbox. orders.get throws the 404 exception when no order has the ID. The domain returns false for a repeated payment, and then nothing is saved.

The web layer in depth#

The web layer and security · Chapter 13· 37 min read· Quick reference

The web layer of the order service turns HTTP into calls of the use cases, and back. Its controllers hold no rule. Records carry the JSON in and out, and small mappers convert them. One platform class turns every exception into an RFC 9457 problem with a traceId. This chapter follows one request through the web framework, and measures what each part does when something fails.
