One request through Spring MVCnew#

An agent ships an order. The browser sends POST /orders/{orderId}/ship with a token. Before the controller method runs, several parts of Spring look at the request. Each part can stop it. When a part stops the request, another part writes the answer. A C# developer knows the same idea as the middleware pipeline of ASP.NET Core.

The web framework of Spring is called Spring model-view-controller (MVC). It runs inside a web server that follows the Jakarta Servlet standard.

The chapter Controllers, routing and binding teaches the basics of a controller, a servlet filter and an interceptor. For the filters and interceptors, see the section Middleware. This section puts all the parts in order:

Each part has one job in the order service:

PartWhat it does hereWhat it answers when it stops the request
servlet filtersSpring Security checks the token401, written by the security chain
DispatcherServletfinds the controller method for the path and the HTTP method404 or 405, written by the advice
interceptorsthe platform's MDC interceptor copies orderId, lineId and noteId into the MDCnothing, it only adds log context
argument resolutionreads the JSON body, runs @Valid, and converts path and query values400, written by the advice
the controller methodbuilds value objects and calls one use case400, 403, 404, 409, 422 or 503, written by the advice
the message converterwrites the returned record as JSON, or the problem as application/problem+jsonnothing, it writes what it is given

Spring Security's checks are filters, so a request without a valid token never reaches Spring MVC. The platform's advice therefore never sees a 401. For how the security chain writes the 401 problem itself, see the section One request through the checks. The test aRequestWithoutATokenIsA401ProblemBeforeAnyController proves that no use case runs:

@Test
void aRequestWithoutATokenIsA401ProblemBeforeAnyController() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(VALID_ORDER))
            .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized())
            .andExpect(header().exists("WWW-Authenticate"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Unauthorized"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value(401));
    verifyNoInteractions(orders);
}

The request has a valid body and no token. verifyNoInteractions(orders) checks that the mocked use case was never called. The test is in the nested class OrderControllerTest.Security.

A run for this book recorded every callback of a normal request. The order was the filter, preHandle, the controller, postHandle, afterCompletion, and the filter again. In ASP.NET Core, routing chooses the endpoint inside the middleware pipeline, and filters wrap the action. The closest match for an interceptor is an action filter.

What an interceptor sees when a request failstrap#

An interceptor has three callbacks. preHandle runs before the controller method, postHandle runs after it returns, and afterCompletion runs at the very end. afterCompletion has a parameter ex for an exception. A C# developer expects that parameter to hold the exception of every failed request.

PredictAn interceptor after a business rule fails#
The ship use case throws OrderNotPaidException. The platform's advice turns it into a 422 problem. Which value of ex does this afterCompletion receive?
@Override
public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler,
                            Exception ex) {
    names.forEach(MDC::remove);
}
Show the answer
null

An exception that an advice handled is not passed to afterCompletion. The advice resolved the exception and wrote the 422. Spring MVC then treats the request as handled. A run recorded afterCompletion ex=null status=422, and postHandle did not run. Only an exception that no advice handles arrives in ex. To see a failure, read response.getStatus().

The platform's interceptor does not need ex. It removes its values in every case. The runs for this book recorded these callbacks:

The requestpreHandleThe controllerpostHandleafterCompletion
a normal requestruns, with the path variablesrunsrunsruns, ex is null
the use case throws, and the advice answers 422runsrunsdoes not runruns, ex is null
the method throws, and no advice handles itrunsrunsdoes not runruns, ex is the exception
a body that fails @Validrunsdoes not rundoes not runruns, ex is null
DELETE on a path that has only GET, a 405does not rundoes not rundoes not rundoes not run
a path with no controller, a 404runs, with no path variablesdoes not rundoes not runnot recorded in the run

A body that fails @Valid runs preHandle first. Spring MVC checks the body while it resolves the method's arguments, and that happens after preHandle. An exception that no advice handles leaves the servlet as ServletException: Request processing failed. The order service never gets there, because its advice has a handler for Exception.

For a 405, Spring refuses the HTTP method while it looks up the handler. Spring does that before any interceptor runs. So the run recorded only the filter and the advice for a DELETE on a GET path.

For a path with no controller, the run showed that Spring gave the request to its handler for static files. That handler then answered 404. The interceptor ran, and the attribute of the path variables was null.

Both cases change what the platform's interceptor can put into the mapped diagnostic context (MDC), the logging context of the thread. For the log lines of these cases, see the section Path variables in the MDC, with an interceptor.

Controllers that only translatetwist#

The order controller is the HTTP door of the order feature. Its documentation states what it does, and what it never does:

/**
 * The HTTP API of orders. It translates HTTP into calls of the use cases, and back. It holds no
 * rule, uses no repository, and catches no exception: the platform turns every exception into
 * a problem response.
 *
 * <p>Each method names the scope it needs with {@link OrdersRead} or {@link OrdersWrite}. This
 * is where callers enter, so this is where permissions are checked. Spring MVC reads and
 * validates the body before it calls the method, so a caller without the scope who sends an
 * invalid body gets 400, not 403. Path IDs are converted inside the methods, after the check.
 *
 * <p>The OpenAPI annotations describe each operation and its errors. springdoc builds the
 * document from them, and the build fails when {@code contracts/openapi.yaml} differs.
 */
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
@Tag(name = "orders")
class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final OrderApiMapper mapper;

    OrderController(OrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }
Reading the code
@RestController

Spring writes the return value of each method to the response body, as JSON. For the basics, see the section A controller.

@RequestMapping("/orders")

Every path of the class starts with /orders.

@Tag(name = "orders")

This annotation comes from the Swagger annotations, which springdoc reads. It groups the operations in the OpenAPI document. See the chapter API and event contracts.

class OrderController {

The class is package-private. No other package calls a controller, so nothing outside order.api can use it.

OrderController(OrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper) {

The controller needs two things, the use cases and the mapper. Each one is a bean, so Spring passes both to the constructor.

A controller method has the same three steps every time. It reads values from the request, calls one use case, and turns the result into a response. The ship method is the shortest example:

@OrdersWrite
@PostMapping("/{orderId}/ship")
// ...
ResponseEntity<Void> ship(@PathVariable String orderId) {
    orders.ship(OrderId.of(orderId));
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
Reading the code
@OrdersWrite

The caller needs the orders.write scope. For permissions, see the chapter Security in depth.

@PostMapping("/{orderId}/ship")

Shipping is a POST to a path that ends with a verb.

orders.ship(OrderId.of(orderId));

The method builds the typed ID and calls one use case. If the order cannot ship, the use case throws, and the platform writes the problem.

The // ... line stands for the OpenAPI annotations. The chapter API and event contracts explains them.

A change of state is an action-style POST, with a verb in the path. The order service has four of them, for picking a line, shipping, cancelling and resolving a note. A PUT of the whole order would let a client set the status to SHIPPED directly. The order must decide whether it may ship, so the client asks for the action and the domain answers. The quick reference lists all ten endpoints.

Three things never appear in a controller:

  • A rule. "An order ships only when it is paid" is in the domain. For where each rule goes, see the chapter Where each rule goes.
  • A repository. The controller calls the use case, and the use case loads and saves. For the use cases, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.
  • A try/catch block. The platform's advice turns every exception into a problem. See the section One handler for every problem.

Notes belong to an order, so the paths of the note controller start with the path of the order:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders/{orderId}/notes")
@Tag(name = "notes")
class NoteController {

The class prefix itself holds a path variable, {orderId}. Each method of the class then declares @PathVariable String orderId to read it. The lookup lists have a third controller, ReferenceDataController, at /reference-data/{type}. The UI uses those lists to fill its drop-down lists.

A C# controller often returns NotFound() or BadRequest(). The controllers of the order service never build an error response. The domain throws, and the platform's advice writes the problem. A success is the returned record, or a ResponseEntity for 201 and 204.

IDs in the path: text in, value objects insidetwist#

C#
[HttpGet("{orderId}")]
public OrderResponse Get([FromRoute] Guid orderId) =>
    mapper.ToResponse(orders.Get(new OrderId(orderId)));
Java 25
@OrdersRead
@GetMapping("/{orderId}")
// ...
OrderResponse get(@PathVariable String orderId) {
    return mapper.toResponse(orders.get(OrderId.of(orderId)));
}

The Java method takes the ID as a String, not as a UUID. It converts the text with OrderId.of, inside the method. OrderId checks the format in its constructor, and throws an InvalidValueException that names the field:

protected Identifier(String value, String fieldName) {
    String normalised = value == null ? null : value.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
    if (normalised == null || !UUID_FORMAT.matcher(normalised).matches()) {
        throw new InvalidValueException(fieldName, "must be a valid identifier");
    }
    this.value = normalised;
}

OrderId passes "orderId" as the fieldName of this constructor. The platform's advice turns the InvalidValueException into a 400, and its errors list names that field. The test anInvalidIdInThePathIsA400ThatNamesTheField sends GET /orders/not-a-uuid. It expects orderId as the first field in the errors.

The text parameter has two more effects:

  • The permission check runs before the conversion. A read-only caller who sends a bad ID to a write endpoint gets 403. With @PathVariable UUID, the conversion runs first, and the caller gets 400. See the section Three places to check a permission, measured.
  • One class, Identifier, checks every ID in the same way, so the domain decides what a valid ID is. It accepts upper and lower case, and stores the value in lower case. Spring's conversion to UUID would fail with another exception, MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException, and another message.

The C# pane wraps a Guid that ASP.NET Core has already converted. The Java method gets the raw text and converts it itself. The note feature uses the light style. So the note controller gives the note ID to the use case as a plain String. A malformed note ID is then not a 400. The use case finds no note with that ID, and the answer is a 404. For the three levels of Domain-Driven Design (DDD), see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

Request and response DTOs as recordstwist#

A class that only carries data into or out of the API is called a data transfer object (DTO). The body that places an order is a record with Bean Validation annotations. Its nested records describe the customer, the lines and the notes:

@Schema(description = "An order to place, with its first notes")
public record PlaceOrderRequest(
        @NotNull @Valid CustomerRequest customer,
        @Schema(description = "A DELIVERY_METHOD code", example = "STANDARD") @NotBlank String deliveryMethod,
        @NotEmpty @Size(max = 50) List<@Valid LineRequest> lines,
        @Schema(description = "Notes saved with the order, in the same transaction")
        @Size(max = 20) List<@Valid NoteRequest> notes) {

    public record CustomerRequest(
            @Schema(example = "Jo Bloggs") @NotBlank @Size(max = 200) String name,
            @Schema(example = "jo@example.com") @NotBlank @Email String email) {
    }

    public record LineRequest(
            @Schema(example = "MUG-001") @NotBlank String productCode,
            @Schema(example = "2") @Min(1) @Max(999) int quantity) {
    }
    // ...
}
Reading the code
@NotNull @Valid CustomerRequest customer,

@NotNull requires the customer object. @Valid tells the validator to check the constraints inside it as well. Without @Valid, a blank name would pass. See the section A nested object needs its own @Valid.

@NotEmpty @Size(max = 50) List<@Valid LineRequest> lines,

The list needs at least one line and at most 50. @Valid on the element type checks each line.

@Size(max = 20) List<@Valid NoteRequest> notes) {

The notes are optional, so the list has no @NotNull. A missing list is null, and the mapper turns it into an empty list.

@Schema(example = "MUG-001")

@Schema adds a description or an example to the OpenAPI document. It changes nothing at run time.

The nested records are declared inside PlaceOrderRequest, so a reader sees the whole body in one file. Java calls them PlaceOrderRequest.CustomerRequest and so on. For the constraint annotations, see the section Constraint annotations.

When the body is invalid, the client gets every bad field at once. The test invalidFieldsAreAllListed sends a blank name, a bad email address and no lines:

@Test
void invalidFieldsAreAllListed() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(AGENT).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("""
                    { "customer": { "name": "", "email": "not-an-email" }, "deliveryMethod": "STANDARD", "lines": [] }
                    """))
            .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Invalid request"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors.length()").value(3))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'customer.name')]").exists())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'customer.email')]").exists())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'lines')]").exists());
}

A field of a nested record is named with a dot, as in customer.name. A failed @Valid throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, and the platform's advice turns it into this 400. See the section One handler for every problem.

The domain checks the same values again. CustomerContact refuses a blank name with the field name customer.name, the same name that the DTO's error uses. The DTO's annotations give a friendly list of errors. The domain's check is the one that counts, because every caller of a use case passes through the domain, with or without a DTO. The record's own documentation says so.

The response is a record too:

/** An order as clients see it. It is a separate class from the domain, so either can change. */
public record OrderResponse(
        String orderId,
        @Schema(allowableValues = {"NEW", "PAID", "SHIPPED", "CANCELLED"}) String status,
        String deliveryMethod,
        Instant placedAt,
        Instant shippedAt,
        Instant cancelledAt,
        List<LineResponse> lines,
        PaymentResponse lastPayment) {

    public record LineResponse(String lineId, String productCode, int quantity,
                               @Schema(allowableValues = {"WAITING", "PICKED"}) String status, Instant pickedAt) {
    }

    public record PaymentResponse(String reference, BigDecimal amount, String currency, Instant paidAt) {
    }
}

Jackson writes a record by its accessor names, so orderId() becomes the member "orderId". A record needs no getters and no annotations for this. The status is a String, not the domain's enum. @Schema(allowableValues = ...) still lists the four values in the OpenAPI document.

Why a separate class, when Order already has these fields? The JSON is a contract with the UI and with other teams. The domain changes when the business rules change. With a separate record, a new field in Order does not appear in the API, and a renamed field does not break a client. So the domain and the API can each change on its own. The domain class also holds things that a client must never see, such as the version for optimistic locking.

One more record completes the order API. OrderPlacedResponse holds the IDs of the new order and of its notes. The note feature and the lookup lists have records of the same kind. Each feature keeps them in a dto package next to its controller.

API mapperstwist#

Each feature has one class that converts between its DTOs and the types of the application layer. The order mapper has four methods:

/** Converts between the order API's DTOs and the application layer's types. */
@Component
class OrderApiMapper {

    List<OrderItem> toItems(PlaceOrderRequest request) {
        return request.lines().stream()
                .map(line -> new OrderItem(new ProductCode(line.productCode()), line.quantity()))
                .toList();
    }

    /** Notes are optional in the request, so a missing list means no notes. */
    List<NewNote> toNewNotes(PlaceOrderRequest request) {
        List<PlaceOrderRequest.NoteRequest> notes = request.notes() == null ? List.of() : request.notes();
        return notes.stream().map(note -> new NewNote(note.text(), note.category(), note.actionRequired())).toList();
    }

    OrderPlacedResponse toResponse(PlacedOrder placed) {
        return new OrderPlacedResponse(placed.orderId(), placed.noteIds());
    }
    // ...
}
Reading the code
@Component

The mapper is a bean, so Spring passes it to the controller's constructor.

class OrderApiMapper {

The class is package-private, like the controller. Only order.api uses it.

new OrderItem(new ProductCode(line.productCode()), line.quantity())

The mapper builds domain value objects from the request. ProductCode checks its own format, so a bad code fails here with a 400.

request.notes() == null ? List.of() : request.notes();

A missing list of notes becomes an empty list. The use case never sees null.

The fourth method, toResponse(OrderView), builds the nested response records from a view of the application layer. For views, see the chapter Use cases: the application service. The note feature's mapper has one method, because the note controller builds its request objects in place:

@Component
class NoteApiMapper {

    NoteResponse toResponse(NoteView note) {
        return new NoteResponse(note.noteId(), note.text(), note.category(), note.actionRequired(),
                note.needsAction(), note.createdAt(), note.actionResolvedAt());
    }
}

The mapper is plain code that you write. A mapping library, such as MapStruct, would generate the same methods. Plain code has three advantages here. A record's constructor needs every component, so a new component in NoteResponse is a compile error in the mapper until someone fills it. A debugger steps through the mapping. And the null check for the notes is visible where it happens. Choose a library when a feature has many large DTOs that copy fields one to one.

The mapper converts, and nothing else. It has no rule and no call to a repository. A test of the controller covers it, because the slice test imports the real mapper with @Import(OrderApiMapper.class).

201 with a Location, 204 with no bodytwist#

C#
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult Add(string orderId, AddNoteRequest request)
{
    var noteId = notes.AddNote(orderId, new NewNote(request.Text, request.Category, request.ActionRequired));
    return Created($"/orders/{orderId}/notes/{noteId}", new NoteAddedResponse(noteId));
}
Java 25
ResponseEntity<NoteAddedResponse> add(@PathVariable String orderId, @Valid @RequestBody AddNoteRequest request) {
    String noteId = notes.addNote(orderId, new NewNote(request.text(), request.category(), request.actionRequired()));
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + orderId + "/notes/" + noteId))
            .body(new NoteAddedResponse(noteId));
}
Reading the code
ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + orderId + "/notes/" + noteId))

created sets the status 201 and the Location header. It takes a java.net.URI, and URI.create builds one from the text.

.body(new NoteAddedResponse(noteId));

body finishes the response with a JSON body.

The C# pane gives Created the URI as a string. The Spring method created takes a URI object. A command that returns nothing ends with ResponseEntity.noContent().build(), and its return type is ResponseEntity<Void>. A plain read returns the record itself, and Spring answers 200. For the other helpers, see the section Returning results.

The tests check the status and the header. OrderControllerTest.placingReturns201WithTheLocation expects Location: /orders/{id}, and NoteControllerTest.resolvingReturns204 expects 204. The Location of a new order is the URL of GET /orders/{orderId}, so a client can read the new order at once.

Paging: PageQuery in, PageResponse outnew#

An agent lists the orders that are waiting. A shop has thousands of orders, so the list comes one page at a time. Every shop service lists data in the same way. So the platform defines one type for the request and one for the answer, and every service uses them.

The list method reads three query parameters:

@OrdersRead
@GetMapping
// ...
PageResponse<OrderResponse> list(@RequestParam(required = false) OrderStatus status,
                                 @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                                 @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size) {
    return PageResponse.from(orders.list(status, new PageQuery(page, size)), mapper::toResponse);
}
Reading the code
@RequestParam(required = false) OrderStatus status,

The status filter is optional, so a missing value is null. Spring converts the text to the enum OrderStatus. An unknown value such as LOST is a 400 that names the field status.

@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,

Without the default, a missing page would be a 400. See the section Model binding.

new PageQuery(page, size)

The controller builds the platform's page request, which checks both numbers.

PageResponse.from(orders.list(status, new PageQuery(page, size)), mapper::toResponse);

The use case returns a page of views. PageResponse.from maps each view to its response record, and keeps the numbers of the page. mapper::toResponse is a method reference.

PageQuery is a value object in the platform's domain package. It holds no Spring type, so a use case can take it:

public record PageQuery(int page, int size) implements ValueObject {

    public static final int MAX_SIZE = 100;
    public static final int DEFAULT_SIZE = 20;

    public PageQuery {
        if (page < 0) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("page", "must not be negative");
        }
        if (size < 1 || size > MAX_SIZE) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("size", "must be between 1 and " + MAX_SIZE);
        }
    }
Reading the code
public PageQuery {

This is a compact constructor. It checks the values before the record stores them.

throw new InvalidValueException("size", "must be between 1 and " + MAX_SIZE);

A size of 1,000 would load 1,000 orders in one request. The limit protects the database. The exception names the field size, so the client sees what to correct.

The test thePageSizeIsLimited sends ?size=1000. It expects a 400 that names the field size. The answer has one shape in every service:

public record PageResponse<T>(List<T> items, int page, int size, long totalItems, int totalPages) {

    /** Converts a page from the application layer, mapping each item to its response DTO. */
    public static <S, T> PageResponse<T> from(PageResult<S> result, Function<? super S, ? extends T> mapper) {
        return new PageResponse<>(result.items().stream().<T>map(mapper).toList(),
                result.page(), result.size(), result.totalItems(), result.totalPages());
    }
}
Reading the code
public record PageResponse<T>(List<T> items, int page, int size, long totalItems, int totalPages) {

A generic record. Its five components become the five members of the JSON, from items to totalPages.

Function<? super S, ? extends T> mapper

Function is like Func<S, T> in C#. The question marks are wildcards. They let the method accept a mapper written for a supertype of S.

result.items().stream().<T>map(mapper).toList(),

<T>map names the type argument of map explicitly, so the result is a List<T>.

PageResult is the platform's page in the domain package. It has the same numbers and computes totalPages from them. The test listsOrdersAsAPage expects totalItems 1 and totalPages 1 for one order.

Spring Data has its own types for a page, Pageable and Page. A feature could pass them from the controller to the repository. That is less code, and it is a good choice for a simple feature. The order service does not use them in its API, for two reasons. The use cases and the domain would then depend on Spring Data. And the JSON of a page would follow Spring Data's shape, not a shape that the shop owns and keeps the same in every service. The adapter that stores the order aggregate turns a PageQuery into a query. For how it does that, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

Jackson 3: what changed for request bodiestrap#

Spring Boot 4 reads and writes JSON with Jackson 3. Boot 3 used Jackson 2. Most code works the same, but one default changed in a way that breaks clients without a warning. An agent adds a note and does not say whether it needs action. The note's request record has a boolean for that:

PredictA request body that leaves out a boolean#
Spring Boot 4.1 reads this body with its default Jackson settings. The body leaves out actionRequired. What does the client get?
public record AddNoteRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 2000) String text,
        @Schema(description = "A NOTE_CATEGORY code", example = "DELIVERY") @NotBlank String category,
        @Schema(description = "Whether an agent must act on the note before the order ships") boolean actionRequired) {
}
mvc.perform(post("/orders/" + ORDER_ID + "/notes").with(AGENT).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                        { "text": "FYI", "category": "GENERAL" }
                        """))
Show the answer
400 Bad Request. Jackson cannot read the body, and the note is not added.

Jackson 3 refuses a missing primitive. In Jackson 3.1.7, the feature FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES is on by default, and Boot keeps it on. A missing value counts as null. A primitive boolean cannot hold null. So Jackson throws MismatchedInputException. Spring MVC wraps it in HttpMessageNotReadableException, and answers 400.

Jackson 2 had the feature off, so the same body gave false on Boot 3. System.Text.Json also gives false. The platform turns the feature off.

The platform restores the old behaviour for every service, in its defaults file:

# Jackson 3 rejects a JSON body that leaves out a primitive field (boolean, int). Treat a missing
# primitive as its default value instead, so an omitted "actionRequired" means false.
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-null-for-primitives=false

spring.jackson.deserialization is a map of Jackson's features. The key is the feature's name in lower case, with dashes. With the value false, a missing primitive gets its default value. A boolean is then false, and an int is 0. An explicit "actionRequired": null is false too. The test NoteControllerTest.anOmittedFlagMeansFalse sends the body above and expects 201, with false passed to the use case. For how the platform's defaults file works, see the chapter Configuration in depth.

The setting is a choice. A strict API could keep Jackson's default, and require every client to send every field. That catches a client that forgot a field. The shop chose the lenient form, because actionRequired is a flag whose natural default is false. A field without a natural default should be a wrapper type, such as Boolean or Integer, with @NotNull. Then a missing value is a 400 that names the field.

Gotcha

A service that moves from Boot 3 to Boot 4 can start to refuse requests that worked before. A client that leaves out a boolean or an int got the default value on Boot 3. On Boot 4, the same request gets a 400, because Jackson cannot read the body. No compiler and no unit test of the domain notices it. Only a controller test with a body that leaves out the field finds it.

Two other defaults matter for the service, and both match what a C# developer expects:

  • Unknown properties are ignored. A body with an extra member, such as "extra": 1, is read without an error. Jackson 3 and Boot's mapper both have FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off. A plain Jackson 2 mapper had it on.
  • An Instant is an ISO-8601 string. Jackson 3 writes "2026-01-15T09:00:00Z" with no extra module. Jackson 2 needed a module for java.time.

The test OrderControllerTest.listsOrdersAsAPage relies on the second default. It expects placedAt to be exactly the string 2026-01-15T09:00:00Z. In .NET, a UTC DateTime is written with the same Z. A DateTimeOffset is written with +00:00 instead. A client that compares the text must expect the Z form from the shop.

One handler for every problemnew#

An agent tries to ship an order that is not paid. The domain throws OrderNotPaidException. The client must get a 422 with the code ORDER_NOT_PAID, in the same format as every other error of every shop service. No feature should write code for that.

The rule is that the kind of the exception decides the status. The domain has exactly three kinds of exception, and each feature extends one of them. For the exception classes themselves, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java. The platform maps each kind to a status:

The exceptionStatusWhat the problem adds
InvalidValueException, a failed @Valid, unreadable JSON, a value of the wrong type400errors, a list of the fields with a message each
AccessDeniedException, from method security403nothing, the detail is "You are not allowed to do this"
NotFoundException404code, such as ORDER_NOT_FOUND
OptimisticLockingFailureException, or a write conflict409code CONCURRENT_UPDATE
BusinessRuleViolationException422code, such as ORDER_NOT_PAID
DownstreamServiceException503nothing, and the log names the service that failed
anything else500nothing, and the log holds the exception

One class does this for every service. The platform registers it as a bean, so a service gets it by adding the library:

@RestControllerAdvice
@Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class GlobalExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);
    private static final String INVALID_REQUEST = "Invalid request";

    @ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> notFound(NotFoundException ex) {
        return respond(domainProblem(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Not found", ex));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InvalidValueException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> invalidValue(InvalidValueException ex) {
        ProblemDetail problem = domainProblem(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, INVALID_REQUEST, ex);
        problem.setProperty("errors", List.of(fieldError(ex.field(), ex.getMessage())));
        return respond(problem);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(BusinessRuleViolationException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> businessRule(BusinessRuleViolationException ex) {
        return respond(domainProblem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Business rule violated", ex));
    }
Reading the code
@RestControllerAdvice

The class is a controller advice. Its handlers apply to the exceptions of every controller. For the basics, see the section Global exception handling.

@Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE)

This advice is asked last. See the section Two advices, and why @Order decides.

extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

The base class comes with Spring MVC. It handles Spring MVC's own exceptions, such as a 405 or a 415. The platform inherits those handlers.

@ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)

This method handles NotFoundException and every subclass of it, such as OrderNotFoundException.

problem.setProperty("errors", List.of(fieldError(ex.field(), ex.getMessage())));

setProperty adds a member to the problem. Spring writes it at the top level of the JSON, next to title and status.

The helper domainProblem builds the problem with the message of the exception as the detail. It also adds the code of the exception:

private static ProblemDetail domainProblem(HttpStatus status, String title, DomainException ex) {
    ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetails.problem(status, title, ex.getMessage());
    problem.setProperty("code", ex.code());
    return problem;
}

ex.getMessage() becomes the detail, and ex.code() becomes the member code.

A run for this book made the same calls in a small test application. It wrote this body for a 422. Its title is the default title of Spring, because the run set no title. The platform sets the title "Business rule violated" instead:

{"detail":"not paid","instance":"/orders/42/rule","status":422,"title":"Unprocessable Content","code":"ORDER_NOT_PAID","traceId":"t-123"}

The members code and traceId are at the top level. The test aBrokenBusinessRuleIsA422WithItsCode expects code to be ORDER_NOT_PAID. A client may rely on the code, so a feature never changes it.

The other handlers of the class answer 403, 503 and 500:

@ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> accessDenied(AccessDeniedException ex) {
    return respond(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN, "Forbidden", "You are not allowed to do this"));
}

@ExceptionHandler(DownstreamServiceException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> downstream(DownstreamServiceException ex) {
    log.warn("Dependency {} is unavailable", ex.dependency(), ex);
    return respond(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "Dependency unavailable",
            "A service this request depends on is unavailable. Try again later."));
}

@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> unexpected(Exception ex) {
    log.error("Unexpected error", ex);
    return respond(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Internal error",
            "Something went wrong. Quote the traceId if you contact support."));
}
Reading the code
"You are not allowed to do this"

The 403 says nothing about which scope is missing, or which record the caller tried to reach.

log.warn("Dependency {} is unavailable", ex.dependency(), ex);

The 503 is logged as a warning, with the name of the service, such as stock. An outage of the stock service is then visible in the logs. For the stock client and its retries, see the chapter Calling other services.

@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)

The catch-all for everything else. It logs the exception as an error, with its stack trace, and answers with a text that reveals nothing.

Inside one advice class, the closest match wins. A run showed that a ResponseEntityExceptionHandler subclass with a handler for Exception still sends MethodArgumentNotValidException to the base class. So the catch-all does not take the 400s. AccessDeniedException still gets its own handler, and its 403.

The platform overrides three of the inherited handlers, so that every 400 has the same shape. The first one lists the fields of a failed @Valid:

@Override
protected @Nullable ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
                                                                        HttpHeaders headers,
                                                                        HttpStatusCode status,
                                                                        WebRequest request) {
    ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, INVALID_REQUEST,
            "One or more fields are invalid");
    problem.setProperty("errors", ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(error -> fieldError(error.getField(), String.valueOf(error.getDefaultMessage())))
            .toList());
    return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problem);
}
Reading the code
protected @Nullable ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,

This method of the base class handles a failed @Valid. The platform overrides it. @Nullable comes from JSpecify, and says that the method may return null. A second advice class for the same exception would compete with this one. See the section One advice class, not two.

ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()

The exception holds one error for each field that failed. Each becomes a {"field": ..., "message": ...} entry.

The second override is handleHttpMessageNotReadable. It answers JSON that cannot be read with a 400. Its detail says that the body is not valid JSON, or that a value has the wrong type. A third override, handleTypeMismatch, names the field of a query parameter of the wrong type, such as ?status=LOST.

The InvalidValueException handler serves one more case. A delivery method must be an active value of a lookup list. The reference feature checks that for the other features:

public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
    boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
            .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
    if (!known) {
        throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
    }
}

The caller passes the name of its request field as field, such as deliveryMethod. An unknown code then throws an InvalidValueException. That is a 400 that names the field, not a 422. The client sent a value that is not allowed, as with a bad email address. It breaks no rule about the order itself.

The status is chosen by the kind, in one place. The careful alternative is a handler in each feature, written next to the feature's exceptions. It keeps the HTTP status close to the code that throws, and a reader of the feature sees both in one package. But each feature would repeat the same mapping, and the shapes would drift apart. The domain also must not know about HTTP. An architecture rule forbids Spring in the domain. With the mapping by kind, a new rule is one new subclass, and its status needs no new code. A handler in a feature is the better choice only for an exception that no kind describes, and that should be rare.

In ASP.NET Core, AddProblemDetails() and an IExceptionHandler do the same job:

C#
public class DomainExceptionHandler(IProblemDetailsService problems) : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(HttpContext context, Exception exception, CancellationToken token)
    {
        if (exception is not InvalidOperationException) return false;
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status422UnprocessableEntity;
        return await problems.TryWriteAsync(new() { HttpContext = context, Exception = exception });
    }
}
Java 25
@ExceptionHandler(BusinessRuleViolationException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> businessRule(BusinessRuleViolationException ex) {
    return respond(domainProblem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Business rule violated", ex));
}

The C# handler returns false for an exception it does not handle, and the next handler gets a turn. The Java method names its exception type in the annotation, and Spring chooses the method. A run of the C# handler on ASP.NET Core 10 wrote a 422 problem with a traceId. The controller tests of the order service check every row of the status table. The quick reference lists them.

A traceId on every problemtrap#

Support staff ask a customer for the traceId of a failed request. With it, they find every log line of that request, in every service it reached. So every problem must carry it. The platform's helper adds it when it builds a problem:

/** Creates a problem with a title, a detail text and the trace ID. */
public static ProblemDetail problem(HttpStatusCode status, String title, String detail) {
    ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, detail);
    problem.setTitle(title);
    return withTraceId(problem);
}

/** Adds the trace ID to a problem that someone else created, such as Spring MVC. */
public static ProblemDetail withTraceId(ProblemDetail problem) {
    String traceId = MDC.get(TRACE_ID);
    if (traceId != null) {
        problem.setProperty(TRACE_ID, traceId);
    }
    return problem;
}
Reading the code
String traceId = MDC.get(TRACE_ID);

Micrometer Tracing puts the trace ID of the request into the mapped diagnostic context (MDC), under the key traceId. A run showed that the ID is there even when the trace is not sampled. For tracing, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

if (traceId != null) {

A slice test runs no tracing, so the MDC can be empty. Then the problem has no traceId, and nothing fails.

Every handler of the platform calls ProblemDetails.problem. But the handlers that the class inherits from ResponseEntityExceptionHandler build their own problems. That base class has handlers for 20 exception types of Spring MVC. They include a 405, a 415, a missing parameter and a path with no controller.

Gotcha

A traceId added only in your own handlers is missing from Spring MVC's problems. An advice that calls a helper like ProblemDetails.problem in each of its own handlers looks complete. But a bad enum in the query, a 405, a 404 for an unknown path and a 415 all go to the inherited handlers. Their problems then carry no traceId. The support desk cannot find the logs of exactly those requests.

Every inherited handler ends in one method of the base class, handleExceptionInternal. The platform overrides that one method:

/**
 * Every handler of {@link ResponseEntityExceptionHandler} passes through this method, so the
 * trace ID reaches the problems Spring MVC creates itself, such as 405 and 415.
 */
@Override
protected @Nullable ResponseEntity<Object> handleExceptionInternal(Exception ex, @Nullable Object body,
                                                                   HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode statusCode,
                                                                   WebRequest request) {
    ResponseEntity<Object> response = super.handleExceptionInternal(ex, body, headers, statusCode, request);
    if (response != null && response.getBody() instanceof ProblemDetail problem) {
        ProblemDetails.withTraceId(problem);
    }
    return response;
}
Reading the code
ResponseEntity<Object> response = super.handleExceptionInternal(ex, body, headers, statusCode, request);

The base class builds the response first. For most exceptions, the body argument is null, and super creates the problem. So the method adds the ID to the result of super, not to the argument.

response.getBody() instanceof ProblemDetail problem

A type pattern. It checks that the body is a ProblemDetail, and names it problem in one step.

ProblemDetails.withTraceId(problem);

The platform's helper adds the traceId member.

A run with this override gave every inherited case a traceId. The run tried six cases. They were a bad enum in the query, a 405, a 404 with no handler, a 415, broken JSON and an invalid body. The order service tests the same cases in the nested class OrderControllerTest.TraceId:

@BeforeEach
void startATrace() {
    // In a slice test no tracing runs, so the test puts a trace ID where tracing would.
    MDC.put("traceId", "trace-1");
}
// ...
@Test
void onAMethodThatIsNotAllowed() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(delete("/orders/" + ORDER_ID).with(AGENT))
            .andExpect(status().isMethodNotAllowed())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.traceId").value("trace-1"));
}

The class has seven tests, one for each case of the run and one for a missing token. The 401 gets its traceId from the security chain's own entry point, which uses the same helper.

In ASP.NET Core, AddProblemDetails() adds a traceId to the problems that it writes. A run of the 422 above showed it, and the automatic 400 of [ApiController] has one too. In Spring, nothing adds it for you. In the same run, a 405 of ASP.NET Core 10 had an empty body. So a 405 is a case where the Spring service gives the client more than the default ASP.NET Core service does.

422 Unprocessable Content, and 409 only for a concurrent updatetwist#

C#
context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status422UnprocessableEntity;
Java 25
return respond(domainProblem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Business rule violated", ex));

Spring Framework 7 names the status 422 UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, with the reason phrase "Unprocessable Content". The old name, UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, still exists and is deprecated. The test matchers changed in the same way. The new matcher is status().isUnprocessableContent(), and the old isUnprocessableEntity() is deprecated. In .NET 10, StatusCodes has only Status422UnprocessableEntity. The enum HttpStatusCode has both names.

The order service answers 422 for every broken business rule, and 409 only for a concurrent update. A careful team can choose differently. The name of 409 is Conflict. A team may read a rule that the current state breaks as such a conflict. Shipping a cancelled order conflicts with the state of the order, so that team answers 409 for it. The reading is sound, and it keeps 422 for a request that is wrong in itself.

The shop still keeps 409 and 422 apart, because each status asks the client for a different reaction:

StatusWhat happenedWhat the client does
409 CONCURRENT_UPDATEsomeone else changed the same order at the same momentreload the order, and try the same action again
422 with a code, such as ORDER_NOT_PAIDthe order's rules refuse the actionshow the reason to the user, and do not retry

With one status for both, a client must read the code to know whether a retry can work. With two statuses, a client can act on the status alone. The 422 always carries a stable code, and the OpenAPI contract lists the codes of each operation. The test aBrokenBusinessRuleIsA422WithItsCode records the 422, and the tests of the next sections record the 409.

Two advices, and why @Order decidestrap#

The platform has two advices. The global handler is one. The 409 handler in the mongo package is the other. Both could answer an OptimisticLockingFailureException, because the global handler has a catch-all for Exception. A C# developer expects the more specific handler to win.

Gotcha

Spring chooses the advice before it chooses the method. It asks the advices in order. The first advice that has any matching handler answers, even if a later advice has a closer match. So a catch-all in the first advice wins over a specific handler in the second. A run with two advices and no @Order showed that the class names then decide:

The two advices, with no @OrderWho answered a ConflictException
AaaCatchAll and ZzzSpecificthe catch-all, with 500
AaaSpecific and ZzzCatchAllthe specific advice, with 409

Nothing warns you, and a renamed class changes the answer.

@Order fixes the order. A lower number comes first. The platform gives the catch-all the lowest precedence, and the specific advice the highest:

@RestControllerAdvice
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class OptimisticLockingExceptionHandler {

The constant Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE is Integer.MIN_VALUE. The constant Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE is Integer.MAX_VALUE. A run with these two values let the specific advice answer 409, whatever the class names were. So the rule is short. Give a catch-all advice the lowest precedence. Give every specific advice a higher one.

Spring Boot has its own advice for problem details too. It is switched on only by spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled, and it backs off when a ResponseEntityExceptionHandler bean exists. The platform's handler is such a bean, so Boot's advice is never created. For more, see the section ProblemDetail.

ASP.NET Core also tries its handlers one after the other. A run registered a catch-all IExceptionHandler before a specific one. The catch-all answered with 500. So in both platforms, the order decides. In ASP.NET Core, the order of registration is visible in Program.cs. In Spring, without @Order, the order is hidden.

The 409 handler in the mongo packagenew#

Two agents pick lines of the same order at the same moment. Each request loads the order, changes it and saves it. The second save finds that the stored version has changed. For how the version works, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB. The client of the second request must get a 409, and then reload and try again.

The exception that signals this comes from Spring Data and MongoDB. The platform's web code should not know about MongoDB. So the 409 handler is in the platform's mongo package, next to the technology that throws. The web package knows nothing about it:

@ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> staleVersion(OptimisticLockingFailureException ex) {
    return conflict();
}

@ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> dataIntegrity(DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
    if (WriteConflicts.isWriteConflict(ex)) {
        return conflict();
    }
    log.error("Unexpected data error", ex);
    return ResponseEntity.internalServerError().body(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
            "Internal error", "Something went wrong. Quote the traceId if you contact support."));
}

private static ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> conflict() {
    ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Concurrent update",
            "Someone else changed this at the same time. Reload it and try again.");
    problem.setProperty("code", "CONCURRENT_UPDATE");
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).body(problem);
}
Reading the code
@ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)

Outside a transaction, Spring Data throws this exception when the stored version differs.

@ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)

Inside a transaction, MongoDB usually stops the second writer earlier, with a write conflict. Spring translates that into a DataIntegrityViolationException.

if (WriteConflicts.isWriteConflict(ex)) {

The same Spring exception also covers real data errors. So the handler checks the cause, and answers 409 only for a write conflict. Any other data error is a 500.

problem.setProperty("code", "CONCURRENT_UPDATE");

The code tells the client to reload and retry.

The check looks for MongoDB's error code for a write conflict, anywhere in the chain of causes:

public static boolean isWriteConflict(Throwable error) {
    for (Throwable cause = error; cause != null; cause = cause.getCause()) {
        if (cause instanceof MongoException mongo
                && (mongo.getCode() == WRITE_CONFLICT
                || mongo.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL))) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

WRITE_CONFLICT is 112, MongoDB's error code. The label TransientTransactionError marks an error after which the whole transaction may be tried again. For write conflicts and transactions in depth, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

The handler is registered by an auto-configuration of the mongo package, and only in a web application:

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = ConditionalOnWebApplication.Type.SERVLET)
public class PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    OptimisticLockingExceptionHandler optimisticLockingExceptionHandler() {
        return new OptimisticLockingExceptionHandler();
    }
}

@ConditionalOnWebApplication creates the bean only in a servlet web application, so a worker with no web server gets no handler. For auto-configurations, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

Two controller tests cover the two shapes. aStaleVersionIsA409 throws an OptimisticLockingFailureException. aWriteConflictInsideATransactionIsAlsoA409 builds the exception that MongoDB would send:

@Test
void aWriteConflictInsideATransactionIsAlsoA409() throws Exception {
    MongoCommandException writeConflict = new MongoCommandException(
            BsonDocument.parse("{ok: 0, code: 112, codeName: 'WriteConflict', errmsg: 'Write conflict'}"),
            new ServerAddress());
    doThrow(new DataIntegrityViolationException("Write conflict", writeConflict)).when(orders).cancel(any());

    mvc.perform(post("/orders/" + ORDER_ID + "/cancel").with(AGENT))
            .andExpect(status().isConflict())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.code").value("CONCURRENT_UPDATE"));
}

The test builds a MongoCommandException with the code 112. It puts that exception inside a DataIntegrityViolationException, as the translation of Spring would. The slice imports the web auto-configuration of the mongo package, so the real handler answers. The closest match in ASP.NET Core is a handler that you write for DbUpdateConcurrencyException.

What a problem never containsnew#

A problem goes to the client, and often to the browser of a customer-service agent. Anything in it can appear in a screenshot or a support ticket. So two things never appear in a problem of the shop. One is personal data. The other is a stack trace or any internal detail.

The message of a domain exception becomes the detail of the problem. So the message must hold IDs, and never a name, an email address or an address. The base class of every domain exception states the rule:

/**
 * The base of every exception the domain throws. It has exactly three kinds, and the kind
 * decides the HTTP status, so a feature never writes an exception handler.
 *
 * <ul>
 *   <li>{@link NotFoundException}: the thing does not exist (404).</li>
 *   <li>{@link InvalidValueException}: a value has the wrong format (400).</li>
 *   <li>{@link BusinessRuleViolationException}: the request breaks a business rule (422).</li>
 * </ul>
 *
 * <p>The class is sealed, so no other direct subclass can exist. Extend one of the three kinds.
 * The message is returned to the caller, so it must never hold personal data. IDs are fine.
 */
public abstract sealed class DomainException extends RuntimeException
        permits NotFoundException, InvalidValueException, BusinessRuleViolationException {

The class is a sealed type. Its permits clause names the three kinds, so no fourth kind can appear by accident. OrderNotPaidException follows the rule. Its message is "Order 7b1e... cannot ship before it is paid", with the order's ID and nothing about the customer. An invalid email address gives the message "customer.email has an invalid format". It names the field, and not the value that the client sent.

For every other exception, the catch-all answers with a fixed text, "Something went wrong. Quote the traceId if you contact support." The details go only to the log, with the traceId. The 409 handler does the same for a data error that is not a write conflict. The test anUnexpectedErrorIsA500WithoutItsMessage throws an exception with a secret in its message. It checks that the answer is a 500 with the fixed text, and that the body does not contain the secret.

Spring Boot also has an error response of its own. The platform's defaults switch off the parts of it that could leak:

# Boot's own error responses never contain a stack trace or an exception message. Both values
# are Boot's defaults, restated. Boot 4 renamed the keys, and it ignores the old server.error.* keys.
spring.web.error.include-stacktrace=never
spring.web.error.include-message=never

These two settings say when the error response of Spring Boot includes the stack trace and the exception message. With never, the response includes no stack trace and no message.

Gotcha

Boot 4 has new names for these two keys. The configuration metadata of Boot 4.1.2 marks server.error.include-stacktrace and server.error.include-message as deprecated since 4.0.0, at the level error. Their replacements are spring.web.error.include-stacktrace and spring.web.error.include-message. A run for this book set the old include-message key to always, and Boot 4.1.2 still left the message out. So Boot 4.1.2 ignores the old key. A service that copies the key from a Boot 3 service loses the setting, and must use the new name.

The default of each new key is never, so the two lines change nothing today. The platform keeps them as a statement of the rule, as its comment says. For the run and for the other keys that Boot 4 renamed, see the section Boot 4 keys that changed their names.

A 401 never reaches the advice. The security chain writes it, with the same title, status and traceId. See the section One request through the checks. For masking personal data in the logs, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

The MDC interceptornew#

Support staff look for every log line about one order. So the platform copies chosen path variables, such as orderId, into the mapped diagnostic context (MDC) for each request. The MDC is the logging context of the thread. Every log line of the request then carries the values.

This section shows the three parts of the interceptor that belong to Spring MVC. They are its callbacks, the request attribute that holds the path variables, and its registration. For the setting and the log lines, see the section Path variables in the MDC, with an interceptor.

The constructor of the interceptor takes the names to copy. They come from the setting platform.logging.mdc-path-variables:

public class PathVariableMdcInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {

    private final List<String> names;

    public PathVariableMdcInterceptor(List<String> names) {
        this.names = List.copyOf(names);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler) {
        if (request.getAttribute(HandlerMapping.URI_TEMPLATE_VARIABLES_ATTRIBUTE) instanceof Map<?, ?> variables) {
            for (String name : names) {
                if (variables.get(name) instanceof String value) {
                    MDC.put(name, value);
                }
            }
        }
        return true;
    }

    @Override
    public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler,
                                Exception ex) {
        names.forEach(MDC::remove);
    }
}
Reading the code
public class PathVariableMdcInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {

HandlerInterceptor has the three callbacks. Each one is a default method of the interface, so the class implements only the two it needs.

request.getAttribute(HandlerMapping.URI_TEMPLATE_VARIABLES_ATTRIBUTE)

Spring MVC stores the path variables of the matched method in this request attribute, as a map. For POST /orders/42/ship, the map is {orderId=42}.

instanceof Map<?, ?> variables) {

A type pattern. The attribute has the type Object, and it can be null. The pattern is false for null, so the code needs no separate null check. The type arguments of a map are not known at run time, so the pattern writes Map<?, ?>, a map of unknown types.

if (variables.get(name) instanceof String value) {

A second pattern. A name that the path does not have gives null, and nothing is put into the MDC.

return true;

true lets the request continue. false would stop it here.

names.forEach(MDC::remove);

afterCompletion runs at the end of the request, even after an exception. So the interceptor removes its values there.

Spring MVC fills the attribute only after it has matched a controller method. So an interceptor is the right place to read path variables. A servlet filter runs earlier, and it has no path variables yet. The attribute holds an empty map for a path with no variables, and it is null when no controller method matched. For the measured cases, see the section Path variables in the MDC, with an interceptor.

The platform registers the interceptor through a WebMvcConfigurer bean:

/** Registers the MDC interceptor. A {@link WebMvcConfigurer} bean is how a library adds to Spring MVC. */
@Bean
WebMvcConfigurer platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer(PlatformLoggingProperties properties) {
    PathVariableMdcInterceptor interceptor = new PathVariableMdcInterceptor(properties.getMdcPathVariables());
    return new WebMvcConfigurer() {
        @Override
        public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
            registry.addInterceptor(interceptor);
        }
    };
}
Reading the code
WebMvcConfigurer platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer(PlatformLoggingProperties properties) {

Spring MVC reads its settings from the WebMvcConfigurer beans. So a library adds to Spring MVC with a bean of its own, and a service can still have its own bean too.

return new WebMvcConfigurer() {

An anonymous class that implements the interface. It overrides one method, and keeps the defaults of the others.

registry.addInterceptor(interceptor);

The interceptor now runs for every controller method.

The closest match in C# is context.Request.RouteValues["orderId"], read in a middleware. For the interceptor's test, and for how the MDC compares with ILogger.BeginScope, see the section Path variables in the MDC, with an interceptor.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe order service takes @PathVariable String orderId, and calls OrderId.of(orderId) inside the method. Why not declare the parameter as a UUID?
Three reasons. The permission check then runs before the conversion, so a read-only caller who sends a bad ID gets 403, not 400. The domain's Identifier decides what a valid ID is, the same way for every ID. And its InvalidValueException gives a 400 whose errors list names the field orderId.
2
An expert asksWhy does GlobalExceptionHandler override handleExceptionInternal, when every one of its own handlers already adds the traceId?
The class also inherits handlers for 20 exception types of Spring MVC, such as a 405, a 415 and a bad enum in the query. Those handlers build their own problems, without the traceId. Every one of them ends in handleExceptionInternal. So one override adds the traceId to all of them.
3
The platform has a catch-all advice and a specific 409 advice. What decides which one answers an OptimisticLockingFailureException, and how does the platform make it reliable?
Spring asks the advices in order, and the first advice with any matching handler answers. Without @Order, the class names decide. The platform gives the catch-all @Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE) and the 409 advice @Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE), so the 409 advice always answers.
4
TranslateWrite this action as a method of the shop's note controller, whose class maps /orders/{orderId}/notes. It needs the orders.write scope: 
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult Add(string orderId, AddNoteRequest request)
{
    var noteId = notes.AddNote(orderId, new NewNote(request.Text, request.Category, request.ActionRequired));
    return Created($"/orders/{orderId}/notes/{noteId}", new NoteAddedResponse(noteId));
}
@OrdersWrite
@PostMapping
// ...
ResponseEntity<NoteAddedResponse> add(@PathVariable String orderId, @Valid @RequestBody AddNoteRequest request) {
    String noteId = notes.addNote(orderId, new NewNote(request.text(), request.category(), request.actionRequired()));
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + orderId + "/notes/" + noteId))
            .body(new NoteAddedResponse(noteId));
}

@Valid is needed, or the constraints of the record are never checked. ResponseEntity.created takes a URI, and sets 201 and the Location header. body adds the JSON.

API and event contracts#

The web layer and security · Chapter 14· 34 min read· Quick reference

A contract is the shape of an API or an event that other teams build against. The order service generates its OpenAPI file from the code, commits it, and fails the build when the committed file differs. This chapter compares that code-first way with contract first, and says when each is right. It then covers the JSON schemas of events, versions, and tolerant readers.
