twistMicrosoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, with OpenAPI 3.1springdoc, with OpenAPI 3.1both generate the document from the code, but only springdoc brings Swagger UI in the same dependency Why
newa schema for each message, if the team writes onecontracts/events/OrderPlacedV1.json, beside the record OrderPlacedV1the schema is the contract for other teams, and a test checks each published event against it Why
twista version in the type name, such as OrderShippedV1OrderShippedV1, a recordwithin V1, fields are only added, and a breaking change is published as V2 beside V1 Why
twistGuid.NewGuid() as the message IDIntegrationEvent.newEventId(), called once when the event is createda resend keeps the ID, so the consumer's inbox detects the duplicate Why
twistJsonSerializer ignores an unknown property by default@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) on the consumer's recordJackson 3 ignores them by default too, and the annotation keeps that true whatever the mapper's settings Why
twist[JsonRequired] on each propertya compact constructor that refuses a missing fielda wrong subscription then fails loudly, and the message is not lost Why
newa shared NuGet package of message classesour own copy of a consumed event, a record and a schema with only the fields we useeach team owns its classes, and a contract change is checked by reading one file Why
newno equivalentan IntegrationEventMapper that returns Optional.empty() for internal eventsevery published event is a contract to keep, so the service publishes only what others need Why

Why the service publishes contractsnew#

The shop's web application shows orders to customer-service agents. Another team builds it. The QA team tests the order service with its own tools. The stock service reads the events that the order service publishes. None of these teams reads the Java code. Each of them builds against a description of what the order service accepts and returns.

That description is called a contract. The order service has two kinds:

ContractFormatWho builds against it
the HTTP APIan OpenAPI 3.1 document, contracts/openapi.yamlthe web application, QA, and any other caller
each published eventa JSON Schema file, such as contracts/events/OrderPlacedV1.jsoneach service that consumes the event

Both are files in the repository of the service, in the folder contracts:

order-service/
  contracts/
    openapi.yaml                        the HTTP API, generated from the code
    events/
      OrderPlacedV1.json                the events that the service publishes
      OrderShippedV1.json
      OrderCancelledV1.json
      consumed-PaymentReceivedV1.json   the part of a consumed event that the service reads
  src/

A change to a contract is then a change to a file in contracts, and a pull request shows it as a diff.

Teams share the contracts, and not a library of the order service's classes. A shared library of request records and event records has a real strength. Both sides compile against one definition, so some breaking changes are compile errors. It is a good choice when one team owns the producer and every consumer, and they always deploy together. But between teams, a shared library ties every consumer to Java, and to the same versions of Jackson and Spring. An upgrade of the library becomes a release that every team must take. And a library invites behaviour into the shared classes. A file in a standard format has none of these costs. Each team generates or writes its own classes from it.

The OpenAPI file also documents the records of the web layer. These records are called data transfer objects (DTOs). For why the API uses them and not the domain classes, see the section Request and response DTOs as records.

A hand-written contract driftstrap#

A team writes contracts/openapi.yaml itself, before it builds the endpoints. It agrees the file with the UI team and QA. The pull request template has a line, "the controller and openapi.yaml match". This is the careful version of a hand-written contract, and it gets two things right. The API is agreed before anyone writes code, and the file is reviewed like code.

Six months later, the file and the code differ, in ways like these:

  • Several operations list no 401 and no 403, although every endpoint needs a token and a scope.
  • An operation that takes an ID in the path lists no 400, although a malformed ID gets one.
  • A list operation lists no 400 for a page size that is too large.
  • A path parameter declares an enum of allowed values, but the code accepts any value, and answers 200 [] for an unknown one.
Gotcha

Nothing fails when a hand-written contract and the code differ. The build compiles the code and never reads the file. A test calls the code, not the file. The pull request checklist line is ticked by a person, who checks what they remember to check. So each change that forgets the file adds one more difference, and nobody notices. The UI team then builds against a file that is wrong.

There are two standard fixes. Both make the build compare the file with the code:

FixWhere the truth isWhat fails the build
code firstthe controllers and DTOs, and the file is generated from thema test, when the committed file differs from the generated one
contract firstthe file, and code is generated from itthe compiler, when a controller no longer matches the generated interface

The order service uses code first. The documentation of its order controller says so:

* <p>The OpenAPI annotations describe each operation and its errors. springdoc builds the
* document from them, and the build fails when {@code contracts/openapi.yaml} differs.

The words the build fails are the difference from a checklist line.

Code first: springdoc reads the codenew#

The library springdoc-openapi builds an OpenAPI document from a running application of Spring model-view-controller (MVC). It reads the controllers, their mappings, and the records they take and return. It also reads the annotations of Jakarta Validation on those records. The platform library adds the dependency, so every service gets it:

<!-- The generated OpenAPI document at /v3/api-docs, and Swagger UI -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
</dependency>

The dependency springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui has no version here. The platform has a parent Project Object Model (POM), and that file sets the version to 3.2.0. A POM that other POMs inherit from is called a parent POM. For parent POMs, see the chapter The build: a parent POM and a platform library. As of October 2026, 3.2.0 is the latest release. It was released on 24 October 2026, and its own parent POM is spring-boot-starter-parent 4.1.2. The springdoc site's compatibility matrix maps Spring Boot 4.1.x to springdoc 3.1.x and 3.2.x, and Boot 4.0.x to springdoc 3.0.x.

A run of springdoc 3.2.0 on Boot 4.1.2 showed what it serves:

PathWhat it returns
/v3/api-docsthe document as JSON, starting with "openapi":"3.1.0"
/v3/api-docs.yamlthe same document as YAML
/swagger-ui.htmla redirect to /swagger-ui/index.html
/swagger-ui/index.htmlSwagger UI, a page to read and call the API in a browser

The run also showed what springdoc reads from the code:

In the codeIn the document
@NotBlank on a componentthe field is listed under required
@Size(max = 20)maxLength 20 and minLength 0
@Min(1) @Max(99)minimum 1 and maximum 99
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0")default 0
@Schema(example = ...) and @Operation(summary = ...)copied as they are
an Instanttype string, with format date-time
a primitive int with no constraintnot listed in required
the media type of a response*/* unless the mapping declares produces

The committed contract shows the same rules on the shop's records. This is the schema of a line of a new order:

LineRequest:
  type: object
  properties:
    productCode:
      type: string
      example: MUG-001
      minLength: 1
    quantity:
      type: integer
      format: int32
      example: 2
      maximum: 999
      minimum: 1
  required:
  - productCode

productCode has @NotBlank, so it is listed under required, and it has a minimum length of 1. quantity is a primitive int. Its two constraints give it a minimum and a maximum, but it is not listed under required.

The platform sets four springdoc settings for every service:

# The OpenAPI document lists properties in a fixed order, so the committed file changes only
# when the API changes.
springdoc.writer-with-order-by-keys=true
# The services answer JSON, so the document says so instead of "*/*".
springdoc.default-produces-media-type=application/json
# The OpenAPI document stays on: it needs a token like every other path, and the drift check
# reads it. Swagger UI is off, and the local profile turns it on.
springdoc.api-docs.enabled=true
springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false
Reading the code
springdoc.writer-with-order-by-keys=true

The document lists keys in alphabetical order. Without a fixed order, two builds of the same code could write the members in another order, and the drift check would fail for nothing.

springdoc.default-produces-media-type=application/json

Without it, every response would say */*. The committed contract says application/json.

springdoc.api-docs.enabled=true

The document stays on in every environment. It is not public, because the security chain asks for a token on /v3/api-docs too.

springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false

Swagger UI is off, except in the local profile. springdoc logs a warning at startup when the document or the UI is enabled by default. A setting that states the choice is clearer.

The local profile turns on Swagger UI, and makes the two paths public. A developer can then open http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html without a token. For the public paths, see the section The platform's filter chain.

Code first has one limit by its nature. The contract exists only after the code. A team that must agree an API before anyone builds it needs a way around that. See the section Choosing code first or contract first.

The OpenAPI annotations the service usestwist#

The code cannot say everything that a client needs. It cannot say why an operation exists, or which business codes a 422 can carry. The service adds that with annotations that springdoc reads. They come from the Swagger project, in the package io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations. The springdoc dependency brings them:

C#
[HttpPost("{orderId}/ship")]
[EndpointSummary("Ship an order")]
[ProducesResponseType(StatusCodes.Status204NoContent)]
[ProducesResponseType(StatusCodes.Status422UnprocessableEntity)]
public IActionResult Ship(string orderId) => NoContent();
Java 25
@OrdersWrite
@PostMapping("/{orderId}/ship")
@Operation(operationId = "shipOrder", summary = "Ship an order",
        description = "The order must be paid, every line picked, and no note may need action.")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "204", description = "Shipped")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "400", ref = PlatformOpenApi.INVALID_REQUEST)
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", ref = PlatformOpenApi.NOT_FOUND)
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "409", ref = PlatformOpenApi.CONCURRENT_UPDATE)
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "422",
        description = "Business rule violated: ORDER_FINISHED, ORDER_NOT_PAID, UNPICKED_LINES, ORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONS",
        content = @Content(mediaType = PlatformOpenApi.PROBLEM_JSON, schema = @Schema(ref = PlatformOpenApi.PROBLEM_SCHEMA)))
Reading the code
@Operation(operationId = "shipOrder", summary = "Ship an order",

operationId names the operation. A client generator uses it as the method name, so the service sets it, and never changes it. summary is the one-line text, and description the longer one.

@ApiResponse(responseCode = "204", description = "Shipped")

One annotation for each response. The annotation can be repeated on one method.

@ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", ref = PlatformOpenApi.NOT_FOUND)

ref points to a shared response, defined once for every service. PlatformOpenApi.NOT_FOUND is the string #/components/responses/NotFound.

description = "Business rule violated: ORDER_FINISHED, ORDER_NOT_PAID, UNPICKED_LINES, ORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONS",

The 422 lists the business codes that this operation can return. A client may rely on them.

content = @Content(mediaType = PlatformOpenApi.PROBLEM_JSON, schema = @Schema(ref = PlatformOpenApi.PROBLEM_SCHEMA)))

The 422 body is a problem, of the media type application/problem+json.

The C# attributes compile on .NET 10. This book did not compare the documents that they produce. The annotations the service uses are few:

AnnotationWhereWhat it adds
@Tag(name = "orders")on the controller classgroups the operations, by feature
@Operation(operationId, summary, description)on each methodthe operation's name and its texts
@ApiResponse(responseCode, description or ref, content)on each method, once for each statusthe responses, including the errors
@Schema(description, example, allowableValues)on a record componentthe texts, an example, and the allowed values of a String
@Parameter(schema = @Schema(allowableValues = ...))on a method parameterthe allowed values of a path or query parameter

The service's status field is a String, so springdoc would not know its values. @Schema(allowableValues = {"NEW", "PAID", "SHIPPED", "CANCELLED"}) on the response record lists them as an enum in the document.

The parts that are the same for every operation are not written on each method. The service describes itself once, in one bean:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class OpenApiConfig {

    @Bean
    OpenAPI orderServiceOpenApi() {
        return new OpenAPI()
                .info(new Info()
                        .title("order-service")
                        .version("1")
                        .description("""
                                The shop's orders, the notes customer-service agents keep on them, and the \
                                lookup values they use.

                                Every request needs a bearer token. Reads need the orders.read scope, and \
                                changes need orders.write.

                                Every error is an RFC 9457 problem (application/problem+json) with a traceId. \
                                A broken business rule (422) carries a stable code that clients may rely on."""))
                .addServersItem(new Server().url("http://localhost:8080").description("Local (docker compose)"))
                .addTagsItem(new Tag().name("orders").description("Orders, their lines and their shipping"))
                .addTagsItem(new Tag().name("notes").description("Customer-service notes on an order"))
                .addTagsItem(new Tag().name("reference-data").description("Lookup values"));
    }
}
Reading the code
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)

A configuration class whose @Bean methods do not call each other. For what proxyBeanMethods changes, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

OpenAPI orderServiceOpenApi() {

springdoc starts from this OpenAPI object, and adds the paths it finds in the controllers.

.description("""

A text block. A backslash at the end of a line joins it to the next line, so the text has no line break there.

.addServersItem(new Server().url("http://localhost:8080").description("Local (docker compose)"))

A fixed server URL. See the section Exporting the contract, and the drift check.

.addTagsItem(new Tag().name("orders").description("Orders, their lines and their shipping"))

The tags are declared here, once, with their texts. The controllers only name them. springdoc then keeps this order of the tags.

The parts that every shop service shares come from the platform. An OpenApiCustomizer bean changes the document after springdoc built it:

@Bean
OpenApiCustomizer platformOpenApiCustomizer() {
    return openApi -> {
        Components components = openApi.getComponents() == null ? new Components() : openApi.getComponents();
        openApi.setComponents(components);
        components.addSecuritySchemes("bearerAuth", new SecurityScheme()
                .type(SecurityScheme.Type.HTTP).scheme("bearer").bearerFormat("JWT"));
        openApi.addSecurityItem(new SecurityRequirement().addList("bearerAuth"));
        components.addSchemas("Problem", problemSchema());
        PlatformOpenApi.SHARED_RESPONSES.forEach((name, description) ->
                components.addResponses(name, problemResponse(description)));

        if (openApi.getPaths() != null) {
            openApi.getPaths().values().forEach(path -> path.readOperations().forEach(operation -> {
                operation.getResponses().computeIfAbsent("401", code -> new ApiResponse().$ref(PlatformOpenApi.UNAUTHORIZED));
                operation.getResponses().computeIfAbsent("403", code -> new ApiResponse().$ref(PlatformOpenApi.FORBIDDEN));
            }));
        }
    };
}
Reading the code
components.addSecuritySchemes("bearerAuth", new SecurityScheme()

The document says once that the API takes a bearer token, a JSON Web Token (JWT).

openApi.addSecurityItem(new SecurityRequirement().addList("bearerAuth"));

Every operation needs that token, so the requirement is set for the whole document.

components.addSchemas("Problem", problemSchema());

The schema of every error body, with code, traceId and errors.

components.addResponses(name, problemResponse(description)));

The shared responses, such as NotFound and ConcurrentUpdate. A controller names them with ref.

operation.getResponses().computeIfAbsent("401", code -> new ApiResponse().$ref(PlatformOpenApi.UNAUTHORIZED));

Every operation gets a 401 and a 403, because every endpoint needs a token and a scope. A controller never has to remember them.

The result is in the committed file. This is the start of it:

openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  # ...
  title: order-service
  version: "1"
servers:
- description: Local (docker compose)
  url: http://localhost:8080
security:
- bearerAuth: []

The servers entry comes from OpenApiConfig. The security entry comes from the platform's customizer.

The Problem schema documents the members of the RFC 9457 problems, plus the shop's own members:

Problem:
  type: object
  description: An RFC 9457 problem. Every error response has this shape.
  properties:
    code:
      type: string
      description: "A stable code (404, 409, 422), such as ORDER_NOT_PAID"
    detail:
      type: string
    errors:
      type: array
      description: "The invalid fields, for a 400"
      items:
        type: object
        properties:
          field:
            type: string
          message:
            type: string

The members code and errors are the shop's own. Each error response uses the media type application/problem+json and this schema. For the problems themselves, see the section One handler for every problem.

A generated file looks different from a hand-written one in three places:

  • Paged lists. A hand-written file often builds a page with allOf. It combines a shared schema of the page numbers with a list of items. springdoc writes one complete schema for each item type instead. PageResponseOrderResponse is one of them. Each such schema repeats the five members of PageResponse. The document is longer, and a client sees the same shape.
  • Shared parameters. A hand-written file often declares the paging parameters once, under components.parameters. Each operation then refers to them. springdoc writes them again in each operation instead, with the defaults of each @RequestParam. A change to the default then shows in every operation of the diff.
  • Fields that may be null. shippedAt has no value until the order ships. The document writes it as type: string, and leaves it out of required. In a run for this book, a plain Jackson 3 mapper wrote the missing value as "shippedAt": null. OpenAPI 3.1 allows a list of types for one field. The ASP.NET Core run in the section OpenAPI in ASP.NET Core 10 wrote such a list, ["integer", "string"]. In another run, a JSON Schema validator accepted null for the type [string, "null"]. springdoc does not write that form for the shop's records. So a client must treat a field that is not required as one that can be missing or null.

A 201 that springdoc cannot seetrap#

springdoc reads the method's signature. It does not run the method. A C# developer who knows TypedResults.Created expects the status to appear in the document by itself.

PredictA method that returns ResponseEntity.created#
springdoc builds the document from this method. Suppose the // ... line holds no @ApiResponse annotation. Which success status does the document list for POST /orders?
@OrdersWrite
@PostMapping
// ...
ResponseEntity<OrderPlacedResponse> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest request) {
    PlacedOrder placed = orders.place(
            new CustomerContact(request.customer().name(), request.customer().email()),
            new DeliveryMethod(request.deliveryMethod()),
            mapper.toItems(request),
            mapper.toNewNotes(request));
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + placed.orderId())).body(mapper.toResponse(placed));
}
Show the answer
200 OK. The 201 that the method really returns is not in the document.

springdoc sees the return type, not the status. The type is ResponseEntity<OrderPlacedResponse>. The status is chosen inside the method, at run time. springdoc cannot read that, so it writes its default, 200. A run for this book showed "200": OK for such a method.

Declare the status with @ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = ...). The order service does that on both methods that create something.

The real method carries the annotation, and the committed contract has the 201:

@ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Placed. The Location header names the new order.")

The description names the Location header, which the document does not show otherwise. In ASP.NET Core 10, TypedResults.Created(...) in a minimal API is documented as 201 with no annotation. A controller action that returns IActionResult is like the Spring method. A run of such an action with Created(...) listed only 200 in the document.

The drift check cannot catch this mistake. It compares the file with what springdoc generates, and springdoc generates the wrong status every time. So a test of the controller must check the real status, as OrderControllerTest.placingReturns201WithTheLocation does. A review of the diff of the contract is the second check. A new POST that shows "200" is a sign that the annotation is missing.

Exporting the contract, and the drift checknew#

A developer adds a field to OrderResponse, and forgets the contract. The build must fail, and say how to update the file. The order service does that with one test:

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@ActiveProfiles("wiring")
class OpenApiContractTest {

    private static final Path COMMITTED = Path.of("contracts/openapi.yaml");
    private static final Path GENERATED = Path.of("target/openapi.yaml");

    @Autowired
    MockMvc mvc;

    @Test
    void theCommittedContractMatchesTheCode() throws Exception {
        String generated = mvc.perform(get("/v3/api-docs.yaml").with(jwt()))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        write(GENERATED, generated);
        if (Boolean.getBoolean("openapi.update")) {
            write(COMMITTED, generated);
        }

        assertThat(COMMITTED).as("contracts/openapi.yaml is missing; run mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true").exists();
        assertThat(Files.readString(COMMITTED))
                .as("contracts/openapi.yaml differs from the code. Review target/openapi.yaml, "
                        + "then run mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true and commit the file.")
                .isEqualTo(generated);
    }
Reading the code
@SpringBootTest

The test starts the whole application, so springdoc sees every controller.

@AutoConfigureMockMvc

The test calls the application through MockMvc, with no server and no port.

@ActiveProfiles("wiring")

The wiring profile gives every setting a value, and connects to nothing. So the test needs no database, no queue and no token issuer. For that profile, see the chapter Testing in depth.

mvc.perform(get("/v3/api-docs.yaml").with(jwt()))

The document needs a token, as every path does. jwt() gives the request a caller without a real token.

write(GENERATED, generated);

Every build writes the generated file to target/openapi.yaml. A developer can compare it with the committed file.

if (Boolean.getBoolean("openapi.update")) {

Boolean.getBoolean reads a system property. With -Dopenapi.update=true, the test overwrites the committed file.

.isEqualTo(generated);

The committed file must match the generated one exactly. The message says how to fix a failure.

So the workflow for an API change has three steps:

  1. Change the controller or a request or response record. mvn verify fails in OpenApiContractTest.
  2. Read target/openapi.yaml, and check that the change is the one you meant.
  3. Run mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true, and commit contracts/openapi.yaml with the change.

The pull request then shows every change to the API as a diff of the contract. A reviewer sees a removed field or a renamed operation in that diff, even when the Java change looks harmless. The UI team can watch the file, and nobody has to remember a checklist line.

Gotcha

springdoc writes the server URL from the request, so a generated file changes with the port. A run exported the file twice, once from a server on port 18089 and once through MockMvc. The two files differed in exactly one line, url: http://localhost:18089 against url: http://localhost. A drift check would fail whenever the file is generated in another way. The service fixes the URL in OpenApiConfig, with addServersItem. Then springdoc writes no server of its own.

springdoc also has a plugin for Maven, springdoc-openapi-maven-plugin, version 1.5 as of October 2026. Its README says that the application must be running. The plugin works in the integration-test phase, together with the start and stop goals of the Spring Boot Maven plugin. A run on Boot 4.1.2 started the application on a port, wrote the file, and stopped the application. So it works. The order service uses the test instead, for three reasons:

  • The test needs no port and no running service, so it runs in every plain mvn verify.
  • The plugin needs the real settings of the service, or a profile like the wiring profile, to start. The test already has that profile.
  • The test compares as well as exports. With the plugin, a second step must still compare the files.

The pages of springdoc that this book checked describe no way to export the document without starting the application. Both the plugin and the test start it.

In CI, the plain build runs the test. A pull request that changes the API without the contract fails there. The contract test is listed in the README of the service as the contract kind of test, next to the unit and slice tests.

Contract first: openapi-generatornew#

Contract first reverses the direction. The team writes the OpenAPI file first, and agrees it with the UI team or a partner. A generator then writes Java code from the file, at every build. The controller implements the generated code. If the controller no longer matches the file, the compiler fails.

The common tool for Spring is openapi-generator-maven-plugin, from the OpenAPI Generator project. Its latest version is 7.26.0, as of October 2026. The same project has a generator for ASP.NET Core, named aspnetcore. It writes controller classes from the file. Its input is a file like the shop's committed contract. This is one operation of it:

/orders/{orderId}/cancel:
  post:
    operationId: cancelOrder
    parameters:
    - in: path
      name: orderId
      required: true
      schema:
        type: string
    responses:
      "204":
        description: Cancelled

From operations like this, the generator for Spring writes interfaces, with one method per operation. With the option useTags, it writes one interface for each tag. The operationId becomes the name of the method. A run of version 7.26.0 against Boot 4.1.2 generated this:

  • An interface, such as OrderControllerApi. Each method carries the mapping annotations and the parameter annotations. It also carries @Valid, and the constraints from the file, such as @Min.
  • The springdoc annotations on each method, such as @Operation and @ApiResponse.
  • Each method returns a ResponseEntity, because the option useResponseEntity is on by default.
  • One model class for each schema, such as PlaceOrderRequest and OrderResponse.

The controller then implements the interface, and writes only the bodies of the methods. The mappings come from the interface, so the controller has none of its own.

The platform's parent POM has the generator ready, in a Maven profile that a service switches on:

<!--
  Contract first: mvn verify -Dcontract-first generates Java interfaces and models from the
  service's committed contracts/openapi.yaml, before the code compiles. A service that
  writes its contract first implements the generated interfaces in its controllers, so the
  compiler finds a controller that no longer matches the contract. The order service
  writes its code first, so for it the profile only proves that its contract generates
  code that compiles.
  Both conditions must hold, so a module without the file, such as the platform, skips it.
-->
<profile>
    <id>contract-first</id>
    <activation>
        <property>
            <name>contract-first</name>
        </property>
        <file>
            <exists>${basedir}/contracts/openapi.yaml</exists>
        </file>
    </activation>
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.openapitools</groupId>
                <artifactId>openapi-generator-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>${openapi-generator.version}</version>
                <executions>
                    <execution>
                        <goals>
                            <goal>generate</goal>
                        </goals>
                        <configuration>
                            <inputSpec>${project.basedir}/contracts/openapi.yaml</inputSpec>
                            <generatorName>spring</generatorName>
                            <apiPackage>com.acme.contract.api</apiPackage>
                            <modelPackage>com.acme.contract.model</modelPackage>
                            <configOptions>
                                <interfaceOnly>true</interfaceOnly>
                                <useSpringBoot4>true</useSpringBoot4>
                                <useJackson3>true</useJackson3>
                                <openApiNullable>false</openApiNullable>
                                <skipDefaultInterface>true</skipDefaultInterface>
                                <useTags>true</useTags>
                            </configOptions>
                        </configuration>
                    </execution>
                </executions>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</profile>
Reading the code
<activation>

The profile switches itself on when both conditions hold. Maven requires every condition of an activation. The property condition holds when the command line has -Dcontract-first. The file condition holds only in a module that has the contract. So the platform's own modules skip the generator, even in a build of the whole companion.

<inputSpec>${project.basedir}/contracts/openapi.yaml</inputSpec>

The input is the committed contract of the service, the same file that the drift check compares.

<generatorName>spring</generatorName>

The generator for Spring MVC. It writes interfaces with the mapping annotations, and models.

<apiPackage>com.acme.contract.api</apiPackage>

The generated code goes into its own packages, outside the service's base package. The architecture tests import com.acme.orderservice only, so they never check generated code.

<configOptions>

The options of the run described above. The table below explains each one.

A run of mvn verify -Dcontract-first on the order service, in October 2026, generated three interfaces from the contract. OrdersApi had six methods, NotesApi three and ReferenceDataApi one. It also generated 16 model classes, such as PlaceOrderRequest and Problem, into target/generated-sources/openapi. All of it compiled with the service, and the tests passed. The generator also printed a warning, "OpenAPI 3.1 support is still in beta". The committed contract is an OpenAPI 3.1 file, because springdoc writes that version. So a team that starts contract first should review the generated code of each new generator version. The operation above became the method ResponseEntity<Void> cancelOrder(@PathVariable("orderId") String orderId), with an @Operation annotation that lists the five problem answers of the contract.

The order service writes its code first, so no controller implements these interfaces. For this service, the profile proves only that the committed contract generates code that compiles. A service that writes its contract first switches the profile on in every build, and its controllers implement the interfaces.

The plugin has many options. These are the ones that matter for a Boot 4 service, with their defaults in 7.26.0. The last column says what the help of the generator or the run showed:

OptionDefaultIn the runWhat the help or the run showed
interfaceOnlyfalsetruethe run generated only the interfaces and the models
useSpringBoot3truenot setthe help says that it also turns on useJakartaEe
useSpringBoot4falsetruethe help says "Generate code and provide dependencies for use with Spring Boot 4.x"
useJackson3falsetruethe help says that it is allowed only when useSpringBoot4 is set
useJakartaEefalsenot setturned on by useSpringBoot3, as the help of that option says
useJspecifyfalsenot setwithout it, the models import the deprecated org.springframework.lang.Nullable
openApiNullabletruefalseits effect was not checked for this book
skipDefaultInterfacefalsetruewith it, a controller that misses a method does not compile
useBeanValidationtruenot setthe generated interface carried @Valid and @Min from the file
useResponseEntitytruenot setevery generated method returned a ResponseEntity

The run also set useTags, so the interface is named after the tag. With these options, the controller compiled against Boot 4.1.2.

Then the run changed the contract. The path parameter orderId got format: uuid. The next compile failed:

rw.cf.OrderController is not abstract and does not override abstract method get(java.util.UUID,...) in rw.cf.api.OrderControllerApi#
Means
The contract changed a parameter's type, so the generated interface has a new method signature. The controller still implements the old one.
Fix
Change the controller's method to the new signature, here with a UUID parameter. Or change the contract back, if the change was not meant.

So the compiler catches a changed signature. It does not catch every change. An added field in a response model, or a different status code, leaves the Java signature as it was. A controller that returns 200 where the file says 201 still compiles. This conclusion comes from reading the generated code, and was not run. So contract first still needs controller tests that check the statuses, as code first does.

Gotcha

Version 7.26.0 has no option useRecords. The generator's web page lists useRecords, "Generate models as Java records where possible". That page documents a newer build. The help of 7.26.0 does not contain the word "record". A run with <useRecords>true</useRecords> still generated classes, such as public class PlaceOrderRequest {, with getters, setters and fluent setters.

Contract first has real costs, besides the options to tune:

  • The generated code shapes the controllers. Every method returns a ResponseEntity. A query parameter with a default becomes a boxed Integer. A format: uuid becomes a UUID parameter, so the conversion runs before the permission check. The order service avoids that with a text parameter, which it turns into a value object inside the method. See the section IDs in the path: text in, value objects inside.
  • The DTOs are generated classes. They are mutable classes with setters, not records, as of version 7.26.0. A team that wants records must write its own and map, or wait for a newer generator.
  • The mappings are out of sight. A reader of the controller does not see its paths. They are in generated code under target.
  • A generator upgrade can change the generated code. A new version of the plugin is then a change to every controller's supertype, and needs a careful review.

Choosing code first or contract firstnew#

Both ways stop the drift. They differ in where the truth is, and when the contract exists. The right one depends on who must agree the API, and when:

QuestionCode first, as in the order serviceContract first
Where is the truth?the controllers and DTOsthe OpenAPI file
When does the contract exist?after the controller and DTOs are writtenbefore any code
What catches a difference?the drift test, at every buildthe compiler, for a changed signature only
What does an API change look like?a Java change, plus a diff of the generated filea diff of the file, plus a Java change
Who can write the change?any developer of the serviceanyone who can edit YAML, including other teams
What does the code look like?the team's own records and controllersgenerated interfaces and model classes
What needs tuning?a few springdoc settings and annotationsthe generator's options, and its upgrades

The order service records its choice in the decisions of its README:

**The contract is generated, committed and checked.** springdoc builds `contracts/openapi.yaml`
from the controllers. `OpenApiContractTest` writes it to `target/openapi.yaml` in every build,
and fails when the committed file differs; `mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true` updates it. Every
API change is then a visible diff in the pull request. To agree an API early, write the
controller and DTOs with stub methods first.

The words stub methods first answer the main objection to code first. The paragraphs below explain it.

The recommendation for an internal service is code first. Generate the file with springdoc, commit it, and let CI fail when the regenerated file differs. Every API change is then a visible diff in the pull request. The developers keep writing plain records and controllers, which this part teaches.

Code first seems to prevent an early agreement on the API. It does not. To agree an API before you build it, write the controller and the DTOs first, with methods that do nothing yet. Generate the file, and open a pull request with it. The UI team reviews the diff of the contract, as it would review a hand-written file. The use cases follow in later pull requests.

Choose contract first in two cases. The first is a UI or partner team that must sign off the API before any code exists. That happens when the teams work in parallel from the first day, or when the API is part of an agreement. The second is an API shared outside the team or the company. There, the contract is the product, and its owners may not be developers of the service. In both cases the file comes first, and code that follows it is the safer direction.

Pragmatic choice: The OpenAPI contract is generated from the code

The strict rule. Design the API first. Write the contract, agree it with every consumer, and only then build the service.

What we do. The order service writes its controllers and DTOs first. springdoc generates contracts/openapi.yaml from them, and OpenApiContractTest fails the build when the committed file differs.

Why. The consumers of the API are teams of the same company, and they can review a pull request. The generated file can never drift from the code. The team writes plain records and controllers, not generated ones. An early agreement is still possible, with a controller whose methods do nothing yet.

When to stop. Stop when a consumer must sign off the API before any code exists, or when the API is published outside the company. Then switch to contract first, with the generator and its options set as in the section Contract first: openapi-generator.

OpenAPI in ASP.NET Core 10twist#

C#
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapOpenApi();
pom.xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
</dependency>

ASP.NET Core 10 has OpenAPI built in, in the package Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi. AddOpenApi() registers it, and MapOpenApi() serves the document. In Spring, a library adds it, and the dependency alone switches it on. The two differ in the details:

QuestionASP.NET Core 10springdoc 3.2.0
Where is the document?/openapi/v1.json, for the document named v1/v3/api-docs, and /v3/api-docs.yaml
Which OpenAPI version?3.1 by default, and the run wrote 3.1.13.1.0
YAMLonly when the route is mapped with a .yaml suffixalways, at its own path
A UInone, so Swagger UI or Scalar is added separatelySwagger UI in the same dependency
Export at build timethe property OpenApiGenerateDocumentsOnBuildthe Maven plugin, or a test such as OpenApiContractTest
How the export worksit starts the app's entry point with a mock serverthe plugin starts the app on a port, and the test uses MockMvc
A 201 from a result helperTypedResults.Created is documented as 201ResponseEntity.created needs @ApiResponse

Both platforms start the application to export the file. ASP.NET Core does it with a mock server, and its run printed that the entry point ran. A C# record needs one more detail. A data annotation on a positional record parameter must target the property, as in [property: MaxLength(20)]. Without property:, the run's schema had no maxLength. A Java record component needs no such target.

Note

The build of the ASP.NET Core 10 run warned NU1903: Package 'Microsoft.OpenApi' 2.0.0 has a known high severity vulnerability. That version comes in with Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.8, as of October 2026.

Event contracts: a JSON schema for each eventnew#

When an order is placed, the order service publishes OrderPlacedV1. The stock service reads it to keep its hold on the products. The stock team writes its code against a description of the event, so the event needs a contract too. The service publishes it through a transactional outbox. For how, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

The event is a record in the service:

@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS)
public record OrderPlacedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId, String deliveryMethod,
                            List<Line> lines) implements IntegrationEvent {

    public record Line(String productCode, int quantity) {
    }
}

It holds IDs and facts in plain types, such as String, Instant and int. It holds no domain class, so the domain can change without changing the event. It also holds nothing about the customer, because the stock service does not need it. The contract for other teams is a JSON Schema file beside the code:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "order-service/OrderPlacedV1",
  "title": "OrderPlacedV1",
  "description": "An order was placed. Published to the order-events SNS topic. Within V1, fields may be added but never removed or renamed, so consumers must accept fields they do not know.",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId", "deliveryMethod", "lines"],
  "properties": {
    "eventId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid", "description": "Unique per event, and the same on a resend: use it to detect duplicates." },
    "occurredAt": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" },
    "orderId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },
    "deliveryMethod": { "type": "string", "description": "A DELIVERY_METHOD code, for example STANDARD." },
    "lines": {
      "type": "array",
      "minItems": 1,
      "maxItems": 50,
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "required": ["productCode", "quantity"],
        "properties": {
          "productCode": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z0-9-]{1,30}$" },
          "quantity": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 999 }
        },
        "additionalProperties": true
      }
    }
  },
  "additionalProperties": true
}
Reading the code
"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",

The schema follows JSON Schema, draft 2020-12. Validators in many languages read it, so the stock team needs no Java.

"$id": "order-service/OrderPlacedV1",

The ID names the owner, the order service, and the event with its version.

"required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId", "deliveryMethod", "lines"],

Every event carries these five fields. A consumer may rely on them.

"eventId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid", "description": "Unique per event, and the same on a resend: use it to detect duplicates." },

format: uuid describes the text. See the next paragraph for what a validator does with it.

"additionalProperties": true

An event may carry fields that the schema does not list. So a consumer that validates an event does not reject a field that V1 adds later.

A run for this book validated events against this schema with a JSON Schema validator. These were the results:

The eventThe result
every required field, with the right typesvalid
an extra field, giftWrapvalid, because additionalProperties is true
an extra field, with additionalProperties set to falserefused, giftWrap was unexpected
deliveryMethod removedrefused, deliveryMethod is a required property
deliveryMethod set to nullrefused, because null is not a string
orderId set to not-a-uuidvalid, unless the validator checks formats

The last row matters. A validator does not always check format. The run's validator refused the bad universally unique identifier (UUID) only with its format checker switched on. So a consumer that relies on a UUID should switch the format check on, or check the value itself.

The service's README lists every event with its direction and its schema:

## Events

| Direction | Event | Where | Schema |
|---|---|---|---|
| out | `OrderPlacedV1` | SNS topic `order-events` | `contracts/events/OrderPlacedV1.json` |
| out | `OrderShippedV1` | SNS topic `order-events` | `contracts/events/OrderShippedV1.json` |
| out | `OrderCancelledV1` | SNS topic `order-events` | `contracts/events/OrderCancelledV1.json` |
| in | `PaymentReceivedV1` | SQS queue `order-service-payment-received` | `contracts/events/consumed-PaymentReceivedV1.json` |

A developer who adds an event adds a row here, and a schema file. The table answers three questions. Which events does the service publish? Which does it consume? Where is the contract of each one?

The schema and the record describe the same event twice, and nothing compares them by itself. This is the drift problem again, for events. Suppose a document of the team says that OrderShippedV1 holds shippedAt, the record holds occurredAt, and the schema says something else again. A consumer then cannot know which one is right. The cure is the same as for the API. Make one of them the source, and let the build compare.

The order service makes the record the source, and the schema the contract that a test checks. The test turns each domain event into its integration event with the real mapper. It writes the event with the application's JSON mapper, which the sender for Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) uses too. Then it validates the JSON against the committed schema:

@JsonTest
class PublishedEventSchemaTest {

    /** Draft 2020-12 treats "format" as a note only. The setting makes "uuid" and "date-time" checks. */
    private static final SchemaRegistry SCHEMAS = SchemaRegistry.withDefaultDialect(SpecificationVersion.DRAFT_2020_12,
            registry -> registry.schemaRegistryConfig(SchemaRegistryConfig.builder().formatAssertionsEnabled(true).build()));

    @Autowired
    JsonMapper json;

    static Stream<DomainEvent> publishedDomainEvents() {
        OrderId id = OrderId.newId();
        return Stream.of(new OrderPlaced(id, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, NOW), new OrderShipped(id, NOW),
                new OrderCancelled(id, NOW));
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("publishedDomainEvents")
    void eachPublishedEventMatchesItsSchema(DomainEvent domainEvent) throws IOException {
        IntegrationEvent event = new OrderIntegrationEventMapper().toIntegrationEvent(domainEvent).orElseThrow();

        List<Error> errors = schemaOf(event).validate(json.writeValueAsString(event), InputFormat.JSON);

        assertThat(errors).isEmpty();
    }

    // ...
    /**
     * The schemas have a relative {@code $id}, such as {@code order-service/OrderPlacedV1}. The
     * validator refuses a relative ID without a base, so the file's own location is the base.
     */
    private static Schema schemaOf(IntegrationEvent event) throws IOException {
        Path file = Path.of("contracts/events", event.getClass().getSimpleName() + ".json");
        return SCHEMAS.getSchema(SchemaLocation.of(file.toUri().toString()), Files.readString(file), InputFormat.JSON);
    }
}
Reading the code
@JsonTest

A slice test that starts only Jackson's part of Spring Boot. The injected JsonMapper is the one that Boot configures for the application, with the platform's defaults. So the test writes the JSON that SNS would receive.

SchemaRegistry.withDefaultDialect(SpecificationVersion.DRAFT_2020_12,

The validator is com.networknt:json-schema-validator, version 3.0.8 as of October 2026. Version 3 reads its input with Jackson 3, like Boot 4. The parent POM gives it to every service with the test scope. The registry reads schemas of draft 2020-12, the draft that the files name in $schema.

formatAssertionsEnabled(true)

In draft 2020-12, format is a note by default, not a check. This option turns it into a check, so an orderId that is not a UUID fails. The test anOrderIdThatIsNotAUuidBreaksItsSchema shows it.

@MethodSource("publishedDomainEvents")

The test runs once for each domain event that leaves the service. These are the events of a placed, a shipped and a cancelled order.

schemaOf(event).validate(json.writeValueAsString(event), InputFormat.JSON);

validate returns the list of errors. An empty list means that the JSON matches the schema.

SchemaLocation.of(file.toUri().toString())

The schemas have a relative $id, such as order-service/OrderPlacedV1. The first run of the test failed with InvalidSchemaException: 'order-service/OrderPlacedV1' is not a valid $id. A relative ID needs a base, so the test gives the file's own location as the base.

Another test, anEventWithoutARequiredFieldBreaksItsSchema, removes orderId from the JSON of a shipped order, and expects an error that names the field. It proves that the check can fail. A test that cannot fail records nothing.

Together, the two tests catch a renamed or removed field in the record, in the mapper or in the schema, in a plain mvn verify. The consumed event works the other way. Its test, PaymentReceivedV1Test, reads JSON that the payment service would send. Its schema file records the part of that contract that the order service relies on.

Versions in names: what may change within V1twist#

C#
public record OrderShippedV1(string EventId, DateTimeOffset OccurredAt, string OrderId);
Java 25
/**
 * A versioned message that crosses the service boundary, such as {@code OrderShippedV1}. It is
 * a contract with other teams, so it changes carefully:
 *
 * <ul>
 *   <li>The version is in the name. Within a version, add fields freely, but never remove or
 *       rename one. For a breaking change, publish {@code V2} next to {@code V1} until every
 *       consumer has moved.</li>
 *   <li>It holds IDs and facts in plain types, and no more personal data than a consumer needs.</li>
 *   <li>The event ID is created once, with the event. A resend keeps it, so a consumer's inbox
 *       can detect the duplicate.</li>
 * </ul>
 */
public interface IntegrationEvent {

    String eventId();

    Instant occurredAt();

The C# record has the version in its name too. The Java side states the rules in the interface that every published event implements. The interface requires eventId() and occurredAt(). A consumer reads the version from the name of the event, so a consumer of V1 knows which fields it can rely on. The rules for a change are these:

The changeAllowed within V1Why
add a fieldyesa tolerant reader ignores it, and the schema allows extra fields
remove a fieldnoa consumer that reads it would get nothing
rename a fieldnoa rename is a removal and an addition, for the consumer
change the type of a fieldnoa consumer's parser would fail
make an optional field requirednoan event from an older producer, or one already in a queue, may lack it
change what a field meansnothe consumer would compute the wrong thing, and nothing fails

A change that is not allowed needs a new event, OrderShippedV2. The service publishes V2 next to V1, and every consumer moves to V2 in its own time. When no consumer reads V1 any more, the service stops publishing it. That needs a list of who consumes what, which is one more reason for the events table in the README.

The eventIdtwist#

C#
var eventId = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
Java 25
/** Returns a new, random event ID. Call it once, when the event is created. */
static String newEventId() {
    return UUID.randomUUID().toString();
}

The two lines do the same. What matters is when the ID is made. The mapper calls newEventId() once, when it turns a domain event into an integration event. The outbox stores the event with its ID. If the service must send the event again, it sends the stored event, with the same ID. For the resend, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

Every consumer can then detect a duplicate by its eventId. The schema says so in the description of the field, so a consumer in another language knows it too. The order service does the same for the events it consumes. For the inbox, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

An ID made again at each send would defeat this. Each resend would look like a new event, and a consumer would process it twice.

Tolerant readerstwist#

C#
public record PaymentReceivedV1(
    [property: JsonRequired] string EventId,
    [property: JsonRequired] string OrderId);
Java 25
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
record PaymentReceivedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId, String paymentReference,
                         BigDecimal amount, String currency, Instant paidAt) implements IntegrationEvent {

    PaymentReceivedV1 {
        Objects.requireNonNull(eventId, "eventId");
        Objects.requireNonNull(occurredAt, "occurredAt");
        Objects.requireNonNull(orderId, "orderId");
        Objects.requireNonNull(paymentReference, "paymentReference");
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        Objects.requireNonNull(paidAt, "paidAt");
    }
}
Reading the code
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)

Jackson ignores a field that the record does not have. The annotation comes from the package com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation, which Jackson 3 still uses.

record PaymentReceivedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId, String paymentReference,

The record is package-private. Only the payment listener of the order feature reads it.

Objects.requireNonNull(eventId, "eventId");

The compact constructor refuses a missing field. requireNonNull throws a NullPointerException with the field's name as the message.

A consumer that ignores what it does not know is called a tolerant reader. The payment service may add a field to PaymentReceivedV1 at any time, within V1. The order service must keep working when that happens.

Jackson 3 already ignores unknown fields by default, and so does the mapper that Boot builds. The annotation still has a purpose. It makes the rule part of the record, so it holds whatever the settings of the mapper are. A plain Jackson 2 mapper refused unknown fields by default. In .NET, JsonSerializer ignores an unknown property by default, and [JsonRequired] makes a missing one fail. A run on .NET 10 refused a payment without its orderId in this way.

The other half of a tolerant reader is strict. A field that the consumer needs must be present. The record's documentation explains why the check matters here:

* <p>The compact constructor refuses missing fields. A wrong subscription, without SNS raw
* message delivery, delivers the SNS envelope instead of the event; Jackson would then build a
* record whose fields are all {@code null}, and the message would be acknowledged and lost. With
* the check, the message fails, is retried, and ends in the dead-letter queue, where someone
* sees it.

The SNS envelope is the wrapper that Amazon SNS puts around a message, with members such as Type and MessageId. None of its members matches the record. Because the reader ignores unknown fields, Jackson would read the envelope without an error. Every field would then be null. The compact constructor turns that silent loss into a failure. For raw message delivery and the dead-letter queue, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

The tests check both halves:

@Test
void readsTheEventAndIgnoresFieldsItDoesNotUse() {
    PaymentReceivedV1 event = json.readValue("""
            { "eventId": "e-1", "occurredAt": "2026-01-15T09:00:00Z", "orderId": "o-1",
              "paymentReference": "PAY-1", "amount": 12.50, "currency": "GBP",
              "paidAt": "2026-01-15T09:00:00Z", "cardScheme": "VISA" }
            """, PaymentReceivedV1.class);

    assertThat(event.paymentReference()).isEqualTo("PAY-1");
}

The first test sends a field the record does not have, cardScheme, and the event is read. The second test, refusesAnSnsEnvelopeInsteadOfTheEvent, sends an envelope. It expects a NullPointerException with the message eventId as the root cause. Both use a plain JsonMapper from tools.jackson.databind.json, so they need no Spring.

Our copy of a consumed contractnew#

The payment service owns PaymentReceivedV1. Its schema is in the payment service's repository. The order service needs to know which part of that contract it relies on. And when the payment team changes the event, someone must check whether the order service is affected.

The order service keeps its own copy of the part it uses:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "payment-service/PaymentReceivedV1",
  "title": "PaymentReceivedV1 (consumed)",
  "description": "Owned by the payment service. This is the part of their contract that order-service relies on, kept here so a change on their side is easy to check. Received on the order-service-payment-received SQS queue, with raw message delivery.",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId", "paymentReference", "amount", "currency", "paidAt"],
  "properties": {
    "eventId": { "type": "string" },
    "occurredAt": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" },
    "orderId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },
    "paymentReference": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 50 },
    "amount": { "type": "number", "minimum": 0, "multipleOf": 0.01 },
    "currency": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z]{3}$" },
    "paidAt": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" }
  }
}
Reading the code
"$id": "payment-service/PaymentReceivedV1",

The ID names the owner, the payment service. The file name starts with consumed-, so nobody mistakes it for a contract of the order service.

"required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId", "paymentReference", "amount", "currency", "paidAt"],

These are the fields the order service reads. The payment service's own schema may have more.

"paymentReference": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 50 },

The limits are the ones the order service relies on. The domain's PaymentReference checks the same limit.

The file has no additionalProperties. A run validated an event with an extra member, cardScheme, against this file, and the event was valid. That suits a tolerant reader. The record in the code holds the same seven fields and no more. So three things describe the same part of the contract. They are the consumed schema, the record, and the record's test.

When the payment team announces a change, a developer compares their new schema with this file. If the change touches none of the seven fields, nothing needs to change. If it removes or renames one of them, the payment service must publish PaymentReceivedV2, and the order service moves to it.

The alternative is to read the producer's schema directly, or to use a class from the producer. That gives one definition, and it can be the better choice inside one team. But the consumer then depends on fields it never reads. A copy of only the used part makes the dependency visible and small.

Publish as few events as needednew#

The order aggregate raises five domain events, from OrderPlaced to OrderCancelled. Each of them is useful inside the service. But every event that leaves the service is a contract, with a schema, a version and consumers to look after. One class decides which events leave:

/**
 * Decides which order events leave the service. Placed, shipped and cancelled orders are
 * published; picked lines and recorded payments stay internal. Every published event is a
 * contract to maintain, so publish only what another service needs.
 */
@Component
class OrderIntegrationEventMapper implements IntegrationEventMapper {

    @Override
    public Optional<IntegrationEvent> toIntegrationEvent(DomainEvent event) {
        return switch (event) {
            case OrderPlaced placed -> Optional.of(new OrderPlacedV1(newEventId(), placed.occurredAt(),
                    placed.orderId().value(), placed.deliveryMethod().code(),
                    placed.items().stream()
                            .map(item -> new OrderPlacedV1.Line(item.product().value(), item.quantity()))
                            .toList()));
            case OrderShipped shipped -> Optional.of(new OrderShippedV1(newEventId(), shipped.occurredAt(),
                    shipped.orderId().value()));
            case OrderCancelled cancelled -> Optional.of(new OrderCancelledV1(newEventId(), cancelled.occurredAt(),
                    cancelled.orderId().value()));
            default -> Optional.empty();
        };
    }
}
Reading the code
return switch (event) {

A switch expression with type patterns. Each case tests the type of the domain event.

placed.orderId().value(), placed.deliveryMethod().code(),

The mapper turns value objects into plain types. The event holds the text of the ID, not an OrderId.

default -> Optional.empty();

Every other event stays inside the service. LinePicked and PaymentRecorded are internal.

An event is published when another service needs it. The stock service needs OrderPlacedV1 to keep its hold on the products. The shipped and cancelled events tell other services that an order is finished. No service needs to know that a line was picked, so LinePicked has no integration event. If a service needs it one day, the team adds LinePickedV1, with a schema and a row in the README. Adding an event is easy. Removing one that consumers use is hard.

The test keepsInternalEventsInternal records the decision. It passes a LinePicked to the mapper and expects an empty result. For how the published events reach SNS, and how each feature registers its mapper, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe order service generates its OpenAPI file with springdoc. Why does it commit the file and check it in a test, instead of serving it only at /v3/api-docs?
The committed file makes every API change a diff in the pull request, so a reviewer and the UI team see it. The test fails when the code and the file differ, so the file can never drift. A document served only at run time shows the current API, but nobody sees what changed.
2
An expert asksWhen is contract first the better choice for a Spring service?
Contract first is better in two cases. A UI or partner team must sign off the API before any code exists. Or the API is shared outside the team or the company. Then the file is the agreement, and the generator makes the compiler check that the controllers follow it. For an internal API, code first with a committed file and a drift test is simpler.
3
The order service's OpenApiConfig sets a fixed server URL. What would happen without it?
springdoc would write the server URL from the request. A file exported through MockMvc would say http://localhost, and one exported from a running server would name its port. The drift test would then fail whenever the file was generated in another way.
4
Within OrderPlacedV1, which changes may the order service make, and what does it do for any other change?
It may add fields. It may not remove or rename a field, change a field's type or meaning, or make an optional field required. For such a change, it publishes OrderPlacedV2 next to V1, until every consumer has moved.
5
TranslateWrite this C# event as the Java record that the order service publishes. It must go to the SNS topic order-events: 
public record OrderShippedV1(string EventId, DateTimeOffset OccurredAt, string OrderId);
@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS)
public record OrderShippedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId) implements IntegrationEvent {
}

Instant takes the place of DateTimeOffset. IntegrationEvent requires eventId() and occurredAt(), which the record's components provide. @Externalized tells Spring Modulith to send the event to the topic after the transaction commits.

Security in depth#

The web layer and security · Chapter 15· 58 min read· Quick reference

The order service trusts a caller only after it checks a signed JSON Web Token (JWT). Spring Security checks the token in a chain of servlet filters. Each controller method then names the scope it needs. This chapter follows one request through every check. It explains where a permission check belongs, and covers messages with no user, the service's own token, audit, tests and a local token issuer.

Who calls the order service, and what each caller may donew#

A customer-service agent opens an order in the shop's web application. The browser sends the agent's token with the request. A minute later, the payment service reports a payment on a queue. No user takes part in that. When an agent places an order, the order service also calls the stock service, and that call needs a token too.

So the service has four kinds of caller. Each kind answers the question "who acts, and may they do this?" in its own way:

CallerHow it proves who it isWhat it may do
an agent, over HTTPa JWT from the shop's token issuer, in the Authorization headerwhat the scopes in the token allow
the payment service, with a message on a queueit proves nothing in the message, because the service trusts the queuerecord a payment, as the system actor
the orchestrator's health probesno token at allread /actuator/health and /actuator/info, and nothing else
the order service, calling the stock serviceits own token, from the client-credentials grantreserve stock, with the scope stock.reserve

A scope is a word in the token that names one permission. The order service knows two scopes. Reads need orders.read, and changes need orders.write. The quick reference at the end of the chapter lists every endpoint with its scope.

Each controller method says which scope it needs. Here is the method that reads one order:

@OrdersRead
@GetMapping("/{orderId}")
// ...
OrderResponse get(@PathVariable String orderId) {
    return mapper.toResponse(orders.get(OrderId.of(orderId)));
}

@OrdersRead is an annotation of the service's own. It means that the caller needs the orders.read scope. The method itself contains no security code. The platform library checks the token before the method runs. Spring checks the annotation when the method is called. The sections below follow this one request through every check, from the token to the audit record.

The platform's filter chaintwist#

Every service of the shop needs the same rule. Each request needs a valid token, except the requests of the health probes. If every service wrote its own security code, one service would forget a line at some point. So the platform library, shop-platform, declares the chain once, as an auto-configuration. Each service gets it by adding the library. For how a library adds beans to a service, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

The chain is a bean of type SecurityFilterChain. It is built with the domain-specific language (DSL) of HttpSecurity, which the chapter Security introduces:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(SecurityFilterChain.class)
SecurityFilterChain platformSecurityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http, PlatformSecurityProperties properties) {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(requests -> requests
                    .requestMatchers(properties.getPublicPaths().toArray(String[]::new)).permitAll()
                    .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(resourceServer -> resourceServer
                    .jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())
                    .authenticationEntryPoint(new ProblemAuthenticationEntryPoint()))
            // Tokens, not cookies, prove who the caller is: no session, and so no CSRF risk.
            .sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable);
    return http.build();
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(SecurityFilterChain.class)

Spring creates this bean only when the service has no SecurityFilterChain of its own. So a service that needs other rules declares its own chain, and the platform's chain is not created.

.requestMatchers(properties.getPublicPaths().toArray(String[]::new)).permitAll()

The public paths come from a setting. permitAll() lets a request on those paths through without a token. String[]::new is a method reference. Here it tells toArray how to create an array of the right size.

.anyRequest().authenticated())

Every other path needs a valid token. This rule checks no scope. The scopes are checked on the controller methods.

.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())

The chain accepts bearer tokens that are JWTs. withDefaults() takes the settings from application.yml. For those settings, see the section Where the signing keys come from.

.authenticationEntryPoint(new ProblemAuthenticationEntryPoint()))

This object writes the 401 response. See the section One request through the checks.

.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable);

This line and the line above it switch off sessions and the protection against cross-site request forgery (CSRF). For what the two lines really change, see the section No session, and no CSRF token.

The public paths are a setting with a default. The default is the two Actuator paths that the orchestrator calls without a token:

/**
 * Paths that need no token. The default is the health probes, which the orchestrator calls
 * without a token. Every other path needs a valid JWT.
 */
private List<String> publicPaths = new ArrayList<>(List.of("/actuator/health/**", "/actuator/info"));

The field publicPaths is bound from the setting platform.security.public-paths. The local profile adds the OpenAPI document and Swagger UI, so a developer can open them in a browser without a token:

platform:
  # ...
  security:
    # Swagger UI and the OpenAPI document need no token locally.
    public-paths: /actuator/health/**, /actuator/info, /v3/api-docs/**, /swagger-ui/**, /swagger-ui.html

The list in public-paths replaces the default as a whole. So the local profile repeats the two Actuator paths. Without them, the probes would need a token on a developer's machine.

In ASP.NET Core, each service calls AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer() and AddAuthorization() in its own Program.cs. The closest match for a shared chain is a shared library on NuGet that registers the same setup. In Spring, the library declares the bean, and the service writes no line of security setup.

One request through the checksnew#

An agent with only the orders.read scope sends POST /orders with a body that is not valid. Several parts of Spring look at that request, one after the other. The filter chain comes first. Spring model-view-controller (MVC) comes after it. Each part can stop it, and each part answers with its own status. The order of the parts decides which answer the agent gets.

The filter chain runs before Spring MVC sees the request. A run for this book printed the 13 filters of a chain like the platform's. The quick reference lists them in order. Five of them matter here:

FilterWhat it does in the order service
SecurityContextHolderFiltergives the request a security context, and clears the thread's context when the request ends
BearerTokenAuthenticationFilterreads the bearer token, checks it, and stores the caller for this request only
AnonymousAuthenticationFilterputs an anonymous authentication into the context when the request has no caller
ExceptionTranslationFilterturns a missing login into 401, and a refusal into 403
AuthorizationFilterchecks the URL rules in order, and it is the last filter by default

The chain of Spring Security 7.1.2 also has a new filter, OAuth2ProtectedResourceMetadataFilter. It belongs to the protected resource metadata of RFC 9728, which the 401 header points to. The order service does not use it.

The 401 needs extra work. It is decided in the filter chain, before Spring MVC runs. So the platform's exception handler, which writes every other problem response, never sees it. The platform adds the problem body in an authentication entry point. Spring Security uses an authentication entry point when a request needs a login and has none:

public class ProblemAuthenticationEntryPoint implements AuthenticationEntryPoint {

    private final AuthenticationEntryPoint bearer = new BearerTokenAuthenticationEntryPoint();
    private final JsonMapper json = JsonMapper.builder().build();

    @Override
    public void commence(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                         AuthenticationException authException) throws IOException, ServletException {
        bearer.commence(request, response, authException);
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Unauthorized",
                "A valid bearer token is required");
        response.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
        json.writeValue(response.getOutputStream(), asMap(problem));
Reading the code
private final AuthenticationEntryPoint bearer = new BearerTokenAuthenticationEntryPoint();

This is the entry point that Spring Security uses by default for bearer tokens. It sets the status 401 and the WWW-Authenticate header, and writes no body.

bearer.commence(request, response, authException);

The platform's class calls the default first, so the status and the header stay as Spring Security writes them.

ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Unauthorized",

This is the platform's helper for a ProblemDetail. It adds the traceId, as in every other problem response. For the problem format, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

json.writeValue(response.getOutputStream(), asMap(problem));

The class writes the body itself, with a Jackson JsonMapper. No Spring MVC message converter runs here, because the request never reached Spring MVC.

The header of a 401 names the problem. These are the values that Spring Security 7.1.2 sent in a run for this book:

CaseStatusWWW-Authenticate header
no token401Bearer resource_metadata="http://localhost/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
a token that fails a check401Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="An error occurred while attempting to decode the Jwt: ...", plus error_uri and resource_metadata
a valid token without the scope403Bearer error="insufficient_scope", error_description="The request requires higher privileges than provided by the access token."

The test OrderControllerTest.aRequestWithoutATokenIsA401ProblemBeforeAnyController checks the 401 response. It expects the header, the title "Unauthorized" and the status in the body, and it checks that the controller's service was never called.

A 403 can come from two places. A URL rule in the chain refuses the request in AuthorizationFilter. Then ExceptionTranslationFilter writes the 403, and the body was empty in the run. A permission annotation refuses the call inside Spring MVC. Then the platform's exception handler writes a 403 problem with a traceId. The section How method security works shows that handler.

Gotcha

The authorization filter checks every dispatch, not only the first one. One pass of a request through the filters is called a dispatch. An error page or a forward is a second dispatch. So a rule can refuse the error page of a request that has already failed. For the trap this causes with CSRF and the /error page, see the section Two chain traps: rule order and CSRF.

Why the platform's chain is created before Boot'snew#

Spring Boot also brings security chains of its own. Each of them is created only when the application has no SecurityFilterChain yet. So when two libraries offer a chain, only the first one that Spring creates is used. The platform makes sure that its chain is first:

@AutoConfiguration(beforeName = {
        "org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.SecurityAutoConfiguration",
        "org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.web.servlet.ServletWebSecurityAutoConfiguration",
        "org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.actuate.web.servlet.ManagementWebSecurityAutoConfiguration",
        "org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.server.resource.autoconfigure.web.OAuth2ResourceServerWebSecurityAutoConfiguration",
        "org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.client.autoconfigure.servlet.OAuth2ClientWebSecurityAutoConfiguration"})
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = ConditionalOnWebApplication.Type.SERVLET)
@EnableMethodSecurity
@EnableConfigurationProperties(PlatformSecurityProperties.class)
public class PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration {
Reading the code
@AutoConfiguration(beforeName = {

This annotation marks the class as an auto-configuration. beforeName lists other auto-configurations by their class names. Spring Boot processes this class before each of them.

"org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.web.servlet.ServletWebSecurityAutoConfiguration",

This Boot class creates the default chain, with form login and HTTP Basic. The class ManagementWebSecurityAutoConfiguration creates a chain for the Actuator, and OAuth2ResourceServerWebSecurityAutoConfiguration creates a JWT chain when a JwtDecoder bean exists.

"org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.client.autoconfigure.servlet.OAuth2ClientWebSecurityAutoConfiguration"})

This Boot class creates a chain of its own, named oauth2SecurityFilterChain, with OAuth2 login. It applies when the classes of the OAuth2 client are present and an OAuth2AuthorizedClientService bean exists. The service has both, because it calls the stock service with the OAuth2 client. So the platform's class must come before this class too.

@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = ConditionalOnWebApplication.Type.SERVLET)
