The class applies only to a servlet web application. A worker with no web server gets no chain.

@EnableMethodSecurity

This switches on the permission annotations. See the section How method security works.

Each Boot chain carries the condition @ConditionalOnDefaultServletWebSecurity. Inside, the condition is @ConditionalOnMissingBean(SecurityFilterChain.class), plus a check that the classes are present. SecurityAutoConfiguration creates no chain. The platform names it anyway, which does no harm.

A condition such as "no bean of this type exists yet" is checked in the order in which Spring Boot processes the auto-configurations. A run for this book offered a "platform" chain with that condition, next to Boot's chains, and changed only the ordering and the package name:

The platform's auto-configurationThe chain that was created
with beforeName, in a package named aaa.platformthe platform's chain
with beforeName, in a package named zzz.platformthe platform's chain
no ordering, in aaa.platformthe platform's chain
no ordering, in zzz.platform, with issuer-uri setBoot's jwtSecurityFilterChain
no ordering, in zzz.platform, without issuer-uriBoot's defaultSecurityFilterChain

Without an ordering, Spring Boot starts from the alphabetical order of the class names. A library in a com. package sorts before org.springframework, so it works by accident. The same code in another package loses, and nothing warns you. beforeName makes the order the same in every package.

The service tests this. ApplicationWiringTest.theContextStartsWithThePlatformsBeans starts the whole application and expects exactly one chain, named platformSecurityFilterChain.

Note

Boot 4.1.2 deprecated the condition annotation @ConditionalOnDefaultWebSecurity for removal. Its replacement is @ConditionalOnDefaultServletWebSecurity, new in 4.1.2. A library that writes its own condition with the old name gets a deprecation warning on 4.1.2.

Where the signing keys come fromtwist#

The chain checks each token with settings from application.yml. The issuer's URL comes from an environment variable, so each environment can name its own issuer:

C#
builder.Services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(o =>
    {
        o.Authority = "https://login.shop.example/default";
        o.Audience = "order-service";
    });
application.yml
security:
  oauth2:
    resourceserver:
      jwt:
        # Spring Security downloads the issuer's signing keys and checks the "iss" claim.
        # It also checks the token's "typ" header: "JWT", or no typ header, passes. "at+jwt" is refused.
        issuer-uri: ${OAUTH_ISSUER_URI}
        # Tokens must be issued for this service.
        audiences: order-service
Reading the code
issuer-uri: ${OAUTH_ISSUER_URI}

This is the URL of the token issuer. ${OAUTH_ISSUER_URI} reads an environment variable. issuer-uri is like Authority in the JwtBearer options. Spring uses the URL twice. It finds the signing keys from it, and it compares every token's iss claim with it.

audiences: order-service

Every token must name order-service in its aud claim. This setting is like Audience in the JwtBearer options.

With issuer-uri, Spring Boot does not contact the issuer at startup. It registers a decoder that builds the real decoder when the first token arrives. A run for this book counted the requests to the issuer. There were none after startup, and none after a request without a token. The first valid token caused two requests:

Each step has a measured fact behind it:

  • A JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) is a JSON document with the issuer's public keys. Each key has an ID, called the kid. Each token names the kid of the key that signed it.
  • Spring tries the discovery document at {issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration. The reference names two other places that an issuer may use instead.
  • Five more requests with the same key made no further request to the issuer. The library that checks the signatures is called Nimbus. Its default cache time is 300,000 milliseconds, which is 5 minutes.
  • A token signed with a key that the issuer had not published yet got 401, after exactly one new fetch of the key set. Once the issuer published the key, the next token caused one more fetch and got 200. So the issuer can rotate its keys while the service runs.
  • The calls to the issuer time out after 30 seconds by default.
Gotcha

If the issuer cannot be reached, the first token fails with an exception, not with a 401. A test with an issuer host that does not exist got JwtDecoderInitializationException: Failed to lazily resolve the supplied JwtDecoder instance. Even a header such as Bearer abc, which is not a JWT, started the discovery. The status that a real client sees in this case was not measured.

A second setting, jwk-set-uri, gives the URL of the key set directly. With both settings, Spring fetches no discovery document. It reads the keys from jwk-set-uri, and it still compares the iss claim with issuer-uri. A run confirmed both. It also showed that Spring then builds the decoder at startup, but still fetches no keys before the first token. The local profile uses this pair. See the section A local token issuer, and the issuer-versus-keys trick.

Use issuer-uri alone in production. Add jwk-set-uri only when the service cannot reach the discovery document at the issuer's own URL.

Gotcha

A JwtDecoder bean of your own replaces Boot's decoder, with its checks. A decoder that you build yourself does not get Boot's issuer and audience checks, unless you add them. And a decoder built with JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation calls the issuer at once, so the service then needs the issuer at startup. Prefer the settings. Declare a decoder only in tests. See the section Testing security in a controller slice.

What Spring checks in each tokentrap#

A token can be refused for many reasons. A C# developer expects the checks of AddJwtBearer. Several of the Spring checks differ. Spring Boot builds the list of checks from these parts:

  • The default checks of Spring Security. They check the typ header, the time claims exp and nbf, and tokens that are bound to a certificate.
  • The issuer check, when issuer-uri is set.
  • The audience check, when audiences is set.
  • Every bean of type OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> in the application.

The signature is checked too, with the key that the token's kid names. A run for this book sent one bad token for each check. The WWW-Authenticate header of the 401 ends with the reason. For an expired token, it looked like this:

WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token",
  error_description="An error occurred while attempting to decode the Jwt: Jwt expired at ...",
  error_uri="https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6750#section-3.1",
  resource_metadata="http://localhost/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"

The reason is the end of error_description. These are the reasons the run printed:

The tokenSpring Security 7.1.2The reason in the header
signed with a key the issuer does not publish401Signed JWT rejected: Another algorithm expected, or no matching key(s) found
signed with the wrong key401Signed JWT rejected: Invalid signature
not a JWT at all401Malformed token
iss is another issuer401The iss claim is not valid
aud does not name order-service, or is missing401The aud claim is not valid
exp was 30 seconds ago200none, because the clock skew is 60 seconds
exp was 90 seconds ago401Jwt expired at ...
nbf is 90 seconds in the future401Jwt used before ...
no exp claim at all200none, because exp is checked only when present
typ header at+jwt401the given typ value needs to be one of [JWT]

The clock skew is how far the clocks of the issuer and the service may differ. Spring allows 60 seconds. A token with an aud list passes when one entry matches one entry of audiences. A token whose exp is before its iat fails even earlier, while Spring builds the token object, with the message expiresAt must be after issuedAt.

Gotcha

Spring Security accepts a token with no exp claim. ASP.NET Core refuses the same token with "The token has no expiration". A token without an expiry is valid for ever. The shop's issuer always sets exp, so the service relies on it. If you do not trust an issuer to set it, add a validator bean that requires the claim.

Gotcha

Spring Security 7 refuses a token whose typ header is at+jwt. The check is new in Spring Security 6.5. It is on by default in version 7. It accepts JWT, or no typ header. An issuer that follows RFC 9068 sends at+jwt. Such tokens need a custom validator in every Spring service. ASP.NET Core accepted at+jwt in the same run. The local token issuer sends typ: JWT, so the local tokens pass.

The defaults of ASP.NET Core differ in several places. A run of Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer 10.0.12 printed its defaults and sent the same kinds of token:

CheckASP.NET Core 10, AddJwtBearerSpring Security 7.1.2
clock skew5 minutes, so exp 4 minutes ago is accepted60 seconds, so exp 90 seconds ago is refused
a token with no exprefused, because RequireExpirationTime is trueaccepted
typ header at+jwtaccepted, because ValidTypes is nullrefused with 401
audiencechecked by default, because ValidateAudience is truechecked only when audiences is set
claim namesMapInboundClaims renames sub to a long URI claim typethe claims keep their names from the token
a 401 without a tokenthe header WWW-Authenticate holds only the word Bearerthe header adds resource_metadata
a 403no WWW-Authenticate headererror="insufficient_scope" in the header

The audience check matters most in practice. A Spring service without audiences accepts any token from its issuer, including a token meant for the stock service. Set audiences in every service.

From scopes to authoritiestwist#

Spring Security does not check scopes directly. It turns each scope into an authority. An authority is a plain string that a rule can ask for. The local token issuer gives an agent this token:

{
  "requestParam": "client_id",
  "match": "agent",
  "claims": {
    "sub": "local-agent",
    "aud": ["order-service"],
    "scope": "orders.read orders.write"
  }
},

The scope claim holds two scopes, separated by a space. Spring Security 7 gives the agent these authorities:

AuthorityWhere it comes from
SCOPE_orders.readthe first scope, with the prefix SCOPE_
SCOPE_orders.writethe second scope, with the prefix SCOPE_
FACTOR_BEARERadded by Spring Security 7 to every JWT login

The default converter reads the claim scope, as a string with spaces, or the claim scp, as a list. A run gave the same two authorities for both forms. The converter reads no other claim. A roles claim gives no authority until you map it. See the section Three ways a method rule fails.

FACTOR_BEARER is new in Spring Security 7. Its class is FactorGrantedAuthority. Its name says that the caller proved who they are with a bearer token. The order service never checks it. But a test that compares the whole list of authorities gets a different answer in production, because the test helper jwt() does not add it.

The caller's name is the sub claim. For the token above, authentication.getName() returns local-agent. The principal object is a Jwt. With a real token, its class is JwtAuthenticatedPrincipal, a private subclass of Jwt. Code that declares a Jwt works with both. Code that compares the exact class does not.

Boot builds the converter from settings, unless the application declares a JwtAuthenticationConverter bean. The settings change the claim, the prefix, the separator and the claim used for the name. The quick reference lists them. The order service keeps the defaults.

In ASP.NET Core, a policy that requires a scope needs code that splits the claim:

builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("orders.write", p => p.RequireAssertion(c =>
        c.User.FindAll("scope")
            .SelectMany(claim => claim.Value.Split(' '))
            .Contains("orders.write")));

A run showed why. RequireClaim("scope", "orders.write") passed for the scope string orders.write. It failed with 403 for orders.read orders.write, because it compared the whole string. A token with the claim scp failed too, because MapInboundClaims had renamed the claim. Spring splits the scopes and reads both claim names, so hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders.write') needs no extra code.

No session, and no CSRF tokentwist#

Two lines of the platform's chain switch off sessions and CSRF protection:

// Tokens, not cookies, prove who the caller is: no session, and so no CSRF risk.
.sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable);

A C# developer reads these lines as "without them, the API would use sessions and need CSRF tokens". Runs for this book showed that this is not true for requests with a bearer token:

  • The resource server already switches CSRF protection off for every request that carries a bearer token. With CSRF protection on, a POST with a bearer token and no CSRF token got 201.
  • A POST to a public path with no bearer token got 403 with CSRF protection on. So the csrf line changes only requests without a bearer token.
  • A bearer request creates no session, with or without STATELESS. The filter stores the caller for the one request only, and no response had a Set-Cookie header.
  • STATELESS also stops every other part of the chain from using a session. It replaces the store of the security context and the cache of saved requests with versions that store nothing.

The service keeps both lines, for two reasons. First, the lines make the design visible in the code. No part of the service keeps state for a caller between requests. Second, the lines let a public POST work without a CSRF token. A run with CSRF protection on and without STATELESS showed the difference in the chain. It had a CsrfFilter after the HeaderWriterFilter, and no SessionManagementFilter. For what a CSRF attack is, see the section Two chain traps: rule order and CSRF.

Keep CSRF protection on for anything that a browser calls with cookies. The order service has no such endpoint.

In ASP.NET Core, an API built with AddControllers() and AddJwtBearer() needs no line about antiforgery. The ASP.NET Core documentation says that AddControllers() does not switch on antiforgery tokens. It also says that CSRF is a concern when a cookie carries the token. It is not a concern when the client keeps the token in local storage and sends it as a bearer token. Spring works in the opposite way. CSRF protection is on by default, and the resource server skips it for each request with a bearer token.

The security context: one per threadnew#

The audit log must record who placed an order. The use case does not receive the caller as a parameter. Spring Security stores the caller where any code of the request can read it. That place is called the security context. The platform reads it in one small class:

C#
public class CurrentActor(IHttpContextAccessor accessor)
{
    public string Id() =>
        accessor.HttpContext?.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value ?? "system";
}
Java 25
public class SecurityContextCurrentActor implements CurrentActor {

    @Override
    public String id() {
        Authentication authentication = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
        if (authentication == null || !authentication.isAuthenticated()
                || authentication instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken) {
            return SYSTEM;
        }
        return authentication.getName();
    }
}
Reading the code
accessor.HttpContext?.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value

In ASP.NET Core, MapInboundClaims renames sub to the claim type ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier. So the C# code reads that name.

SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

SecurityContextHolder is a class with static methods. getContext() returns the security context of the current thread. getAuthentication() returns the caller, or null when the thread has none.

authentication instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken) {

On a request without a caller, such as a probe on a public path, the anonymous filter puts an AnonymousAuthenticationToken into the context. Its name is anonymousUser, and isAuthenticated() returns true for it. So the class must check the type, and it treats the token as no caller.

return authentication.getName();

For a JWT, the name is the token's sub claim.

Three objects are involved, one inside the other:

ObjectWhat it holdsASP.NET Core
SecurityContextHolderthe strategy that stores one context for each threadIHttpContextAccessor
SecurityContextone Authentication, or noneHttpContext, for this purpose
Authenticationthe caller's name, its authorities and the principal, here a JwtClaimsPrincipal

By default, SecurityContextHolder keeps the context in a ThreadLocal. A ThreadLocal holds one value for each thread. The holder has three strategies, named by constants:

StrategyWhat it doesUse it
MODE_THREADLOCALone context for each thread, and the defaultalways, in a web service
MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCALa new thread starts with a copy of its parent's contextnever with a thread pool, because a pool thread keeps its first copy
MODE_GLOBALone context for the whole JVMonly in a desktop application with one user

The system property spring.security.strategy selects the strategy. Spring reads it once, when the class is loaded.

Think of the context as a name badge that one worker wears. Any task the worker does carries the badge. A second worker does not wear it, even when the first worker passes a task on. The comparison stops at the badge itself. A Java thread can wear a context that belongs to no person. And code can swap the badge for another one.

The bearer token filter puts the caller into the context of the thread that handles the request. It also stores the context for this one request only, in a request attribute. When the request ends, SecurityContextHolderFilter clears the thread's context in a finally block. So the next request on the same pool thread starts with no caller.

Read the context through a small interface, such as CurrentActor. Do not call SecurityContextHolder from the domain or the application layer. The reference also advises one thing for code that sets a caller. Build a new context with SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext(), and do not change the shared one with getContext().setAuthentication(...). This avoids race conditions between threads.

The caller does not follow work to other threadstrap#

ASP.NET Core and Spring behave in opposite ways here. In ASP.NET Core, the caller flows with the ExecutionContext, so it follows an await and a Task.Run:

[HttpGet("/flow"), Authorize]
public async Task<string> Flow()
{
    string Name() => accessor.HttpContext?.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value ?? "none";
    var before = Name();
    var inTaskRun = await Task.Run(Name);   // the caller flows into Task.Run
    return before + inTaskRun;
}

A run of the same idea in ASP.NET Core 10 found the caller in four places. They were before the await, after it, inside Task.Run and on a new Thread. Only ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem and ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow() lost it.

Spring's default ThreadLocal does the opposite. Nothing follows the work unless a wrapper copies it. A run with the user alice signed in gave these results:

Where the code ranWhat getAuthentication() saw
a new platform threadnull
a new virtual threadnull
CompletableFuture.supplyAsyncnull
a task on a plain fixed thread poolnull
an @Async method, on Boot's default executornull
an @Async method, with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=truenull
a DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable on a new threadalice
a DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService over a fixed poolalice, and the next plain task on that pool thread saw null
the same wrapper over Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()alice
an @Async method, on a DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutoralice

A wrapper copies the caller's context into the task, runs it, and clears the context afterwards. A virtual thread behaves like any other thread here. For @Async, the wrapper is set in an AsyncConfigurer bean. For more about @Async, see the section @Async.

Gotcha

The inheritable mode copies the caller once, when a pool creates its thread. With MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL, a pool thread created while alice was signed in kept alice. A later task from bob ran on that thread and still saw alice. So that mode gives one user's identity to another user's work. Never use it with a thread pool.

The order service starts no threads in its use cases. If a use case must run work on another thread, pass the actor's ID to that work as a plain value. A plain value cannot leak to another task. Use a wrapper only for code that must check permissions on the other thread. The ASP.NET Core documentation gives the same advice for HttpContext. It says to pass the required data to background work, not the context itself.

The order service has no background work today. The platform's test ActorOnAnotherThreadTest shows both ways side by side, with alice signed in on the test's thread. The first way reads the actor before the work starts:

/** The recommended way: read the actor on the request's thread, and pass the work a value. */
@Test
void passTheActorToTheWorkAsAPlainValue() throws Exception {
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        String actor = currentActor.id();
        Future<String> actorSeenByTheWork = executor.submit(() -> actor);
        Future<String> actorOfTheOtherThread = executor.submit(currentActor::id);

        assertThat(actorSeenByTheWork.get()).isEqualTo("alice");
        assertThat(actorOfTheOtherThread.get()).isEqualTo(CurrentActor.SYSTEM);
    }
}
Reading the code
String actor = currentActor.id();

This line runs on the caller's thread, where the security context holds alice. The work receives only the string.

Future<String> actorOfTheOtherThread = executor.submit(currentActor::id);

The same CurrentActor, called on the other thread, finds no authentication there. So it answers system. Code that read the context on the other thread would record the wrong actor, with no error.

The second way wraps the executor:

/**
 * Only for work that must check permissions itself: the wrapper copies the caller's context
 * into each task when it is submitted, and clears it when the task ends.
 */
@Test
void wrapTheExecutorWhenTheWorkMustCheckPermissions() throws Exception {
    try (ExecutorService executor = new DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService(
            Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor())) {
        Future<String> actorOfTheOtherThread = executor.submit(currentActor::id);

        assertThat(actorOfTheOtherThread.get()).isEqualTo("alice");
    }
}

DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService is a wrapper from Spring Security. It takes the caller's context when a task is submitted, sets it on the thread that runs the task, and clears it afterwards. So the task sees alice. Choose it only when the work checks permissions itself, for example with @PreAuthorize on a method it calls. A plain value is easier to read and to test, and it cannot carry more than the work needs.

How method security worksnew#

The controller method carries @OrdersWrite, and no line of the method checks anything. Something must read the annotation and refuse the call. That something is method security. The annotation @EnableMethodSecurity on the platform's auto-configuration switches it on. Without it, every permission annotation is ignored, and nothing warns you.

Method security works through a proxy, as @Transactional does. For what a proxy is, see the chapter How Spring actually works. Spring creates a subclass of the controller with the Code Generation Library (CGLIB). Spring MVC calls the subclass, and the subclass runs a list of interceptors before it calls your method:

Each annotation has its own interceptor. For @PreAuthorize, the interceptor is AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor. It asks a PreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager to evaluate the expression of the annotation. The expression is written in the Spring Expression Language (SpEL).

Each interceptor has an order, and the lower number runs first. These are the values in Spring Security 7.1.2:

InterceptorOrderWhen it runs
@PreFilter100before the method
@PreAuthorize200before the method
@Secured300before the method
JSR-250 annotations such as @RolesAllowed400before the method
@AuthorizeReturnObject450after the method, and it wraps the result
@PostAuthorize500after the method returns
@PostFilter600after the method, and it filters the returned collection
@TransactionalInteger.MAX_VALUEaround the method, inside every security interceptor

So the permission check runs outside the transaction. A run with a transaction manager that recorded its events showed it. A refused call began no transaction. An allowed call began one and committed it. The offset attribute of @EnableMethodSecurity moves all security interceptors at once.

In the order service, the check is on the controller, and the controller has no transaction. The use case starts its transaction later. So the order matters only when one bean has both annotations.

Gotcha

A refusal by @PostAuthorize comes after the commit. @PostAuthorize checks the return value, after the method has run. Its order, 500, is lower than the transaction's. So the transaction has already committed when the check refuses the call. The reference names this case. If the refusal must roll back the change, it says to put @EnableTransactionManagement before @EnableMethodSecurity. This case was not run for this book.

A refusal throws AuthorizationDeniedException. That class is a subclass of AccessDeniedException, so a handler for AccessDeniedException catches it. The platform's controller advice turns it into a 403 problem:

@ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> accessDenied(AccessDeniedException ex) {
    return respond(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN, "Forbidden", "You are not allowed to do this"));
}

The same advice has a handler for Exception, which answers 500. The handler for the more specific type wins, so a refusal still gets 403. The test OrderControllerTest.aCallerWithoutTheWriteScopeIsA403AndNothingRuns expects the title "Forbidden". OrderJourneyIT.aCallerWithoutTheWriteScopeIsForbidden expects a traceId in the body.

Two more facts about the proxy matter for the service:

  • The controller class and its methods are package-private. The check still runs on them. The 403 tests of the controller prove it.
  • A call from inside the same object skips the proxy, so it skips the check. This is called self-invocation. A run for this book confirmed it for @PreAuthorize. A controller method is called only by Spring MVC, through the proxy. So a check on a controller cannot be skipped this way. For the trap in full, see the section Self-invocation: a call from inside the class.

ASP.NET Core has no proxy for this. An [Authorize] attribute on an action is evaluated before model binding, so before the action runs. The closest match for a permission check on any class is a decorator that you write and register yourself.

Other method security annotations#

The order service needs only @PreAuthorize. The other annotations solve other problems. Most of them were run for this book:

AnnotationWhat it doesWhat the run showed
@PostFilterremoves elements from the returned collection that fail the expressionwith filterObject.startsWith(authentication.name) as alice, [alice-1, bob-1, alice-2] became [alice-1, alice-2]
@AuthorizeReturnObjectreturns a proxy of the result, so the result's own annotated methods are checkedit works on a plain class, but a record result failed with ClassCastException
@HandleAuthorizationDeniednames a handler that returns a fallback value instead of throwingnew in Spring Security 6.3, read from the source, and not run
annotation templateslet a meta-annotation take a value, as in @HasScope("orders.write")needs a bean of type AnnotationTemplateExpressionDefaults, new in Spring Security 6.4

A record is final, so Spring cannot subclass it. For a record, @AuthorizeReturnObject makes an interface proxy, and that proxy is not of the record's type. Use the annotation only on methods that return a class that is not final, or an interface.

Spring can also weave method security into the bytecode with AspectJ, instead of using proxies. The setting is @EnableMethodSecurity(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ). The weaving makes the build more complex, so the shop does not use it.

Permission annotations: each scope string written oncetwist#

C#
[HttpPost("/orders"), Authorize(Policy = "orders.write")]
public IActionResult Place(PlaceOrder body) => StatusCode(201);
Java 25
/** The caller needs the {@code orders.write} scope. Put it on each controller method that changes data. */
@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders.write')")
public @interface OrdersWrite {
}
Reading the code
@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})

@Target says where the annotation may be written. Here it is a method or a class. On a class, it applies to every method of the class.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)

The annotation stays in the compiled class, so Spring can read it while the program runs. Without it, Spring would never see the annotation. See the section Retention: the concept C# lacks.

@Documented

The annotation becomes part of the public contract of each method that carries it. So Javadoc shows it on those methods.

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders.write')")

An annotation on an annotation is called a meta-annotation. Spring Security finds the @PreAuthorize on @OrdersWrite, and applies it to each method that carries @OrdersWrite. A run for this book confirmed that a meta-annotation refuses a read-only caller.

public @interface OrdersWrite {

@interface declares an annotation type. For more, see the section Declaring one.

The C# attribute names a policy, and the policy holds the rule. The Java annotation holds the rule itself. In both, the rule is written once. In Java, a misspelled annotation name does not compile. A misspelled scope inside @PreAuthorize compiles, and the rule then never matches. So the scope string is in one file for each scope, and the controllers use the names.

@OrdersRead is the same, with orders.read. Both annotations are in the shared.security package, because every feature uses them. For the rules about the shared package, see the chapter Features, layers and the rules.

A service with many scopes can use an annotation template instead. One annotation, such as @HasScope("orders.write"), then serves every scope. For what it needs, see the section Other method security annotations. With two scopes, two named annotations are easier to read and to search for.

Three places to check a permission, measuredtrap#

A permission check can be in three places. It can be a URL rule in the filter chain, an annotation on the controller method, or an annotation on the application service. The place decides which status a caller gets when two things are wrong at once. A C# developer expects an attribute on the action to answer 403 first.

PredictA read-only caller posts an invalid order#
A caller whose token has only the orders.read scope posts an order with an empty customer name. Which status does the caller get?
@OrdersWrite
@PostMapping
// ...
ResponseEntity<OrderPlacedResponse> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest request) {
    PlacedOrder placed = orders.place(
            new CustomerContact(request.customer().name(), request.customer().email()),
            new DeliveryMethod(request.deliveryMethod()),
            mapper.toItems(request),
            mapper.toNewNotes(request));
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + placed.orderId())).body(mapper.toResponse(placed));
}
Show the answer
400 Bad Request, with the field errors. Not 403.

Spring MVC reads and validates the body before the method is called. The token is valid, so the filter chain lets the request through. Spring MVC then resolves the method's arguments. It reads the JSON and runs @Valid. Validation fails, so Spring MVC throws before it calls the method. The proxy's check would run only at the call, so it never runs.

In ASP.NET Core, [Authorize(Policy = ...)] on the action gave 403 in the same case. Authorization runs before model binding there. If 403 must come first in Spring, use a URL rule in the filter chain.

A run for this book measured the three places with the same endpoint. The body failed @NotBlank and @Min(1) when it was invalid. The table also shows the two ASP.NET Core forms from a run on .NET 10:

Where the check iswrite scope, invalid bodyread scope, invalid bodyread scope, valid bodyread scope, broken JSONno token
a URL rule in the filter chain400403403403401
@PreAuthorize on the controller method400400403400401
@PreAuthorize on the service method the controller calls400400403400401
ASP.NET Core, [Authorize(Policy)] on the action400403403403401
ASP.NET Core, AuthorizeAsync inside the action400400403400401

A path variable behaves like the body. With @PathVariable UUID, a read-only caller who sent not-a-uuid got 400 for the controller check and for the service check. A valid universally unique identifier (UUID) got 403.

So only the URL rule answers 403 before the body is read. The C# attribute behaves like the Spring URL rule. The C# check in code behaves like @PreAuthorize. A missing or bad token is always 401 first, because the filter chain checks the token before anything else.

The order service records its own behaviour in two tests:

/**
 * Records what a caller without the write scope gets when the body is also invalid.
 * Spring MVC reads and validates the body while it resolves the method's arguments, which
 * is before the method, and its permission check, runs. So the answer is 400, not 403.
 */
@Test
void aCallerWithoutTheScopeWhoSendsAnInvalidBodyGets400() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(READ_ONLY).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("""
                    { "customer": { "name": "", "email": "x" }, "deliveryMethod": "", "lines": [] }
                    """))
            .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
    verifyNoInteractions(orders);
}

/**
 * Records the same case for an invalid ID in the path. The controller turns the text into
 * an {@code OrderId} inside the method, after the permission check, so the answer is 403.
 */
@Test
void aCallerWithoutTheScopeWhoSendsAnInvalidPathIdGets403() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders/not-a-uuid/ship").with(READ_ONLY))
            .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
}
Reading the code
.andExpect(status().isBadRequest());

The first test records the 400 for an invalid body. It is a test of the trade-off, so a change to the behaviour fails the build and is noticed.

verifyNoInteractions(orders);

orders is a mock of the use case. This line proves that no use case ran. The 400 tells the caller about the body, but the caller changed nothing.

mvc.perform(post("/orders/not-a-uuid/ship").with(READ_ONLY))

The controller takes the order ID as a String, and converts it inside the method. So the check runs first, and a bad ID from a read-only caller gets 403.

The three places differ in more than the status:

QuestionURL rule in the chainAnnotation on the controllerAnnotation on the service
When the check runsbefore Spring MVC reads anythingafter the arguments are read and validatedwhen the use case is called
A read-only caller with an invalid body403400400
The body of the 403empty, unless the chain also writes a problemthe platform's problem, with a traceIdthe platform's problem, with a traceId
Where the rule is writtenin a list of paths, apart from the controllerson the method it protectson the use case it protects
A new endpoint that nobody protectedit gets only the authenticated rulethe architecture rule fails the builddepends on whether the endpoint calls a protected method
Other features and message listenersnot affectednot affectedchecked too, so they need a caller with scopes

A URL rule for the shop would look like requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders.write"). The rules are matched in order, and the first match decides. So every path of every controller must appear in the right place in that list. A renamed path in a controller does not change the list, and nothing warns you.

Choosing the place by the shape of the servicenew#

No place is right for every service. The right place depends on where users enter. A door for users is called an entry point here. It is a way for a user's request to reach a use case. An HTTP controller is an entry point. So is a GraphQL resolver, or a queue that carries commands from users with their tokens.

A message from another service, a scheduled job and a call from another feature are not user entry points. No user stands behind them. The service itself decided to do the work.

One entry point for users. Users reach the use cases only through the HTTP API. This is the order service, and many microservices. Check the permission at the entry point:

  • Put a permission annotation on each controller method. This is the default.
  • Add an architecture rule that fails the build for an endpoint without one.
  • Put no permission annotation on the application services. Other features, listeners and jobs then call them directly.
  • If a caller must get 403 before 400, use URL rules in the chain instead. Choose this for an API that callers outside the company use. For the cost, see the section Three places to check a permission, measured.

Several entry points for users. Users reach the same use cases through two or more doors, such as REST and GraphQL. Then each door needs its own check, and the checks must be kept in step. Move the check to the use case, the application service method that the users call. Each new door is then protected without a new line. A check on the use case has a second strength. A reader of the use case sees its permission next to its steps. Three conditions keep this safe:

  • Internal callers never call a method that has a permission check. A listener or a job calls a use case of its own, written for the system.
  • A use case for the system is a different business action with its own name, such as recordPayment. It is not a copy of a user's use case without the annotation.
  • An architecture rule stops the entry points from calling the use cases that are meant for the system.

If the same action must be started by a user and by the system, these conditions cannot hold. Then put the check on each entry point after all, with the same permission annotation on each one. @PreAuthorize works on the method of any bean, not only on a controller.

A check on both the controller and the service has one strength. If one check is forgotten, the other one still refuses the caller. But it brings back the problem of the service checks, because the internal callers still meet them. A URL rule together with controller annotations is safe, but it is two lists to keep in step. Choose one place for each service, and let an architecture rule guard it.

The order service shows the first shape in its code. The application service says so in its own documentation:

 * <p>The class has no permission annotation. Permissions are checked on the controllers, where
 * users enter. Every method here can therefore be called by another feature or by a message
 * listener without a second, unprotected copy of the method.
 *
 * <p>With about ten use cases, split the class by area, such as {@code OrderFulfilmentService},
 * not into a read side and a write side.
 */
@Service
public class OrderService {

The class carries @Service and nothing more. The note feature calls OrderService.requireExists. The order feature calls NoteService.addNotes and NoteService.countNeedingAction. The payment listener calls OrderService.recordPayment. None of these calls needs a caller with scopes, because no service method checks one.

Pragmatic choice: Permissions on the controllers, not on the use cases

The strict rule. In a layered Domain-Driven Design (DDD) service, the application layer is the boundary of the use cases. A strict reading says that it also decides who may run them.

What we do. Each controller method carries @OrdersRead or @OrdersWrite. The application services carry no permission annotation. An architecture rule fails the build for an endpoint without one.

Why. Users enter the order service through one door, the HTTP API. Every other caller of a use case is the service itself, such as another feature, the payment listener or a job. A check at the door runs once for each user request. The internal calls need no identity.

When to stop. Stop when users reach the same use cases through a second door, such as GraphQL or a queue of user commands. Then choose again, by the rules of the section Choosing the place by the shape of the service.

Pragmatic choice: 400 before 403 for an invalid body

The strict rule. Refuse a caller without the permission before you tell it anything about its request.

What we do. A caller without the scope who sends an invalid body gets 400, with the names of the fields that failed. Two tests record this.

Why. Every caller already has a valid token from the shop's issuer. The errors describe only the shape of the API, and the published OpenAPI contract shows that shape anyway. A URL rule would be a second list of paths to keep in step with the controllers.

When to stop. Stop when callers outside the company use the API, or when a validation message would reveal data, such as "this email address is already registered". Then add URL rules for the paths that change data.

Why an identity-swapping helper is a warning signtrap#

Picture the order service with its checks on the use cases instead. A developer puts @OrdersWrite on OrderService.recordPayment, because "every use case needs a permission". The payment listener calls that method. The shop's listener is short:

@Override
protected void handle(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    Payment payment = new Payment(new PaymentReference(event.paymentReference()),
            new Money(event.amount(), event.currency()), event.paidAt());
    orders.recordPayment(OrderId.of(event.orderId()), payment);
}

The listener's thread has no security context. So the check on recordPayment finds no caller. A run for this book showed what happens then. Method security does not refuse with 403. It throws another exception:

AuthenticationCredentialsNotFoundException: An Authentication object was not found in the SecurityContext#
Means
A method with a permission annotation was called on a thread that has no caller, such as a message listener or a scheduled job.
Fix
Check permissions where users enter, and call the use case from the listener without a check. Do not invent a caller for the thread.

The message fails, the queue delivers it again, and in the end it moves to the dead-letter queue. For that path, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

Developers often try one of two quick fixes. Both make the problem worse.

The first quick fix is a helper that swaps the identity for one call. A careless version grants every scope to a made-up user. A careful developer writes a better one, and the book must answer that one. In the shop, it would look like this:

  • It grants only the scope that the inner call needs. For recordPayment, that is orders.write, and nothing else.
  • Its getName() returns the real caller. So in a request, the audit log still names the agent. In the payment listener, it names system.
  • It builds a new context, and restores the old one in a finally block, even after an exception.
  • It runs the call on the same thread, so the call joins the outer transaction.
  • It has one name, so a search finds every place that uses it.

That version gets a lot right. The audit stays true, the extra rights are small, and the context cannot leak to the next task on the thread. A careless version fails on each of these points. But the careful version is still a warning sign, for six reasons:

  1. It is an elevation of privilege that your own code grants. The security check exists to refuse callers without the scope. The helper decides, in code, to give the scope anyway. That decision is made in every place that calls the helper, not in one place.
  2. A caller gets more than its token allows. Suppose a read use case, reached with orders.read, calls a write use case through the helper. An agent with only orders.read cannot call the write use case directly. Yet code inside the agent's request now runs with orders.write.
  3. The inner check protects nothing that a user can reach directly. It says that a caller with orders.write may record a payment. But no user ever records a payment. The check guards a door that users cannot open. The helper only lets the internal callers pass the check.
  4. It fails without a warning when the work moves. The helper sets the context of the current thread only. If the inner call later moves to another thread, or becomes @Async, it runs with no caller. See the section The caller does not follow work to other threads. The call then throws, or a careless fix grants more.
  5. Every caller and every test must know about it. A new listener must use the helper, or it fails. A test of the listener must set up the same identity.
  6. It exists only because of where the check is. Without the check on a method that internal callers use, the helper would have nothing to do.

The second quick fix is a twin. A copy of the method without the annotation serves the internal callers. The twin is public, so a later controller can call it, and skip the check. The compiler cannot tell the twins apart, and a review may miss it.

Both fixes have one cause. The check is on a method that internal callers use too. So the real fix is to move the check to the door. In the order service, recordPayment carries no annotation, because the controllers carry them. The listener calls it directly. The audit log records system, which is the truth.

A helper that empties the context is different. The platform's message handler clears the context before it calls the use case, and restores it afterwards. It invents no identity and grants no scope. See the section Messages and jobs: the system actor.

Rules about one record: in the domain, with the actor passed innew#

A scope says which kind of action a caller may take. It cannot say which records. An agent with orders.write may resolve notes, but only a note of the order in the URL. A rule like this is about one record. It needs the record, so it can run only after the record is loaded.

The shop's note checks that it belongs to the order in the URL. ASP.NET Core offers an authorization handler for a rule about one resource. The order service writes the rule in the note class itself:

C#
public class NoteOwnerHandler : AuthorizationHandler<BelongsToOrder, Note>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context, BelongsToOrder requirement, Note note)
    {
        if (note.OrderId == requirement.OrderId) context.Succeed(requirement);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
Java 25
/**
 * Refuses a note that belongs to another order than the one in the URL, as not found.
 * Answering 403 would tell the caller that the note exists under another order.
 */
public void requireBelongsTo(String expectedOrderId) {
    if (!orderId.equals(expectedOrderId)) {
        throw new NoteNotFoundException(id);
    }
}

The C# handler calls context.Succeed(requirement) when the note belongs to the order, and the controller answers 403 otherwise. The Java method requireBelongsTo is part of the note class, and it throws when the order differs. The use case loads the note and asks the note to check itself, before it changes anything:

@Transactional
public void resolveAction(String orderId, String noteId) {
    Note note = notes.findById(noteId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoteNotFoundException(noteId));
    note.requireBelongsTo(orderId);
    note.resolveAction(currentActor.id(), clock);
    saveAndPublish(note, AuditActions.NOTE_ACTION_RESOLVED);
}

The line note.requireBelongsTo(orderId) comes before note.resolveAction(currentActor.id(), clock). A note of another order gets 404, the same answer as a note that does not exist. A 403 would tell the caller that the note exists under another order. In ASP.NET Core, the controller calls Forbid() when the handler does not succeed, and Forbid() answers 403. A run for this book measured that. The Java rule throws a "not found" exception instead, and the platform turns it into 404.

Some rules depend on who acts. The note has one. The agent who wrote a note that needs action may not resolve it, so a second person checks the work. Write such a rule in the domain too, and pass the actor in as a plain value. The application service gets the actor from CurrentActor, and passes the actor's ID to the domain method. That is the currentActor.id() in the use case above. The note compares it with the author that it stored when it was written:

/**
 * Resolves the action. The agent who wrote the note may not resolve it, so a second person
 * checks the work. The use case passes the actor's ID in as a plain value, so the note never
 * reads the security context.
 */
public void resolveAction(String actorId, Clock clock) {
    if (!actionRequired) {
        throw new NoteHasNoActionException(id);
    }
    if (actionResolvedAt != null) {
        throw new NoteActionAlreadyResolvedException(id);
    }
    if (actorId.equals(createdBy)) {
        throw new NoteResolvedByItsAuthorException(id);
    }
    actionResolvedAt = clock.instant();
    events.add(new NoteActionResolved(id, orderId, actionResolvedAt));
}

The note never reads SecurityContextHolder. It gets a String, like any other value, so a plain unit test can check the rule with two made-up agents:

/** A rule that depends on who acts: the actor comes in as a plain value, like any other. */
@Test
void theAgentWhoWroteTheNoteCannotResolveItsAction() {
    Note note = Note.create(ORDER_ID, "Call back", "DELIVERY", true, AUTHOR, CLOCK);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> note.resolveAction(AUTHOR, CLOCK)).isInstanceOf(NoteResolvedByItsAuthorException.class);
    assertThat(note.needsAction()).isTrue();
}

NoteResolvedByItsAuthorException is a business rule violation, so the platform answers 422 with the code NOTE_RESOLVED_BY_ITS_AUTHOR. The journey test OrderJourneyIT shows it end to end. The agent agent-1 places an order with a note. The same agent then tries to resolve the note, and gets 422. A second agent resolves it, and gets 204.

Keep the security types out of the domain. The architecture rule domainIsPlainJava fails the build if a class in a domain package uses a class from org.springframework. It also refuses several other technical libraries. The note is a light-style entity with Spring Data annotations. It is in a model package, not in a domain package, so that rule does not check it. The note still takes the actor as a value. So the rule about who acts reads the same in both styles.

Another form is a guard bean, called from @PreAuthorize. For that form, see the section Method-level authorisation. The guard loads the record again, outside the use case, and keeps the rule outside the domain. It is good enough for a simple feature. For the order service, the rule is with the record. For where each rule belongs, see the chapter Where each rule goes.

Messages and jobs: the system actornew#

A payment arrives from a queue. No user sent it, and the message carries no token. The platform's base class for listeners makes this explicit. It empties the security context for the call:

protected final void process(T event) {
    Map<String, String> context = new HashMap<>(logContext(event));
    context.put("eventId", event.eventId());
    SecurityContext callerContext = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
    SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();
    try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.with(context)) {
        inbox.process(consumer, event, this::handle);
    } finally {
        SecurityContextHolder.setContext(callerContext);
    }
}
Reading the code
SecurityContext callerContext = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();

The method keeps the thread's current context, whatever it is.

SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();

The thread now has no caller. Any code that asks who acts gets the system actor.

try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.with(context)) {

This is a try-with-resources block. It puts the event's IDs into the logging context, and removes them at the end. For the logging context, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

SecurityContextHolder.setContext(callerContext);

The finally block puts the old context back, even after an exception. So the thread is as it was before.

A listener thread has no caller anyway. Clearing the context makes the rule hold for every caller of process. Even on a thread with a signed-in user, the use case runs as the system.

The use case that the message starts carries no permission check, and says why:

/**
 * Records a payment from the payment service. A message starts this use case, so no user
 * acts, and the audit log records the system actor.
 *
 * <p>It joins the transaction of the inbox that called it. The one {@code if} here is not a
 * business rule: the domain decided to ignore the payment, so there is nothing to save.
 */
@Transactional
public void recordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment) {

Who may send a payment, then? The order service trusts the queue, not the message. Only the payment service should be able to send to that queue. That is a setting in AWS, not in the code.

A scheduled job behaves the same way. The platform's outbox resender runs on a scheduler thread, which has no security context. Any audit record it causes names system. For the resender, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

The current actor, and the audit recordnew#

Each change to an order writes an audit record. The record says what happened, to which order, and who acted. The audit log asks one small interface who acts:

public interface CurrentActor {

    /** The actor for work that no user started, such as handling a message from a queue. */
    String SYSTEM = "system";

    /** Returns the actor's ID: the token's subject, or {@link #SYSTEM}. */
    String id();
}

SYSTEM is a constant of the interface, the actor for work that no user started. The platform registers the implementation that reads the security context. For that class, see the section The security context: one per thread. The bean is replaceable, like every platform bean:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
CurrentActor currentActor() {
    return new SecurityContextCurrentActor();
}

@ConditionalOnMissingBean lets a service define its own CurrentActor instead. The audit log asks for the actor each time it writes a record:

@Override
public void record(String action, String resourceType, String resourceId) {
    Document entry = new Document("action", action)
            .append("resourceType", resourceType)
            .append("resourceId", resourceId)
            .append("actor", currentActor.id())
            .append("at", clock.instant());
    String traceId = MDC.get(ProblemDetails.TRACE_ID);
    if (traceId != null) {
        entry.append("traceId", traceId);
    }
    mongo.insert(entry, COLLECTION);
}
Reading the code
.append("actor", currentActor.id())

The actor is the token's sub claim for a request, and system for a message or a job.

String traceId = MDC.get(ProblemDetails.TRACE_ID);

The record also gets the trace ID from the mapped diagnostic context (MDC), so support can find the request's log lines.

mongo.insert(entry, COLLECTION);

The record is written in the use case's transaction, so it is stored only with the change. For audit records in full, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

The interface has three uses. The application services and the audit log never touch Spring Security. A test can supply a fixed actor. And a service with another identity model can replace the bean.

The journey test checks the actors of a whole order's life. An agent places, picks and ships the order. The payment arrives as a message in between:

// The audit log: every change once, by the agent, except the payment, which the system recorded.
List<Document> orderAudit = mongo.find(query(where("resourceId").is(orderId)).with(Sort.by("at")),
        Document.class, "audit_log");
assertThat(orderAudit).extracting(entry -> entry.getString("action"))
        .containsExactly("ORDER_PLACED", "PAYMENT_RECORDED", "LINE_PICKED", "ORDER_SHIPPED");
assertThat(orderAudit).extracting(entry -> entry.getString("actor"))
        .containsExactly("agent-1", "system", "agent-1", "agent-1");

The test's token has the subject agent-1. The payment came from the queue, so its actor is system. With an identity-swapping helper, the second entry would name the made-up identity, and the test could not tell a person from the system.

Note

The sub claim of a user's token is the user's ID at the issuer. Keep it as an ID. Do not put a name or an email address in the audit record, because the audit log keeps its records for a long time.

The service's own token for the stock servicenew#

Placing an order calls the stock service, which also requires a token. The local stub of the stock service answers 401 to a request without one. The order service has two choices. It can forward the agent's token, or it can send a token of its own.

The shop sends a token of its own. The agent's token names order-service as its audience, so a stock service that checks its audience refuses it. A payment message has no user token to forward. And the stock service should trust the order service, not every agent. A service gets its own token with the client-credentials grant. The service sends its client ID and secret to the issuer, and gets a token back. No user takes part.

The registration is in application.yml:

client:
  # The service's own identity, for its calls to the stock service (client credentials).
  registration:
    stock-service:
      provider: shop-identity
      client-id: ${STOCK_CLIENT_ID:order-service}
      client-secret: ${STOCK_CLIENT_SECRET}
      authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
      scope: stock.reserve
  provider:
    shop-identity:
      token-uri: ${OAUTH_TOKEN_URI}
Reading the code
stock-service:

This is the registration ID. The stock client names it to get its token.

client-id: ${STOCK_CLIENT_ID:order-service}

The client ID comes from an environment variable. After the colon is the default, order-service.

client-secret: ${STOCK_CLIENT_SECRET}

The secret has no default, so it must come from the environment. A secret never goes into this file.

scope: stock.reserve

The service asks for this scope only. It needs nothing more from the stock service.

token-uri: ${OAUTH_TOKEN_URI}

This is the issuer's token endpoint, where the service asks for its token.

The client registration needs the starter spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client on Boot 4.1.2. The old name, spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client, still exists in 4.1.2, and its description says that it is deprecated. The platform's HttpClientFactory adds the token to each call of a client whose settings name a registration:

/**
 * Adds a client-credentials token to each request.
 *
 * <p>The token belongs to this service, not to the user of the current request. So the
 * principal is fixed to the registration ID: every request shares one cached token, and a
 * call works on a thread with no user, such as a message listener.
 */
private OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor tokenInterceptor(String registrationId) {
    Authentication thisService = new AnonymousAuthenticationToken(registrationId, registrationId,
            AuthorityUtils.createAuthorityList("ROLE_SERVICE"));
    OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor interceptor = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(tokenManager.get());
    interceptor.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(request -> registrationId);
    interceptor.setPrincipalResolver(request -> thisService);
    return interceptor;
}
Reading the code
new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(tokenManager.get());

This interceptor of RestClient adds a bearer token to each request. The token manager fetches the token from the issuer, and keeps it.

interceptor.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(request -> registrationId);

Every request of this client uses the registration stock-service.

interceptor.setPrincipalResolver(request -> thisService);

The token manager stores each token under a principal, and this line fixes the principal. The next paragraphs explain why it matters.

Authentication thisService = new AnonymousAuthenticationToken(registrationId, registrationId,

The fixed principal is an object that names the service. It is never put into a security context. It is only the key under which the token is stored.

The token manager is an AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager, which the platform builds. A run for this book showed that this manager gets a token on any thread, including a thread with no security context. Boot created no token manager of its own in that run.

Gotcha

By default, the interceptor caches the token for each signed-in user. The default principal resolver reads the caller from the security context. A run made three calls with no caller, and they shared one token, stored for anonymousUser. Then a call as alice and a call as bob each caused a new token request. Each user caused a token request of their own, for the same service. Under load, that is one call to the issuer for each user. Only setPrincipalResolver fixed it. An attribute on the request alone changed nothing.

The stock adapter's test checks the fix against a real HTTP server, with a token endpoint. The server is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK):

@Test
void twoDifferentUsersShareOneServiceToken() {
    SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(new TestingAuthenticationToken("agent-1", null));
    adapter.reserve(OrderId.newId(), TWO_MUGS);
    SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(new TestingAuthenticationToken("agent-2", null));
    adapter.reserve(OrderId.newId(), TWO_MUGS);

    assertThat(reservationCalls).hasValue(2);
    assertThat(tokenCalls).hasValue(1);
}

Two agents call, and tokenCalls is 1, so the issuer saw one token request. Another test, sendsTheServicesTokenAndTheOrderIdAsTheIdempotencyKey, checks that the stock service receives Bearer token-1. The test sets the context directly, because it runs on one thread and clears the context after each test.

In ASP.NET Core, the closest match is a DelegatingHandler on the HttpClient that adds the token. For timeouts, retries and the rest of the stock client, see the chapter Calling other services.

Testing security in a controller slicenew#

A controller test should run the real chain, the real permission annotations and the real error handling, without a token issuer. The platform supplies an annotation for this:

@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
@WebMvcTest
@ImportAutoConfiguration({
        PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformWebAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration.class})
@Import(TestJwtDecoderConfiguration.class)
public @interface PlatformWebMvcTest {

    /** The controllers to test. */
    @AliasFor(annotation = WebMvcTest.class, attribute = "controllers")
    Class<?>[] value() default {};
}
Reading the code
@WebMvcTest

This starts a test slice with Spring MVC and the controllers only. For slices, see the section Test slices.

PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration.class,

The slice imports the platform's chain, so the test runs the same security as production.

@Import(TestJwtDecoderConfiguration.class)

This adds a decoder for tests. The next example shows it.

@AliasFor(annotation = WebMvcTest.class, attribute = "controllers")

@AliasFor passes the value of this annotation to @WebMvcTest. So @PlatformWebMvcTest(OrderController.class) means @WebMvcTest(controllers = OrderController.class). A run for this book confirmed that such a slice loads only the named controller.

The slice needs a JwtDecoder, because the chain accepts JWTs. Without an issuer-uri and without a decoder, a run of a slice failed at startup:

Method api in sec.SecurityConfig required a bean of type 'org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtDecoder' that could not be found.#
Means
The security chain accepts JWTs, but the test has no issuer setting and no decoder bean.
Fix
Give the slice a decoder for tests, such as the platform's TestJwtDecoderConfiguration, and authenticate with jwt().

The platform's decoder for tests refuses every real token:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class TestJwtDecoderConfiguration {

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder() {
        return token -> {
            throw new BadJwtException("Tests authenticate with SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()");
        };
    }
}

JwtDecoder has one method, so a lambda can implement it. A run showed both sides. A test with jwt() got 200, and a real bearer token got 401 with the decoder's message. So the slice starts without an issuer, needs no network, and a stray real token fails as it would in production.

The tests then authenticate with jwt(), from spring-security-test. It puts an authentication straight into the security context of the MockMvc request, and never calls the decoder. The controller test defines two callers:

/** A customer-service agent's token: a subject and both scopes. */
private static final JwtRequestPostProcessor AGENT = jwt().jwt(token -> token.subject("agent-1"))
        .authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.read"), new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.write"));
private static final JwtRequestPostProcessor READ_ONLY = jwt()
        .authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.read"));
Reading the code
jwt().jwt(token -> token.subject("agent-1"))

The inner jwt(...) changes the claims of the token. Here the subject is agent-1, which the audit log would record.

.authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.read"), new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.write"));

authorities(...) replaces the authorities. Write them with the SCOPE_ prefix, as the converter would produce them.

Without changes, jwt() gives the name user and the one authority SCOPE_read. Its principal is a Jwt. A scope claim set with jwt(t -> t.claim("scope", "orders.read")) goes through the same converter as in production. It gave SCOPE_orders.read in a run. jwt() does not add FACTOR_BEARER.

The security tests of the controller check the 401 and the 403, and that nothing ran:

@Test
void aRequestWithoutATokenIsA401ProblemBeforeAnyController() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(VALID_ORDER))
            .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized())
            .andExpect(header().exists("WWW-Authenticate"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Unauthorized"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value(401));
    verifyNoInteractions(orders);
}

@Test
void aCallerWithoutTheWriteScopeIsA403AndNothingRuns() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(READ_ONLY).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(VALID_ORDER))
            .andExpect(status().isForbidden())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Forbidden"));
    mvc.perform(post("/orders/" + ORDER_ID + "/ship").with(READ_ONLY))
            .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    verifyNoInteractions(orders);
}

Both tests end with verifyNoInteractions(orders), so no use case ran. Each permission test has a partner. One caller without the scope gets 403, and one caller with it succeeds. The test theReadScopeIsEnoughToRead is the other half for reads.

Gotcha

@WithMockUser passes a scope check, but gives no Jwt. @WithMockUser(authorities = "SCOPE_orders.write") made a POST pass hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders.write') with 201 in a run. But its authentication is a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, and its principal is a User. Code that reads a claim from the Jwt gets the wrong type. In a resource server, use jwt().

In Boot 4.1.2, @WebMvcTest includes the resource server auto-configuration. So a plain slice with issuer-uri in application.yml builds the lazy decoder. Tests with jwt() pass without a network. But a request with a real Authorization: Bearer header makes the slice try to reach the issuer.

For the general rules of test slices and of the platform's test annotations, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Security in the journey testtwist#

The journey test starts the whole service, with a real database and a real queue. It still needs no token issuer:

@SpringBootTest(properties = {
        "spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=",
        "spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=http://localhost:1/jwks",
Reading the code
"spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=",

The issuer setting is empty. So Spring adds no issuer check, and the environment variable of application.yml is not needed.

"spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=http://localhost:1/jwks",

Nothing listens on port 1. But with jwk-set-uri, Spring fetches keys only for a real token, and jwt() never sends one. So the URL is never called.

The journey test uses jwt() as the slice tests do. Its security tests check what only the whole service can show:

@Test
void aCallerWithoutTheWriteScopeIsForbidden() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.read")))
                    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                    .content("{ %s, \"deliveryMethod\": \"STANDARD\", %s }".formatted(CUSTOMER, VALID_LINES)))
            .andExpect(status().isForbidden())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.traceId").exists());
}

Here the 403 carries a traceId, which the tracing of the full service sets. The test aRequestWithoutATokenIsRejectedButTheProbesArePublic checks the other side of the chain. A request without a token gets 401, and the liveness and readiness probes get 200 without one. The wiring test uses the same two settings in its profile application-wiring.yml.

A rule that every endpoint names its permissionnew#

With checks on the controllers, the danger is a new endpoint without a permission annotation. Any caller with a valid token could then call it. A review can miss that. So the platform states the rule as an ArchUnit rule, which fails the build:

/**
 * Every endpoint names the permission it needs, with an annotation that wraps
 * {@code @PreAuthorize}, such as {@code @OrdersRead}. A new endpoint without one fails the build.
 */
public static ArchRule everyEndpointHasAPermission() {
    return methods().that().areDeclaredInClassesThat().areAnnotatedWith(RestController.class)
            .and().areMetaAnnotatedWith(RequestMapping.class)
            .should().beMetaAnnotatedWith(PreAuthorize.class)
            .as("Every endpoint has a permission annotation");
}
Reading the code
methods().that().areDeclaredInClassesThat().areAnnotatedWith(RestController.class)

The rule looks at the methods of every @RestController class.

.and().areMetaAnnotatedWith(RequestMapping.class)

It keeps the methods that handle requests. @GetMapping and @PostMapping carry @RequestMapping, so "meta-annotated" finds them.

.should().beMetaAnnotatedWith(PreAuthorize.class)

Each such method needs @PreAuthorize, directly or through an annotation such as @OrdersRead.

The service calls the rule in ArchitectureTest.everyEndpointHasAPermission. A second test proves that the rule fails for code that breaks it:

@RestController
static class ForgetfulController {

    @GetMapping("/forgotten")
    String forgotten() {
        return "anyone with a token can call this";
    }
}
// ...
@Test
void anEndpointWithoutAPermissionFailsTheBuild() {
    JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter().importClasses(ForgetfulController.class);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> ArchitectureRules.everyEndpointHasAPermission().check(classes))
            .isInstanceOf(AssertionError.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("forgotten");
}

The test expects an AssertionError whose message contains forgotten. A rule that never fails proves nothing. This test shows that the rule names the endpoint it catches.

The rule also covers endpoints that seem harmless. The lookup lists of reference data, such as the delivery methods, need orders.read too. Without the rule, it is easy to leave such an endpoint open to any token.

The rule checks that an annotation exists, not that it is the right one. A write method with @OrdersRead passes the rule. The pair of 403 and success tests in each controller test catches that. For ArchUnit and the other rules, see the chapter Testing in depth.

A local token issuer, and the issuer-versus-keys tricktwist#

A developer needs real tokens on their own machine, for curl, Swagger UI and the end-to-end tests. The local environment runs a token issuer in Docker. It is mock-oauth2-server, version 6.1.3, the latest release as of October 2026:

# Issues JWTs for local calls, for Playwright, and for the services' own client-credentials calls.
mock-oauth2:
  image: ghcr.io/navikt/mock-oauth2-server:6.1.3
  ports: ["8090:8080"]
  environment:
    JSON_CONFIG_PATH: /config/config.json
  volumes: ["./mock-oauth2:/config"]
Reading the code
ports: ["8090:8080"]

The server listens on port 8080 in its container. The host reaches it on port 8090.

JSON_CONFIG_PATH: /config/config.json

This environment variable names the configuration file, mounted from the folder mock-oauth2.

The configuration gives each client ID its own subject and scopes. The first mapping gives agent both scopes. See the section From scopes to authorities. The second mapping gives read-only one scope:

{
  "interactiveLogin": false,
  "tokenCallbacks": [
    {
      "issuerId": "default",
      "tokenExpiry": 3600,
      "requestMappings": [
        // ...
        {
          "requestParam": "client_id",
          "match": "read-only",
          "claims": {
            "sub": "local-read-only",
            "aud": ["order-service"],
            "scope": "orders.read"
          }
        },
Reading the code
"issuerId": "default",

The issuer's URL ends in /default.

"tokenExpiry": 3600,

The token is valid for 3,600 seconds, one hour. A run confirmed that the value is in seconds.

"match": "read-only",

The mapping applies when the request's client_id is exactly read-only. The server also accepts "*" and regular expressions.

"aud": ["order-service"],

The token names the order service as its audience, so it passes the audiences check.

The third mapping is for the order service itself. It gives order-service the scope stock.reserve and the audience stock-service, for the client-credentials call. In a run, the server ignored the scope that the client asked for, and used the mapping's claims. The token's header was typ: JWT, so the token passes Spring's typ check.

A developer gets a token with curl:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8090/default/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=agent -d client_secret=any | jq -r .access_token

The command asks for a client-credentials token as the client agent. The secret can be anything. jq -r .access_token prints only the token from the JSON answer. The token is not a real user's token. Locally, a client ID stands for a kind of user, and that is enough to test the scopes.

One detail makes the local setup harder. The server puts the URL that the caller used into the token's iss claim. A run showed it. A token asked for through localhost had a localhost issuer. A token asked for through 127.0.0.1 had an issuer with that address.

The developer's curl calls localhost:8090. So the token's iss is http://localhost:8090/default. The order service runs in a container. Inside a container, localhost is the container itself, so the service cannot fetch keys from that URL. The local profile solves this with two URLs:

security:
  oauth2:
    resourceserver:
      jwt:
        # The mock OAuth2 server puts the URL the caller used into the token's "iss" claim.
        # Get tokens from http://localhost:8090/default/token, as curl and Playwright on your
        # machine do. The service then checks that issuer, and reads the signing keys over the
        # docker network.
        issuer-uri: http://localhost:8090/default
        jwk-set-uri: http://mock-oauth2:8080/default/jwks

The issuer-uri is the URL that the developer's tools call. The jwk-set-uri is the URL that the container can reach, by the container name mock-oauth2.

With both settings, Spring never calls issuer-uri. It only compares the token's iss with it. It fetches the keys from jwk-set-uri, by the container's name on the Docker network. A run reproduced the mechanism on one machine, with localhost and 127.0.0.1 as the two names.

A run of the whole local environment in Docker, on 25 October 2026, confirmed it. A token from http://localhost:8090/default/token had the iss http://localhost:8090/default, and the order service container accepted it with 200 and 201. A token asked for at http://127.0.0.1:8090 had another iss. The container refused it with 401. Its WWW-Authenticate header said "The iss claim is not valid". So the service compares the issuer and fetches the keys from the container name, as described.

The run did not use the image ghcr.io/navikt/mock-oauth2-server:6.1.3. The registry refused the pull with 403 Forbidden on that machine, also without stored credentials. So the same version ran from its jar on Maven Central, in a Java container under the same name and port. The compose file keeps the pinned image.

The service's own token request goes to http://mock-oauth2:8080/default/token. So the token's iss is the container URL. That is fine, because the stock service stub does not check the issuer. When the service runs in an IDE on the host, the README of the service overrides jwk-set-uri and the token URI with localhost:8090. For the whole local environment, see the chapter Running locally and shipping.

The JwtBearer options of ASP.NET Core have two settings for the same idea. MetadataAddress names where to fetch the metadata, and TokenValidationParameters.ValidIssuer names the expected issuer. This book did not run that pair against the local issuer.

AWS credentials: a role, never a keytwist#

The service publishes to Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) and reads from Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). Both need AWS credentials. The settings name only the region:

cloud:
  aws:
    # Credentials come from the task's or pod's IAM role, never from configuration.
    region:
      static: ${AWS_REGION:eu-west-2}

The line static: ${AWS_REGION:eu-west-2} sets the region, with a default. Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the AWS service that decides who may call which AWS action. In production, the deployment gives the service's task or pod an IAM role, and the role holds the permissions. So no access key is in a file, in an environment variable or in the image.
