Only the local profile sets keys, the dummy values local, for the AWS emulator.

Spring Cloud AWS 4.1.0 builds the credentials provider in its class CredentialsProviderAutoConfiguration. The source shows the choice. Apart from connection details, which a test can supply, each of these adds a provider:

  • a key pair, in spring.cloud.aws.credentials.access-key and secret-key
  • the instance profile, when spring.cloud.aws.credentials.instance-profile is true
  • a named profile, in spring.cloud.aws.credentials.profile.name
  • a web identity token file, named in the settings or in the environment variable AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE. This provider is added only when the SDK's sts module is present.

When none of these applies, the class returns the AWS SDK's DefaultCredentialsProvider. The comment of that class, in the SDK version 2.47.4 that the service uses, lists where it looks, in this order:

PlaceWhat it reads
Java system propertiesaws.accessKeyId and aws.secretAccessKey
environment variablesAWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
a web identity tokenthe token file named in a system property or an environment variable
the profile file~/.aws/credentials, shared with the AWS command-line tool
the container credentialsthe credentials that Amazon ECS delivers, when AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI is set
the instance profilethe credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service

So the production service, with no credential settings, finds the role of its task or pod through this chain. The first place that has credentials wins. A forgotten AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in the environment would therefore win over the role.

Gotcha

A web identity token file needs a module that the service does not have. Both places that can read the file need the SDK's sts module. Spring Cloud AWS adds its web identity provider only when a class of that module is present. The web identity step of DefaultCredentialsProvider needs the module too. Without it, the SDK logs that web identity tokens need the sts module on the class path. Then the chain goes on to the next place.

The order service's dependencies have no software.amazon.awssdk:sts. So a deployment that hands the role over as a web identity token file needs that dependency. Without it, the service never reads the file. The version of sts needs no entry of its own. The list of versions that Spring Cloud AWS publishes imports the list of versions of the AWS SDK. The container credentials and the instance profile are in the SDK's auth module, which the service already has.

The role needs one permission that surprises people:

/**
 * Spring Cloud AWS turns this name into the topic's ARN by calling {@code CreateTopic}, which
 * returns the ARN of an existing topic. So the service's IAM role needs {@code sns:CreateTopic}
 * as well as {@code sns:Publish}, and a typo here silently creates a new, empty topic.
 */
public static final String ORDER_EVENTS = "order-events";

An ARN is the full Amazon Resource Name of the topic. Spring Cloud AWS finds it by calling CreateTopic, which returns the ARN of a topic that exists already. The service's README lists the role's permissions. For the other way, an ARN in the settings, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe order service checks permissions on its controllers. Why can the payment listener then record a payment without any identity?
The permission check runs at the door that users use, the HTTP API. The application service has no check. The listener calls recordPayment directly, on a thread with an empty security context. Nothing asks for a scope, so no identity is needed. The audit log records system, which is the truth, because no user acted.
2
An expert asksA developer puts @OrdersWrite on a use case that a message listener calls. Then they write a helper that runs the call as a made-up user with every scope. Why is the helper a warning sign?
Even a careful helper is an elevation of privilege that the code grants itself. Code runs with a scope that the caller's token may not hold. The inner check guards an action that no user starts. The helper breaks when the call moves to another thread, and every caller and test must know it. It exists only because the check is on a method that internal callers use. Move the check to the entry point.
3
A token's exp was 30 seconds ago. Does Spring Security 7 accept it? Does ASP.NET Core with the defaults of AddJwtBearer?
Both accept it. Spring allows a clock skew of 60 seconds, and ASP.NET Core allows 5 minutes. At 90 seconds, Spring refuses the token with "Jwt expired at", and ASP.NET Core still accepts it.
4
The stock client adds a client-credentials token with OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor. Two agents place orders, one after the other. How many token requests does the default principal resolver cause, and what does the platform change?
The default resolver stores the token under the signed-in user, so each agent causes a token request of their own. The platform calls setPrincipalResolver with a fixed principal for the service. Then all callers share one token. StockAdapterTest.twoDifferentUsersShareOneServiceToken checks it.
5
TranslateIn C#, this code reads the caller inside work that runs on another thread. It works, because the caller flows into Task.Run: 
string seen = await Task.Run(() => currentActor.Id());
Write the Java for work on a virtual thread from an ExecutorService, so that the work sees the caller.
try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    String actor = currentActor.id();
    Future<String> actorSeenByTheWork = executor.submit(() -> actor);
    // ...
}

Read the actor on the request's thread, and give the work the plain value. A call of currentActor.id() inside the work would answer system, because the security context stays on its own thread. Wrap the executor in DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService only when the work must check permissions itself.

The settings of the resource server and the client, as Boot 4.1.2 reads them:

SettingDefaultWhat it does

spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-urinonefetches the keys from this URL, with no discovery

The filters of a stateless resource server chain in Spring Security 7.1.2, in order, as a run printed them:

Storing aggregates in DocumentDB#

Storing and changing data · Chapter 16· 41 min read· Quick reference

The order service stores each order as one document, with its lines inside. Notes have a collection of their own. The order feature keeps its stored shape in a separate document class with a mapper. The note feature stores the entity itself. This chapter covers both styles, optimistic locking with @Version, the types to store, the queries, and the connection to Amazon DocumentDB.
