One aggregate, one documentnew#

An agent opens an order. The service must check the shipping rule, so it needs the order, every line and the last payment. With a relational database, that is three tables and a join. In the order service, it is one read of one document.

The rule of the service is short. One aggregate is stored as one document. The aggregate is the unit that a use case loads, changes and saves. So the document holds exactly the data that the rules of the aggregate need. A read returns the whole aggregate, and a write replaces the whole aggregate. For what an aggregate is, see the chapter Finding the aggregates. For documents and collections in general, see the chapter Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API.

The service and its platform library write to nine collections. A collection has the same purpose as a table in a relational database. Each collection has one owner, and only the owner writes to it:

CollectionOwnerWhat one document holds
ordersthe order featureone order, with its lines and its last payment
notesthe note featureone note, with the ID of its order
reference_datathe reference featureone lookup value, such as the delivery method EXPRESS
audit_logthe platform's audit logone record of who changed what, and when
event_publicationSpring Modulith, the outboxone event for one listener, until it is sent
processed_messagesthe platform's inboxthe key of one event that was processed
schema_migrationsthe platform's migration runnerthe ID of one migration that ran
schema_migrations_lockthe platform's migration runnerthe lock, while one instance migrates
scheduler_locksShedLock, for the outbox resenderthe lock of one scheduled job

Only the first three collections hold aggregates or lookup data. The others belong to the platform. For the outbox, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox. For the inbox, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox. For the migration runner, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

The service writes no code to connect. The platform library depends on one starter:

<!-- DocumentDB, through the MongoDB API -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>

With spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb on the classpath, Spring Boot creates a MongoTemplate bean. MongoTemplate is the class that sends commands to the database. The Spring Data repositories use it too. The platform adds only what DocumentDB needs on top. For that part, see the section Driver settings that DocumentDB needs.

Embed the lines, keep the notes aparttwist#

An order has lines and notes. Both belong to one order. The service embeds the lines in the order's document, and stores the notes in a collection of their own. The document class says why in its comment:

/**
 * How an order is stored: one document per aggregate, with its lines and last payment embedded.
 *
 * <p>The lines are embedded because they are few (at most 50) and every order rule needs them.
 * Notes are not: they have no limit, and embedding them would rewrite the whole order for each
 * new note. A document must stay under 16 MB.
 *
 * <p>Only plain types are stored. Enums and codes are strings, so renaming a Java class never
 * breaks stored data. Money is DECIMAL128, so it is exact. The class and its fields are
 * package-private: nothing outside this package knows the storage shape.
 */

The comment gives the reasons in short. It names two limits, 50 lines for an order and 16 MB for the whole document. It also says why money is DECIMAL128. Three questions decide whether to embed something:

QuestionLinesNotes
Do the rules of the order need it?yes, picking and shipping check every lineno, only the count of open actions matters
Is the number limited?yes, at most 50 lines, checked by Order.placeno, an agent can add notes for years
Does it change on its own?no, a line changes only through the orderyes, an agent adds and resolves notes without changing the order

Embed what passes all three questions. A document on Amazon DocumentDB may hold at most 16 MiB, as of October 2026. Fifty lines are far below that limit. An unlimited list of notes is not.

A save replaces the whole document. So with embedded notes, each new note would rewrite the order and every earlier note. The note would also take the order's version. An agent who adds a note would then conflict with a warehouse worker who picks a line at the same moment.

Embedding the notes has a careful version, and it has real strengths. One read returns the order with its notes. One write stores both, with no transaction. A limit on notes, such as 100, would keep the document small. But the strengths do not help the order service. The shipping rule needs only a count, which an indexed query returns. The notes would still share the order's version, so unrelated work would conflict. Embed notes when they are few, limited, and always read and changed with the order. For why the note is an aggregate of its own, see the section Why order and note are separate aggregates.

The MongoDB .NET driver embeds a nested object or a list in the same way. For the basic rule, see the section Embed or reference.

The full style: a document classtwist#

The order feature uses the full style. The domain class Order holds the rules and knows nothing about storage. A second class, OrderDocument, holds what is stored:

@Document("orders")
class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

    String customerName;
    String customerEmail;
    String deliveryMethod;
    String status;
    Instant placedAt;
    Instant shippedAt;
    Instant cancelledAt;
    List<LineDocument> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    PaymentDocument lastPayment;
    // ...
    static class PaymentDocument {
        String reference;
        @Field(targetType = FieldType.DECIMAL128)
        BigDecimal amount;
        String currency;
        Instant paidAt;
    }
}
Reading the code
@Document("orders")

This annotation from Spring Data MongoDB names the collection. Each OrderDocument is one document in orders.

class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

The class has no access modifier, so it is package-private. Only the classes of the persistence package can use it. BaseDocument is the platform's base class. It adds the ID and the version. See the section Optimistic locking with @Version.

String customerName;

The fields are package-private too, and they have no getters or setters. Spring Data reads and writes fields directly. So the mapper in the same package can set them, and nothing else can. Each field is stored under its own name, such as customerName.

String status;

The status is a String, not the enum OrderStatus. See the section The types to store.

List<LineDocument> lines = new ArrayList<>();

A list of nested objects becomes an array of embedded documents. The class LineDocument is shown in the section An embedded field named id.

static class PaymentDocument {

A static nested class does not need an instance of the outer class. Spring Data can create it on its own when it reads a document.

The stored shape and the domain can now change apart from each other. The domain can rename a field, and the stored name stays the same. The domain keeps its Money type with a currency, and the document stores two plain values. The cost is a second class and a mapper for every aggregate.

An architecture rule keeps every @Document class in a persistence package or a model package. The model package is the home of a light-style entity. For the rule and the three levels, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

In C#, the MongoDB driver maps a class with attributes such as [BsonElement] on its properties. The same split works in C#, with a document class in an infrastructure project. In Java, the package-private class keeps the document inside its package.

The mapper: from the aggregate to the document and backtwist#

The platform defines the shape of every mapper. A mapper converts one aggregate into one document, and back:

/**
 * Converts between an aggregate and its stored document.
 *
 * <p>{@link #toDocument} copies the aggregate's data; {@link MongoAggregateRepository} sets the
 * ID and the version. {@link #toDomain} rebuilds the aggregate with its {@code rehydrate}
 * factory, passing {@code getId()} and {@code getVersion()}, so loading applies no rules and
 * raises no events.
 *
 * @param <A> the aggregate
 * @param <D> the document
 */
public interface DocumentMapper<A, D extends BaseDocument> {

    D toDocument(A aggregate);

    A toDomain(D document);
}

D extends BaseDocument limits the type parameter. A mapper can only produce a document that has an ID and a version. In C#, the same limit is written where D : BaseDocument.

The order's mapper implements both directions:

@Component
class OrderDocumentMapper implements DocumentMapper<Order, OrderDocument> {

    @Override
    public OrderDocument toDocument(Order order) {
        OrderDocument document = new OrderDocument();
        document.customerName = order.customer().name();
        document.customerEmail = order.customer().email();
        document.deliveryMethod = order.deliveryMethod().code();
        document.status = order.status().name();
        document.placedAt = order.placedAt();
        document.shippedAt = order.shippedAt();
        document.cancelledAt = order.cancelledAt();
        document.lines = order.lines().stream().map(OrderDocumentMapper::lineDocument).toList();
        document.lastPayment = paymentDocument(order.lastPayment());
        return document;
    }

    @Override
    public Order toDomain(OrderDocument document) {
        return Order.rehydrate(
                OrderId.of(document.getId()),
                document.getVersion(),
                new CustomerContact(document.customerName, document.customerEmail),
                new DeliveryMethod(document.deliveryMethod),
                document.placedAt,
                document.lines.stream().map(OrderDocumentMapper::line).toList(),
                OrderStatus.valueOf(document.status),
                payment(document.lastPayment),
                document.shippedAt,
                document.cancelledAt);
    }
Reading the code
@Component

The mapper is a bean, so Spring injects it into the adapter. It is package-private, like the document.

document.status = order.status().name();

name() returns the name of the enum constant, such as PAID. Every Java enum has this method.

OrderStatus.valueOf(document.status),

valueOf turns the stored name back into the constant. An unknown name throws IllegalArgumentException. So renaming an enum constant needs a migration of the stored data.

return Order.rehydrate(

rehydrate is the factory for a stored order. It applies no rules and raises no events, because loading is not a business action. New orders come from Order.place, which applies the rules. For both factories, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

document.getVersion(),

The mapper passes the stored version into the aggregate. It never sets the ID or the version of a document. The platform's base class does that. See the section The adapter and the platform's base class.

The mapper handles a missing payment too. An order that is not paid stores no lastPayment, so the field is null when the order is read:

private static Payment payment(OrderDocument.PaymentDocument document) {
    return document == null ? null : new Payment(new PaymentReference(document.reference),
            new Money(document.amount, document.currency), document.paidAt);
}

payment returns null for a missing payment, and the domain accepts an order with no payment. The developer writes the whole mapper. A mapping library, such as MapStruct, could generate the copying of fields. The service does not use one, because the domain is built through a factory with checked value objects, not through setters. A hand-written mapper shows each conversion where a reviewer reads it.

The adapter and the platform's base classnew#

A use case loads an order through the port OrderRepository. The port is a plain Java interface in the domain. It names findById, save and exists, plus the order's own queries. Something must implement the port with MongoDB. That class is called the persistence adapter. Without help, every aggregate's adapter would write the same load and save code. So the platform writes it once:

public abstract class MongoAggregateRepository<A extends AggregateRoot<ID>, ID extends Identifier, D extends BaseDocument>
        implements Repository<A, ID> {

    protected final MongoRepository<D, String> documents;
    protected final DocumentMapper<A, D> mapper;

    protected MongoAggregateRepository(MongoRepository<D, String> documents, DocumentMapper<A, D> mapper) {
        this.documents = documents;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<A> findById(ID id) {
        return documents.findById(id.value()).map(mapper::toDomain);
    }

    /**
     * Saves the aggregate and returns it rebuilt from the stored document, with the new version.
     *
     * <p>The version is copied from the aggregate into the document. Without that copy, every
     * save would be sent as an insert. The service assigns the IDs, so the insert of a stored
     * aggregate would fail with {@code DuplicateKeyException} instead of a version conflict.
     */
    @Override
    public A save(A aggregate) {
        D document = mapper.toDocument(aggregate);
        document.setId(aggregate.id().value());
        document.setVersion(aggregate.version());
        return mapper.toDomain(documents.save(document));
    }

    @Override
    public boolean exists(ID id) {
        return documents.existsById(id.value());
    }
Reading the code
public abstract class MongoAggregateRepository<A extends AggregateRoot<ID>, ID extends Identifier, D extends BaseDocument>

The class has three type parameters. A is the aggregate root, ID its typed identifier, and D its document. The limits make sure that each one has what the class needs, such as a version.

protected final MongoRepository<D, String> documents;

This is a Spring Data repository for the document. Its ID type is String, because the typed OrderId is stored as its text.

return documents.findById(id.value()).map(mapper::toDomain);

findById returns an Optional. map converts the document into an aggregate only when one was found. mapper::toDomain is a method reference to the mapper's method.

document.setVersion(aggregate.version());

The base class copies the ID and the version from the aggregate into the new document. So Spring Data knows whether to insert or to update, and which version to check.

return mapper.toDomain(documents.save(document));

documents.save writes the document and sets its new version. The base class then rebuilds the aggregate from that document. So the caller gets a new Order with the new version.

The comment above save says what a missing copy of the version would do. The order's ID is assigned by the service, so a save with no version is an insert of an existing ID. That insert fails with a duplicate key, not with a version conflict. The section The order that was passed to save shows the run. Only an aggregate whose ID the database generates would get a second document without an error.

The order's adapter extends the base class, and adds the two list queries of the port:

@Component
class OrderPersistenceAdapter extends MongoAggregateRepository<Order, OrderId, OrderDocument> implements OrderRepository {

    private static final Sort NEWEST_FIRST = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "placedAt");

    private final OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments;

    OrderPersistenceAdapter(OrderMongoRepository orderDocuments, OrderDocumentMapper mapper) {
        super(orderDocuments, mapper);
        this.orderDocuments = orderDocuments;
    }

    @Override
    public PageResult<Order> findAll(PageQuery page) {
        return toPageResult(orderDocuments.findAll(pageable(page, NEWEST_FIRST)));
    }

    @Override
    public PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page) {
        return toPageResult(orderDocuments.findByStatus(status.name(), pageable(page, NEWEST_FIRST)));
    }
}
Reading the code
class OrderPersistenceAdapter extends MongoAggregateRepository<Order, OrderId, OrderDocument> implements OrderRepository {

The adapter inherits load, save and exists, and implements the port. It is package-private, so a use case can only reach it through OrderRepository.

private static final Sort NEWEST_FIRST = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "placedAt");

Sort is Spring Data's description of a sort order. Every list query names its order, because Amazon DocumentDB guarantees no order of results without one, as of October 2026.

super(orderDocuments, mapper);

The constructor passes the Spring Data repository and the mapper to the base class. It also keeps the repository with its own type, because only OrderMongoRepository has findByStatus.

The port declares only what a use case calls. It has no saveAll, because no use case saves several orders at once. A method that no one calls still needs code, tests and care in every adapter. The same rule keeps the light style small. Its repository declares only the two queries that the note service uses.

The same thinking applies to an annotation that repeats a default. The stock client's response record keeps @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true), although the JSON setup of Spring Boot already ignores unknown fields. It stays, because it states the rule where a reader looks. For that record, see the chapter Calling other services.

The same base class can be written in C#, with generics and constraints. The important part is the mapper. The base class never stores the aggregate itself. It stores a document that a mapper built.

The light style: the note is its own documenttwist#

The note feature uses the light style. The class Note holds the rules, and it is also the stored document. It carries the Spring Data annotations itself. Its constructor is marked @PersistenceCreator, and its list of events is @Transient. For the class and each annotation, see the section The light level: the note feature.

Storage needs four things from a light-style entity:

NeedHow Note meets itWhy storage needs it
a way to create a stored notethe constructor marked @PersistenceCreatorSpring Data calls it with the stored values, and it applies no rules
a version that can change@Version private Long version, not finalSpring Data writes the new version into the object after each save
nothing stored that is not data@Transient on the list of eventsthe events are published after the save, and never stored
a stable stored name for each fieldthe field names, which are the stored namesrenaming a field of the entity renames the stored field

The last row is the price of the light style. In the full style, a field of the domain can be renamed freely, because the document keeps its own names. In the light style, a renamed field stores new documents under the new name, and reads old documents with the field missing. Keep the stored name with @Field("oldName") on the renamed field. @Field stores a field under another name. For the annotation, see the section What the stored document holds.

A test checks that the events are not stored:

@Test
void storesTheNoteButNotItsEvents() {
    Note note = Note.create(ORDER_ID, "Call back", "DELIVERY", true, "agent-1", CLOCK);   // one event pending

    notes.save(note);

    Document stored = mongo.findById(note.id(), Document.class, "notes");
    assertThat(stored).doesNotContainKey("events").containsEntry("orderId", ORDER_ID);
    Note loaded = notes.findById(note.id()).orElseThrow();
    assertThat(loaded.pullEvents()).isEmpty();
    assertThat(loaded.needsAction()).isTrue();
}
Reading the code
Document stored = mongo.findById(note.id(), Document.class, "notes");

This line reads the stored note as a raw org.bson.Document, not as a Note. A Document is a map of field names to values. So the test sees exactly what is in the database.

assertThat(stored).doesNotContainKey("events").containsEntry("orderId", ORDER_ID);

The stored note has no field events. It does have the order's ID.

assertThat(loaded.pullEvents()).isEmpty();

A note that is loaded has no pending events. Only a change raises events.

The note service injects the Spring Data repository NoteRepository directly. It has no port and no adapter. So the service can call every method that Spring Data offers, such as deleteAll. The light style accepts that risk in exchange for less code. Code review guards it.

The reference feature goes one step further. ReferenceItemDocument is a record with its own @Id, and it does not extend BaseDocument. Lookup values are only read by the service, and the migrations write them. Nothing can change a lookup value at the same time, so it needs no version. For that level, see the section The simple level: the reference feature.

The types to storetwist#

A document outlives the code that wrote it. In a year, a new version of the service reads documents that the old version wrote. Another team may read them with a script. So the service stores plain types whose meaning does not depend on a Java class:

Value in the domainStored asWhy
OrderStatus, an enuma string, such as "PAID"the value is readable, and the enum class can move or be renamed
DeliveryMethod and ProductCode, value objectsa string, the codethe code is the business value, and the Java wrapper is not stored
OrderId, LineId and PaymentReferencea stringthe ID is text in every service that refers to it
Moneya Decimal128 amount and a string currencythe amount stays exact, and the currency stays with it
Instant, a point in timea BSON datea BSON date is a point in time in UTC, so it matches Instant
a calendar date, such as a birthdayan ISO string, such as "2026-10-25"a calendar date has no time zone, so it must not become a point in time

BSON is the binary format of MongoDB documents. It has types that JSON lacks, such as dates and Decimal128.

The enum is stored by its name. The MongoDB .NET driver stores a C# enum as a number by default. In a run for this book, it stored "Status": 0. A number breaks when someone reorders the constants. A name breaks only when someone renames a constant, and then valueOf fails loudly.

Money uses Decimal128, which keeps every decimal digit exactly. A double cannot hold 0.1 exactly. The document says so on its field, with @Field(targetType = FieldType.DECIMAL128). The platform also sets the representation for every BigDecimal, and for every universally unique identifier (UUID):

# How UUIDs are stored. The driver has no default, so writing a UUID fails without this.
# Spring Modulith's outbox stores each publication's ID as a UUID.
spring.mongodb.representation.uuid=standard

# Store every BigDecimal as DECIMAL128, so money stays exact even where a field has no
# @Field(targetType = DECIMAL128), for example in an event stored in the outbox.
spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimal=decimal128
Reading the code
spring.mongodb.representation.uuid=standard

A UUID can be stored in more than one binary form, and standard names one of them. The service's own IDs are strings. The outbox of Spring Modulith stores real UUIDs. Spring Boot's upgrade notes for Boot 4 say that an explicit configuration is expected for both representations.

spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimal=decimal128

Boot 4 sets no representation for a BigDecimal, and a run stored it as a Decimal128 anyway. The platform states the choice, so a later default cannot change it. An event in the outbox has no @Field, so only this setting covers its amounts.

A run for this book checked the comment. It used Boot 4.1.2 with the MongoDB driver 5.8.1, and no representation set. It inserted a record with a UUID field through MongoTemplate. Then it inserted a raw Document with a UUID value. Both inserts failed before anything reached the database:

org.bson.codecs.configuration.CodecConfigurationException: The uuidRepresentation has not been specified, so the UUID cannot be encoded.#
Means
The driver has no default form for a UUID, and no setting chose one.
Fix
Set spring.mongodb.representation.uuid=standard, as the platform does. Use another value only for data that older code wrote in another form.

So the platform's setting is not a detail. Without it, the outbox could not store its first event, because each publication has a UUID as its ID.

Boot 3 stored a BigDecimal as a string. For what an upgrade from Boot 3 means for stored amounts, see the section Money: how a BigDecimal is stored.

A calendar date needs care. A run for this book stored the LocalDate 3 October 2026 as 2026-10-02T23:00:00Z, on a machine in British summer time. Spring Data converted the date through the time zone of the machine. Another machine, in another time zone, would read it as another date. So store a LocalDate as its ISO text, with date.toString(), and read it with LocalDate.parse(text). In the full style, the mapper does that, and the document has a String field. In the light style, the entity keeps the String field and returns a LocalDate from its method. The order has no calendar date, so the companion has no code for it.

An Instant has no such problem. It is a point in time, and a BSON date is one too. The order stores placedAt and paidAt as dates, so queries can sort and compare them.

An embedded field named idtwist#

Each line of an order has an ID, because warehouse staff pick one line at a time. The obvious name for that field is id. The service names it lineId instead:

/**
 * An embedded line. Its ID field is named {@code lineId}, not {@code id}: Spring Data maps a
 * property named {@code id} to {@code _id}, even in an embedded document, so queries written
 * outside Spring Data, and tools such as mongosh, would not find {@code lines.id}.
 */
static class LineDocument {
    String lineId;
    String productCode;
    int quantity;
    Instant pickedAt;
}

Spring Data stores a field named id as _id, also inside an embedded document. The MongoDB .NET driver does the same with a property named Id of a nested class. A run for this book measured what this means, with a line class whose field was named id:

Who asksThe queryFound the order
Spring Data, with where("lines.id").is("L1")sent {"lines._id": "L1"}yes
Spring Data, the derived findByLinesId("L1")sent {"lines._id": "L1"}yes
the raw driver, or mongosh, or another service{lines.id: "L1"}no, the count was 0
a document written by another program as {lines: [{id: "L9"}]}read through Spring Datathe field was dropped, and the line's id was null
a line id of 24 hexadecimal charactersstored as an ObjectId, not as a stringSpring's own queries match, but a query with the string does not

So Spring's own code works, and everything else fails without an error. That includes an index that a migration names directly as lines.id. An ObjectId is the binary ID type of MongoDB.

There are two fixes. Give the field another name, as the shop does with lineId. Or keep the name and write @Field("id") on it. The run tested it on a list named marks. With @Field("id"), the field was stored as id. The query of Spring Data then used marks.id. The shop prefers the other name, because it reads the same in Java, in the database and in every tool. Spring Data's reference does not mention the rule for embedded documents. Only the runs show it.

A test checks the stored shape against a real MongoDB:

@Test
void storesPlainTypesAndNamesTheLineIdLineId() {
    Order order = newOrder();
    order.recordPayment(payment(NOW));
    orders.save(order);

    Document stored = mongo.findById(order.id().value(), Document.class, "orders");

    assertThat(stored.getList("lines", Document.class).getFirst()).containsKey("lineId").doesNotContainKey("_id");
    assertThat(stored.get("lastPayment", Document.class).get("amount")).isInstanceOf(Decimal128.class);
    assertThat(stored.getString("status")).isEqualTo("PAID");
}
Reading the code
stored.getList("lines", Document.class).getFirst()

The stored lines are a list of embedded documents. getFirst() returns the first element of a list. It is new in Java 21.

.containsKey("lineId").doesNotContainKey("_id");

The line stores lineId, and no _id.

.isInstanceOf(Decimal128.class);

The amount is a Decimal128, not a string and not a double.

Optimistic locking with @Versiontwist#

Two warehouse workers open the same order. The first picks a line and saves. The second cancels the order a moment later, with the copy that they loaded before the pick. Without a check, the second save would write the old line status back, and the pick would be lost. This is called a lost update.

The fix is called optimistic locking. Each document carries a version number. A save succeeds only if the stored version is still the one that was loaded. Otherwise someone else saved in between, and the save fails. In .NET with the MongoDB driver, you write this check yourself. In Spring Data, one annotation does it:

MongoDB .NET driver
long expected = order.Version;
order.Version = expected + 1;
ReplaceOneResult result = await orders.ReplaceOneAsync(
    o => o.Id == order.Id && o.Version == expected, order);
if (result.MatchedCount == 0)
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException("Someone else changed the order.");
}
Spring Data MongoDB
public abstract class BaseDocument {

    @Id
    private String id;

    @Version
    private Long version;
Reading the code
o => o.Id == order.Id && o.Version == expected, order);

The C# filter matches the document only when its version is still the expected one. A run for this book showed what happens with a stale copy. Nothing threw, and the result said matched=0 modified=0. So the C# code must check MatchedCount itself.

@Id

This @Id is from org.springframework.data.annotation. It maps the field to _id.

@Version

This annotation is from the same package. Spring Data adds the version to the filter of every update, and raises it by one. When nothing matches, Spring Data throws OptimisticLockingFailureException.

private Long version;

The type is the wrapper Long, not the primitive long. A null version means "never saved". The table below shows why that matters.

The closest match in .NET is the MongoDB EF Core Provider. It supports [ConcurrencyCheck] and row versioning with [Timestamp]. On a conflict, the SaveChanges method of EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. The plain driver has no version support in its documentation, as of October 2026.

A run for this book measured what Spring Data MongoDB 5.1.2 does with a version field:

CaseWhat Spring Data sentThe result
a Long version that is nullan insertstored with version 0, even when the ID was already set
a primitive long versionan insertstored with version 1, because 0 counts as never saved
a version that is seta full replacement, filtered on _id and the old versionthe version went up by one, and there was no $set
a stale versionthe same replacement, which matched nothingOptimisticLockingFailureException, and the stored document was unchanged
a mutable classsavethe same object came back, with the new version set on it
a record, or a class with final fields and no setterssavea new object came back, and the object passed in kept its old version
a failed save of a mutable objectsavethe object's version was raised before the update was sent

The exception in the run said Cannot save entity m-1 with version 2 to collection v_mutable; Has it been modified meanwhile. The message names version 2, although the filter asked for version 1. Spring Data had already raised the version on the object.

org.springframework.dao.OptimisticLockingFailureException: Cannot save entity m-1 with version 2 to collection v_mutable; Has it been modified meanwhile#
Means
Someone saved the document after this copy was loaded. The stored document is unchanged.
Fix
Load the aggregate again, apply the change again, and save that. Never save the failed copy a second time.

The last row of the table is the trap of the light style. The note service saves a mutable Note. After a failed save, the note already holds the newer version. A second save of the same object would pass the check and overwrite the other change. For that trap and its test, see the section Versions after a save.

The full style is safe from this trap. The mapper builds a new OrderDocument for every save. A failed save raises the version of that document, and the document is thrown away. The Order keeps its old version, because the field is final. A retry with the same order sends the old version again, and fails again. It never overwrites.

The order that was passed to savetrap#

A use case saves an order, and then changes it again. The repository's save returns a new Order. A C# developer is used to an entity that the save updates in place.

PredictSaving the same order a second time#
The test then saves original a second time. What happens?
Order original = newOrder();

Order saved = orders.save(original);
saved.pickLine(saved.lines().getFirst().id(), CLOCK);
Order savedAgain = orders.save(saved);
Show the answer
The save throws DuplicateKeyException.

The order passed to save keeps the version it had. original was never saved before, so its version is null. The version field is final, so the save cannot change it. The base class copies null into the document. Spring Data sees no version and sends an insert. The order's _id exists already, so the insert fails with error 11000.

Continue with the order that save returns, as saved does here. With an ID from the database, the second insert would succeed silently, as a second document.

The test is OrderPersistenceAdapterIT.saveReturnsTheStoredCopyWithTheNewVersion. It also checks that saved has version 0, and savedAgain version 1.

The failure depends on the version of the stale order. An order that was never saved has the version null, so its second save is an insert, and it fails with a duplicate key. An order that was loaded has a version, so its second save is an update with the old version, and it fails with OptimisticLockingFailureException. Either way, nothing is overwritten. The service's use cases continue with the copy that save returns. For that rule in the use cases, see the section Continue with the saved copy.

org.springframework.dao.DuplicateKeyException: ... E11000 duplicate key error collection: research.v_mutable index: _id_ dup key: { _id: "m-1" }#
Means
Spring Data sent an insert, because the document had no version. A document with that ID exists already.
Fix
Save the copy that the last save returned. Check that the mapper or the base class copies the version into the document.

A conflict inside a transactiontrap#

Most use cases of the order service run in a transaction. Inside a transaction, MongoDB usually finds the conflict before Spring Data checks the version. A test shows the second shape of the same conflict:

/**
 * Inside transactions, the same conflict shows up earlier and differently: MongoDB aborts the
 * second writer with a write conflict, which Spring translates to
 * {@code DataIntegrityViolationException}. The platform answers both with 409.
 */
@Test
void aConcurrentUpdateInsideTransactionsIsAWriteConflict() throws Exception {
    Order saved = orders.save(newOrder());
    TransactionTemplate transactions = new TransactionTemplate(transactionManager);
    CountDownLatch firstHasWritten = new CountDownLatch(1);
    CountDownLatch secondHasTried = new CountDownLatch(1);

    CompletableFuture<Void> first = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
        Order copy = orders.get(saved.id());
        copy.cancel(CLOCK);
        orders.save(copy);
        firstHasWritten.countDown();
        await(secondHasTried);          // keep the transaction open while the second one writes
    }));
    firstHasWritten.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    Throwable secondError = null;
    try {
        transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            Order copy = orders.get(saved.id());
            copy.pickLine(copy.lines().getFirst().id(), CLOCK);
            orders.save(copy);
        });
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        secondError = e;
    } finally {
        secondHasTried.countDown();
    }
    first.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

    assertThat(secondError).isNotNull();
    assertThat(WriteConflicts.isTranslatedWriteConflict(secondError)).as(String.valueOf(secondError)).isTrue();
    assertThat(orders.get(saved.id()).status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
}
Reading the code
TransactionTemplate transactions = new TransactionTemplate(transactionManager);

A TransactionTemplate runs a block of code in a transaction. For the class, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

CountDownLatch firstHasWritten = new CountDownLatch(1);

A CountDownLatch lets one thread wait until another thread calls countDown(). The two latches force the order of events. The first transaction writes, and stays open while the second transaction tries.

CompletableFuture<Void> first = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {

The first transaction runs on another thread. It cancels the order and saves it, but does not commit yet.

copy.pickLine(copy.lines().getFirst().id(), CLOCK);

The second transaction loaded the same version. It picks a line and saves.

assertThat(WriteConflicts.isTranslatedWriteConflict(secondError)).as(String.valueOf(secondError)).isTrue();

The second save failed with a write conflict, not with OptimisticLockingFailureException. The cancelled order stayed.

The research for this book ran the same race. MongoDB aborted the second writer with error 112, WriteConflict, labelled TransientTransactionError. Spring translated it to DataIntegrityViolationException. The second writer failed in this way also when the first transaction had already committed, but only after the second one started. So catch (OptimisticLockingFailureException e) around a transactional use case misses these conflicts. For every case that the research measured, see the section Write conflicts, and what Spring retries.

The platform answers both shapes with the same 409 response:

@ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> staleVersion(OptimisticLockingFailureException ex) {
    return conflict();
}

@ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> dataIntegrity(DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
    if (WriteConflicts.isWriteConflict(ex)) {
        return conflict();
    }
    log.error("Unexpected data error", ex);
    return ResponseEntity.internalServerError().body(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
            "Internal error", "Something went wrong. Quote the traceId if you contact support."));
}
Reading the code
@ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)

A stale version outside a transaction becomes 409 with the code CONCURRENT_UPDATE.

if (WriteConflicts.isWriteConflict(ex)) {

DataIntegrityViolationException also covers real data errors. So the handler checks the cause for error 112 or the label. Only a write conflict becomes 409. Every other data error is a 500.

The agent sees the text "Someone else changed this at the same time. Reload it and try again." The handler is in the platform's mongo package, next to the technology that throws the exceptions. The web code of the platform knows nothing about MongoDB. For whether the service should retry a write conflict itself, see the section Write conflicts, and what Spring retries.

Queries from method namestwist#

Each feature declares its queries as methods of a Spring Data repository. Spring Data writes the implementation when the application starts. It reads the query from the name of the method:

MongoDB .NET driver
IFindFluent<Note, Note> page = notes.Find(n => n.OrderId == orderId);

long open = await notes.CountDocumentsAsync(n =>
    n.OrderId == orderId && n.ActionRequired && n.ActionResolvedAt == null);
Spring Data MongoDB
public interface NoteRepository extends MongoRepository<Note, String> {

    Page<Note> findByOrderId(String orderId, Pageable pageable);

    /** Counts the notes on an order that still need action. Spring Data reads the rule from the name. */
    long countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull(String orderId);
}
Reading the code
public interface NoteRepository extends MongoRepository<Note, String> {

MongoRepository brings the usual methods, such as save and findById. Note is the stored type, and String is the type of its ID.

Page<Note> findByOrderId(String orderId, Pageable pageable);

findBy starts a query, and OrderId names the field orderId. The Pageable adds the page and the sort. See the section Paging.

long countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull(String orderId);

countBy returns a number instead of documents. The name has three conditions, joined by And. OrderId takes the parameter. ActionRequiredTrue asks for actionRequired to be true. ActionResolvedAtIsNull asks for no resolution time.

In C#, the query is a lambda, and the driver turns it into a filter. In Java, the query is the method name. A Java lambda cannot be read as data, so it cannot describe a query.

The other two features declare one query each. The order's query takes the status as a string, because the document stores a string:

interface OrderMongoRepository extends MongoRepository<OrderDocument, String> {

    Page<OrderDocument> findByStatus(String status, Pageable pageable);
}

The adapter calls findByStatus with status.name(), and the domain never sees the string.

The reference feature names its sort in the method name:

@Cacheable("reference-data")
List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);

OrderByCodeAsc adds a sort on code. In a run for this book, findByStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc sent the filter {"status": "NEW"} with the sort {"placedAt": -1}. @Cacheable keeps the result in a cache. For the cache, see the chapter Caching and scheduling.

Each query of the service has an index, created by a migration. A query without an index reads the whole collection. For the indexes, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data. For more about derived queries, see the section Repositories and derived queries.

Pagingtwist#

An agent lists the orders that are paid, twenty at a time. The domain asks for a page with its own type, PageQuery, which knows nothing about Spring. The base class converts it into Spring Data's types, and the result back:

protected static Pageable pageable(PageQuery query, Sort sort) {
    return PageRequest.of(query.page(), query.size(), sort);
}

protected PageResult<A> toPageResult(Page<D> page) {
    return new PageResult<>(page.map(mapper::toDomain).getContent(),
            page.getNumber(), page.getSize(), page.getTotalElements());
}
Reading the code
return PageRequest.of(query.page(), query.size(), sort);

PageRequest implements Pageable. It holds the page number, counted from 0, the page size, and the sort.

page.map(mapper::toDomain).getContent(),

Page.map converts each document into an aggregate, and keeps the paging numbers. getContent() returns the items of this page as a list.

page.getNumber(), page.getSize(), page.getTotalElements());

These are the page number, the page size, and the number of items on all pages. PageResult is the platform's own type, so the domain port returns no Spring type.

A run for this book measured a Page query. For page 1 with a size of 2, Spring Data sent a find with skip 2 and limit 2, and then a count. The count was an aggregation with $match and $group. On the last page, which held fewer items than the page size, Spring Data sent no count. It already knew the total.

So a Page costs two queries on most pages. The order service shows the total in its responses, so it pays for the count.

The light style does the same conversion in the service, because it has no adapter:

public PageResult<NoteView> list(String orderId, PageQuery page) {
    orders.requireExists(orderId);
    Page<Note> found = notes.findByOrderId(orderId, PageRequest.of(page.page(), page.size(), NEWEST_FIRST));
    return new PageResult<>(found.getContent(), found.getNumber(), found.getSize(), found.getTotalElements())
            .map(NoteView::from);
}

PageRequest.of builds the Pageable here, and PageResult.map turns each note into a view.

MongoTemplate for writes that are not aggregatesnew#

Some writes store no aggregate. The inbox checks a key and inserts it. The audit log inserts a record. The migration runner inserts a lock. A Spring Data repository needs a class for each of them. MongoTemplate needs none. It works with raw org.bson.Document values and a collection name:

import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Criteria.where;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Query.query;
// ...
        try {
            transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                if (mongo.exists(query(where("_id").is(key)), COLLECTION)) {
                    log.info("Skipping event {}, which was processed before", event.eventId());
                    return;
                }
                handler.accept(event);
                mongo.insert(new Document("_id", key).append("processedAt", clock.instant()), COLLECTION);
            });
Reading the code
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Criteria.where;

A static import lets the code write where(...) instead of Criteria.where(...). C# has using static for the same purpose.

mongo.exists(query(where("_id").is(key)), COLLECTION)

where("_id").is(key) builds a Criteria, one condition. query(...) wraps it in a Query. exists asks whether any document in the collection matches.

mongo.insert(new Document("_id", key).append("processedAt", clock.instant()), COLLECTION);

new Document(...) builds a raw document. append adds a field and returns the same document. insert writes it into the named collection.

The research for this book measured the template's raw methods:

CallWhat happened
insert(document, "seed")the same Document came back, with an ObjectId in _id when it had none
insert(document) with no collection nameMappingException, because the template cannot know the collection of a raw Document
upsert(query, new Update().set(...).setOnInsert(...), "seed")one update with upsert true, which inserted the first time and updated after
the same upsert with unchanged valuesmatched 1 and modified 0, which is not an error
where("type").is("a").and("type").is("b")InvalidMongoDbApiUsageException, because one Criteria cannot hold the same field twice
updateFirst(query, new Update().set("status", PAID), Order.class)a $set on one field, while save replaces the whole document

MongoTemplate has the same purpose as IMongoDatabase and IMongoCollection<T> in the MongoDB .NET driver. Update describes a change to some fields, such as set or inc. A repository's save always replaces the whole document. So use Update when only one field changes and no aggregate rule is involved. The seed data of the reference feature is written this way, with upsert. For that code, see the section Seed data, upserted by a natural key.

Never change an aggregate with Update. An update of one field skips the rules of the aggregate, and it skips the version check. Change an aggregate only through the root, and save the whole aggregate.

MongoTemplate also joins the transaction that is running on the thread. So the inbox key, the audit record and the change are committed together. For transactions, see the chapter Transactions in depth. For more methods, see the section MongoTemplate for the rest.

Changing the shape of stored documentsnew#

A new version of the service adds a field to the order, such as a delivery note. Orders that were stored before have no such field. A relational database would need a column added before the release. A document database accepts the new field at once, and the old documents stay as they are. So the code must deal with both shapes.

There are two ways, and the choice depends on the field:

WayWhat to doChoose it when
handle the missing field on loadthe mapper treats a missing value as "none", or gives it a defaultthe field is optional in the domain, such as a note to the courier
migrate the stored documentsa migration sets the default in every old documentevery order must have the value, or a query must find old documents by it

The mapper already handles one missing value. An order that was never paid has no lastPayment, so the mapper returns no payment:

return document == null ? null : new Payment(new PaymentReference(document.reference),

A new optional field works the same way. The document field is null in old documents, and the mapper turns null into "none" in the domain. A field with a primitive type, such as int, cannot be null. Use the wrapper type, such as Integer, for a field that old documents lack.

A required field needs a migration. The migration runs once, before the new code takes traffic, and writes the default into every document that lacks the field. A migration of this kind should be safe to run twice, so it changes only documents where the field is missing. For migrations, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

The note got such a field. Each note now stores createdBy, the agent who wrote it, for the rule that another agent resolves its action. Notes written before have no author, and every note must have one. So a migration writes a value into the old notes:

/**
 * Gives every stored note an author. Notes written before the field {@code createdBy} existed
 * have none, and every note must have one, so they get the value {@code unknown}. Only notes
 * without the field change, so the migration is safe to run twice.
 */
@Component
class V003AddNoteAuthors implements MongoMigration {

    static final String UNKNOWN_AUTHOR = "unknown";

    @Override
    public String id() {
        return "V003-add-note-authors";
    }

    @Override
    public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        mongo.updateMulti(query(where("createdBy").exists(false)),
                new Update().set("createdBy", UNKNOWN_AUTHOR), "notes");
    }
}
Reading the code
query(where("createdBy").exists(false))

The filter selects only the notes that have no field createdBy. A second run finds none, so it changes nothing.

new Update().set("createdBy", UNKNOWN_AUTHOR)

The update sets the one field, and leaves the rest of each note as it is. The value unknown is no agent's ID, so any agent may resolve an old note.

mongo.updateMulti(

updateMulti changes every matching document in one command, on the server. The service loads no note.

A test runs it against a real MongoDB, twice:

@Test
void givesEveryOldNoteAnAuthorAndLeavesTheOthersAlone() {
    mongo.insert(new Document("_id", "old-note").append("text", "Call back"), "notes");
    mongo.insert(new Document("_id", "new-note").append("text", "Refund").append("createdBy", "agent-1"), "notes");

    new V003AddNoteAuthors().migrate(mongo);
    new V003AddNoteAuthors().migrate(mongo);   // a second run finds no note without an author

    assertThat(mongo.findById("old-note", Document.class, "notes")).containsEntry("createdBy", "unknown");
    assertThat(mongo.findById("new-note", Document.class, "notes")).containsEntry("createdBy", "agent-1");
}

The test writes raw documents, as an older version of the service would have stored them. One note has no author, and one has. After two runs, the old note has unknown, and the other note keeps its author.

Three changes are harder than adding a field:

  • Renaming a field. In the full style, rename the domain field and keep the document field. In the light style, keep the stored name with @Field("oldName").
  • Renaming an enum constant. Old documents hold the old name, and valueOf fails on it. Migrate the stored values first, or map the old name in the mapper.
  • Changing a type. For example, an amount stored as a string by Boot 3 becomes a Decimal128 on Boot 4. One collection then holds both forms. Convert the old documents in a migration.

The full style has one more option. The mapper can read two shapes, such as an old field and a new one, while a migration converts the documents. The domain never sees the old shape.

The connection string and the Boot 4 keytrap#

The connection string comes from an environment variable. Each environment sets its own:

mongodb:
  # The Spring Boot 4 key. Boot 4 ignores the old spring.data.mongodb.uri without a warning.
  # DocumentDB: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<cluster>:27017/orders?tls=true&replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=primary
  # The platform forces retryWrites=false, which DocumentDB needs.
  uri: ${MONGO_URI}
Reading the code
mongodb:

This key is under spring:, so the full name is spring.mongodb.uri. Boot 4 moved every connection key from spring.data.mongodb to spring.mongodb.

uri: ${MONGO_URI}

${MONGO_URI} reads the environment variable MONGO_URI. The deployment sets it from the secrets manager, because the string holds a password.

Gotcha

Boot 4 ignores spring.data.mongodb.uri without a warning. Boot 4 deprecated the old key at the level "error", so it has no effect. In a run for this book, an application had only the old key, with a working URI. The client went to localhost:27017, the default, and failed with "Connection refused". Nothing was logged about the old key. A service that was upgraded from Boot 3 works on a laptop with a local MongoDB, and fails in every other environment.

A test catches the mistake without Docker. The wiring test starts the whole application, and checks the address that Boot will use:

/** Spring Boot 4 reads spring.mongodb.uri; the old spring.data.mongodb.uri would be ignored silently. */
@Test
void usesTheConfiguredMongoUri() {
    ConnectionString used = context.getBean(MongoConnectionDetails.class).getConnectionString();

    assertThat(used.getHosts()).containsExactly("localhost:1");
    assertThat(used.getDatabase()).isEqualTo("wiring-test");
}

MongoConnectionDetails is the bean in which Boot keeps the resolved connection. The wiring profile sets the URI to port 1 and the database wiring-test. With the old key, the test would find localhost and the database test.

The comment shows the parameters for Amazon DocumentDB, the database of Amazon Web Services (AWS). Transport Layer Security (TLS) encrypts the connection. A replica set is a primary instance that takes the writes, and replicas that copy them. Each parameter has a reason:

ParameterValueWhy
tlstrueAmazon DocumentDB uses TLS by default, and the platform trusts the AWS certificate bundle
replicaSetrs0AWS recommends connecting as a replica set, so the driver follows the cluster's instances
readPreferenceprimaryevery read goes to the primary instance, so a read sees the write before it
retryWritesfalse, forced by the platformDocumentDB supports retryable writes only from engine 8.0.2, as of October 2026

AWS says that reads from the primary are read-after-write consistent, and reads from replicas are eventually consistent. The order service often reads right after a write. An agent places an order, and the next screen shows it. So the service reads from the primary. The example connection string of the short chapter on document data uses secondaryPreferred, which spreads reads over the replicas. That suits a service with many reads that accepts slightly old data. For that parameter, see the section Two parameters that change behaviour.

AWS states that replicaSet=rs0 fails through an SSH tunnel. A developer who connects from a laptop through a tunnel removes it. For a run from an integrated development environment (IDE) against the local MongoDB, the service's README adds directConnection=true. The local replica set tells the driver that its member is mongo:27017, a name that only containers can resolve.

Driver settings that DocumentDB needstwist#

A connection string is easy to copy and easy to get wrong. A service copies a URI without retryWrites=false. AWS states that most current drivers switch retryable writes on by default. As of October 2026, every write then fails on an engine before 8.0.2, or on an elastic cluster. The platform therefore sets the driver options that DocumentDB needs in code, after the URI is applied:

MongoDB .NET driver
MongoClientSettings settings = MongoClientSettings.FromConnectionString(connectionString);
settings.RetryWrites = false;
return new MongoClient(settings);
Spring Data MongoDB
public class DocumentDbClientSettingsCustomizer implements MongoClientSettingsBuilderCustomizer {

    private final DocumentDbProperties properties;

    public DocumentDbClientSettingsCustomizer(DocumentDbProperties properties) {
        this.properties = properties;
    }

    @Override
    public void customize(MongoClientSettings.Builder settings) {
        settings.retryWrites(false);
        if (StringUtils.hasText(properties.getCaBundle())) {
            SSLContext sslContext = sslContextTrusting(Path.of(properties.getCaBundle()));
            settings.applyToSslSettings(ssl -> ssl.enabled(true).context(sslContext));
        }
    }
Reading the code
public class DocumentDbClientSettingsCustomizer implements MongoClientSettingsBuilderCustomizer {

MongoClientSettingsBuilderCustomizer is a Boot interface, in the package org.springframework.boot.mongodb.autoconfigure. Boot calls every bean of this type while it builds the client. The platform registers this class as a bean.

settings.retryWrites(false);

This line switches retryable writes off. A retryable write is a write that the driver sends once more after a network error. A run showed that this line wins over retryWrites=true in spring.mongodb.uri.

if (StringUtils.hasText(properties.getCaBundle())) {

hasText is true for a string that is not null and not blank. Locally, no bundle is set, and the connection uses no TLS.

settings.applyToSslSettings(ssl -> ssl.enabled(true).context(sslContext));

With a bundle, the driver uses TLS, and trusts the certificates in the bundle. See the section TLS with the AWS certificate bundle.

Boot calls the customizers after it has applied the connection string. The run confirmed it. Without the customizer, an insert carried "txnNumber": 1, the mark of a retryable write. With the customizer, the insert had none. In C#, you set RetryWrites on MongoClientSettings yourself, in the code that builds the client.

Boot's documentation names a limit. If a service defines its own MongoClientSettings bean, Boot uses it without modification. So the customizer would change nothing, and a service must never declare that bean.

A unit test checks the setting with no database:

@Test
void turnsRetryableWritesOffWhateverTheConnectionStringSays() {
    MongoClientSettings.Builder settings = MongoClientSettings.builder()
            .applyConnectionString(new ConnectionString("mongodb://localhost/shop?retryWrites=true"));

    new DocumentDbClientSettingsCustomizer(new DocumentDbProperties()).customize(settings);

    MongoClientSettings built = settings.build();
    assertThat(built.getRetryWrites()).isFalse();
    assertThat(built.getSslSettings().isEnabled()).isFalse();
}

The test builds the settings from a URI with retryWrites=true, runs the customizer, and expects getRetryWrites() to be false. With no bundle, TLS stays off.

Pragmatic choice: Retryable writes off on every cluster

The strict rule. Configure each environment for what its database supports. From engine version 8.0.2, Amazon DocumentDB supports retryable writes, as of October 2026.

What we do. The platform switches retryable writes off for every service and every cluster, whatever the connection string says.

Why. On an engine before 8.0.2, and on an elastic cluster, every write fails with retryable writes on. One setting in the platform removes that failure for every service. The writes that matter most run in transactions, and AWS states that writes inside a transaction are not retryable anyway.

When to stop. Stop when every cluster of the company runs engine 8.0.2 or later on instance-based clusters. Then retryable writes protect single writes outside a transaction from a failover, and the line can go.

TLS with the AWS certificate bundletrap#

Amazon DocumentDB uses TLS by default. The driver must trust the certificate authority (CA) that signed the cluster's certificate. AWS publishes the CA certificates in one file, global-bundle.pem. The deployment mounts that file, and sets one property:

/**
 * The path of the AWS certificate bundle, such as {@code /certs/global-bundle.pem}. The
 * deployment mounts the file and sets this property. Leave it empty locally.
 */
private String caBundle;

The field caBundle is bound from platform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundle. The deployment sets it with the environment variable PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLE.

Gotcha

The Java driver ignores tlsCAFile in the connection string. AWS's connection strings for other languages contain tlsCAFile. AWS's Java page shows it in a URI too, as of October 2026. But the MongoDB Java driver's TLS page lists no such parameter. In a run against a MongoDB that accepts only TLS, a URI with tlsCAFile failed with "PKIX path building failed". It failed exactly as with no trust at all. So the trust must come from code or from Boot.

The platform builds the trust from the file:

private static SSLContext sslContextTrusting(Path pemFile) {
    try (InputStream pem = Files.newInputStream(pemFile)) {
        Collection<? extends Certificate> certificates =
                CertificateFactory.getInstance("X.509").generateCertificates(pem);
        if (certificates.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("The DocumentDB CA bundle " + pemFile + " holds no certificate");
        }
        KeyStore trustStore = KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType());
        trustStore.load(null, null);
        int index = 0;
        for (Certificate certificate : certificates) {
            trustStore.setCertificateEntry("documentdb-ca-" + index++, certificate);
        }
        TrustManagerFactory trustManagers = TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm());
        trustManagers.init(trustStore);
        SSLContext sslContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS");
        sslContext.init(null, trustManagers.getTrustManagers(), null);
        return sslContext;
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not read the DocumentDB CA bundle " + pemFile, e);
    } catch (GeneralSecurityException e) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("The DocumentDB CA bundle " + pemFile + " is not valid", e);
    }
}
Reading the code
try (InputStream pem = Files.newInputStream(pemFile)) {

This is a try-with-resources statement. It closes the stream at the end, like using in C#. Files.newInputStream opens the file at the Path.

CertificateFactory.getInstance("X.509").generateCertificates(pem);

CertificateFactory reads certificates in the X.509 format. generateCertificates reads every certificate in the file, not only the first. The AWS bundle holds many.

KeyStore trustStore = KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType());

A KeyStore holds keys and certificates. Here it is a trust store, which holds only the certificates to trust. load(null, null) creates it empty, in memory.

trustStore.setCertificateEntry("documentdb-ca-" + index++, certificate);

Each certificate needs a name, called an alias. The loop numbers them.

TrustManagerFactory trustManagers = TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm());

A TrustManagerFactory creates the objects that decide whether a server's certificate is trusted. init(trustStore) makes them trust exactly the certificates of the store.

SSLContext sslContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS");

An SSLContext holds the TLS settings of a connection. init gives it the trust managers. The first null means that the service sends no client certificate.

throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not read the DocumentDB CA bundle " + pemFile, e);

IOException is a checked exception, and customize may not throw one. UncheckedIOException wraps it as an unchecked exception. The startup fails, with the file name in the message.

These classes are part of the Java Development Kit (JDK), in java.security and javax.net.ssl. AWS's instructions for C# import the same certificates into the Windows root store, as global-bundle.p7b. The Java code builds a store of trusted certificates in memory, and gives it to this one connection.

Two tests check the trust. trustsTheCaBundleWhenOneIsConfigured loads a test CA and finds TLS on, with a context. failsAtStartupWhenTheCaBundleIsMissing names a file that does not exist, and expects UncheckedIOException with the file name. So a wrong mount fails at startup, not at the first query.

There are two other ways, and both work. Both were tested against a MongoDB that accepts only TLS:

WayHowWhat it gets rightWhy the platform does not use it
a Boot SSL bundlespring.ssl.bundle.pem.docdb.truststore.certificate and spring.mongodb.ssl.bundle=docdbconfiguration only, and Boot loads every certificate of the PEM fileevery service repeats two settings, and the platform cannot test them once
a JVM trust storea JKS file made with keytool, and -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStoreno code, and the way that AWS's Java guide describesevery host needs the file and its password, and the setting lives outside the service
the platform's customizerplatform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundleone property, and one tested implementation for every serviceit is code to maintain, about 30 lines

The Boot SSL bundle is the better choice for a single service without a platform library. It needs no code, and Boot supports it. For its settings, see the section Connecting to Amazon DocumentDB. For the trust store made with keytool, see the section A trust store made with keytool.

MongoDB locally, DocumentDB in productiontrap#

Amazon DocumentDB runs only inside AWS. AWS offers no local edition, as of October 2026. So developers and tests use MongoDB, which offers the same API. The local environment pins the image:

# Stands in for DocumentDB. Use the MongoDB version that your DocumentDB cluster is compatible with.
# It runs as a single-node replica set, because transactions need one.
mongo:
  image: mongo:8.0.34
  command: ["--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]

--replSet rs0 starts MongoDB as a replica set named rs0. A driver sees a DocumentDB cluster under the same name.

DocumentDB emulates the MongoDB API on its own engine. As of October 2026, AWS lists engine versions 3.6, 4.0, 5.0 and 8.0. Engine 3.6 reached its end of life in March 2026. Engine 8.0 also supports applications built with the MongoDB API versions 6.0 and 7.0. Spring Data MongoDB 5.1 states that it is tested against MongoDB 6 to 8. So the shop uses engine 8.0 clusters, and a MongoDB 8.0 image locally.

Gotcha

A test that succeeds on MongoDB can fail on DocumentDB. MongoDB accepts features that DocumentDB lacks or changes, as of October 2026. Some examples matter for this service:

  • A transaction on DocumentDB cannot create a collection. A MongoDB 8.0 container allows it.
  • DocumentDB guarantees no order of results without a sort. A test against MongoDB cannot prove that every list query names its sort.
  • Elastic clusters have no transactions at all.
  • Spring's transaction manager opens a causally consistent session, and DocumentDB does not support causal consistency. This was never tested on a cluster.

The first item has a fix in the platform. A migration creates every collection that a transaction writes to, before the first transaction runs. For that migration, see the section The limits of a transaction on Amazon DocumentDB.

The platform's test configuration says the same in its comment:

/**
 * Starts MongoDB in Docker for a test, and points Spring Boot at it.
 *
 * <p>{@link ServiceConnection} sets the connection details from the running container, so the
 * test needs no {@code spring.mongodb.uri}. {@code withReplicaSet()} starts MongoDB as a
 * single-node replica set. Without it, MongoDB runs stand-alone and every transaction fails, but
 * DocumentDB always runs as a replica set.
 *
 * <p>MongoDB is not DocumentDB. Keep at least one test stage against a real DocumentDB cluster,
 * and use the MongoDB version your cluster is compatible with.
 */
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class MongoTestContainerConfiguration {

    public static final String IMAGE = "mongo:8.0.34";

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    MongoDBContainer mongoDbContainer() {
        return new MongoDBContainer(IMAGE).withReplicaSet();
    }
}
Reading the code
@ServiceConnection

Boot reads the address of the running container, and connects the application to it. The test sets no URI.

return new MongoDBContainer(IMAGE).withReplicaSet();

The container runs as a single-node replica set, so transactions work. See the section Testing the storage.

So the shop's tests run against MongoDB in Docker, for speed. That covers the slice tests and the journey test, which runs the whole service. The comment asks for one more stage, against a real DocumentDB cluster, before a release. Only that stage catches the differences in the list above. For the full list of differences, see the section What Amazon DocumentDB does not do and the section More differences.

Testing the storagenew#

A mapper can lose a field without a compile error. A version that is not copied breaks optimistic locking without a failing unit test. So every aggregate gets a test against a real MongoDB. The platform provides one annotation for it:

/**
 * A persistence slice test against MongoDB in Docker, with the platform's transaction manager
 * and DocumentDB settings. Name such tests {@code *IT}, because they need Docker.
 *
 * <p>Migrations are off, so each test sees only the data it writes. Add the adapter and mapper
 * under test with {@code @Import}.
 */
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
@DataMongoTest(properties = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled=false")
@ImportAutoConfiguration(PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)
@Import(MongoTestContainerConfiguration.class)
public @interface PlatformDataMongoTest {
}
Reading the code
@DataMongoTest(properties = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled=false")

@DataMongoTest is the test slice of Spring Boot for MongoDB. It starts the Spring Data repositories and MongoTemplate, and no web layer. The property switches the migration runner off.

@ImportAutoConfiguration(PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)

A slice starts only Boot's own MongoDB setup. This line adds the platform's transaction manager and the DocumentDB settings.

@Import(MongoTestContainerConfiguration.class)

This line adds the container from the section above.

The test of optimistic locking is the one that every aggregate needs. It loads two copies, changes and saves the first, and expects the second save to fail:

@Test
void rejectsAStaleCopy() {
    Order saved = orders.save(newOrder());
    Order firstCopy = orders.get(saved.id());
    Order secondCopy = orders.get(saved.id());

    firstCopy.cancel(CLOCK);
    orders.save(firstCopy);
    secondCopy.pickLine(secondCopy.lines().getFirst().id(), CLOCK);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> orders.save(secondCopy)).isInstanceOf(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class);
}

The test runs without a transaction, so the conflict is OptimisticLockingFailureException. The test in the section A conflict inside a transaction covers the other shape. The note has the same test, NoteRepositoryIT.rejectsAStaleCopyAndStillChangesItsVersion.

The test class imports only what it tests, with @Import({OrderPersistenceAdapter.class, OrderDocumentMapper.class}). The slice rolls nothing back after a test. So the tests create new orders with new IDs, and never count all documents of a collection.

Gotcha

The new MongoDBContainer starts no replica set by default. Testcontainers 2 has a new class, org.testcontainers.mongodb.MongoDBContainer. It starts a replica set only after withReplicaSet(). The old class, org.testcontainers.containers.MongoDBContainer, is deprecated and always starts one. An upgrade to Boot 4 often changes only the import. Then every transaction in the tests fails. Boot 4.1 accepts both classes with @ServiceConnection. Its support for the old class is marked for removal in Boot 4.2.0.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe order service stores its own IDs as strings. Why does the platform still set spring.mongodb.representation.uuid=standard?
The MongoDB driver has no default form for a UUID. Without the setting, a write of a UUID fails with CodecConfigurationException before it reaches the database. The outbox of Spring Modulith stores a UUID as the ID of every publication. So without the setting, the outbox could not store its first event.
2
A connection string for Amazon DocumentDB contains tlsCAFile=global-bundle.pem. What does the MongoDB Java driver do with it, and how does the platform trust the AWS certificates?
The Java driver ignores tlsCAFile. A run against a MongoDB that accepts only TLS failed exactly as with no trust at all. The platform reads the bundle file that platform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundle names, and builds an SSLContext that trusts its certificates.
3
A service on Spring Boot 4 sets only spring.data.mongodb.uri. What happens?
Boot 4 ignores the old key without a warning. The client uses the default, localhost:27017. It works on a laptop with a local MongoDB, and fails everywhere else. The key is spring.mongodb.uri.
4
Why does an embedded line of the order store its ID as lineId, not as id?
Spring Data stores a field named id as _id, also in an embedded document. Spring rewrites its own queries, but mongosh, raw driver queries, hand-named indexes and other services look for lines.id and find nothing. A run counted 0 matches.
5
TranslateWrite this query as a method of the order's persistence adapter. The domain passes an OrderStatus and a PageQuery, and gets a PageResult<Order>, newest first: 
List<OrderDocument> items = await orders.Find(o => o.Status == status)
    .SortByDescending(o => o.PlacedAt)
    .Skip(pageNumber * pageSize)
    .Limit(pageSize)
    .ToListAsync();
long total = await orders.CountDocumentsAsync(o => o.Status == status);
@Override
public PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page) {
    return toPageResult(orderDocuments.findByStatus(status.name(), pageable(page, NEWEST_FIRST)));
}

orderDocuments.findByStatus(String, Pageable) is a derived query of OrderMongoRepository. The helper pageable builds a PageRequest. NEWEST_FIRST sorts on placedAt, descending. Spring Data sends the skip, the limit and the count. toPageResult maps each document back to an Order.

Quick reference#

The storage settings of the order service, with the value the platform or the service sets:

SettingValue in the shopWhat it does
spring.mongodb.uri${MONGO_URI}the connection string, and the Boot 4 key
spring.mongodb.representation.uuidstandard, from the platformthe binary form of a stored UUID
spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimaldecimal128, from the platformstores every BigDecimal as a Decimal128, and Boot's default is unspecified
spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creationfalse, from the platformSpring creates no index at startup, because migrations create them
platform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundlenone locally, a mounted file in AWSthe CA bundle that TLS trusts
platform.mongo.migrations.enabledtrue, and false in slice and wiring testsruns the migrations at startup

Migrations, indexes and seed data#

Storing and changing data · Chapter 17· 30 min read· Quick reference

A migration is one versioned change to the database, such as new indexes or lookup values. The platform runs each migration once in each environment, at startup, before the service takes traffic. A lock lets only one instance migrate at a time. This chapter covers the runner, the lock, named indexes, unique and time-to-live (TTL) indexes, and seed data that is upserted and never deleted.

KindC#JavaNote
