Why Spring creates no index at startuptwist#

Spring Data can create indexes when the application starts. A field gets @Indexed, and Spring creates the index on the first start. The platform switches this off for every service:

# Indexes are created by migrations (MongoMigration), never by Spring at startup.
# Startup index creation is invisible, nobody reviews it, and it can block on a large collection.
spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation=false

The setting spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation keeps its old name on Boot 4. Spring Data's own default is already off, so this line states the choice where a reader sees it. For the trap of @Indexed without this setting, see the section Indexes.

Automatic index creation has a careful version, and it has real strengths. The index stands next to the field it serves. A new field with an index needs no second file. On a new, empty collection, the index is created at once. For a prototype or a small internal tool, that is the simpler choice.

The platform still uses migrations, for four reasons:

  • A failed build stops the service. In a run for this book, automatic index creation met a collection that already held two equal values for a unique index. The application failed to start, with a DuplicateKeyException.
  • A build can block the collection. AWS states that the default index build on Amazon DocumentDB is a foreground build, which blocks all other operations on the collection. DocumentDB also allows only one index build on a collection at a time, as of October 2026.
  • Nobody sees it. An annotation on a field looks like a small change in a pull request. A migration shows the index, its name and its options as a change of its own.
  • It runs on every start. A migration runs once, and the runner records it.

In C#, the MongoDB .NET driver has no index attribute. A run for this book found no attribute named like an index in the driver's assemblies. So a C# service creates its indexes in code, with Indexes.CreateOneAsync. The shop does the same in Java, inside a migration.

One migration: an interface and a beantwist#

A migration is a class that implements one interface of the platform:

/**
 * One versioned change to the database, such as creating indexes or loading seed data. It runs
 * once in each environment, at startup, before the service takes traffic.
 *
 * <p>Write each migration as a {@code @Component} in the service's {@code migration} package.
 * The rules:
 *
 * <ul>
 *   <li>IDs are unique and sort in run order, such as {@code V001-create-indexes}. Platform
 *       migrations start with {@code P}, so they run first.</li>
 *   <li>Never change or delete a migration that has run anywhere. Add a new one.</li>
 *   <li>Make each migration safe to run twice, because a crash part-way runs it again.</li>
 *   <li>Use no transaction: DocumentDB cannot create a collection inside one.</li>
 * </ul>
 */
public interface MongoMigration {

    String id();

    void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo);
}
Reading the code
String id();

The ID names the migration forever. The runner sorts by it, and records it when the migration has run.

void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo);

The change itself. The runner passes the MongoTemplate, so a migration can create indexes and write documents of any collection.

Each rule in the comment has its own section below. The service's first migration creates the indexes. EF Core migrations have the same purpose for a relational database:

EF Core migrations
public partial class CreateIndexes : Migration
{
    protected override void Up(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
    {
        migrationBuilder.CreateIndex(
            name: "notes_orderId_createdAt",
            table: "notes",
            columns: ["OrderId", "CreatedAt"]);
    }
}
The order service
@Component
class V001CreateIndexes implements MongoMigration {

    @Override
    public String id() {
        return "V001-create-indexes";
    }

    @Override
    public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        // GET /orders?status=PAID, newest first
        mongo.indexOps("orders").createIndex(new Index()
                .on("status", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("placedAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)
                .named("orders_status_placedAt"));
        // ...
    }
}
Reading the code
@Component

The migration is a bean. Spring finds it by component scanning, and the platform collects every bean of type MongoMigration. A new migration needs no registration.

class V001CreateIndexes implements MongoMigration {

The class is package-private. Nothing in the service calls a migration. Only the runner does.

return "V001-create-indexes";

The ID starts with V001, so it sorts before V002. The words after it describe the change.

The class name and the ID say the same thing, but only the ID counts. Renaming the class is safe. Changing the ID makes the runner see a new migration, and run it once more.

EF Core generates its migration classes from the model, and the command dotnet ef database update applies them. The shop writes each migration itself, and the service applies it at startup. For Flyway, which is the closest match for a relational database in Java, see the section Migrations.

The service's migrations are in their own package, migration, beside the features. The package's comment says why:

/**
 * The service's database changes: indexes and seed data, as {@code MongoMigration} beans. The
 * platform's runner applies each one once, in ID order, before the service takes traffic.
 *
 * <p>This is not a feature. It changes the storage of every feature, so it sits beside them.
 * Never edit a migration that has run anywhere; add the next one.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.migration;

A file named package-info.java holds the comment of a package, here package com.acme.orderservice.migration. One migration often touches the collections of several features, so no single feature owns it.

IDs, their order, and the platform's migrations firsttwist#

The platform has migrations of its own. The audit log, the inbox and the outbox need their collections and indexes in every service. Their IDs start with P:

/**
 * The platform's index on the audit log, for finding the history of one resource.
 *
 * <p>Its ID starts with {@code P}, so it sorts, and runs, before every service migration,
 * whose IDs start with {@code V}.
 */
public class AuditLogIndexes implements MongoMigration {

    @Override
    public String id() {
        return "P001-audit-log-indexes";
    }

    @Override
    public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        mongo.indexOps(MongoAuditLog.COLLECTION).createIndex(new Index()
                .on("resourceType", Sort.Direction.ASC)
                .on("resourceId", Sort.Direction.ASC)
                .on("at", Sort.Direction.ASC)
                .named("audit_log_resource"));
    }
}
Reading the code
public class AuditLogIndexes implements MongoMigration {

This class has no @Component. The platform's auto-configuration declares it as a bean, so a service gets it by adding the library.

.named("audit_log_resource"));

The index serves one question. It finds the history of one resource, in time order.

The runner sorts the migrations by their ID, as text. The letter P sorts before V, so the platform's migrations run first. So these are the migrations of the order service, in run order:

IDOwnerWhat it does
P000-audit-log-collectionthe platform's audit logcreates the collection audit_log
P000-messaging-collectionsthe platform's outbox and inboxcreates the collections event_publication and processed_messages
P001-audit-log-indexesthe platform's audit logthe index audit_log_resource
P002-inbox-indexesthe platform's inboxthe TTL index processed_messages_ttl
P003-outbox-indexesthe platform's outboxthe index event_publication_incomplete
V000-create-collectionsthe order servicecreates the collections orders, notes and reference_data
V001-create-indexesthe order serviceone index for each query of the three features
V002-seed-reference-datathe order servicethe delivery methods and the note categories
V003-add-note-authorsthe order servicewrites an author into the notes that have none
V004-replace-open-actions-indexthe order servicereplaces the index of the shipping rule

The migrations with the number 000 create collections. On a new database, each one runs before the migrations that create indexes on the same collections. For these migrations, see the section Collections first, outside any transaction.

Text sorts character by character. So V10 sorts before V2. The second character decides, and the digit 1 comes before the digit 2. The shop pads every number to three digits, so V010 sorts after V002. Choose the width once, for the life of the service.

Two migrations with the same ID would make the record ambiguous. The runner refuses them when it is created:

private static void requireUniqueIds(List<MongoMigration> migrations) {
    Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (MongoMigration migration : migrations) {
        if (!seen.add(migration.id())) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Two migrations have the ID " + migration.id());
        }
    }
}

seen.add(migration.id()) returns false when the ID is in the set already. The startup then fails. The test MongoMigrationRunnerTest.refusesTwoMigrationsWithTheSameId checks the message.

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Two migrations have the ID V001-indexes#
Means
Two beans of type MongoMigration return the same ID, often after a copy and paste.
Fix
Give the newer migration the next free ID. Never change the ID of a migration that has run.

The runner: each migration once, before trafficnew#

A new instance of the service starts. Its code needs an index that does not exist yet, and a lookup value that is not stored yet. If the service took requests now, the first query would read a whole collection, and the first order would fail validation. So the migrations must run before the first request and the first message.

The platform declares the runner as a bean, with every migration bean in ID order:

/** Runs the migrations at startup. Slice and wiring tests turn it off with the property. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
MongoMigrationRunner mongoMigrationRunner(MongoTemplate mongo, ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations, Clock clock,
                                          @Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl) {
    return new MongoMigrationRunner(mongo, migrations.orderedStream().toList(), clock, lockTtl);
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)

The runner exists unless the property is false. matchIfMissing = true means that a service without the property gets the runner.

ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations

An ObjectProvider gives access to every bean of a type. orderedStream() returns them as a stream. The runner sorts them by ID itself. For ObjectProvider, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

@Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl)

@Value reads one setting. The text after the colon is the default. PT15M is the ISO 8601 form of 15 minutes, and Spring converts it into a Duration.

The runner does its work in one method. Spring calls it once every singleton bean of the application exists:

@Override
public void afterSingletonsInstantiated() {
    acquireLock();
    try {
        Set<String> applied = appliedIds();
        for (MongoMigration migration : migrations) {
            if (!applied.contains(migration.id())) {
                run(migration);
            }
        }
    } finally {
        releaseLock();
    }
}

private void run(MongoMigration migration) {
    log.info("Running migration {}", migration.id());
    Instant started = clock.instant();
    migration.migrate(mongo);
    mongo.insert(new Document("_id", migration.id())
            .append("appliedAt", clock.instant())
            .append("durationMs", Duration.between(started, clock.instant()).toMillis()), HISTORY);
}

private Set<String> appliedIds() {
    Set<String> ids = new HashSet<>();
    mongo.findAll(Document.class, HISTORY).forEach(document -> ids.add(document.getString("_id")));
    return ids;
}
Reading the code
public void afterSingletonsInstantiated() {

This method comes from the interface SmartInitializingSingleton. Spring calls it at the end of the phase in which it creates the singleton beans. The source of Spring says that all regular singleton beans exist by then.

acquireLock();

Only one instance may migrate at a time. See the section The lock between instances.

} finally {

The lock is released, also when a migration throws. The other instances then do not wait for the TTL.

Set<String> applied = appliedIds();

The runner reads every ID from schema_migrations once. It runs only the migrations whose ID is missing.

mongo.insert(new Document("_id", migration.id())

After a migration succeeds, the runner records it. The ID is the document's _id, so it can be recorded only once. The record also holds the time and the duration.

So no HTTP request and no message can arrive while a migration runs. Spring starts the web server and the listener containers of Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) only after this method returns. For the order of startup, with a diagram, see the section Work at startup: migrations before traffic.

A failed migration stops the startup. The exception leaves afterSingletonsInstantiated, and the application context fails. The new instance never becomes ready, so it takes no traffic. Fix the migration, and deploy again. The test MongoMigrationRunnerTest.releasesTheLockWhenAMigrationFails checks that the lock is released in that case.

The history collection shows what ran where. A document in schema_migrations looks like {_id: "V001-create-indexes", appliedAt: ..., durationMs: 41}. The duration helps to plan the lock TTL.

Tests switch the runner off. @PlatformDataMongoTest sets platform.mongo.migrations.enabled=false, so each test sees only its own data. The wiring test does the same in its profile, because it connects to no database:

platform:
  # ...
  mongo:
    migrations:
      enabled: false

With enabled: false, the condition of the bean fails, and no runner exists. The journey test keeps the runner on. It starts the whole service against MongoDB, so it proves that the migrations run.

The lock between instancesnew#

The orchestrator starts three instances of a new version at once. Each one runs the runner. Without a lock, all three would create the same indexes and load the same seed data at the same time. Each would try to record the same migration. The runner takes a lock first:

private void acquireLock() {
    Instant giveUpAt = clock.instant().plus(lockTtl);
    while (true) {
        try {
            mongo.insert(new Document("_id", LOCK_ID)
                    .append("owner", owner)
                    .append("expiresAt", clock.instant().plus(lockTtl)), LOCK);
            return;
        } catch (DuplicateKeyException lockedByAnotherInstance) {
            // A lock left by a crashed instance has expired: remove it, and try again.
            mongo.remove(query(where("_id").is(LOCK_ID).and("expiresAt").lt(clock.instant())), LOCK);
            if (clock.instant().isAfter(giveUpAt)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Timed out waiting for the migration lock", lockedByAnotherInstance);
            }
            log.info("Waiting for another instance to finish the migrations");
            sleep(pollInterval);
        }
    }
}

private void releaseLock() {
    mongo.remove(query(where("_id").is(LOCK_ID).and("owner").is(owner)), LOCK);
}
Reading the code
mongo.insert(new Document("_id", LOCK_ID)

The lock is one document with the fixed _id lock. Every collection has a unique index on _id. So only one insert can succeed, and the database decides which one.

.append("owner", owner)

owner is a random universally unique identifier (UUID) that each runner creates. It says which instance holds the lock.

.append("expiresAt", clock.instant().plus(lockTtl)), LOCK);

The lock carries the time after which it counts as abandoned.

} catch (DuplicateKeyException lockedByAnotherInstance) {

A failed insert means that another instance holds the lock. Spring translates the server's error 11000 into DuplicateKeyException.

mongo.remove(query(where("_id").is(LOCK_ID).and("expiresAt").lt(clock.instant())), LOCK);

The runner removes the lock only if it has expired. lt means "less than". So a lock left by a crashed instance goes away, and a live lock stays.

sleep(pollInterval);

The runner waits two seconds, and tries again.

mongo.remove(query(where("_id").is(LOCK_ID).and("owner").is(owner)), LOCK);

An instance releases only its own lock. If its lock had expired and another instance took it, this line removes nothing.

The time to give up is the lock TTL, 15 minutes by default. An instance that waits longer fails its startup. The orchestrator starts it again, and by then the first instance has usually finished.

The runner waits with Thread.sleep, which can be interrupted:

private static void sleep(Duration duration) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(duration);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        // Restore the flag, so the code that interrupted this thread can see it.
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new IllegalStateException("Interrupted while waiting for the migration lock", e);
    }
}
Reading the code
} catch (InterruptedException e) {

InterruptedException is a checked exception. Another thread asked this thread to stop, for example during a shutdown.

Thread.currentThread().interrupt();

A method that throws InterruptedException first clears the interrupted status of the thread. This line sets it again, so the code higher up can still see the request to stop. The documentation of Thread asks for this whenever code throws another exception instead.

throw new IllegalStateException("Interrupted while waiting for the migration lock", e);

The runner then gives up, with an unchecked exception. The startup fails.

Gotcha

A lock TTL shorter than the slowest migration lets two instances migrate. The first instance runs a long migration. After the TTL, a second instance finds the lock expired, removes it and takes the lock. It then runs the same migrations again, while the first one is still running. The runner's comment says what to do. Set platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl longer than the slowest migration, and split a long data migration into smaller ones.

The lock needs only the unique _id of a collection. ShedLock, which the outbox resender uses, also keeps its locks in MongoDB, in the collection scheduler_locks. For that lock, see the chapter Caching and scheduling.

Waiting at startup, and the probestrap#

An instance that waits for the lock has not started its web server yet. So it answers no HTTP request at all, also no probe. The orchestrator may count every failed probe. With a short startup probe, it restarts the instance while it waits. The new instance waits too, and the deployment never finishes.

Gotcha

The startup probe must allow for the whole lock TTL. A waiting instance has no HTTP port open for up to platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl, 15 minutes by default. The service's README gives the rule:

**Migrations run before the service takes traffic, and the startup probe allows for the lock.**
The platform's runner runs in `afterSingletonsInstantiated`, before the web server and the SQS
listeners start, so no request or message arrives before the indexes and seed data exist. An
instance that waits for another's migration lock waits up to `platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl`
(15 minutes by default) with no HTTP port open. Give the orchestrator's startup probe at least
that long, for example `failureThreshold: 90` with `periodSeconds: 10`, or lower the TTL.

The values failureThreshold: 90 and periodSeconds: 10 allow 90 failures, ten seconds apart, which are 15 minutes. Or lower the TTL, if every migration is quick.

The local Docker Compose file of the service follows the same rule on a small scale:

healthcheck:
  # The image has no curl, so bash opens the TCP connection itself. "Ready" means the database is reachable.
  test: ["CMD", "bash", "-c", "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/localhost/8080 && printf 'GET /actuator/health/readiness HTTP/1.0\\r\\n\\r\\n' >&3 && grep -q UP <&3"]
  interval: 10s
  retries: 12
  # Migrations run before the web server starts, and an instance may wait for another's
  # migration lock. Allow for that before failed checks count.
  start_period: 60s

As the comment says, start_period gives the container 60 seconds before failed checks count. The waiting time of a local start is short, because one developer starts one instance.

Two other places could run the migrations. An ApplicationRunner runs after the web server has started, so the probes are answered, and readiness stays down. A separate job runs the migrations once, before the rollout. For the comparison of the three places, see the section Work at startup: migrations before traffic.

Pragmatic choice: The service migrates its own database at startup

The strict rule. A change of the database is a deployment step of its own. It runs once, before the new version starts, and it can be watched and stopped.

What we do. Each instance runs the platform's runner at startup. A lock lets one instance migrate, and the others wait.

Why. The order service's migrations create indexes and upsert a few dozen lookup values. They take seconds. One mechanism for every service needs no extra step in the pipeline, and a new environment migrates itself.

When to stop. Stop when one migration takes longer than a few minutes, such as a change of every stored order. Then run that migration as a separate job, and keep the startup probes short.

Why not Mongock or Flamingock, as of October 2026new#

Writing a migration runner looks like work that a library should do. Two libraries exist for MongoDB in Java. The platform's README gives its decision:

- **Our own migration runner.** Mongock has no Spring Boot 4 artifact. Flamingock says it supports
  Boot 4, but lists Spring Data MongoDB only up to 4.x. The runner is about 150 lines; re-evaluate
  when a library supports this stack.

The bullet names both libraries, Mongock and Flamingock. The research for this book checked both in October 2026:

LibraryWhat the sources say, as of October 2026
Mongockthe latest version is 5.5.1, from March 2025, and no artifact for Spring Boot 4 exists
Mongockits README says that it is sunsetting, in maintenance mode, and reaches its end of life at the end of 2026
Flamingockthe successor of Mongock, under the Apache-2.0 licence, with version 1.4.5 from August 2026
Flamingockits Spring Boot integration says that it is compatible with Spring Boot 2.x to 4.x
Flamingockits target system for Spring Data MongoDB lists Spring Data MongoDB 3.1.x to 4.x
the shop's stackSpring Boot 4.1.2 manages Spring Data MongoDB 5.1.2, which is outside that range

Flamingock is the careful alternative, and it deserves a fair look. It is maintained, and its licence is open. It keeps an audit of the changes, and it is the successor of Mongock. It may well work with Spring Data MongoDB 5.1.2. But its own page does not say so, and nobody ran it for this book. Its page on moving from Mongock mentions DocumentDB only in a list of systems that Mongock supported.

The shop's runner is small. It runs each migration once, in order, under a lock, and records it. It needs nothing that a library adds, such as rollback steps or several target systems. Re-evaluate when Flamingock lists Spring Data MongoDB 5, and when a test against DocumentDB succeeds. Then the runner can go, and the migrations stay much the same.

An older form of this standard used Mongock. A service that still uses it must move before Mongock's end of life. The research checked the names in Mongock 5.5.1, in its source and its documentation, in October 2026:

Mongock 5What it marksIn the shop's runner
@ChangeUnit(id, order, author)a class that is one migration, where author may be left outa class that implements MongoMigration, with id()
@Executionthe method that makes the changemigrate(MongoTemplate mongo)
@RollbackExecutionthe method that undoes the changenothing, because a later migration repairs instead
@BeforeExecutionan optional method that runs outside the change unit's transaction, for changes that a transaction does not allownothing, because no migration runs in a transaction
@RollbackBeforeExecutionthe undo of @BeforeExecution, required when that method existsnothing
mongock.migration-scan-packagethe setting that names the packages with change unitsthe migration beans, found by component scanning

All five annotations are in the package io.mongock.api.annotations. @ChangeUnit has four more attributes, among them runAlways and transactional. The attribute transactional is true by default. The documentation says that @BeforeExecution runs outside the transaction. It is meant for operations that change the structure of the database, which some databases do not allow inside a transaction, and it names MongoDB. Creating an index or a collection changes the structure. So, as that documentation advises, a Mongock change unit creates its index in @BeforeExecution, and changes documents in @Execution.

A named index for each querynew#

Each query of the service reads one collection. Without an index, MongoDB reads every document of the collection to answer it. So the first migration creates one index for each query, and names it:

@Override
public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
    // GET /orders?status=PAID, newest first
    mongo.indexOps("orders").createIndex(new Index()
            .on("status", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("placedAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)
            .named("orders_status_placedAt"));

    // GET /orders/{orderId}/notes, newest first
    mongo.indexOps("notes").createIndex(new Index()
            .on("orderId", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("createdAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)
            .named("notes_orderId_createdAt"));

    // The shipping rule: count the notes on an order that still need action
    mongo.indexOps("notes").createIndex(new Index()
            .on("orderId", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("actionRequired", Sort.Direction.ASC)
            .on("actionResolvedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC)
            .named("notes_orderId_openActions"));

    // Lookup by type; the unique index also guarantees that a code appears once in its list
    mongo.indexOps("reference_data").createIndex(new Index()
            .on("type", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("code", Sort.Direction.ASC)
            .unique().named("reference_data_type_code"));
}
Reading the code
mongo.indexOps("orders").createIndex(new Index()

indexOps returns the index operations of one collection. createIndex creates the index and returns its name. The method ensureIndex does the same, but it is deprecated.

.on("status", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("placedAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)

Each on adds a field to the index, with a direction. An index of several fields is called a compound index. This one holds the status first, and then the time, newest first. That is the filter and the sort of the query findByStatus.

.named("orders_status_placedAt"));

The name is the collection and the fields. A later migration can find the index by this name, and drop or change it.

.on("actionResolvedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC)

This index serves the count of open actions. It holds the three fields of the condition in countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull.

.unique().named("reference_data_type_code"));

A unique index refuses a second document with the same type and code. See the section Unique and TTL indexes.

Each index has a comment that names its query, an endpoint or a rule. So a reviewer can check two things. Every query has an index, and every index has a query.

A run for this book showed what createIndex sends. An index on a status and a time, created in the same way, was sent as {"key": {"status": 1, "createdAt": -1}, "name": "idx_status_createdAt"}. 1 means ascending, and -1 descending.

In C#, the driver builds the keys with Builders<T>.IndexKeys, and the name goes into the options:

MongoDB .NET driver
await notes.Indexes.CreateOneAsync(new CreateIndexModel<Note>(
    Builders<Note>.IndexKeys.Ascending(n => n.OrderId).Descending(n => n.CreatedAt),
    new CreateIndexOptions { Name = "notes_orderId_createdAt" }));
The order service
// GET /orders/{orderId}/notes, newest first
mongo.indexOps("notes").createIndex(new Index()
        .on("orderId", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("createdAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)
        .named("notes_orderId_createdAt"));

The C# side names the fields with lambdas, so the compiler checks them. The Java side names them as strings, and the compiler checks nothing. Write the field names exactly as they are stored, and check them in review.

Name every index after its collection and its fields, as the shop does. A short name that hides a field, such as notes_orderId for the index on orderId and createdAt, misleads the next reader. As of October 2026, AWS allows index names of 1 to 255 characters on DocumentDB 5.0 and later. On 4.0 and earlier, the collection name and the index name together may hold only 3 to 63 characters.

Unique and TTL indexes, and what DocumentDB supportstwist#

Two indexes of the service do more than speed up a query. The unique index on reference_data guarantees that a code appears once in its list. The time-to-live index of the inbox deletes old documents by itself:

@Override
public String id() {
    return "P002-inbox-indexes";
}

@Override
public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
    mongo.indexOps(Inbox.COLLECTION).createIndex(new Index()
            .on("processedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC)
            .expire(properties.getInbox().getRetention())
            .named("processed_messages_ttl"));
}
Reading the code
.on("processedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC)

A TTL index is on one date field. Here it is the time at which the inbox processed the event.

.expire(properties.getInbox().getRetention())

expire sets the time after which the database deletes a document. The setting platform.messaging.inbox.retention holds it, 14 days by default. A run showed that expire became expireAfterSeconds in the command.

The inbox keeps each key only as long as a repeated message could arrive. Nothing in the service deletes old keys. For the inbox, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

The runs for this book showed four details of these options:

DetailWhat the run showed
expire(Duration.ofMillis(1500))expireAfterSeconds 1, because the value is cut to whole seconds without an error
.unique()"unique": true in the command
a duplicate on a unique compound indexDuplicateKeyException, E11000, with the name of the index and the values
.partial(PartialIndexFilter.of(where("actionRequired").is(true)))a partialFilterExpression, which indexes only the matching documents

DocumentDB does not support every kind of index. AWS lists these, as of October 2026:

Index or propertyEngine 5.0Engine 8.0Note
single field, compound, multikeyyesyesevery index of the shop is one of these kinds, and some add a property from the rows below
uniqueyesyesa missing field counts as null, so two documents without the field collide
TTLyesyeslisted for a single field and multikey only, so a compound TTL index is not listed
partialyesyesnot on 3.6 or 4.0, and only a few operators in the filter
sparseyesyesbut unique and sparse together on a nested field is not supported
hashed, wildcard, 2dnonouse a single field or a compound index

AWS adds two limits for a TTL index. The deletion is best effort, with no guaranteed time. And a TTL index starts to delete only after its build has finished. AWS also limits a collection to 64 indexes, and a compound index to 32 fields.

So never rely on a TTL index for a rule, such as "a reservation is gone after 15 minutes". Check the time in the query or the code too. The inbox can use one, because an old key that stays a little longer does no harm.

In C#, the same options are Unique = true and ExpireAfter in CreateIndexOptions.

Never edit a migration that rantrap#

The notes of an order must now be listed by category too. A developer opens V001CreateIndexes, which already creates the notes indexes, and adds one more index there. It is the obvious place.

PredictAn index added to V001 after it ran#
Production ran V001 last month. The developer adds a new index to V001, as above, and deploys. What happens in production?
Set<String> applied = appliedIds();
for (MongoMigration migration : migrations) {
    if (!applied.contains(migration.id())) {
        run(migration);
    }
}
Show the answer
Nothing. The new index is never created in production.

The runner decides by ID, not by content. V001-create-indexes is in schema_migrations already. So the runner skips it, and no error appears. A new environment runs the edited V001, and gets the index. So the environments now differ.

Add the index in a new migration, such as V005-index-notes-by-category. MongoMigrationRunnerTest.skipsTheMigrationsThatHaveRun tests the skipping.

Flyway checks a checksum of every migration that ran, and stops the startup when one changed. The shop's runner stores no checksum, so an edit goes unnoticed. The rule is therefore in the comment of MongoMigration and of the migration package. A reviewer must refuse an edit of a migration that has run anywhere. For Flyway's checksum, see the section Migrations.

Changing an existing index is harder than adding one. A run for this book tried each change with createIndex:

ChangeResult
the same name, keys and options againnothing happened, and the name came back, so a migration can run twice
the same name, with other keysDataIntegrityViolationException, error 86, IndexKeySpecsConflict
the same keys, with another nameerror 85, IndexOptionsConflict, "Index already exists with a different name"
the same name and keys, with another TTLerror 85, "An equivalent index already exists with the same name but different options"

So a changed index needs a new migration that drops the old index by its name, and creates the new one. An edit of the old migration would also fail on every environment that has the index already, with one of the errors above.

Index already exists with a different name#
Means
A migration creates an index whose keys match an existing index, under another name.
Fix
Keep the existing name, or drop the old index by its name in a new migration and create the new one.

The service has one such change. The shipping rule counts the notes on an order that still need action. V001 gave it an index on three fields of every note. V004 replaces it with a smaller index, which holds only the notes that need action:

/**
 * Replaces the index of the shipping rule with a smaller one. V001's index holds every note;
 * this one holds only the notes that need action, because the rule counts only those. An index
 * cannot be changed in place, so the migration drops the old one by its name and creates the
 * new one under a new name.
 *
 * <p>Dropping an index that does not exist fails, so the old index is dropped only when it is
 * there. Creating an index that exists already changes nothing. So the migration is safe to
 * run twice. DocumentDB supports partial indexes from version 5.0, on instance-based clusters.
 */
@Component
class V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex implements MongoMigration {

    static final String OLD_INDEX = "notes_orderId_openActions";
    static final String NEW_INDEX = "notes_orderId_needingAction";

    @Override
    public String id() {
        return "V004-replace-open-actions-index";
    }

    @Override
    public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        IndexOperations notes = mongo.indexOps("notes");
        boolean oldIndexExists = notes.getIndexInfo().stream().anyMatch(index -> index.getName().equals(OLD_INDEX));
        if (oldIndexExists) {
            notes.dropIndex(OLD_INDEX);
        }
        notes.createIndex(new Index()
                .on("orderId", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("actionResolvedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC)
                .partial(PartialIndexFilter.of(where("actionRequired").is(true)))
                .named(NEW_INDEX));
    }
}
Reading the code
notes.getIndexInfo().stream().anyMatch(index -> index.getName().equals(OLD_INDEX));

getIndexInfo lists the indexes of the collection. The migration drops the old index only when it is there. A second run finds no old index, so it drops nothing.

notes.dropIndex(OLD_INDEX);

The old index goes by its name. This is why V001 named every index.

.partial(PartialIndexFilter.of(where("actionRequired").is(true)))

A partial index holds only the documents that match its filter. A note without an action is not in this index at all, so the index stays small. A query can use it only when its own filter includes the same condition. The shipping rule's query does, because it asks for notes with actionRequired true.

.named(NEW_INDEX));

The new index gets a new name. Creating it again with the same name, keys and options changes nothing, as the table above showed.

The test runs V001, then V004 twice, against a real MongoDB:

@Test
void replacesTheIndexOfTheShippingRuleAndCanRunTwice() {
    new V001CreateIndexes().migrate(mongo);

    new V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex().migrate(mongo);
    new V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex().migrate(mongo);   // the old index is gone, so nothing is dropped

    List<IndexInfo> indexes = mongo.indexOps("notes").getIndexInfo();
    assertThat(indexes).extracting(IndexInfo::getName)
            .contains(V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex.NEW_INDEX).doesNotContain(V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex.OLD_INDEX);
    assertThat(indexes).filteredOn(index -> index.getName().equals(V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex.NEW_INDEX))
            .singleElement().satisfies(index -> assertThat(index.getPartialFilterExpression()).contains("actionRequired"));

    // The query of the shipping rule uses the new index.
    Document shippingRuleQuery = new Document("orderId", "order-1").append("actionRequired", true)
            .append("actionResolvedAt", null);
    Document plan = mongo.getCollection("notes").find(shippingRuleQuery).explain();
    assertThat(plan.toJson()).contains(V004ReplaceOpenActionsIndex.NEW_INDEX);
}

The test checks three things. The old index is gone, and the new one exists. The new index has its partial filter. And MongoDB's plan for the shipping rule's query names the new index, so the query really uses it. explain() returns that plan as a document.

Check the index features of the database you run. Amazon DocumentDB supports partial indexes on its 5.0 and 8.0 engines, on instance-based clusters, and not on elastic clusters, as of October 2026. Its supported filter operators include $eq, which is(true) uses. The test ran on MongoDB 8.0.34, not on DocumentDB.

Seed data follows the same rule. See the section Seed data, upserted by a natural key.

Safe to run twice, and no transactionnew#

The runner runs a migration, and records it afterwards. An instance can crash between the two steps, for example when the orchestrator stops it. The next start finds no record, and runs the same migration again. So every migration must be safe to run twice. This property is called idempotent.

The comment of V001CreateIndexes says so for indexes:

/**
 * One named index for each query the service runs. A query without an index reads the whole
 * collection. The names say what each index is for, so a later migration can find and change it.
 * Creating an index that exists already, with the same keys and options, changes nothing, so the
 * migration is safe to run twice.
 */
@Component
class V001CreateIndexes implements MongoMigration {

The last sentence of the comment is why V001CreateIndexes can run twice. The two kinds of migration in the shop are idempotent by nature:

  • An index. createIndex with the same name, keys and options changes nothing. The run in the section above showed it.
  • Seed data. An upsert by a natural key updates the existing value, or inserts it once. A second run changes nothing.

A migration that changes stored documents must be written for it. Change only the documents that still need the change, such as those where the new field is missing. Never add or subtract a value relative to the stored one, because a second run would apply it twice.

A transaction would seem to solve the crash. The migration and its record would commit together. But the platform uses no transaction in migrations. AWS states that a transaction on Amazon DocumentDB cannot create a collection. MongoDB behaves differently. In a run for this book on MongoDB 8.0.34, the first index and the first insert each created a missing collection, also inside a transaction. A migration often creates an index or inserts a document. The comment of MongoMigration gives the reason in one line.

For indexes themselves, AWS states no rule. The research checked the pages on transactions, on indexes and on the functional differences, and AWS's table of supported commands, in October 2026. None says whether DocumentDB builds an index inside a transaction. The only link is an AWS support article, which says that long-running transactions can delay index creation, or make it fail. Mongock's documentation also keeps structure changes on MongoDB out of its transactions. So keep index changes out of transactions. Then the question never arises.

So idempotence is the only protection. It is enough, because an index and an upsert are naturally safe to repeat.

Collections first, outside any transactiontwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
foreach (string name in new[] { "orders", "notes", "reference_data" })
{
    if (!(await database.ListCollectionNames().ToListAsync()).Contains(name))
    {
        await database.CreateCollectionAsync(name);
    }
}
The order service
/**
 * Creates the service's collections before a use case writes to them inside a transaction,
 * which Amazon DocumentDB cannot do for a collection that does not exist. On a new database,
 * the ID sorts first, so the collections exist before V001 creates their indexes.
 */
@Component
class V000CreateCollections extends CreateCollections {

    V000CreateCollections() {
        super("V000-create-collections", List.of("orders", "notes", "reference_data"));
    }
}
Reading the code
class V000CreateCollections extends CreateCollections {

CreateCollections is a migration class of the platform. It creates each collection of its list that does not exist yet. The service only gives it an ID and the names.

super("V000-create-collections", List.of("orders", "notes", "reference_data"));

The ID has the number 000, so it sorts before V001-create-indexes. The three names are the collections of the three features.

A new environment has no collections. On Amazon DocumentDB, the first use case would then fail, because its transaction cannot create the collection that it writes to. MongoDB creates the collection on the fly, so a local test never shows the problem. So the collections are created at startup, in a migration, and no migration runs in a transaction.

CreateCollections asks collectionExists before it creates a collection. So a second run changes nothing, and the migration is safe to run twice. The platform creates its own collections the same way, in P000-audit-log-collection and P000-messaging-collections. A new feature with a new collection adds it in a new migration, because V000 has run already. For the platform's class, the DocumentDB limit and the test CreateCollectionsIT, see the section The limits of a transaction on Amazon DocumentDB.

The C# pane does the same with the MongoDB .NET driver. It lists the names, and creates each missing collection with CreateCollectionAsync.

Seed data, upserted by a natural keynew#

An agent chooses a delivery method when they place an order. The service checks that the code is an active value of the list. The list must exist in every environment, the same everywhere, and be versioned with the code. So the values are JSON files in the service:

[
  { "code": "STANDARD", "label": "Standard delivery (3 to 5 days)", "active": true },
  { "code": "EXPRESS", "label": "Express delivery (next day)", "active": true },
  { "code": "COLLECT", "label": "Collect from a store", "active": true },
  { "code": "SECOND_CLASS_POST", "label": "Second-class post (no longer offered)", "active": false }
]

The code SECOND_CLASS_POST is no longer offered, so it is inactive. It is not deleted. Orders from last year still store this code, and the service must still show its label. The other file, note-categories.json, keeps PHONE_CALL in the same way.

The second migration loads both files:

/**
 * Loads the lookup values from {@code resources/seed/}. Each value is upserted by its type and
 * code, so the migration is safe to run twice.
 *
 * <p>To change the values, edit the JSON file and add a new migration that runs the same upserts.
 * Never edit this one: environments where it has run would not see the change.
 */
@Component
class V002SeedReferenceData implements MongoMigration {

    private static final String COLLECTION = "reference_data";

    @Override
    public String id() {
        return "V002-seed-reference-data";
    }

    @Override
    public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        SeedFiles.upsert(mongo, COLLECTION, "seed/delivery-methods.json",
                Map.of("type", ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD), "code");
        SeedFiles.upsert(mongo, COLLECTION, "seed/note-categories.json",
                Map.of("type", ReferenceTypes.NOTE_CATEGORY), "code");
    }
}
Reading the code
SeedFiles.upsert(mongo, COLLECTION, "seed/delivery-methods.json",

The platform's helper reads the file from the classpath, and upserts each entry into reference_data.

Map.of("type", ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD), "code");

Every entry of the file gets the field type, with the value DELIVERY_METHOD. The type and the code together identify an entry. That pair is the natural key, a key that comes from the business, not from the database.

The helper does the upserts:

MongoDB .NET driver
await referenceData.UpdateOneAsync(
    r => r.Type == type && r.Code == code,
    Builders<ReferenceItem>.Update.Set(r => r.Label, label).Set(r => r.Active, active),
    new UpdateOptions { IsUpsert = true });
The platform
public static void upsert(MongoTemplate mongo, String collection, String classpathFile,
                          Map<String, Object> fixedFields, String keyField) {
    for (Document entry : read(classpathFile)) {
        Criteria key = Criteria.where(keyField).is(entry.get(keyField));
        fixedFields.forEach((field, value) -> key.and(field).is(value));

        Update values = new Update();
        entry.forEach((field, value) -> {
            if (!field.equals(keyField)) {
                values.set(field, value);
            }
        });
        mongo.upsert(Query.query(key), values, collection);
    }
}

/** Reads a JSON array of objects. BSON parses only objects, so the array is wrapped in one. */
public static List<Document> read(String classpathFile) {
    try {
        String json = new ClassPathResource(classpathFile).getContentAsString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        return Document.parse("{\"entries\": " + json + "}").getList("entries", Document.class);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not read the seed file " + classpathFile, e);
    }
}
Reading the code
Criteria key = Criteria.where(keyField).is(entry.get(keyField));

The filter starts with the code of the entry.

fixedFields.forEach((field, value) -> key.and(field).is(value));

Each fixed field joins the filter. So the filter is "this code in this type". A Criteria can hold each field only once. A run showed that a second condition on the same field throws InvalidMongoDbApiUsageException.

values.set(field, value);

Every field of the entry except the code becomes a $set. So the label and the flag active are written.

mongo.upsert(Query.query(key), values, collection);

upsert updates the matching document, or inserts one when none matches. A run showed one update command with upsert: true. The first call inserted, and the next calls updated.

String json = new ClassPathResource(classpathFile).getContentAsString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

ClassPathResource finds a file on the classpath, such as seed/delivery-methods.json inside the Java archive (JAR) of the service. getContentAsString reads it as text in UTF-8.

return Document.parse("{\"entries\": " + json + "}").getList("entries", Document.class);

Document.parse reads only a JSON object, not an array. So the helper wraps the array in an object with one field, and reads that field as a list.

throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not read the seed file " + classpathFile, e);

getContentAsString throws the checked IOException. The helper wraps it in the unchecked UncheckedIOException, so migrate needs no throws clause. The startup fails, with the file in the message.

The C# version is one call per entry, with IsUpsert = true. The Java helper works for any seed file, because it builds the filter and the update from the JSON.

A run showed that an upsert with unchanged values reports matched=1 modified=0. That is not an error. It means that the value was already right.

Gotcha

Removing a field from a seed file does not remove it from the database. The helper sets only the fields that are in the file. A field that was in an earlier version of the file stays in the stored document. To remove one, write a migration that unsets it.

The reference feature reads the values, and the order feature checks them:

public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
    boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
            .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
    if (!known) {
        throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
    }
}

requireActive accepts a code only when item.active() is true. So a new order needs an active value. A stored order with an inactive value is still read and shown. The journey test anInactiveDeliveryMethodIsRejectedBeforeTheStockServiceIsCalled places an order with SECOND_CLASS_POST, and expects a 400 for the field deliveryMethod.

To change a value, follow the comment of V002. Edit the JSON file, and add a new migration, such as V005-seed-reference-data-again, that runs the same upserts. The order matters:

  • An environment that ran V002 skips it. It runs V005, which reads the edited file.
  • A new environment runs V002 with the edited file, and then V005 with the same file. The second run changes nothing.

So every environment ends with the same values. Editing only the JSON file would change new environments and leave the old ones as they were.

Never delete a value. Mark it "active": false. A deleted code would leave stored orders and notes with a code that the service cannot explain, and the label would be lost.

Testing the runner and the migrationsnew#

The runner has a unit test with a mocked MongoTemplate, and an integration test against MongoDB. The unit test checks the order of runs:

@Test
void runsThePendingMigrationsInIdOrder() {
    MongoMigration second = migration("V002-seed");
    MongoMigration first = migration("V001-indexes");
    MongoMigration platform = migration("P001-audit");
    when(mongo.findAll(Document.class, MongoMigrationRunner.HISTORY)).thenReturn(List.of());

    runner(List.of(second, first, platform), Duration.ofMinutes(1)).afterSingletonsInstantiated();

    InOrder order = inOrder(platform, first, second);
    order.verify(platform).migrate(mongo);
    order.verify(first).migrate(mongo);
    order.verify(second).migrate(mongo);
}
Reading the code
when(mongo.findAll(Document.class, MongoMigrationRunner.HISTORY)).thenReturn(List.of());

The mocked history is empty, so every migration is pending. For Mockito in this service, see the chapter Testing in depth.

runner(List.of(second, first, platform), Duration.ofMinutes(1)).afterSingletonsInstantiated();

The list is in the wrong order on purpose. The test calls the method that Spring would call.

InOrder order = inOrder(platform, first, second);

InOrder checks the order of the calls. The platform's migration comes first, then V001, then V002.

The other unit tests cover the rest of the runner without a database:

TestWhat it proves
skipsTheMigrationsThatHaveRuna recorded ID is skipped, and only the pending migration is recorded
refusesTwoMigrationsWithTheSameIdthe runner fails at creation, with the ID in the message
givesUpWhenAnotherInstanceHoldsTheLockTooLonga lock that never goes away ends in "Timed out waiting for the migration lock"
releasesTheLockWhenAMigrationFailsa failing migration still removes the lock

The integration test runs the lock against a real MongoDB, because the lock depends on the unique _id:

@Test
void waitsForALiveLockAndThenGivesUp() {
    mongo.insert(new Document("_id", "lock").append("owner", "another-instance")
            .append("expiresAt", Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(10))), MongoMigrationRunner.LOCK);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> runner(List.of(recording("V001-a")), Duration.ofMillis(300)).afterSingletonsInstantiated())
            .hasMessage("Timed out waiting for the migration lock");
    assertThat(ran).isEmpty();
}

@Test
void takesOverAnExpiredLockLeftByACrashedInstance() {
    mongo.insert(new Document("_id", "lock").append("owner", "crashed-instance")
            .append("expiresAt", Instant.now().minusSeconds(1)), MongoMigrationRunner.LOCK);

    runner(List.of(recording("V001-a")), Duration.ofMinutes(1)).afterSingletonsInstantiated();

    assertThat(ran).containsExactly("V001-a");
}
Reading the code
.append("expiresAt", Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(10))), MongoMigrationRunner.LOCK);

The first test inserts a live lock of another instance, which expires in ten minutes.

runner(List.of(recording("V001-a")), Duration.ofMillis(300))

The runner gets a TTL of 300 milliseconds, so the test gives up quickly. A test constructor of the runner also takes a short poll interval.

.append("expiresAt", Instant.now().minusSeconds(1)), MongoMigrationRunner.LOCK);

The second test inserts a lock that expired a second ago. The runner removes it, takes the lock, and runs the migration.

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Timed out waiting for the migration lock#
Means
Another instance held the migration lock for longer than platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl. Its migrations may still be running.
Fix
Look at the logs of the instance that holds the lock. Set the TTL longer than the slowest migration, and give the startup probe at least as long.

SeedFilesTest.readsAJsonArrayOfObjects reads a small test file and checks the values, with no database. CreateCollectionsIT runs the collection migration twice against a real MongoDB. NoteMigrationsIT runs V003 and V004 twice each, on raw documents and real indexes. The journey test covers all the service's migrations at once. OrderJourneyIT.lookupValuesAreSeededAndCached reads the delivery methods through the API, and finds SECOND_CLASS_POST with active false. So the collections, the indexes and the seed data exist when the service starts against an empty MongoDB.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe migration lock is the insert of a document with the fixed _id lock. Why not read the collection first, and insert a lock only when none is there?
Two instances could both read "no lock" at the same moment, and both insert one. An insert with a fixed _id lets the database decide, because the _id is unique. Exactly one insert succeeds. The other gets DuplicateKeyException, and waits. The expiry time lets a crashed instance's lock go away.
2
An expert asksWhy are lookup values upserted by their type and code, and never deleted?
An upsert by the natural key makes the migration safe to run twice, and an edited entry updates the stored value in place. A value is never deleted, because stored orders and notes still hold its code. An old value is marked "active": false. New data cannot use it, and old data can still show it.
3
Why does the migration P001-audit-log-indexes run before V001-create-indexes?
The runner sorts the IDs as text. P sorts before V, so the platform's migrations run before every service migration. The numbers are padded to three digits, because V10 would sort before V2.
4
Why does the shop use its own migration runner, as of October 2026?
Mongock has no artifact for Spring Boot 4, and it reaches its end of life at the end of 2026. Flamingock says that it supports Boot 4, but its Spring Data target lists Spring Data MongoDB only up to 4.x. Boot 4.1.2 uses 5.1.2. The runner is about 150 lines.
5
TranslateWrite this index as a call in a migration of the order service, on the MongoTemplate named mongo: 
await notes.Indexes.CreateOneAsync(new CreateIndexModel<Note>(
    Builders<Note>.IndexKeys.Ascending(n => n.OrderId).Descending(n => n.CreatedAt),
    new CreateIndexOptions { Name = "notes_orderId_createdAt" }));
mongo.indexOps("notes").createIndex(new Index()
        .on("orderId", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("createdAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)
        .named("notes_orderId_createdAt"));

indexOps("notes") selects the collection. Each on adds a field with its direction, and named sets the name. The field names are strings, so they must match the stored names exactly.

Quick reference#

The settings of migrations and indexes:

SettingDefaultWhat it does
platform.mongo.migrations.enabledtrueruns the migration runner at startup, and tests set false

Transactions in depth#

Storing and changing data · Chapter 18· 25 min read· Quick reference

Each change in the order service runs in one transaction. The transaction stores the aggregate, its outbox events and its audit record together, or none of them. The platform registers the transaction manager for MongoDB. This chapter covers @Transactional and TransactionTemplate, joining, rollback, write conflicts and retries, the limits of Amazon DocumentDB, and tests without a database.

KindC#JavaNote

trapno equivalenta MongoTransactionManager bean from the platformwithout it, @Transactional does nothing on MongoDB, and every write commits on its own Why

twistpassing the same session to a second methodpropagation REQUIRED, the defaultthe inner method joins the running transaction, so the order and its notes commit together Why
trapcatching an exception of an inner call, and committingcatching an exception that an inner @Transactional method threwthe inner method marked the transaction rollback-only, so the commit throws UnexpectedRollbackException Why
