What one transaction holds in the order servicenew#

A warehouse worker ships an order. Three things must be stored. The order gets the status SHIPPED. The event OrderShipped goes into the outbox, so the shop's other services hear about it. And the audit log records who shipped the order. If the service stored only some of the three, the data would contradict itself. An order could be shipped with no event, or an event could announce a shipment that never happened.

So every use case that changes data runs in one transaction. The transaction commits all three writes, or none of them. The simplest use case shows the shape:

@Transactional
public void pickLine(OrderId orderId, LineId lineId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    order.pickLine(lineId, clock);
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.LINE_PICKED);
}

saveAndPublish saves the order, publishes its events and records the audit, all inside the transaction that @Transactional started. The use cases of the order service use four forms:

Use caseHow it gets its transactionWhy this form
OrderService.placeTransactionTemplate, after the stock callonly part of the method may be transactional
pickLine, ship, cancel, addNote, resolveAction@Transactional on the methodthe whole method is the change
OrderService.recordPayment@Transactional, joining the inbox's transactionthe inbox key and the payment commit together
NoteService.addNotes@Transactional, joining placethe order and its first notes commit together
get, list, countNeedingActionno transactiona read changes nothing, so it needs no transaction

For the basics of @Transactional, propagation and the rollback rule, see the chapter Transactions, propagation and isolation. This chapter shows how the order service uses them on MongoDB and Amazon DocumentDB.

The transaction manager, and what happens without ittrap#

A transaction manager is the object that begins, commits and rolls back transactions for Spring. Spring Boot creates one for a relational database. For MongoDB, Boot 4.1 creates none. The platform therefore registers one for every service:

/**
 * Sets up DocumentDB for every service: transactions, the driver settings DocumentDB needs,
 * and the migration runner.
 *
 * <p>Spring Boot creates no transaction manager for MongoDB. Without one, {@code @Transactional}
 * silently does nothing: each write commits on its own. This class registers a
 * {@link MongoTransactionManager} before Spring Boot's transaction setup runs, so
 * {@code @Transactional} and {@code TransactionTemplate} both use it.
 */
@AutoConfiguration(beforeName = {
        "org.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.autoconfigure.DataMongoAutoConfiguration",
        "org.springframework.boot.transaction.autoconfigure.TransactionAutoConfiguration"})
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DocumentDbProperties.class)
public class PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(TransactionManager.class)
    MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory databaseFactory) {
        return new MongoTransactionManager(databaseFactory);
    }
Reading the code
@AutoConfiguration(beforeName = {

Spring Boot processes this class before the two Boot classes it names. A run showed that Boot adds its TransactionTemplate bean only when a transaction manager exists. So the manager must be registered first. For the ordering of auto-configurations, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean(TransactionManager.class)

Spring creates this bean only when the service has no transaction manager of its own. A service that needs another manager declares it, and the platform's manager is not created.

MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory databaseFactory) {

MongoTransactionManager is the transaction manager of Spring Data MongoDB. MongoDatabaseFactory gives it the database. Boot creates the factory from the connection settings.

A run for this book showed both states on Boot 4.1.2:

QuestionWith no managerWith a MongoTransactionManager
TransactionManager beansnoneone, named transactionManager
TransactionTemplate beansnoneone, which Boot adds
Is the service a proxy?noyes
isActualTransactionActive() inside @Transactionalfalsetrue
What the driver senteach insert on its own, as a retryable writestartTransaction with the first write, then commit or abort
An unchecked exception after an insertthe document stayedthe document was rolled back
A bean that needs a PlatformTransactionManagerthe startup failedthe startup succeeded

The worst row is the second to last. Without the manager, @Transactional compiles, the application starts, and nothing warns you. Each write commits on its own. For the run as a prediction, see the section Transactions.

No qualifying bean of type 'org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager' available#
Means
A bean needs a transaction manager, but none exists. On MongoDB, Spring Boot creates none.
Fix
Declare a MongoTransactionManager bean, or add the platform library, which declares one.

The wiring test checks the bean without Docker. ApplicationWiringTest.theContextStartsWithThePlatformsBeans expects the PlatformTransactionManager to be a MongoTransactionManager.

The condition names TransactionManager, and the inbox asks for a PlatformTransactionManager. The two types differ. The bytecode of Spring Framework 7.0.10 shows how they relate:

TypeWhat it isWho uses it in the service
TransactionManageran interface with no methods, the parent of every kind of transaction managerthe platform's condition, so any kind of manager counts as present
PlatformTransactionManagerthe interface for blocking code, with getTransaction, commit and rollbackTransactionTemplate and @Transactional on ordinary methods
ReactiveTransactionManagerthe interface for reactive codenothing in the order service

MongoTransactionManager extends AbstractPlatformTransactionManager, which implements PlatformTransactionManager. So the platform's condition backs off for any manager, also a reactive one. And the inbox's constructor can ask for the blocking kind that TransactionTemplate needs.

One transaction manager, also for Spring Modulithtwist#

The outbox of the order service is Spring Modulith's event publication registry. Spring Modulith's MongoDB module can create its own transaction manager. A property switches that on, and its default is true. The platform switches it off:

# The outbox: Spring Modulith's event publication registry, collection "event_publication".
# Delete a publication once it has been sent, so the collection stays small.
spring.modulith.events.completion-mode=delete
# The platform's mongo package already provides the transaction manager.
spring.modulith.events.mongodb.transaction-management.enabled=false
Reading the code
spring.modulith.events.mongodb.transaction-management.enabled=false

With true, Spring Modulith registers a MongoTransactionManager and a TransactionTemplate. Both are conditional on a missing bean, as the platform's own manager is. The metadata of the property says that it requires a replica set.

Both registrations back off when a manager exists. So the setting looks unnecessary. It is still useful, because it removes a question of order. Without it, the service would get the manager of whichever auto-configuration ran first. With it, there is exactly one place that creates the manager, the platform's mongo package. A reader who looks for the manager finds one answer. For the outbox itself, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

@Transactional on a use casetwist#

Most use cases are transactional from their first line to their last. They carry @Transactional:

MongoDB .NET driver
using IClientSessionHandle session = await client.StartSessionAsync();
await session.WithTransactionAsync(async (s, ct) =>
{
    await orders.ReplaceOneAsync(s, o => o.Id == order.Id, order, cancellationToken: ct);
    return true;
});
The order service
/** Ships the order. The rule across the order and its notes is checked by the domain service. */
@Transactional
public void ship(OrderId orderId) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);                                         // load
    long notesNeedingAction = notes.countNeedingAction(orderId.value());       // ask the note feature
    shippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction);                   // rule across aggregates
    order.ship(clock);                                                         // rule and change
    saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_SHIPPED);                         // save, publish, audit
}
Reading the code
await orders.ReplaceOneAsync(s, o => o.Id == order.Id, order, cancellationToken: ct);

In C#, every call that belongs to the transaction takes the session s. A call without it compiles, and runs outside the transaction.

@Transactional

A proxy around OrderService starts a transaction before the method runs. It commits when the method returns, and rolls back when an unchecked exception leaves the method.

Order order = orders.get(orderId); // load

The repository takes no session. MongoTemplate finds the transaction that is bound to the current thread, and joins it. So the read, the count of notes, the save, the outbox row and the audit record all run in the same transaction.

The C# code needs a session parameter on every call. The Java code needs none, because the transaction is bound to the thread. The cost is the proxy. A call from another method of the same class skips it, and runs with no transaction. For the proxy trap, see the section The proxy trap, again.

Gotcha

The plain MongoDB .NET driver ignores TransactionScope. A C# developer may expect an ambient transaction, as with SQL Server. A run for this book wrapped an insert of the MongoDB .NET driver in a TransactionScope, and disposed the scope without Complete(). The document stayed, and nothing threw. The MongoDB EF Core Provider goes further, and throws when it meets an ambient transaction. So the .NET match for @Transactional on MongoDB is a session, not a scope.

The reads of the service carry no @Transactional. Spring Data's reference says that @Transactional(readOnly = true) still starts a transaction on MongoDB, with the session on every request. A read of one document needs no transaction, so the service saves that cost.

On Amazon DocumentDB, AWS states that a transaction's read concern of local, available or majority is upgraded to snapshot. The service sets no isolation on @Transactional. For isolation levels in general, see the section Isolation.

TransactionTemplate, when only part of a method is transactionalnew#

Placing an order needs the stock service. It must hold the products before the order exists. That call goes over HTTP, and it can take seconds. If the call ran inside the transaction, the transaction would stay open for those seconds. On Amazon DocumentDB, a transaction may run for one minute at most, as of October 2026. A slow stock service would then abort the order's transaction.

The rule of the service is short. Call other services before the transaction starts. So place cannot carry @Transactional, which covers the whole method. It uses a TransactionTemplate for the part that writes:

/**
 * Places an order and saves its first notes with it, in one transaction: the order and all
 * its notes are stored, or none are.
 *
 * <p>The stock call happens before the transaction starts. A DocumentDB transaction has time
 * and size limits, and a slow HTTP call inside it would hold it open. That is why this method
 * uses {@link TransactionTemplate} instead of {@code @Transactional}: only the lambda is
 * transactional.
 *
 * <p>The order ID is chosen first, because it is the idempotency key of the reservation.
 */
// ...
    StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items);           // outside the transaction

    return transaction.execute(status -> {
Reading the code
StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items); // outside the transaction

The stock call runs first, with no transaction open. If the stock service is slow or down, no transaction waits for it.

return transaction.execute(status -> {

execute begins a transaction, runs the lambda, and commits. It returns the value of the lambda. status is the TransactionStatus, which the lambda could use to mark a rollback.

For the whole method and the order of its steps, see the section Placing an order: the stock call before the transaction. For the template bean that Boot adds, see the section The TransactionTemplate bean.

A run for this book measured the template that Boot creates:

CaseWhat happened
the defaultspropagation REQUIRED, and the default isolation and timeout
execute with a valuethe value came back, in a new transaction that committed
executeWithoutResult with status.setRollbackOnly()the transaction rolled back, and nothing was thrown
an unchecked exception in the callbackthe transaction rolled back, and the same exception reached the caller
a checked exception, thrown in the callbackthe transaction rolled back, and the caller got UndeclaredThrowableException
an execute inside another executethe inner call joined the outer transaction

The fifth row differs from @Transactional. A checked exception rolls the template back, but by default it commits an annotated method. For the annotation's rule, see the section The rollback rule.

The stock call outside the transaction leaves one gap. The stock service may hold the products, and then the transaction fails. The order is not stored, and the hold stays. The service closes the gap in two ways. The order ID is chosen first, and sent as the idempotency key of the reservation. And the stock service releases a hold when no OrderPlacedV1 arrives in time. For that call, see the chapter Calling other services.

The other way is fair too. Put the transactional part in its own bean, such as OrderPlacement, with a method marked @Transactional. The use case calls the stock service, and then that bean. The style stays declarative. But the step list of the use case moves into two classes, and a reader must open both. The template keeps the whole use case in one method, with the transaction boundary in plain sight. Choose the second bean when the transactional part is large, or when several use cases share it.

In C#, the same split is the code before and after StartTransaction on a session. The Java template is the closest match for the session's WithTransactionAsync, but it does not retry. See the section Write conflicts, and what Spring retries.

Joining the caller's transactiontwist#

Placing an order also saves its first notes. The note feature does that, in NoteService.addNotes, a method with @Transactional. Its propagation is REQUIRED, the default. A transaction is already running, the one that place started. So addNotes joins it, and starts none of its own. In a run for this book, an inner method saw the name of the outer transaction, and both inserts carried the same transaction number. If a caller had no transaction, addNotes would start one. For the method and its journey test, see the section One request that saves the order and its first notes.

The payment works in the same way. The inbox starts a transaction, and the handler calls OrderService.recordPayment, which joins it. The inbox builds its own template from the transaction manager:

public Inbox(MongoTemplate mongo, PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager, Clock clock) {
    this.mongo = mongo;
    this.transactions = new TransactionTemplate(transactionManager);
    this.clock = clock;
}

new TransactionTemplate(transactionManager) creates a template with the default settings. The inbox runs its work with executeWithoutResult, the variant for a lambda that returns nothing. The key of the event and the recorded payment then commit together. For the inbox, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

For the other propagation modes, see the section Propagation. The order service uses only REQUIRED.

Gotcha

Catching the exception of a joined method does not save the transaction. A method that joined the transaction throws. The proxy of that method marks the whole transaction as rollback-only. The caller catches the exception and returns normally. Spring then tries to commit, finds the mark, and rolls back. In a run for this book, the caller got UnexpectedRollbackException, and the driver sent abortTransaction. No document remained. In the order service, never catch a domain exception inside a transaction to continue. Let it leave the use case.

org.springframework.transaction.UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only#
Means
A method that joined the transaction threw, and the caller caught the exception and returned normally. Spring could not commit.
Fix
Let the exception leave the transaction. If a part must fail on its own, give it its own transaction, and only for work that does not share the caller's documents.

Rollback, and the domain's exceptionstwist#

Spring rolls a transaction back for an unchecked exception, and commits for a checked one. Every exception of the domain is unchecked, because the base class extends RuntimeException:

public abstract sealed class DomainException extends RuntimeException
        permits NotFoundException, InvalidValueException, BusinessRuleViolationException {
Reading the code
public abstract sealed class DomainException extends RuntimeException

Every domain exception is a RuntimeException, so every broken rule rolls the transaction back. No method needs rollbackFor.

permits NotFoundException, InvalidValueException, BusinessRuleViolationException {

The class is sealed, so only these three kinds may extend it. For the kinds and their statuses, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

In C#, every exception is unchecked, so a C# developer has no habit for this rule. The rule matters only where code throws a checked exception inside a transaction, such as an IOException. The service has no such code inside a transaction. The platform's helpers wrap checked exceptions in unchecked ones, for example UncheckedIOException in the seed loader.

A rule can also fail after a save, inside the same transaction. For that case, see the section One aggregate per transaction, and the order with its notes.

The outbox row and the audit record in the same transactionnew#

A use case saves an order, publishes its events and records the audit. The three writes go to three collections, through three pieces of code. None of them takes a transaction parameter. They all join the transaction of the thread. The audit log says so in its comment:

/**
 * Writes audit records to the {@code audit_log} collection.
 *
 * <p>{@link MongoTemplate} joins the transaction that is running on the thread. A use case
 * that records audit inside its transaction therefore stores the record only with its change.
 */
public class MongoAuditLog implements AuditLog {

MongoAuditLog inserts a raw document with MongoTemplate. The outbox works in the same way. Spring Modulith writes one row for each transactional listener of an event, in the current transaction. The comment of the platform's publisher explains it:

* <p>Spring Modulith writes one row to {@code event_publication} for each transactional listener
* of an event, in the current transaction. The row is therefore stored only if the change is
* stored. An event with no such listener writes no row and reaches no one.

So a rollback removes all three writes. A failed shipment leaves no event in event_publication and no record in audit_log. After the commit, Spring Modulith sends the events, outside the transaction. For the sending, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

The other way is to write the audit record in a transaction of its own, with REQUIRES_NEW. Then a failed attempt leaves a record too. That suits an audit of attempts, such as failed logins. The order service audits changes, not attempts. A record of a change that was rolled back would be false, so the record shares the change's transaction.

Refusing to publish outside a transactiontrap#

A developer adds a scheduled job that changes an order, and forgets the transaction. The job publishes an event. Spring Modulith writes the outbox row at once, but it sends events only after a commit, and no commit comes. So the row is stored and never sent. The platform's publisher therefore checks for a transaction before it publishes anything:

if (!TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException(
            "Publish domain events inside the use case's transaction, so they are stored with the change");
}

TransactionSynchronizationManager holds the transaction state of the current thread. isActualTransactionActive() is true only when a real transaction runs on this thread. A run showed it false inside @Transactional with no transaction manager, and true with one. So the check also catches a service that has no transaction manager. For the run of an event published with no transaction, and the whole publisher, see the section Publishing outside a transaction.

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Publish domain events inside the use case's transaction, so they are stored with the change#
Means
Code published domain events on a thread with no transaction. The outbox row would never be sent.
Fix
Publish from a use case that runs in a transaction, with @Transactional or a TransactionTemplate.

The tests of the publisher run it inside a TransactionTemplate with a transaction manager that does nothing. See the section A transaction manager that does nothing, for unit tests.

Write conflicts, and what Spring retriestrap#

Two transactions change the same document at the same moment. MongoDB lets only one of them write. It aborts the other with a write conflict. The research for this book measured the cases:

CaseWhat MongoDB 8.0.34 answeredWhat Spring threw
two transactions insert the same _id, and the first has not committederror 112, WriteConflict, at once, with the label TransientTransactionErrorDataIntegrityViolationException
the second transaction started before the first committed, and wrote after iterror 112, WriteConflictDataIntegrityViolationException
the first committed before the second transaction beganerror 11000, a duplicate key, with no labelDuplicateKeyException
a write outside any transaction, against an open transactionthe write waited until the other transaction committed, and then failed with 11000DuplicateKeyException
two transactions update the same versioned documenterror 112, before the version checkDataIntegrityViolationException

A label is a tag on a MongoDB error. TransientTransactionError says that the whole transaction may succeed if it runs again. The MongoDB manual says that the operations inside a transaction are not retryable on their own. Only the whole transaction is.

Spring Data translates error 112 to DataIntegrityViolationException, the same type as many real data errors. A WriteConflict never becomes a transient exception in Spring, because the translator checks the code first. So the platform checks the cause itself:

public final class WriteConflicts {

    /** MongoDB's error code for a write conflict. */
    public static final int WRITE_CONFLICT = 112;

    private WriteConflicts() {
    }

    /** Returns whether the exception, or one of its causes, is a MongoDB write conflict. */
    public static boolean isWriteConflict(Throwable error) {
        for (Throwable cause = error; cause != null; cause = cause.getCause()) {
            if (cause instanceof MongoException mongo
                    && (mongo.getCode() == WRITE_CONFLICT
                    || mongo.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL))) {
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
Reading the code
for (Throwable cause = error; cause != null; cause = cause.getCause()) {

The loop walks the chain of causes. Spring's exception wraps the driver's exception.

if (cause instanceof MongoException mongo

This is a type pattern. When the cause is a MongoException, it is bound to the variable mongo. C# writes the same test as cause is MongoException mongo.

|| mongo.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL))) {

The label counts too, so a transient error with another code is also a conflict.

The test WriteConflictsTest builds a MongoCommandException with code 112, and one with code 121. Only the first counts as a conflict. So a broken validation rule in the database stays a 500, and is not answered as a conflict.

Gotcha

Spring retries nothing. The MongoDB .NET driver's WithTransactionAsync runs its callback again after a TransientTransactionError. In a run for this book, it ran the callback three times, and the third run succeeded. Spring's TransactionTemplate ran its callback exactly once, and the write conflict reached the caller. MongoTransactionManager uses the core transaction API of the driver, which has no retry logic. Its source says that it ignores error labels by default.

Spring Data's reference recommends Spring Retry for errors with these labels. The order service does not retry inside the service. It answers 409, and the caller decides:

Who caused the conflictWhat the service doesWhat happens next
an agent, over HTTPthe platform's handler answers 409, with the code CONCURRENT_UPDATEthe agent reloads the order and tries again
a message from SQSthe inbox throws ConcurrentDeliveryException, and the transaction rolls backSQS delivers the message again, and the inbox finds its key or processes it

A retry inside the service has a careful version. Retry only on the label TransientTransactionError. Run the whole transaction again, and load the aggregate again inside it. Retry two or three times at most, with a short pause. Put no call to another service inside the retried part. This version is safe, and it hides short conflicts from the user. It is the better choice for a background job that changes hot documents, where nobody can press "try again".

The order service still answers 409 for two reasons. A conflict means that someone else changed the same order a moment ago. The agent should see the new state before acting again, because a pick or a cancellation may have changed it. And conflicts are rare in the service, because notes have their own documents. A retry would add code for a case that the agent can handle better.

A commit can also fail with an unknown result. The network fails after the commit was sent, and the driver cannot tell whether it succeeded. The source of MongoTransactionManager shows how a subclass could retry the commit on the label constant UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION_COMMIT_RESULT_LABEL. A failed commit raises TransactionSystemException. The service does not override this, so the caller sees a 500.

com.mongodb.MongoCommandException: Command execution failed on MongoDB server with error 112 (WriteConflict): 'Caused by :: WiredTigerIdIndex::_insert: index: _id_ ... Please retry your operation or multi-document transaction.'#
Means
Another transaction wrote the same document first. MongoDB aborted this transaction, and Spring translated the error to DataIntegrityViolationException.
Fix
Answer 409 and let the caller reload, or run the whole transaction again for an error with the label TransientTransactionError.

The DocumentDB pages that the research checked document error 251, not error 112. Amazon DocumentDB may answer the same race differently. Nobody ran it on a cluster for this book.

The limits of a transaction on Amazon DocumentDBtrap#

A transaction that works on a local MongoDB can fail on Amazon DocumentDB. AWS documents these limits, as of October 2026:

LimitWhat AWS statesWhat it means for the order service
engine versiontransactions need engine 4.0 or laterthe shop's clusters run engine 8.0
elastic clustersno ACID transactions at allthe service needs an instance-based cluster
durationa transaction may run for one minuteno HTTP call inside a transaction, as in place
sizethe transaction log must be less than 32 MBone order with a few notes is far below it
document locksa write lock on a document times out after one minute, and this cannot be configureda long transaction can block other writers for that long
sessionsa session times out after 30 minutesMongoTransactionManager opens a session when a transaction begins
new collectionsa transaction cannot create a collection, or query one that does not existevery collection must exist before its first transaction
cursorsno cursors within a transactionread single documents or small results inside a transaction
causal consistencynot supported, with error 303Spring opens a causally consistent session, which was never tested on a cluster
isolationa lower read concern is upgraded to snapshot, and a lower write concern to majoritythe service sets neither

AWS also limits the open transactions of an instance. On engine 8.0, an instance of the class T3.medium allows 50, R5.large allows 200, and R5.2xlarge allows 800. A service whose transactions stay open long uses these up first.

AWS's page contradicts itself on counting. Its table lists countDocuments() as unsupported in a transaction, and its list of limits recommends it. The shipping rule counts notes inside the transaction of ship, with a derived count query:

/** For the order feature's shipping rule: a plain number, so no note crosses the boundary. */
public long countNeedingAction(String orderId) {
    return notes.countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull(orderId);
}

The research did not record which command Spring Data sends for countByOrderIdAndActionRequiredTrueAndActionResolvedAtIsNull. Test the shipping rule on a real cluster before a release.

Gotcha

A collection that does not exist yet breaks the first transaction. On a new environment, the first save of a note may happen inside a transaction. On Amazon DocumentDB, that save cannot create the collection notes. MongoDB 8.0 allows it, so tests do not show the problem. Create every collection before its first transaction.

An index would seem to create the collection on the way. On MongoDB 8.0.34 it does, in a run for this book. On DocumentDB, no AWS page that the research checked says so, as of October 2026. So the platform does not rely on it. It creates each collection explicitly, outside any transaction, in a migration:

/**
 * Creates the collections that a transaction writes to, before the first transaction does.
 *
 * <p>Amazon DocumentDB cannot create a collection inside a transaction. MongoDB creates a
 * missing collection on the first write, even inside a transaction, so a local test never shows
 * the problem. On a new DocumentDB cluster, the first use case would fail instead. So every
 * collection that a transaction writes to is created here, outside any transaction.
 *
 * <p>A collection that exists already is left alone, so the migration is safe to run twice.
 * Give the ID a {@code 000} number, such as {@code V000-create-collections}, so that on a new
 * database it runs before the migrations that create indexes on the same collections.
 */
public class CreateCollections implements MongoMigration {

    private final String id;
    private final List<String> collections;

    public CreateCollections(String id, List<String> collections) {
        this.id = id;
        this.collections = List.copyOf(collections);
    }

    @Override
    public String id() {
        return id;
    }

    @Override
    public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        for (String collection : collections) {
            if (!mongo.collectionExists(collection)) {
                mongo.createCollection(collection);
            }
        }
    }
}
Reading the code
if (!mongo.collectionExists(collection)) {

collectionExists asks the database for the collection by its name. On MongoDB 8.0.34, a second create of an existing collection with the same options gave no error, in a run for this book. DocumentDB was not checked, so the migration asks first, and stays safe to run twice on both.

mongo.createCollection(collection);

This creates an empty collection with the default options. The migration runner calls it before the web server and the listeners of Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) start, and never inside a transaction.

Every collection that a transaction writes to has an owner, and each owner lists its own. The order service lists the collections of its three features in the migration V000-create-collections. For that migration and its place in the run order, see the section Collections first, outside any transaction.

The platform lists the collections of its own parts. The outbox of Spring Modulith writes to event_publication in the use case's transaction, and the inbox writes to processed_messages in the listener's transaction. So the messaging auto-configuration creates both:

/**
 * The outbox and the inbox are written inside the use case's transaction, so both
 * collections must exist before it. See {@link CreateCollections}.
 */
@Bean
CreateCollections messagingCollections() {
    return new CreateCollections("P000-messaging-collections", List.of(OutboxIndexes.COLLECTION, Inbox.COLLECTION));
}

The ID P000-messaging-collections sorts before the platform's index migrations. The audit log writes to audit_log in the same transactions, so the audit auto-configuration adds P000-audit-log-collection the same way. The collections that no transaction writes to need no entry. The migration runner writes schema_migrations and its lock, and the resender's lock writes scheduler_locks, all outside transactions.

The test CreateCollectionsIT runs the migration twice against a real MongoDB. It finds the missing collection created, and the existing one unchanged. No test can show the DocumentDB failure on MongoDB. Run one use case on a new DocumentDB cluster before the first release.

For the basic list of these limits, see the section Transactions on Amazon DocumentDB.

A local replica settwist#

MongoDB supports transactions only on a replica set. A stand-alone MongoDB refuses them. Amazon DocumentDB always runs as a replica set. So the local environment starts MongoDB as a replica set with one member, and initialises it in its health check:

mongo:
  image: mongo:8.0.34
  command: ["--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]
  ports: ["27017:27017"]
  healthcheck:
    # Also initialises the replica set the first time it runs
    test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval",
           "try { rs.status().ok } catch (e) { rs.initiate({_id: 'rs0', members: [{_id: 0, host: 'mongo:27017'}]}).ok }"]
    interval: 5s
    retries: 30
Reading the code
command: ["--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]

MongoDB starts as a member of the replica set rs0. --bind_ip_all lets other containers connect.

"try { rs.status().ok } catch (e) { rs.initiate({_id: 'rs0', members: [{_id: 0, host: 'mongo:27017'}]}).ok }"]

A replica set must be initiated once. The check asks for the status, and initiates the set when the status fails. So the first check sets it up, and the later checks only report.

host: 'mongo:27017'

The member is named by its container name. Other containers reach it by that name. A program on the host machine cannot resolve it, so the README adds directConnection=true for a run from an IDE.

The tests start their MongoDB with withReplicaSet(), for the same reason. For that, and the trap of the new Testcontainers class, see the section Testing the storage. In a run for this book, a transaction on a stand-alone MongoDB container failed. For that error, see the entry UncategorizedMongoDbException.

One aggregate per transaction, and the order with its notesnew#

An aggregate is the boundary of its own rules. So one transaction should change one aggregate. A use case that changes two aggregates in one transaction couples them. Each makes the transaction of the other larger and slower, and each can conflict with writers of the other. The usual answer is an event. The first aggregate commits, and an event changes the second one later, in its own transaction.

The order service keeps this rule in every use case but one. Placing an order stores the new order and its first notes in one transaction. The decision has a callout of its own, "One transaction for an order and its first notes". For the decision, its reasons and the sign to stop, see the section One request that saves the order and its first notes. This section shows what the transaction holds.

The transaction of place holds the order, one document for each note, an outbox row for each event and an audit record for each change. If a note fails its category check, the unchecked exception leaves the lambda, and all of these are rolled back. The journey test OrderJourneyIT.anOrderAndItsNotesAreStoredTogetherOrNotAtAll proves it against a real MongoDB.

The transaction stays far inside the limits of Amazon DocumentDB. Both aggregates are new, so no other writer can cause a write conflict on them. It holds a few documents, and it calls no other service, because the stock call runs before it. The service's README gives the rule for such a transaction:

**One request saves two aggregates.** Placing an order with its first notes stores both in one
transaction, because the agent sees it as one action. Keep such transactions small, and never
let them span services.

The words Keep such transactions small name the limit in transaction terms. A transaction that grows past a few documents, or that changes an existing aggregate of another feature, is the sign to use an event instead.

Three other designs avoid the shared transaction. Each one has something it gets right. The service still does not use them. For the reasons, see the section One request that saves the order and its first notes.

For the reasons on the side of the domain, see the section Why order and note are separate aggregates. Between services, the rule is stricter still. No transaction ever spans two services. For that, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

A transaction manager that does nothing, for unit teststwist#

A unit test of OrderService runs with no Spring context and no database. But place calls a TransactionTemplate, and the outbox publisher checks for a transaction. A mocked template would not run the lambda at all. So the platform provides a real transaction manager that does nothing:

/**
 * A transaction manager that does nothing, for unit tests.
 *
 * <p>With it, a real {@code TransactionTemplate} runs its callback, and Spring reports an active
 * transaction, but nothing touches a database. A unit test can then check the order of the
 * steps inside the transaction without MongoDB.
 */
public class NoOpTransactionManager extends AbstractPlatformTransactionManager {

    @Override
    protected Object doGetTransaction() {
        return new Object();
    }

    @Override
    protected void doBegin(Object transaction, TransactionDefinition definition) {
        // Nothing to begin.
    }

    @Override
    protected void doCommit(DefaultTransactionStatus status) {
        // Nothing to commit.
    }

    @Override
    protected void doRollback(DefaultTransactionStatus status) {
        // Nothing to roll back.
    }
}
Reading the code
public class NoOpTransactionManager extends AbstractPlatformTransactionManager {

AbstractPlatformTransactionManager is the base class of Spring for transaction managers. It handles propagation, joining and the state of the thread. A subclass only begins, commits and rolls back.

protected Object doGetTransaction() {

The base class asks for an object that stands for the transaction. Any object will do here.

// Nothing to commit.

The real work of the other methods is empty. The base class still marks the thread as being in a transaction, so isActualTransactionActive() is true inside the callback.

The test builds the service with new, and passes a real template:

private final OrderService service = new OrderService(orders, notes, referenceData, stock, new ShippingPolicy(),
        events, audit, new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager()), CLOCK);

new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager()) runs the lambda of place, and returns its value. The test reservesStockThenSavesTheOrderAndItsNotesAndPublishesOrderPlaced then checks the order of the steps with InOrder. The stock call comes first, then the save, the event, the audit and the notes. The test cannot prove a rollback, because nothing is stored. The journey test proves that against MongoDB.

The publisher's own test uses the same manager. OutboxDomainEventPublisherTest.publishesEachDomainEventAndItsIntegrationEvent publishes inside transaction.executeWithoutResult, and the publisher sees an active transaction. A C# test of code with sessions would need a mock of IClientSessionHandle. The Java test needs no mock, because the template itself is real. NoOpTransactionManager extends the same base class as MongoTransactionManager.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksA method that joined the use case's transaction throws a domain exception. The use case catches it, and returns normally. What happens, and why?
The commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException, and nothing is stored. The proxy of the inner method marked the whole transaction as rollback-only when the exception left it. The outer code cannot undo that mark. So never catch a domain exception inside a transaction to continue. Let it leave the use case.
2
An expert asksA write conflict aborts a transaction. Why does Spring not retry it, as WithTransactionAsync does in .NET, and what does the order service do instead?
MongoTransactionManager uses the driver's core transaction API, which has no retry, and it ignores error labels. The conflict reaches the caller as DataIntegrityViolationException. The service answers an agent with 409, so the agent reloads the order. A message is redelivered by SQS.
3
What does spring.modulith.events.mongodb.transaction-management.enabled=false do in the platform?
It stops Spring Modulith from registering its own MongoTransactionManager and TransactionTemplate. The default is true. The platform's mongo package already registers the manager, so exactly one place creates it.
4
On Amazon DocumentDB, why must a collection exist before the first transaction that writes to it?
AWS states that a transaction cannot create a collection, or query one that does not exist, as of October 2026. On a new environment, the first save inside a transaction would fail. MongoDB 8.0 allows it, so local tests do not show the problem. Create the collections first, for example in a migration.
5
TranslateWrite the transactional part of the platform's inbox in Java. The template for transactions is transactions, and the MongoTemplate is mongo. The collection name is COLLECTION: 
using IClientSessionHandle session = await client.StartSessionAsync();
await session.WithTransactionAsync(async (s, ct) =>
{
    if (await processed.Find(s, new BsonDocument("_id", key)).AnyAsync(ct))
    {
        return false;
    }
    await handler();
    await processed.InsertOneAsync(s,
        new BsonDocument { { "_id", key }, { "processedAt", clock.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime } },
        cancellationToken: ct);
    return true;
});
transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
    if (mongo.exists(query(where("_id").is(key)), COLLECTION)) {
        log.info("Skipping event {}, which was processed before", event.eventId());
        return;
    }
    handler.accept(event);
    mongo.insert(new Document("_id", key).append("processedAt", clock.instant()), COLLECTION);
});

executeWithoutResult runs a lambda that returns nothing, in one transaction. The handler joins the same transaction, so the key and the handler's changes commit together. No call takes a session. One difference stays. WithTransactionAsync retries a transient error, and the template does not.

Calling other services#

Talking to other services · Chapter 19· 35 min read· Quick reference

The order service asks the stock service to hold the products of each new order. The use case sees only a small interface in its own words. Behind it, Spring generates the HTTP client, and an adapter translates the answer. The platform gives every call timeouts, tracing, a token, a circuit breaker and safe retries. A call that still fails becomes a 503.
