Why the order service calls the stock servicenew#

An agent places an order for two mugs. The shop must not sell mugs that it does not have. The stock service knows how many mugs are in the warehouse. So the order service asks it to hold the mugs for the new order, before it saves the order.

The service's README states the rule. An order is placed only if the stock service confirms and holds every product. The use case place makes the call first, and opens its transaction afterwards:

public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
                         List<NewNote> firstNotes) {
    referenceData.requireActive(ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD, deliveryMethod.code(), "deliveryMethod");
    OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();
    StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items);           // outside the transaction

    return transaction.execute(status -> {
        Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);
        Order saved = saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_PLACED);        // aggregate 1
        List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction
        return new PlacedOrder(saved.id().value(), noteIds);
    });
}
Reading the code
OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();

The use case chooses the order's ID before anything else. The ID travels to the stock service as the idempotency key. The section Retry only what is safe to repeat explains why.

StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items); // outside the transaction

stock is the port to the stock service. The call returns a value object of the order service, not the stock service's JSON. It runs before the transaction, so a slow stock service never holds a database transaction open.

return transaction.execute(status -> {

Only the code inside this lambda is transactional. Order.place then decides what the answer means. For the TransactionTemplate, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

One call to the stock service passes through five pieces. Each piece has one job:

The sections below follow the call from the use case to the network, and then back through every way it can fail.

The port: the question in the service's own wordstwist#

C#
public interface IStockChecker
{
    Task<StockAvailability> ReserveAsync(OrderId order, IReadOnlyList<OrderItem> items);
}
Java 25
public interface StockChecker {

    /**
     * Asks the stock service to confirm that the items are available, and to hold them for the
     * order. The stock service keeps the hold until it sees {@code OrderPlacedV1}, or releases it
     * after a timeout if the order is never placed.
     *
     * <p>Calling it twice for the same order holds nothing twice, because the order ID is the
     * idempotency key.
     */
    StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);
}
Reading the code
StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);

The method takes and returns types of the order service. OrderId, OrderItem and StockAvailability belong to the domain model. Nothing here says HTTP, JSON or sku.

The stock service keeps the hold until it sees {@code OrderPlacedV1}, or releases it

The comment states the contract with the stock service. A hold for an order that is never saved does not last for ever.

The Java method returns the answer directly, and the C# method returns a Task. The Java call blocks its thread. On a virtual thread that is the normal way. For the reason, see the chapter HTTP clients and resilience.

A port is an interface that the application layer owns, and an adapter elsewhere implements it. This port is in the package order.application.port, not in the domain. Calling another service is a step of the use case, and the domain only judges the answer. A unit test of OrderService replaces the port with a Mockito mock, and needs no server. The journey test does the same with @MockitoBean StockChecker stock. For ports in general, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

The HTTP interface: Spring writes the clienttwist#

Refit
public interface IStockHttpClient
{
    [Post("/stock/reservations")]
    Task<ReservationResponse> ReserveAsync([Header("Idempotency-Key")] string idempotencyKey,
                                           [Body] ReservationRequest request);
}
Spring HTTP interface
@HttpExchange("/stock")
interface StockHttpClient {

    /**
     * Holds stock for an order.
     *
     * <p>A POST that creates something is not safe to repeat: if the response is lost, a retry
     * would hold the stock twice. The {@code Idempotency-Key} header makes it safe. The stock
     * service remembers the key, and answers a repeated request with the first answer.
     */
    @PostExchange("/reservations")
    ReservationResponse reserve(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey,
                                @RequestBody ReservationRequest request);
}
Reading the code
@HttpExchange("/stock")

This annotation on the interface gives the start of every path. It is in the package org.springframework.web.service.annotation.

@PostExchange("/reservations")

This method sends a POST to /stock/reservations, like [Post] in Refit.

@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey,

The argument becomes the header Idempotency-Key. The annotation is the same one that a controller uses to read a header.

@RequestBody ReservationRequest request);

The argument is written as the JSON body. The answer is read into a ReservationResponse.

The interface has no access modifier, so it is package-private. Only the client package can use it. Spring creates the implementation at runtime. The platform asks HttpServiceProxyFactory for it, and the factory returns a proxy. A run for this book looked at such a client, created by Boot. It was a proxy of the Java Development Kit (JDK), an object that implements the interface and turns each method call into an HTTP request.

Boot 4 can also create the bean itself, with @ImportHttpServices and the settings spring.http.serviceclient.<group>.*. For that form, see the section Declarative clients. The order service builds its clients through the platform instead, so every client gets the same timeouts, tracing and token. See the section The platform's HttpClientFactory.

Their DTOs stay in the client packagetwist#

C#
[JsonUnmappedMemberHandling(JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Skip)]
public record ReservationResponse(string Result, List<string> ShortSkus);
Java 25
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public record ReservationResponse(String result, List<String> shortSkus) {
}

The record ReservationResponse is the stock service's answer. A data transfer object (DTO) is a class that only carries data over the wire. The stock service has its own words. It calls a product code a sku, and its answer is RESERVED or INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. The order service copies those words into two records in the package order.client.dto. The request is the other one:

/** The stock service's request body, in its own words: it calls a product code a {@code sku}. */
public record ReservationRequest(String orderId, List<Line> lines) {

    public record Line(String sku, int quantity) {
    }
}

Line is a record inside a record, so its full name is ReservationRequest.Line. Only the adapter uses these records. The use case and the domain never see them. So a renamed field on the stock service's side changes one package of the order service.

The answer reads only the fields that the order service uses. The stub of the stock service also sends reservationId, and the record has no such field. A reader that takes what it needs and ignores the rest is called a tolerant reader. The stock service can then add fields without breaking the order service.

Jackson 3 already ignores unknown fields. A run for this book confirmed that FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is off, in Jackson 3 and in the mapper that Boot builds. In Jackson 2 it was on by default. The annotation @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) states the rule on the class itself. It keeps the record safe if a later setting turns the check on. Its package is still com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation, because Jackson 3 kept the annotations of the 2.x line. For Jackson 3 in full, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

The adapter: the anti-corruption layernew#

The stock service may one day answer PARTIALLY_RESERVED. If the order service passed the stock service's words through, that new word would reach the domain. A rule would then treat it as a success or a failure by accident. Something must stand between the two models.

That something is called an anti-corruption layer. It translates the other service's model into this service's model, in one place. In the order service, it is the adapter that implements the port:

@Component
class StockAdapter implements StockChecker {

    static final String DEPENDENCY = "stock";

    private final StockHttpClient http;
    private final ResilientCalls resilientCalls;

    StockAdapter(StockHttpClient http, ResilientCalls resilientCalls) {
        this.http = http;
        this.resilientCalls = resilientCalls;
    }

    @Override
    public StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items) {
        ReservationRequest request = new ReservationRequest(order.value(), items.stream()
                .map(item -> new ReservationRequest.Line(item.product().value(), item.quantity()))
                .toList());
        ReservationResponse response = resilientCalls.callWithRetry(DEPENDENCY,
                () -> http.reserve(order.value(), request));
        return translate(response);
    }

    /** Translates their answer into ours. An answer this service does not know is a bug to report. */
    static StockAvailability translate(ReservationResponse response) {
        return switch (response.result()) {
            case "RESERVED" -> StockAvailability.allAvailable();
            case "INSUFFICIENT_STOCK" -> StockAvailability.unavailable(
                    response.shortSkus().stream().map(ProductCode::new).toList());
            default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unknown stock reservation result: " + response.result());
        };
    }
}
Reading the code
class StockAdapter implements StockChecker {

The class is package-private, and @Component makes it a bean. Spring injects it wherever a StockChecker is needed. Nothing outside the client package can name the class.

static final String DEPENDENCY = "stock";

The name of the dependency. It chooses the circuit breaker and the retry settings in ResilientCalls, and it appears in the log when the call fails.

.map(item -> new ReservationRequest.Line(item.product().value(), item.quantity()))

The adapter builds their request from our items. A ProductCode becomes the text that the stock service calls a sku.

() -> http.reserve(order.value(), request));

The call is passed as a lambda, and ResilientCalls decides when to run it. Its type is Supplier<ReservationResponse>. See the section The platform's HttpClientFactory.

return switch (response.result()) {

This is a switch expression on a string. Each case with -> gives the value of the whole switch, as an arm of a switch expression does in C#.

default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unknown stock reservation result: " + response.result());

A default arm may throw instead of giving a value. An answer that the order service does not know is a bug to report, not a guess to make.

.map(ProductCode::new)

ProductCode::new is a method reference to the constructor. It turns each sku into a ProductCode of the order service.

The method translate is static and has no dependencies. So a test can call it with a ReservationResponse and check the result, with no server. The test StockAdapterTest.refusesAnAnswerItDoesNotKnow sends MAYBE, and expects the IllegalStateException with that message.

An unknown answer is not a 503. The stock service answered, and the order service did not understand it. So the exception reaches the platform's handler for any other exception, and the caller gets 500. The log then shows a bug, which a person must fix.

Note

The stock service never sees the domain classes, and the domain never sees the DTOs. Keep the translation in the adapter, in both directions. A use case that reads ReservationResponse would bring the stock service's model into the order service's model.

The platform's HttpClientFactorynew#

Every service of the shop calls other services. Each client needs the same things. It needs a base URL, two timeouts, the trace ID on each request, and often a token. If each team wrote this code, one client would sooner or later have no timeout. So the platform builds every client in one method:

public <T> T create(Class<T> clientType, HttpClientProperties properties) {
    HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .connectTimeout(properties.getConnectTimeout())
            .build();
    JdkClientHttpRequestFactory requestFactory = new JdkClientHttpRequestFactory(httpClient);
    requestFactory.setReadTimeout(properties.getReadTimeout());

    RestClient.Builder builder = restClientBuilders.get()
            .baseUrl(properties.getBaseUrl().toString())
            .requestFactory(requestFactory);
    if (StringUtils.hasText(properties.getTokenRegistrationId())) {
        builder.requestInterceptor(tokenInterceptor(properties.getTokenRegistrationId()));
    }

    return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(builder.build()))
            .build()
            .createClient(clientType);
}
Reading the code
public <T> T create(Class<T> clientType, HttpClientProperties properties) {

A generic method. Class<T> is the interface to implement, such as StockHttpClient.class, and the method returns a T.

HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newBuilder()

This is the HTTP client of the JDK, in the package java.net.http. It opens the connections.

.connectTimeout(properties.getConnectTimeout())

The connect timeout belongs to the JDK client.

requestFactory.setReadTimeout(properties.getReadTimeout());

JdkClientHttpRequestFactory lets Spring's RestClient send its requests through the JDK client. The read timeout belongs to this factory.

RestClient.Builder builder = restClientBuilders.get()

A new builder from Spring Boot. The next section shows why it must come from Boot.

builder.requestInterceptor(tokenInterceptor(properties.getTokenRegistrationId()));

When the settings name a token registration, every request gets the service's own token. See the section The service's own token on every call.

HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(builder.build()))

RestClientAdapter lets the proxy factory send requests through the finished RestClient.

.createClient(clientType);

The factory reads the annotations of the interface and returns the proxy.

So three Spring types stand between the interface and the network:

TypeWhat it doesWhere its settings come from
HttpServiceProxyFactoryturns the interface into a proxy, one request for each method callthe annotations of the interface
RestClientsends the request, writes and reads JSON, runs the interceptorsBoot's builder, plus the base URL and the token interceptor
JdkClientHttpRequestFactoryhands each request to the JDK's HttpClient, with a read timeoutthe client's settings

The factory receives its builders as a Supplier<RestClient.Builder>. A Supplier<T> is a functional interface with one method, get(), and no parameters. It does the same as Func<T> in C#. The platform uses three of these interfaces:

JavaC#Where the platform uses it
Supplier<T>Func<T>the builders here, and the call that ResilientCalls runs
Consumer<T>Action<T>the handler that the inbox runs for a message
Function<T, R>Func<T, TResult>the type of a lambda such as item -> new ReservationRequest.Line(...)

For lambdas and these types in full, see the section Lambdas. The platform's auto-configuration creates the factory:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
HttpClientFactory httpClientFactory(ObjectProvider<RestClient.Builder> restClientBuilders,
                                    ObjectProvider<ClientRegistrationRepository> registrations,
                                    ObjectProvider<OAuth2AuthorizedClientService> authorizedClients) {
    Supplier<OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager> tokenManager = () -> {
        ClientRegistrationRepository repository = registrations.getIfAvailable();
        if (repository == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("A client asks for a token, but no "
                    + "spring.security.oauth2.client.registration is configured");
        }
        return new AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(repository, authorizedClients.getObject());
    };
    return new HttpClientFactory(restClientBuilders::getObject, tokenManager);
}
Reading the code
ObjectProvider<RestClient.Builder> restClientBuilders,

An ObjectProvider asks the container for a bean each time it is called, not once. For ObjectProvider, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

return new HttpClientFactory(restClientBuilders::getObject, tokenManager);

restClientBuilders::getObject is a method reference, used as the Supplier. Each call to get() asks the container for a builder.

ClientRegistrationRepository repository = registrations.getIfAvailable();

The token manager is built only when a client asks for a token. A service without client registrations still starts.

The Supplier is also the seam for tests. StockAdapterTest passes the method reference RestClient::builder, so it needs no Spring container. See the section Testing the client against a real HTTP server.

The platform's factory has the same purpose as IHttpClientFactory in ASP.NET Core. It creates a typed client from an interface and one settings object, and every client gets the same setup.

Why the factory uses Boot's injected buildertrap#

The platform's comment is short. Never use RestClient.create(). The reason is the trace ID. The trace ID travels to the next service in a header named traceparent. A run for this book sent requests from three clients to a JDK HttpServer that recorded the headers. The application had spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry on its classpath. This is the run's own code:

PredictThree ways to build a RestClient#
b1 is Boot's RestClient.Builder bean. Each line sends one request to the recording server. Which of the three requests carry a traceparent header?
var b1 = ctx.getBean(RestClient.Builder.class);
// ...
b1.baseUrl(base).build().get().uri("/stock/a").retrieve().toBodilessEntity();
// ...
RestClient.create(base).get().uri("/stock/a").retrieve().toBodilessEntity();
// ...
RestClient.builder().baseUrl(base).build().get().uri("/stock/a").retrieve().toBodilessEntity();
Show the answer
Only the request through b1, Boot's builder, carries traceparent. The other two requests carry none.

Only Boot's builder carries the tracing setup. Spring Boot creates and configures a RestClient.Builder bean, and the run shows that its setup includes tracing. The static methods RestClient.create and RestClient.builder make a bare client that knows nothing of Boot.

A second run showed the effect. A request that called itself through the static builder started a new trace. Through Boot's builder, the inner request kept the trace of the outer one. So always take the builder from the container.

The builder bean is named restClientBuilder, and its scope is prototype. A prototype bean is created new for each request to the container. Two calls to getBean returned two instances in a run. This matters, because a builder is a mutable object. The factory sets a base URL and an interceptor on it. With one shared builder, the second client would get the first client's settings too. So the factory asks for a new builder for each client, through ObjectProvider::getObject.

Boot's builder brings more than tracing. The platform's comment also names metrics, and the reference of Boot says that it creates and pre-configures the builder. For traces and metrics, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

Gotcha

A test that builds the client with RestClient::builder has no tracing. That is right for StockAdapterTest, which tests the call, the JSON and the retries. A test that must check the trace ID needs the builder from a Spring context.

Timeouts, and the Boot 4 key namestwist#

C#
builder.Services.AddHttpClient("stock", c =>
{
    c.BaseAddress = new Uri(stockUrl);
    c.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3);
});
application.yml
clients:
  stock:
    base-url: ${STOCK_SERVICE_URL}
    read-timeout: 3s
    # Each call carries a token from this client registration
    token-registration-id: stock-service
Reading the code
base-url: ${STOCK_SERVICE_URL}

The URL comes from an environment variable, so each environment names its own stock service.

read-timeout: 3s

The order service waits at most 3 seconds for the stock service's answer. The connect timeout keeps the platform's default of 2 seconds.

The keys clients.stock.* are the platform's own. Each client binds them into a HttpClientProperties object:

@Validated
public class HttpClientProperties {

    /** The root URL of the other service, such as {@code https://stock.internal}. */
    @NotNull
    private URI baseUrl;

    /** How long to wait for a connection. */
    @NotNull
    private Duration connectTimeout = Duration.ofSeconds(2);

    /** How long to wait for the response once connected. */
    @NotNull
    private Duration readTimeout = Duration.ofSeconds(5);
Reading the code
@Validated

Spring validates the object when it binds the settings. A missing base-url stops the service at startup, not at the first call.

private URI baseUrl;

java.net.URI holds a parsed address. A value that is not a valid URI fails at binding.

private Duration connectTimeout = Duration.ofSeconds(2);

The default applies when the setting is missing. A text such as 3s binds to a Duration.

The two timeouts guard against two different problems. Runs for this book measured both, with a connect timeout of 500 ms and a read timeout of 1 second:

SituationTimeout that firesWhat the caller got
the address cannot be reached, here 10.255.255.1connect timeout, after 507 msResourceAccessException, caused by HttpConnectTimeoutException
the server is reached, and answers after 3 secondsread timeout, after 1071 msResourceAccessException, caused by HttpTimeoutException with the message Request cancelled

Both failures arrive as ResourceAccessException, Spring's exception for an input or output error. So the platform can treat them as one kind of failure. See the section Which failures are worth a retry.

The C# pane sets one Timeout on the HttpClient. The platform sets two limits, because a slow connection and a slow answer are different problems. Without a limit, a stock service that never answers would hold the order service's request for as long as the socket stays open. See the section Timeouts.

Spring Boot 4 also has its own keys, for the clients that Boot builds. They apply to Boot's builder and to an @ImportHttpServices client. Their names changed in Boot 4:

Boot 4 keyDeprecated key, since 4.0.0What it does
spring.http.clients.connect-timeoutspring.http.client.connect-timeoutthe time to wait for a connection, for every client Boot builds
spring.http.clients.read-timeoutspring.http.client.read-timeoutthe time to wait for an answer, for every client Boot builds
spring.http.clients.imperative.factoryspring.http.client.factorywhich HTTP library the blocking clients use
spring.http.serviceclient.<group>.read-timeoutnonethe same, for one @ImportHttpServices group

The plural clients is easy to miss. A run with spring.http.clients.read-timeout=1s failed a 3-second reply after 1070 ms. With no other HTTP client library on the classpath, Boot chose the JdkClientHttpRequestFactory, the same one that the platform uses.

The platform's factory passes its own request factory to the builder, with the client's timeouts. So the settings clients.stock.* decide the stock call's timeouts. Use Boot's keys for a client that Boot builds, and the platform's keys for a client that the factory builds.

Wiring one clienttwist#

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class StockClientConfig {

    /** Binds the platform's reusable properties class to this client's prefix. */
    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")
    HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties() {
        return new HttpClientProperties();
    }

    @Bean
    StockHttpClient stockHttpClient(HttpClientFactory clients, HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties) {
        return clients.create(StockHttpClient.class, stockClientProperties);
    }
}
Reading the code
@ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")

On a @Bean method, this annotation binds the returned object to the prefix. So the platform's one class serves every client, each with its own prefix. For binding, see the chapter Configuration in depth.

StockHttpClient stockHttpClient(HttpClientFactory clients, HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties) {

The parameter name stockClientProperties matches the bean name. With a second client, two beans of type HttpClientProperties exist, and the name chooses one.

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)

No method of this class calls another @Bean method, so Spring needs no Code Generation Library (CGLIB) subclass of it.

This class completes the client. A new client for another service needs five files in the feature's client package and in its port package:

FileExampleWhat it holds
the portapplication/port/StockCheckerthe question, in this service's types
the HTTP interfaceclient/StockHttpClientthe other service's endpoints, as annotated methods
the DTOsclient/dto/ReservationRequest, ReservationResponsetheir JSON, in their words
the adapterclient/StockAdapterthe call through ResilientCalls, and the translation
the configurationclient/StockClientConfigthe settings prefix and the client bean

Add the settings under clients.<name>, a stub in the local environment, and the adapter's test. Only the adapter and the configuration are beans. The port is the only type that the rest of the service sees.

The service's own token on every calltwist#

C#
builder.Services.AddHttpClient("stock")
    .AddHttpMessageHandler<ClientCredentialsTokenHandler>();
Java 25
/**
 * The Spring Security client registration that issues this client's tokens, such as
 * {@code stock-service}. When it is set, every call carries a client-credentials token.
 * Leave it empty only for a service that needs no token.
 */
private String tokenRegistrationId;

The stock service needs a token, and its stub answers 401 without one. The field tokenRegistrationId is bound from the setting token-registration-id, which the stock client sets to stock-service. The value names a client registration of Spring Security. When the field is set, the factory adds an interceptor that puts a client-credentials token on every request. In the C# pane, ClientCredentialsTokenHandler stands for a DelegatingHandler that you write yourself.

The token belongs to the order service, not to the agent. Spring Security fetches it at the first call, and keeps it until 60 seconds before it expires. The platform fixes the principal under which the token is stored, so all agents share one token. The test StockAdapterTest.twoDifferentUsersShareOneServiceToken proves it with two agents and one token request.

Security has its home in another chapter. For the registration and the interceptor, see the section The service's own token for the stock service. That section also explains the trap of one token for each user.

Retry and circuit breaker: what each one is fornew#

The stock service restarts during a deployment, and one request gets no answer. A second try a moment later would work. Later that day, the stock service is down for ten minutes. Every request waits 3 seconds for nothing, and agents see slow failures.

The two cases need two tools. A retry repeats a call that failed for a short time. A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, and fails at once instead. After a wait, it lets a few test calls through. If they work, it closes again.

Think of the circuit breaker as a fuse box in a house. When a device keeps failing, the fuse trips, and the device gets no power until someone tests it. The comparison stops at the reset. A circuit breaker tests the line by itself after its wait, and no person is needed.

The platform puts both tools in one class, ResilientCalls. It uses the core modules of the library Resilience4j, version 2.4.0. Its constructor builds the two registries:

public ResilientCalls(ResilienceProperties properties) {
    ResilienceProperties.CircuitBreaker breaker = properties.getCircuitBreaker();
    this.circuitBreakers = CircuitBreakerRegistry.of(CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
            .failureRateThreshold(breaker.getFailureRateThreshold())
            .slidingWindowSize(breaker.getSlidingWindowSize())
            .minimumNumberOfCalls(breaker.getMinimumNumberOfCalls())
            .waitDurationInOpenState(breaker.getWaitDurationInOpenState())
            .recordException(ResilientCalls::isTransient)
            .ignoreExceptions(HttpClientErrorException.class)
            .build());

    ResilienceProperties.Retry retry = properties.getRetry();
    this.retries = RetryRegistry.of(RetryConfig.custom()
            .maxAttempts(retry.getMaxAttempts())              // calls in total, not retries
            .intervalFunction(IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff(
                    retry.getInitialInterval().toMillis(), retry.getMultiplier()))
            .retryOnException(ResilientCalls::isTransient)
            .build());
}
Reading the code
this.circuitBreakers = CircuitBreakerRegistry.of(CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()

A registry holds one circuit breaker for each name, all with this configuration. The builder CircuitBreakerConfig.custom() starts from the library's defaults.

.failureRateThreshold(breaker.getFailureRateThreshold())

The breaker opens when this percentage of the recent calls failed. The platform's value is 50.

.slidingWindowSize(breaker.getSlidingWindowSize())

The rate is computed over the last 20 calls.

.minimumNumberOfCalls(breaker.getMinimumNumberOfCalls())

No rate is computed before 10 calls. See the section When the breaker opens.

.waitDurationInOpenState(breaker.getWaitDurationInOpenState())

An open breaker refuses calls for 30 seconds, then lets test calls through.

.recordException(ResilientCalls::isTransient)

Only transient failures count as failures. See the section What the breaker counts.

.maxAttempts(retry.getMaxAttempts()) // calls in total, not retries

Three attempts in total, including the first call.

.intervalFunction(IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff(

The waits between attempts grow, and each wait has a random part.

.retryOnException(ResilientCalls::isTransient)

The retry uses the same test as the breaker. A 4xx answer is never retried.

The values come from the platform's settings, under platform.resilience.*. The quick reference at the end of the chapter lists them with the library's defaults. The services rarely change them.

A circuit breaker has three states. These are the states of CircuitBreaker.State that the service meets:

StateWhat happens to a callWhen the state changes
CLOSEDthe call runs, and its result is countedthe failure rate reaches 50% of the last 20 calls, after at least 10 calls
OPENthe call does not run, and CallNotPermittedException is thrown at oncethe wait of 30 seconds ends
HALF_OPENa few test calls run, 10 by defaultthe test calls decide whether it closes or opens again

How many times a retry callstrap#

The setting is called maxAttempts, and its value is 3. A test sends a reservation to a stub that always answers 503:

PredictA stock service that always answers 503#
The retry has maxAttempts = 3. How many requests reach the stock service before the adapter gives up?
@Test
void retriesServerErrorsThenReportsTheServiceAsUnavailable() {
    status = 503;
    body = "{}";

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> adapter.reserve(OrderId.newId(), TWO_MUGS)).isInstanceOf(DownstreamServiceException.class);
Show the answer
3 requests: the first call and 2 retries. The test's next line checks it with assertThat(reservationCalls).hasValue(3).

Resilience4j counts the first call as an attempt. Its documentation defines maxAttempts as the maximum number of attempts, including the initial call. A run with an always-failing call ran it 3 times.

Polly counts differently. MaxRetryAttempts = 3 makes 4 calls, and so does @Retryable(maxRetries = 3) in Spring Framework 7. When you copy a value between libraries, check what it counts.

The platform's settings say it in a comment, because the name misleads:

/** The number of attempts in total, including the first one. 3 means up to 2 retries. */
private int maxAttempts = 3;

/** The wait before the first retry. Later waits grow by the multiplier, with random spread. */
private Duration initialInterval = Duration.ofMillis(200);

/** How much each wait grows before the random spread. 2.0 doubles it. */
private double multiplier = 2.0;

The default of Resilience4j is also 3 attempts, with a fixed wait of 500 ms. The platform changes the wait. Its initialInterval is 200 ms, and its multiplier is 2.0. IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff starts at 200 ms and doubles each time, with a random spread around each value. A run with 200 ms, 2.0 and a randomization factor of 0.5 gave four waits of 115, 447, 988 and 1410 ms. Without the random part, ofExponentialBackoff waited exactly 200, 400, 800 and 1600 ms.

The random part matters when many instances fail at the same moment. With fixed waits, they all retry at the same moment too, and the stock service gets a wave of calls just as it starts again. Random waits spread the wave.

Count the total time as well. Three attempts with a read timeout of 3 seconds can keep the agent waiting for about 9 seconds, plus the waits. Keep the read timeout short when the call is retried.

When the breaker openstwist#

A breaker over the last 20 calls seems to wait for 20 calls before it decides. Or two failures out of the first two calls seem to be a rate of 100%, enough to open it. Both guesses are wrong. The setting minimumNumberOfCalls decides.

A run for this book configured a breaker with a threshold of 50%, a window of 20 and a minimum of 10 calls. Every call failed:

Failed calls so farStateFailure rate that the breaker reported
8CLOSED-1.0, which means not computed yet
9CLOSED-1.0
10OPEN100.0
the next callOPENthe call did not run, and CallNotPermittedException was thrown
Gotcha

The breaker cannot open before minimumNumberOfCalls calls, whatever the size of its window. Before that, it reports no failure rate at all.

The library's default minimum is 100, which is high for a service with modest traffic. The platform sets 10. Its comment gives the reason. Two early failures never open the breaker.

/** The failure rate, in percent, that opens the breaker. */
private float failureRateThreshold = 50;

/** The number of recent calls the failure rate is computed over. */
private int slidingWindowSize = 20;

/** The breaker computes no rate before this many calls, so two early failures never open it. */
private int minimumNumberOfCalls = 10;

/** How long the breaker stays open before it lets a few test calls through. */
private Duration waitDurationInOpenState = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

The platform's test ResilientCallsTest.opensTheBreakerAfterManyFailuresAndThenStopsCalling makes 10 failing calls through call, which does not retry. It then expects the state OPEN, and checks that the next call never ran.

Polly's breaker has the same idea under another name. A run with Polly 8.8.0 set FailureRatio = 0.5 and MinimumThroughput = 10. Calls 9 and 10 went through, and call 11 threw BrokenCircuitException. That is the same point as Resilience4j. The window differs. Polly measures over a time, by default 30 seconds. The platform measures over a count of calls.

What the breaker countstrap#

Some answers of a service are not failures of that service. A 404 for an unknown product means that the caller asked for something that does not exist. A breaker that counts 404s would open when users mistype, and block good requests too. So the platform tells the breaker which errors to record.

PredictA breaker that records only transient errors#
transientFailure accepts only ResourceAccessException and HttpServerErrorException. Fifteen calls each throw a 404. What does the breaker count?
CircuitBreaker cb2 = CircuitBreaker.of("stock2", CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .slidingWindowSize(20).minimumNumberOfCalls(10).recordException(ResilienceTest::transientFailure).build());
for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
  try { cb2.executeSupplier(() -> { throw HttpClientErrorException.create(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "nf", null, null, null); }); } catch (Exception ignored) {}
}
Show the answer
15 successful calls and 0 failed calls. The state is CLOSED.

An exception that the predicate does not record counts as a success. It is not left out of the count. The documentation says that all other exceptions count as a success, unless ignoreExceptions names them.

So 404s fill the window with successes. Ten 503s among many 404s then stay under 50%, and the breaker never opens. Add ignoreExceptions(HttpClientErrorException.class). An ignored exception is not counted at all.

The platform uses both settings, and its comment explains the pair:

* <p>The breaker uses two settings for this on purpose. {@code recordException} decides which
* errors count as failures, but it counts every other error as a success. {@code ignoreExceptions}
* keeps 4xx answers out of the failure rate entirely, so many 404s neither open the breaker nor
* hide the 5xx answers that should.

So ignoreExceptions is not a detail. The test ResilientCallsTest.clientErrorsNeitherOpenTheBreakerNorCountAsSuccesses sends 20 404s, and expects the breaker to stay CLOSED. The ignored exception still reaches the caller unchanged. The adapter may then turn a 404 into an answer of its own.

Which failures are worth a retrynew#

A retry helps only when the next attempt may work. A timeout may work next time. A 400 Bad Request will fail the same way every time, because the request itself is wrong. So the platform sorts the failures into two kinds, with one method:

static boolean isTransient(Throwable error) {
    return error instanceof ResourceAccessException || error instanceof HttpServerErrorException;
}

A failure that may pass by itself is called transient. The method isTransient names two exception types of Spring:

FailureException from RestClientTransientRetried, and counted by the breaker
connect timeout, refused connection, read timeoutResourceAccessExceptionyesyes
503, 502, 500 and every other 5xxHttpServerErrorExceptionyesyes
400, 401, 404 and every other 4xxHttpClientErrorExceptionnono, and the breaker ignores it
an answer that the adapter does not knowIllegalStateException, from translatenono, because it happens after the call

A 5xx answer may be a bug in the other service, not a short outage. The platform still treats it as transient. Three attempts cost little, and the breaker stops the calls if the bug stays.

A 401 is not transient either. A missing or expired token is fixed by a new token, not by the same request again. The token manager fetches a new token 60 seconds before the old one expires, by default.

The test ResilientCallsTest.doesNotRetryClientErrors throws a 400, and expects exactly 1 attempt. The test retriesTransientFailuresThenSucceeds fails twice with a 502, and succeeds on attempt 3.

Retry outside, circuit breaker insidetwist#

Polly 8
var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
    .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions { ShouldHandle = transient, MaxRetryAttempts = 2 })
    .AddCircuitBreaker(new CircuitBreakerStrategyOptions { ShouldHandle = transient })
    .Build();
Java 25
public <T> T callWithRetry(String dependency, Supplier<T> call) {
    CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker = circuitBreakers.circuitBreaker(dependency);
    Retry retry = retries.retry(dependency);
    Supplier<T> protectedCall = Retry.decorateSupplier(retry, CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(circuitBreaker, call));
    return translateFailures(dependency, protectedCall);
}
Reading the code
CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker = circuitBreakers.circuitBreaker(dependency);

The registry returns the breaker of this name, and creates it on first use.

Supplier<T> protectedCall = Retry.decorateSupplier(retry, CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(circuitBreaker, call));

Each decorateSupplier wraps a Supplier in another Supplier. The breaker wraps the call, and the retry wraps the breaker. Nothing runs yet.

return translateFailures(dependency, protectedCall);

Only here is the call made, through both wrappers.

The order changes what the breaker counts. A run for this book compared the two orders, with 3 attempts:

OrderWhat the breaker counted for one call that always failed
Retry(CircuitBreaker(call)), as in the platform3 calls, one for each attempt
CircuitBreaker(Retry(call))1 call for the same 3 attempts

With the retry outside, the breaker sees every attempt, so it opens sooner when a service is really down. In the run, the second failing call opened the breaker after its first attempt, and ended with CallNotPermittedException. The documentation of Resilience4j gives the same order for its Spring Boot aspects. Retry is the outermost, and CircuitBreaker comes next.

The retry tests only isTransient. CallNotPermittedException is not transient, so the retry does not repeat a call that an open breaker refused. In a run, a retry predicate that excluded that exception stopped retrying into an open breaker.

Polly behaves in the same way when the retry is added first. A run for this book with Polly 8.8.0 added a retry with MaxRetryAttempts = 2, then a breaker that opens after 3 failures. The first call made 3 attempts and opened the breaker. The second call threw BrokenCircuitException at once, without a retry. With the breaker added first, the second call made 3 more attempts.

A failed call becomes a 503new#

The stock service is down, and an agent places an order. The agent should learn that a service that the shop depends on is unavailable, and that a later try may work. A 500 would say that the order service has a bug. So the platform translates the failures of a call:

private static <T> T translateFailures(String dependency, Supplier<T> call) {
    try {
        return call.get();
    } catch (CallNotPermittedException | ResourceAccessException | HttpServerErrorException e) {
        throw new DownstreamServiceException(dependency, e);
    }
}
Reading the code
return call.get();

This runs the decorated call, with its retries.

} catch (CallNotPermittedException | ResourceAccessException | HttpServerErrorException e) {

A multi-catch block catches any of the three types. It is like a catch with when (e is A or B) in C#. The three types are an open breaker, and the two transient failures after the last retry.

throw new DownstreamServiceException(dependency, e);

The platform's exception keeps the name of the dependency, and the original exception as its cause.

A 4xx answer is not in the list. It reaches the adapter as HttpClientErrorException, and the adapter decides what it means. The platform's controller advice answers the platform's exception:

@ExceptionHandler(DownstreamServiceException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> downstream(DownstreamServiceException ex) {
    log.warn("Dependency {} is unavailable", ex.dependency(), ex);
    return respond(ProblemDetails.problem(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "Dependency unavailable",
            "A service this request depends on is unavailable. Try again later."));
}

The line log.warn names the dependency, and the response does not. A caller learns that a dependency failed, but not which one or why. The response is a ProblemDetail with a traceId, like every other error. The test OrderControllerTest.anUnavailableDependencyIsA503 lets the use case throw DownstreamServiceException, and expects 503. For the problem format, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

Only the requests that call the stock service fail. The service's README states what each dependency affects:

DependencyUsed forWhen it is down
stock serviceplacing an orderonly POST /orders answers 503, and everything else works
token issuerchecking tokens, and the stock call's own tokenrequests get 401, and placing an order gets 503
SNSpublishing eventsevents wait in the outbox and are resent
SQSpaymentspayments wait in the queue

An agent can still read, pick and ship orders while the stock service is down. A service that keeps working in part when a dependency fails is said to degrade gracefully. Write such a table for every service, and test the row of each HTTP dependency.

ResilientCalls also reports the state of a breaker, for tests and health checks:

/** Returns the breaker's state, for tests and health checks. */
public CircuitBreaker.State state(String dependency) {
    return circuitBreakers.circuitBreaker(dependency).getState();
}

The method state returns one of the three states of the breaker. Do not put an open breaker into the readiness probe. The orchestrator would then stop all traffic to the order service, although only one endpoint needs the stock service. For probes, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

Retry only what is safe to repeatnew#

The order service sends a reservation, and the read timeout fires after 3 seconds. Did the stock service hold the mugs? It may have held them and then been slow to answer. A retry of that POST would then hold the mugs twice, and the shop would refuse the next customer.

The rule is to retry only an idempotent call. A call is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. A read is idempotent. A POST that creates something is not, unless the other service can recognise the repeat. So the platform offers two methods:

/**
 * Calls once, through the dependency's circuit breaker. Use it for a call that must not run
 * twice, such as a POST that creates something without an idempotency key: if a timed-out
 * POST was retried, the other service could create the thing twice.
 */
public <T> T call(String dependency, Supplier<T> call) {
    CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker = circuitBreakers.circuitBreaker(dependency);
    return translateFailures(dependency, CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(circuitBreaker, call));
}

call runs once, through the breaker. callWithRetry also retries. The test ResilientCallsTest.callsANonIdempotentOperationOnlyOnce expects exactly one attempt from call, even for a 503.

The reservation is a POST, and the adapter still uses callWithRetry. An idempotency key makes the POST safe. The key is a value that the caller chooses once and sends with every attempt. The other service remembers each key with its first answer. A repeated request with the same key gets the first answer, and changes nothing.

The order ID is the key. The use case chooses the ID before the call, so every attempt carries the same value. The adapter passes it as the first argument of http.reserve, which the interface sends as the header Idempotency-Key. The test StockAdapterTest.sendsTheServicesTokenAndTheOrderIdAsTheIdempotencyKey checks that the stock service receives the order ID in that header.

An ID created on each attempt would defeat the key. So would an ID created by the stock service. The key must exist before the first attempt, and the caller must keep it.

The callIdempotentUse
GET of a product, or of a priceyescallWithRetry
POST with an idempotency key that the other service honoursyescallWithRetry
PUT that replaces a whole resourceusually yescallWithRetry, after checking the other service's contract
POST without a key, such as sending an emailnocall

The key works only if the other service honours it. Ask the other team. Their documentation or their contract must say it. A key that the other service ignores makes the retry unsafe again, and nothing warns you.

Pragmatic choice: The stock hold before the transaction

The strict rule. A use case's changes and its effects commit together, or not at all.

What we do. The use case reserves the stock before its transaction. If the transaction then fails, the hold stays in the stock service. The stock service releases it after a timeout, because no OrderPlacedV1 arrives.

Why. A DocumentDB transaction has time and size limits. A slow HTTP call inside it would hold it open, and a retry would hold it open longer. A hold that expires by itself is cheap, and a lost sale is not.

When to stop. Stop when the stock service cannot release a hold by itself, or when a stale hold costs real money. Then the order service must cancel the hold when its transaction fails. If several services must agree, a saga or a process manager is the next step.

One circuit breaker for each dependencytwist#

ReservationResponse response = resilientCalls.callWithRetry(DEPENDENCY,
        () -> http.reserve(order.value(), request));

The first argument, DEPENDENCY, is the name of the dependency, here stock. The registry keeps one breaker for each name. If the stock service fails and its breaker opens, a call with another name, such as payment, still has a closed breaker. The test opensTheBreakerAfterManyFailuresAndThenStopsCalling opens the breaker named failing. It then expects the breaker named another to stay CLOSED.

Use one name for each service you call, not one for each endpoint. A service that is down is down for all its endpoints, and one breaker learns that faster. Use one name for each endpoint only when the endpoints fail on their own, for example when they run on different servers.

Compared with Pollytwist#

A .NET developer writes the same policy as a Polly pipeline. This pipeline matches the platform's settings, and it compiles with Polly.Core 8.8.0:

var transient = new PredicateBuilder()
    .Handle<HttpRequestException>()
    .Handle<TaskCanceledException>();

return new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
    .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions
    {
        ShouldHandle = transient,
        MaxRetryAttempts = 2,
        Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200),
        BackoffType = DelayBackoffType.Exponential,
        UseJitter = true
    })
    .AddCircuitBreaker(new CircuitBreakerStrategyOptions
    {
        ShouldHandle = transient,
        FailureRatio = 0.5,
        MinimumThroughput = 10,
        BreakDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)
    })
    .Build();
Reading the code
MaxRetryAttempts = 2,

Polly counts only the retries. So 2 here gives the same 3 calls as maxAttempts(3) in Resilience4j.

ShouldHandle = transient,

The predicate has the same purpose as isTransient. It names the failures that the strategy handles.

The Java side is the constructor of ResilientCalls. See the section Retry and circuit breaker: what each one is for. The two libraries differ in several defaults and names:

PointPolly 8.8.0Resilience4j 2.4.0, as the platform uses it
retry countMaxRetryAttempts = 2 makes 3 callsmaxAttempts = 3 makes 3 calls
retry defaultsa constant delay of 2 seconds, without jitter3 attempts, with a fixed wait of 500 ms
breaker windowa time, SamplingDuration, 30 seconds by defaulta count of calls, here the last 20
breaker minimumMinimumThroughput, 100 by defaultminimumNumberOfCalls, 100 by default and 10 in the platform
breaker defaultsFailureRatio 0.1, BreakDuration 5 secondsa threshold of 50%, and 60 seconds open
orderthe first strategy added is the outermostthe outer decorator is the outermost

AddStandardResilienceHandler in .NET adds a whole pipeline to an HttpClient in one line. It chains five strategies. The outermost is a rate limiter. Then come a total timeout of 30 seconds, a retry and a circuit breaker. The innermost is an attempt timeout of 10 seconds. Its retry makes 3 retries with exponential waits and jitter. Its breaker uses a failure ratio of 10% and a minimum of 100 calls. The retry is outside the breaker there too.

The closest match in the platform is ResilientCalls plus the two timeouts of the factory. The platform has no rate limiter and no total timeout. A total timeout would be the next thing to add, if agents wait too long during an outage.

Resilience4j core, its starter, or Spring's @Retryabletwist#

/**
 * Wraps calls to other services in a circuit breaker, and retries the calls that are safe to
 * repeat. It uses the plain-Java core modules of Resilience4j, so it works the same with any
 * Spring Boot version.
// ...
public class ResilientCalls {

The class ResilientCalls depends on two plain-Java modules, resilience4j-circuitbreaker and resilience4j-retry, at 2.4.0. It calls their decorators in its own code. A Spring service has two other choices, and both have real strengths:

ChoiceHow a call is protectedWhat it does well
Resilience4j core, as in the platforma method call, such as callWithRetry(...)one policy in one class, with no tie to the Boot version
the Resilience4j starter, resilience4j-spring-boot4 2.4.0@Retry(name = "stock") and @CircuitBreaker(name = "stock") on the methodthe policy is visible on the method, and each name has its own values in YAML
@Retryable from Spring Framework 7@Retryable on the method, with @EnableResilientMethodsno extra library at all, for a service that needs only a retry

The starter's settings for each name are under resilience4j.retry.instances.<name> and resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.<name>. An operator can change a value without a build. The library documents the order of its aspects, and it is the platform's order, with the retry outside. For both annotation styles in code, see the section Resilience: the Polly answer.

@Retryable counts only the retries, as Polly does. Its defaults are 3 retries, 1 second apart, on any exception, so the default makes 4 calls. Spring Framework 7 has no circuit breaker, no bulkhead and no time limiter. So the order service would still need Resilience4j for its breaker.

The book still recommends the core modules in a platform library, for four reasons:

  1. No tie to the Boot version. The core is plain Java. A new Boot version needs no new starter, so the platform can move first.
  2. One policy, written once. The rule "retry only transient failures, and ignore 4xx in the breaker" is in one method. With annotations, each method or each YAML instance must repeat it.
  3. No proxy. The annotations of the starter and @Retryable work through a proxy. So a call from inside the same class is not protected. For that trap, see the section Self-invocation: a call from inside the class. A method call on ResilientCalls always works.
  4. The choice is in the code. callWithRetry and call are two names. A reviewer sees at once which calls retry.

Choose the starter for a single service without a platform library, or when operators must tune each instance without a release. Choose @Retryable for a service that needs a retry and no breaker. Do not mix the styles in one service. Two places that decide the retry are harder to check than one.

The stock stubs in the local environmenttwist#

{
  "name": "stock-service: the product OUT-OF-STOCK is never available (for testing the 422 path)",
  "priority": 1,
  "request": {
    "method": "POST",
    "urlPath": "/stock/reservations",
    "headers": { "Authorization": { "matches": "Bearer .+" } },
    "bodyPatterns": [ { "matchesJsonPath": "$.lines[?(@.sku == 'OUT-OF-STOCK')]" } ]
  },
  "response": {
    "status": 200,
    "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    "jsonBody": { "result": "INSUFFICIENT_STOCK", "shortSkus": ["OUT-OF-STOCK"] }
  }
}
Reading the code
"priority": 1,

When several stubs match a request, the lowest number wins. This stub beats the default answer, which has priority 10.

"headers": { "Authorization": { "matches": "Bearer .+" } },

The stub matches only a request with a bearer token, as the real stock service would.

"bodyPatterns": [ { "matchesJsonPath": "$.lines[?(@.sku == 'OUT-OF-STOCK')]" } ]

A JSON path selects the lines whose sku is OUT-OF-STOCK. The stub matches when the path finds one.

The local environment runs WireMock in Docker, with four stubs for the stock service:

StubPriorityAnswer
a line with the product OUT-OF-STOCK1200 INSUFFICIENT_STOCK, so the agent gets 422
a line with the product SERVICE-DOWN1503, so the retries run and the agent gets 503
any reservation with a token and an Idempotency-Key10200 RESERVED
any reservation without a token20401

A run with WireMock 3.13.2 confirmed the priorities. A stub with priority 1 and a matchesJsonPath beat a catch-all with priority 10. A stub with no priority beat priority 10, because the default priority is 5. So give every stub a priority, or a stub without one may win.

A tester can try each path of the client with a product code, without changing any code. QA's Playwright tests use the same stubs, so the stubs must stay realistic. For the local environment, see the chapter Running locally and shipping.

Testing the client against a real HTTP servertwist#

@BeforeEach
void start() throws IOException {
    server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("localhost", 0), 0);
    server.createContext("/token", exchange -> {
        tokenCalls.incrementAndGet();
        respond(exchange, 200, """
                {"access_token":"token-1","token_type":"Bearer","expires_in":3600}""");
    });
    server.createContext("/stock/reservations", exchange -> {
        reservationCalls.incrementAndGet();
        authorization = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Authorization");
        idempotencyKey = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Idempotency-Key");
        respond(exchange, status, body);
    });
    server.start();
    String baseUrl = "http://localhost:" + server.getAddress().getPort();

    HttpClientProperties properties = new HttpClientProperties();
    properties.setBaseUrl(URI.create(baseUrl));
    properties.setTokenRegistrationId("stock-service");
    ResilienceProperties resilience = new ResilienceProperties();
    resilience.getRetry().setInitialInterval(Duration.ofMillis(1));

    HttpClientFactory factory = new HttpClientFactory(RestClient::builder, () -> tokenManager(baseUrl + "/token"));
    adapter = new StockAdapter(factory.create(StockHttpClient.class, properties), new ResilientCalls(resilience));
}
Reading the code
server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("localhost", 0), 0);

com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer is a small HTTP server in the JDK. Port 0 asks the system for a free port, so tests never clash.

server.createContext("/token", exchange -> {

Each context handles one path. This one plays the token issuer, and counts its calls.

idempotencyKey = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Idempotency-Key");

The stock path records the headers, so a test can check what the client sent.

resilience.getRetry().setInitialInterval(Duration.ofMillis(1));

The retries wait 1 ms, so the test of three attempts stays fast.

HttpClientFactory factory = new HttpClientFactory(RestClient::builder, () -> tokenManager(baseUrl + "/token"));

The test builds the real factory with plain builders and a real token manager. Only the servers are local.

The test exercises the real code from the adapter to the socket. The JSON is real, the headers are real, the token request is real, and the retries are real. It needs no Docker, no WireMock and no Spring context, so it runs in the normal build. The tests of the class are these:

TestWhat it proves
translatesAReservationIntoOurModelRESERVED becomes allAvailable(), and the unknown field reservationId is ignored
translatesMissingStockWithTheProductsINSUFFICIENT_STOCK becomes unavailable(...) with the product codes
sendsTheServicesTokenAndTheOrderIdAsTheIdempotencyKeythe request carries Bearer token-1 and the order ID as the key
twoDifferentUsersShareOneServiceTokentwo agents cause one token request
retriesServerErrorsThenReportsTheServiceAsUnavailablea 503 is tried 3 times, then becomes DownstreamServiceException
refusesAnAnswerItDoesNotKnowthe answer MAYBE throws IllegalStateException

The rules of ResilientCalls have their own tests in the platform, with plain lambdas and no HTTP. So the adapter's test checks the wiring, and the platform's test checks the policy.

In ASP.NET Core, a test of a typed client often uses an HttpMessageHandler that returns fixed answers. That test never opens a socket. The JDK server costs a few lines more, and also tests the timeouts, the request factory and the real JSON writer. For test kinds and WireMock in tests, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe stock reservation is a POST, which creates a hold. Why may the order service still retry it, and what would make the retry unsafe?
The order ID is the idempotency key. The use case chooses it before the call, and every attempt sends it in the Idempotency-Key header. The stock service answers a repeated key with its first answer. The retry becomes unsafe if each attempt makes a new key, or if the stock service ignores the key.
2
An expert asksWhy does the platform build each client from Spring Boot's injected RestClient.Builder, and ask for a new one for each client?
Boot's builder carries the tracing setup, so each request sends a traceparent header. A client from RestClient.create() sends none, and the trace breaks. The builder bean is a prototype and is mutable. A shared builder would pass one client's base URL and interceptor to the next client.
3
TranslateWrite this C# translation of the stock service's answer in Java, as a static method of the adapter: 
public static StockAvailability Translate(ReservationResponse response) => response.Result switch
{
    "RESERVED" => StockAvailability.AllAvailable(),
    "INSUFFICIENT_STOCK" => StockAvailability.Unavailable(
        response.ShortSkus.Select(sku => new ProductCode(sku)).ToList()),
    _ => throw new InvalidOperationException($"Unknown stock reservation result: {response.Result}")
};
static StockAvailability translate(ReservationResponse response) {
    return switch (response.result()) {
        case "RESERVED" -> StockAvailability.allAvailable();
        case "INSUFFICIENT_STOCK" -> StockAvailability.unavailable(
                response.shortSkus().stream().map(ProductCode::new).toList());
        default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unknown stock reservation result: " + response.result());
    };
}

The Java switch writes case and ->. It writes default in place of _. ProductCode::new is a constructor reference, and toList() ends the stream.

Publishing events: the outbox#

Talking to other services · Chapter 20· 31 min read· Quick reference

When an order ships, other services must hear about it, and only if the change was saved. The order service writes each outgoing event to an outbox collection, in the same transaction as the change. Spring Modulith sends it to Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) after the commit. A scheduled job sends again whatever failed. This chapter covers what leaves, what is guaranteed, and what can go wrong.

KindC#JavaNote
newno equivalentthe event stored in the change's transaction, then senta direct send to SNS can lose an event or announce a change that rolled back Why
twista record that implements IDomainEventa record that implements DomainEventa domain event is internal and may change with the model, so it never leaves the service as it is Why
twista versioned message class, such as OrderShippedV1a record that implements IntegrationEventan integration event is a contract with other teams, so it changes carefully Why
twista switch expression with type patternsswitch (event) { case OrderShipped shipped -> ... }one mapper per feature decides which domain events leave, and in which shape Why
newno equivalentOutboxDomainEventPublisherthe platform publishes each domain event and its integration events through Spring's event bus Why
trapno equivalentpublishEvent outside a transactionthe outbox row is stored but never sent, so the platform's publisher refuses with IllegalStateException Why
newthe outbox table of MassTransit or NServiceBusSpring Modulith's event publication registryone document for each event and transactional listener, written in the publisher's transaction Why
twistno equivalentspring.modulith.events.completion-mode=deletea sent row is deleted, so the collection holds only what is still to be sent Why
twistPublish(message) through the bus outbox@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS) on the recordSpring Modulith sends the event to the SNS topic after the commit, on another thread Why
trapno equivalentthe topic name order-eventsSpring Cloud AWS finds the ARN by calling CreateTopic, so the role needs sns:CreateTopic and a typo creates a topic Why
twistMessageId set by the buseventId, created once in the mappera resend keeps the ID, so a consumer's inbox can detect the duplicate Why
newno equivalentthe event ID and the order ID in every log linethe SNS message carries no trace ID by default, so flows are followed by their IDs Why
newno equivalentOutboxResender and IncompleteEventPublicationsa scheduled job sends again the rows that are older than five minutes and still not sent Why
trapno equivalenta row left RESUBMITTED by an instance that diedthe resender skips it for ever, unless the staleness monitor is turned on, as the platform does Why
twistno equivalentShedLock's lock in MongoDBevery instance schedules the resender, but only one runs it at a time Why
newno equivalent@ApplicationModuleListenerit runs after the commit in its own transaction, and its outbox row brings a retry after a failure Why
twista MediatR INotificationHandler@EventListenerit runs at once on the publisher's thread, inside its transaction, with no outbox row Why
newno equivalentat least once, never for a rolled-back changean event can be sent twice, so every consumer must be idempotent Why
twistUsingAmazonSqs against a local emulatorthe journey test with Floci, and the outbox collection empty at the endturning externalisation off in a test also stops the outbox rows Why
newno equivalentthe externaliser of Spring Cloud AWS 4.1it is built on a class that Spring Modulith 2.1 deprecated for removal, so drain the outbox before that upgrade Why
