The dual-write problemnew#

An agent ships an order. The order service saves the order, then sends OrderShippedV1 to a topic of Amazon SNS. Other services subscribe to that topic. The service crashes between the two steps. The order is shipped in the database, and no other service ever hears of it.

Swap the two steps, and the opposite happens. The service sends the event, then the save fails, and the transaction rolls back. Every subscriber now believes in a shipment that never happened.

Writing to two systems that share no transaction is called the dual-write problem. The database and SNS cannot commit together. No order of the two calls is safe. A careful version sends after the commit, from a transaction callback. It is right in the normal case, and it still loses the event when the process dies after the commit and before the send.

The fix is called the transactional outbox. The service writes the event into its own database, in the same transaction as the change. A separate step reads the stored events and sends them. The change and the event are then stored together, or not at all.

In the order service, every use case ends with the same private method. It saves, publishes and audits in the use case's transaction:

private Order saveAndPublish(Order order, String auditAction) {
    List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();
    Order saved = orders.save(order);
    events.publish(raised);
    audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.ORDER, saved.id().value());
    return saved;
}
Reading the code
List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();

The aggregate collected its events while its methods ran, such as OrderShipped from ship. pullEvents returns them and empties the list. For how the aggregate collects events, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

events.publish(raised);

events is the port DomainEventPublisher. Its implementation writes the events to the outbox. It sends nothing yet.

The use case never calls SNS. The rest of this chapter follows the events from this line to the topic.

Domain events and integration eventstwist#

C#
public record OrderShipped(OrderId OrderId, DateTimeOffset OccurredAt) : IDomainEvent;
Java 25
/** An order was shipped. It leaves the service as {@code OrderShippedV1}. */
public record OrderShipped(OrderId orderId, Instant occurredAt) implements DomainEvent {
}

A domain event tells that something happened inside the service, and its name is in the past tense. In the order service, each one is a record. OrderShipped holds an OrderId, a value object of the domain. It may change whenever the model changes, because only the order service reads it.

The event that leaves the service is a different record:

/** Published when an order ships. The schema is in {@code contracts/events/OrderShippedV1.json}. */
@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS)
public record OrderShippedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId) implements IntegrationEvent {
}

OrderShippedV1 is an integration event. It is a versioned message for other services, and so a contract with other teams. It holds plain types, such as a String for the order ID, and an eventId that the domain event does not need. The two kinds differ in every way that matters for change:

QuestionDomain eventIntegration event
Who reads itcode in this serviceother services, owned by other teams
Its typesvalue objects of the domain, such as OrderIdplain types, such as String and Instant
Its namethe business fact, OrderShippedthe fact and a version, OrderShippedV1
When it may changewhenever the model changesonly by rules that keep consumers working
Where it is declaredorder/domain/eventorder/messaging/event

The separation lets the domain evolve without breaking consumers. If one record served both purposes, a renamed field of the domain would break the payment service. Some teams publish the domain events directly, to save a mapper and a class per event. That works while one team owns both sides. It stops working when the first consumer belongs to another team, because every refactoring of the model then needs their agreement.

The mapper decides what leavestwist#

C#
public IIntegrationEvent? ToIntegrationEvent(IDomainEvent domainEvent) => domainEvent switch
{
    OrderShipped shipped => new OrderShippedV1(NewEventId(), shipped.OccurredAt, shipped.OrderId.Value),
    OrderCancelled cancelled => new OrderCancelledV1(NewEventId(), cancelled.OccurredAt, cancelled.OrderId.Value),
    _ => null
};
Java 25
@Component
class OrderIntegrationEventMapper implements IntegrationEventMapper {

    @Override
    public Optional<IntegrationEvent> toIntegrationEvent(DomainEvent event) {
        return switch (event) {
            case OrderPlaced placed -> Optional.of(new OrderPlacedV1(newEventId(), placed.occurredAt(),
                    placed.orderId().value(), placed.deliveryMethod().code(),
                    placed.items().stream()
                            .map(item -> new OrderPlacedV1.Line(item.product().value(), item.quantity()))
                            .toList()));
            case OrderShipped shipped -> Optional.of(new OrderShippedV1(newEventId(), shipped.occurredAt(),
                    shipped.orderId().value()));
            case OrderCancelled cancelled -> Optional.of(new OrderCancelledV1(newEventId(), cancelled.occurredAt(),
                    cancelled.orderId().value()));
            default -> Optional.empty();
        };
    }
}
Reading the code
return switch (event) {

A switch on an object, with a type pattern in each arm. It is like a switch expression with type patterns in C#. Java needs Java 21 or later for it.

case OrderShipped shipped -> Optional.of(new OrderShippedV1(newEventId(), shipped.occurredAt(),

When the event is an OrderShipped, the arm binds it to shipped, and builds the integration event from it. newEventId() is a static method of IntegrationEvent, imported with a static import.

default -> Optional.empty();

Every other event stays inside the service. Java needs the default here, because DomainEvent is an open interface, and the compiler cannot list its types.

public Optional<IntegrationEvent> toIntegrationEvent(DomainEvent event) {

The platform's interface returns an Optional, where the C# version returns null. An empty Optional means "this event does not leave the service".

The order feature raises five domain events. The mapper publishes three of them:

Domain eventLeaves the service asWhy
OrderPlacedOrderPlacedV1the stock service keeps its hold on the products when it sees it
OrderShippedOrderShippedV1other services act on a shipment
OrderCancelledOrderCancelledV1other services must undo what the order started
LinePickednothingno other service needs to know which line was picked
PaymentRecordednothingthe payment service sent the payment, so it knows already

The note feature's events, NoteAdded and NoteActionResolved, have no mapper at all. They stay inside the service too.

Each feature that publishes events has one mapper bean. The platform's interface says why in its comment:

/**
 * Decides which domain events leave the service, and in which shape. Each feature that
 * publishes events has one mapper bean.
 *
 * <p>Return an empty {@link Optional} for an internal event. Every event you publish is a
 * contract you must maintain, so publish as few as other services need.
 */
public interface IntegrationEventMapper {

    Optional<IntegrationEvent> toIntegrationEvent(DomainEvent event);
}

The method toIntegrationEvent is the whole interface. Every published event is a contract to maintain. A consumer may start to depend on it the day it appears, and the order service can no longer remove it. So the default answer for a new domain event is Optional.empty(). Publish it when another service asks for it.

The mapper is also the one place to read the answer to "what does the order feature tell the world?". That question gets an answer in one file per feature, which keeps event flows easy to follow. The test OrderIntegrationEventMapperTest.keepsInternalEventsInternal passes a LinePicked, and expects an empty result.

The platform's publishernew#

The use case calls the port DomainEventPublisher with a list of domain events. Something must turn them into outbox rows. The platform's implementation hands every event to Spring's event bus, and Spring Modulith writes the rows:

@Override
public void publish(List<DomainEvent> events) {
    if (events.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }
    if (!TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Publish domain events inside the use case's transaction, so they are stored with the change");
    }
    for (DomainEvent event : events) {
        publisher.publishEvent(event);
        mappers.stream()
                .map(mapper -> mapper.toIntegrationEvent(event))
                .flatMap(Optional::stream)
                .forEach(publisher::publishEvent);
    }
}
Reading the code
if (!TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()) {

This static method tells whether the current thread runs inside a real transaction. The next section explains why the publisher refuses to work without one.

publisher.publishEvent(event);

The field publisher holds Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher. The domain event itself is published first, so a listener in this service can react to it. See the section Reacting inside the service.

.map(mapper -> mapper.toIntegrationEvent(event))

Every mapper bean of the service is asked. Most answer with an empty Optional.

.flatMap(Optional::stream)

Optional::stream turns an empty Optional into an empty stream, and a full one into a stream of one element. So only the real integration events go on.

.forEach(publisher::publishEvent);

Each integration event is published too. It is @Externalized, so Spring Modulith sends it to SNS after the commit.

The publisher knows no feature and no topic. It receives the list of every IntegrationEventMapper bean from the auto-configuration:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DomainEventPublisher.class)
OutboxDomainEventPublisher domainEventPublisher(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher,
                                                ObjectProvider<IntegrationEventMapper> mappers) {
    return new OutboxDomainEventPublisher(publisher, mappers.orderedStream().toList());
}

mappers.orderedStream() returns every mapper bean of the service. A new feature adds a mapper, and the publisher uses it with no change. A service may still replace the whole publisher, because of @ConditionalOnMissingBean.

The test OutboxDomainEventPublisherTest.publishesEachDomainEventAndItsIntegrationEvent publishes two domain events. It expects each domain event, followed by its integration event, if it has one.

An older design used a port for each feature, such as an OrderEvents interface, with an adapter that called ApplicationEventPublisher for each event type. That design is explicit. A reader of the adapter sees every event that the feature sends. But each feature repeated the same adapter, and nothing stopped a publish outside a transaction. The platform's publisher keeps the explicit part in the mapper, and writes the adapter once.

Publishing outside a transactiontrap#

A developer adds a job that cancels old orders. The job has no @Transactional, and it publishes the events of each cancelled order. A run for this book did the same with an @Externalized event and no transaction at all:

PredictAn externalised event published with no transaction#
OrderPlacedV1 carries @Externalized(&quot;order-events&quot;). No transaction is active. What does the outbox hold afterwards, and does the event reach SNS?
events.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedV1("o-8", false));
Thread.sleep(500);
System.out.println("  SNS calls so far=" + ctx.getBean(FakeSns.class).calls.get());
rows(jdbc);
Show the answer
The outbox holds a row with status PUBLISHED. The event never reaches SNS.

The row is written, but the listener that sends it waits for a commit that never comes. Spring Modulith stores the row when the event is published. The sending listener is a transactional listener. Without a transaction, it does not run, because its fallbackExecution is false by default.

At shutdown, the registry logged "Shutting down with the following publications left unfinished". So the platform's publisher refuses to publish outside a transaction.

The refusal turns a silent loss into a loud error. The test OutboxDomainEventPublisherTest.refusesToPublishOutsideATransaction expects the IllegalStateException, and checks that nothing reached Spring's publisher.

Do not rely on the resender for such a row. Fix the caller. Put the job's work into a use case with @Transactional, or run it in a TransactionTemplate. For both, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

An empty list needs no transaction. The publisher returns before the check, so a use case that raised no events never fails. anEmptyListNeedsNoTransaction tests that.

Spring Modulith's event publication registrynew#

The outbox itself comes from a library. Spring Modulith is a Spring project for structuring an application into modules. One of its parts is the event publication registry. It records each event that a transactional listener must receive, and it marks the record complete when the listener has run. That registry is the order service's outbox.

The platform library adds these modules:

<!--
  The outbox (Spring Modulith's event publication registry in MongoDB, sent to SNS) and SQS.
  The platform needs no spring-modulith-events-jackson. The MongoDB store keeps each event
  as an embedded document, and never uses a serializer. SNS writes JSON with Boot's JsonMapper.
-->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.modulith</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-modulith-events-api</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.modulith</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-modulith-events-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.modulith</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-modulith-events-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-modulith-events-sns</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-modulith-events-api</artifactId>

The annotations and interfaces that code uses, such as @Externalized, @ApplicationModuleListener and IncompleteEventPublications.

<artifactId>spring-modulith-events-core</artifactId>

The registry itself, and the multicaster that writes the rows.

<artifactId>spring-modulith-events-mongodb</artifactId>

The store in MongoDB. It was not run against DocumentDB for this book, so test the outbox on a real cluster early.

<artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-modulith-events-sns</artifactId>

The part that sends @Externalized events to SNS. It comes from Spring Cloud AWS, not from Spring Modulith.

The comment names a module that the platform leaves out on purpose. spring-modulith-events-jackson holds the serializer that writes events as JSON. The store for Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) uses it. The MongoDB store keeps the event as an embedded document instead, and its source never calls the serializer. The SNS sender writes JSON with the JsonMapper bean of Boot, as the source of Spring Cloud AWS shows. Nothing else in the core of Spring Modulith uses the serializer. So the platform removed the module, and the tests, the journey test with SNS among them, still pass.

The versions are 2.1.2 for Spring Modulith and 4.1.0 for Spring Cloud AWS, as of October 2026. The parent Project Object Model (POM) sets them. For the parent POM, see the chapter The build: a parent POM and a platform library.

The registry works through Spring's event bus. A call of publishEvent reaches Spring Modulith's multicaster. For each matching transactional listener, the multicaster writes one row. The sender to SNS counts as such a listener. Facts from the source and from runs:

  • Only transactional listeners create a row. @ApplicationModuleListener and the SNS sender are transactional listeners. A plain @EventListener is not.
  • The row is written in the publisher's transaction. Before the commit, the row was already there with status PUBLISHED. After a rollback, there was no row and no SNS call.
  • An event that no transactional listener receives creates no row, and nobody hears it.
  • A row belongs to one event and one listener. OrderPlaced has a listener that counts orders, so it gets a row for that listener. OrderPlacedV1 gets a row for the SNS sender.

In MongoDB, the rows are documents in the collection event_publication. The source of the MongoDB store gives their fields:

FieldWhat it holds
_ida UUID for the publication
publicationDatewhen the event was published, inside the transaction
listenerIdthe listener that must receive the event, as a method signature
eventthe event itself, as an embedded document, not as a JSON string
statusPUBLISHED, PROCESSING, COMPLETED, FAILED or RESUBMITTED
completionDatewhen the listener finished, empty until then
completionAttemptshow many times a listener tried, 1 at first
lastResubmissionDatewhen the resender last took the row

A failed listener marks its row FAILED. In a run, the row went FAILED, then COMPLETED with completionAttempts 2 after a resend.

A run of the local environment, on 25 October 2026, recorded one row in MongoDB 8.0.34. The order service ran in Docker, and the SNS emulator was stopped, so the send failed and the row stayed. mongosh printed it as follows. Only the array lines is joined onto one line here:

{
  _id: UUID('0680c15d-37e7-478a-86c7-695ebc121f43'),
  publicationDate: ISODate('2026-10-25T22:30:54.689Z'),
  listenerId: 'org.springframework.modulith.events.support.DelegatingEventExternalizer.externalize(java.lang.Object)',
  event: {
    eventId: '14970a89-d74a-4ec3-b3bc-2d2bbf3621c8',
    occurredAt: ISODate('2026-10-25T22:30:54.677Z'),
    orderId: '9ade9c6c-c572-4a45-80ab-7ac67746370d',
    deliveryMethod: 'STANDARD',
    lines: [ { productCode: 'MUG-001', quantity: 1 } ],
    _class: 'com.acme.orderservice.order.messaging.event.OrderPlacedV1'
  },
  lastResubmissionDate: ISODate('2026-10-25T22:30:54.689Z'),
  completionAttempts: 1,
  status: 'FAILED',
  _class: 'org.springframework.modulith.events.mongodb.MongoDbEventPublication'
}

The output is not an excerpt of the companion. It is what the database held. Four details matter:

  • _id is a universally unique identifier (UUID) in the standard binary form, which mongosh prints as UUID(...). That form comes from the platform's setting spring.mongodb.representation.uuid=standard.
  • The event is an embedded document with its own _class, the full name of the record. Its Instant became a BSON date. So the class name is part of the stored row. Spring Data reads it when it loads the row for a resend. This book did not run a rename, so send every row of an event before its record is renamed or moved.
  • The listener is the SNS sender, named by its method signature. That is the only row, because OrderPlacedV1 has no other transactional listener.
  • The row has no completionDate field at all, because the send never completed. With completion-mode=delete, a successful send removes the row.

The platform uses this registry rather than an outbox of its own, because the registry already does the three hard parts. It stores the row in the publisher's transaction. It sends after the commit, on another thread. And it keeps the rows in MongoDB, with a resend API. An outbox written in-house would need all three, plus their tests. The cost is a dependency on the registry's design, which the section What the sender depends on describes.

Spring Modulith 2.1 added a second mode, spring.modulith.events.externalization.mode=outbox. It sends events through the Namastack Outbox library. The reference of Spring Modulith says that this mode is available only for relational databases. The README of Namastack Outbox 1.11.0 lists MongoDB among its stores, as of October 2026. The two sources disagree, and nobody ran the mode on MongoDB for this book. So the order service on DocumentDB uses the default mode, the registry itself.

The registry's settings, and whytwist#

# The outbox: Spring Modulith's event publication registry, collection "event_publication".
# Delete a publication once it has been sent, so the collection stays small.
spring.modulith.events.completion-mode=delete
# The platform's mongo package already provides the transaction manager.
spring.modulith.events.mongodb.transaction-management.enabled=false
# OutboxResender sends unsent events on a schedule, so a restart need not resend them as well.
spring.modulith.events.republish-outstanding-events-on-restart=false
# ...
spring.modulith.events.externalization.enabled=true
Reading the code
spring.modulith.events.completion-mode=delete

The default is update, which keeps each completed row with its completion date. delete removes it. archive moves it to event_publication_archive. In a run with delete, completed rows vanished, and failed or unsent rows stayed.

spring.modulith.events.mongodb.transaction-management.enabled=false

The default is true. Spring Modulith then registers its own MongoTransactionManager. The platform's mongo package registers one already, so this line keeps one manager.

spring.modulith.events.republish-outstanding-events-on-restart=false

This is the default anyway. When true, each instance resends every unfinished row at startup. The reference warns against that with several instances, because other instances may still be sending those rows.

spring.modulith.events.externalization.enabled=true

The default too. Externalisation is the step that sends @Externalized events to SNS. The line states the platform's intent where a reader looks.

The file is in the platform's jar, under META-INF/platform-defaults/. It gives every service these values as defaults, and a service's own settings override them. For how a library adds defaults, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

The choice of delete keeps the collection small. Only rows still to be sent remain, so an operator who counts the documents counts the backlog. The cost is the history. Choose archive if support must answer "was this event ever sent?" from the database. Then give the archive collection a time-to-live (TTL) index, so it cleans itself.

@Externalized: from the outbox to SNStwist#

/**
 * Published when an order is placed. The stock service uses it to keep its hold on the products.
 *
 * <p>{@link Externalized} tells Spring Modulith to send the event to the SNS topic after the
 * transaction commits. The schema is in {@code contracts/events/OrderPlacedV1.json}.
 */
@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS)
public record OrderPlacedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId, String deliveryMethod,
                            List<Line> lines) implements IntegrationEvent {

    public record Line(String productCode, int quantity) {
    }
}
Reading the code
@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS)

The value is the target, here the topic name order-events. A target may also carry a routing key, written "target::key". The key may be an expression of the Spring Expression Language (SpEL), such as #{orderId()}, evaluated on the event.

public record Line(String productCode, int quantity) {

The lines use the shop's own words, productCode, because this is the order service's contract. The stock service's word sku stays in the client package.

The sending itself happens later, and elsewhere. A run for this book recorded each send to a fake SNS:

  • Before the commit, the count of SNS calls was 0.
  • Every send ran on a thread named task-N, and outside any transaction.
  • The sender is a method with @ApplicationModuleListener(propagation = SUPPORTS). So it runs after the commit, on Spring's task executor.

Two consequences follow. The request's thread does not wait for SNS, so a slow SNS never slows the agent's request. And an error from SNS never reaches the use case. It appears in the log, on a task- thread, and the row stays for the resender.

Gotcha

An @Externalized event declared outside the application's package is not sent. By default, Spring Modulith considers only events in the auto-configuration packages, the package of @SpringBootApplication and below. This is read from the source and was not run. Declare integration events in the service, as the order service does in order/messaging/event, never in a shared library.

A FIFO topic needs a routing key, because SNS requires a message group ID there. Spring Cloud AWS uses the routing key as that group ID. In a run, the target "order-events.fifo::#{orderId()}" sent with the group ID of the order. The order service uses a standard topic, so it has no key.

From a topic name to an ARNtrap#

The order feature names its topic once, in a constant:

/**
 * Spring Cloud AWS turns this name into the topic's ARN by calling {@code CreateTopic}, which
 * returns the ARN of an existing topic. So the service's IAM role needs {@code sns:CreateTopic}
 * as well as {@code sns:Publish}, and a typo here silently creates a new, empty topic.
 */
public static final String ORDER_EVENTS = "order-events";

SNS needs the full Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of a topic, such as arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:000000000000:order-events. The constant ORDER_EVENTS holds only the name. Spring Cloud AWS resolves the name, and the source shows how:

  • SnsTemplate uses a CachingTopicArnResolver around a DefaultTopicArnResolver. A service may replace them with a resolver bean of its own.
  • DefaultTopicArnResolver passes a value that starts with arn: through. For a name, it calls CreateTopic. That call returns the ARN of a topic that exists already.
  • The result is cached for each name.
Gotcha

A typo in the topic name creates a new, empty topic. CreateTopic with order-evnets succeeds, and the events go to a topic that nobody reads. And the service's Identity and Access Management (IAM) role needs sns:CreateTopic as well as sns:Publish. Without it, the resolution fails, although publishing is allowed.

There are two ways to avoid the call. Put the full ARN in the target, which every environment must then set. Or declare a TopicsListingTopicArnResolver bean, which pages through ListTopics and never creates a topic. The order service keeps the name, because one constant serves every environment. Its README lists both permissions for the role. For the role itself, see the section AWS credentials: a role, never a key.

The event ID and the versiontwist#

/**
 * A versioned message that crosses the service boundary, such as {@code OrderShippedV1}. It is
 * a contract with other teams, so it changes carefully:
 *
 * <ul>
 *   <li>The version is in the name. Within a version, add fields freely, but never remove or
 *       rename one. For a breaking change, publish {@code V2} next to {@code V1} until every
 *       consumer has moved.</li>
 *   <li>It holds IDs and facts in plain types, and no more personal data than a consumer needs.</li>
 *   <li>The event ID is created once, with the event. A resend keeps it, so a consumer's inbox
 *       can detect the duplicate.</li>
 * </ul>
 */
public interface IntegrationEvent {

    String eventId();

    Instant occurredAt();

    /** Returns a new, random event ID. Call it once, when the event is created. */
    static String newEventId() {
        return UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    }
}
Reading the code
String eventId();

Every integration event has an ID. A record implements this method with its component of the same name, eventId.

static String newEventId() {

An interface may have a static method in Java. The mapper calls it once for each event. A UUID as text is unique without a database.

The mapper creates the ID, inside the use case's transaction. The integration event, with its ID, is then stored in the outbox row. A resend reads the same row, so it sends the same ID. A consumer that has seen the ID knows that the message is a duplicate. For that consumer, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

An ID made at send time would break this. Each resend would then carry a new ID, and every duplicate would look new.

The other rules in the comment keep consumers working:

  • The version is part of the name, as in OrderShippedV1. A new optional field is safe, because consumers ignore fields they do not know.
  • A removed or renamed field breaks a consumer. Publish OrderShippedV2 next to V1, until every consumer has moved.
  • Plain types only, such as String and Instant. A consumer in another language can read them.
  • IDs and facts, and no personal data beyond what a consumer needs. OrderPlacedV1 carries no customer name or email address.

Each published event has a JSON schema in contracts/events/. For schemas, versions and how to check them, see the chapter API and event contracts.

Keeping event flows traceablenew#

An agent asks why the stock service still holds the mugs of a shipped order. Support must follow one order from the HTTP request, through the outbox and SNS, to the stock service's log. Events make that harder than a direct call, because the send happens later, on another thread.

Plan for it. The order service uses four practices:

  • Business IDs in every event. Each integration event carries the orderId. A search for the order ID finds the request, the audit record, the event and the consumer's log lines.
  • The event ID in every consumer's log. The inbox puts the eventId into the logging context. See the section Log lines that name the message.
  • One mapper per feature. The question "which events does the order feature send?" has one answer, in one file.
  • A schema for every event. The files in contracts/events/ list what each event contains.

The trace ID of the request does not travel with the event. In a run with no header extractor configured, the SNS notification had no headers at all. So a consumer starts a new trace, and the order ID connects the two traces. A service that needs one trace across the event must add the trace context as a message header itself. How Spring Cloud AWS maps such headers to SNS message attributes was not checked.

Here is the schema of one event, with the fields that a support engineer searches for:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "order-service/OrderShippedV1",
  "title": "OrderShippedV1",
  "description": "An order was shipped. Published to the order-events SNS topic.",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId"],
  "properties": {
    "eventId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },
    "occurredAt": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" },
    "orderId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" }
  },
  "additionalProperties": true
}

"additionalProperties": true tells consumers that new fields may appear. The three required fields are the ones every flow is traced by.

A flow that spans many services and days needs more than IDs. Then use a workflow engine or a process manager, which keeps the state of the whole flow in one place. For that choice, see the section What keeps a DDD service readable.

Resending what was not sentnew#

SNS is unavailable for a few minutes. Every send in that time fails, and its row stays in the outbox as FAILED. Nothing sends it again by itself. So the platform runs a job that resends old rows:

@Scheduled(initialDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}",
        fixedDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}")
void resend() {
    LockConfiguration lock = new LockConfiguration(clock.instant(), LOCK_NAME,
            properties.getLockAtMostFor(), properties.getResendInterval().dividedBy(2));
    locks.executeWithLock((Runnable) this::resendNow, lock);
}

private void resendNow() {
    Duration olderThan = properties.getResendOlderThan();
    log.debug("Resending outbox events older than {}", olderThan);
    incompletePublications.resubmitIncompletePublicationsOlderThan(olderThan);
}
Reading the code
fixedDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}")

The job runs once a minute by default, and each run starts after the previous run ended. For @Scheduled with durations from settings, see the section @Scheduled with durations from settings.

locks.executeWithLock((Runnable) this::resendNow, lock);

The run happens only if this instance gets the lock, which ShedLock keeps. See the section One instance at a time: ShedLock.

incompletePublications.resubmitIncompletePublicationsOlderThan(olderThan);

The Spring Modulith interface IncompleteEventPublications sends each unfinished row again, if it is older than five minutes.

The five minutes protect the rows that are still being sent. A row written a second ago is unfinished too, because its send is running on a task thread. Resending it would send the event twice for no reason. The age counts from the first publication date, not from the last resend. In a run, resubmitIncompletePublicationsOlderThan(PT1H) did nothing for a fresh failure, and PT0S resent it at once.

The settings are in MessagingProperties.Outbox, bound from platform.messaging.outbox.*:

/** Turns the scheduled resender on. Tests turn it off, so no background job runs. */
private boolean resendEnabled = true;

/** How often the resender runs. */
private Duration resendInterval = Duration.ofMinutes(1);

/** Only events older than this are resent, so events still being sent are left alone. */
private Duration resendOlderThan = Duration.ofMinutes(5);

/** The longest one instance may hold the resender lock, in case it dies while holding it. */
private Duration lockAtMostFor = Duration.ofMinutes(5);

The field resendEnabled switches the whole job. The platform's messaging auto-configuration declares the resender in a nested configuration, together with @EnableScheduling. So scheduling is on only when the resender is on. A service that has jobs of its own declares @EnableScheduling itself. For that trap and the platform's callout on it, see the section Scheduling, switched on by the platform.

The setting republish-outstanding-events-on-restart stays false, because this job already resends. Two mechanisms would only send more duplicates.

Gotcha

A row that an instance took just before it died stays RESUBMITTED, and the resender skips it for ever. The resend claims each row in one atomic update. The update sets the status RESUBMITTED, and only for a row that is not RESUBMITTED already. So a row is never claimed twice. But if the process dies after the claim, no later run takes the row. Only Spring Modulith's staleness monitor moves it back to FAILED. The monitor is off by default. It registers only when one of the settings spring.modulith.events.staleness.published, .processing or .resubmitted is set.

The claim comes from the source of the MongoDB store. A run with two instances on MongoDB is pending. The platform therefore switches the monitor on, in its defaults:

# Spring Modulith's staleness monitor. A row that has stayed RESUBMITTED for this long goes back
# to FAILED, so the resender takes it again. A row stays RESUBMITTED for ever when an instance
# dies during a resend. Keep the value longer than the longest resend run (lock-at-most-for,
# 5 minutes), or a resend that is still running would send its events a second time.
spring.modulith.events.staleness.resubmitted=PT15M
Reading the code
spring.modulith.events.staleness.resubmitted=PT15M

A row that has been RESUBMITTED for 15 minutes goes back to FAILED. The next run of the resender takes it again. The monitor measures from the row's last resubmission date, or from its publication date when it has none.

Keep the value longer than the longest resend run (lock-at-most-for,

A resend that is still running has rows in RESUBMITTED too. If the monitor marked them FAILED, the next run would send them a second time. The resender's lock lasts at most five minutes, so no run takes longer than that. Fifteen minutes leaves a margin.

The monitor checks once a minute by default, with spring.modulith.events.staleness.check-interval. It registers through SchedulingConfigurer, so it runs only when scheduling is on, and so only together with the resender. For how it is scheduled, see the section Scheduling, switched on by the platform. Each instance runs the monitor, with no lock. Marking a row FAILED a second time should change nothing, but this book did not run two monitors at once.

Watch the backlog as well. With completion-mode=delete, the number of documents in event_publication is the number of events not yet sent. A number that only grows means that SNS or a listener keeps failing. For metrics and alerts, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

One instance at a time: ShedLocktwist#

/** ShedLock's lock in MongoDB, in the collection {@code scheduler_locks}. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
LockingTaskExecutor lockingTaskExecutor(MongoTemplate mongo) {
    return new DefaultLockingTaskExecutor(new MongoLockProvider(mongo.getCollection("scheduler_locks")));
}

When the order service runs on three instances, each one schedules the resender. Without a lock, all three would read the same rows every minute, and send them again. ShedLock is a small library that lets only one instance run a scheduled job at a time. This bean keeps its lock as a document in the collection scheduler_locks. An instance that finds the lock taken skips its run, and does not wait. For the lock, its two durations, its tests and a prediction, see the section Several instances, and the lock.

The lock reduces duplicates, and it does not remove them. An instance can stop after a send and before it marks the row complete. The next run then sends that event again. So every consumer must be idempotent. ShedLock's README does not mention DocumentDB, and the provider was not run against a DocumentDB cluster.

Reacting inside the servicenew#

A developer wants to count shipped orders, as a business metric. The obvious tool is a listener for the domain event OrderShipped. Spring has two kinds of listener for this, and they behave very differently. A run for this book published one event to each, inside a transaction:

PredictTwo listeners for two domain events#
Each event is published inside a transaction that then commits. For each listener, how many rows appear in the outbox, and when and on which thread does it run?
@Component
public class Listeners {

    @EventListener
    void on(Events.NoteAdded e) {
        System.out.println("  @EventListener NoteAdded on thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName()
            + ", inTx=" + TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive());
    }

    @ApplicationModuleListener
    void on(Events.PaymentRecorded e) {
        System.out.println("  @ApplicationModuleListener PaymentRecorded on thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName()
            + ", inTx=" + TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive());
    }
}
Show the answer
The @EventListener creates no row, and runs at once on the publisher's thread, inside its transaction. The @ApplicationModuleListener creates one row, and runs after the commit on the thread task-1, in a new transaction.

Only a transactional listener gets an outbox row. @ApplicationModuleListener combines three annotations. They are @Async, @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) and @TransactionalEventListener. The default phase of the last one is after the commit.

A plain @EventListener runs synchronously, during publishEvent. Spring Modulith records nothing for it. If it fails, the use case fails with it. If the use case later rolls back, the listener has already acted.

The order service counts its orders with the second kind:

@ApplicationModuleListener
void on(OrderPlaced event) {
    placed.increment();
}

@ApplicationModuleListener
void on(OrderShipped event) {
    shipped.increment();
}

Each method on receives a domain event, and increments a counter of Micrometer. A rolled-back order is never counted, because the listener runs only after a commit. A failed listener is resent, because it has a row. The journey test reads the counter shop.orders with the tag shipped, and expects at least 1.

The two kinds of listener compare like this:

Question@EventListener@ApplicationModuleListener
When it runsat once, inside publishEventafter the commit
Which threadthe publisher's threada thread of Spring's task executor, such as task-1
Which transactionthe publisher's transaction, if anya new one of its own
An outbox rownoyes, one for each event
After a failurethe use case fails toothe row stays, and the resender tries again

Choose @ApplicationModuleListener for a side effect that may happen a moment later, and must not slow or break the use case. Examples are metrics, a cache refresh, or a step of another feature. Keep a rule that must hold at once in the use case itself, in its transaction. A plain @EventListener is right only for work that must share the publisher's transaction, and that is rare.

Spring Modulith turns on @EnableAsync by itself for these listeners, unless the application has its own async configuration. In ASP.NET Core, a plain listener behaves as a MediatR notification handler does. A run showed that Publish in MediatR runs its handlers on the caller's thread, and a failing handler fails the caller.

Note

A domain event that no mapper publishes and no listener receives is dropped. It creates no row, and nobody hears it. That is correct for LinePicked today. To react to such an event later, add an @ApplicationModuleListener. The publisher already publishes every domain event, so no other change is needed.

What the outbox guaranteesnew#

A consumer team asks what they can rely on. The answer comes from the steps of the outbox, and from what can fail between them:

What fails, and whenWhat the consumers see
the use case throws, and the transaction rolls backno event, because the row rolled back with the change
the process dies before the commitno event, for the same reason
SNS is down after the committhe event, later, when the resender sends it
the process dies after the send, before the row is marked completethe event twice
two instances resend in one momentthe event once in that round, because the claim is atomic, as the source shows

The resender's own comment names the case of the duplicate:

* <p>Consumers must still be idempotent: an event can be sent twice, for example when an
* instance stops after sending and before marking the row complete.

The comment's first words, Consumers must still be idempotent, state the price of the outbox. So the outbox gives three guarantees:

  • A saved change always produces its event. The row commits with the change, and stays until it is sent.
  • A rolled-back change never produces an event. The row was never committed.
  • An event may arrive more than once. This is called at-least-once delivery. Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) adds its own duplicates on top.

Two things are not guaranteed. The order of events is not guaranteed, because each send runs on a task thread, and a resent event arrives late. And the delay is not guaranteed. A failed event waits at least five minutes.

Consumers handle both. A consumer detects duplicates by the eventId, and its domain ignores a late message. The order service does the same as a consumer of payments. For that side, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

The outbox needs a database transaction, with every write of the use case inside it. For transactions on DocumentDB and their limits, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

Testing the outboxtwist#

// The outbox sent the published events to SNS, and SNS delivered them to the subscribed queue.
List<String> received = new ArrayList<>();
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() -> {
    aws.sqs.receiveMessage(request -> request.queueUrl(aws.orderEventsQueueUrl).maxNumberOfMessages(10))
            .messages().stream().map(Message::body).forEach(received::add);
    assertThat(received).anySatisfy(body -> assertThat(body).contains(orderId, "\"deliveryMethod\":\"STANDARD\""))
            .anySatisfy(body -> assertThat(body).contains(orderId).doesNotContain("deliveryMethod"));
});

// Completed publications are deleted, so the outbox empties once every listener has run.
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() ->
        assertThat(mongo.findAll(Document.class, "event_publication")).isEmpty());
Reading the code
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() -> {

Awaitility repeats the block until it passes, or 20 seconds have gone. The send happens on another thread after the commit, so the test must wait for it.

aws.sqs.receiveMessage(request -> request.queueUrl(aws.orderEventsQueueUrl).maxNumberOfMessages(10))

The test subscribed its own queue to the topic order-events, with raw message delivery. It reads what SNS delivered there.

.anySatisfy(body -> assertThat(body).contains(orderId).doesNotContain("deliveryMethod"));

One message is OrderPlacedV1, with the delivery method. Another is OrderShippedV1, without it.

assertThat(mongo.findAll(Document.class, "event_publication")).isEmpty());

Every row was completed and deleted, the counting listener's rows too.

The journey test runs the service against Floci, a free emulator of SNS and SQS, in Docker. It proves the whole path. The path is the row, the commit, the send, SNS and the subscription. The platform's unit tests cover the parts without Docker:

TestWhat it proves
OutboxDomainEventPublisherTestthe refusal outside a transaction, and each domain event followed by its integration event
OrderIntegrationEventMapperTestwhich events leave, their plain types, and that internal events stay inside
OutboxResenderTestthe resend with the five-minute age, and the skip when the lock is taken
OutboxResenderLockITtwo executors on a real MongoDB, and only one runs

A second design keeps SNS out of the test. Point the SNS endpoint at an address where nothing listens, then check that the row stays in event_publication. That test needs no emulator, and it shows the outbox directly. It has two weak points. The failed send appears later, on another thread, as an error in the log. And it proves nothing about the topic or the subscription.

Gotcha

Turning off externalisation in a test also turns off the outbox rows. With spring.modulith.events.externalization.enabled=false, an @Externalized event produced no row in a run. The sender is the transactional listener behind the row. Without the sender, the event has no listener, so no row is written. Turn off platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled instead, as the journey test does.

For Floci, Testcontainers and the other test kinds, see the chapter Testing in depth.

What the sender depends onnew#

The libraries behind the outbox moved recently. Spring Modulith had its own AWS modules once. It removed them in version 1.4, in favour of the modules of Spring Cloud AWS. Version 1.4.0 came out on 27 May 2025, and 2.0.0 on 21 November 2025. So a guide that names the old modules is older than 1.4.

The current sender comes from spring-cloud-aws-modulith-events-sns 4.1.0. The platform's parent POM sets the versions:

<!-- Libraries that Spring Boot does not manage -->
<spring-modulith.version>2.1.2</spring-modulith.version>
<spring-cloud-aws.version>4.1.0</spring-cloud-aws.version>

The comment says why spring-modulith.version and spring-cloud-aws.version are set at all. Spring Boot does not manage these two libraries. The sender of Spring Cloud AWS 4.1 is built on DelegatingEventExternalizer. Spring Modulith 2.1 deprecated that class for removal, with the advice to use EventExternalizerModuleListener instead.

The deprecation matters for the rows. Each row names its listener by a method signature. In a run, the sender's rows had the listener ID ...DelegatingEventExternalizer.externalize(java.lang.Object). A later Spring Cloud AWS may move to the new class. Rows written before that upgrade would then name a listener that no longer exists. The source shows that the multicaster then logs "Listener ... not found" and marks the row failed. This is read from the source, not run.

Pragmatic choice: An outbox sender on a deprecated class

The strict rule. Do not build on a class that is deprecated for removal.

What we do. The platform uses the SNS sender of Spring Cloud AWS 4.1, which is built on DelegatingEventExternalizer. That class is deprecated for removal in Spring Modulith 2.1.

Why. It is the SNS sender that Spring Cloud AWS provides, and Spring Modulith removed its own. It works with Spring Modulith 2.1.2 and Boot 4.1.2, as the journey test shows. Writing a sender of our own would mean owning the retry and the completion logic.

When to stop. Stop when a Spring Cloud AWS release moves to EventExternalizerModuleListener, or when Spring Modulith removes the old class. Before that upgrade, let the outbox drain to zero documents, stop the services, then deploy.

MassTransit's outbox in MongoDB, from the package MassTransit.MongoDb. The C# pane compiles with MassTransit 8.5.12.

The bus outbox stores the messages that the code publishes, until they are sent.

In Java, a service writes no setup. The platform's auto-configuration runs after the mongo one, which provides the transaction manager.

MassTransit's documentation describes its bus outbox as adding published and sent messages to the database context. Its consumer outbox combines an inbox and an outbox. The documentation also says that the outbox does not replace idempotent business logic. Spring Modulith's registry has the same purpose as the bus outbox. The order service writes its inbox itself, which the next chapter shows.

The licences differ, and they changed recently. As of October 2026:

LibraryLicenceNote
MassTransit v9commercial, source-availablea paid licence is needed once annual revenue exceeds one million US dollars
MassTransit v8Apache 2.08.5.12 came out on 21 October 2026, and an archived notice ends official maintenance after 2026, with no exact date

MassTransit 9.0.0 came out on 6 January 2026. A team that moves from v8 to v9 must check the licence first. NServiceBus deduplicates by MessageId, and supports MongoDB among its stores. Its documentation warns that messages sent through IMessageSession are not handled by the outbox. That is the same trap as a publish outside a transaction.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy can the order service not send OrderShippedV1 to SNS right after it saves the order, even from an after-commit callback?
The database and SNS share no transaction. Sending before the commit announces a change that may roll back. Sending after the commit loses the event if the process dies between the commit and the send. The outbox writes the event in the change's transaction, and sends it later, so the change and the event are stored together.
2
An expert asksWhy does the mapper create the eventId, and not the code that sends the event?
The mapper runs inside the use case's transaction, so the ID is stored in the outbox row with the event. Every resend reads the same row and sends the same ID. A consumer's inbox then recognises the duplicate. An ID made at send time would differ on each resend, and every duplicate would look new.
3
An instance of the order service dies just after the resender claimed an outbox row. What happens to the row, and what brings it back?
The row stays RESUBMITTED, and later resends skip it, because the claim takes only rows that are not RESUBMITTED. Only Spring Modulith's staleness monitor moves it back to FAILED, and the monitor is off until spring.modulith.events.staleness.resubmitted is set.
4
TranslateWrite this C# mapper as the Java mapper of the order feature, for the cancelled order only, so that every other event stays inside: 
public IIntegrationEvent? ToIntegrationEvent(IDomainEvent domainEvent) => domainEvent switch
{
    OrderCancelled cancelled => new OrderCancelledV1(NewEventId(), cancelled.OccurredAt, cancelled.OrderId.Value),
    _ => null
};
public Optional<IntegrationEvent> toIntegrationEvent(DomainEvent event) {
    return switch (event) {
        // ...
        case OrderCancelled cancelled -> Optional.of(new OrderCancelledV1(newEventId(), cancelled.occurredAt(),
                cancelled.orderId().value()));
        default -> Optional.empty();
    };
}

The Java switch uses a type pattern in each case. default returns an empty Optional where the C# version returns null. The // ... stands for the arms of the other published events.

Consuming events: SQS and the inbox#

Talking to other services · Chapter 21· 27 min read· Quick reference

The order service reads the payment service's events from a queue of Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). SQS may deliver the same message twice. So the order service keeps the ID of each event it has handled, in an inbox, in the same transaction as the change. Its domain also ignores a repeated payment. This chapter covers the listener, failures, the dead-letter queue and the inbox.
