Why every consumer needs an inboxnew#

The payment service publishes PaymentReceivedV1 to its topic in Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS). SNS copies it into the order service's queue in SQS. The order service reads it, and marks the order paid. SQS sometimes delivers the same message twice, and the payment service's own outbox may send it twice as well.

The AWS documentation is direct about this. A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery. More than one copy of a message might be delivered, and the order is only best effort. It tells consumers to be idempotent. A consumer is idempotent when handling a message twice has the same effect as handling it once.

The journey test does what SQS may do. It sends the same payment event twice:

// The payment service's event arrives through SQS, twice, as at-least-once delivery allows.
String payment = paymentEvent(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), orderId);
aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(payment));
aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(payment));
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() ->
        mvc.perform(get("/orders/" + orderId).with(agent)).andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value("PAID")));
Reading the code
String payment = paymentEvent(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), orderId);

One event, with one eventId. Both messages carry the same text.

aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(payment));

The test writes straight to the queue, through the AWS SDK, as SNS would.

Later, the same test reads the audit log, and finds exactly one PAYMENT_RECORDED for the order. So the service handled the event once, although it received it twice.

The order service uses two defences. The first is the inbox. An inbox is a collection where a consumer stores the ID of each event that it has handled. It stores the ID in the same transaction as the change. A copy that arrives later finds the ID, and is skipped. The second defence is the domain itself, which ignores a payment that is not newer than the last one. The sections below show both, after the listener that receives the message.

For messaging in general and Kafka, see the chapter Messaging and WebSockets. For the outbox on the sending side, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

The listener: @SqsListenertwist#

AWS.Messaging
public class PaymentReceivedHandler(IOrderService orders) : IMessageHandler<PaymentReceivedV1>
{
    public async Task<MessageProcessStatus> HandleAsync(MessageEnvelope<PaymentReceivedV1> envelope,
        CancellationToken token = default)
    {
        PaymentReceivedV1 e = envelope.Message;
        await orders.RecordPaymentAsync(e.OrderId, e.PaymentReference, e.Amount, e.Currency, e.PaidAt);
        return MessageProcessStatus.Success();
    }
}
Spring Cloud AWS
/** The queue name comes from configuration, so each environment can name its own queue. */
@SqsListener("${messaging.queues.payment-received}")
void on(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    process(event);
}
Reading the code
@SqsListener("${messaging.queues.payment-received}")

This annotation of Spring Cloud AWS 4.1 makes the method a listener of one queue. The value is a property placeholder, so the queue name comes from application.yml.

void on(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {

The parameter's type tells Spring Cloud AWS how to read the message body. The JSON becomes a PaymentReceivedV1.

process(event);

The method passes the event to the platform's base class. See the section The base class of every listener.

The C# handler returns a status. The Java method returns nothing, and an exception means failure. The C# pane compiles with AWS.Messaging 1.6.0.

The queue name has a default in the service's settings, and each environment may override it with an environment variable:

messaging:
  queues:
    payment-received: ${PAYMENT_RECEIVED_QUEUE:order-service-payment-received}

The variable PAYMENT_RECEIVED_QUEUE overrides the default name. The key messaging.queues.payment-received belongs to the service, not to Spring. A run for this book confirmed that @SqsListener("${...}") resolves such a placeholder. Behind the method, Spring Cloud AWS runs a listener container. The container polls the queue, converts each message, calls the method, and deletes the message when the method returns. In the same run, a JSON body with an extra field paidBy became the record, and the extra field was ignored.

The container also passes the message's metadata as headers. A parameter with @Header(name = "eventType") receives an SQS message attribute. The run listed the headers that the container adds:

HeaderWhat it holds
Sqs_Msa_ApproximateReceiveCounthow many times SQS has delivered this message, the first delivery included
Sqs_QueueName and Sqs_QueueUrlthe queue the message came from
Sqs_ReceiptHandlethe handle that a delete or a visibility change needs
Sqs_VisibilityTimeoutthe visibility timeout of the receive
Sqs_RawMessageIdthe message ID that SQS gave the message

The service's own copy of the eventtwist#

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
record PaymentReceivedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId, String paymentReference,
                         BigDecimal amount, String currency, Instant paidAt) implements IntegrationEvent {

The payment service owns PaymentReceivedV1. The order service does not share a library with it. It declares its own record, with only the fields it uses. The payment service can add fields, and the order service ignores them. The test PaymentReceivedV1Test.readsTheEventAndIgnoresFieldsItDoesNotUse reads an event with an extra field cardScheme.

The record is package-private, in order.messaging. Only the listener uses it. It implements the platform's IntegrationEvent, so it has an eventId for the inbox. The fields are plain types. amount is a BigDecimal, never a double, because it is money.

The service also keeps a copy of the part of their schema that it relies on:

"$id": "payment-service/PaymentReceivedV1",
"title": "PaymentReceivedV1 (consumed)",
"description": "Owned by the payment service. This is the part of their contract that order-service relies on, kept here so a change on their side is easy to check. Received on the order-service-payment-received SQS queue, with raw message delivery.",
"type": "object",
"required": ["eventId", "occurredAt", "orderId", "paymentReference", "amount", "currency", "paidAt"],

The required list is the order service's side of the contract. When the payment service plans a change, both teams compare their schema with this file. For event contracts and their checks, see the chapter API and event contracts.

The SNS envelope, and the null traptrap#

SNS wraps each message in a JSON envelope before it puts it on a queue, unless the subscription asks for raw message delivery. The envelope holds fields such as Type, MessageId and TopicArn. It holds the event itself as a string, in the field Message. A run for this book sent such an envelope to a listener that expects the event:

PredictAn SNS envelope on a queue that expects the event#
The listener expects PaymentReceivedV1. The queue delivers the SNS envelope, with the event as a string inside Message. What does the listener receive, and what happens to the message?
public record PaymentReceivedV1(String eventId, String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {}
// ...
    @SqsListener("envelope-plain")
    void onEnvelopePlain(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
        System.out.println("  envelope-plain listener got " + event);
    }
// ...
    var envelope = "{\"Type\":\"Notification\",\"MessageId\":\"m-1\",\"TopicArn\":\"arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:000000000000:payment-events\","
        + "\"Message\":\"{\\\"eventId\\\":\\\"e-3\\\",\\\"orderId\\\":\\\"o-3\\\",\\\"amount\\\":5}\",\"Timestamp\":\"2026-10-25T10:00:00.000Z\","
        + "\"SignatureVersion\":\"1\",\"Signature\":\"x\",\"SigningCertURL\":\"https://x\",\"UnsubscribeURL\":\"https://x\"}";
    SQS.send("envelope-plain", envelope, Map.of());
Show the answer
PaymentReceivedV1[eventId=null, orderId=null, amount=null], with no error. The message is acknowledged and deleted, so the payment is lost.

Jackson 3 ignores unknown fields, so the envelope's fields are dropped, and the record's fields are simply absent. No field of the envelope has the name of a record component. Nothing fails, so the listener returns normally. The container acknowledges a message on success, and an acknowledgement deletes it.

Turn on raw message delivery on the subscription. And make the record refuse missing fields, so a wrong subscription fails loudly.

The local environment turns raw delivery on for every subscription it creates:

# subscribe <topic-arn> <queue-url>: raw delivery, so the message body is the event itself and
# not an SNS envelope around it.
subscribe() {
  queue_arn=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$2" --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)
  aws sns subscribe --topic-arn "$1" --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint "$queue_arn" \
    --attributes RawMessageDelivery=true >/dev/null
}
Reading the code
queue_arn=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$2" --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)

A subscription needs the queue's Amazon Resource Name (ARN), not its URL. This line asks SQS for it.

--attributes RawMessageDelivery=true >/dev/null

With raw delivery, SNS sends the message as it is, with no envelope. The AWS documentation says that SNS then strips its metadata.

The infrastructure code of each environment must set the same attribute. The service's README says that the subscription must use raw message delivery. But a setting in another repository can be forgotten, so the order service also defends itself in code:

PaymentReceivedV1 {
    Objects.requireNonNull(eventId, "eventId");
    Objects.requireNonNull(occurredAt, "occurredAt");
    Objects.requireNonNull(orderId, "orderId");
    Objects.requireNonNull(paymentReference, "paymentReference");
    Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
    Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
    Objects.requireNonNull(paidAt, "paidAt");
}
Reading the code
PaymentReceivedV1 {

A compact constructor. It runs every time the record is created, also when Jackson creates it from JSON.

Objects.requireNonNull(eventId, "eventId");

java.util.Objects.requireNonNull throws a NullPointerException with the given message when the value is null.

Now an envelope cannot become a record. The conversion fails, the message is not acknowledged, and SQS delivers it again. After the maximum number of receives, SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue, where someone sees it. The test PaymentReceivedV1Test.refusesAnSnsEnvelopeInsteadOfTheEvent reads an envelope, and expects the root cause NullPointerException with the message eventId. The journey test aMessageThatIsNotTheEventEndsInTheDeadLetterQueue proves the whole path with Floci.

A third way exists. The annotation @SnsNotificationMessage on the parameter unwraps the envelope. In the same run, it gave PaymentReceivedV1[eventId=e-3, orderId=o-3, amount=5]. Choose it only when raw delivery cannot be turned on. With raw delivery, the same listener also works for a message that another source sends straight to the queue.

Note

With raw delivery on, SNS can send at most 10 message attributes. The AWS documentation says that a message with more is discarded as a client-side error. Keep the attributes few.

Acknowledged on success, deleted in batchestwist#

* <p>If the handler throws, the transaction rolls back and the message is not acknowledged.
* SQS delivers it again after the visibility timeout, and after the queue's maximum receive
* count it moves the message to the dead-letter queue.

The comment says that a failed message is not acknowledged. An acknowledgement is the container's signal that a message is done. In SQS, acknowledging a message is the same as deleting it from the queue. The default acknowledgement mode of the container is ON_SUCCESS. So the outcome of the listener method decides:

The listener methodWhat the container doesWhat SQS does
returns normallydeletes the message, in a batchnothing more, because the message is gone
throws an exceptionnothing, so no delete and no visibility changemakes the message visible again when the visibility timeout ends

A run for this book confirmed both rows. A successful message was followed by deleteMessageBatch. A failing message was received again after each timeout, with no delete and no call to change its visibility.

The deletes are batched. On a standard queue, the container deletes every second, or every 10 messages. On a FIFO queue, it deletes at once. In the run, the deletes came about 1.0 second after the receive.

Other defaults of the container, from its source and the same run:

DefaultValueWhy it matters
messages per poll10one receive call returns up to 10 messages
poll timeout10 seconds, which is long pollingan empty queue costs few requests
messages in flight per queue10at most 10 messages of one queue are handled at once
listener shutdown timeout20 secondsthe time that running handlers get when the service stops
message attributesAllevery SQS attribute reaches the listener as a header

The other modes are ALWAYS and MANUAL. The order service keeps ON_SUCCESS, because the outcome of the inbox's transaction must decide.

The visibility timeouttrap#

When a consumer receives a message, SQS hides it from other consumers for a while. That time is called the visibility timeout. Its default is 30 seconds, and its maximum is 12 hours. If the message is not deleted before the timeout ends, it becomes visible again, and another receive gets it.

A C# developer who used AWS.Messaging may expect the timeout to look after itself. That framework extends the visibility timeout while a handler runs. Spring Cloud AWS's default container does not. The run saw no visibility call at all.

Gotcha

A visibility timeout shorter than the handler plus about one second delivers every message twice, even when nothing fails. The container deletes in batches, up to one second after the handler ends. In a run with a simulated timeout of 700 ms, every successful message was delivered twice before its delete arrived. Size the queue's timeout for the slowest handler, plus the batch interval.

The local environment's script says the same where the queue is created:

# The visibility timeout must be longer than the slowest handler plus about 1 second: Spring
# Cloud AWS acknowledges (deletes) messages in batches, every second or every 10 messages, and
# does not extend the timeout while a handler runs. A shorter timeout delivers each message twice.
queue() {
  dlq_url=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1-dlq" --query QueueUrl --output text)
  dlq_arn=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$dlq_url" --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)
  aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1" \
    --attributes "{\"VisibilityTimeout\":\"30\",\"RedrivePolicy\":\"{\\\"deadLetterTargetArn\\\":\\\"$dlq_arn\\\",\\\"maxReceiveCount\\\":\\\"5\\\"}\"}" \
    --query QueueUrl --output text
}
Reading the code
dlq_url=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1-dlq" --query QueueUrl --output text)

The dead-letter queue comes first, because the main queue's policy names it.

--attributes "{\"VisibilityTimeout\":\"30\",\"RedrivePolicy\":\"{\\\"deadLetterTargetArn\\\":\\\"$dlq_arn\\\",\\\"maxReceiveCount\\\":\\\"5\\\"}\"}" \

Two attributes in one JSON text. VisibilityTimeout is 30 seconds. The redrive policy names the dead-letter queue and the receive count. The quoting looks hard, because the policy is JSON inside JSON inside a shell string.

The payment handler is short, so 30 seconds is plenty. A handler that calls a slow service needs a longer timeout, or a call that extends it. The duplicates of a short timeout reach the inbox, which skips them. But each one costs a read and a transaction.

Failures, redrive and the dead-letter queuetwist#

this.paymentDeadLetterQueueUrl = sqs.createQueue(queue -> queue.queueName(PAYMENT_QUEUE + "-dlq")).queueUrl();
String redrive = "{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"" + queueArn(paymentDeadLetterQueueUrl)
        + "\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"" + MAX_RECEIVES + "\"}";
this.paymentQueueUrl = sqs.createQueue(queue -> queue.queueName(PAYMENT_QUEUE).attributes(Map.of(
        QueueAttributeName.REDRIVE_POLICY, redrive,
        QueueAttributeName.VISIBILITY_TIMEOUT, "2"))).queueUrl();
Reading the code
String redrive = "{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"" + queueArn(paymentDeadLetterQueueUrl)

The redrive policy is JSON text. It names the dead-letter queue by its ARN.

+ "\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"" + MAX_RECEIVES + "\"}";

The journey test uses 2 receives, so a bad message reaches the dead-letter queue in seconds.

QueueAttributeName.VISIBILITY_TIMEOUT, "2"))).queueUrl();

A failed message becomes visible again after 2 seconds.

The journey test creates its queues as the local script does, with the AWS SDK for Java. A message that always fails is called a poison message. Without a limit, SQS would deliver it again and again, and it would use the listener's capacity for ever.

A dead-letter queue is a second queue that receives such messages. The source queue's redrive policy names it, with a maxReceiveCount. The AWS documentation defines that count. It is the number of times a consumer can receive a message before SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue. The local queues use 5. The journey test uses 2, so it finishes quickly.

The move is a feature of SQS. Spring Cloud AWS does not do it, and the order service has no code for it. So the path of a failing payment is this:

  1. The handler throws, and the inbox's transaction rolls back. The order is unchanged, and no inbox key is written.
  2. The container does not acknowledge, so the message stays in the queue.
  3. After the visibility timeout, SQS delivers it again. The header Sqs_Msa_ApproximateReceiveCount grows by one.
  4. After 5 receives, SQS moves the message to order-service-payment-received-dlq.
  5. Someone looks at the message, fixes the cause, and moves it back.

SQS can move messages from the dead-letter queue back to the source queue, with the API StartMessageMoveTask. The dead-letter queue of a standard queue must be a standard queue, and that of a FIFO queue must be a FIFO queue.

Alert on a dead-letter queue that is not empty. A message there means a payment that the order service never recorded. For metrics and alerts, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

A transient failure, such as a database that is briefly unavailable, takes the same path, and may succeed on a later receive. So the receive count also works as a slow retry. It does not need Resilience4j.

A queue that does not existtrap#

A deployment sets PAYMENT_RECEIVED_QUEUE with a typo. At startup, the container looks up the queue's URL, and finds no queue. What it does then is a setting, spring.cloud.aws.sqs.queue-not-found-strategy. The platform sets it to fail:

# Stop at startup when a queue does not exist. The default creates the missing queue,
# which then has no dead-letter queue, so a failing message would be retried for ever.
spring.cloud.aws.sqs.queue-not-found-strategy=fail

The comment names the danger. The property queue-not-found-strategy takes a value of the type QueueNotFoundStrategy.

Gotcha

By default, Spring Cloud AWS creates a queue that does not exist. The default of QueueNotFoundStrategy in the code is CREATE. The new queue has no dead-letter queue and no subscription. So the service listens to an empty queue, and a poison message on it would be retried for ever. The setting's metadata gives no default, and the code does.

With fail, the service stops at startup, and the orchestrator shows the error at once. Queues belong to the infrastructure code and to the local script, never to the service. This matches the rule for topics in the chapter Publishing events: the outbox, with one difference. A topic name is resolved by CreateTopic, and no setting stops that.

The inboxnew#

The same payment arrives twice. Without an inbox, the order service handles it twice. For a payment, the domain ignores the second copy. Most handlers are not so forgiving. A handler that sends an email or adds a line would act twice. So the platform gives every consumer an inbox:

public <T extends IntegrationEvent> void process(String consumer, T event, Consumer<T> handler) {
    String key = consumer + ":" + event.eventId();
    try {
        transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            if (mongo.exists(query(where("_id").is(key)), COLLECTION)) {
                log.info("Skipping event {}, which was processed before", event.eventId());
                return;
            }
            handler.accept(event);
            mongo.insert(new Document("_id", key).append("processedAt", clock.instant()), COLLECTION);
        });
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
        // DuplicateKeyException is a DataIntegrityViolationException; so is a translated write conflict.
        if (e instanceof DuplicateKeyException || WriteConflicts.isWriteConflict(e)) {
            log.info("Event {} was processed by another delivery at the same time", event.eventId());
            throw new ConcurrentDeliveryException(key, e);
        }
        throw e;
    }
}
Reading the code
public <T extends IntegrationEvent> void process(String consumer, T event, Consumer<T> handler) {

A generic method for any integration event. The handler is a Consumer<T>, a function that takes the event and returns nothing. It does the same as Action<T> in C#.

String key = consumer + ":" + event.eventId();

The key combines the consumer's name and the event's ID, such as order-service.payment-received:3f2a.... Two consumers of one event in the same service have two keys.

transactions.executeWithoutResult(status -> {

Everything in the lambda runs in one transaction of a TransactionTemplate.

if (mongo.exists(query(where("_id").is(key)), COLLECTION)) {

The key is the document's _id in processed_messages. If it exists, the event was handled before, and the method returns.

handler.accept(event);

The handler runs inside the same transaction. The use case that it calls joins it.

mongo.insert(new Document("_id", key).append("processedAt", clock.instant()), COLLECTION);

The key is inserted after the handler, with the time. The commit stores the change and the key together.

The order of the steps matters. The key is written after the handler, in the same transaction. If the handler fails, the key rolls back with the change, so a redelivery runs the handler again. If the key were committed first, a failure after it would lose the event for ever.

The test InboxIT.processesARepeatedEventOnlyOnce handles one event twice against a real MongoDB, and finds one stored parcel. rollsBackTheHandlersChangesWhenItFails lets the handler throw after a write. Afterwards the test finds no write and no key.

The inbox is platform code, a few dozen lines long. MassTransit offers an inbox in .NET, as part of its consumer outbox. The platform did not use a library for it in Java. The research looked for one in October 2026, and found none that is maintained and supports MongoDB:

CandidateWhat the research found
Spring Modulith 2.1.2an outbox with a MongoDB store, and no inbox, which its source and its issues do not mention
Namastack Outbox 1.11.0an outbox for JDBC, JPA and MongoDB, with no inbox, and a guarantees page that asks for idempotent handlers
Spring Integration 7.1.2IdempotentReceiverInterceptor with a MetadataStore such as MongoDbMetadataStore, made for the message handlers of Spring Integration
small starters on GitHub with 2026 commitsan inbox for JDBC, R2DBC, PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle, and none for MongoDB

Spring Integration's interceptor is the careful alternative. It is maintained, and its MongoDB store keeps the keys across restarts. It fits a service that already uses Spring Integration for its messages. The order service receives messages with Spring Cloud AWS's listener container, not with Spring Integration. Adding Spring Integration only for the inbox would bring a second messaging model into the service. The platform's inbox is short, it shares the use case's transaction, and its tests run against MongoDB. Re-evaluate when Spring Modulith or Namastack adds an inbox with a MongoDB store.

The inbox needs transactions, as the outbox does. The inbox and the outbox were tested on MongoDB 8.0.34, not on Amazon DocumentDB. Test both on a real DocumentDB cluster early in a project. For DocumentDB transactions, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

Two copies at the same momenttwist#

SQS can deliver two copies of one message to two instances at nearly the same time. Both inboxes check the key, and both find nothing. Both handlers run. Both transactions try to insert the same _id. A C# developer expects the second insert to fail with a duplicate-key error. The platform's integration test records what MongoDB really does:

PredictTwo deliveries of one event, in two transactions at once#
Both deliveries pass the existence check, and both handlers have run. Which exception does the losing delivery's insert of the key cause?
@Test
void aConcurrentDuplicateRollsBackAndIsSkippedOnRedelivery() throws Exception {
    ParcelArrivedV1 event = new ParcelArrivedV1("event-3", Instant.EPOCH);
    CyclicBarrier bothHandled = new CyclicBarrier(2);
    Consumer<ParcelArrivedV1> handler = arrived -> {
        storeParcel(arrived);
        await(bothHandled);
    };
Show the answer
A write conflict, MongoDB's error 112, which Spring translates to DataIntegrityViolationException. It is not a DuplicateKeyException. The inbox then throws ConcurrentDeliveryException.

Inside two open transactions, the collision on the key is a write conflict. The first transaction has inserted the key and not yet committed. The second insert fails at once with code 112 and the label TransientTransactionError. Spring translates code 112 to DataIntegrityViolationException.

Only a copy that starts after the first commit gets DuplicateKeyException, code 11000. An inbox that catches only the duplicate key treats the race as an unknown failure. So the platform checks for both.

The test then checks the outcome:

assertThat(failures).singleElement().isInstanceOfSatisfying(ConcurrentDeliveryException.class,
        error -> assertThat(error.getCause().getMessage()).contains("WriteConflict"));
assertThat(mongo.findAll(Document.class, "parcels")).hasSize(1);

inbox.process(CONSUMER, event, this::storeParcel);   // the redelivery of the losing copy
assertThat(mongo.findAll(Document.class, "parcels")).hasSize(1);
Reading the code
assertThat(failures).singleElement().isInstanceOfSatisfying(ConcurrentDeliveryException.class,

Exactly one delivery failed, with the platform's exception.

error -> assertThat(error.getCause().getMessage()).contains("WriteConflict"));

Its cause names the write conflict.

assertThat(mongo.findAll(Document.class, "parcels")).hasSize(1);

Both handlers wrote a parcel, but the loser's write rolled back. One parcel remains.

inbox.process(CONSUMER, event, this::storeParcel); // the redelivery of the losing copy

SQS would deliver the losing copy again. That delivery finds the key, and skips.

The platform's helper WriteConflicts.isWriteConflict walks the causes of the exception. It looks for a MongoDB exception with code 112 or with the label TransientTransactionError. The Spring type alone is not enough, because DataIntegrityViolationException also covers real data errors.

The losing copy is not an error to alert on. ConcurrentDeliveryException reaches the container, so the message is not acknowledged. Its redelivery finds the key of the winner, and is skipped. MongoDB does not retry the transaction by itself, and Spring does not retry it either. The redelivery of SQS is the retry.

The .NET driver reports the same server error, and its callback API retries the transaction. For that difference, see the section Write conflicts, and what Spring retries. The answer of DocumentDB to the same race was not measured.

The inbox cleans itself: a TTL indextwist#

@Override
public String id() {
    return "P002-inbox-indexes";
}

@Override
public void migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
    mongo.indexOps(Inbox.COLLECTION).createIndex(new Index()
            .on("processedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC)
            .expire(properties.getInbox().getRetention())
            .named("processed_messages_ttl"));
}
Reading the code
return "P002-inbox-indexes";

This is a migration of the platform, with an ID that never changes. The migration runner applies it once. For the runner, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

.expire(properties.getInbox().getRetention())

A time-to-live (TTL) index deletes each document a fixed time after the date in the field processedAt.

.named("processed_messages_ttl"));

A named index can be found and changed later by its name.

Without the index, the collection would grow by one document for every message, for ever. The retention is 14 days, from MessagingProperties.Inbox. SQS keeps a message for 4 days by default, and for 14 days at most. So no copy of a message can arrive after its key is gone. A queue with a shorter retention could use a shorter inbox retention.

The deletes are not exact. The DocumentDB documentation says that deletes from a TTL index are best effort, with no fixed timing. And DocumentDB lists TTL for single-field indexes, so the index has one field. For TTL indexes in full, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

The base class of every listenernew#

Every listener needs the same steps. It needs the inbox, the event's IDs in the log, and the system as the actor. If each listener wrote these steps, one would forget the inbox. So the platform puts them in an abstract base class, and a listener writes only the part that differs:

public abstract class InboxMessageHandler<T extends IntegrationEvent> {

    private final String consumer;
    private final Inbox inbox;

    /**
     * @param consumer a stable name, such as {@code order-service.payment-received}; never change
     *                 it, or the inbox treats every old event as new
     * @param inbox    the platform's inbox
     */
    protected InboxMessageHandler(String consumer, Inbox inbox) {
        this.consumer = consumer;
        this.inbox = inbox;
    }

    protected final void process(T event) {
        Map<String, String> context = new HashMap<>(logContext(event));
        context.put("eventId", event.eventId());
        SecurityContext callerContext = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
        SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();
        try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.with(context)) {
            inbox.process(consumer, event, this::handle);
        } finally {
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(callerContext);
        }
    }

    /** Translates the event and calls the application service. */
    protected abstract void handle(T event);

    /** Returns the business IDs to add to the MDC, such as the order ID. Only IDs, never personal data. */
    protected Map<String, String> logContext(T event) {
        return Map.of();
    }
}
Reading the code
public abstract class InboxMessageHandler<T extends IntegrationEvent> {

A generic abstract class. T is the event type, and it must be an integration event, so it has an eventId.

protected final void process(T event) {

final means that no subclass can override the method. So no listener can skip the inbox. It is like a method without virtual in C#.

SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();

The work runs with no user, as the system actor. The finally block restores the thread's earlier context.

inbox.process(consumer, event, this::handle);

this::handle is a method reference to the subclass's handle, passed as the inbox's Consumer.

protected abstract void handle(T event);

The one method that each listener must write.

protected Map<String, String> logContext(T event) {

A listener may override it to add business IDs to the log. The default adds none.

The base class is an example of the template method pattern. A pattern of this name fixes the steps of an algorithm in a base class, and lets subclasses fill in one step. The order service's listener extends it:

@Component
class PaymentReceivedListener extends InboxMessageHandler<PaymentReceivedV1> {

    /** The inbox key prefix. Never change it, or every old event looks new. */
    static final String CONSUMER = "order-service.payment-received";

    private final OrderService orders;

    PaymentReceivedListener(Inbox inbox, OrderService orders) {
        super(CONSUMER, inbox);
        this.orders = orders;
    }

The constructor passes the consumer name to super, the base class's constructor. The name is a constant, written once.

Gotcha

A new consumer name makes every old event look new. The inbox key starts with the name. After a rename, no old key matches. If SQS still holds a message that was handled before the deploy, it runs again. Treat the name like a database column name, and never change it. A refactoring that renames the class must keep the constant.

The security part has its home in another chapter. For why a message runs as the system actor, and what the audit log records, see the section Messages and jobs: the system actor.

An older design wrote each listener in full. The listener opened a TransactionTemplate itself, asked the inbox alreadyProcessed(...), called the use case, and then called record(...). That design is explicit, and a reader sees every step in one method. Its weakness is repetition. Each listener must repeat the steps in the right order, and a listener that records the key outside the transaction loses events. The base class keeps the order in one place, and final keeps it there.

Pragmatic choice: Every listener goes through the inbox

The strict rule. Add machinery only where a case needs it. A handler that is idempotent by nature, such as "set the status to PAID", needs no inbox.

What we do. Every listener extends InboxMessageHandler, so every message costs a check and a write in processed_messages. The payment handler is idempotent in its domain as well.

Why. Few handlers stay idempotent by nature. A later change, such as a notification email, makes a repeat visible. With one base class for every listener, nobody has to judge each handler again after each change.

When to stop. Stop for a queue with very high volume, where the extra write per message matters. Its handler must be idempotent by design, and tested as such. Then call the use case without the inbox, and write down why.

A thin listenertwist#

@Override
protected void handle(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    Payment payment = new Payment(new PaymentReference(event.paymentReference()),
            new Money(event.amount(), event.currency()), event.paidAt());
    orders.recordPayment(OrderId.of(event.orderId()), payment);
}

The method handle translates the event into value objects, and calls one use case. It holds no rule. A listener is an adapter, like a controller. Its job is to turn a message into a call of the application layer. OrderId.of checks the ID's format, so a bad ID fails here, and the message goes the way of every failure.

The use case joins the inbox's transaction:

@Transactional
public void recordPayment(OrderId orderId, Payment payment) {
    Order order = orders.get(orderId);
    if (order.recordPayment(payment)) {
        saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.PAYMENT_RECORDED);
    }
}

@Transactional has the propagation REQUIRED by default. So recordPayment runs in the transaction that the inbox opened. The order, its events in the outbox, the audit record and the inbox key commit together. For propagation, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

The test PaymentReceivedListenerTest.translatesTheEventAndCallsTheUseCase mocks the inbox to run the handler, and checks the Payment that reaches the use case. The amount 12.5 arrives as Money.of("12.50", "GBP").

The domain is idempotent tootwist#

/**
 * Records a payment, unless it is not later than the last one.
 *
 * <p>SQS can deliver a message twice, and messages can arrive out of order. Both cases leave
 * the order unchanged. A payment for a shipped or cancelled order is still recorded, on
 * purpose: the money was received, and the payment service handles any refund.
 *
 * @return whether the order changed, so the caller knows whether to save it
 */
public boolean recordPayment(Payment payment) {
    if (lastPayment != null && !payment.paidAt().isAfter(lastPayment.paidAt())) {
        return false;
    }
    lastPayment = payment;
    if (status == OrderStatus.NEW) {
        status = OrderStatus.PAID;
    }
    raise(new PaymentRecorded(id(), payment.reference(), payment.amount(), payment.paidAt()));
    return true;
}

The aggregate's method recordPayment ignores a payment that is not later than the last one. It returns false, and the use case saves nothing. So a repeat of the same payment changes nothing, and a late, older payment changes nothing either.

The inbox and the domain guard against different cases:

CaseThe inboxThe domain
the same message twice, within 14 daysskips it by its keyignores it, because paidAt is not later
the same payment with a new eventId, from a bug in the payment servicedoes not recognise itignores it
an older payment that arrives after a newer onedoes not recognise it, because the ID is newignores it
the same message after the inbox key expireddoes not recognise itignores it

So the second defence covers what the inbox cannot. The inbox stays the general defence, because most handlers have no field like paidAt to compare. For rules in the aggregate, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java.

Log lines that name the messagetwist#

@Override
protected Map<String, String> logContext(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    return Map.of("orderId", event.orderId());
}

A message arrives on a thread of the listener container, with no HTTP request around it. So nothing puts a trace ID or an order ID into the mapped diagnostic context (MDC). The base class adds the eventId itself, and the listener's logContext adds the orderId. Every log line of the handler then carries both.

The platform's LogContext sets the entries for a block, and puts the earlier values back when the block ends. So nested blocks with the same key work, and the container's thread is clean for the next message. Put only IDs into the MDC, never personal data, because every log line repeats them. For the MDC, structured logs and tracing, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

ILogger.BeginScope in ASP.NET Core has the same purpose. A support engineer then searches the logs for an order ID, and finds the agent's request, the payment service's log lines, and this message.

Testing the consumertwist#

@Test
void aMessageThatIsNotTheEventEndsInTheDeadLetterQueue() {
    String envelope = """
            { "Type": "Notification", "MessageId": "%s", "Message": "{}" }""".formatted(UUID.randomUUID());
    aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(envelope));

    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(60)).untilAsserted(() ->
            assertThat(aws.sqs.receiveMessage(request -> request.queueUrl(aws.paymentDeadLetterQueueUrl)).messages())
                    .extracting(Message::body).anySatisfy(body -> assertThat(body).contains("Notification")));
}

The test aMessageThatIsNotTheEventEndsInTheDeadLetterQueue sends an envelope to the payment queue, and waits until it appears in the dead-letter queue. The journey's queue uses a visibility timeout of 2 seconds and a receive count of 2, so the test needs seconds, not minutes. JourneyAwsResources creates the queues in Floci, as the local script does. The consumer has tests at every level:

TestLevelWhat it proves
PaymentReceivedV1Testunit, no Springunknown fields are ignored, and an envelope fails with eventId
PaymentReceivedListenerTestunit, with Mockitothe event becomes value objects and one use case call
InboxTestunit, with Mockitoa new event runs and records its key, and a known one is skipped
InboxITMongoDB in Dockera repeat runs once, a failure leaves nothing, and a concurrent copy is a write conflict
OrderJourneyITthe whole service, MongoDB and Flocia payment sent twice records once, and a bad message reaches the dead-letter queue

Most tests need no queue. The wiring test starts the whole service with the SQS auto-configuration turned off:

cloud:
  aws:
    sqs:
      enabled: false

The line enabled: false sets spring.cloud.aws.sqs.enabled, which turns off the SQS client, the template and the listener container factory. So no container tries to reach a queue. What an @SqsListener bean does with no factory was not run, but the wiring test starts.

On a developer's machine, a payment can be sent as the payment service would send it. The local environment's README shows the command:

docker run --rm --network local-dev -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=local -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=local \
  -e AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=eu-west-2 -e AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://floci:4566 amazon/aws-cli:2.27.0 \
  sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:000000000000:payment-events --message \
  '{"eventId":"e-1","occurredAt":"2026-10-25T09:00:00Z","orderId":"<order id>","paymentReference":"PAY-1","amount":12.50,"currency":"GBP","paidAt":"2026-10-25T09:00:00Z"}'
Reading the code
docker run --rm --network local-dev

The AWS command-line tool runs in a container on the local network, so it reaches Floci by its container name.

sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:000000000000:payment-events --message \

The command publishes to the topic, not to the queue. So the test also passes through the subscription with raw delivery.

Replace <order id> with the ID of an order, then read the order. Its status is PAID. Run the command twice, and the audit log still shows one payment. For the local environment, see the chapter Running locally and shipping. For the test kinds, see the chapter Testing in depth.

FIFO queues, the other choicenew#

SQS has a second kind of queue. A FIFO queue keeps the order of messages within a message group, and the AWS documentation promises exactly-once processing. Its name must end in .fifo. So why does the order service not use one, and drop the inbox?

The careful version of that choice is strong. A FIFO topic feeds a FIFO queue, and the message group is the order ID. Payments of one order then arrive in order, and SQS removes duplicates. The container acknowledges at once, with no batch. On the sending side, Spring Modulith's routing key gives the group ID, as in "order-events.fifo::#{orderId()}".

The book still recommends a standard queue with an inbox for the order service, for these reasons:

PointFIFO queueStandard queue and inbox
duplicatesremoved by SQS, within a window of 5 minutesskipped by the inbox, within 14 days
throughput300 transactions per second for each API action, or up to 3,000 messages with batches of 10not limited by the FIFO quota
orderkept within a message groupbest effort, so the domain handles a late message
setupa FIFO dead-letter queue, and a message group ID on every message of a FIFO topicstandard queues and topics, with no group ID
the sender's outboxa resend after 5 minutes is not removed as a duplicatethe inbox skips it by eventId

The last row decides for the order service. The outbox resends an event after five minutes. A duplicate after that window passes the FIFO deduplication. So the consumer would need its inbox anyway. High-throughput mode raises the FIFO quota in some regions, to up to 70,000 transactions per second in us-east-1, us-west-2 and eu-west-1.

Choose FIFO when the order of messages within a group is a business rule that the domain cannot restore, and the volume fits the quota. For the routing key, see the section @Externalized: from the outbox to SNS. The order service's own topic is a standard one:

public static final String ORDER_EVENTS = "order-events";

The constant ORDER_EVENTS names a standard topic. A FIFO topic would need the suffix .fifo and a routing key on each event.

Compared with .NET consumerstwist#

An ASP.NET Core developer consumes SQS in one of two ways. The plain way calls ReceiveMessageAsync and DeleteMessageAsync of AWSSDK.SQS in a loop. AWS's own example is a console loop. Running that loop in a hosted service of the application is a pattern of this book, not of an AWS page. The other way is the AWS Message Processing Framework for .NET, AWS.Messaging:

builder.Services.AddAWSMessageBus(bus =>
{
    bus.AddSQSPoller("https://sqs.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/000000000000/order-service-payment-received");
    bus.AddMessageHandler<PaymentReceivedHandler, PaymentReceivedV1>();
});
Reading the code
bus.AddSQSPoller("https://sqs.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/000000000000/order-service-payment-received");

The poller is a long-running background service of the application, which receives from the queue.

bus.AddMessageHandler<PaymentReceivedHandler, PaymentReceivedV1>();

This registers the handler of the section The listener: @SqsListener for the message type.

AWS.Messaging reached version 1.0.0, its first stable release, on 5 May 2025. The latest is 1.6.0, from 10 August 2026. The two frameworks compare like this:

PointAWS.Messaging 1.6.0Spring Cloud AWS 4.1.0
the handlerIMessageHandler<T>, which returns MessageProcessStatusa method with @SqsListener, which returns or throws
successMessageProcessStatus.Success()the method returns, and the message is deleted in a batch
failureMessageProcessStatus.Failed() leaves the message in the queuean exception leaves the message in the queue
visibility timeoutextended while a handler runsnot extended, so size the queue's timeout
duplicatesyour own inbox, or MassTransit'sthe platform's inbox

The row about the visibility timeout is the one to remember. A .NET habit of long handlers on a short timeout turns into duplicates in Spring. For a whole inbox and outbox in .NET, MassTransit's consumer outbox is the closest match. Its inbox state tracks received messages by MessageId for each endpoint. For its licence as of 2026, see the section Compared with MassTransit and NServiceBus.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe order service has an inbox. Why does Order.recordPayment still ignore a payment that is not later than the last one?
The inbox recognises only the same eventId, and only for 14 days. A repeated payment with a new event ID, an older payment that arrives late, or a message after its key expired all pass the inbox. The domain compares paidAt, so it ignores all of them. The two defences cover different cases.
2
An expert asksWhy can a queue with a visibility timeout of one second deliver every successful message twice in a Spring Cloud AWS service?
The container deletes successful messages in batches, every second or every 10 messages. It does not extend the visibility timeout while the handler runs. If the timeout ends before the batch delete, SQS makes the message visible again, and it is delivered a second time. Size the timeout for the slowest handler plus about one second.
3
A developer renames the listener class, and its consumer name changes with it. What happens to messages that are still in the queue?
The inbox key starts with the consumer name, so no old key matches the new name. Every message that was handled before the deploy, and is delivered again, runs a second time. The name must never change.
4
TranslateWrite this C# handler as a Java listener of the order service, using the platform's base class: 
public class PaymentReceivedHandler(IOrderService orders) : IMessageHandler<PaymentReceivedV1>
{
    public async Task<MessageProcessStatus> HandleAsync(MessageEnvelope<PaymentReceivedV1> envelope,
        CancellationToken token = default)
    {
        PaymentReceivedV1 e = envelope.Message;
        await orders.RecordPaymentAsync(e.OrderId, e.PaymentReference, e.Amount, e.Currency, e.PaidAt);
        return MessageProcessStatus.Success();
    }
}
@SqsListener("${messaging.queues.payment-received}")
void on(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    process(event);
}

@Override
protected void handle(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    Payment payment = new Payment(new PaymentReference(event.paymentReference()),
            new Money(event.amount(), event.currency()), event.paidAt());
    orders.recordPayment(OrderId.of(event.orderId()), payment);
}

The class extends InboxMessageHandler<PaymentReceivedV1>. The method with @SqsListener passes the event to process, which runs the inbox. Success is a normal return, and failure is an exception.

The SQS limits that the chapter uses, from the AWS documentation:

LimitValue
visibility timeout30 seconds by default, 12 hours at most
message retention4 days by default, 14 days at most

Logging, tracing and health#

Running the service · Chapter 22· 30 min read· Quick reference

When an order fails in production, support staff need to find out what happened. The order service writes JSON log lines, and every line carries a trace ID and the order's ID. Traces follow a request into other services. Metrics count orders, and health probes tell the orchestrator when to send traffic. A separate audit log stores who changed what.
