What the service keeps, and who reads itnew#

A customer calls the shop. Their order says "placed", but the warehouse never saw it. A support engineer opens the logs. They need every line about that order, from every service the request reached, in the order they were written. Later the business asks who cancelled the order. That answer must be exact, and it must still exist in a year.

These are different questions, and the service answers each one with a different tool:

ToolWhat it answersWho reads itKept for
log lines, in JSONwhat happened in this request, step by stepdevelopers and supportdays or weeks
a tracewhere the time went, across servicesdevelopersdays
metricshow many orders, how many errors, how fastoperations and the businessmonths
health probescan this instance take traffic nowthe orchestratornot kept
the audit logwho changed which order, and whensupport, auditors, the businessas long as the data

Most of this comes from the platform library, shop-platform. Two starters in its build file bring the tools:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- ... -->
<!-- Tracing: trace and span IDs in every log line, passed on with every HTTP call -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>

The Actuator starter adds the health endpoints and Micrometer, the metrics library. For the Actuator endpoints in general, see the chapter Actuator and observability.

<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry</artifactId>

This starter adds tracing with OpenTelemetry. It is new in Boot 4. See the section Tracing with the OpenTelemetry starter.

The service itself adds very little. It names the path variables to log, it counts its orders, and each use case writes an audit entry. Everything else is a platform default that every shop service gets.

SLF4J and Logback in the servicetwist#

The platform's exception handler logs a failure of the stock service. Each class keeps one logger in a static final field:

C#
public class GlobalExceptionHandler(ILogger<GlobalExceptionHandler> log)
{
    public void Downstream(DownstreamServiceException ex) =>
        log.LogWarning(ex, "Dependency {Dependency} is unavailable", ex.Dependency);
}
Java 25
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);
// ...
@ExceptionHandler(DownstreamServiceException.class)
ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> downstream(DownstreamServiceException ex) {
    log.warn("Dependency {} is unavailable", ex.dependency(), ex);
Reading the code
LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);

The code calls the Simple Logging Facade for Java (SLF4J). Logback does the writing, because Boot uses it by default. The logger's name is the class's full name, so the level setting of its package applies.

log.warn("Dependency {} is unavailable", ex.dependency(), ex);

The {} is filled with the first argument. The last argument is an exception, and no placeholder is left for it. So SLF4J prints the exception's stack trace under the message.

A run for this book logged the same call. It printed the message, then the exception and its stack trace:

WARN cf.Slf4jRunTest -- Dependency stock is unavailable
java.lang.IllegalStateException: connection refused
	at cf.Slf4jRunTest.run(Slf4jRunTest.java:9)

C# passes the exception first, as its own parameter. SLF4J takes it last. A Java message template has no names, so the JSON line has no Dependency member. The value is only in the message text. A .NET run of the C# pane kept it as a member of "State".

The same class has a handler for every other exception. It calls log.error("Unexpected error", ex), so the stack trace is in the log. The 500 response holds a traceId, but never the exception's message. The test OrderControllerTest.anUnexpectedErrorIsA500WithoutItsMessage checks that the body does not contain the message. For the rules, see the section What a problem never contains.

The local profile raises the level for the shop's own code:

logging:
  level:
    com.acme: DEBUG

The setting logging.level.com.acme applies to the package com.acme and every package below it. So the platform and the service both log at DEBUG on a developer's machine. Other environments do not set it.

JSON logs, switched on by the platformtwist#

In production, a log collector reads each service's console output. It can search a field such as orderId only if each line is JSON. Boot writes JSON itself with one setting, logging.structured.format.console. The platform sets it for every service, unless the service switches it off:

if (environment.getProperty("platform.logging.structured", Boolean.class, true)) {
    environment.getPropertySources().addLast(new MapPropertySource("platform-defaults:structured-logging",
            Map.of("logging.structured.format.console", "ecs")));
}
Reading the code
environment.getProperty("platform.logging.structured", Boolean.class, true)

This line reads the platform's own setting. Its default is true, so a service that says nothing gets JSON logs.

addLast(new MapPropertySource("platform-defaults:structured-logging",

The setting is added last, with the lowest precedence. So a service can still set logging.structured.format.console to another format in its application.yml.

Map.of("logging.structured.format.console", "ecs")));

ecs stands for the Elastic Common Schema (ECS). It is one of the three JSON formats that Boot writes.

A class that Spring Boot calls before the application starts, and before logging starts, is called an environment post-processor. This code runs in one. A properties file cannot say "only if another setting is true", so this one default is code. For how the platform adds its other defaults, see the chapter Configuration in depth.

The platform's setting is bound to a small class, so it appears in the IDE's completion:

@ConfigurationProperties("platform.logging")
public class PlatformLoggingProperties {

    /** Write JSON (ECS) logs. Set it to false locally for readable console logs. */
    private boolean structured = true;

    /** Path variables to copy into the MDC for each request, such as {@code orderId}. */
    private List<String> mdcPathVariables = new ArrayList<>();

The field structured starts as true, so JSON is the default. The list mdcPathVariables names the path variables that go into the mapped diagnostic context (MDC). An interceptor copies them there, as the section Path variables in the MDC, with an interceptor shows.

The local profile and the tests switch JSON off. A developer then reads plain lines on the console:

platform:
  logging:
    structured: false          # readable console logs

With structured: false, the post-processor adds nothing, and Boot writes its plain-text format.

The test PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessorTest checks both cases. With no setting, logging.structured.format.console is ecs. With platform.logging.structured=false, it is not set at all.

A run for this book logged one line in each of Boot's three formats. Here is the ECS line of a request that put orderId into the logging context:

{"@timestamp":"2026-10-25T19:46:49.460581Z","log":{"level":"INFO","logger":"rw.logging.LogWebMain"},
 "process":{"pid":77217,"thread":{"name":"http-nio-auto-1-exec-1"}},
 "service":{"name":"order-service","node":{}},
 "message":"Handling order 42 (MDC traceId=4acdfe93505af32476c1dc16458821e3)",
 "traceId":"4acdfe93505af32476c1dc16458821e3","spanId":"898fa9e5bedf816f","orderId":"42",
 "ecs":{"version":"8.11"}}
Reading the code
"service":{"name":"order-service","node":{}},

ECS takes the service name from spring.application.name. So the collector can tell the services apart.

"traceId":"4acdfe93505af32476c1dc16458821e3","spanId":"898fa9e5bedf816f","orderId":"42",

Every value in the logging context becomes a member at the top level. The trace ID is written as traceId, its name in the context, not as ECS's own name trace.id.

The three formats differ in their member names:

FormatA context value orderId=42 appears asService name
ecs"orderId":"42" at the top level"service":{"name":"order-service"}
logstash"orderId":"42" at the top levelnot written
gelf"_orderId":"42", with an underscore before each extra member"host":"order-service"

Boot can change the members with settings. In the run, each of these worked:

SettingEffect in the run
logging.structured.json.exclude=log.logger,ecs.versionremoved the members, but left empty objects such as "ecs":{}
logging.structured.json.rename.orderId=order.idwrote "order.id":"42"
logging.structured.json.customizer=a class nameran code that adds or changes members, as the platform's masking does

In ASP.NET Core, a service calls AddJsonConsole() in Program.cs. With IncludeScopes = true, the scope values appear in a "Scopes" array. In Spring Boot, the service writes no code for it. The context values are members at the top level of the line.

The MDC: values for every line of one threadtwist#

Every log line about an order should carry its ID. Passing the ID into every log call would be easy to forget. So Java logging keeps a map of values for the current thread. This map is called the mapped diagnostic context (MDC). Each log line includes what the map holds when the line is written.

The MDC has three methods that matter. The audit log uses one of them to read the trace ID:

String traceId = MDC.get(ProblemDetails.TRACE_ID);
if (traceId != null) {
    entry.append("traceId", traceId);
}

MDC.get returns null when the thread has no trace ID, so the audit entry then has no traceId field.

CallWhat it does
MDC.put("orderId", id)adds a value for the current thread, until code removes it
MDC.get("orderId")reads the value, or returns null
MDC.remove("orderId")removes the value

MDC.put is like logger.BeginScope in C#, but it returns nothing to dispose.

MDC is in the package org.slf4j. Logback stores the map in a ThreadLocal, so each thread has its own map. A run showed that the class behind it is ch.qos.logback.classic.util.LogbackMDCAdapter.

A value stays until code removes it. Spring reuses each request thread for many requests. So a value that nobody removes appears in the lines of the next request on that thread, which may be about another order. Every piece of code that puts a value must remove it. The next three sections show how the platform does that in each case.

Path variables in the MDC, with an interceptornew#

Support staff search the logs for one order. Most requests name the order in the URL, as in POST /orders/{orderId}/ship. The platform copies such values into the MDC once, for every controller. A Spring model-view-controller (MVC) interceptor does this. An object whose methods Spring MVC calls before and after a controller method is called an interceptor.

The platform's interceptor is PathVariableMdcInterceptor. Its method preHandle runs before the controller method. It reads the path variables of the request, and puts each configured name into the MDC with MDC.put. Its method afterCompletion runs at the end of the request, also after an exception. It removes the same names, so the thread is clean for the next request.

For the code of the interceptor, its callbacks, and how the platform registers it with Spring MVC, see the section The MDC interceptor. The registration needs no code in the service.

The service names its variables in one setting:

platform:
  logging:
    # Added to every log line of a request, next to traceId
    mdc-path-variables: orderId, lineId, noteId

The value of mdc-path-variables is a list separated by commas. It binds to a List<String> in PlatformLoggingProperties, and the spaces are trimmed. The names must match the names in the controllers' paths, such as {orderId}.

The interceptor reads the path variables from a request attribute that Spring MVC fills. The attribute's value depends on the request. A run for this book recorded three cases:

The requestThe attribute in preHandleWhat reaches the MDC
a path with variables, such as GET /orders/42a map, {orderId=42}orderId=42
a path with no variables, such as POST /ordersan empty mapnothing
a path with no controller, a 404null, because the handler for static files took the requestnothing

The null attribute is harmless. The interceptor tests the attribute with instanceof, and that test is false for null. So the log lines of a 404 simply have no orderId.

Other requests skip some of the callbacks. For every case that the runs recorded, see the section What an interceptor sees when a request fails. One more case matters for the MDC. It is a 405, and it is the case to understand.

PredictA 405 for a path with an orderId#
The interceptor above is registered. A client sends DELETE /orders/42, but the path allows only GET. Spring MVC answers 405. Does a line that is logged while Spring MVC handles this request carry orderId=42?
@Override
public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler) {
    if (request.getAttribute(HandlerMapping.URI_TEMPLATE_VARIABLES_ATTRIBUTE) instanceof Map<?, ?> variables) {
        for (String name : names) {
            if (variables.get(name) instanceof String value) {
                MDC.put(name, value);
            }
        }
    }
    return true;
}
Show the answer
No. For a 405, no method of the interceptor runs at all.

Spring MVC rejects a wrong HTTP method while it looks for the controller method. An interceptor belongs to a matched controller method. A request with the wrong method matches none. So Spring MVC throws HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException before any interceptor runs. A run recorded only the filter and the exception handler for the 405.

A value that every request needs belongs in a servlet filter. A filter runs for every request, before Spring MVC.

The platform accepts this gap. A path variable exists only after a match, so the 405 cannot know it anyway. The trace ID is different, because every request needs it. The tracing setup puts it into the MDC without the interceptor. A run for this book sent the same 405 to an application with the OpenTelemetry starter. The exception handler for the 405 found a traceId in the MDC.

A servlet filter sees every request, also a 405. It runs before Spring MVC and again after it, so it also sees the final status after the advice wrote the problem. The order service needs no other value for every request, so it has no filter of its own. If a service needs one, such as a tenant ID from a header, write a servlet filter. For filters and the request path, see the section One request through Spring MVC.

The platform's interceptor ignores the parameter ex of afterCompletion, and removes its values in every case. That is on purpose. An exception that an advice handled reaches afterCompletion as null. For the prediction about it, see the section What an interceptor sees when a request fails.

The test PathVariableMdcInterceptorTest needs no Spring. It sets the attribute on a MockHttpServletRequest itself, and checks three things. Only the configured names are copied. The values are removed when the request completes, even with an exception. And a request without path variables adds nothing.

In ASP.NET Core, a middleware can read context.Request.RouteValues["orderId"] and open a logging scope with ILogger.BeginScope. A scope ends when it is disposed. The MDC has no scope object. The interceptor must remove its values itself. In Spring, the interceptor is the place where the matched path variables are known. Scopes and the MDC also differ for nested values and for other threads. See the sections The log context for message handlers and The MDC does not follow work to other threads.

The log context for message handlersnew#

A payment arrives from a queue. No HTTP request and no interceptor take part. The handler's lines still need the order ID and the event ID. The platform has a small class for this, LogContext. It puts values into the MDC for one block of code, and puts the MDC back as it was:

public final class LogContext implements AutoCloseable {

    private final Map<String, String> previous = new HashMap<>();

    private LogContext(Map<String, String> entries) {
        entries.forEach((key, value) -> {
            if (value != null) {
                previous.put(key, MDC.get(key));
                MDC.put(key, value);
            }
        });
    }

    /** Adds the entries to the MDC until {@link #close()}. */
    public static LogContext with(Map<String, String> entries) {
        return new LogContext(Objects.requireNonNull(entries, "entries"));
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        previous.forEach((key, earlierValue) -> {
            if (earlierValue == null) {
                MDC.remove(key);
            } else {
                MDC.put(key, earlierValue);
            }
        });
    }
}
Reading the code
public final class LogContext implements AutoCloseable {

AutoCloseable does the same as IDisposable in C#. Its one method is close().

if (value != null) {

A null value is left out. So a missing ID never makes the caller fail.

previous.put(key, MDC.get(key));

Before it puts a value, the class remembers the value that the key had. That is null when the key had none.

MDC.put(key, earlierValue);

On close, a key that had a value gets that value back. A key that had none is removed.

The class is used with a try-with-resources block. That block is the Java form of a using block. It calls close() at the end, also after an exception. The platform's base class for message listeners opens one around every event:

protected final void process(T event) {
    Map<String, String> context = new HashMap<>(logContext(event));
    context.put("eventId", event.eventId());
    SecurityContext callerContext = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
    SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();
    try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.with(context)) {
        inbox.process(consumer, event, this::handle);
    } finally {
        SecurityContextHolder.setContext(callerContext);
    }
}
Reading the code
Map<String, String> context = new HashMap<>(logContext(event));

logContext is a method that a listener may override, to add its business IDs.

try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.with(context)) {

The variable is called ignored, because the block only needs its close(). Every line that the inbox and the handler write carries the IDs.

SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();

The same method also runs the handler as the system actor. See the section Messages and jobs: the system actor.

The payment listener adds the order ID:

protected Map<String, String> logContext(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    return Map.of("orderId", event.orderId());
}

So a payment's log lines carry eventId and orderId, as a request's lines carry orderId. Support staff search one field, whatever started the work.

Nested blocks with the same key work as nested scopes do in C#:

C#
using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["eventId"] = "outer" }))
{
    using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["eventId"] = "inner" }))
    {
        log.LogInformation("Inner scope");
    }
    log.LogInformation("After inner scope");   // the scope holds only "outer"
}
Java 25
try (LogContext outer = LogContext.with(Map.of("eventId", "outer"))) {
    try (LogContext inner = LogContext.with(Map.of("eventId", "inner"))) {
        assertThat(MDC.get("eventId")).isEqualTo("inner");
    }
    assertThat(MDC.get("eventId")).isEqualTo("outer");
}
assertThat(MDC.get("eventId")).isNull();

The Java pane is the test LogContextTest.restoresTheOuterValueOfANestedBlock. After the inner block, MDC.get("eventId") is outer again, as the scope in C# holds only outer again. The two languages behave differently inside the inner block. A .NET run with AddJsonConsole(IncludeScopes = true) wrote both values in the "Scopes" array of the inner line, because scopes stack. The MDC holds one value for each key, so the inner block replaces the outer value until it closes.

Gotcha

SLF4J's own MDC.putCloseable loses the outer value. SLF4J has a method that returns a closeable value. A run nested it with the same key, as orderId=outer and then inner. After the inner one closed, orderId was null, not outer. Its close() only removes the key. The outer code then logs without the order ID, and nothing warns you. Use a helper that remembers the earlier value, as LogContext does.

Put only IDs into the MDC. Every line repeats each value, and logs are copied to many places. A name or an e-mail address there would be in every line of the request. The section Personal data in logs shows the other defences.

The MDC does not follow work to other threadstrap#

In ASP.NET Core, a log scope flows with the ExecutionContext. A .NET run for this book logged inside Task.Run and on a new Thread. Both lines still had the scope's orderId:

using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["orderId"] = "42" }))
{
    await Task.Run(() => log.LogInformation("On a thread-pool thread"));   // has orderId
    var t = new Thread(() => log.LogInformation("On a new thread")); t.Start(); t.Join();   // has orderId
}

The comments after Task.Run and the new thread say what the run printed. The MDC belongs to one thread, so it does the opposite. A Java run put orderId=42 on the calling thread, and then read it elsewhere:

Where the code ranWhat MDC.get("orderId") returned
the calling thread42
a new virtual threadnull
a task on a thread poolnull
a virtual thread that first called MDC.setContextMap(copy)42

So a line written on another thread has no order ID, and no other value of the MDC. The fix is a copy. The caller takes MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(), and the task calls MDC.setContextMap(copy) before it logs. The task must also clear the map at its end, or the pool thread keeps the values for its next task.

This is the same rule as for the caller's identity. For the measured cases with a wrapper, see the section The caller does not follow work to other threads. The order service starts no threads in its use cases, so it needs no copy. Spring Modulith runs the metrics listener on another thread. Its lines carry no order ID, and it writes none.

Personal data in logsnew#

A developer writes log.info("Placing an order for {}", contact) while tracking a problem. The log now holds a customer's name and e-mail address. Logs are kept for weeks, copied to a log service, and read by many people. So personal data must not reach them.

Java and C# records behave alike here. Each one prints every component by default. A run printed the same record in both languages:

LanguageWhat printing the record wrote
C#CustomerContact { Name = Jo Bloggs, Email = jo@example.com }
JavaCustomerContact[name=Jo Bloggs, email=jo@example.com]

The first defence is in the value object itself. CustomerContact overrides toString():

public record CustomerContact(String name, String email) implements ValueObject {
    // ...
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "CustomerContact[masked]";
    }
}

So logging a contact by mistake prints CustomerContact[masked]. The Note entity does the same in another way. Its toString() prints the note's ID, the order's ID and the length of the text, but not the text. Views and integration events leave the customer out completely.

The second defence is a safety net in the JSON writer. Boot lets a class change the members of each structured log line. The platform's class masks personal data:

public class PersonalDataMaskingCustomizer implements StructuredLoggingJsonMembersCustomizer<Object> {

    /** Member names whose values are always personal data. */
    static final Set<String> PERSONAL_FIELDS = Set.of("email", "phone", "address", "customerName");

    private static final Pattern EMAIL = Pattern.compile("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+(\\.[\\w-]+)+");
    private static final Pattern LONG_NUMBER = Pattern.compile("\\d[\\d -]{7,}\\d");

    @Override
    public void customize(JsonWriter.Members<Object> members) {
        members.applyingValueProcessor(JsonWriter.ValueProcessor.of(String.class, value -> "[masked]")
                .whenHasPath(path -> PERSONAL_FIELDS.contains(path.name())));
        members.applyingValueProcessor(JsonWriter.ValueProcessor.of(String.class, PersonalDataMaskingCustomizer::mask)
                .whenHasPath("message"));
    }
Reading the code
implements StructuredLoggingJsonMembersCustomizer<Object> {

Boot calls a class of this interface when it builds the JSON writer for the log lines. The class can add, remove or change members.

members.applyingValueProcessor(JsonWriter.ValueProcessor.of(String.class, value -> "[masked]")

A value processor changes a value just before it is written. This one replaces any string with [masked].

.whenHasPath(path -> PERSONAL_FIELDS.contains(path.name())));

The first processor applies only to members with a personal name, such as email. Such members appear when code puts them into the MDC.

.whenHasPath("message"));

The second processor applies to the message text. Its mask method replaces e-mail addresses with [email]. It replaces long numbers, such as a phone number, with [number]. A long number is a run of at least nine digits, spaces and dashes that starts and ends with a digit.

One line of the platform's defaults switches it on for every service:

# Mask personal data in JSON logs (a safety net; see the class).
logging.structured.json.customizer=com.acme.platform.core.logging.PersonalDataMaskingCustomizer

The setting logging.structured.json.customizer names the class, and Boot creates it when logging starts.

The test PersonalDataMaskingCustomizerTest builds a JSON writer shaped like a log line. The message "Contact jo.bloggs@example.com on 07700 900123 about order 42" becomes "Contact [email] on [number] about order 42". A member email becomes "[masked]", and other members stay as they are.

Gotcha

A value processor without a path condition masks every string. A research run added a processor with no whenHasPath. It masked the service name too, so the line said "service":{"name":"***"}. Always limit a processor to the members it is meant for.

The net has holes, and the platform's class says so. It cannot recognise a name or a street address inside a message. It works only for the JSON formats, so the readable local console is not masked. So the main defence stays in the code. Value objects with personal data override toString(), and code never logs a whole request body.

Tracing with the OpenTelemetry starternew#

An order is placed. The order service calls the stock service, which calls the warehouse. One of the three is slow. Each service has its own logs, so the engineer needs one ID that all three share. That ID is called the trace ID. Each service's part of the work is called a span, and has a span ID.

The starter spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry does this with no code. It brings Micrometer Tracing and the OpenTelemetry libraries. Each incoming request gets a trace ID, or keeps the one that the caller sent. The IDs go into the MDC, so every log line carries them. Outgoing calls through Boot's HTTP clients pass them on in the W3C traceparent header.

In ASP.NET Core, the service writes the setup itself:

builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .WithTracing(tracing => tracing
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter());

The calls AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation() and AddOtlpExporter() choose what is traced and where it goes. In the order service, no line of code mentions tracing. The platform's defaults set one value:

# Tracing. Every request gets a traceId in the MDC, even when it is not sampled.
# Lower the sampling rate in production if volumes are high.
management.tracing.sampling.probability=1.0

The setting management.tracing.sampling.probability is a share from 0 to 1. Sampling decides which traces are recorded and sent to a tracing system. Boot's default is 0.1, so it samples 10% of requests. The platform samples every request. The default sampler is named parent-based-trace-id-ratio. Its name says that it follows the decision of the caller, when the caller sent one.

A trace ID exists even when the trace is not sampled. A run with the default 0.1 read MDC.get("traceId") in a controller, and got the trace ID. The plain-text log line carried it too, in brackets with the span ID. So every log line and every problem response has a traceId, whatever the sampling rate:

INFO 77203 --- [o-auto-1-exec-1] [60a2b527bd6d398c29ef021abb69176e-351506590893af3a] rw.logging.LogWebMain : Handling order 42

The first part, 60a2b527bd6d398c29ef021abb69176e, is the trace ID. The part after the dash is the span ID. Only the outgoing traceparent header shows whether the trace is sampled. It ended in -02 with the default sampling, and in -03 with sampling 1.0. The last bit of that flag says "sampled".

The platform's problem responses read the same MDC value:

/** The MDC key under which Micrometer Tracing stores the current trace ID. */
public static final String TRACE_ID = "traceId";

ProblemDetails reads the MDC value under TRACE_ID, and adds the value to every problem response. A caller who gets an error quotes this ID to support. Support finds every line of the request, in every service it reached. For the problem format, see the chapter The web layer in depth.

Pragmatic choice: Every request is sampled

The strict rule. Sample a fraction of the requests, as Boot does by default, so the tracing system stores and costs less.

What we do. The platform sets management.tracing.sampling.probability to 1.0, so every request is traced once an export is configured.

Why. A shop service handles a modest number of requests. A support case starts from one traceId, and an engineer wants the whole trace for that request, not a 10% chance of it.

When to stop. Stop when the tracing system's storage or bill grows with the traffic. Then lower the rate per service in its application.yml. The log lines keep their trace IDs at any rate.

Where traces and metrics go: off until an endpoint is settrap#

Traces and metrics leave the service through the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP). A collector receives them and forwards them to a tracing system. The trace export needs the setting management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint. It has no default, so no trace leaves the service until a deployment sets it. A run without it logged no errors.

The metrics export behaves differently:

PredictThe OpenTelemetry starter with no collector#
A Boot 4.1 service adds this starter and sets no OTLP setting. No collector runs. Does anything about metrics appear in its log?
<!-- Tracing: trace and span IDs in every log line, passed on with every HTTP call -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry</artifactId>
</dependency>
Show the answer
Yes. It logs "Publishing metrics for OtlpMeterRegistry every 1m to http://localhost:4318/v1/metrics", and later a WARN "Failed to publish metrics to OTLP receiver", with "Connection refused".

The starter also brings the OTLP metrics registry, and switches it on. The setting management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled is true by default. With no URL set, the registry pushes to a collector on localhost:4318. In a container, nothing listens there, so every push fails with a warning.

Switch the export off until a real collector exists, as the platform does.

The platform switches the metrics export off, and says how to switch it on:

# Traces are exported only when management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint is set.
# Metrics would be exported to localhost:4318 by default, so they are off until a service
# sets management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled=true and management.otlp.metrics.export.url.
management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled=false

With management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled=false, nothing is pushed. So locally and in tests, no warning appears. A deployment that runs a collector sets the two endpoints as environment variables. The metrics still exist inside the service, so a test can read them. See the section Business metrics.

Note

The Boot 3 key for the trace endpoint was management.otlp.tracing.endpoint. Boot 4.0 deprecated it at level error, so the old name no longer works. The new key is management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint. Logs have an exporter of their own, management.opentelemetry.logging.export.otlp.endpoint, which the service does not use. Its logs go to the console, where a log collector reads them.

The trace follows only the injected client buildertrap#

The trace ID must travel with every call to another service. Boot adds the traceparent header through the RestClient.Builder bean that it creates. A client built in any other way sends no header. A run for this book compared three ways to build a client:

How the client was builttraceparent sentTrace in the called service
from Boot's injected RestClient.Builder00-7d38...1265-5a72...dd38-02the same trace ID as the caller
RestClient.create(base)nonea new trace ID
the static RestClient.builder()nonea new trace ID

In the end-to-end run, a request with trace 94d3...b992 called itself twice. The call through the static builder started the new trace 5daa...705b. The call through Boot's builder kept 94d3...b992. Nothing failed, and nothing warned. The link between the two services was simply gone.

So the platform builds every client from the injected builder. Its client factory asks the container for a new builder each time:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
HttpClientFactory httpClientFactory(ObjectProvider<RestClient.Builder> restClientBuilders,
                                    ObjectProvider<ClientRegistrationRepository> registrations,
                                    ObjectProvider<OAuth2AuthorizedClientService> authorizedClients) {

The parameter ObjectProvider<RestClient.Builder> lets the factory ask for a builder whenever it builds a client. The builder bean has the scope prototype, so each request for it returns a new builder. For the client factory and the stock client, see the chapter Calling other services.

A C# developer does not expect this trap. A .NET 10 run with only the ASP.NET Core tracing instrumentation called a second endpoint with new HttpClient(). The request carried a traceparent header, and the called endpoint saw the same trace ID. In Spring, the way a client is built decides whether the trace continues.

Business metricstwist#

Boot already records HTTP, client and MongoDB metrics. The business also wants to know how many orders are placed, shipped and cancelled. The service counts them with a listener for its domain events:

@Component
class OrderMetrics {

    private final Counter placed;
    private final Counter shipped;
    private final Counter cancelled;

    OrderMetrics(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.placed = registry.counter("shop.orders", "event", "placed");
        this.shipped = registry.counter("shop.orders", "event", "shipped");
        this.cancelled = registry.counter("shop.orders", "event", "cancelled");
    }

    @ApplicationModuleListener
    void on(OrderPlaced event) {
        placed.increment();
    }
Reading the code
registry.counter("shop.orders", "event", "placed");

One metric named shop.orders, with a tag event. Each tag value is its own series. The tag has three values, so the number of series stays small.

@ApplicationModuleListener

This Spring Modulith annotation makes the method a listener that runs after the transaction commits, on another thread. So an order that was rolled back is never counted.

For counters and tags in general, see the section Metrics. Spring Modulith stores each delivery to the listener in the outbox, and retries it. For more, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox. The journey test reads the counter at the end of an order's life:

assertThat(meters.counter("shop.orders", "event", "shipped").count()).isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(1);

The test checks isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(1), because other tests of the same run also ship orders.

The counters exist inside the service. To reach a monitoring system, a registry must export them. Boot 4.1.2 has export registries for Prometheus, OTLP, Datadog and many others, but none for Amazon CloudWatch. CloudWatch export comes from Spring Cloud AWS, as of October 2026:

NeedArtifactNote
the auto-configurationio.awspring.cloud:spring-cloud-aws-starter-metricslatest 4.2.0, and the service uses Spring Cloud AWS 4.1.0
the registry itselfio.micrometer:micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2the Micrometer registry that writes to CloudWatch

The service adds no registry. Its README says that export stays off until a deployment sets an OTLP endpoint, or adds the CloudWatch registry. So nothing is exported locally or in tests, and the counters are still there for the test.

The health probes: liveness without the databasetwist#

The orchestrator asks each instance two questions. Is the process alive, or should it be restarted? Is it ready for traffic, or should requests go elsewhere? Actuator answers at two paths, /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness.

The database is down for five minutes. If liveness included the database, every instance would report "not alive". The orchestrator would restart all of them, again and again. The restarts fix nothing, because the database is still down. So liveness must not depend on any other system. Readiness does include the database. While it is down, no traffic is sent, and the instances keep running until it returns.

The platform's mongo defaults add the database to readiness:

C#
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck("mongo", () => HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy("database down"), tags: ["ready"]);

app.MapHealthChecks("/health/live", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = _ => false });
app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = check => check.Tags.Contains("ready") });
mongo.properties
# The service is ready for traffic only when the database is reachable.
# Liveness deliberately leaves the database out: a database outage must not restart every instance.
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,mongo
Reading the code
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,mongo

A health group is a named set of health checks. This line puts two checks into the readiness group. readinessState is the readiness state that Boot keeps for the application. mongo is the health check that Boot provides for MongoDB.

Predicate = _ => false

In ASP.NET Core, liveness runs no check at all. A .NET run added an unhealthy mongo check. The path /health/live answered 200 Healthy. The path /health/ready answered 503 Unhealthy.

Boot also keeps other checks out of its two probes. By default, it puts no other health indicator into the two groups. A run with a failing check named stock measured two cases:

Setting/actuator/healthlivenessreadiness
none503 DOWN200 UP200 UP
readiness.include=readinessState,stock503 DOWN200 UP503 DOWN

So without the platform's line, readiness would stay UP while the database is down. The orchestrator would keep sending requests that all fail. The service's README states the result for each dependency. When DocumentDB is down, readiness is DOWN, and liveness stays UP.

The core defaults choose what is reachable:

# Health probes for the orchestrator (a Boot default, restated):
#   /actuator/health/liveness  - is the process alive? Never include other services or the database.
#   /actuator/health/readiness - can it take traffic? The mongo defaults add the database.
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=never
Reading the code
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true

This adds the two probe paths. It is already the default in Boot 4.1.

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info

Only these two endpoints are reachable over HTTP. Boot's default is health alone, so the platform adds info.

management.endpoint.health.show-details=never

The answer says only UP or DOWN, with no details of the checks. This is also the default of Boot.

Two of the three lines restate a default of Boot 4.1. The file's own comment gives the reason. The behaviour of every service is visible in one file. And a Boot upgrade that changes a default cannot change the platform's behaviour.

The probes need no token. The platform's security chain lets /actuator/health/** and /actuator/info through, as the section The platform's filter chain shows. The journey test checks this. A request to /orders without a token gets 401, and both probes answer 200, with readiness UP.

The service's own docker-compose.yml uses readiness as the container's health check:

healthcheck:
  # The image has no curl, so bash opens the TCP connection itself. "Ready" means the database is reachable.
  test: ["CMD", "bash", "-c", "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/localhost/8080 && printf 'GET /actuator/health/readiness HTTP/1.0\\r\\n\\r\\n' >&3 && grep -q UP <&3"]
  interval: 10s
  retries: 12
Reading the code
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/localhost/8080

Bash treats the path /dev/tcp/host/port as a network connection. This line opens one as file descriptor 3, for reading and writing.

printf 'GET /actuator/health/readiness HTTP/1.0\\r\\n\\r\\n' >&3

The command writes a minimal HTTP request to the connection.

grep -q UP <&3

grep reads the answer and succeeds only if it contains UP.

The image has no curl, and a smaller image has fewer tools to patch. For the startup probe that allows for the migration lock, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

Graceful shutdowntwist#

A deployment stops an old instance while it still handles requests. Graceful shutdown lets those requests finish first:

C#
builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o => o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(20));
core.properties
# Finish the requests in flight when the service is stopped (graceful is a Boot default, restated).
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s

Graceful shutdown is the default in Boot 4.1, with all three embedded web servers. The value server.shutdown=immediate turns it off. So the line server.shutdown=graceful restates the default. The line spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s is a real change. Boot waits at most 30 seconds by default, and the platform waits 20. A .NET run printed the default of HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, which is also 30 seconds.

Every run for this book logged two lines when it stopped:

INFO o.s.boot.tomcat.GracefulShutdown : Commencing graceful shutdown. Waiting for active requests to complete
INFO o.s.boot.tomcat.GracefulShutdown : Graceful shutdown complete

GracefulShutdown is the class in Boot that waits for Tomcat's requests. Keep the wait shorter than the time the orchestrator allows before it kills the process. Otherwise the process is killed in the middle of the wait.

The audit log: a business record, not a log linenew#

An order was cancelled, and the customer says they did not do it. The business needs to know who cancelled it, and when. A log line is the wrong place for that answer. Logs are kept for weeks, can be sampled or lost, and may say that something happened when the transaction then rolled back. So the service keeps an audit log. It is a collection in the database, written in the same transaction as the change.

The platform defines the audit log as one small interface:

/**
 * Records who did what to which resource. This is a business record for support and audit,
 * not a log line, so it is stored in the database in the same transaction as the change.
 *
 * <p>Never put personal data in the action or the resource ID.
 */
public interface AuditLog {
    // ...
    void record(String action, String resourceType, String resourceId);
}

The method record takes three strings. The caller names only what happened, and to which resource. The implementation adds who acted, when, and the trace ID. Each record in the collection audit_log has six fields:

FieldWhere it comes fromExample
actionthe use caseORDER_SHIPPED
resourceTypethe use caseorder
resourceIdthe use casethe order's ID
actorCurrentActor, the token's subject or systemagent-1
atthe Clock beanthe time of the change
traceIdthe MDC, when tracing has onethe request's trace ID

For the code that writes the record, and for where the actor comes from, see the section The current actor, and the audit record. The record is written with MongoTemplate, which joins the transaction that runs on the thread. So the record is stored only if the change is stored. For transactions, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

The platform provides the storage as an auto-configuration that a service can replace:

@AutoConfiguration(after = PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)
public class PlatformMongoAuditAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(AuditLog.class)
    MongoAuditLog auditLog(MongoTemplate mongo, CurrentActor currentActor, Clock clock) {
        return new MongoAuditLog(mongo, currentActor, clock);
    }

    @Bean
    AuditLogIndexes auditLogIndexes() {
        return new AuditLogIndexes();
    }

    /** A use case writes its audit record inside its transaction. See {@link CreateCollections}. */
    @Bean
    CreateCollections auditLogCollection() {
        return new CreateCollections("P000-audit-log-collection", List.of("audit_log"));
    }
}
Reading the code
@AutoConfiguration(after = PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)

This class is processed after the platform's MongoDB setup, which creates the transaction manager and the template that it needs.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean(AuditLog.class)

A service that defines its own AuditLog bean replaces this one. For example, a service could send its records to a central audit service.

AuditLogIndexes auditLogIndexes() {

A migration creates an index on the type, the ID and the time, to find the history of one resource quickly. For migrations, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

CreateCollections auditLogCollection() {

A second migration creates the collection audit_log itself, before any use case writes a record inside its transaction. Amazon DocumentDB cannot create a collection inside a transaction. For that limit, see the section The limits of a transaction on Amazon DocumentDB.

The action names are constants in one class, so they stay the same everywhere and a search finds them:

public final class AuditActions {

    public static final String ORDER = "order";
    public static final String NOTE = "note";

    public static final String ORDER_PLACED = "ORDER_PLACED";
    public static final String LINE_PICKED = "LINE_PICKED";
    public static final String ORDER_SHIPPED = "ORDER_SHIPPED";
    public static final String ORDER_CANCELLED = "ORDER_CANCELLED";
    public static final String PAYMENT_RECORDED = "PAYMENT_RECORDED";
    public static final String NOTE_ADDED = "NOTE_ADDED";
    public static final String NOTE_ACTION_RESOLVED = "NOTE_ACTION_RESOLVED";

A use case passes AuditActions.ORDER and a constant such as ORDER_PLACED, never a string typed in place.

The audit is the last step of every change. Each use case loads the aggregate, lets the domain apply its rules, saves it, publishes its events, and records the audit. The order feature does the last three steps in one private method:

private Order saveAndPublish(Order order, String auditAction) {
    List<DomainEvent> raised = order.pullEvents();
    Order saved = orders.save(order);
    events.publish(raised);
    audit.record(auditAction, AuditActions.ORDER, saved.id().value());
    return saved;
}

Every caller of saveAndPublish runs inside a transaction. So the order, its events in the outbox and its audit record are stored together, or not at all. NoteService has the same method for notes. For the steps of a use case, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

The journey test checks the notes' records too:

assertThat(mongo.find(query(where("resourceId").is(noteId)), Document.class, "audit_log"))
        .extracting(entry -> entry.getString("action")).containsExactly("NOTE_ADDED", "NOTE_ACTION_RESOLVED");

A note gets NOTE_ADDED when it is added, and NOTE_ACTION_RESOLVED when its action is resolved. The same test checks the order's records and their actors. The agent appears for each change, and system for the payment, which came from a queue.

Keep personal data out of the action and the resource ID. The audit log keeps its records as long as the data, and longer than any log. The actor is the token's subject, which is an ID at the issuer, not a name.

ASP.NET Core with Entity Framework Core uses the same design. The code adds an audit row to the same DbContext before it calls SaveChangesAsync(). The EF Core documentation says that all changes in one call of SaveChanges are applied in one transaction, when the database supports transactions. The idea is the same in both. The audit record is data, and it commits with the change it describes.

Seeing what the stubs did, locallytwist#

Locally, WireMock replaces the stock service. When a call fails, a developer needs to see which stub answered. The local environment starts WireMock with --verbose:

wiremock:
  image: wiremock/wiremock:3.13.0
  command: ["--global-response-templating", "--verbose"]

A run of WireMock 3.13.2 for this book compared the two modes. The local environment pins 3.13.0. Without --verbose, WireMock logged only a request that no stub matched, with a table of the closest stub. With --verbose, it also logged every request, the stub that matched it, and the response, with the header Matched-Stub-Id. Use it locally only. For the local environment, see the chapter Running locally and shipping.

Check yourself
1
The platform samples every request, but a team lowers the sampling rate to 0.1. Do the log lines of an unsampled request still carry a traceId?
Yes. The trace ID is put into the MDC for every request, sampled or not, so the log lines and the problem responses carry it. Sampling decides only whether the trace is exported. The traceparent header shows it in its last flag, -02 for not sampled and -03 for sampled.
2
An expert asksWhy does the order service's liveness probe leave out the database, while its readiness probe includes it?
A failed liveness probe makes the orchestrator restart the instance. If liveness included the database, a database outage would restart every instance, and the restarts would fix nothing. Readiness only stops traffic. So during an outage, no requests arrive, and the instances keep running until the database is back.
3
An expert asksWhy is the audit record written to the database in the use case's transaction, and not as a log line?
The audit answers who changed what, and the business needs that answer for as long as the data exists. Logs are kept for weeks and can be lost. A log line can also say that a change happened when the transaction then rolled back. A record in the same transaction exists exactly when the change exists.
4
TranslateWrite this C# in the order service's platform, for a message handler that runs the inbox with the event's ID in every log line: 
var scope = new Dictionary<string, object> { ["eventId"] = message.EventId };
using (logger.BeginScope(scope))
{
    inbox.Process(consumer, message, Handle);
}
Map<String, String> context = new HashMap<>(logContext(event));
context.put("eventId", event.eventId());
// ...
try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.with(context)) {
    inbox.process(consumer, event, this::handle);
} finally {
    SecurityContextHolder.setContext(callerContext);
}

The finally block restores the security context, which the C# code does not touch. LogContext is the platform's AutoCloseable. It puts the values into the MDC and restores the earlier values on close. The try-with-resources block calls close(), like the end of the using block. this::handle is a method reference to the handler.

Quick reference#

Caching and scheduling#

Running the service · Chapter 23· 19 min read· Quick reference

The order service reads the same lookup lists on almost every request, so it keeps them in memory. One annotation on the repository does that. The service also runs a job every minute, which sends again the events that were not sent. This chapter shows where the cache belongs, why it never expires, and how one lock keeps several instances from running the same job.

KindC#JavaNote
newno equivalentlookup lists read on every orderthe delivery method of each new order is checked against a list that changes only with a deployment Why
twistbuilder.Services.AddMemoryCache()@EnableCaching and spring-boot-starter-cachethe annotation switches the caching proxy on, and the starter brings the cache manager Why
twistan IMemoryCache with no size limitConcurrentMapCacheManagerwith no cache library present, Boot keeps each cache in a ConcurrentHashMap that it makes on first use Why
newcache.GetOrCreateAsync(type, ...) in a repository class@Cacheable("reference-data") on the Spring Data repository methodthe cache is a storage concern, and its callers are other beans, so every call passes the proxy Why

twistthe key passed to GetOrCreatethe method's one argumentone argument is the key itself, and two arguments make a SimpleKey of both Why
newAbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow on each entryno expiry and no evictionthe lists change only with a deployment, and a deployment restarts every instance Why
twistcache.Remove(key)@CacheEvict, or spring.cache.type=caffeine with a specan eviction reaches one instance only, so data that changes at run time needs an expiry Why
