Why the service caches its lookup listsnew#

An agent places an order with the delivery method EXPRESS. Before anything else, the service checks that EXPRESS is an active delivery method. The list of delivery methods is in the database, in the collection reference_data. Every order placement reads it, and so does every call of GET /reference-data/{type}.

The reference feature reads and checks these lists. It uses the simple level, one of the three levels of Domain-Driven Design (DDD) in this part, with no aggregate and no events. For the levels, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service. Its service has two methods:

public List<ReferenceItemView> list(String type) {
    if (!ReferenceTypes.ALL.contains(type)) {
        throw new UnknownReferenceTypeException(type);
    }
    return items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream().map(ReferenceItemView::from).toList();
}

/**
 * Throws a 400 for the field unless the code is an active value of the list.
 *
 * @param field the request field the client must correct, such as {@code deliveryMethod}
 */
public void requireActive(String type, String code, String field) {
    boolean known = items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type).stream()
            .anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());
    if (!known) {
        throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");
    }
}
Reading the code
items.findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(type)

items is the feature's Spring Data repository. Both methods call the same repository method with the type, such as DELIVERY_METHOD.

.anyMatch(item -> item.code().equals(code) && item.active());

A code passes only if it is in the list and active. An old code stays in the list, inactive, because stored orders still use it.

throw new InvalidValueException(field, "is not a known value");

The platform turns this exception into a 400 that names the field.

The lists are small, and they change only when a deployment runs a seed migration. Reading them from the database on every request costs a round trip each time, for the same answer. So the service keeps them in memory. For the seed migration, see the chapter Migrations, indexes and seed data.

Switching caching on, and the default cache managertwist#

Caching in Spring has two parts. An annotation switches the caching proxy on, and a cache manager stores the entries. The reference feature switches the proxy on in its own configuration class:

C#
builder.Services.AddMemoryCache();
Java 25
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@EnableCaching
class ReferenceConfig {
}
Reading the code
@EnableCaching

This annotation makes Spring wrap every bean that has a cache annotation in a proxy. Without it, every cache annotation does nothing. For that trap, see the section Caching.

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)

The class declares no @Bean methods, so it needs no proxy of its own. false tells Spring not to create one.

The class is in the reference package, because that feature is the only user of the cache. It is still a setting for the whole application. Any bean of the service with a cache annotation now gets a proxy.

The cache manager comes from a starter. The service's build file adds one dependency on top of the platform:

<!-- Only what this service needs on top. Test libraries come from the parent. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>

With spring-boot-starter-cache and no cache library such as Caffeine, Boot creates a ConcurrentMapCacheManager. It keeps each cache in a ConcurrentHashMap, inside the process. A run for this book listed the caches of such a manager. It made each cache on first use, by its name, with no setting. The map has no size limit and no expiry. For the reference lists, that is exactly right. The section Why the cache never expires explains why.

Where the cache goes: on the repositorynew#

The cache could go on the service or on the repository. The order service puts it on the repository method:

/**
 * Reads lookup values, and caches each list by its type.
 *
 * <p>The cache is on the repository, not on the service, for a reason. {@code @Cacheable} works
 * through a proxy around the bean, so only calls from another bean pass through it. The service
 * calls this method from two of its own methods; if the cache were on the service, the call from
 * {@code requireActive} to {@code list} would skip the proxy and the cache.
 *
 * <p>The cached list is shared by every caller, so callers must not change it.
 */
public interface ReferenceItemRepository extends MongoRepository<ReferenceItemDocument, String> {

    @Cacheable("reference-data")
    List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);
}
Reading the code
public interface ReferenceItemRepository extends MongoRepository<ReferenceItemDocument, String> {

A Spring Data repository is an interface. Spring Data writes its implementation at startup, from the method's name.

@Cacheable("reference-data")

@Cacheable names the cache. Before the method runs, the proxy looks for the argument in the cache reference-data. On a hit, the database is not read. On a miss, the method runs, and the proxy stores its result.

List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);

The name means "find by type, ordered by code, ascending". Spring Data builds the query from it.

There are two reasons for this place. Both are worth knowing, because the same choice comes back with every cache.

The cache is a storage concern. Its job is to save database reads. The service decides what the lists mean, and it should not care where they come from. With the cache on the repository, the service reads the same way with or without it. In a feature of the full style, the place would be the persistence adapter, for the same reason. The domain and the use cases never see it.

The proxy rule. @Cacheable works through a proxy around the bean. Only a call from another bean passes through the proxy. A call from a method to another method of the same object skips it. This is called self-invocation. A run for this book called a cached method twice from inside its own bean. The method loaded twice, so the cache did nothing. For the same trap with @Transactional, see the prediction in the chapter How Spring actually works.

Here, the service is the only caller of the repository, and it is another bean. So every call passes the proxy. Picture the cache on the service's list method instead. If requireActive called list, that call would skip the cache, and every order placement would read the database again.

The careful version of "cache on the service" has a real point. A cache on the service can store the views, which are already mapped. Then a hit does less work. It is safe if every caller of the cached method is another bean, and a test proves the hits. The book still recommends the repository, because the next developer who adds a call inside the service breaks the cache, and nothing fails. Put the cache on the service only when the mapping is the expensive part.

Gotcha

A field of a proxied bean reads as null. A run gave a cached bean a public field and read it through the injected bean. The injected bean was the class CacheApp$ReferenceData$$SpringCGLIB$$0, a subclass made for the proxy. The field read returned null, because nothing ever sets the proxy object's own fields. Call methods on a proxied bean, never read its fields.

The cached list is one object, shared by every caller. A caller that changed it would change it for everyone. The service never changes it. It maps each item to a new ReferenceItemView with stream().map(...).toList(), and toList() returns a list that cannot be changed.

The journey test checks the cache with the real application:

@Test
void lookupValuesAreSeededAndCached() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/reference-data/DELIVERY_METHOD").with(agent))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$[?(@.code == 'SECOND_CLASS_POST')].active").value(false));

    assertThat(caches.getCache("reference-data").get("DELIVERY_METHOD")).isNotNull();
}
Reading the code
mvc.perform(get("/reference-data/DELIVERY_METHOD").with(agent))

The request reads the delivery methods through the controller, the service and the repository.

.andExpect(jsonPath("$[?(@.code == 'SECOND_CLASS_POST')].active").value(false));

The seed data has an inactive method, and the list still contains it.

assertThat(caches.getCache("reference-data").get("DELIVERY_METHOD")).isNotNull();

caches is the CacheManager bean. The entry under the key DELIVERY_METHOD exists, so the proxy stored the list.

Cache keystwist#

The test above finds the entry under the plain string DELIVERY_METHOD. That is the default key for a method with one argument:

C#
public Task<List<ReferenceItem>?> FindByType(string type) =>
    cache.GetOrCreateAsync(type, _ => store.FindByTypeAsync(type));
Java 25
@Cacheable("reference-data")
List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);

In C#, GetOrCreateAsync takes the key as its first argument. In Spring, the proxy builds the key from the arguments. A run for this book printed the default keys:

ArgumentsThe key
one, such as "delivery"the argument itself, a java.lang.String
two, such as "delivery" and "en"SimpleKey [delivery, en]
noneSimpleKey []

A key needs a correct equals and hashCode. A string, a record and a typed ID such as OrderId all have them. The cache name separates the lists of different methods. So two methods may cache by the same type string, if their caches have different names. For keys written as expressions, see the section Cache keys, conditions and eviction.

Why the cache never expiresnew#

A cache that never expires sounds like a bug. Here it is the design. The lookup lists change in one way only. A developer adds a seed migration, and a deployment runs it. A deployment starts new instances and stops the old ones. Each new instance starts with an empty cache, and reads the new lists on first use. The class that switches caching on says so:

/**
 * Turns on Spring's caching, which the reference repository uses.
 *
 * <p>Lookup values change only when a deployment runs a seed migration, and a deployment
 * restarts every instance, which empties the cache. So the cache needs no expiry and no
 * eviction. With no cache library on the classpath, Spring Boot uses a simple in-memory map.
 */

The comment names the condition that makes this safe, in the words restarts every instance, which empties the cache. The data changes only together with a restart of every instance. There is no admin endpoint that changes a list while the service runs. The default map has no size limit, but the seed data holds nine values in two lists, so their size is fixed.

Pragmatic choice: A cache with no expiry and no size limit

The strict rule. Every cache has an expiry and a size limit, so stale data disappears and memory stays bounded. The section Choosing the cache store calls the unbounded default map a memory leak.

What we do. The reference lists stay in Boot's default map until the instance stops. No entry expires, and no code evicts one.

Why. The lists change only with a deployment, which restarts every instance. Their number and size are fixed by the seed data. An expiry would only add database reads and a library.

When to stop. Stop when anything changes the lists while the service runs, such as an admin endpoint or another service. Stop also when a cache holds data with no fixed size, such as one entry for each order. Then add an expiry and a size limit, as the next section shows.

When the data changes while the service runstwist#

Suppose the business wants to switch a delivery method off at once, without a deployment. An admin endpoint changes the list in the database. The cached copy is now stale. There are three ways to deal with it, and they differ in what they guarantee:

ChoiceHowWhat it guarantees
evict on change@CacheEvict on the method that changes the datathis instance is fresh at once, and the other instances are not
expire after a timespring.cache.type=caffeine with an expireAfterWrite in its specevery instance is fresh within that time
one shared cacheRedis behind @Cacheableevery instance reads the same entries

@CacheEvict(value = "reference-data", key = "#type") removes one entry when its method runs. A run for this book on Spring 7.0.9 confirmed that it removes the entry, and that the next call loads again. For its attributes, see the section Cache keys, conditions and eviction.

The instances are the problem. Each instance of the service has its own map in its own memory. The admin request reaches one instance, so only that instance evicts. The other instances keep the old list until something else clears it. A C# developer with IMemoryCache has the same limit, because that cache is also kept in one process:

public class ExpiringReferenceItems(IMemoryCache cache, IReferenceStore store)
{
    public Task<List<ReferenceItem>?> FindByType(string type) =>
        cache.GetOrCreateAsync(type, entry =>
        {
            entry.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);
            return store.FindByTypeAsync(type);
        });

    public void Changed(string type) => cache.Remove(type);
}

In C#, AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow sets the expiry for each entry, in code. In Spring, the expiry belongs to the cache store, and is a setting. A run for this book on Boot 4.1.2 used Caffeine 3.2.4, the version that Boot manages. It set spring.cache.type=caffeine and spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=500,expireAfterWrite=1s. Boot then created a CaffeineCacheManager. Two calls loaded once. A third call after 1.5 seconds loaded again. The dependency is com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine, with no version, because Boot manages it. A service that needs an expiry adds that dependency and the two settings, and its @Cacheable methods stay as they are. The order service has no Caffeine, for the reason in the first item below, so the companion has no code for it.

The recommendation follows from the guarantee that the data needs:

  • Data that changes only with a deployment needs nothing. This is the order service.
  • Data where a few minutes of staleness are harmless needs an expiry. Caffeine with expireAfterWrite is enough, and an eviction on change makes the instance that took the change fresh at once.
  • Data that must be fresh everywhere at once does not belong in an in-process cache. Use Redis, or read the database every time.

The .NET caches, comparedtwist#

.NET has several cache APIs, and Spring has one annotation over several stores. Two of the .NET APIs matter here:

.NETSpringNote
IMemoryCache@Cacheable with the default map, or with Caffeineone process, and Caffeine adds size limits and expiry
HybridCacheno single providerHybridCache has two levels, over IMemoryCache and IDistributedCache

HybridCache has a call much like the code of the order service:

public class HybridReferenceItems(HybridCache cache, IReferenceStore store)
{
    public ValueTask<List<ReferenceItem>> FindByType(string type) =>
        cache.GetOrCreateAsync(type, async _ => await store.FindByTypeAsync(type));
}

Its GetOrCreateAsync returns a ValueTask. HybridCache keeps its entries at two levels, in memory and in a distributed cache. Boot lists Caffeine and Redis among its cache providers, but no provider with two levels. A Spring service that needs two levels must build them itself. The order service needs only the level in memory.

The bigger difference is where the code is. In C#, the cache call is inside the method. In Spring, the annotation leaves the method's body as a plain database read, and the proxy adds the cache around it. That is why the proxy rule of the section Where the cache goes: on the repository matters in Spring and never comes up in C#.

Scheduling, switched on by the platformtrap#

Events that the outbox could not send must be sent again. The platform's OutboxResender does this every minute. For what the resender sends, and why, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox. This chapter covers how the job is scheduled.

A scheduled method runs only when something switches scheduling on, with @EnableScheduling. The order service never writes that annotation. The platform does, inside its messaging auto-configuration:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableScheduling
static class OutboxResendConfiguration {

    /** ShedLock's lock in MongoDB, in the collection {@code scheduler_locks}. */
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    LockingTaskExecutor lockingTaskExecutor(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        return new DefaultLockingTaskExecutor(new MongoLockProvider(mongo.getCollection("scheduler_locks")));
    }

    @Bean
    OutboxResender outboxResender(IncompleteEventPublications incompletePublications, LockingTaskExecutor locks,
                                  MessagingProperties properties, Clock clock) {
        return new OutboxResender(incompletePublications, locks, properties, clock);
    }
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)

The nested class applies only when the property is true, or missing. So the resender is on by default.

@EnableScheduling

The annotation is on the same nested class as the resender. So scheduling is on exactly when the resender is on.

OutboxResender outboxResender(IncompleteEventPublications incompletePublications, LockingTaskExecutor locks,

The resender is a @Bean, not a scanned class. Its @Scheduled method still runs. A research run confirmed that Spring finds scheduled methods on any bean, however it was registered.

@EnableScheduling is not limited to the class that carries it. A research run put it into a library's auto-configuration only, and the application had none. Spring still registered its scheduling processor for the whole application. So every @Scheduled method of the service runs, although the service never switched scheduling on.

Scheduling also runs a task that the service never sees. The platform's defaults set spring.modulith.events.staleness.resubmitted=PT15M, so Spring Modulith adds its staleness monitor. The monitor registers through SchedulingConfigurer, an interface that the scheduling processor reads. So it runs only when scheduling is on. A run of the local environment logged its check once a minute, on the thread scheduling-1. That is the one thread of the scheduler, which the resender uses too. For what the monitor does, see the section Resending what was not sent.

Gotcha

A service's own job can depend on a platform setting without saying so. Suppose the order service adds a nightly job with @Scheduled, and writes no @EnableScheduling. The job runs, because the platform switched scheduling on. The tests set platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled=false, so that no background job runs during a test. That setting also switches scheduling off for the whole application. And a service with platform.messaging.enabled=false gets no scheduling at all. The job then stops, and nothing warns you. A service that has a job of its own writes @EnableScheduling itself.

The test profile switches the resender off:

messaging:
  outbox:
    resend-enabled: false

With resend-enabled: false, the wiring test starts the whole application with no job and no lock. Scheduling is off too, so the staleness monitor does not run either. The journey test sets the same property.

Pragmatic choice: The platform switches scheduling on

The strict rule. An application switches on the features it uses itself. A library adds beans, and does not change how the whole application behaves.

What we do. The platform's messaging auto-configuration carries @EnableScheduling, next to the resender, behind one property.

Why. The resender is part of the outbox, which every service with events needs. Without scheduling, unsent events would wait for ever, and a service author would have to remember one more annotation. Tying it to resend-enabled keeps it visible in one property.

When to stop. Stop when a service has jobs of its own. That service writes @EnableScheduling in its own configuration, so its jobs do not depend on the platform's property.

@Scheduled with durations from settingstwist#

C#
public class OutboxResender : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            await ResendAsync(stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}
Java 25
@Scheduled(initialDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}",
        fixedDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}")
void resend() {
    LockConfiguration lock = new LockConfiguration(clock.instant(), LOCK_NAME,
            properties.getLockAtMostFor(), properties.getResendInterval().dividedBy(2));
    locks.executeWithLock((Runnable) this::resendNow, lock);
}
Reading the code
fixedDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}")

The next run starts one interval after the previous run ends. The value is a placeholder for the setting. The part after the colon, PT1M, is the default.

initialDelayString = "${platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval:PT1M}",

The first run waits one interval after startup too. Without it, the first run would start right after startup.

locks.executeWithLock((Runnable) this::resendNow, lock);

The job takes a lock before it does any work. See the section Several instances, and the lock.

PT1M is an ISO-8601 duration, which means one minute. PT30S means 30 seconds, and PT1H one hour. A research run confirmed that @Scheduled accepts placeholders with ISO durations in its ...String attributes. The setting itself is bound to a Duration field with the same default:

/** Turns the scheduled resender on. Tests turn it off, so no background job runs. */
private boolean resendEnabled = true;

/** How often the resender runs. */
private Duration resendInterval = Duration.ofMinutes(1);

/** Only events older than this are resent, so events still being sent are left alone. */
private Duration resendOlderThan = Duration.ofMinutes(5);

/** The longest one instance may hold the resender lock, in case it dies while holding it. */
private Duration lockAtMostFor = Duration.ofMinutes(5);

The annotation reads resendInterval as a placeholder, and the method reads it from properties. Both have the default of one minute, so they agree when the setting is missing. A service changes both with one line, such as platform.messaging.outbox.resend-interval: PT5M.

The C# loop and the Spring method behave alike in one way. Each one waits for its work to finish before the next run can start. Spring's scheduler has one thread by default. So a slow job delays every other job of the service. For that and for cron expressions, see the section Scheduling.

Several instances, and the locktrap#

The order service runs as three instances. Each one has the same @Scheduled method. Every instance runs its own copy of the job, as a BackgroundService does in each instance of an ASP.NET Core service. A research run measured it with two instances on one database for 3 seconds. Without a lock, the job ran 7 times in one instance and 6 times in the other.

For the resender, that is waste and a risk. Without a lock, every instance reads the same unsent rows each minute, and sends them again. So the resender takes a lock first. A C# developer expects the second instance to wait for the lock, as lock does in C#. ShedLock behaves differently. The library is ShedLock, version 7.10.1 as of October 2026. Its 7.x line supports Spring Boot 4. The platform uses its core and its MongoDB provider:

<!-- A lock in MongoDB, so only one instance runs the outbox resender at a time -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.javacrumbs.shedlock</groupId>
    <artifactId>shedlock-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.javacrumbs.shedlock</groupId>
    <artifactId>shedlock-provider-mongo</artifactId>
</dependency>

The artifact shedlock-provider-mongo has no version here. The version comes from shedlock-bom 7.10.1, which the parent Project Object Model (POM) imports. The provider keeps each lock as a document in the collection scheduler_locks.

PredictTwo instances reach the resender at the same time#
Two instances of the order service run this method at the same moment. Instance A takes the lock first and is still working. What does instance B do?
void resend() {
    LockConfiguration lock = new LockConfiguration(clock.instant(), LOCK_NAME,
            properties.getLockAtMostFor(), properties.getResendInterval().dividedBy(2));
    locks.executeWithLock((Runnable) this::resendNow, lock);
}
Show the answer
B skips the run. It does not wait for the lock, and it does not run later.

ShedLock skips a run when the lock is taken. The LockingTaskExecutor tries once to take the lock. If another instance holds it, the task is not run, and the call returns. B's next chance is its next scheduled run.

A research run with the lock ran the job 7 times in total, all in one instance. The other instance skipped every time. So a lock fits a job that may skip a turn. A job that must run once for every trigger needs a job store, such as Quartz.

The two durations of the lock protect against two different problems:

ValueIn the platformWhat it protects against
lockAtMostForlock-at-most-for, PT5M by defaultan instance that dies while it holds the lock, because the lock is freed after this time
lockAtLeastForhalf the resend intervalclocks that differ a little, so a second instance does not run just after the first

The resender calls ShedLock's LockingTaskExecutor directly. ShedLock also offers an annotation, @SchedulerLock, that does the same through a proxy and needs @EnableSchedulerLock. The platform's README gives the reason for the direct call. The library then needs no proxy and no global annotation in each service.

Two tests cover the lock. OutboxResenderTest gives the resender a lock that is free, then one that is taken:

@Test
void skipsTheRunWhenAnotherInstanceHoldsTheLock() {
    LockProvider takenLock = configuration -> Optional.empty();

    resender(takenLock).resend();

    verifyNoInteractions(publications);
}

A LockProvider returns an empty Optional when the lock is taken. The test then checks with verifyNoInteractions that nothing was resent. OutboxResenderLockIT uses the real MongoDB provider in a test container. One LockingTaskExecutor holds the lock, and a second one, on another thread, gets no run. The test needs the second thread. ShedLock remembers the locks that a thread holds. When the same thread asks for the same lock again, ShedLock runs the task without a check. A real second instance is another process, so another thread is the closer copy.

Gotcha

ShedLock on Amazon DocumentDB was not verified. The provider ran against MongoDB in the integration test. The ShedLock README does not mention DocumentDB, and no run for this book used it. Run OutboxResenderLockIT against a DocumentDB cluster once before you rely on it there.

A lock is enough when a skipped turn is harmless. The resender is such a job, because the next run sends what this one skipped. Some jobs need more, such as retries of one run, a history, or a run that must not be lost:

Need.NETJava
a job that may skip a turn, once across instancesa BackgroundService with a lock of your own@Scheduled with ShedLock
jobs kept in a databaseHangfire, which stores each recurring job in persistent storageJobRunr, which keeps jobs in your database and has a dashboard
a scheduler with a cluster of nodes and a shared job storeQuartz.NET, clustered with its AdoJobStoreQuartz, with spring-boot-starter-quartz and job-store-type jdbc

Quartz.NET clusters only with its AdoJobStore, and its documentation names load balancing and fail-over as the benefits. Boot's Quartz starter keeps jobs in memory by default, and in a database with spring.quartz.job-store-type=jdbc.

A job acts as the systemnew#

A scheduled job runs on a scheduler thread. No user started it, and the thread has no security context. If the job called a method that checks a permission, the call would fail with AuthenticationCredentialsNotFoundException. The order service avoids this by design. Its application services check no permission:

* <p>The class has no permission annotation. Permissions are checked on the controllers, where
* users enter. Every method here can therefore be called by another feature or by a message
* listener without a second, unprotected copy of the method.

With no permission annotation on the class, nothing on the scheduler thread asks for a caller. So a future job, such as one that cancels orders unpaid after a week, calls OrderService.cancel directly. The audit log then records the actor system, because the thread has no caller. That is the truth, because no user acted. For the reasons, see the sections Messages and jobs: the system actor and Why an identity-swapping helper is a warning sign.

The resender itself calls no use case. It asks Spring Modulith to resend publications, and the publications carry the events that a use case already recorded.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy does the order service put @Cacheable on the repository method and not on the service method that lists the values?
The cache saves database reads, so it is a storage concern, and the service reads the same way without it. And @Cacheable works through a proxy. Only calls from another bean pass it. The service calls the repository from two of its own methods, and each call passes the proxy. A cache on a service method would be skipped by any call from inside the service.
2
An expert asksAn admin endpoint changes a lookup list, and its method carries @CacheEvict. The service runs as three instances with the default cache. Why do some requests still see the old list?
Each instance keeps its own cache in its own memory. The admin request reaches one instance, so only that instance evicts the entry. The other two keep the old list. An expiry, such as Caffeine's expireAfterWrite, bounds how long they keep it. A shared cache such as Redis, or no cache, makes every instance fresh at once.
3
The order service writes no @EnableScheduling. What switches scheduling on, and which setting switches it off again?
The platform's messaging auto-configuration carries @EnableScheduling, on the nested configuration of the outbox resender. The setting platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled=false removes that configuration, and with it scheduling for the whole application. platform.messaging.enabled=false does the same.
4
TranslateThe order service reads lookup lists through a Spring Data repository. Write the Java for this cached read: 
public Task<List<ReferenceItem>?> FindByType(string type) =>
    cache.GetOrCreateAsync(type, _ => store.FindByTypeAsync(type));
public interface ReferenceItemRepository extends MongoRepository<ReferenceItemDocument, String> {

    @Cacheable("reference-data")
    List<ReferenceItemDocument> findByTypeOrderByCodeAsc(String type);
}

The proxy uses the argument type as the key, and stores the result in the cache reference-data. Spring Data writes the query from the method's name. The application also needs @EnableCaching once, on a configuration class.

Writing the platform library#

Running the service · Chapter 24· 25 min read· Quick reference

The platform library holds the code that every shop service needs, such as errors, security, storage and messaging. A service adds one dependency, and Spring Boot sets everything up through auto-configuration. The service writes no line of setup. This chapter shows how the library is built, ordered and switched. It shows how a service replaces a default, and what must never go in the library.

What the library gives a servicenew#

The shop has ten services. Each one needs the same error format, the same token checks and the same way to store an aggregate. If each team wrote its own, the ten versions would differ within a year. So the shop writes that code once, in the library shop-platform. Its Project Object Model (POM) lists its five packages:

<!--
  The platform library: the one dependency that every shop service adds.

    com.acme.platform.domain     DDD building blocks in plain Java (no Spring imports)
    com.acme.platform.core       errors, security, logging, tracing, HTTP clients, audit, OpenAPI
    com.acme.platform.mongo      DocumentDB settings, transactions, base persistence classes, migrations
    com.acme.platform.messaging  the outbox to SNS and the inbox for SQS
    com.acme.platform.test       test annotations, test containers and architecture rules

  Every feature is Spring Boot auto-configuration. The library holds no business code.
-->
<!-- ... -->
    <artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>

The artifact is named shop-platform, and its comment lists the packages. Each package is one area. A service's code uses classes from domain, such as AggregateRoot, and the others give it beans at startup. The platform's README lists what a service gets from each package:

PackageWhat a service gets
com.acme.platform.domainAggregateRoot, Entity, Identifier, ValueObject, DomainEvent, DomainEventPublisher, Repository, Guard, PageQuery, PageResult and the three exception kinds, in plain Java
com.acme.platform.coreproblem responses with traceId, the resource server chain, method security, the MDC interceptor, LogContext, JSON log masking, HttpClientFactory, ResilientCalls, Clock, CurrentActor, AuditLog and the shared OpenAPI parts
com.acme.platform.mongothe transaction manager, the DocumentDB driver settings, BaseDocument, MongoAggregateRepository, DocumentMapper, the migration runner and seed files, the audit log store and the 409 handler
com.acme.platform.messagingthe outbox, with OutboxDomainEventPublisher and OutboxResender, and the inbox, with Inbox and InboxMessageHandler
com.acme.platform.test@PlatformWebMvcTest, @PlatformDataMongoTest, the MongoDB and Floci test containers, NoOpTransactionManager and ArchitectureRules

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is the approach of the whole part. The building blocks in the first row are its base classes. For each of them, see the chapter The domain model in plain Java. Each other row has a home chapter too. The mapped diagnostic context (MDC) and the log masking are in the chapter Logging, tracing and health. The clients are in the chapter Calling other services. This chapter explains how the library is put together, not what each class does.

The README is also the place to look up a setting. Its properties table is in the quick reference at the end of this chapter.

What never goes in the platform librarynew#

The order service and the invoice service both need Money. Both need an order ID. A developer suggests a shared library with Money, OrderId and perhaps Order itself. Then nobody writes them twice. The shop says no, and writes the rule at the top of the platform's README:

The parent POM and the library that every shop service uses. It holds no business code and no
domain model: services share contracts (OpenAPI files and event schemas), never domain classes,
because a shared domain library would tie their release cycles together.

The README says that the library holds no business code. The rule has two parts. The platform holds no business code. And no other shared library holds domain classes either. Services share contracts. A contract is the OpenAPI file of an API, or the JSON schema of an event.

The reason is the release cycle. Suppose Order is in a shared library. The order service adds a field for a new rule. Now the invoice service must take a new version of the library, though nothing changed for it. Or it stays on the old version, and the two services disagree about what an order is. Either way, a change in one service touches the others. A contract is different. The order service can add a field to OrderPlacedV1, and a consumer that does not read the field does not change.

The careful version of a shared domain library has a fair point. Some types really are the same everywhere, such as an amount of money with a currency. A team that writes Money in every service writes the same rounding rule ten times, and one copy will be wrong. The book's answer is to look at what a shared type must contain. The platform's domain package holds building blocks with no business meaning. It holds the base class of an aggregate, an identifier and a guard for simple checks. Those change rarely, and they mean the same in every service:

/**
 * The building blocks of a domain model, in plain Java.
 *
 * <p>Nothing in this package imports Spring, MongoDB or Jackson. A service's {@code domain}
 * packages may use these classes and still stay plain Java. The classes hold no business
 * concepts: they remove code that every aggregate would otherwise repeat, such as equality by
 * identity, the version for optimistic locking, the list of raised events and simple checks.
 */
package com.acme.platform.domain;

The comment draws the line. It says that the classes hold no business concepts. The package removes code that every aggregate repeats, such as equality by identity. It never says what an order is. Money is a business concept, with a rule about decimals that belongs to the shop's own pricing. So each service that needs it writes it, and each copy can follow its own service's rules.

The other parts of the library follow the same test. Problem responses, token checks and the outbox are technical, and identical in every service. A rule such as "an order ships only when it is paid" is business, and it stays in the order service.

Pragmatic choice: Money written in each service, not shared

The strict rule. One concept has one implementation, so a fix is made once.

What we do. Each service writes its own value objects, such as Money. The platform shares only building blocks with no business meaning.

Why. A shared business type ties every service to one release cycle. A copy of a small record costs a few lines, and each service can change its copy alone.

When to stop. Stop when the same rule inside such a type is copied into many services, and the copies must never differ. A legal rounding rule is an example. Then make it a small library of its own, with no other business types in it, and version it carefully.

How Spring Boot finds the library's setupnew#

The order service's main class is in com.acme.orderservice. Component scanning looks only in that package and below it. The platform's classes are in com.acme.platform, so the scan never finds them. Yet the service gets the platform's filter chain, its error handler and its transaction manager.

The answer is a file in the library's Java archive (JAR). Spring Boot reads every file with this name on the classpath at startup:

com.acme.platform.core.PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.core.PlatformWebAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.core.PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.core.openapi.PlatformOpenApiAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.mongo.PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.mongo.PlatformMongoAuditAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.mongo.PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration
com.acme.platform.messaging.PlatformMessagingAutoConfiguration

The file is META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Each line names one class, such as com.acme.platform.core.PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration. Boot treats each class as an auto-configuration. It sorts them, checks their conditions and creates their beans. A line that starts with # is a comment. For the basic idea, see the section Auto-configuration.

The main class of the service says why it registers nothing:

* <p>{@code @SpringBootApplication} scans this package and every package below it for
* components. The platform's beans come from its auto-configuration instead, because the
* platform's packages are not below this one.

The comment says that @SpringBootApplication scans only its own package and the packages below it. So the library's beans are added in a different way from the service's own beans. The scan finds @Component classes in the service. The imports file names the platform's configuration classes. An auto-configuration runs after the service's own configuration, so its conditions can see the service's beans.

In ASP.NET Core, a library offers an extension method on IServiceCollection, and Program.cs calls it. A run for this book wrote one:

C#
public static class ShopPlatformServiceCollectionExtensions
{
    // An extension method: Program.cs calls builder.Services.AddShopPlatform().
    public static IServiceCollection AddShopPlatform(this IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
        return services;
    }
}
PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration.java
@AutoConfiguration(afterName = "org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.client.autoconfigure.OAuth2ClientAutoConfiguration")
@EnableConfigurationProperties({PlatformLoggingProperties.class, ResilienceProperties.class})
public class PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration {

    /** The clock that the domain reads the time from. Code never calls {@code Instant.now()}. */
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    Clock clock() {
        return Clock.systemUTC();
    }

The C# library does nothing until the service calls AddShopPlatform(). The Java library needs no call. Its class is in the imports file, so adding the dependency is enough. The @Bean method clock() does the same job as TryAddSingleton. For the conditions and the order, see the sections below.

Gotcha

A misspelt imports file is silently ignored. A run with the file named ...AutoConfigurations.imports, with one letter too many, gave no error. The class was not loaded. The file spring.factories is not read for auto-configurations either, though older tutorials use it. If the platform's beans are missing, check the file name first. The conditions report of --debug lists every auto-configuration that Boot considered. A class that is missing from the report was never found. For the report, see the section Asking Boot what it configured.

The eight auto-configurationsnew#

The library has one auto-configuration class for each area. Each class says when it applies, and where it runs in the order:

ClassApplies whenOrderBeans
PlatformCoreAutoConfigurationalwaysafter Boot's OAuth2 client setupClock, CurrentActor, HttpClientFactory, ResilientCalls
PlatformWebAutoConfigurationin a servlet web applicationno orderGlobalExceptionHandler, and a WebMvcConfigurer for the MDC interceptor
PlatformSecurityAutoConfigurationin a servlet web applicationbefore Boot's security chainsthe SecurityFilterChain, with method security on
PlatformOpenApiAutoConfigurationwhen springdoc's OpenAPI class is on the classpathno orderan OpenApiCustomizer with the shared parts
PlatformMongoAutoConfigurationalwaysbefore Boot's MongoDB and transaction setupMongoTransactionManager, the DocumentDB customizer, the migration runner
PlatformMongoAuditAutoConfigurationalwaysafter PlatformMongoAutoConfigurationMongoAuditLog, AuditLogIndexes
PlatformMongoWebAutoConfigurationin a servlet web applicationno orderOptimisticLockingExceptionHandler
PlatformMessagingAutoConfigurationunless platform.messaging.enabled is falseafter PlatformMongoAutoConfigurationthe outbox publisher, the inbox, and the resender with its lock

The core class holds the beans that every service needs, web or not:

/**
 * The beans every service gets, whether it is a web application or not.
 *
 * <p>Each bean is {@link ConditionalOnMissingBean}: a service that defines its own bean of the
 * same type replaces the platform's one. A test, for example, defines a fixed {@link Clock}.
 */
@AutoConfiguration(afterName = "org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.client.autoconfigure.OAuth2ClientAutoConfiguration")
@EnableConfigurationProperties({PlatformLoggingProperties.class, ResilienceProperties.class})
public class PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration {
    // ...
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    CurrentActor currentActor() {
        return new SecurityContextCurrentActor();
    }
Reading the code
@AutoConfiguration(afterName = "org.springframework.boot.security.oauth2.client.autoconfigure.OAuth2ClientAutoConfiguration")

@AutoConfiguration marks the class as an auto-configuration. It does what @Configuration does, and it also takes ordering attributes. afterName makes Boot process this class after the named one, which sets up the OAuth2 client registrations.

@EnableConfigurationProperties({PlatformLoggingProperties.class, ResilienceProperties.class})

This line creates the two @ConfigurationProperties beans and binds them from the settings, such as platform.resilience.retry.max-attempts. For binding, see the chapter Configuration in depth.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean

Without a type, the condition takes the method's return type. So this bean is created only when no CurrentActor bean exists yet.

The class name of an auto-configuration ends in AutoConfiguration, by convention. The class is public, but its @Bean methods are package-private. Spring can still call them, and no service needs to.

The web class shows how a library adds to Spring model-view-controller (MVC):

/** The web defaults: one error format for every service, and path variables in the MDC. */
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = ConditionalOnWebApplication.Type.SERVLET)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(PlatformLoggingProperties.class)
public class PlatformWebAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    GlobalExceptionHandler globalExceptionHandler() {
        return new GlobalExceptionHandler();
    }

    /** Registers the MDC interceptor. A {@link WebMvcConfigurer} bean is how a library adds to Spring MVC. */
    @Bean
    WebMvcConfigurer platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer(PlatformLoggingProperties properties) {
        PathVariableMdcInterceptor interceptor = new PathVariableMdcInterceptor(properties.getMdcPathVariables());
        return new WebMvcConfigurer() {
            @Override
            public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
                registry.addInterceptor(interceptor);
            }
        };
    }
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = ConditionalOnWebApplication.Type.SERVLET)

The class applies only in a servlet web application. A batch job that uses the library gets no error handler and no interceptor. A run for this book checked the condition. In an application of the type NONE, the bean was absent. In a servlet application, it was there.

WebMvcConfigurer platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer(PlatformLoggingProperties properties) {

Spring MVC collects every WebMvcConfigurer bean and calls each one. So the library adds an interceptor by declaring a bean. The service's own configurers still work beside it.

return new WebMvcConfigurer() {

This is an anonymous class. It implements the interface on the spot, with one method.

The bean platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer has no @ConditionalOnMissingBean. A service may have many WebMvcConfigurer beans, so the condition would switch the platform's interceptor off by accident. A bean that is one of many has no such condition.

The 409 handler for optimistic locking is in the mongo package, not in the web package:

/**
 * Registers the 409 handler for optimistic locking, only in web applications.
 *
 * <p>It lives in the mongo package, next to the technology that throws the exception, so the
 * platform's web code knows nothing about MongoDB.
 */
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = ConditionalOnWebApplication.Type.SERVLET)
public class PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration {

So PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration is a small class of its own. If the library later splits into modules, the web module needs no MongoDB, and the mongo module brings its own handler.

The messaging class has a nested configuration:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableScheduling
static class OutboxResendConfiguration {

A nested configuration is a static class inside the auto-configuration. Its conditions apply only to its own beans. Here @EnableScheduling is on the nested class. So scheduling is on only when the resender is on, and a service controls both with one property. For the resender, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

The security class and its order are taught in the section Why the platform's chain is created before Boot's.

The order of auto-configurations, and its trapstrap#

A condition such as "no Clock bean exists yet" depends on what Spring has already processed. So the order of the auto-configurations decides the result. Spring Boot's reference says the same, and it recommends bean conditions only on auto-configuration classes. Two libraries offer a greeter. One offers a default with a condition, and one offers its own bean. The two libraries do not say which one comes first:

PredictA default and a provider with no order between them#
A service asks Spring for the one TrapGreeter bean. What happens?
@AutoConfiguration
public class AaaTrapDefaultsAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    TrapGreeter defaultTrapGreeter() { return new TrapGreeter("default"); }
}

@AutoConfiguration
public class CccTrapProviderAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    TrapGreeter providedTrapGreeter() { return new TrapGreeter("provided"); }
}
Show the answer
Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: "expected single matching bean but found 2: defaultTrapGreeter,providedTrapGreeter".

The condition is checked when its own class is processed, not at the end. With no order, Boot processed the default first. No greeter existed then, so the default was created. The provider then added its unconditional bean. Both beans were registered.

In .NET, two AddSingleton calls for one type give no error. A run showed that GetRequiredService returns the last one.

Order the default after the provider, with after or afterName. The same run then left one bean, the provider's.

The classes in the prediction are from a run for this book. Their code is shortened here. The run also found a worse effect. In its first version, a third class declared an order against the provider. Boot's sorting then moved the provider ahead of the default as well, and the trap did not appear. So a default can work by luck, because of another class's order. The luck ends when that other class changes.

An auto-configuration states its order with four attributes of @AutoConfiguration:

AttributeTakesUse it when
beforeclassesthe other class is always on the library's compile classpath
afterclassesthe same, for a class that must come first
beforeNameclass names as stringsthe other class is in a module that may be missing, or the library should not compile against it
afterNameclass names as stringsthe same, for a class that must come first

The platform uses each kind. The audit class names a class of its own library:

/** Stores the audit log in MongoDB, unless the service defines its own {@link AuditLog}. */
@AutoConfiguration(after = PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)
public class PlatformMongoAuditAutoConfiguration {

after = PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class is a class literal, so the compiler checks it. The mongo class names Boot's classes as strings:

/**
 * Sets up DocumentDB for every service: transactions, the driver settings DocumentDB needs,
 * and the migration runner.
 *
 * <p>Spring Boot creates no transaction manager for MongoDB. Without one, {@code @Transactional}
 * silently does nothing: each write commits on its own. This class registers a
 * {@link MongoTransactionManager} before Spring Boot's transaction setup runs, so
 * {@code @Transactional} and {@code TransactionTemplate} both use it.
 */
@AutoConfiguration(beforeName = {
        "org.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.autoconfigure.DataMongoAutoConfiguration",
        "org.springframework.boot.transaction.autoconfigure.TransactionAutoConfiguration"})
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DocumentDbProperties.class)
public class PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(TransactionManager.class)
    MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory databaseFactory) {
        return new MongoTransactionManager(databaseFactory);
    }
Reading the code
"org.springframework.boot.transaction.autoconfigure.TransactionAutoConfiguration"})

Boot's transaction setup creates a TransactionTemplate once a transaction manager exists. A run with Boot 4.1.2 showed it. With no manager, there was no template either. With the manager, Boot added the bean transactionTemplate. So the platform's manager must exist before Boot's class runs.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean(TransactionManager.class)

The condition names a type. A service that declares any transaction manager of its own keeps it, and the platform creates none.

The names in beforeName are checked by no compiler. The run for this book confirmed that each of these names exists in Boot 4.1.2. A second run gave the web class a beforeName that names no class at all. The service started, and its wiring test passed. Nothing reported the wrong name.

Gotcha

A wrong name in beforeName or afterName is not reported. The order is then simply not applied. Boot 4 moved many classes into new packages, so a name copied from a Boot 3 library is often wrong. Check each name against the Boot jars after every major upgrade. A wiring test that starts the whole service, such as ApplicationWiringTest, catches the effect when an ordering matters for a bean.

The wiring test checks the result of two orderings at once:

@Test
void theContextStartsWithThePlatformsBeans() {
    assertThat(context.getBean(PlatformTransactionManager.class)).isInstanceOf(MongoTransactionManager.class);
    assertThat(context.getBeansOfType(SecurityFilterChain.class)).containsOnlyKeys("platformSecurityFilterChain");
}

The first line checks that the transaction manager is the platform's MongoTransactionManager. The second line checks that exactly one filter chain exists, the platform's own. If an order broke, one of the two lines would fail. For the wiring test, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Conditions: when a bean or a class appliesnew#

A condition decides whether Spring creates a bean, or applies a whole class. The platform uses four of them:

ConditionThe bean or class is created whenUsed by the platform for
@ConditionalOnMissingBeanno bean of the type exists yet, and the type is the return type when none is namedevery default that a service may replace, such as Clock and AuditLog
@ConditionalOnPropertya setting has the given value, compared without case, and matchIfMissing decides when it is absentthe migrations, the messaging and the resender, which a service can switch off
@ConditionalOnWebApplicationthe application has the given web type, such as SERVLETthe error handler, the security chain and the 409 handler
@ConditionalOnClassa class is on the classpaththe OpenAPI customizer, which needs springdoc

A switch with @ConditionalOnProperty looks like this:

/** Runs the migrations at startup. Slice and wiring tests turn it off with the property. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
MongoMigrationRunner mongoMigrationRunner(MongoTemplate mongo, ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations, Clock clock,
                                          @Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl) {
    return new MongoMigrationRunner(mongo, migrations.orderedStream().toList(), clock, lockTtl);
}
Reading the code
havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)

The bean is created when the setting is true, and also when the setting is absent. A run for this book checked the three cases. With the setting missing, the bean was present. With false, it was absent. With TRUE in capitals, it was present.

ObjectProvider<MongoMigration> migrations

An ObjectProvider asks for beans when the code needs them. orderedStream() returns every MongoMigration bean, sorted by @Order. For ObjectProvider, see the chapter Wiring the service: the container in depth.

@Value("${platform.mongo.migrations.lock-ttl:PT15M}") Duration lockTtl)

One setting, read directly, with the default after the colon.

The OpenAPI class depends on a class from another library:

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(OpenAPI.class)
public class PlatformOpenApiAutoConfiguration {

@ConditionalOnClass(OpenAPI.class) applies the class only when springdoc's OpenAPI class is on the classpath. The library adds springdoc today. The condition keeps the class safe if a service ever leaves springdoc out.

Boot's reference recommends bean conditions, such as @ConditionalOnMissingBean, only on auto-configuration classes. A @Configuration class of the service is processed before the auto-configurations. So a bean condition on it sees only part of the beans. The platform keeps every bean condition on its auto-configurations.

Replacing a default: a bean of your own, or a settingtwist#

A test needs a fixed time. A service needs its audit log in another store. Each of them replaces one default of the platform. There are two ways. A service defines its own bean of the same type, or it sets a property.

C#
var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddSingleton<TimeProvider>(new FixedTime());
services.AddShopPlatform();
Java 25
/** The clock that the domain reads the time from. Code never calls {@code Instant.now()}. */
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
Clock clock() {
    return Clock.systemUTC();
}

In the run for this book, the service's FixedTime won, and only one TimeProvider was registered. TryAddSingleton adds nothing when the type is registered already. But the order matters in .NET. When the service registered its own clock after AddShopPlatform(), both registrations existed. GetRequiredService returned the service's one, because the last one wins.

In Spring, the order of the service's code does not matter. The service's own configuration is processed before the auto-configurations. So @ConditionalOnMissingBean always sees the service's Clock, and the platform's one is never created. A run for this book showed that a user's bean makes the condition back off, and one bean remains.

These are the beans a service can replace:

TypeThe platform's defaultA reason to replace it
ClockClock.systemUTC()a test that needs a fixed time
CurrentActorSecurityContextCurrentActora service that reads the actor from somewhere else
AuditLogMongoAuditLog, in the collection of the platforman audit store outside the service's database
SecurityFilterChainthe resource server chaina service with other rules, such as URL rules
TransactionManagerMongoTransactionManagera service that does not use MongoDB
DomainEventPublisherOutboxDomainEventPublishera service with another way to publish
GlobalExceptionHandlerthe platform's problem responsesrarely, because every service should answer errors the same way

A setting is the lighter way. The platform reads its settings from @ConfigurationProperties classes. A service sets platform.security.public-paths, for example, and keeps the platform's chain. Prefer a setting when one exists. A bean of your own takes over the whole object, and the platform's later fixes to it no longer reach the service.

A service finds the settings in its IDE. The shop's parent POM runs Spring Boot's configuration processor when the library is compiled. The processor writes the file META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json into the library's jar. The file holds each key's type and description, and the default of most keys. So an IDE completes platform.security.public-paths and shows what it does. Write a Javadoc comment on every field of a properties class, because that comment becomes the key's description. For the file and its limits, see the section Completion in the IDE: the configuration metadata.

Default settings, loaded with the lowest precedencenew#

Every service needs some settings that the platform chooses. Indexes must never be created at startup. A missing queue must stop the service. Health probes must be on. If each service wrote those lines in its application.yml, some would forget them. So the platform keeps them in files of its own:

# Defaults that every service gets from the platform's mongo package.

# Indexes are created by migrations (MongoMigration), never by Spring at startup.
# Startup index creation is invisible, nobody reviews it, and it can block on a large collection.
spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation=false

# The service is ready for traffic only when the database is reachable.
# Liveness deliberately leaves the database out: a database outage must not restart every instance.
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,mongo

Each package has its own file, core.properties, mongo.properties and messaging.properties. Each line carries the reason for the setting. The key spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation switches off the indexes that Spring Data would create at startup.

Some lines restate a default of Spring Boot. The core file says why:

# Defaults that every service gets from the platform's core package.
# They have the LOWEST precedence: a service's application.yml overrides any of them.
# Some keys restate a Spring Boot 4.1 default. They stay here on purpose: the platform's
# behaviour is visible in one file, and a Boot upgrade that changes a default cannot change it.

The comment says that the defaults have the LOWEST precedence. A Boot upgrade could change a default. A line in the file keeps the platform's choice, so server.shutdown=graceful stays graceful after any upgrade.

The files are not read by Spring Boot on its own. An environment post-processor of the platform, PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor, adds them to the environment, before the application context exists. It adds each file with addLast, so the defaults have the lowest precedence, and every setting of the service wins. For the class, its order and its test, see the section The platform's defaults, below everything else.

For the author of the library, three rules follow from that design:

  • A new package of the library adds its own file in META-INF/platform-defaults. The processor finds every file in that folder, in every jar, so no code changes.
  • Each key carries a comment with its reason. Then a reviewer can tell a decision from a leftover.
  • A default that depends on another setting cannot be a line in a file. It goes into the processor's code. The switch to JSON logs in the Elastic Common Schema (ECS) is an example.

The class is not in the imports file. An imports file names auto-configurations, and this class must run before any of them. So Boot finds it through the older file META-INF/spring.factories:

# EnvironmentPostProcessor is still registered here, not in the AutoConfiguration.imports file.
org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor=\
com.acme.platform.core.config.PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor

The key is the interface's full name, org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor. The old key, in the package org.springframework.boot.env, still works in Boot 4.1.2, but it is deprecated. So a library registers its processor under the new key.

Switching a whole area offtwist#

A small service sends and receives no events. With one library, it still has the outbox, the inbox and Spring Cloud AWS on its classpath. It switches them off with four settings:

A service that sends and receives no events sets these four properties together:
`platform.messaging.enabled=false`, `spring.cloud.aws.sns.enabled=false`,
`spring.cloud.aws.sqs.enabled=false` and `spring.modulith.events.externalization.enabled=false`.

The first setting, platform.messaging.enabled=false, is the platform's own. It switches off the whole messaging class, because the class carries the condition:

@AutoConfiguration(after = PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "platform.messaging.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(MessagingProperties.class)
public class PlatformMessagingAutoConfiguration {

The condition is on the class PlatformMessagingAutoConfiguration itself. A condition on the class applies to every bean in it, and to its nested configuration. So platform.messaging.enabled=false removes the outbox publisher, the inbox and the resender together.

The other three settings belong to Spring Cloud AWS and Spring Modulith. They are settings of those libraries, so the service sets them too. Turning messaging off completely takes four properties, because three libraries are involved. Each property switches off one part:

PropertySwitches off
platform.messaging.enabled=falsethe platform's outbox publisher, the inbox and the resender
spring.cloud.aws.sns.enabled=falsethe SNS client of Spring Cloud AWS
spring.cloud.aws.sqs.enabled=falsethe SQS client and the listener containers
spring.modulith.events.externalization.enabled=falsethe sending of events to other services by Spring Modulith

The README lists the four together, because one without the others leaves a part running. The wiring profile of the order service sets spring.cloud.aws.sqs.enabled: false, so its test needs no queue.

The migrations and the resender have switches of the same kind, platform.mongo.migrations.enabled and platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled. The slice tests and the wiring test use them.

Test support, shipped in the librarynew#

Each service tests its controllers with the platform's security and error handling, as in production. Each service tests its persistence against MongoDB in a container. If each team wrote that setup, the tests would differ. So the library ships the setup in its package com.acme.platform.test. The web slice is an annotation:

/**
 * A web slice test with the platform's security, error handling and MDC interceptor, the same
 * as in production. Only the controllers and Spring MVC start, so the test runs in about a
 * second.
 *
 * <pre>{@code
 * @PlatformWebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
 * class OrderControllerTest { ... }
 * }</pre>
 *
 * <p>{@code @WebMvcTest} loads no auto-configuration from libraries, so this annotation imports
 * the platform's web-related ones by name.
 */
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
@WebMvcTest
@ImportAutoConfiguration({
        PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformWebAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration.class})
@Import(TestJwtDecoderConfiguration.class)
public @interface PlatformWebMvcTest {

    /** The controllers to test. */
    @AliasFor(annotation = WebMvcTest.class, attribute = "controllers")
    Class<?>[] value() default {};
}

@WebMvcTest starts a test slice with only Spring MVC and the named controllers. It does not start the auto-configurations of a library. So the annotation @PlatformWebMvcTest carries @WebMvcTest, and names the platform's four web-related auto-configurations in @ImportAutoConfiguration. A service writes one annotation, and its slice runs the platform's security and error handling. The chapter on testing explains each line of the annotation. It also shows what goes wrong with a plain @WebMvcTest. See the section API slices through the platform's own annotation.

The package holds these classes:

ClassWhat a service's test gets
@PlatformWebMvcTesta controller slice with the platform's security, errors and MDC
@PlatformDataMongoTesta persistence slice against MongoDB in Docker, with the platform's transaction manager and migrations off
MongoTestContainerConfigurationMongoDB 8.0.34 as a one-node replica set, connected with @ServiceConnection
AwsTestContainerConfigurationthe Floci emulator for SNS and SQS
TestJwtDecoderConfigurationa decoder that refuses every real token, for tests that use jwt()
NoOpTransactionManagera transaction manager that does nothing, for unit tests of a use case
ArchitectureRulesthe design rules as ArchUnit rules

This code is in the library's main source, not in its tests. Only then can a service use it. So the library must compile against the test libraries, without passing them on to a service. For how the POMs do that, see the chapter The build: a parent POM and a platform library.

The library tests itself too, in its own repository. As of October 2026, it has 16 test classes and four integration tests. ResilientCallsTest, AggregateRootTest and SeedFilesTest are three of the test classes. A library has no application class, so its slice tests start from one in the test folder:

/**
 * The configuration that the platform's own slice tests start from. A library has no
 * application class, but {@code @DataMongoTest} looks upwards from the test's package for one.
 */
@SpringBootApplication
class PlatformTestApplication {
}

PlatformTestApplication is in the package com.acme.platform, the root of every test package of the library. So every slice test of the library finds it. For the other kinds of test, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Versions, and the rules for upgradingnew#

The platform changes a default. The service that upgrades first is surprised in production. So the platform's versions follow rules, written in its README:

Semantic versions. A breaking change comes only in a major version, with upgrade notes. Services
stay at most one minor version behind. Upgrading Spring Boot for every service means changing
the parent and releasing a new platform version.

The README says Semantic versions. A semantic version has three numbers, such as 1.4.2. The first is the major version, the second the minor and the third the patch. A patch fixes a bug. A minor version adds something, and changes nothing that a service relies on. A major version may break things.

For a library like this one, "breaking" covers more than a Java signature. These changes are breaking, so they wait for a major version:

  • A property is renamed or removed, such as platform.security.public-paths.
  • A default changes its value, such as the public paths or the retry count.
  • A bean is removed, or a bean loses its @ConditionalOnMissingBean.
  • A class or a method of the domain or test packages changes its signature.
  • A Spring Boot major version, such as Boot 3 to Boot 4.

These changes are minor, because no service breaks:

  • A new bean with @ConditionalOnMissingBean, which a service may replace.
  • A new property with a default that keeps today's behaviour.
  • A new architecture rule. A service runs a rule only after it adds a test that calls it, and it can freeze its old violations first. For freezing, see the chapter Testing in depth.

The rule "at most one minor version behind" keeps all services close together. A security fix then needs at most one upgrade step for any service. A service that falls three versions behind must make three sets of changes at once, at the worst moment.

The upgrade notes are the platform team's duty. Each note says what changed, why, and what a service must do. With the parent and the library at the same version, a service changes one number. For the steps, see the section Upgrading Spring Boot for every service.

One library, not one per concernnew#

Spring Boot itself has a starter per concern, such as web, security and data. A platform could do the same, with one module per package. The modules would have names such as shop-platform-core and shop-platform-mongo. A service would add only what it uses. The shop chose one library. Its README says why:

- **One library, not one per concern.** One dependency and one version for every service. The
  cost is that every capability is on the classpath, which is why messaging can be switched off.
  The packages stay separate, so the library can be split later.

The README names the cost: every capability is on the classpath. The case for modules is strong. A service with no events would not carry the AWS libraries. Its startup would check fewer conditions. And the boundaries between the areas would be enforced by the build, not by discipline.

The case for one library is stronger while the shop is small. Every service has the same set of platform code. A bug report names one version, not four that must match. A new service adds one dependency. And nearly every shop service uses all the areas. The cost is the classpath, and the switch for messaging removes most of it.

The design keeps a later split easy. Each area is a package with its own auto-configurations. The 409 handler is in the mongo package, so the web code has no MongoDB import. A split would move each package to a module, with its own imports file, and almost no code would change.

Split the library when one of these happens:

  • Several services do not use an area, and its libraries slow their startup or enlarge their image.
  • An area needs its own release rhythm, for example because the messaging changes every month.
  • Services in another language or framework need part of it. Then that part is no longer a Spring Boot library at all.

When to build the library, and what to do before it existsnew#

A company starts its first DDD services. The platform library does not exist yet. Two mistakes are common. One team waits for a complete platform before it writes a service. Or every team writes its own cross-cutting code, and eight or ten services later the company has eight or ten error formats.

The better path is to build the library together with the first services. The first service needs an error handler, so the error handler is written once, in a form that the library can take. The second service then uses it.

Until the library exists, a service keeps the shared code in its shared package, with the package names that the library will have. The service's own shared package already says where such code belongs:

/**
 * Small helpers that every feature of this service uses: the permission annotations, the audit
 * names and the OpenAPI description. It holds no business logic. Code that several services
 * need belongs in the platform instead.
 */
package com.acme.orderservice.shared;

The comment's last sentence is the rule. Code that several services need belongs in the platform. Before the platform exists, such code waits in shared, under names such as shared.platform.core.error. When the library arrives, the code moves, and only the imports change.

Pragmatic choice: Platform code inside a service, for a while

The strict rule. Cross-cutting code comes from the platform library, and a service holds none of it.

What we do. Before the library exists, the first services keep such code in their shared package. It uses the package names that the library will use.

Why. A library built before any service guesses what services need. A library built from the first two services contains what they really used.

When to stop. Stop when a second service needs the same code. Then move it into the library, release it, and delete the copies.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksThe platform's Clock bean has @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Why does a service's own Clock bean always win, whatever the order of the service's code?
Spring processes the service's own configuration before the auto-configurations. So when the platform's condition is checked, the service's Clock already exists, and the platform's bean is not created. In .NET, TryAddSingleton backs off only if the service registered its own bean before calling the library.
2
An expert asksWhy does a shared domain library tie the release cycles together, when a shared OpenAPI file or event schema does not?
A domain class changes with the rules of the service that owns it. Every other service must then take a new version of the library, or disagree about the concept. A contract changes only when the API or the event changes. A consumer that does not read a new field needs no change.
3
An expert asksThe platform's Clock bean carries @ConditionalOnMissingBean, but its bean platformMdcWebMvcConfigurer does not. Why?
A service may have many WebMvcConfigurer beans of its own, and Spring MVC calls each one. With the condition, any configurer of the service would switch off the platform's MDC interceptor by accident. A bean that is one of many has no such condition.
4
Why is PlatformDefaultsEnvironmentPostProcessor registered in spring.factories, and not in the imports file?
The imports file names auto-configurations only. An environment post-processor must run before any bean exists, so Boot finds it under the key org.springframework.boot.EnvironmentPostProcessor in META-INF/spring.factories.
5
TranslateWrite this .NET registration as a bean of the platform's core auto-configuration. A service may replace it with its own: 
services.TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
Clock clock() {
    return Clock.systemUTC();
}

@ConditionalOnMissingBean with no type takes the return type, Clock. The class that holds the method is listed in the imports file, so no service calls it.

Testing in depth#

Testing, shipping and changing it · Chapter 25· 49 min read· Quick reference

The order service has eleven kinds of test. Most of them run in milliseconds, with no Spring and no Docker. A few start only the web layer of Spring. One starts the whole service with nothing to connect to. Three need Docker. This chapter shows each kind, who owns it, what it proves and what it costs. It ends with the architecture rules that keep the design in place.

The kinds of test, who owns each, and what each costsnew#

A developer changes the shipping rule and runs the tests. If every test starts the whole service and a database, the run takes minutes. The developer stops running the tests before each commit. So the service splits its tests into kinds. Each kind proves one thing, and starts only what that one thing needs.

The basics of each tool are taught elsewhere. For JUnit, Mockito and Testcontainers, see the chapter Testing. For test slices and @SpringBootTest, see the chapter Testing Spring Boot. This chapter shows how the order service combines them.

These are the kinds. The time is what the test reports gave for each class in one run of the companion on 25 October 2026. Read the times as an order of size, not as a promise:

KindExampleWhat startsOwnerTime for one classCommand
domain unitOrderTest, 15 testsnothingthe feature's developer0.05 smvn verify
application unitOrderServiceTest, 7 testsnothing, with Mockito mocksthe feature's developer0.5 smvn verify
API sliceOrderControllerTest, 23 teststhe web layer and the platform's web beansthe feature's developer6.1 smvn verify
HTTP clientStockAdapterTest, 6 testsan HTTP server from the Java librarythe developer who adds the client0.4 smvn verify
messaging unitPaymentReceivedListenerTest, 1 testnothingthe feature's developer0.05 smvn verify
mappingNoteMappingTest, 2 teststhe MongoDB converter, with no databasethe feature's developer0.2 smvn verify
wiringApplicationWiringTest, 2 teststhe whole service, connected to nothingthe service team4.0 smvn verify
