architectureArchitectureTest, 10 testsnothing, ArchUnit reads the compiled classesthe platform team writes the rules, and each service calls them1.0 smvn verify
persistenceOrderPersistenceAdapterIT, 6 testsMongoDB in Dockerthe feature's developer9.7 smvn verify -Pit

end-to-endPlaywright tests across servicesevery service and the local environmentthe QA team, in its own repositorynot measured hereQA's own command

In that run, the 112 tests of mvn verify took about 18 seconds in total. The 19 tests that need Docker took about 38 seconds more. The domain and application tests are the largest group, and they are the fastest. That is on purpose. A rule that is tested in milliseconds is tested on every change.

The last row belongs to another team. A Playwright test drives the shop's web pages, and the pages call several services. Such a test proves that the services work together. It does not belong in the repository of one service, because no single service owns it. QA runs it against the shared local environment. For that environment, see the chapter Running locally and shipping.

Each test class of the order feature is in the same package as the code it tests:

src/test/java/com/acme/orderservice/order/
  domain/model/OrderTest.java            domain unit
  domain/service/ShippingPolicyTest.java domain unit
  application/OrderServiceTest.java      application unit
  api/OrderControllerTest.java           API slice
  client/StockAdapterTest.java           HTTP client
  messaging/PaymentReceivedListenerTest.java  messaging unit
  persistence/OrderPersistenceAdapterIT.java  persistence, needs Docker

The folder src/test/java mirrors src/main/java. A test in the same package can call package-private code, so the classes under test need not be public.

In ASP.NET Core, a team often makes one test project for each layer, such as Orders.Domain.Tests and Orders.Api.Tests. Maven has one test folder for each module. So the order service puts every kind in src/test/java, in the package of the code under test. The kind shows in the class name and in what the class starts, not in a project name.

*Test and *IT: the name decides when a test runstwist#

Every test class of the order service ends in Test or in IT. The suffix decides which command runs the class. The shop's parent Project Object Model (POM) tells the surefire plugin to skip every *IT class:

<!-- mvn verify runs the fast tests only: *Test.java. The *IT.java tests need Docker. -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <argLine>@{argLine} -javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}</argLine>
        <excludes>
            <exclude>**/*IT.java</exclude>
        </excludes>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

So mvn verify runs every *Test class, and needs no Docker. A developer runs it before every commit. mvn verify -Pit also runs every *IT class, through the failsafe plugin in the profile it. The build server runs it on every pull request. A class with another name, such as OrderCheck, never runs, and nothing warns you. The build chapter owns this topic. For the trap and the plugins, see the section The name of a test class decides whether it runs. For the two commands, see the section Fast tests and integration tests.

The same parent POM gives every service its test libraries, with the scope test. They are JUnit, AssertJ, Mockito, the Spring test slices, spring-security-test, Testcontainers, ArchUnit and Awaitility. A service declares none of them. See the section Test libraries for every service, from the parent.

In .NET, a test can carry [Trait("Category", "Integration")], and the build filters on it with dotnet test --filter. In Maven, the class name is the filter.

Domain tests: plain JUnit, no Spring, no mocksnew#

The business says that an order ships only when it is paid and every line is picked. That rule is in the Order aggregate, so the test of the rule needs only an Order. It needs no database, no Spring and no mock. The class comment of the test says so:

/**
 * The order's rules, in plain JUnit: no Spring, no mocks, a few milliseconds. If a test here
 * needed Spring, the code under test would be in the wrong place.
 */
class OrderTest {
    // ...
    @Nested
    class Shipping {

        @Test
        void shipsAPaidOrderWithEveryLinePicked() {
            Order order = readyToShip();

            order.ship(CLOCK);

            assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.SHIPPED);
            assertThat(order.shippedAt()).isEqualTo(NOW);
            assertThat(order.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new OrderShipped(order.id(), NOW));
        }

        @Test
        void refusesAnUnpaidOrder() {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> newOrder().ship(CLOCK)).isInstanceOf(OrderNotPaidException.class);
        }
Reading the code
@Nested

JUnit runs the tests of an inner class as a group. The report shows OrderTest, then Shipping, then each test. The test class has five groups, one for each behaviour. They are placing, picking, shipping, cancelling and payments. A group is named after a behaviour, not after a method.

Order order = readyToShip();

This method comes from the shared test data, with a static import. It returns an order that is paid and fully picked. The next section shows it.

assertThat(order.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new OrderShipped(order.id(), NOW));

The test checks the event too. pullEvents() returns the events that the order raised, and clears them. containsExactly passes only for exactly this list, in this order. The event is a record, so it compares by value.

assertThatThrownBy(() -> newOrder().ship(CLOCK)).isInstanceOf(OrderNotPaidException.class);

This AssertJ check runs the lambda and expects it to throw this type.

The domain tests use a small set of AssertJ checks again and again. Each one reads as a sentence:

AssertJ checkWhat it checksWhere the service uses it
assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)equal by equalsalmost every test
assertThatThrownBy(() -> ...).isInstanceOf(T.class)the code throws this typeevery rule that refuses a change
.hasMessage("...") or .hasMessageContaining("...")the exception's message, whole or in partValueObjectTest, for the text of each refusal
assertThatCode(() -> ...).doesNotThrowAnyException()the code throws nothingShippingPolicyTest, the allowed case
containsExactly(a, b)exactly these elements, in this orderthe raised events
singleElement().satisfies(x -> ...)exactly one element, which passes the checks insidethe one line of a new order
extracting(Order::id)a list of one value from each elementthe page of orders in the persistence test
isInstanceOfSatisfying(T.class, x -> ...)this type, then the checks inside on itthe mapper test of the published events
hasToString("...")the result of toString()CustomerContact hides its personal data
hasValue(3)the value of an AtomicIntegercounting the calls in the client test

Two other domain tests follow the same style. ValueObjectTest checks Money, CustomerContact and the codes. ShippingPolicyTest checks the domain service with the rule across an order and its notes. The light-style NoteTest is plain JUnit too, because the note entity still holds its own rules. For the levels of Domain-Driven Design (DDD), see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The class comment of OrderTest states a rule about design. If a domain test needs Spring, the code under test is in the wrong place. Suppose a test of the shipping rule needs a Spring context. Then the rule depends on a bean, a setting or a repository. That dependency belongs in the application service, which passes plain values to the domain. So the test becomes the first warning, before any review. The architecture rule domainIsPlainJava gives the same warning in the build. See the section The architecture rules in the platform's test package.

The careful version of the other view deserves a fair answer. Some teams test their rules through the whole application, with @SpringBootTest. They say that such a test also proves the wiring, the settings and the mapping. That is true. But it starts a context for each set of settings, it needs a database, and a failure can be in any layer. The order service proves the wiring once, in the wiring test, and the rules hundreds of times, in milliseconds. Use a full test for a rule only where the rule needs the database, such as a unique index.

A light-style entity is also the stored document. So the order service adds a test of how Spring Data stores it, still without a database. NoteMappingTest builds the same converter that MongoTemplate uses, and turns a note into a document and back:

@Test
void theRaisedEventsAreNotStored() {
    Note note = Note.create(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), "Call back", "DELIVERY", true, "agent-1", CLOCK);   // has an event

    Document stored = new Document();
    converter.write(note, stored);

    assertThat(stored).containsKeys("_id", "orderId", "text", "category", "actionRequired", "createdAt", "createdBy")
            .doesNotContainKey("events");
}

converter.write fills a Document from the BSON library, so the test sees exactly what would be stored. The check proves that the list of raised events is not stored. For how the converter maps a document, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

Shared test data with a fixed clocktwist#

C#
public static class TestData
{
    public static readonly DateTimeOffset Now = new(2026, 1, 15, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
    public static readonly TimeProvider Clock = new FixedTimeProvider(Now);
}

public sealed class FixedTimeProvider(DateTimeOffset now) : TimeProvider
{
    public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => now;
}
TestData.java
/** Shared values for tests, with a fixed clock so every time is predictable. */
public final class TestData {

    public static final Instant NOW = Instant.parse("2026-01-15T09:00:00Z");
    public static final Clock CLOCK = Clock.fixed(NOW, ZoneOffset.UTC);

    public static final CustomerContact CUSTOMER = new CustomerContact("Jo Bloggs", "jo@example.com");
    public static final DeliveryMethod STANDARD = new DeliveryMethod("STANDARD");
    public static final List<OrderItem> TWO_MUGS = List.of(new OrderItem(new ProductCode("MUG-001"), 2));

    private TestData() {
    }

    /** A new order with no raised events, so each test starts clean. */
    public static Order newOrder() {
        Order order = Order.place(OrderId.newId(), CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, StockAvailability.allAvailable(), CLOCK);
        order.pullEvents();
        return order;
    }
Reading the code
public static final Clock CLOCK = Clock.fixed(NOW, ZoneOffset.UTC);

Clock comes from java.time. A fixed clock always returns the same instant. The domain receives the clock as a parameter, such as order.ship(CLOCK), so every time that a test sees is NOW. TimeProvider has the same purpose in .NET 8 and later.

private TestData() {

The private constructor stops anyone from creating an object of this class. The class is a holder for static members, like a static class in C#.

order.pullEvents();

Placing an order raises OrderPlaced. The helper pulls that event, so a test of shipping sees only the events that shipping raises.

The C# pane shows the same idea with a TimeProvider of its own. The two differ in one way. Java has a fixed clock in the Java Development Kit (JDK), so the test needs no class of its own.

The helper readyToShip() builds on newOrder(). It records a payment and picks every line, then pulls the events. One helper per state keeps the tests short, and each helper goes through the real methods of the aggregate. A test never builds an order in a state that the rules would not allow.

Application service tests with Mockitotwist#

An application service decides the order of the steps. It loads, lets the domain decide, saves, publishes and records the audit. Its test runs those steps with the real domain and with a Mockito mock of each port. No Spring context starts. The test creates the service with new:

private final OrderRepository orders = mock(OrderRepository.class);
private final NoteService notes = mock(NoteService.class);
private final ReferenceDataService referenceData = mock(ReferenceDataService.class);
private final StockChecker stock = mock(StockChecker.class);
private final DomainEventPublisher events = mock(DomainEventPublisher.class);
private final AuditLog audit = mock(AuditLog.class);

private final OrderService service = new OrderService(orders, notes, referenceData, stock, new ShippingPolicy(),
        events, audit, new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager()), CLOCK);
Reading the code
mock(OrderRepository.class)

This call creates a mock of the repository port. An unstubbed method of a mock does nothing, and returns null, an empty value or zero. For the basics, see the section Mocking.

new ShippingPolicy()

The domain service is real, not a mock. The test then checks the steps together with the real rule.

new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager())

A real transaction template runs the transactional part, with a transaction manager that does nothing. See the section A transaction manager that does nothing.

The constructor of OrderService takes every dependency as a parameter, so a test can create the service with new. This works because the service uses constructor injection. A service that read its dependencies from fields filled by Spring could not be built this way.

The most useful application test checks what does not happen. When the stock service refuses, nothing may be saved, published or audited:

C# 12, Moq
[Fact]
public void SavesNothingWhenTheStockIsNotAvailable()
{
    stock.Setup(s => s.Reserve(It.IsAny<OrderId>(), It.IsAny<IReadOnlyList<OrderItem>>()))
         .Returns(StockAvailability.Unavailable(["MUG-001"]));
    var service = new OrderService(orders.Object, stock.Object, notes.Object, events.Object);

    Assert.Throws<ProductsUnavailableException>(() => service.Place(TwoMugs));
    orders.Verify(o => o.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Never());
    notes.VerifyNoOtherCalls();
    events.VerifyNoOtherCalls();
}
Java 25
@Test
void savesNothingWhenTheStockIsNotAvailable() {
    when(stock.reserve(any(), any())).thenReturn(StockAvailability.unavailable(List.of(new ProductCode("MUG-001"))));

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.place(CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, firstNotes))
            .isInstanceOf(ProductsUnavailableException.class);
    verify(orders, never()).save(any());
    verifyNoInteractions(notes, events, audit);
}
Reading the code
when(stock.reserve(any(), any())).thenReturn(

when(...).thenReturn(...) stubs a method, like Setup(...).Returns(...) in Moq. any() matches every argument, like It.IsAny<T>(). Mockito needs no lambda around the call, because the mock records the call itself.

verify(orders, never()).save(any());

This check fails if save was called at all. It does the same as Times.Never() in Moq.

verifyNoInteractions(notes, events, audit);

This check fails if any method of these three mocks was called. The closest match in Moq is VerifyNoOtherCalls(), which fails on any call that the test did not verify.

The C# pane compiled, and its test passed, with .NET 10, Moq 4.20.72, xUnit 2.9.3 and small stand-in types. Mockito has no .Object property, because the mock is the object.

A mock can also throw. doThrow(...).when(mock).method(...) stubs a method that returns nothing. The test checksTheDeliveryMethodBeforeCallingTheStockService uses it to make the lookup check fail. Then it expects verifyNoInteractions(stock). So the service never calls another service for an order that it would refuse anyway.

A mocked repository has no database behind it. But save must return the saved copy with its next version, because the use case continues with that copy. So the test gives the mock an answer that behaves like the real adapter:

/** Makes the mocked repository behave like the real one: save returns a stored copy with the next version. */
private void saveReturnsTheStoredCopy() {
    when(orders.save(any())).thenAnswer(call -> {
        Order order = call.getArgument(0);
        long next = order.version() == null ? 0 : order.version() + 1;
        return Order.rehydrate(order.id(), next, order.customer(), order.deliveryMethod(), order.placedAt(),
                order.lines(), order.status(), order.lastPayment(), order.shippedAt(), order.cancelledAt());
    });
}

thenAnswer runs the lambda for each call, like Returns with a function in Moq. call.getArgument(0) is the order that the service passed. For why save returns a new copy, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

The light-style NoteService uses a Spring Data repository directly. Its test mocks that interface in the same way, because a Spring Data repository is an ordinary Java interface. One test of the note service also shows a small Java detail:

@Test
void listingTheNotesOfAnUnknownOrderIsNotFound() {
    // NotFoundException is non-sealed with a protected constructor, so a test can subclass it.
    doThrow(new NotFoundException("ORDER_NOT_FOUND", "Order not found") {
    }).when(orders).requireExists(ORDER_ID);

The constructor of the platform's NotFoundException is protected, and the test is in another package. So the test cannot call the constructor directly, but a subclass can. The empty braces after the constructor call create an anonymous subclass. An anonymous class is a class with no name, which the expression declares on the spot. For another use of it, see the section Getting type information back.

Another test of the note service records a decision, not a rule. aNoteNeedingActionCanStillBeAddedAfterTheOrderShipped proves that the shipping rule holds only at the moment of shipping. Its comment says that the team accepted this gap, and names the README section that explains it. A test like this keeps a known gap visible. If someone closes the gap later, the test fails, and the decision is reviewed.

Checking the order of the stepstwist#

Placing an order has six steps, and their order matters. The lookup check comes first, the stock service second, and the notes last. The test checks the order with an InOrder object, and reads the order ID with an ArgumentCaptor:

PlacedOrder placed = service.place(CUSTOMER, STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, firstNotes);

ArgumentCaptor<OrderId> reservedFor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(OrderId.class);
ArgumentCaptor<Order> saved = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class);
InOrder order = inOrder(referenceData, stock, orders, events, audit, notes);
order.verify(referenceData).requireActive("DELIVERY_METHOD", "STANDARD", "deliveryMethod");
order.verify(stock).reserve(reservedFor.capture(), eq(TWO_MUGS));          // the other service first
order.verify(orders).save(saved.capture());                                // then the order
order.verify(events).publish(List.of(new OrderPlaced(reservedFor.getValue(), STANDARD, TWO_MUGS, NOW)));
order.verify(audit).record("ORDER_PLACED", "order", reservedFor.getValue().value());
order.verify(notes).addNotes(reservedFor.getValue().value(), firstNotes);  // then its notes

assertThat(saved.getValue().id()).isEqualTo(reservedFor.getValue());       // the reserved ID is the order's ID
Reading the code
InOrder order = inOrder(referenceData, stock, orders, events, audit, notes);

An InOrder object checks calls across these mocks in the order of the verify lines. A call that happened in another order fails the test.

order.verify(stock).reserve(reservedFor.capture(), eq(TWO_MUGS));

capture() records the argument, which here is the order ID that the service chose. eq(...) matches an argument that equals TWO_MUGS.

assertThat(saved.getValue().id()).isEqualTo(reservedFor.getValue());

The service chose the ID before it called the stock service, because the ID is the idempotency key of the reservation. This line proves that the saved order has the same ID.

The order is the application layer's job, so this is the right place to test it. The domain test cannot see the stock service, and the journey test sees only the result. For why the stock call comes before the transaction, see the chapter Use cases: the application service.

Moq checks an order with a MockSequence, and the mocks must be strict for that. A strict mock throws on every call that has no setup. Mockito checks the order after the calls, with ordinary mocks. For captors and strict mocks in general, see the section Capturing an argument, and strict mocks.

A transaction manager that does nothingnew#

OrderService.place runs part of its work in a transaction. It calls the stock service first, and only then starts the transaction, with a TransactionTemplate. A unit test has no database. But the lambda inside the template holds the steps that the test must check. The platform's test package solves this with a transaction manager that does nothing:

public class NoOpTransactionManager extends AbstractPlatformTransactionManager {

    @Override
    protected Object doGetTransaction() {
        return new Object();
    }

    @Override
    protected void doBegin(Object transaction, TransactionDefinition definition) {
        // Nothing to begin.
    }

    @Override
    protected void doCommit(DefaultTransactionStatus status) {
        // Nothing to commit.
    }

    @Override
    protected void doRollback(DefaultTransactionStatus status) {
        // Nothing to roll back.
    }
}
Reading the code
extends AbstractPlatformTransactionManager {

Spring's base class does the bookkeeping of every transaction manager. It tracks whether a transaction is active, joins an existing one, and calls the four methods below at the right moments. A subclass only says how to begin, commit and roll back.

return new Object();

The base class needs an object that stands for the transaction. Any object works, because nothing reads it.

The test passes new TransactionTemplate(new NoOpTransactionManager()) to the service. The template runs the lambda, and the steps inside run in order. The class comment adds that Spring then reports an active transaction. So code that refuses to run outside a transaction, such as the platform's outbox publisher, runs in the test too.

The other way is to mock the TransactionTemplate. The careful version stubs execute with an answer that calls the callback, and that works. It costs a stub in every test class, and the stub must copy what the template does. The do-nothing manager keeps the real template, so the test runs the code that production runs, minus the database.

The methods with @Transactional, such as ship, need nothing at all. The test creates the service with new, so no proxy wraps it, and the annotation is ignored. For why a proxy is needed, see the chapter How Spring actually works. That is fine for a test of the steps. Whether the transaction really rolls back is tested in the journey test, against a real database.

API slices through the platform's own annotationtwist#

A controller test should run the real security, the real validation and the real error responses. It should not start the database or the stock client. Spring Boot's @WebMvcTest starts only Spring model-view-controller (MVC), which is the web layer of Spring. The platform adds its own web beans to that slice with a composed annotation:

/**
 * A web slice test with the platform's security, error handling and MDC interceptor, the same
 * as in production. Only the controllers and Spring MVC start, so the test runs in about a
 * second.
 *
 * <pre>{@code
 * @PlatformWebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
 * class OrderControllerTest { ... }
 * }</pre>
 *
 * <p>{@code @WebMvcTest} loads no auto-configuration from libraries, so this annotation imports
 * the platform's web-related ones by name.
 */
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
@WebMvcTest
@ImportAutoConfiguration({
        PlatformCoreAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformWebAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration.class,
        PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration.class})
@Import(TestJwtDecoderConfiguration.class)
public @interface PlatformWebMvcTest {

    /** The controllers to test. */
    @AliasFor(annotation = WebMvcTest.class, attribute = "controllers")
    Class<?>[] value() default {};
}
Reading the code
@WebMvcTest

The new annotation carries @WebMvcTest. So a class with @PlatformWebMvcTest is a web slice, as if it carried @WebMvcTest itself. An annotation on an annotation is called a meta-annotation.

@ImportAutoConfiguration({

This annotation adds the listed auto-configurations to the slice. A slice starts only a fixed set of auto-configurations, so the platform's security chain, error handler and log interceptor must be named here.

PlatformMongoWebAutoConfiguration.class})

This one holds the web part of the platform's MongoDB support. It answers a stale version with 409. It needs no database.

@Import(TestJwtDecoderConfiguration.class)

This adds a token decoder that refuses every real token. For why the slice needs it, see the section Testing security in a controller slice.

@AliasFor(annotation = WebMvcTest.class, attribute = "controllers")

@AliasFor passes the value of this attribute to @WebMvcTest. So @PlatformWebMvcTest(OrderController.class) means @WebMvcTest(controllers = OrderController.class). Without the alias, Spring would not know that value belongs to the inner annotation.

Class<?>[] value() default {};

An attribute named value is special in Java. It is the one attribute that can be written without its name, as in @PlatformWebMvcTest(OrderController.class).

A run for this book built the same kind of annotation and checked it. The slice loaded only the named controller. A path of another controller answered 404. A @MockitoBean replaced the service, and the beans of the imported auto-configuration were present. For @Target, @Retention and @Documented, see the section Permission annotations: each scope string written once.

A controller test uses the annotation with the controller, its mapper and a mock of the use case:

@PlatformWebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@Import(OrderApiMapper.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
    // ...
    @Autowired
    MockMvc mvc;

    @MockitoBean
    OrderService orders;
Reading the code
@Import(OrderApiMapper.class)

The slice creates only controllers and web beans. The mapper is a plain @Component, so the test adds it by name. The real mapper runs, so the test also checks the translation between the request classes and the use case.

@MockitoBean

This puts a Mockito mock of OrderService into the context, in place of a real bean. It comes from Spring Framework, and it replaces Boot's old @MockBean. See the section Boot 4: @MockBean becomes @MockitoBean.

Gotcha

A controller written as a static nested class slips past the slice's filter. In a run for this book, two controllers were nested classes of the @SpringBootApplication class. @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) then loaded the other controller too. Spring registers the nested classes of a configuration class directly, so the slice's filter never sees them. Keep every controller in a top-level class.

In ASP.NET Core, the closest match is a subclass of WebApplicationFactory that replaces services, and that every test class shares:

public class ShopApiFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    public Mock<IOrderService> Orders { get; } = new();

    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder) =>
        builder.ConfigureTestServices(services => services.AddSingleton(Orders.Object));
}

This factory compiled with .NET 10 and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing 10.0.12. ConfigureTestServices replaces one service, and the factory starts the whole host, with every service except the replaced one. The Spring slice starts less. It creates no use case, no repository and no client. So a forgotten mock fails at startup with a missing bean, not with a call to a real database.

Why a plain @WebMvcTest is not enoughtrap#

A developer new to the platform writes @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class), as a Spring tutorial shows. The test compiles, and the context starts. A run for this book tried it in a copy of the order service. The test asked for an order that the mocked service reported as missing:

What the run looked atWith a plain @WebMvcTest
the security chains in the contextBoot's oauth2SecurityFilterChain, not the platform's chain
the controller advices in the contextnone
GET /orders/{id} for a missing orderperform threw a ServletException, caused by OrderNotFoundException
Gotcha

Without the platform's beans, an exception never becomes a problem response. The platform's exception handler turns OrderNotFoundException into a 404 with the code ORDER_NOT_FOUND. A plain slice has no such handler. So MockMvc passes the exception to the test, and the test fails with an error, not with a wrong status. The security in the test is also the chain of Spring Boot, not the chain that runs in production. Use @PlatformWebMvcTest for every controller test.

With the platform's annotation, the same request gets the answer that production gives:

@Test
void aMissingOrderIsA404WithItsCode() throws Exception {
    OrderId id = OrderId.of(ORDER_ID);
    when(orders.get(id)).thenThrow(new OrderNotFoundException(id));

    mvc.perform(get("/orders/" + ORDER_ID).with(AGENT))
            .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.code").value("ORDER_NOT_FOUND"));
}

The mock throws OrderNotFoundException, and the platform's handler answers 404 with the code ORDER_NOT_FOUND. This is the reason the platform ships the annotation. A slice tests the HTTP contract, and the error responses are part of that contract. The 404, 409, 422 and 503 answers are all written by the platform. A slice without them tests a contract that does not exist.

A second run measured the damage. It removed only @ImportAutoConfiguration from the platform's annotation, and ran OrderControllerTest. At that time the class had 22 tests, and 18 of them failed. Eleven were in the nested class Security, and seven in TraceId. With the import back, all 22 passed.

MockMvc and JSONPath: checking the HTTP contracttwist#

A MockMvc test sends a request through Spring MVC without a server, and checks the response. The controller test checks each kind of error. Here an invalid body must list every field that failed:

@Test
void invalidFieldsAreAllListed() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(AGENT).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("""
                    { "customer": { "name": "", "email": "not-an-email" }, "deliveryMethod": "STANDARD", "lines": [] }
                    """))
            .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Invalid request"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors.length()").value(3))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'customer.name')]").exists())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'customer.email')]").exists())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'lines')]").exists());
}
Reading the code
mvc.perform(post("/orders").with(AGENT).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("""

post builds the request. with(AGENT) adds a caller with both scopes. The body is a text block, which starts and ends with three double quotes. A text block keeps a JSON body readable, with no escaped quotes. For text blocks, see the section Text blocks.

.andExpect(status().isBadRequest())

Each andExpect adds one check. The checks come from the class MockMvcResultMatchers, with static imports.

.andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors.length()").value(3))

JSONPath is a small language for finding values in JSON. $ is the whole document, and length() counts the elements of the list.

.andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[?(@.field == 'customer.name')]").exists())

The part in square brackets is a filter. It keeps the elements whose field is customer.name, and @ is the element being tested. So the check does not depend on the order of the errors.

The test class has one test for each answer that the platform writes. Together they fix the error contract of the API:

TestThe answer it expects
invalidFieldsAreAllListed400, with every invalid field in errors
anInvalidIdInThePathIsA400ThatNamesTheField400, with the field orderId
aMissingOrderIsA404WithItsCode404, with the code ORDER_NOT_FOUND
aBrokenBusinessRuleIsA422WithItsCode422, with the code ORDER_NOT_PAID
aStaleVersionIsA409409, with the code CONCURRENT_UPDATE
aWriteConflictInsideATransactionIsAlsoA409409, with the same code, for MongoDB's write conflict
anUnavailableDependencyIsA503503, when the stock client reports the service as unavailable
thePageSizeIsLimited400, with the field size, for a page of 1,000
aRequestWithoutATokenIsA401ProblemBeforeAnyController401, with the WWW-Authenticate header
aCallerWithoutTheWriteScopeIsA403AndNothingRuns403, and the use case is never called
anUnexpectedErrorIsA500WithoutItsMessage500, with a fixed text, and never the message of the exception

The last test in the table guards against a leak. Any exception that the platform does not know is a bug, and its message may hold a secret. So the test throws an exception with a secret in its message, and checks that the body does not contain it:

/** Any other exception is a bug. The answer is a fixed text, and never the exception's message. */
@Test
void anUnexpectedErrorIsA500WithoutItsMessage() throws Exception {
    doThrow(new IllegalStateException("secret: the database password is hunter2")).when(orders).ship(any());

    mvc.perform(post("/orders/" + ORDER_ID + "/ship").with(AGENT))
            .andExpect(status().isInternalServerError())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Internal error"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Something went wrong. Quote the traceId if you contact support."))
            .andExpect(content().string(not(containsString("hunter2"))));
}

content().string(...) checks the whole body as text. not and containsString are matchers from the Hamcrest library, with static imports from org.hamcrest.Matchers. Together they pass only if the secret is absent. The detail asks the caller for the traceId, so support can find the full error in the logs.

A nested class named TraceId checks one more promise. Every problem carries the traceId, even the problems that Spring MVC creates itself, such as a 405. In a slice, no tracing runs. So the test puts a trace ID into the log context before each test, with MDC.put("traceId", "trace-1"), and removes it after. For the log context, see the chapter Logging, tracing and health.

The journey test needs a value from one response for the next request. It reads the value with Jayway's JsonPath.read:

String orderId = JsonPath.read(placed, "$.orderId");
String noteId = JsonPath.read(placed, "$.noteIds[0]");

placed is the body of the response, as a string. JsonPath.read returns the value at the path, with the type of the variable. In C#, the closest match is JsonDocument.Parse(body).RootElement.GetProperty("orderId").GetString().

Security in tests, in shorttwist#

Every controller test sends its requests as a caller with a token. It does so with jwt() from spring-security-test:

/** A customer-service agent's token: a subject and both scopes. */
private static final JwtRequestPostProcessor AGENT = jwt().jwt(token -> token.subject("agent-1"))
        .authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.read"), new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_orders.write"));

jwt() puts an authentication straight into the security context of the request. It never calls the token decoder, so the test needs no token issuer. The chapter on security owns this topic. The section Testing security in a controller slice covers the defaults of jwt() and the decoder for tests. It also covers the 401 and 403 tests, and the trap of @WithMockUser. For the rule that every endpoint names a permission, see the section A rule that every endpoint names its permission.

One habit from that chapter applies to every feature. Each permission test has a partner. One caller without the scope gets 403, and one caller with the scope succeeds. A rule that only refuses could refuse everyone.

The HTTP client against a real server from the JDKtwist#

The stock client turns a reservation into JSON, adds the service's token and an idempotency key, retries a 503, and translates the answer. A mock of the client would test none of that. So StockAdapterTest starts a real HTTP server inside the test. The server is the one in the JDK, in the package com.sun.net.httpserver:

private HttpServer server;
private final AtomicInteger reservationCalls = new AtomicInteger();
private final AtomicInteger tokenCalls = new AtomicInteger();
private volatile int status = 200;
private volatile String body = """
        {"result":"RESERVED","shortSkus":[],"reservationId":"r-1"}""";
private volatile String authorization;
private volatile String idempotencyKey;
private StockAdapter adapter;

@BeforeEach
void start() throws IOException {
    server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("localhost", 0), 0);
    server.createContext("/token", exchange -> {
        tokenCalls.incrementAndGet();
        respond(exchange, 200, """
                {"access_token":"token-1","token_type":"Bearer","expires_in":3600}""");
    });
    server.createContext("/stock/reservations", exchange -> {
        reservationCalls.incrementAndGet();
        authorization = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Authorization");
        idempotencyKey = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Idempotency-Key");
        respond(exchange, status, body);
    });
    server.start();
    String baseUrl = "http://localhost:" + server.getAddress().getPort();

    HttpClientProperties properties = new HttpClientProperties();
    properties.setBaseUrl(URI.create(baseUrl));
    properties.setTokenRegistrationId("stock-service");
    ResilienceProperties resilience = new ResilienceProperties();
    resilience.getRetry().setInitialInterval(Duration.ofMillis(1));

    HttpClientFactory factory = new HttpClientFactory(RestClient::builder, () -> tokenManager(baseUrl + "/token"));
    adapter = new StockAdapter(factory.create(StockHttpClient.class, properties), new ResilientCalls(resilience));
}
Reading the code
server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("localhost", 0), 0);

Port 0 lets the system choose a free port when the server binds. So two test runs on one machine never fight over a port. getAddress().getPort() later reads the port that was chosen.

server.createContext("/token", exchange -> {

Each context answers one path. The first one plays the token issuer, so the client-credentials flow runs for real. The second one plays the stock service and records the headers it received.

private volatile int status = 200;

server.start() starts the server in a new background thread, and the server handles every request on that thread. The test sets status on its own thread, and the server reads it on the other. volatile makes each write visible to the other thread. For more, see the section volatile means more in Java.

private final AtomicInteger reservationCalls = new AtomicInteger();

The server thread counts the calls. An atomic variable adds one safely from any thread. For more, see the section Atomics.

resilience.getRetry().setInitialInterval(Duration.ofMillis(1));

The platform's default waits 200 milliseconds before the first retry, and about twice as long before the next one. The test sets 1 millisecond, so a test of retries does not wait.

new HttpClientFactory(RestClient::builder, () -> tokenManager(baseUrl + "/token"));

The test builds the client with the platform's real factory, as Spring would. So the timeouts, the token interceptor and the error handling are the production ones.

The tests then change the answer and check the result. This one proves the retries:

@Test
void retriesServerErrorsThenReportsTheServiceAsUnavailable() {
    status = 503;
    body = "{}";

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> adapter.reserve(OrderId.newId(), TWO_MUGS)).isInstanceOf(DownstreamServiceException.class);
    assertThat(reservationCalls).hasValue(3);
}

hasValue(3) proves that three calls reached the server, which is one call and two retries. Then the adapter reported the service as unavailable, and the platform answers that with 503. The other tests of the class check the translation of each answer, the token and the idempotency key. They also check an unknown answer, and one service token shared by two users. The client chapter explains each behaviour. See the chapter Calling other services.

The platform's own ResilientCallsTest uses the same trick for fast retries:

private static ResilienceProperties fastRetries() {
    ResilienceProperties properties = new ResilienceProperties();
    properties.getRetry().setInitialInterval(Duration.ofMillis(1));
    return properties;
}

The method sets setInitialInterval(Duration.ofMillis(1)), the same one line as the client test.

Why not WireMock? WireMock is the better tool when a test needs delays, faults or many stubs, and the local environment uses it. For a test of one client, the JDK server needs no library and starts in milliseconds. The test reads the received headers from plain fields. For WireMock in a test, see the section WireMock: faking an HTTP dependency. A .NET developer would use WireMock.Net here. Both choices are sound.

Messaging unit teststwist#

Two classes of the order feature touch messages. The mapper decides which domain events leave the service. The listener turns a payment event into a call of the use case. Both are tested without a queue.

The mapper test checks the published events and the events that stay inside:

@Test
void keepsInternalEventsInternal() {
    assertThat(mapper.toIntegrationEvent(new LinePicked(OrderId.newId(), LineId.newId(), NOW))).isEmpty();
}

toIntegrationEvent returns an Optional, and an empty one means "not published". A picked line is an internal fact, so no other service hears about it. The other two tests check that a placed order and a shipped order become versioned events with plain types.

The listener test is harder. The listener calls the platform's inbox, and the inbox calls the listener's handler back. The inbox is platform code with tests of its own. So this test replaces it with a mock that only passes the event through:

@Test
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
void translatesTheEventAndCallsTheUseCase() {
    doAnswer(call -> {
        ((Consumer<PaymentReceivedV1>) call.getArgument(2)).accept(call.getArgument(1));
        return null;
    }).when(inbox).process(eq("order-service.payment-received"), any(PaymentReceivedV1.class), any());
    OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();

    listener.on(new PaymentReceivedV1("event-1", NOW, orderId.value(), "PAY-1", new BigDecimal("12.5"), "GBP", NOW));

    ArgumentCaptor<Payment> payment = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Payment.class);
    verify(orders).recordPayment(eq(orderId), payment.capture());
    assertThat(payment.getValue().amount()).isEqualTo(Money.of("12.50", "GBP"));
}
Reading the code
doAnswer(call -> {

doAnswer stubs a method that returns nothing with code that runs on each call. Here the code plays the inbox. It takes the handler and the event from the call, and runs the handler.

((Consumer<PaymentReceivedV1>) call.getArgument(2)).accept(call.getArgument(1));

The third argument of process is the handler, a Consumer. Mockito returns it with no type argument, because generics are erased at run time. So the test casts it. For erasure, see the section What erasure takes away.

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")

The compiler cannot check that cast, and warns about it. This annotation tells the compiler that the test accepts the risk. Put it on the smallest scope that needs it, here one method.

assertThat(payment.getValue().amount()).isEqualTo(Money.of("12.50", "GBP"));

The event carried 12.5, and the captured payment holds 12.50 in pounds. So the test proves the translation into the domain's money.

A third test, PaymentReceivedV1Test, reads JSON into the consumed event with a real Jackson mapper. It proves that unknown fields are ignored. It also proves that an envelope of Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) is refused, instead of being read as an event full of nulls. For that trap, see the section The SNS envelope, and the null trap.

MongoDB in Docker: the replica settrap#

The persistence tests need a real MongoDB. The platform starts one in Docker, with Testcontainers, in a test configuration that every service imports:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class MongoTestContainerConfiguration {

    public static final String IMAGE = "mongo:8.0.34";

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    MongoDBContainer mongoDbContainer() {
        return new MongoDBContainer(IMAGE).withReplicaSet();
    }
}
Reading the code
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)

This is a configuration class for tests only. A test adds it with @Import.

@Bean

The container is a bean. Spring starts it when the context starts, and stops it when the context closes. The context is cached and shared by test classes with the same configuration, so they share one container too. For the context cache, see the section Test configuration.

@ServiceConnection

Spring Boot reads the address of the running container, and sets the MongoDB connection from it. The test needs no spring.mongodb.uri.

public static final String IMAGE = "mongo:8.0.34";

The image names an exact version, and the local environment uses the same version. Use the MongoDB version that your DocumentDB cluster is compatible with.

PredictA MongoDB container without withReplicaSet()#
Spring Boot 4 uses Testcontainers 2. A developer removes .withReplicaSet() from this configuration, because the container seems to work without it. Then a persistence test saves an order inside a transaction. What happens?
@Bean
@ServiceConnection
MongoDBContainer mongoDbContainer() {
    return new MongoDBContainer(IMAGE).withReplicaSet();
}
Show the answer
The transaction fails with UncategorizedMongoDbException: This MongoDB deployment does not support retryable writes. Please add retryWrites=false to your connection string.

The Testcontainers 2 class starts a stand-alone MongoDB unless you ask for a replica set.

MongoDB runs a transaction only on a replica set. A stand-alone server refuses it.

The old class, org.testcontainers.containers.MongoDBContainer, always started a replica set. The new class, org.testcontainers.mongodb.MongoDBContainer, starts one only after withReplicaSet().

So an upgrade that changes only the import turns transactions off in every test. Keep withReplicaSet(). DocumentDB always runs as a replica set.

Testcontainers 2 has non-generic container classes in new packages. The old generic class still ships, deprecated. Boot 4.1 can still connect to it, but its connection support is marked for removal in Boot 4.2. So move to the new class, and keep the replica set.

Many guides start the container in a static field instead. The test class then carries @Testcontainers, and the field carries @Container and @ServiceConnection. The section Testing without a cluster shows that style. It works, but each test class declares the container again. The bean in a shared configuration declares it once, for every test class and every service.

Testcontainers for .NET does the same job in C#. The two libraries have different code, but the idea is the same. A real database runs in Docker for the length of the tests.

Persistence tests with the platform's data slicetwist#

A persistence test checks that an aggregate goes into MongoDB and comes back whole. It needs the database, the platform's MongoDB setup and the adapter, and nothing else. The platform has a slice annotation for that:

@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
@DataMongoTest(properties = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled=false")
@ImportAutoConfiguration(PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)
@Import(MongoTestContainerConfiguration.class)
public @interface PlatformDataMongoTest {
}
Reading the code
@DataMongoTest(properties = "platform.mongo.migrations.enabled=false")

@DataMongoTest is the slice of Spring Boot for document data. It starts Spring Data MongoDB and the repositories. The property turns the platform's migrations off, so each test sees only the data it writes.

@ImportAutoConfiguration(PlatformMongoAutoConfiguration.class)

This adds the platform's MongoDB setup, such as the transaction manager and the DocumentDB settings. So a test runs with the settings of production.

@Import(MongoTestContainerConfiguration.class)

This adds the container from the section above.

The test of the full-style adapter imports the adapter and its mapper:

/** The full-style adapter, its mapper and optimistic locking against a real MongoDB replica set. */
@PlatformDataMongoTest
@Import({OrderPersistenceAdapter.class, OrderDocumentMapper.class})
class OrderPersistenceAdapterIT {

The class name ends in IT, so only mvn verify -Pit runs it. Its tests check the round trip of a whole aggregate, and the stored names and types. They also check the version after a save, a page of orders, and the conflict between two writers. One test reads the stored document with MongoTemplate, to see the shape that another tool would see:

Document stored = mongo.findById(order.id().value(), Document.class, "orders");

assertThat(stored.getList("lines", Document.class).getFirst()).containsKey("lineId").doesNotContainKey("_id");
assertThat(stored.get("lastPayment", Document.class).get("amount")).isInstanceOf(Decimal128.class);

The check proves two decisions of the storage chapter. The ID of a line is stored as lineId, and money is stored as Decimal128, not as a string. For both decisions, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

@DataMongoTest rolls nothing back after a test, unlike the slice for Jakarta Persistence (JPA). So each test must work beside the data that other tests left behind. No test counts all the documents in a collection. Each test creates orders with new IDs, and looks only at those orders. The page test, for example, checks that the result contains its cancelled order, not that the page holds exactly one.

The light-style note has its own test, NoteRepositoryIT. It uses the same annotation and imports nothing, because Spring Data creates the repository itself.

One optimistic-lock test for each aggregatenew#

Two agents open the same order. One cancels it, and the other picks a line. The second save must fail, or the cancel is lost. The @Version field makes it fail. A test proves it once for each aggregate, because each feature stores its aggregate in its own way:

@Test
void rejectsAStaleCopy() {
    Order saved = orders.save(newOrder());
    Order firstCopy = orders.get(saved.id());
    Order secondCopy = orders.get(saved.id());

    firstCopy.cancel(CLOCK);
    orders.save(firstCopy);
    secondCopy.pickLine(secondCopy.lines().getFirst().id(), CLOCK);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> orders.save(secondCopy)).isInstanceOf(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class);
}

Both copies are loaded with version 0. The first save writes version 1. The second save must throw OptimisticLockingFailureException. It still says version 0, so Spring Data finds no matching document. The platform turns that exception into a 409, which the controller test checks with a mock. This test proves the cause, and the controller test proves the answer.

The note feature has the same test, and it shows a difference of the light style:

assertThatThrownBy(() -> notes.save(secondCopy)).isInstanceOf(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class);
// Spring Data wrote the next version into the object before the update failed, so the
// failed copy must not be saved again: load the note afresh instead.
assertThat(secondCopy.version()).isEqualTo(1L);

The failed save changed the version of the object anyway, so secondCopy.version() is 1. So a retry with the same object would overwrite the other agent's change. The test records that fact, and the rule that follows from it. Load the note again, and never retry with the failed copy.

A third test, aConcurrentUpdateInsideTransactionsIsAWriteConflict, runs two writers inside two open transactions. MongoDB then refuses the second writer earlier, with a write conflict. For the two kinds of conflict, see the chapter Transactions in depth.

The wiring test: the whole service, connected to nothingnew#

A developer renames a setting in application.yml, and every unit test passes. The service then fails to start in the test environment, because a bean needs the old key. No fast test started the whole application. So the order service has one test that starts every bean with every setting, while nothing connects to anything:

/**
 * Starts the whole service with every setting, while nothing connects to anything. It catches a
 * missing bean, a cycle, a bad property or a wrong auto-configuration order in seconds, without
 * Docker. The settings are in {@code application-wiring.yml}.
 */
@SpringBootTest
@org.springframework.test.context.ActiveProfiles("wiring")
class ApplicationWiringTest {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationContext context;

    @Test
    void theContextStartsWithThePlatformsBeans() {
        assertThat(context.getBean(PlatformTransactionManager.class)).isInstanceOf(MongoTransactionManager.class);
        assertThat(context.getBeansOfType(SecurityFilterChain.class)).containsOnlyKeys("platformSecurityFilterChain");
    }

    /** Spring Boot 4 reads spring.mongodb.uri; the old spring.data.mongodb.uri would be ignored silently. */
    @Test
    void usesTheConfiguredMongoUri() {
        ConnectionString used = context.getBean(MongoConnectionDetails.class).getConnectionString();

        assertThat(used.getHosts()).containsExactly("localhost:1");
        assertThat(used.getDatabase()).isEqualTo("wiring-test");
    }
}
Reading the code
@SpringBootTest

This starts the whole application context, as the service does in production. If any bean cannot be created, the test fails, and the message names the bean.

@org.springframework.test.context.ActiveProfiles("wiring")

The profile wiring loads application-wiring.yml from the test resources. That file gives every setting a value that connects to nothing.

.containsOnlyKeys("platformSecurityFilterChain");

Exactly one security chain exists, and it is the platform's. This catches a wrong order of auto-configurations. See the section Why the platform's chain is created before Boot's.

assertThat(used.getHosts()).containsExactly("localhost:1");

The service uses the URI from the setting. Spring Boot 4 ignores the old key spring.data.mongodb.uri without a warning, and would connect to localhost:27017 instead. This line catches that.

The profile makes every connection lazy or impossible:

spring:
  mongodb:
    # Nothing listens on port 1. The driver connects lazily, and gives up after 100 ms.
    uri: mongodb://localhost:1/wiring-test?serverSelectionTimeoutMS=100
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: ""
          jwk-set-uri: http://localhost:1/jwks
      # ...
  cloud:
    aws:
      sqs:
        enabled: false
      credentials:
        access-key: test
        secret-key: test

platform:
  # ...
  mongo:
    migrations:
      enabled: false
  messaging:
    outbox:
      resend-enabled: false

clients:
  stock:
    base-url: http://localhost:1

Each value stops one kind of connection. For example, serverSelectionTimeoutMS=100 makes a query give up after 100 milliseconds:

SettingWhy it lets the service start without a network
spring.mongodb.uri on port 1, with serverSelectionTimeoutMS=100the driver connects only when a query runs, and a query would give up after 100 ms
migrations enabled: falsethe migrations would write to MongoDB at startup
issuer-uri empty, jwk-set-uri on port 1Spring fetches keys only for a real token, and no test sends one
sqs enabled: falsethe SQS listeners would start polling a queue
credentials access-key and secret-keythe AWS client needs some credentials to be created
resend-enabled: falsethe outbox resender would read MongoDB on a schedule
clients.stock.base-url on port 1the client is created with a URL, and is never called

The test took about 4 seconds in the companion's run, with no Docker. It catches the mistakes that only a whole context shows. These are a missing bean, a cycle between beans, and a setting that does not bind. The test also checks results that depend on names in strings. The platform's beforeName lists name Spring Boot's classes as strings, which the compiler cannot check. The test does not read the strings. It checks their effect, one security chain, the platform's. If an upgrade renamed one of those classes and the order went wrong, that check would fail. So run the test after every upgrade of Spring Boot or the platform.

The OpenAPI contract test uses the same profile. Both tests start the same context, so the second one reuses the cached context and starts faster.

In ASP.NET Core, WebApplicationFactory<Program> starts the host in the same way. A .NET team gets a similar test by starting the factory with settings that point nowhere, and resolving a few services. The Spring test also catches a wrong order of auto-configurations. That problem comes from Spring Boot's auto-configuration, so a .NET test has nothing like it to catch.

The journey test: real MongoDB and a real SNS and SQS emulatortwist#

A journey test runs one business story through the whole service. An agent places an order with a note. The order cannot ship while the note needs action. It cannot ship before the payment arrives, or before every line is picked. Then it ships. The test uses a real MongoDB, and Floci, a free emulator of SNS and Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS), both in Docker. Only the stock service is mocked, at its port:

@SpringBootTest(properties = {
        "spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=",
        "spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=http://localhost:1/jwks",
        "spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.stock-service.client-secret=test",
        "spring.security.oauth2.client.provider.shop-identity.token-uri=http://localhost:1/token",
        "clients.stock.base-url=http://localhost:1",
        "messaging.queues.payment-received=" + JourneyAwsResources.PAYMENT_QUEUE,
        "platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled=false"})
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import({MongoTestContainerConfiguration.class, AwsTestContainerConfiguration.class, OrderJourneyIT.Resources.class})
class OrderJourneyIT {
Reading the code
@SpringBootTest(properties = {

The properties are set for this test class only, on top of application.yml. They replace the environment variables that production sets.

"platform.messaging.outbox.resend-enabled=false"})

The scheduled resender is off. So every event in the test is sent by the normal path, right after the commit. The test does not depend on the timing of a schedule.

@AutoConfigureMockMvc

@SpringBootTest gives no MockMvc without this annotation. See the section MockMvc and TestRestTemplate under @SpringBootTest.

@Import({MongoTestContainerConfiguration.class, AwsTestContainerConfiguration.class, OrderJourneyIT.Resources.class})

The test imports the two containers from the platform. Resources is a small configuration inside the test. It creates the topic, the queues and the subscription in Floci, as the local environment's init script does.

In the class, @MockitoBean StockChecker stock replaces the stock port. The test drives the story through MockMvc, and sends the payment through the real queue, twice:

// The payment service's event arrives through SQS, twice, as at-least-once delivery allows.
String payment = paymentEvent(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), orderId);
aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(payment));
aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(payment));
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() ->
        mvc.perform(get("/orders/" + orderId).with(agent)).andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value("PAID")));
Reading the code
aws.sqs.sendMessage(message -> message.queueUrl(aws.paymentQueueUrl).messageBody(payment));

The test sends the same event twice, as SQS may deliver it. The inbox must record the payment once.

await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() ->

The listener handles the message on its own thread, a moment later. Awaitility runs the check again and again until it passes, or until 20 seconds have passed. A fixed sleep would be either too short or too slow.

After the order ships, the test checks the records that no response shows. It reads them with MongoTemplate, and with a queue that listens to the service's topic:

// The audit log: every change once, by the agent, except the payment, which the system recorded.
List<Document> orderAudit = mongo.find(query(where("resourceId").is(orderId)).with(Sort.by("at")),
        Document.class, "audit_log");
assertThat(orderAudit).extracting(entry -> entry.getString("action"))
        .containsExactly("ORDER_PLACED", "PAYMENT_RECORDED", "LINE_PICKED", "ORDER_SHIPPED");
assertThat(orderAudit).extracting(entry -> entry.getString("actor"))
        .containsExactly("agent-1", "system", "agent-1", "agent-1");
Reading the code
mongo.find(query(where("resourceId").is(orderId)).with(Sort.by("at")),

query and where are static imports from two classes of Spring Data. The line reads as a sentence. It finds the audit entries of this order, sorted by time.

.containsExactly("agent-1", "system", "agent-1", "agent-1");

The agent did three things, and the payment listener did one, as the system actor. The payment appears once, although the event arrived twice.

The same test then waits until both published events reach the subscribed queue, and until the outbox collection is empty. So one journey proves the rules, the audit, the inbox, the outbox and the delivery to SNS together.

The other journeys are short. Each checks one thing:

  • An order and its notes are stored together, or not at all.
  • An inactive delivery method is refused before the stock service is called.
  • A caller without a token gets 401, and a caller without the write scope gets 403.
  • The lookup values are seeded and cached.
  • A message that is not the event ends in the dead-letter queue.

Each one checks something that only the whole service with real infrastructure can show.

Pragmatic choice: The stock service is mocked in the journey test

The strict rule. An integration test of a service runs against real copies of everything the service calls.

What we do. The journey mocks the StockChecker port with @MockitoBean. The real stock client is tested against a real HTTP server in StockAdapterTest.

Why. A real stock service would bring its own database and its own dependencies into the test. The port is the boundary that the order service owns. The client test already proves everything on the other side of it.

When to stop. When a bug appears that only the real pair of services shows, such as a disagreement about the JSON. Then add a contract test between the two teams, or a QA journey against the local environment.

An older version of such a test can depend on a failure. If SNS is set to an address where nothing listens, the outbox sends nothing, and the events stay in the outbox. A test can then check the outbox and pass. But that test relies on a network failure and on timing, and it proves nothing about delivery. The order service sends to a real emulator, turns the resender off, and waits for the events to arrive. That proves the path that production uses.

In ASP.NET Core, the same test would use WebApplicationFactory<Program> with containers from Testcontainers for .NET. The design is the same. Only the stock port is replaced, and everything else is real.

The OpenAPI drift testtwist#

The committed file contracts/openapi.yaml is the contract that other teams read. A hand-written file drifts from the code, and nothing warns anyone. So a test generates the document from the controllers, and compares it with the committed file:

@Test
void theCommittedContractMatchesTheCode() throws Exception {
    String generated = mvc.perform(get("/v3/api-docs.yaml").with(jwt()))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    write(GENERATED, generated);
    if (Boolean.getBoolean("openapi.update")) {
        write(COMMITTED, generated);
    }

    assertThat(COMMITTED).as("contracts/openapi.yaml is missing; run mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true").exists();
    assertThat(Files.readString(COMMITTED))
            .as("contracts/openapi.yaml differs from the code. Review target/openapi.yaml, "
                    + "then run mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true and commit the file.")
            .isEqualTo(generated);
}
Reading the code
mvc.perform(get("/v3/api-docs.yaml").with(jwt()))

springdoc serves the document at this path. The test asks for it through MockMvc, so it needs no server and no port. The document needs a token, like every path.

if (Boolean.getBoolean("openapi.update")) {

Boolean.getBoolean reads a system property, not a string. mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true sets it, and the test then writes the committed file.

.as("contracts/openapi.yaml differs from the code. Review target/openapi.yaml, "

as(...) gives the check a message for its failure. The message says what to do, so a developer who never saw the test can fix the build.

The test runs in the wiring profile, so it needs no Docker. Every API change then shows as a diff of contracts/openapi.yaml in the pull request. The contracts chapter owns this topic. For the drift check, see the section Exporting the contract, and the drift check. For code first against contract first, and for event schemas, see the chapter API and event contracts.

The events have a contract test too. PublishedEventSchemaTest turns each published domain event into its integration event with the real mapper. It writes the event with the service's JSON mapper, and validates the JSON against the committed schema in contracts/events. A renamed or removed field then fails the build before a consumer breaks. The test is a @JsonTest slice, so it starts only Jackson. For the schemas and the validator, see the section Event contracts: a JSON schema for each event.

The architecture rules in the platform's test packagetwist#

The order service has rules about its own structure. The domain uses no framework, a controller uses no repository, and features meet only through their services. A rule in a document is forgotten. A rule that fails the build is kept. ArchUnit reads the compiled classes and checks such rules. For the basics, see the section ArchUnit: architecture rules as tests.

The rules belong to the platform, so every service checks the same ones. They are in the library's test package, and a service calls them from a plain JUnit test:

private static final String BASE = "com.acme.orderservice";
/** The features in the full style, whose application layer must use ports only. */
private static final String ORDER = BASE + ".order";

private static final JavaClasses CLASSES = new ClassFileImporter()
        .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
        .importPackages(BASE);

@Test
void domainIsPlainJava() {
    ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava().check(CLASSES);
}
Reading the code
.withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)

The importer skips the test classes. A test may break the rules on purpose, as the next sections show. A run for this book imported no class named *Test with this option, against 15 without it.

.importPackages(BASE);

The importer reads every compiled class of the service. The field is static, so the classes are read once for all the tests of the class.

ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava().check(CLASSES);

check throws an AssertionError that lists every violation. So the test fails like any other test.

The first rule is the most important one:

/** A {@code domain} package uses no framework, no adapter and no other layer. */
public static ArchRule domainIsPlainJava() {
    return noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage(
                    "org.springframework..", "com.mongodb..", "org.bson..", "jakarta..",
                    "tools.jackson..", "com.fasterxml..", "io.awspring..",
                    "..application..", "..api..", "..persistence..", "..client..", "..messaging..",
                    "com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")
            .as("A domain package is plain Java");
}
Reading the code
noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")

The rule is about every class in a package whose name contains domain. Two dots match any part of a package name.

"tools.jackson..", "com.fasterxml..", "io.awspring..",

The classes of Jackson 3 are in tools.jackson, but its annotations are still in com.fasterxml. So the rule names both.

"com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")

The domain may use the platform's domain package, with its base classes, but not the platform's web or storage code.

.as("A domain package is plain Java");

This text replaces the generated sentence in the failure message.

The other rules of the platform follow the same pattern. Each is a method that returns an ArchRule:

RuleWhat it stops
domainIsPlainJavaa framework, an adapter or another layer in the domain
applicationDoesNotUseAdapters(features)HTTP, MongoDB or an adapter in the application layer of a full-style feature
apiDoesNotUsePersistenceOrClientsa controller that reaches past the application layer
controllersDoNotUseRepositoriesa controller that skips the use case and its rules
everyEndpointHasAPermissionan endpoint that anyone with a token can call
documentsOnlyInPersistenceOrModela stored document outside a persistence or model package
httpClientsOnlyInClienta declarative HTTP client outside a client package
entitiesHaveNoPublicSettersan entity that can be changed without its rules
featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication(base)a feature that reaches into another feature's domain or storage
servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities(base)a service that uses another feature's repository or entity

The rules know the three levels of DDD. A rule about the domain package affects only full-style features, because the other features have none. The rule about the application layer takes the full-style features as a parameter. So the light and simple features are not held to rules that they do not need.

Many guides write ArchUnit tests in another style. A class carries @AnalyzeClasses, and each rule is a field with @ArchTest. That style needs ArchUnit's own JUnit engine. The platform's style needs only plain JUnit tests that call methods. The methods can take parameters, such as the base package, and a library can ship them like any other code.

ArchUnitNET is the C# fork of ArchUnit, and its rules read the same way:

IArchRule rule = Types().That().ResideInNamespace("Shop.Domain")
    .Should().NotDependOnAny(Types().That().ResideInNamespace("Microsoft.AspNetCore"));
Assert.True(rule.HasNoViolations(Shop));

This rule compiled, and its test passed, with .NET 10 and ArchUnitNET 0.13.4. Shop is the loaded assembly of the stand-in project.

A custom ArchConditionnew#

Some rules cannot be said with the fluent sentences. "A feature may use another feature only through that feature's application package" is one of them. The rule depends on which feature a class is in, and which feature its dependency is in. So the platform writes the check itself:

public static ArchRule featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication(String basePackage) {
    return classes().that().resideInAPackage(basePackage + "..")
            .should(new ArchCondition<>("use other features only through their application package") {
                @Override
                public void check(JavaClass origin, ConditionEvents events) {
                    String feature = featureOf(basePackage, origin.getPackageName());
                    if (feature == null) {
                        return;
                    }
                    for (Dependency dependency : origin.getDirectDependenciesFromSelf()) {
                        String target = dependency.getTargetClass().getBaseComponentType().getPackageName();
                        String targetFeature = featureOf(basePackage, target);
                        if (targetFeature == null || targetFeature.equals(feature) || targetFeature.equals("shared")) {
                            continue;
                        }
                        String inFeature = target.substring((basePackage + "." + targetFeature).length());
                        boolean allowed = inFeature.startsWith(".application") && !inFeature.startsWith(".application.port");
                        if (!allowed) {
                            events.add(SimpleConditionEvent.violated(dependency, dependency.getDescription()));
                        }
                    }
                }
            })
            .as("Features use each other only through their application package");
}
Reading the code
.should(new ArchCondition<>("use other features only through their application package") {

An ArchCondition is a check that ArchUnit runs on each selected class. The text is the description in the failure message. The class is anonymous and declared on the spot, because only this rule uses it.

public void check(JavaClass origin, ConditionEvents events) {

ArchUnit calls this method once for each class. JavaClass describes the class from its bytecode. events collects the violations.

for (Dependency dependency : origin.getDirectDependenciesFromSelf()) {

Each dependency is one use of another class, such as a field type, a parameter, a method call or a constructor call.

dependency.getTargetClass().getBaseComponentType().getPackageName();

For an array such as Order[], the base component type is Order. So an array cannot hide a forbidden class.

boolean allowed = inFeature.startsWith(".application") && !inFeature.startsWith(".application.port");

Another feature may be used only through its application package, and not through its ports. A port is that feature's own boundary to storage or another service.

events.add(SimpleConditionEvent.violated(dependency, dependency.getDescription()));

This records one violation. The description names the two classes, so the failure says where to look.

A run for this book wrote a condition of this kind, and it reported both of the classes that broke it, each with its message. The helper featureOf takes the part of the package name after the base package. For com.acme.orderservice.note.model, it returns note.

The shared package is open to every feature. It holds the permission annotations and the audit names. A shared package is a common place for code that grows without an owner. Keep it small, and move anything with rules into a feature.

The guardrail rulesnew#

Most rules keep the layers apart. Five rules guard against the mistakes that a pull request review misses most often. Each one is small, and each one has a reason that the rest of the part explains.

No public setter on an entity. An entity changes only through methods that apply its rules. A public setter lets any code skip the rules:

public static ArchRule entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters() {
    DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> entities = assignableTo(Entity.class)
            .or(DescribedPredicate.describe("light-style entities",
                    (JavaClass type) -> type.isAnnotatedWith(Document.class)
                            && !type.getPackageName().contains(".persistence")));
    return methods().that().areDeclaredInClassesThat(entities)
            .and().haveNameMatching("set[A-Z].*")
            .should().notBePublic()
            .allowEmptyShould(true)
            .as("Entities have no public setter");
}
Reading the code
DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> entities = assignableTo(Entity.class)

A predicate selects classes. This one selects every subclass of the platform's Entity, which covers the full-style domain.

(JavaClass type) -> type.isAnnotatedWith(Document.class)

The light-style note is a stored document outside a persistence package. So the predicate selects such documents too. A persistence document only holds data, and may have setters.

.allowEmptyShould(true)

This lets the rule pass when it selects no method at all. A service whose entities have no setters, or that has no entities, then passes.

Features only through services. A service never takes another feature's repository or entity. It asks that feature's service, which checks that feature's rules. The rule servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities states the most common case of the wider rule above. Its failure message is clearer.

No repository in a controller. A controller that calls a repository skips the use case, its rules, its events and its audit:

/** A controller calls a service, never a repository, so every rule and check runs. */
public static ArchRule controllersDoNotUseRepositories() {
    return noClasses().that().areAnnotatedWith(RestController.class)
            .should().dependOnClassesThat(are(assignableTo(org.springframework.data.repository.Repository.class))
                    .or(assignableTo(com.acme.platform.domain.Repository.class)))
            .as("Controllers use no repository");
}

The rule names both kinds of Repository. One is the Spring Data interface, which the light and simple features use. The other is the platform's port, which the full-style feature uses.

A permission on every endpoint. The permission is checked on the controllers, so a new endpoint without an annotation is open to any caller with a token. For the rule and its test, see the section A rule that every endpoint names its permission.

HTTP clients only in client packages. A declarative client is an interface with @HttpExchange. If one appears in a domain or application package, the anti-corruption layer is gone:

/** Declarative HTTP clients live in a client package, behind a port. */
public static ArchRule httpClientsOnlyInClient() {
    return classes().that().areAnnotatedWith(HttpExchange.class)
            .should().resideInAPackage("..client..")
            .as("@HttpExchange interfaces live only in client packages");
}

resideInAPackage("..client..") accepts any package whose name contains client.

A rule that never fails proves nothing. So the service has a test that feeds each guardrail a class that breaks it:

/** A light-style entity, a document outside persistence, that someone gave a setter. */
@Document("parcels")
static class ParcelWithASetter {
    private String status;

    public void setStatus(String status) {
        this.status = status;
    }
}

@Test
void anEntityWithAPublicSetterFailsTheBuild() {
    JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter().importClasses(ParcelWithASetter.class);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> ArchitectureRules.entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters().check(classes))
            .isInstanceOf(AssertionError.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("setStatus");
}

The broken class is a static nested class of the test, so it exists only in the test code. importClasses imports just that one class. The check must fail, and its message must name the setter.
