The same test class does this for the endpoint rule, with a controller that forgot its permission, and with one that did not.

In .NET, ArchUnitNET can state the same rules. The rules are not the hard part in either language. The hard part is agreeing on them as a team, and keeping them in one shared place.

Adding the rules to an existing servicetwist#

A service that is five years old breaks the rules in forty places. If the rules fail the build today, nobody adds them. ArchUnit has an answer, which the platform's class comment names:

* <p>To add the rules to an existing service with old violations, wrap a rule in
* {@code FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule)}. ArchUnit then records today's violations, and only new
* ones fail the build.

So FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule) takes any rule. In the test, the call becomes FreezingArchRule.freeze(ArchitectureRules.domainIsPlainJava()).check(CLASSES). A run for this book with ArchUnit 1.5.1 showed the whole cycle:

StepWhat happened
the plain rule, on a domain class with @Componentthe rule failed
the frozen rule, first runit passed, and wrote a store of today's violations
the frozen rule, same codeit passed again
the frozen rule, after a new violation was addedit failed, and named only the new violation

The store is a folder of text files. Its default name is archunit_store. The first run creates it only if a file named archunit.properties allows it, with freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=true. That setting is false by default. The run also set freeze.store.default.path to choose the folder.

The order service keeps a small example of a frozen rule. Two small controllers model an older service. The old one was written before the rule existed, and its violation is in the store:

class FrozenRuleTest {

    @RestController
    static class OldReportController {

        @GetMapping("/old-report")
        String oldReport() {
            return "written before every endpoint needed a permission";
        }
    }

    @RestController
    static class NewReportController {

        @GetMapping("/new-report")
        String newReport() {
            return "written after the rule, and still without a permission";
        }
    }

    @Test
    void theOldViolationIsRecordedSoTheRulePasses() {
        JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter().importClasses(OldReportController.class);

        FreezingArchRule.freeze(ArchitectureRules.everyEndpointHasAPermission()).check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void aNewViolationFailsTheBuild() {
        JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter().importClasses(OldReportController.class,
                NewReportController.class);

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> FreezingArchRule.freeze(ArchitectureRules.everyEndpointHasAPermission()).check(classes))
                .isInstanceOf(AssertionError.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("newReport")
                .hasMessageNotContaining("oldReport");
    }
}
Reading the code
FreezingArchRule.freeze(ArchitectureRules.everyEndpointHasAPermission()).check(classes);

The platform's rule, frozen. ArchUnit compares today's violations with the store. A violation in the store passes. A violation that is not in the store fails the check.

.hasMessageContaining("newReport")

The second test adds a new controller with the same mistake. The check fails, and its message names only the new method.

.hasMessageNotContaining("oldReport");

The old violation is still known, so the message leaves it out. A reviewer sees only what the change added.

The settings are in archunit.properties, at the root of the test classpath:

# ArchUnit's settings, read from the test classpath.
#
# A frozen rule (FrozenRuleTest) keeps the violations it accepts in a store: a folder of text
# files, committed with the code. Review every change to it in the pull request, because a
# store that grows means that someone froze a new violation.
freeze.store.default.path=src/test/resources/archunit_store

# Never create a store by accident, for example in CI, where it would accept every violation
# without a review. To create the store, set this to true once, run the test, commit the
# folder, and set it back to false.
freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=false
Reading the code
freeze.store.default.path=src/test/resources/archunit_store

The folder of the store, relative to the module, because Maven runs the tests there. It is under src, so it is committed with the code.

freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=false

The default, stated with its reason. With false, a missing store fails the test.

The first run created the store with the setting at true. The store has a file that names each frozen rule, and one file of violations for each rule:

#
#Sun Oct 25 22:12:10 GMT 2026
Every\ endpoint\ has\ a\ permission\ annotation=788271d0-89f0-404a-8ca9-76d9759202a5
Reading the code
Every\ endpoint\ has\ a\ permission\ annotation=788271d0-89f0-404a-8ca9-76d9759202a5

The key is the rule's description. The value names the file that holds the rule's violations.

The file of violations has one line for each violation. Its line here says that the method OldReportController.oldReport() is not meta-annotated with @PreAuthorize, with the source file and line. A pull request that changes the store shows each accepted violation by name.

Commit the store with the code. Review a change to the store in the pull request, because a store that grows means someone froze a new violation.

Optional or required: which rules to adoptnew#

Some teams make the architecture tests optional, so a service may skip them. That choice deserves a fair hearing. Rules cost something. A rule that is too strict blocks a sound pragmatic shortcut, and someone must maintain it. A small team that reviews every change may catch the same mistakes by reading.

If a team keeps only one rule, the book recommends "a domain package is plain Java". That rule protects what DDD is for. Business rules stay testable in milliseconds, and they never depend on a framework. Every other rule can be checked by a careful review. This one is the easiest to break by accident, with one import.

The rules are worth the most in three situations:

  • Many engineers work on the service, and no one reads every change.
  • Code is generated by an AI assistant, which copies whatever pattern it saw last.
  • The service will live for years, and its first authors will leave.

The book recommends the rules as required for a new service, from the first commit. They take about a second of build time, and a new service breaks none of them. For an existing service, freeze them. Then they need no fixes today, and they stop the problem from growing. Make a rule optional only where a feature has a documented reason to break it. Say so in the rule's parameters, as the service does for the full-style features:

@Test
void applicationOfFullStyleFeaturesUsesNoAdapter() {
    ArchitectureRules.applicationDoesNotUseAdapters(ORDER).check(CLASSES);
}

Only the ORDER feature is passed to the rule. The light-style note service uses a Spring Data repository on purpose, so the rule does not apply to it. For the team's guardrails as a whole, see the chapter DDD for a team: the playbook.

Testing the platform librarytwist#

The platform library is code that every service runs. So it has tests of its own, in its own repository. A test of a base class needs a class that uses it. The test declares one inside itself:

static final class ThingId extends Identifier {
    ThingId() {
        super(newValue(), "thingId");
    }
}

record ThingHappened(Instant occurredAt) implements DomainEvent {
}

static final class Thing extends AggregateRoot<ThingId> {
    Thing() {
        super(new ThingId(), null);
    }

    void doSomething() {
        raise(new ThingHappened(Instant.EPOCH));
    }
}

@Test
void pullEventsReturnsTheRaisedEventsAndClearsThem() {
    Thing thing = new Thing();
    thing.doSomething();

    assertThat(thing.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new ThingHappened(Instant.EPOCH));
    assertThat(thing.pullEvents()).isEmpty();
}

ThingId, ThingHappened and Thing exist only for this test. A record or class declared inside another class is nested, and a nested record is always static. So the test needs no domain from a real service, and the library stays free of any service's names. IdentifierTest uses the same trick, with a ParcelId and an InvoiceId, to prove that two IDs of different types are never equal.

The library tests the code that every service relies on most:

Platform codeIts tests
the inboxInboxTest, and InboxIT with a duplicate, a rollback and two copies of one event at once
the outbox publisherOutboxDomainEventPublisherTest, including the refusal outside a transaction
the outbox resender and its lockOutboxResenderTest, and OutboxResenderLockIT with two instances
the migration runnerMongoMigrationRunnerTest for order and duplicate IDs, MongoMigrationRunnerIT for the lock, and CreateCollectionsIT for creating the collections before the first transaction
the log context and the path variables in the MDCLogContextTest and PathVariableMdcInterceptorTest
the DocumentDB settingsDocumentDbClientSettingsCustomizerTest, including a missing certificate bundle
retries and the circuit breakerResilientCallsTest
the base classes of the domainAggregateRootTest, IdentifierTest and GuardTest
the current actor on another threadActorOnAnotherThreadTest, which shows that a new thread loses the caller unless the executor passes it on

This list matters. Code that every service shares is where a missing test costs most. An inbox without a test of two copies at once can lose or repeat payments in every service at once. Each chapter that teaches one of these pieces shows its test. A library also needs one test class that you would not expect. Boot's slices look for a @SpringBootApplication class above the test's package, and a library has none. So the platform declares a small PlatformTestApplication in its test code. For the test support that the library ships to services, see the section Test support, shipped in the library.

A shared NuGet package in .NET would have the same tests. Nothing here is special to Java, except that a nested record or class makes the test types short.

What to test first in an older servicenew#

An older service has few tests, and every change feels risky. Writing tests for all of it first would take months. So start with the tests that cost least and protect the most, in this order:

  1. The wiring test. It is one small class and one file of settings, and it needs no Docker. From then on, it catches a broken bean or setting in seconds, which makes upgrades safer.
  2. The architecture rules, frozen. They need no fixes today, and they stop new code from making the structure worse.
  3. API slice tests for the endpoints you are about to change. Record what each endpoint answers today, including its errors, before you touch it. Such a test is called a characterisation test. It describes the current behaviour, right or wrong, so a change cannot alter it by accident.
  4. Domain tests, as rules move into the domain. Each rule that moves from a service into an aggregate gets its plain JUnit test in the same pull request.
  5. One optimistic-lock test for each aggregate. A lost update is silent, so a missing version check is found only by a test.
  6. The inbox and the outbox against a real database, early. They are where duplicates and lost events hide. Test them against DocumentDB itself in a test environment, because MongoDB in Docker is not DocumentDB.

Do not start with a large journey test. It is slow to write, slow to run, and when it fails it does not say which layer broke. Add journeys after the fast tests exist, one for each story that matters to the business.

Move feature by feature, and only where you are changing code anyway. For the checklist of changing an existing service, see the chapter Changing the service.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksA domain test of the shipping rule needs a Spring context to pass. Why does the book call that a sign that the code is in the wrong place, and not a reason to start Spring?
The rule should depend only on the order and on plain values. If its test needs Spring, the rule reads a bean, a setting or a repository. That dependency belongs in the application service, which can pass the value in. Moving it keeps the rule testable in milliseconds and free of the framework. The architecture rule domainIsPlainJava catches the same mistake in the build.
2
Why does the order service test its controllers with @PlatformWebMvcTest and not with a plain @WebMvcTest?
A plain slice loads none of the platform's auto-configurations. It has Boot's security chain, not the platform's, and no exception handler. So a missing order throws in the test instead of answering a 404 problem. The platform's annotation imports its security, error handling and log interceptor, and a decoder for tests.
3
An expert asksThe unit test of OrderService passes a real TransactionTemplate with a NoOpTransactionManager. What does that give the test that a mock of the template would not?
The real template runs the lambda as production does, so the steps inside run in order with no stub to write. Spring also reports an active transaction, so code that refuses to run outside one still runs. A mock would need an answer that calls the callback, in every test class. That answer would repeat what the template does.
4
TranslateWrite the two checks at the end of this Moq test in Mockito. The test expects that the order was never saved and that the notes, events and audit mocks were never called: 
orders.Verify(o => o.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Never());
notes.VerifyNoOtherCalls();
events.VerifyNoOtherCalls();
audit.VerifyNoOtherCalls();
verify(orders, never()).save(any());
verifyNoInteractions(notes, events, audit);

never() does the same as Times.Never(). verifyNoInteractions fails on any call at all, and takes several mocks at once.

Running locally and shipping#

Testing, shipping and changing it · Chapter 26· 26 min read· Quick reference

A developer runs the order service on their own machine, against local copies of everything it needs. A separate repository, the local environment, holds those copies. They are MongoDB, HTTP stubs, an emulator of AWS messaging and a token issuer. Two commands start everything. The chapter then builds the image that ships, with layers, a user that is not root, and memory settings for a container.

KindC#JavaNote

The local environment: one repository for every servicenew#

The order service needs MongoDB, the stock service, Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS), Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) and a token issuer. The payment service needs most of the same. If each service started its own copies, a developer would run three MongoDB servers to work on two services. The QA team would need yet another setup for its Playwright tests. So the shop keeps the shared dependencies in one repository of their own, called local-environment.

Its compose file says how to use it:

# The shared local dependencies of every shop service. Start them first, then the service:
#
#   docker compose up -d                 (here)
#   docker compose up --build            (in the service's repository)
#
# Everything joins the "local-dev" network, so services reach these containers by name.
# The QA team's Playwright tests run against this same setup. Every image version is pinned,
# so everyone runs the same thing.

name: local-environment
Reading the code
name: local-environment

This is the name of the Compose project. Docker Compose puts it in front of every container name, so the MongoDB container is called local-environment-mongo-1.

The file ends with the network that every container joins:

networks:
  default:
    name: local-dev

A Compose file creates a default network for its containers. These three lines give that network a fixed name, local-dev. A service from another repository can then join the same network, and reach each container by its service name, such as mongo.

The repository's README lists the containers:

ContainerImagePurposeHost port
mongomongo:8.0.34stands in for DocumentDB, as a single-node replica set27017
wiremockwiremock/wiremock:3.13.0stubs of the HTTP services the shop calls8089
flocifloci/floci:2.3.0SNS and SQS, with the API of LocalStack4566
aws-initamazon/aws-cli:2.27.0creates the topics, queues and subscriptions, then stopsnone
mock-oauth2ghcr.io/navikt/mock-oauth2-server:6.1.3issues tokens8090

In .NET, a solution often has its own docker-compose.yml for its dependencies. That works well for one service. The shared repository costs one more checkout, but every service and the QA team then run the same stubs and the same queues. A change to a stub is made once, and every consumer gets it.

MongoDB as a replica set of onenew#

The order service saves an order and its notes in one transaction. MongoDB runs a transaction only on a replica set. So the local MongoDB runs as a replica set with one member:

# Stands in for DocumentDB. Use the MongoDB version that your DocumentDB cluster is compatible with.
# It runs as a single-node replica set, because transactions need one.
mongo:
  image: mongo:8.0.34
  command: ["--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]
  ports: ["27017:27017"]
  healthcheck:
    # Also initialises the replica set the first time it runs
    test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval",
           "try { rs.status().ok } catch (e) { rs.initiate({_id: 'rs0', members: [{_id: 0, host: 'mongo:27017'}]}).ok }"]
    interval: 5s
    retries: 30
Reading the code
command: ["--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]

--replSet rs0 starts the server as a member of a replica set named rs0. --bind_ip_all makes it listen on every network address, so other containers can reach it.

"try { rs.status().ok } catch (e) { rs.initiate({_id: 'rs0', members: [{_id: 0, host: 'mongo:27017'}]}).ok }"]

A new replica set must be initiated once. rs.status() throws while it is not. Then the catch calls rs.initiate, with one member named mongo:27017. On every later run, rs.status() succeeds, and the check only reports health.

interval: 5s

Docker runs the check every 5 seconds. After 30 failed checks in a row, Docker marks the container as unhealthy.

The healthcheck does two jobs. It initiates the replica set on the first start, and it reports health. That saves a separate container for the set-up step. In a run for this book on 25 October 2026, the container was healthy within about 20 seconds. The replica set then listed one member, mongo:27017. That member name matters for the IDE, as the section Running from the IDE shows.

The platform's tests start the same image, mongo:8.0.34, with Testcontainers. So the local environment and the integration tests run one version of MongoDB. Two places with two versions would test against two databases. For the container in tests, see the section MongoDB in Docker: the replica set.

Choose the version by your DocumentDB cluster. DocumentDB emulates the MongoDB 3.6, 4.0, 5.0 and 8.0 APIs. A guide that pins mongo:5.0 "to match DocumentDB" is right for a 5.0 cluster, and wrong for an 8.0 one. Check the engine version of your cluster, then set the same major version in both places.

Gotcha

Local MongoDB is not DocumentDB. MongoDB in Docker accepts features that DocumentDB does not support. A test that passes locally can fail against the cluster. Check an unusual feature, such as a new aggregation stage, against a real DocumentDB cluster in a development environment. For the differences, see the section What Amazon DocumentDB does not do.

WireMock: stubs of the other servicestwist#

The order service calls the stock service. Locally, WireMock answers in its place:

# Imitates the HTTP services that shop services call. The stubs are in wiremock/mappings/<service>/.
wiremock:
  image: wiremock/wiremock:3.13.0
  command: ["--global-response-templating", "--verbose"]
  volumes: ["./wiremock:/home/wiremock"]
  ports: ["8089:8080"]
Reading the code
command: ["--global-response-templating", "--verbose"]

Response templating lets a stub compute part of its answer. The default stub uses it to return a new reservation ID each time. Without --verbose, WireMock logs only the requests that match no stub. With it, WireMock logs every request and the stub that answered it.

volumes: ["./wiremock:/home/wiremock"]

WireMock reads its stubs from mappings and large bodies from __files under this folder. Each service that is stubbed has a folder of its own, such as mappings/stock-service/.

The stubs for the stock service give one answer by default, and other answers for special products. The default stub has a low priority:

{
  "name": "stock-service: every product is available (the default answer)",
  "priority": 10,
  "request": {
    "method": "POST",
    "urlPath": "/stock/reservations",
    "headers": {
      "Authorization": { "matches": "Bearer .+" },
      "Idempotency-Key": { "matches": ".+" }
    }
  },

With "priority": 10, this stub loses to any stub with a smaller number. A special product gets such a stub, which matches on the body:

{
  "name": "stock-service: the product OUT-OF-STOCK is never available (for testing the 422 path)",
  "priority": 1,
  "request": {
    "method": "POST",
    "urlPath": "/stock/reservations",
    "headers": { "Authorization": { "matches": "Bearer .+" } },
    "bodyPatterns": [ { "matchesJsonPath": "$.lines[?(@.sku == 'OUT-OF-STOCK')]" } ]
  },
  "response": {
    "status": 200,
    "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    "jsonBody": { "result": "INSUFFICIENT_STOCK", "shortSkus": ["OUT-OF-STOCK"] }
  }
}
Reading the code
"priority": 1,

When several stubs match a request, WireMock uses the one with the lowest priority number. 1 is the highest priority. A stub without a priority gets 5.

"bodyPatterns": [ { "matchesJsonPath": "$.lines[?(@.sku == 'OUT-OF-STOCK')]" } ]

The stub matches only a body with a line whose sku is OUT-OF-STOCK. The filter in square brackets is JSONPath, as in the controller tests.

"headers": { "Authorization": { "matches": "Bearer .+" } },

The stub needs a bearer token, as the real stock service does. So a missing token fails locally too.

A run for this book sent four requests to these stubs. WireMock named the stub that matched in a response header, Matched-Stub-Name:

RequestAnswerThe stub that matched
a line with MUG-001, a token and an Idempotency-Key200 RESERVED, with a new reservation IDthe default answer, priority 10
a line with OUT-OF-STOCK200 INSUFFICIENT_STOCKthe product OUT-OF-STOCK, priority 1
a line with SERVICE-DOWN503the product SERVICE-DOWN, priority 1
no token401, with the header WWW-Authenticate set to Bearera call without a token, priority 20

The stub for a call without a token has priority 20, the lowest of the four. It matches every reservation, with or without a token. So it must lose to every other stub, and it wins only when no other stub matches.

Gotcha

A stub without a priority beats a stub with priority 10. A run of WireMock 3.13.2 showed it. The default priority is 5, and a lower number wins. So a new stub that leaves out priority takes over from the default answer. Give every stub an explicit priority.

QA's Playwright tests use these special products by name. A tester places an order for OUT-OF-STOCK to see the 422 page, and for SERVICE-DOWN to see the 503 page. So the stubs are shared test data, and the README lists their behaviour. For WireMock inside a Java test, see the section WireMock: faking an HTTP dependency.

The image is wiremock/wiremock:3.13.0. The latest release of 3.13 was 3.13.2, as of October 2026. An upgrade is a change to this line, made and reviewed on purpose.

Floci: SNS and SQS on your machinenew#

The service publishes to SNS and reads from SQS. Locally, Floci answers in place of AWS:

# Local SNS and SQS: Floci, a free emulator with LocalStack's API, on port 4566.
floci:
  image: floci/floci:2.3.0
  ports: ["4566:4566"]

Floci is a free AWS emulator under the MIT licence. Its repository was created in February 2026. It emulates SQS, with standard and FIFO queues, dead-letter queues and the visibility timeout, and SNS, with delivery to SQS. Every service it emulates is on port 4566. The image is floci/floci on Docker Hub. Version 2.3.0 was the latest, released on 15 October 2026.

Many guides use LocalStack for this job, and LocalStack was the usual choice for years. Since March 2026, LocalStack is delivered as one version, and users need an account. Its image localstack/localstack:latest asks for an auth token. Older tags still run, but get no security updates, and the GitHub repository is archived. So, as of October 2026, a team that wants a free emulator with no account uses another one. Floci speaks the same API. A service sets only spring.cloud.aws.endpoint to reach it.

LocalStack is still a sound choice for a team that already pays for it, or that needs an AWS service that Floci does not emulate. Then change one image line and keep the rest.

The integration tests start the same Floci image, from the platform's AwsTestContainerConfiguration:

public static final String IMAGE = "floci/floci:2.3.0";
public static final int PORT = 4566;

The constant IMAGE holds the same tag as the compose file.

A guide may run Floci with the tag latest, and plan to pin it later. Then each developer gets whatever was latest on the day of the pull, and two machines run two emulators. The shop pins the tag from the start, in both places.

aws-init: creating the queues and topicsnew#

An emulator starts empty. The order service expects its queue to exist, and fails at startup if it does not. So a container that runs once creates every topic, queue and subscription:

# Creates the topics, queues and subscriptions that every service expects (aws-init/init.sh).
aws-init:
  image: amazon/aws-cli:2.27.0
  depends_on: [floci]
  entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/init/init.sh"]
  volumes: ["./aws-init:/init"]
  environment:
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: local
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: local
    AWS_DEFAULT_REGION: eu-west-2
    AWS_ENDPOINT_URL: http://floci:4566
Reading the code
entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/init/init.sh"]

The container runs the script and stops. The image is the official AWS command-line tool.

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: local

The tool signs each request with credentials, and it refuses to send a request without them. In a run for this book, the same image with no credentials printed "Unable to locate credentials". Floci accepted these dummy values.

AWS_ENDPOINT_URL: http://floci:4566

This environment variable sends every command of the tool to Floci instead of AWS.

The script waits for Floci, then defines two shell functions:

echo "Waiting for Floci..."
until aws sns list-topics >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done

# queue <name>: creates the queue and its dead-letter queue, and prints the queue URL.
#
# A message moves to the dead-letter queue after 5 failed receives, so a poison message stops
# being retried and someone can look at it.
#
# The visibility timeout must be longer than the slowest handler plus about 1 second: Spring
# Cloud AWS acknowledges (deletes) messages in batches, every second or every 10 messages, and
# does not extend the timeout while a handler runs. A shorter timeout delivers each message twice.
queue() {
  dlq_url=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1-dlq" --query QueueUrl --output text)
  dlq_arn=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$dlq_url" --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)
  aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1" \
    --attributes "{\"VisibilityTimeout\":\"30\",\"RedrivePolicy\":\"{\\\"deadLetterTargetArn\\\":\\\"$dlq_arn\\\",\\\"maxReceiveCount\\\":\\\"5\\\"}\"}" \
    --query QueueUrl --output text
}
Reading the code
until aws sns list-topics >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done

The loop tries a harmless command once a second until Floci answers. The short form depends_on: [floci] only waits until the Floci container has started, not until Floci is ready. Compose waits for a healthy container only with condition: service_healthy, and the Floci container has no healthcheck.

queue() {

This defines a shell function named queue. Inside it, $1 is its first argument, the queue name.

dlq_url=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1-dlq" --query QueueUrl --output text)

First the dead-letter queue. $( ) captures the output of a command. --query QueueUrl --output text prints only the URL, not the whole JSON answer.

"{\"VisibilityTimeout\":\"30\",\"RedrivePolicy\":\"{\\\"deadLetterTargetArn\\\":\\\"$dlq_arn\\\",\\\"maxReceiveCount\\\":\\\"5\\\"}\"}"

The attributes are JSON, and the redrive policy is JSON inside a JSON string, so the quotes are escaped twice. The visibility timeout is 30 seconds. After 5 failed receives, SQS moves a message to the dead-letter queue.

The comment above the function explains the two numbers. A message that fails every time is a poison message. Without a dead-letter queue, SQS would deliver it again for up to four days, its default retention. With maxReceiveCount 5, it moves to the dead-letter queue after five tries, where someone can see it.

The visibility timeout is how long a received message stays hidden from other consumers. Spring Cloud AWS deletes handled messages in batches, and does not extend the timeout while a handler runs. So the timeout must be longer than the slowest handler plus about a second. For the full reasoning, see the section The visibility timeout.

The second function subscribes a queue to a topic, and the script then creates the resources of the order service:

subscribe() {
  queue_arn=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$2" --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)
  aws sns subscribe --topic-arn "$1" --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint "$queue_arn" \
    --attributes RawMessageDelivery=true >/dev/null
}

# --- order-service publishes
aws sns create-topic --name order-events >/dev/null

# --- order-service consumes: payment-events from the payment service
payment_events=$(aws sns create-topic --name payment-events --query TopicArn --output text)
payment_received=$(queue order-service-payment-received)
subscribe "$payment_events" "$payment_received"
Reading the code
--attributes RawMessageDelivery=true >/dev/null

Raw delivery puts the event itself into the queue. Without it, SNS wraps the event in a JSON envelope, and the listener would read the envelope as the event.

payment_received=$(queue order-service-payment-received)

The function prints the queue URL, and $( ) keeps it in a variable for the next line.

The run for this book checked the result. The aws-init container exited with code 0 after printing "AWS resources ready". Floci then listed the queue and its dead-letter queue. The queue had VisibilityTimeout 30 and a RedrivePolicy with maxReceiveCount 5. One subscription linked payment-events to the queue.

Each service adds its own block to this one script. The block names the service in a comment, as the order service does. For the publishing side, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox.

mock-oauth2-server: tokens for each kind of callertwist#

Every request to the order service needs a token. Locally, mock-oauth2-server issues them. Its configuration maps each client ID to a subject and its scopes:

client_idSubjectScopes
agentlocal-agentorders.read orders.write
read-onlylocal-read-onlyorders.read
order-serviceorder-servicestock.reserve, for the order service's own calls to the stock service

The third mapping gives the order service its own token, for its calls to the stock service:

{
  "requestParam": "client_id",
  "match": "order-service",
  "claims": {
    "sub": "order-service",
    "aud": ["stock-service"],
    "scope": "stock.reserve"
  }
}

A request with client_id order-service gets a token for the audience stock-service. A client ID stands for a kind of user, which is enough to test the scopes. The security chapter explains the configuration, the image ghcr.io/navikt/mock-oauth2-server:6.1.3, and why the service checks one issuer URL and fetches keys from another. See the section A local token issuer, and the issuer-versus-keys trick.

Two commands start everythingnew#

A new developer should not follow a page of manual steps. The shop has a rule that two commands start any service with all its dependencies. The service's compose file states them:

# Runs ONLY this service. Its dependencies (MongoDB, WireMock, Floci, the mock OAuth2 server) come
# from the local-environment repository, which must be started first:
#
#   1. in local-environment:   docker compose up -d
#   2. here:                    mvn package && docker compose up --build

services:
  order-service:
    build: .
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: local
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    # ...

networks:
  default:
    name: local-dev
    external: true
Reading the code
docker compose up -d

-d runs the containers in the background, so the terminal is free.

mvn package && docker compose up --build

mvn package builds the jar, and runs the unit tests. The Dockerfile copies that jar, so it must exist first. --build builds the image again from the new jar.

SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: local

This environment variable switches on the profile local, so Spring Boot also reads application-local.yml. It is like ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT in ASP.NET Core.

external: true

This network is not created by this file. It must exist already, created by the local environment. So the service joins the same network as its dependencies, and reaches mongo and wiremock by name.

The profile local holds the container names:

spring:
  mongodb:
    uri: mongodb://mongo:27017/orders?replicaSet=rs0

The URI names the container mongo and the replica set rs0. Inside the network, both names are right. The rest of the profile points the token keys at mock-oauth2, AWS at floci, and the stock client at wiremock.

In the run for this book, the second command built the image and started the container in about 8 seconds. The container was healthy after about 24 seconds. A request without a token got 401, as it should.

The rule has a cost. Every change that needs a new dependency must also change the local environment, so the two commands keep working. The section The rules of the local environment says when.

Running from the IDEtrap#

A developer wants breakpoints, so they run OrderServiceApplication from the IDE on the host. The dependencies still run in Docker. From the host, the container names mean nothing, so the README overrides them with localhost:

--spring.mongodb.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/orders?directConnection=true
--spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=http://localhost:8090/default/jwks
--spring.security.oauth2.client.provider.shop-identity.token-uri=http://localhost:8090/default/token
--spring.cloud.aws.endpoint=http://localhost:4566
--clients.stock.base-url=http://localhost:8089

Each line is a program argument that sets one property. A program argument wins over every file, so these values replace the container names of the local profile. The IDE run still uses the profile local for everything else.

PredictThe local MongoDB URI from the IDE#
A developer runs the service from the IDE with only this change to the local profile, keeping replicaSet=rs0. MongoDB runs in Docker, and port 27017 is open on the host. What happens when the service starts?
--spring.mongodb.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/orders?replicaSet=rs0
Show the answer
The service never opens its HTTP port. The log repeats UnknownHostException: mongo, and the first write waits for a server.

A replica set tells the driver the names of its members.

The driver connects to localhost:27017 and asks for the replica set. The member answers that its name is mongo:27017.

With replicaSet=rs0, the driver then uses that name. The host cannot resolve mongo.

The migrations write before the web server starts, so the port never opens.

Use directConnection=true, which talks only to the host you named.

The run for this book tried three URIs from the host:

URI from the hostResult
mongodb://localhost:27017/orders?replicaSet=rs0no HTTP port after 45 seconds, and an UnknownHostException for mongo in the log
mongodb://localhost:27017/ordersreadiness UP after 13 seconds
mongodb://localhost:27017/orders?directConnection=truereadiness UP after 13 seconds

With one host and no replicaSet, the Java driver also connected directly. But directConnection=true says so in the URI, so a reader does not have to know the driver's default. Keep it in the README.

A .NET service that runs on the host meets the same replica set and the same member name. This book did not run the MongoDB driver for .NET against the local replica set. So check what it does with a URI that has no directConnection=true before you rely on it.

The first request with curltwist#

The README of the service ends its section on running locally with three requests. They get a token, read a lookup list and place an order:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8090/default/token -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=agent -d client_secret=any | jq -r .access_token)
curl -s localhost:8080/reference-data/DELIVERY_METHOD -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/orders -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "customer": { "name": "Jo Bloggs", "email": "jo@example.com" }, "deliveryMethod": "STANDARD",
  "lines": [ { "productCode": "MUG-001", "quantity": 2 } ],
  "notes": [ { "text": "Leave with a neighbour", "category": "DELIVERY", "actionRequired": true } ] }'
Reading the code
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8090/default/token -d grant_type=client_credentials \

The first command asks the local issuer for a token as the client agent, and keeps it in the shell variable TOKEN. jq -r .access_token takes the token out of the JSON answer.

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Each later request sends the token as a bearer token. The agent has both scopes, so it can read and write.

To test a missing scope, ask for a token with client_id=read-only. The place request then gets 403. With "productCode": "OUT-OF-STOCK", it gets 422, because the WireMock stub reports that product as unavailable.

A run against the full local environment, on 25 October 2026, gave these answers:

RequestAnswer
the token, as the client agenta token with iss http://localhost:8090/default, sub local-agent, aud order-service and the scope orders.read orders.write
GET /reference-data/DELIVERY_METHOD200, with the four delivery methods in code order, SECOND_CLASS_POST among them with active false
POST /orders201, with {"orderId": "...", "noteIds": ["..."]}
POST /orders with a read-only token403, with the title Forbidden and a traceId
POST /orders with OUT-OF-STOCK422, with the code PRODUCTS_UNAVAILABLE
POST /orders/{orderId}/notes/{noteId}/resolve, by the same agent422, with the code NOTE_RESOLVED_BY_ITS_AUTHOR

The last row is a business rule. The agent who wrote a note may not resolve its action. Locally, every token of the client agent has the same subject, so resolving a note from curl needs a second client in the issuer's configuration.

The run could not pull the image ghcr.io/navikt/mock-oauth2-server:6.1.3. The registry answered 403 Forbidden, also with no stored credentials. So the same version of the issuer ran from its jar on Maven Central, in a Java container named mock-oauth2 on port 8090. Everything else ran from the compose files as they are. The compose file still names the image on ghcr.io, with its exact version, and a developer normally runs that image. The migrations ran on the new database before the service took traffic, and the readiness probe answered UP.

The local environment's README also shows how to send a payment, as the payment service would. It runs the AWS command-line tool in a container on the same network:

docker run --rm --network local-dev -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=local -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=local \
  -e AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=eu-west-2 -e AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://floci:4566 amazon/aws-cli:2.27.0 \
  sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:000000000000:payment-events --message \
  '{"eventId":"e-1","occurredAt":"2026-10-25T09:00:00Z","orderId":"<order id>","paymentReference":"PAY-1","amount":12.50,"currency":"GBP","paidAt":"2026-10-25T09:00:00Z"}'

--network local-dev puts the tool on the shared network, so it reaches floci by name. --rm removes the container when the command ends. Replace <order id> with the ID from the place request. The order then becomes paid, through SNS, SQS and the inbox. In a browser, Swagger UI is at http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html, in the local profile only.

The rules of the local environmentnew#

The local environment is only useful while it matches what the services need. Its README states four rules:

## Rules

- Add a stub, a topic or a queue in the same piece of work that makes a service call or use it.
- Keep the stubs realistic: QA's tests depend on them.
- Pin every image version.
- Local MongoDB is not DocumentDB. Check unusual features against a real cluster.

Each rule in the list, from Add a stub to Local MongoDB is not DocumentDB, has a reason:

  • The same piece of work. A service that calls a new service, publishes a new event or reads a new queue changes the local environment in the same change. Otherwise the two commands stop working for everyone else, the next morning. For the files each change touches, see the chapter Changing the service.
  • Realistic stubs. QA's Playwright tests run against these stubs. A stub that answers what the real service never answers makes those tests prove the wrong thing. Copy a real response when you write a stub, and keep its field names.
  • Exact image versions. See the section An exact version for every image.
  • Not DocumentDB. See the section MongoDB as a replica set of one.
Pragmatic choice: One shared local environment for all services

The strict rule. Each service owns its whole build and run setup, so it never depends on another repository.

What we do. Every service depends on the shared local-environment repository for its dependencies and stubs.

Why. One copy of each stub, queue and token client serves every service and QA. A change is made once, and nobody runs three databases for two services.

When to stop. When teams change the shared files so often that they block each other, or one team's stub breaks another team's tests. Then give each team its own folder of stubs and its own review, or move a team's stubs into its own repository.

The Dockerfile: a layered jartwist#

The service ships as a container image. The Dockerfile builds it from the jar that mvn package made. For the layered jar and the other ways to ship, see the chapter Packaging and native images. This is the service's file:

# Build the jar first:  mvn package   (from the companion root: mvn -pl order-service -am package)
#
# The image has layers: dependencies change rarely, so they sit in their own layers, and Docker
# reuses them from its cache when only the application code changed.

FROM eclipse-temurin:25.0.4.1_1-jre AS extract
WORKDIR /build
COPY target/order-service-*.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:25.0.4.1_1-jre
# Never run as root
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 --no-create-home app
USER 10001
WORKDIR /app
# Rarely changing layers first, so a code change rebuilds only the last layer
COPY --from=extract /build/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /build/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=extract /build/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /build/extracted/application/ ./
# Size the heap from the container's memory limit. Stop on OutOfMemoryError, so the orchestrator restarts the container.
# Half, not three quarters: the service needs about 220 MB outside the heap, so with 75 percent a
# 512 MB container killed the process before the heap was full (measured, see the memory chapter).
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
Reading the code
FROM eclipse-temurin:25.0.4.1_1-jre AS extract

The first stage only unpacks the jar. A Java Runtime Environment (JRE) is enough for that, because nothing is compiled here. AS extract names the stage, so the second stage can copy from it.

COPY target/order-service-*.jar app.jar

The image is built from the jar, not from the source code. So mvn package runs first, on the developer's machine or on the build server.

RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination extracted

Spring Boot's tool splits the jar into four folders under extracted. --launcher keeps Spring Boot's launcher classes, so the result starts with a class name instead of a jar.

COPY --from=extract /build/extracted/dependencies/ ./

Each COPY makes one image layer. The released libraries change least, so they come first. The service's own classes come last.

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

The launcher class finds the service's classes in BOOT-INF/classes, and the libraries next to them. Then it calls the service's main method.

A run for this book listed the layers of a Boot 4.1.2 jar. They are the dependencies, the Spring Boot loader, the snapshot dependencies and the application, in that order. With the folders copied into one, java org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher started the application. The jar's manifest names the same class as its Main-Class. In the run of the order service image, the folder /app held the folders BOOT-INF, META-INF and org.

The chapter on packaging shows the other form. It extracts without --launcher, and starts the small application.jar that the tool writes. Both forms are correct. The service uses the launcher class, so the start command names no file.

The order of the layers is what makes a build fast. A code change alters only the last layer. Docker reuses the three layers above it from its cache, and a server that pulls the new image downloads only that last layer.

In .NET, the usual Dockerfile copies the output of dotnet publish into an ASP.NET Core runtime image. The layering idea is the same. Spring Boot splits the libraries from the code for you.

A user that is not roottwist#

Two lines of the Dockerfile create a user and switch to it:

# Never run as root
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 --no-create-home app
USER 10001
Reading the code
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 --no-create-home app

useradd creates a system user named app, with the fixed user ID 10001 and no home folder.

USER 10001

Every later line, and the running service, uses this user. The line names the number, not the name. So anyone who reads the image's settings sees a user ID that is not 0, the ID of root.

In the run for this book, id inside the running container printed uid=10001(app) gid=999(app). If an attacker breaks into the service, they get the rights of that user, not root. The service needs no more, because it only reads its own files and listens on port 8080.

The JVM in a container: heap and OutOfMemoryErrortrap#

One line of the Dockerfile sets how much memory the service may use, and what happens at an OutOfMemoryError. The .NET runtime configuration has a setting for the first job:

runtimeconfig.template.json
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 75
  }
}
Dockerfile
# Size the heap from the container's memory limit. Stop on OutOfMemoryError, so the orchestrator restarts the container.
# Half, not three quarters: the service needs about 220 MB outside the heap, so with 75 percent a
# 512 MB container killed the process before the heap was full (measured, see the memory chapter).
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
Reading the code
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) reads the environment variable JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS when it starts, and adds its options. A run printed Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and showed both flags set.

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50

The maximum heap is half of the container's memory limit. With a limit of 512 MB, a run showed a maximum heap of 256 MB.

-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError

At the first OutOfMemoryError, the JVM stops the process.

Gotcha

Without a setting, the JVM uses a quarter of the container's memory for its heap. The default of MaxRAMPercentage is 25. A service in a 1 GB container then gets a 256 MB heap. It can run out of memory while three quarters of the container is unused. The default in .NET is different. In a container with a memory limit, the .NET heap hard limit is 75 percent of that limit, unless you set another value. For the memory model, see the section Containers.

The second flag matters as much. A program that catches OutOfMemoryError can keep running in a broken state. In a run without the flag, such a program printed "still alive after the error" and exited normally. With the flag, the JVM printed a line that starts "Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError", and exited with code 3 at the first error. The orchestrator sees a dead container and starts a new one.

The rest of the container's memory is not wasted. Metaspace, thread stacks and buffers live outside the heap. The chapter on the JVM suggests 70 percent and a limit on metaspace as well. The service used 75 percent until the chapter on memory measured it. The service needs about 220 MB outside the heap, so in a 512 MB container the heap of 384 MB left too little, and the container killed the process. The service now uses 50 percent and no metaspace limit. For the measurement, see the chapter The JVM under the service: memory.

The setting is in the image, as an environment variable. A deployment can still replace JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS without a new build, for example to add a heap dump on error. System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent in .NET has the same purpose as -XX:MaxRAMPercentage. A .NET service seldom sets it, because its default in a container is already 75 percent.

The healthcheck: ready means the database is reachablenew#

Docker Compose, and later the orchestrator, must know when the service can take traffic. The service's compose file asks the readiness probe:

healthcheck:
  # The image has no curl, so bash opens the TCP connection itself. "Ready" means the database is reachable.
  test: ["CMD", "bash", "-c", "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/localhost/8080 && printf 'GET /actuator/health/readiness HTTP/1.0\\r\\n\\r\\n' >&3 && grep -q UP <&3"]
  interval: 10s
  retries: 12
  # Migrations run before the web server starts, and an instance may wait for another's
  # migration lock. Allow for that before failed checks count.
  start_period: 60s
Reading the code
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/localhost/8080

In bash, a redirection to the path /dev/tcp/host/port opens a TCP connection. It is not a real file, because bash handles the name itself. This line opens a connection to the service, as file number 3, for reading and writing.

printf 'GET /actuator/health/readiness HTTP/1.0\\r\\n\\r\\n' >&3

The command writes a minimal HTTP request to the connection.

grep -q UP <&3"]

grep reads the answer, and succeeds only if it contains UP. So the check passes only when the service says that it is ready.

start_period: 60s

For the first 60 seconds, a failed check does not count towards the 12 retries. Startup can be slow, because migrations run first. If a check passes during this time, the container counts as started, and every later failure counts.

The base image has no curl. The run for this book confirmed it, and the check passed with bash alone. Installing curl only for a healthcheck would add a tool that an attacker could use inside the container.

The readiness probe includes the database. The platform's defaults add mongo to the readiness group, and leave the liveness group alone. So a database outage makes the service unready, and the orchestrator stops sending it traffic. It does not restart every instance. In the run, /actuator/health/readiness answered 200 with {"status":"UP"}. For the probes and their groups, see the section The health probes: liveness without the database.

An orchestrator such as Kubernetes uses its own probes, not this healthcheck. The comment about the migration lock applies there too. An instance that waits for another's migration lock opens no HTTP port. So its startup probe must allow for the lock's whole wait. For the lock and the numbers, see the section Waiting at startup, and the probes.

The DocumentDB certificate bundle, mounted at run timenew#

DocumentDB uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) by default, and the service must trust the certificate of the cluster. AWS publishes that certificate in a file, the global bundle. The service does not copy the file into its image. The deployment mounts it when the container starts:

# DocumentDB TLS: the deployment sets PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLE to the mounted AWS
# certificate bundle, for example /certs/global-bundle.pem. It is not set locally.

The environment variable PLATFORM_MONGO_DOCUMENTDB_CA_BUNDLE sets the property platform.mongo.documentdb.ca-bundle, by relaxed binding. The platform then trusts the certificates in that file, as its test DocumentDbClientSettingsCustomizerTest.trustsTheCaBundleWhenOneIsConfigured checks. Locally, the variable is not set, and MongoDB in Docker runs without TLS.

The file stays outside the image for two reasons. The image is then the same in every environment, so the image that was tested is the image that ships. And the bundle can change without a new build of the service. The test failsAtStartupWhenTheCaBundleIsMissing in the same class checks the other side. A setting that names a missing file stops the service at startup, not at the first query.

For how the platform loads the bundle, and the ways that AWS documents for Java, see the section Connecting to Amazon DocumentDB. For the DocumentDB settings of the platform, see the chapter Storing aggregates in DocumentDB.

An exact version for every imagenew#

A developer pulls wiremock:latest in January, and a colleague pulls it in March. They now run two versions, and a stub that works for one may fail for the other. A tag such as latest moves. So every image in the shop names an exact version:

ImageVersionWhere
mongo8.0.34the local environment, and MongoTestContainerConfiguration
wiremock/wiremock3.13.0the local environment
floci/floci2.3.0the local environment, and AwsTestContainerConfiguration
amazon/aws-cli2.27.0the local environment, and the README's payment command
ghcr.io/navikt/mock-oauth2-server6.1.3the local environment
eclipse-temurin25.0.4.1_1-jrethe service's Dockerfile, both stages

The same image in two places, such as MongoDB in the local environment and in the tests, has the same version in both. An upgrade is then one visible change in a pull request, which someone reviews and tests. With latest, an upgrade happens on the day someone pulls, and nobody decides it.

The Java base image names its patch release, 25.0.4.1_1, not just 25. So a rebuild of the same commit gets the same Java release. Moving to a new patch is then a deliberate change. Do it often, because patch releases carry security fixes.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy does the order service keep its dependencies in a shared local-environment repository instead of in its own compose file?
Every service and the QA team need the same MongoDB, stubs, queues and token clients. One repository holds one copy of each, started once. A change to a stub is made once, and the Playwright tests run against the same setup as the developers. The cost is a second checkout, and the rule that a change adds its stub or queue in the same piece of work.
2
The local MongoDB runs with --replSet rs0. Why, when there is only one node?
MongoDB runs a transaction only on a replica set, and the service saves an order and its notes in one transaction. A replica set with one member is enough. The healthcheck initiates it on the first start.
3
An expert asksWhy does the image set -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError?
After an OutOfMemoryError, a JVM can keep running in a broken state, for example when code catches the error. With the flag, the JVM exits at the first error, with code 3. The orchestrator sees a dead container and starts a new one, so the service recovers on its own.
4
TranslateThis .NET runtime configuration limits the heap to 75 percent of the container's memory. Write a Dockerfile line that sets the same limit for the JVM, and also stops the JVM at the first out-of-memory error: 
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 75
  }
}
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"

The JVM reads JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS when it starts. MaxRAMPercentage sets the heap as a share of the container's limit.

Quick reference#

The commands of local work:

TaskCommand
start the shared dependenciesdocker compose up -d, in local-environment
start the order service in Dockermvn package && docker compose up --build, in order-service
run the service from the IDEthe README's program arguments, with localhost and directConnection=true
get a token as an agentcurl -s -X POST localhost:8090/default/token -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=agent -d client_secret=any
open Swagger UIhttp://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html, in the local profile only
stop everythingdocker compose down, in each repository

The host ports of the local environment:

PortContainerInside the network
27017mongomongo:27017
8089wiremockwiremock:8080
4566flocifloci:4566
8090mock-oauth2mock-oauth2:8080
8080order-serviceorder-service:8080
