The JVM under the service: memory#

Testing, shipping and changing it · Chapter 27· 23 min read

The order service passes every test and runs for days on a laptop. In a cluster, a 512 MB container is killed at 03:00. There is no OutOfMemoryError, and the heap of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) never filled. This chapter follows one object from its allocation to the collector, then follows the kill to its cause. Every number comes from the service in a container with a limit.

KindC#JavaNote
twista memory limit on the container, counted on the whole processthe same limit, which the JVM cannot see comingthe kernel counts resident pages, sends SIGKILL at the limit, and no Java code runs afterwards Why
trapthe .NET heap takes 75 percent of a container by default, and that works-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 looked like the same thingthe limit counts the whole process, the JVM keeps about 220 MB outside the heap, and 384 plus 220 is more than 512 Why
twistthe GC heap, and the rest of the processthe Java heap, and the regions outside itmetaspace, the code cache, thread stacks and direct buffers have their own sizes and their own limits Why
twistpointer-bump allocation into generation 0pointer-bump allocation into a thread-local buffer in edenboth runtimes allocate by moving a pointer, and both keep young objects apart from old ones Why
twistworkstation GC, or server GC with one heap per CPUSerial, G1 or ZGC, chosen by the JVM from the container's CPUs and memorya container with one CPU gets Serial, and the service's pauses are then its business Why
twistOutOfMemoryException, and a dump with dotnet-dumpOutOfMemoryError, and a heap dump with jcmd GC.heap_dumpthe JVM reaches its own heap limit first only if the container's limit leaves room for it Why
newno equivalentexit code 137, OOMKilled true, and nothing in the logthe kernel killed the process at the container's limit, and no Java code ran afterwards Why
newno equivalentMaxDirectMemorySize, which defaults to the maximum heapdirect buffers are capped by the JVM at another heap's worth, outside the heap Why
twistdocker stats, and the kernel's cgroup filesNative Memory Tracking, read with jcmdthe JVM's own account of every region, as reserved and committed bytes Why

Scene 1: what memory is to a processtwist#

For the first look at the heap, the collectors and the container limit, see the chapter The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers. For the Dockerfile of the service, see the section The JVM in a container: heap and OutOfMemoryError. This chapter starts with the operating system, because the kill at 03:00 is the operating system's doing. The numbers come from runs on 26 October 2026, in Docker 27.5.1 on a laptop with an Intel i9-8950HK. The service's own image ran inside an image of the Java Development Kit (JDK) 25.0.4.1. The run script is companion/runs/memory/run.sh.

Think of a process as a house. The house has rooms. The Java heap is one room, the biggest. The container's memory limit is not the size of that room. It is the floor area of the whole house, with every room counted. When the house grows past the floor area, the landlord does not knock on the door of the biggest room. The landlord removes the house.

The words behind the picture are these. A process owns virtual memory, which is a set of addresses it may use. The addresses are divided into pages of 4 KB. A page uses no physical memory until the process touches it. Then the kernel gives it a page of physical memory. The pages that are in physical memory right now are called the resident set, and its size is the RSS. A container's memory limit is a limit on the resident memory of every process in the container. The kernel's own data and the file cache that those processes caused count too. The kernel keeps the count in a cgroup, and the file memory.max of the cgroup is the limit. When the count reaches the limit and cannot be reduced, the kernel's out-of-memory killer acts. It picks a process in the cgroup and sends it the signal SIGKILL. That signal cannot be caught. The process is gone, and a shell reports its exit status as 137, which is 128 plus the signal's number 9.

Three facts follow, and the whole chapter rests on them. The limit counts the whole process, not the Java heap. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) cannot see the kill coming, because it is not asked. And no Java code runs after it, so no exception, no log line and no heap dump exist.

The service at rest shows the gap between the heap and the house. The run started the service in a container with -m 512m and one CPU. It sent the service 537 rounds of three requests in a minute, and read docker stats before and after:

279.9MiB / 512MiB   54.67%    idle, just after the start
347.3MiB / 512MiB   67.84%    after a minute of load

Each line is one sample, and 512MiB is the limit on both. The first number is the container's resident memory, and the second is the limit. After a minute the service used 347 MB of its 512. Its heap, as the next scene shows, had 117 MB committed and about 65 MB in use. More than half of the house was not the heap.

The C# reader knows the first half of this. The .NET runtime also keeps memory outside its GC heap. In a container, .NET limits the heap of its garbage collector (GC) to 75 percent of the memory limit by default. The rest is for the runtime, the code and the threads. The Java default is 25 percent, and the service's Dockerfile raised it to 75 to match. That number is the trap of this chapter, and scene 6 pays for it.

What you can see here#

docker stats, whose memory column is the container's resident memory against its limit. The same number in Kubernetes comes from kubectl top pod. Inside the container, /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current is the count the kernel uses, and memory.events has a line oom_kill that counts the kills. After a kill, docker inspect shows the exit code 137 and the flag OOMKilled as true. In Kubernetes, the pod's description shows the reason OOMKilled.

What you can tune here#

The limit itself, and whether the container may use swap. Scene 6 shows why the second setting matters most on a laptop.

Scene 2: the rooms of the housetwist#

The JVM keeps an account of every room, and the run asked for it after the minute of load. The feature is called Native Memory Tracking (NMT). It is off by default, costs five to ten percent when on, and the run switched it on with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary. The summary names each region with two numbers. Reserved is address space the JVM has set aside. Committed is memory the JVM has asked the kernel for, which is what the container counts once it is touched. The rooms that matter in the service, in committed megabytes:

Region, as NMT names itCommittedWhat is in it
Java Heap117 MB, of 384 reservedevery object, from a request's DTO to the cached reference data
Metaspace90 MBthe metadata of every loaded class, more than 20,000 of them in the service
Code58 MBthe machine code that the compilers made, and the interpreter's own
Symbol19 MBthe names of classes, methods and fields, shared by the whole JVM
Class16 MBthe compressed class space, which holds the class pointers that objects carry
Shared class space14 MBthe JDK's own classes, loaded from the class data sharing archive
Native Memory Tracking8 MBthe account itself
Thread7 MB, of 56 reservedthe stacks of the platform threads, 1 MB reserved each and only the touched pages committed
everything elseabout 6 MBGC data, the compiler's working memory, arena chunks, locks, logging

The table is in mebibytes, as NMT and docker stats print them. The total committed was 334 MB, and the container showed 347 MB resident. The two agree, which is the point of the account. Add the rooms outside the heap, and the service needs about 217 MB that is not heap, whatever the heap does. At idle, before the load, it was about 160 MB, so the rooms grow with use. Now the arithmetic of the Dockerfile. With -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 in a 512 MB container, the heap may grow to 384 MB. The run's VM.flags confirmed it, in the flags the JVM chose for itself:

-XX:InitialHeapSize=8388608 -XX:MaxHeapSize=402653184 -XX:MaxRAM=536870912 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.000000 -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=251662336 -XX:+UseCompressedOops -XX:+UseSerialGC

MaxHeapSize is 402,653,184 bytes, which is 384 MB. MaxRAM is the container's 512 MB. 384 plus 217 is 601, and 601 is far more than 512. The heap can be within its limit while the house is over the floor area.

Each room has its own limit, and the table says which. The heap stops at MaxHeapSize. Direct buffers, which scene 7 meets, stop at MaxDirectMemorySize, which defaults to the maximum heap. Metaspace has no limit by default, and MaxMetaspaceSize gives it one. The code cache is reserved at 240 MB with tiered compilation. A thread stack is 1 MB on Linux x64, set by -Xss. A service with a thousand platform threads reserves a gigabyte for stacks. The container caps the sum, and nothing else does.

Two settings of the run shaped the rooms. The JVM saw one CPU and 512 MB, and on such a machine it chooses the Serial collector. The Java 25 tuning guide reserves G1 for a server-class machine, which has at least two processors and 1,792 MB. The GC log's first line said so, Using Serial. And compressed references were on, as they are for any heap below 32 GB. So a reference in an object is 4 bytes and not 8. The .NET runtime makes the same kind of choice. Workstation GC is the default, and server GC gives one heap and one thread per logical CPU, but never on a machine with one.

What you can see here#

jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary, inside the container, where the service is process 1. jcmd 1 VM.native_memory baseline and then summary.diff show what grew since the baseline, which is how the run watched the leaks of the later scenes. jcmd 1 VM.flags prints the flags the JVM chose, such as the collector and the maximum heap. The Actuator has three memory gauges, for used, committed and maximum bytes. Each one carries the tag area, as heap or nonheap, so they show the heap and the JVM's non-heap pools over time. No Actuator metric shows the resident memory of the process. Read it from the cgroup, or from the platform's dashboard.

What you can tune here#

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage, from the arithmetic above and never from a habit. -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, when a service loads classes without end, which a class loader leak does. -Xss, when a service has many platform threads and shallow stacks. And -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, for the libraries that read and write with direct buffers. Every one of these moves a wall between rooms inside the same house.

Scene 3: an allocationtwist#

Now one object, an Order made for one request. Its allocation is a pointer bump. Each thread owns a small piece of the young generation. The piece is called a thread-local allocation buffer, or TLAB. Allocating an object means moving the thread's pointer forward by the object's size. No lock, no search. The .NET runtime allocates the same way, by adding to a pointer, and its documentation says that this is almost as fast as the stack. The difference is how many objects a request makes. Java has no structs. An order with three lines, a customer and money values is a dozen objects, each with a header of 12 bytes, and each allocated. The C2 compiler removes some of them with escape analysis, when an object never leaves the method that made it. The rest go to the heap.

When the thread's buffer is full, it takes another from eden. When eden is full, the collector runs. The run's GC log, from the minute of load, shows what that looks like under the Serial collector:

[92.049s][info][gc] GC(113) Pause Young (Allocation Failure) 78M->47M(112M) 4.909ms

Read the line from the left. The 92.049s is the time since the JVM started, the GC number, the kind of pause, and the cause. "Allocation Failure" is the ordinary cause. It means that an allocation did not fit in eden, not that anything failed. Then the heap before and after the pause, with the committed size in brackets, and the pause's length. Over the whole run the log held 110 young pauses, with a median of 4.8 milliseconds. Each one stopped every thread of the service. A request that arrived during one waited.

The run's heap at that moment, from jcmd 1 GC.heap_info, had the shape the tuning guide describes. The young generation was 36 MB, as eden of 31 MB and two survivor spaces of 4 MB. The old generation, which the Serial collector calls tenured, was 80 MB with 48 MB in use. A young pause copies the objects that are still reachable from eden into a survivor space. An object that survives enough pauses, fifteen by default, is copied into the old generation. Most orders never get there. They are made, sent, and dead before the next pause. That is the generational hypothesis, and the whole design rests on it.

The log also held five full pauses, and four of them came in the first forty seconds, with the cause "Metadata GC Threshold". Those are not about the heap. They are about metaspace. The JVM triggers a collection when the metaspace grows past a threshold, which starts at about 21 MB and is raised after each collection. A service that loads more than 20,000 classes at startup crosses that threshold four times, and the longest of the four pauses took 231 milliseconds. The chapter on starting the service shows where those seconds go.

What you can see here#

The GC log, which the run wrote with -Xlog:gc*:file=/tmp/gc.log. The tag gc alone gives one line per pause. gc* gives the phases, the regions and the metaspace line of each pause too. The Actuator timer jvm.gc.pause gives the same pauses as a metric. Its tags name the collector, the action and the cause. And jcmd 1 GC.heap_info gives the generations at one moment.

What you can tune here#

Nothing in the service's code, for the pointer bump. -XX:MetaspaceSize, the threshold of the full pauses at startup, is the one flag of this scene worth a thought. Think about it only after a measurement like the one above.

Scene 4: the collectors, and a pause you caused yourselftwist#

The service got the Serial collector because of the container's shape, and under that collector every pause stops the world. Three collectors ship in Java 25, and the JVM chooses between the first two by itself:

CollectorWhen the JVM picks itHow it pausesThe price
Serialone CPU, or less than 1,792 MBone thread does all the work, and every collection stops every threadpauses grow with the live data
G1two or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MBregions of equal size, young collections in short stop-the-world pauses, old regions marked concurrently and reclaimed in mixed collections, with a soft goal of 200 ms per pausesome memory for its bookkeeping, and CPU for the concurrent work
ZGConly with -XX:+UseZGCall the expensive work concurrently, with pauses under a millisecond that do not grow with the heap, generational since Java 24throughput, and heap headroom for the concurrent work

The run met a fourth kind of pause, and it caused it. To take the class histogram of the next scene, the run called jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram. The histogram counts live objects, so the JVM first ran a full collection, and the GC log recorded it:

[119.798s][info][gc] GC(114) Pause Full (Heap Inspection Initiated GC) 62M->47M(113M) 344.056ms

The cause in brackets, Heap Inspection Initiated GC, names the diagnostic. That is a third of a second in which the service answered nothing. A heap dump does the same, and a bigger heap pays more. The tools of this chapter are safe to use in production, and they are not free. The reference pages say so, and the log proves it.

In .NET the matching choice is workstation GC against server GC. Since .NET 9 the dynamic adaptation called DATAS resizes the heap on its own. The Java choice is made once, by the JVM or by a flag. The pause goal of G1 is the one setting most services ever touch.

What you can see here#

The Using line at the top of the GC log, which names the collector. The cause in brackets on each pause line, which says who asked. And the Actuator timer jvm.gc.pause, whose tag cause carries the same words.

What you can tune here#

-XX:+UseG1GC or -XX:+UseZGC, with a measurement of the pauses before and after, on the container shape that production uses. A laptop with eight CPUs picks G1 and tells you nothing about a one-CPU container. -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis for G1, which is a goal and not a promise. And the second CPU, which changes the collector by itself and may be the cheaper fix.

Scene 5: the leak the JVM catchestwist#

A leak in Java is an object that is still reachable and should not be. Nothing frees it, because something still points to it. The run made one on purpose, with a class that the chapter on running the service never ships. The experiments jar holds it, and the diagnostics image adds that jar to the classpath only for these runs:

private static byte[] heap(int kb) {
    byte[] block = new byte[kb * 1024];
    block[0] = 1;                                   // touch it, so the page is really used
    return block;
}

The method makes a byte[] block of the asked size and touches its first byte. A worker thread stores one such block every 100 milliseconds in a list that the bean holds. The bean exists as long as the context. Nothing ever removes a block. The run started the service with the Dockerfile's old setting of 75 percent, and with half, which is the setting the Dockerfile has now. Scene 6 tells what happened at 75. At half, the heap may grow to 256 MB, and the GC log of the last second shows the collector losing:

[44.745s][info][gc] GC(104) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 238M->237M(247M) 210.731ms
[44.947s][info][gc] GC(105) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 238M->238M(247M) 200.443ms
[45.099s][info][gc] GC(106) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 238M->238M(247M) 149.471ms
[45.252s][info][gc] GC(107) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 238M->238M(247M) 153.449ms

Each line is a Pause Full, and the numbers before and after the arrow barely move. Four full collections in half a second, each one freeing a megabyte or nothing, each one stopping the service for a fifth of a second. Eighteen full pauses ran in all, and fifteen of them had the cause Allocation Failure. This is what a service looks like just before a heap leak ends it. The CPU is at 112 percent of its one core, the requests crawl, and the log is quiet. Then the JVM gave up:

Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space

The Terminating due to line is the last thing the JVM wrote. The service's image sets -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, so the JVM exited with code 3 at the first error, and the container stopped with that code. The orchestrator would start a new one. This is the good ending of a leak, because it leaves evidence. The log has the error. And with one more flag, the JVM writes the heap to a file before it dies.

The run took the dump itself instead, in a separate run with a 1 GB container. It took it while the leak held about 190 MB, with jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof. The JVM wrote 291 MB in one second, and the file is in the HPROF format. A quicker look is the class histogram, which the run took at the same moment:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
-------------------------------------------------------
   1:        156920      226611000  [B (java.base@25.0.4.1)
   2:        148921        3574104  java.lang.String (java.base@25.0.4.1)
   3:         23538        2970104  java.lang.Class (java.base@25.0.4.1)

The first row is [B, which is the JVM's name for byte[]. In the service at rest, that row held 15 MB. Here it holds 227 MB, and about 200 MB of that is the leak. The histogram counts only live objects, because it runs a full collection first. A histogram names the class of what leaked. It does not name who holds it. For that, open the dump in Eclipse Memory Analyzer and read its dominator tree. An object dominates another when every path from the roots to the second goes through the first. The tree sorts objects by what they keep alive. The LeakExperiment bean is at the top of it, with its list and every block under it.

In .NET, the same investigation is dotnet-dump collect and dotnet-dump analyze, and the exception is OutOfMemoryException. The shape is the same. The difference is in the next scene. The JVM catches a heap leak only if the container's limit leaves room for the heap to fill.

What you can see here#

The full pauses with "Allocation Failure" as their cause, back to back, in the GC log or in jvm.gc.pause. The Terminating due to line. The histogram from jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram, which costs a full pause. The dump from jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump, which costs more. And the old-object sampling of Flight Recorder, which samples objects that stay alive and saves where each one was allocated. With path-to-gc-roots=true it also keeps the chain that holds the object, at the cost of a full collection when the recording ends.

What you can tune here#

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError with -XX:HeapDumpPath pointing at a mounted volume, in the image or in the deployment. The Java 25 reference says the dump is written only for a heap exhaustion, before the error is reported. The service's Dockerfile does not set it. A dump of a 384 MB heap in a container with no volume for it has nowhere to go. Add the volume first, then the flag.

Scene 6: the kill that comes firsttrap#

Now the mystery. The run started the same leak with the Dockerfile's setting of the time, 75 percent, in the same 512 MB container. The container had no swap. The service's resident memory went from 393 MB to 486 MB in five seconds, and then there was no container:

392.7MiB / 512MiB   76.70%    just after the start, with the leak already running
485.9MiB / 512MiB   94.91%    five seconds later
0B / 0B              0.00%    ten seconds later

exit code: 137
OOMKilled by the container: true

The three samples are five seconds apart. The third, 0B / 0B, has no container to measure. The log ended with an ordinary line. The leak had logged "holds 100 MB" and nothing after it. No OutOfMemoryError, no "Terminating", no dump. The GC log showed young pauses at 203 MB and 215 MB of heap, nowhere near the 384 MB limit. Then it showed one full pause for the metaspace threshold. The heap was fine. The JVM was fine. The house had grown past the floor area, and the kernel removed it.

The arithmetic of scene 2 says why, and it says that the leak was not even needed. After a minute of load the service used 347 MB, and 217 MB of it was outside the heap. The heap may grow to 384 MB. So a busy day, with the heap honestly at 250 MB and no leak at all, puts the house at 467 MB. A burst of 50 MB ends it. At 03:00 the nightly job that rebuilds the reference data is such a burst. That is the whole mystery. The Dockerfile had the wrong number, and the number looked right because it is the right number for .NET.

The run did the direct-buffer leak of the next scene the same way. The result was the same, a kill at 496 MB with the heap flat. The two kinds of leak are indistinguishable from outside. And then the run changed one thing, the Dockerfile's percentage, to half. With a heap limit of 256 MB, the house reached 465 MB at most, 47 MB under the limit. The heap leak then ended as scene 5 showed, with the JVM's own error and an exit code of 3. That is the fix, and the companion's Dockerfile now has it.

Pragmatic choice: Half the container for the heap

The strict rule. Size the heap from a measurement of the service's non-heap memory. Set the percentage so that heap plus non-heap stays under the limit with a margin.

What we do. The Dockerfile sets -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50, for every container size.

Why. The non-heap memory of the service is about 220 MB under load, and it does not grow with the container. At 512 MB, half leaves about 40 MB of margin, and the leak run peaked at 465 MB. At 1 GB, half leaves about 290 MB, which is more margin than the service needs. A 512 MB heap is still several times what the service uses. One number for every size is what a team can remember.

When to stop. When a service runs in 2 GB or more, half wastes memory. Then measure the non-heap once, and set the percentage for that size.

One more twist, and it is the reason the first captures of this chapter had to be thrown away. On a laptop, Docker Desktop runs containers in a virtual machine, and that machine has a swap file of 1 GB by default. A container with -m 512m and no --memory-swap may use as much swap again as its limit. The first run with a raised cap on direct memory used that default, and it was not killed. The kernel pushed the leaked pages to swap, the resident memory stayed at 479 MB, and the service kept answering, slowly. A Kubernetes node is the opposite case. The kubelet refuses to start on a Linux node with swap enabled. Its default swap behaviour is NoSwap, under which pods cannot use swap at all. So the laptop said "fine" and the cluster said "killed", for the same image and the same limit. The runs now pass --memory-swap 512m, which gives the container no swap, and the kill appeared.

Kubernetes states the kill plainly. A container that uses more than its memory limit may be terminated by the kernel. The termination happens after the fact, when the kernel detects pressure. The container's reason then shows as OOMKilled. The reference adds that if the killed process is the container's process 1, and the container is restartable, Kubernetes restarts it. A service that is killed and restarted every night looks healthy on every dashboard that measures uptime by the hour.

What you can see here#

The exit code 137 and OOMKilled: true, from docker inspect or kubectl describe pod. A restart count that grows. A resident memory graph that climbs to the limit and drops to zero. And nothing in the application's log, which is the sign that separates this from scene 5.

What you can tune here#

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage, from the arithmetic. The container limit, if the arithmetic cannot fit. And on a laptop, --memory-swap equal to --memory for any test of a memory limit, or the test lies.

Scene 7: the leak outside the heap, and the JVM's second capnew#

Not every leak is in the heap, and a heap-only mind misses the other kind. A library that reads and writes network bytes often uses direct buffers. A direct buffer is a block of memory outside the heap, which the kernel can fill without a copy. The experiments jar can leak those too:

private static ByteBuffer direct(int kb) {
    ByteBuffer block = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(kb * 1024);
    for (int i = 0; i < block.capacity(); i += 4096) {
        block.put(i, (byte) 1);                     // touch every page
    }
    return block;
}

The method calls allocateDirect for a buffer of the asked size. Then it touches one byte in every page of the buffer, so that every page becomes resident. With swap off, the result was scene 6 again, a kill at 496 MB with a flat heap. With swap on, as Docker Desktop allows by default, the run saw something the heap leak never shows. The run script calls this mode direct-swap. The leak stopped by itself, at about 371 MB, and the service kept running:

Exception in thread "leak-experiment" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 1048576 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 389021704, limit: 389283840)
	at java.base/java.nio.Bits.reserveMemory(Bits.java:178)
	at java.base/java.nio.DirectByteBuffer.<init>(DirectByteBuffer.java:108)
	at java.base/java.nio.ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(ByteBuffer.java:367)

The limit in the message is 389,283,840 bytes, which is about 371 MB. The JVM caps direct buffers at MaxDirectMemorySize. When that flag is not set, the JDK's own code sets the cap to Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory(). Under Serial that is the maximum heap minus one survivor space, so a little under 384 MB. A service with a 384 MB heap may therefore also hold about 371 MB of direct buffers. The sum is far over a 512 MB container. The exception was thrown in the leak's own thread, which died. The service's requests ran on other threads and kept working. The run's load loop got 6,165 rounds of 200 and 201 answers in ten minutes. The -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError flag did not fire. That flag exits on an error thrown by the JVM itself, and this one was thrown by Java code in java.nio.

NMT showed where the memory went. The diff against the baseline, after ten minutes, had one line that moved:

-                     Other (reserved=380970KB +272736KB, committed=380970KB +272736KB)

Direct buffers appear under Other, not under the heap, and a diff of the summary is the way to see a room grow. The Actuator gauge jvm.buffer.memory.used, with the tag id as direct, shows the same number over time.

Then the run raised the cap, with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m, which is what a team does when a native library asks for more. With swap, nothing was killed, and the service ran slowly on a swap file. Without swap, the kill came at 507 MB. The lesson is not the flag. The JVM caps the heap and the direct buffers. It does not cap metaspace, threads or a native library's own allocations. The container caps the sum, and the sum is what a team must know.

What you can see here#

The gauge jvm.buffer.memory.used. The lines Other and Internal of the NMT diff. An OutOfMemoryError whose message names direct buffer memory, in the log of a thread nobody watches. And a resident memory that grows while jvm.memory.used for the heap stays flat. That is the one graph that tells the two kinds of leak apart.

What you can tune here#

-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, downwards as often as upwards. A service that never uses direct buffers on purpose can set it low. A library's leak then throws early instead of growing to a heap's worth.

Scene 8: the toolkit, and the image that lacks ittwist#

Every number in this chapter came from one of these tools, and each is one command:

ToolCommandWhat it costs
the container's viewdocker stats, or memory.current in the cgroupnothing
the JVM's accountjcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary, after -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary5 to 10 percent of CPU while tracking is on
the growth since a momentjcmd 1 VM.native_memory baseline, then summary.diffthe same
the heap's shapejcmd 1 GC.heap_infonothing
the GC log-Xlog:gc*:file=/tmp/gc.loga file that grows, rotated by default at 20 MB
the class histogramjcmd 1 GC.class_histogramone full collection
a heap dumpjcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprofone full collection, and a file the size of the heap
the long-lived objectsa Flight Recorder recording with path-to-gc-roots=truea full collection when the recording ends

The service's own image has none of the jcmd commands. It is built on eclipse-temurin:25-jre, a Java Runtime Environment (JRE) image, and the run checked what that image holds. Its bin folder has six tools, among them java and jfr. It has no jcmd, because the module jdk.jcmd is not in a JRE. The other diagnostic tools of that module are missing with it. The runs of this chapter therefore used a second image, with the service's own layers copied into the JDK image. In that image jcmd exists inside the container. A team has three ways out. Build the production image on the JDK image, which is bigger. Build a runtime with jlink and add the module jdk.jcmd, which the run tried and got a 58 MB runtime. Or keep the JRE and use Flight Recorder, whose jfr tool the JRE does have, and the next chapter does.

One more lesson came from a run that went wrong. The run first took the dump inside the 512 MB container, and the container was killed while the file was written. A file written inside the container goes through the kernel's page cache, and the cgroup counts that cache. The dump was the last straw, and the container was killed. Write dumps to a mounted volume, and know that the write itself needs room.

Whichever way, the time to capture is before the restart. A heap dump, an NMT summary and the last GC log of a dying container are worth more than a day of graphs. All three are gone with the container.

What you can see here#

The bin folder of the image, listed with ls. And java --list-modules, which says whether the two diagnostic modules are there before you need them.

What you can tune here#

The base image, between the JRE and the JDK, or a jlink runtime with the two modules. And a volume for the dumps, named in -XX:HeapDumpPath, so that a dump written by a dying process survives it.

Check yourself
1
A service in a 512 MB container with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 is killed every night with exit code 137 and nothing in its log. The heap graph never reached its maximum. What happened, and what is the first thing to change?
The container's limit counts the whole process. The heap may grow to 384 MB. The service keeps about 220 MB outside the heap, in metaspace, the code cache, the class data and the thread stacks. The sum passes 512 MB before the heap is full, and the kernel kills the process with SIGKILL. No Java code runs after it. Lower the percentage so that heap plus non-heap fits with a margin, which for this service is half.
2
An expert asksThe same leak ran twice in the same container. One run ended with OutOfMemoryError and exit code 3. The other ended with a kill and exit code 137. Why?
The two limits race. The JVM throws OutOfMemoryError when the heap reaches its own maximum. The kernel kills the process when the whole container reaches its limit. With a heap maximum of 256 MB the heap filled first, and the exit flag gave code 3. With 384 MB the container filled first, before the heap was full. Swap can hide the kill on a laptop, because the kernel pushes pages out instead.
3
A service's heap is flat, but its resident memory grows until the container kills it. Which two JVM accounts show where the memory went?
Native Memory Tracking, read with jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary.diff against a baseline, which shows the region that grew, such as Other for direct buffers or Metaspace for classes. And the Actuator gauges for the non-heap pools and the buffer pools, such as jvm.buffer.memory.used, over time.
4
TranslateTranslate this .NET container setting into the JVM flag for the order service's Dockerfile. The setting limits the GC heap to 60 percent of the container's memory. 
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 60
  }
}
The same percentage, as a JVM flag in the image's JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. 
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
The JVM reads the flag at startup, and 60 percent of the container's limit becomes the maximum heap. Check first that the service's non-heap memory fits in the other 40 percent.
