The JVM under the service: code, threads and the compiler#

Testing, shipping and changing it · Chapter 28· 35 min read

The order service answers its first request in 0.31 seconds and its second in 0.04. For minutes after every deploy it is slow, and then it is fast. In a quiet minute, one request in a thousand takes ten times the median. This chapter follows one method, OrderService.place, from its class file to machine code and back. The numbers come from one run of the service under load.

KindC#JavaNote
twistCIL and metadata in a PE assembly, not verified for type safety at run timebytecode and a constant pool in a class file, verified when the class is linkedboth runtimes load a class the first time it is needed, and both keep the source's names in the binary Why
twista struct lives inline, and a class carries a 16-byte header on x64every object carries a 12-byte header, and a record is a classcompressed class pointers make the header 12 bytes and not 16, and compact headers make it 8 when switched on Why
twisttwo tiers, quick JIT and then the optimising JIT, with tiered PGOfive tiers, the interpreter, three forms of C1 and then C2the interpreter runs the first 200 calls, C1 the next thousands, and C2 compiles the method after 5,000 Why
trapReadyToRun code ships in the app, so the first minute is finenothing ships but bytecode, so the first minutes belong to the compilersthe run made 17,848 compilations in its first minute on one CPU, and the ahead-of-time cache is the answer Why
twistguarded devirtualisation, from the profile of tier 0inlining behind a class check, and deoptimisation when the check failsthe run had 516 deoptimisations, and none of them was in the service's own code Why
newno log of the stops-Xlog:safepoint, one line per stop with the time to reach itevery thread stops at a poll, for the collector and for a thread dump alike, and the slow request waited for one Why
twista thread is an operating-system thread, and async/await frees it while it waitsa platform thread is the same, and a virtual thread is an object that the JVM mounts on a carrierthe code stays blocking, and the thread under it is taken away while it waits Why
trapawait inside lock is a compile errorsynchronized inside a virtual thread pinned its carrier until Java 24Java 25 no longer pins on synchronized, and the recording of the service on virtual threads showed no pinned thread Why
twistdotnet-trace and dotnet-countersFlight Recorder, started with one flag and read with the jfr toolthe recording costs about one percent, the JRE image has the tool, and the reading happens on your machine Why

Scene 1: the class filetwist#

The chapter before this one cleared the heap. The service did not die of memory, and when it was killed, the kernel did it. This chapter is about the other half of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), the half that runs code. It has two mysteries. After every deploy, the service is slow for minutes, and the graphs show it. And in a quiet minute with a median of 19 ms, one request took 241 ms. The protagonist is one method, place in OrderService. Scene 1 reads its bytes. Scene 7 reads a recording of it. For the first look at how Java runs a program, see the handbook chapter How Java runs your code.

The run. On 26 October 2026 the service ran from its image inside an image of the Java Development Kit (JDK) 25.0.4.1. The host was Docker 27.5.1 on a laptop with an Intel i9-8950HK. The container had one CPU and 512 MB. The JVM ran with three diagnostic flags: -XX:+PrintCompilation, -Xlog:safepoint and a Flight Recorder recording. A script sent requests for two minutes, then timed each request for one more minute. A second, shorter run put Tomcat on virtual threads. The numbers below come from those two runs, unless the text names another chapter. The script is companion/runs/jit/run.sh.

Here is the protagonist as the author wrote it. It checks the delivery method, reserves stock outside the transaction, and then places the order and its first notes in one transaction:

public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact customer, DeliveryMethod deliveryMethod, List<OrderItem> items,
                         List<NewNote> firstNotes) {
    referenceData.requireActive(ReferenceTypes.DELIVERY_METHOD, deliveryMethod.code(), "deliveryMethod");
    OrderId orderId = OrderId.newId();
    StockAvailability availability = stock.reserve(orderId, items);           // outside the transaction

    return transaction.execute(status -> {
        Order order = Order.place(orderId, customer, deliveryMethod, items, availability, clock);
        Order saved = saveAndPublish(order, AuditActions.ORDER_PLACED);        // aggregate 1
        List<String> noteIds = notes.addNotes(saved.id().value(), firstNotes); // aggregate 2, same transaction
        return new PlacedOrder(saved.id().value(), noteIds);
    });
}

Two calls in it matter for this chapter. stock.reserve goes through an interface, the port to the stock service. transaction.execute receives a lambda. The compiler javac turned the ten lines into 60 bytes of bytecode, and the run printed them with javap. Each line is one instruction. The number at the left is its offset in the method, and the comment at the right is the constant pool entry it names:

public PlacedOrder place(CustomerContact, DeliveryMethod, List<OrderItem>, List<NewNote>);
  Code:
     0: aload_0
     1: getfield      #17   // Field referenceData:ReferenceDataService
     4: ldc           #47   // String DELIVERY_METHOD
     6: aload_2
     7: invokevirtual #49   // Method DeliveryMethod.code:()String
    10: ldc           #55   // String deliveryMethod
    12: invokevirtual #57   // Method ReferenceDataService.requireActive
    15: invokestatic  #63   // Method OrderId.newId:()OrderId
    18: astore        5
    20: aload_0
    21: getfield      #21   // Field stock:StockChecker
    24: aload         5
    26: aload_3
    27: invokeinterface #69,  3  // InterfaceMethod StockChecker.reserve
    32: astore        6
    34: aload_0
    35: getfield      #37   // Field transaction:TransactionTemplate
    38: aload_0
    ...
    48: invokedynamic #75,  0   // InvokeDynamic #0:doInTransaction
    53: invokevirtual #79   // Method TransactionTemplate.execute
    56: checkcast     #85   // class PlacedOrder
    59: areturn

The output is shortened to one line per idea, and the package names are cut. The JVM is a stack machine, like the Common Language Runtime (CLR). aload_0 pushes this, and getfield replaces it with the field. A call takes its arguments from the stack. Four kinds of call appear in sixty bytes. The fifth kind, invokespecial, calls constructors and private methods. invokevirtual calls a method on a class, and the JVM picks the override. invokestatic calls a static method, and the target is known at link time. invokeinterface calls through an interface, and here the interface is the port StockChecker. invokedynamic is the lambda. It asks a bootstrap method for the call site at first use, and the lambda class exists only from then on. The checkcast at the end is type erasure at work. execute returns a type parameter, so the compiler inserted the cast to PlacedOrder.

The bytes are stored in a class file. Its layout is fixed by the JVM specification, and it opens with the magic number CAFEBABE. Then come two version numbers, and a Java 25 compiler writes major version 69. A Java 25 JVM accepts every major version from 45 to 69, so old class files run and newer ones are refused. Then the constant pool, which holds every name, every type and every string the class uses. The #17 in the listing is an index into it. Then the fields and the methods. The bytecode of a method is in its Code attribute, behind two numbers. One is the depth of operand stack the method needs, and one is the number of local variable slots. The astore 5 above writes slot five. The names are all there. A class file is not stripped, which is why javap and every stack trace can name the method.

The C# reader has seen this before. A C# compiler emits Common Intermediate Language (CIL) plus metadata into a portable executable (PE) file. The metadata is the constant pool by another name. Both runtimes are stack machines. The difference is where the checking happens. Modern .NET does not verify CIL for type safety at run time. Its just-in-time (JIT) compiler rejects only invalid CIL. The JVM verifies every class when it links it, before any method in it runs.

Loading has three steps, and the JVM does them lazily. Loading finds the bytes and makes a class from them. Linking verifies the class, prepares its static fields, and resolves the symbolic names in the constant pool. Initialisation runs the static initialiser. HotSpot waits until a class is first needed before it loads and links it. It resolves each constant pool entry when an instruction first uses it. So the #69 above is a name until the first order is placed. Then the JVM looks up StockChecker.reserve, finds it, and replaces the lookup with the answer. The first request pays for every lookup on its path. The verifier reads the bytecode once, because a class file since version 50 carries a StackMapTable with the types at each branch target. A class that fails verification throws VerifyError and never links. The histogram in the next scene counts 23,858 java.lang.Class objects in the running service. The recording counts 22,463 loaded classes, and most of them belong to Spring and the JDK. The other Class objects stand for arrays and primitive types.

What you can see here#

javap -c -p on a class in the jar, which prints the bytecode of every method. -v adds the constant pool and the version. The run ran it inside the container against /app/BOOT-INF/classes, where the layered jar keeps the service's own classes. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per loaded class, with its source. The source says whether the class came from a jar or from the class data sharing (CDS) archive.

What you can tune here#

AOT is short for ahead-of-time, and the AOT cache is the first answer to the slow minutes. Java 24 can save the loaded and linked classes of a training run, and Java 25 saves their method profiles too. Spring Boot documents it in three commands. Extract the jar with java -Djarmode=tools -jar order-service.jar extract. Run the extracted application once with -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot and -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh. Then start it with -XX:AOTCache=app.aot. The training run must use the extracted form, or the cache has no effect. The handbook chapter Packaging and native images places it against the other packaging options. The AOT cache does not cache compiled code. Scene 3 says what it does for the compilers instead.

Scene 2: the objecttwist#

place makes objects. An OrderId, an Order, a PlacedOrder, the lambda, and many that the libraries make for it. Scene 3 of the memory chapter followed one of them into a TLAB. This scene looks at its shape. The run asked the JVM for a class histogram after three minutes of load, and the top of it is this:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
-------------------------------------------------------
   1:        159218       15178528  [B (java.base@25.0.4.1)
   2:        151241        3629784  java.lang.String (java.base@25.0.4.1)
   3:         23858        3010528  java.lang.Class (java.base@25.0.4.1)
   4:         78990        2527680  java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap$Node (java.base@25.0.4.1)
   5:         27348        2406624  java.lang.reflect.Method (java.base@25.0.4.1)

The first line is byte arrays, written [B, and most of them are the text of strings. The second line is the strings themselves. Divide the bytes by the instances, and a String is 24 bytes and a ConcurrentHashMap$Node is 32. Those sizes come from three rules. Every object starts with a header. Every reference inside it is 4 bytes in this service. And every object is padded to a multiple of 8.

The header is two words. The mark word is 8 bytes. It holds the lock state, the identity hash code and the age of the object for the collector. The class word points to the class, and it is 4 bytes because compressed class pointers are on by default. So the header is 12 bytes. A String has a reference to its byte array, an int hash and two small fields. That is about 22 bytes, and the padding makes it 24. The C# reader knows the same arithmetic with different numbers. A .NET object on x64 carries a 16-byte header, the object header word and the method table pointer, and a reference is 8 bytes.

Java references are 4 bytes because of compressed ordinary object pointers. The flags of the run showed them as -XX:+UseCompressedOops. The JVM stores a reference as a 32-bit offset from the heap base, in units of 8 bytes, which reaches 32 GB. Any heap below 32 GB gets them by default. Above that, a reference is 8 bytes and every object with references grows. Compressed class pointers are the same idea for the class word. Their flag is deprecated in Java 25, and they are on by default.

Java 25 can make the header 8 bytes. Compact object headers fold a 22-bit class pointer into the mark word, with the hash code and the collector's bits beside it. They were experimental in Java 24 and are a product feature in 25. The flag is -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders, and it is still off by default. The reference says the flag saves 4 bytes per object on average and often improves performance. A future release is expected to turn it on. The histogram above has 159,218 arrays and 151,241 strings. Those two lines alone would lose about 1.2 MB of headers.

Now the twist for the C# reader. Java has no struct. OrderId is a record, and a record is a class that cannot be extended, with java.lang.Record as its superclass. Its instance carries the full header, and a field of that type is a 4-byte reference to it. An Order with an OrderId, a customer and a list of lines is a small graph of objects, not one block. Value classes, which would let the JVM flatten some of them, are a preview feature targeted at Java 28. What Java has instead is the compiler's escape analysis, which scene 4 reaches. When C2 can prove that an object never leaves the compiled method, it allocates nothing and keeps the fields in registers. The status lambda above escapes, because execute receives it. A small record that a hot method makes and reads and drops often does not.

What you can see here#

jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram, inside the container. Its impact is a full collection, and the memory chapter met the pause it causes. For one class, the Java Object Layout tool prints the real layout with the header, as java -jar jol-cli.jar internals com.acme.orderservice.order.domain.model.Order. The flags that jcmd 1 VM.flags prints include UseCompressedOops. When you set it, they include UseCompactObjectHeaders too.

What you can tune here#

-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders, after a test run, because it changes every object. Nothing else in the layout is worth a flag. Keep the heap below 32 GB, so references stay at 4 bytes, and the memory chapter gave the service 256 MB.

Scene 3: the interpreter and the two compilerstwist#

Now the first mystery. The service starts, and for minutes it is slow. The run saw it. The first request of the startup chapter took 0.31 seconds and the second 0.04. In this run, with one CPU, Spring reported Started after 31 seconds, where the laptop needs sixteen. The reason is in the first lines the JVM printed:

242    1       3       java.lang.Object::<init> (1 bytes)
275    2       3       java.lang.Byte::toUnsignedInt (6 bytes)
277    3       3       java.lang.String::hashCode (60 bytes)
285    4     n 0       jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe::getReferenceVolatile (native)
328   27       4       java.lang.String::charAt (25 bytes)
330    7       3       java.lang.String::charAt (25 bytes)   made not entrant: not used
371   67   !   3       java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap::putVal (432 bytes)
593  196 %     3       java.lang.StringCoding::countPositives @ 7 (33 bytes)

These lines come from -XX:+PrintCompilation, and no reference document explains their columns, so here they are from the HotSpot source. The first number is the time in milliseconds since the JVM started. The second is the compile id. Then up to five marks. % is on-stack replacement, and s a synchronized method. ! marks a method with exception handlers, b a blocking compile and n a native wrapper. Then the tier, then the method and its bytecode size, then a message. So String::hashCode was compiled at tier 3 after 277 ms. String::charAt reached tier 4 after 328 ms, and two milliseconds later its tier 3 code was dropped as not used. And countPositives was compiled while a loop in it was running, with @ 7 naming the bytecode offset where the compiled code took over.

The JVM starts every method in the interpreter. HotSpot's interpreter is generated at startup from a template for each bytecode, and it runs the method one instruction at a time. While it runs, it counts. Each method has an invocation counter and a back-edge counter, and the back-edge counter counts loop iterations. The counts decide when the method moves to a compiler. There are two compilers, and together they are the just-in-time (JIT) compiler of the JVM. C1 compiles fast and optimises lightly. C2 compiles slowly and optimises hard, with the profile that C1's code collected. Together they make five tiers. Tier 0 is the interpreter. Tier 1 is C1 without profiling, for methods whose profile would not help. Tier 2 is C1 with the two counters only. Tier 3 is C1 with full profiling, which records which branches are taken and which classes appear at each call. Tier 4 is C2. The normal path is 0, then 3, then 4. Tier 2 appears when the C2 queue is long, because tier 2 code runs faster than tier 3 code. Tier 1 is the end for trivial methods. The run compiled the accessors of the request record at tier 1 and left them there. PlaceOrderRequest::customer, with its 5 bytes, is one of them.

The thresholds are in the HotSpot source, not in any manual. A method goes to tier 3 after 200 invocations. It also goes after 100 invocations when invocations plus loop iterations pass 2,000. It goes to tier 4 after 5,000 invocations, or after 600 when the sum passes 15,000. A loop alone sends a method to on-stack replacement after 60,000 iterations at tier 3. Each threshold is scaled up when the compile queue is long. A busy JVM therefore waits longer before it compiles. The CLR has two tiers in place of five. Tier 0 is the quick JIT and tier 1 the optimising JIT, with dynamic PGO adding the profile from tier 0. ReadyToRun code counts as tier 0 and is replaced when a method gets hot. Java has nothing that counts as compiled code at start. The jar carries bytecode, and every method begins in the interpreter after every deploy.

Here is what that cost the service. The run lasted 217 seconds and the compilation log has 24,992 compilations in it. 8,420 of them happened before Started. By minute, the compilations were 17,848, then 4,391, then 1,836, then 917. The tier 4 compilations alone were 1,910, then 1,362, then 707, then 273. The recording adds the price. Its compiler statistics report a total compile time of 1 minute 47 seconds, in a run of 217 seconds, on one CPU. The JVM had chosen two compiler threads, as CICompilerCount=2 in its flags. Their compile tasks lasted 1 minute 47 seconds in total, most of them in the first minutes. The run did not measure their share of the CPU. But the request threads shared that one CPU with them, and the request code itself still ran in the interpreter or in C1 code. That is the slow start, and it has two parts. The code is slow until it is compiled, and compiling it is work on the same CPU.

The protagonist shows the scale. OrderService::place was called about 2,600 times in the run, once per order. Its line in the log is one:

131048 22717       3       com.acme.orderservice.order.application.OrderService::place (60 bytes)

The line puts OrderService::place at tier 3, after 131 seconds, with compile id 22717. The method never reached C2 in the run, because 2,600 calls are below the tier 4 threshold of 5,000. At 50 orders a second in production it would reach C2 within two minutes of the deploy. Fourteen methods of the service's own code did reach tier 4. Seven of them were property accessors that Spring Data generates. Those run for every field of every saved document. Everything else at tier 4 was the JDK, Spring and the drivers.

Compiled code is kept in the code cache, outside the heap. The memory chapter counted it at 58 MB committed. The run asked for its layout:

CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods': size=120036Kb used=10122Kb max_used=10482Kb free=109913Kb
CodeHeap 'profiled nmethods': size=120036Kb used=24904Kb max_used=33795Kb free=95131Kb
CodeHeap 'non-nmethods': size=5692Kb used=1553Kb max_used=1633Kb free=4139Kb
CodeCache: size=245764Kb, used=36579Kb, max_used=45910Kb, free=209183Kb

The CodeCache line is the whole. It is 240 MB reserved, the default with tiered compilation, and it is split in three since Java 9. The 'profiled nmethods' heap takes tier 2 and 3 code. The counters make that code large, and tier 4 replaces it soon. Its high mark was 33.8 MB and it had 24.9 MB at the end. The difference is the not used code that was dropped. The non-profiled heap takes tier 1 and 4 code, which stays. The third heap takes the interpreter itself and the compilers' buffers. A full code cache stops the compilers. The JVM logs it and raises a Flight Recorder event named jdk.CodeCacheFull. The service used 37 MB of 240, and the cache never filled. But the code cache can stop the service in another way, and scene 5 finds it.

What you can see here#

-XX:+PrintCompilation, whose columns are above, written to the container's standard output. jcmd 1 Compiler.codecache for the layout, and jcmd 1 Compiler.queue for the methods waiting. In a recording, the view compiler-statistics gives the totals and longest-compilations the methods that cost most. In the run the longest single compilation was 1.87 seconds, for a Spring caching method at tier 4. Five of the ten longest were one bean factory method, compiled again and again. Scene 4 says why.

What you can tune here#

Not the thresholds. -XX:CompileThresholdScaling moves them all at once, and a service that needs it is a service without a warm-up plan. -XX:CICompilerCount sets the compiler threads, and the JVM's choice fits the CPUs it sees. The real knob is the AOT cache of scene 1. Java 25 stores the method profiles of the training run in it, so the JIT starts earlier and with better information. It still compiles. The other real knob is the deploy itself. A rolling deploy that sends full traffic to a new instance at once makes the first minutes the user's problem. Warm the instance with its own traffic first. And never -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 for a service. It is for a tool that runs for seconds.

Scene 4: the compiler's betstwist#

C2 is fast because it bets. It reads the profile that tier 3 collected and compiles the method for the cases the profile saw. Three bets matter in place.

The first bet is inlining. A call costs a frame, and it hides the callee from every optimisation of the caller. So C2 copies small callees into the caller. Any method up to 35 bytes of bytecode is inlined where it is called. A hot method is inlined up to a platform limit, which is 325 bytes in the reference's example. C2 inlines up to fifteen levels deep. deliveryMethod.code() is a record accessor of a few bytes, and OrderId.newId() is a small static method. Both disappear into place when C2 compiles it. The CLR inlines too, with its own limits, and the C# reader has written AggressiveInlining for a reason.

The second bet is about the calls that cannot be resolved at compile time. stock.reserve is an invokeinterface. Which class answers it is a run-time question, and a virtual call through a table is the slow way to answer it. C2 has two ways around that. Class hierarchy analysis asks the JVM whether only one loaded class implements the interface. In the running service one adapter implements the port. So the call becomes a direct call, and the compiled code records a dependency on that fact. If the profile shows one receiver class at the call site, C2 inlines that class's method behind a class check. With two classes it inlines both, with two checks. The source calls these sites monomorphic and bimorphic. With more it leaves a virtual call, which the source calls megamorphic. When a call site has seen more than two classes, C2 still inlines the most common one if it covers 90 percent of the calls. Since .NET 8 the CLR makes the same bet by default, under the name guarded devirtualisation, from the profile of an instrumented tier. In both runtimes, an interface with one implementation on a hot path is free. An instanceof chain over five types pays a virtual call.

The third bet is about branches. A branch that the profile never saw taken is compiled as an uncommon trap. The compiled code for that path is a jump out of the compiled method. The same trick removes null checks that never failed and array bounds checks that never failed. Escape analysis is the bet that an object never leaves the method, and it removes the allocation and any lock on that object.

Every bet has a check, and when a check fails the compiled code cannot continue. The JVM then deoptimises. It converts the compiled frame back into interpreter frames, at the exact bytecode, with every local variable restored. The method continues in the interpreter as if it had never been compiled. The source calls this an uncommon trap when C2 planted it. Each trap carries a reason and an action. The reasons say which bet failed, and the actions say what to do with the compiled code. maybe_recompile keeps the code and asks for a new compilation with the new profile. reinterpret throws the code away and resets the inline cache of the call, and the JVM may compile the method again later. make_not_entrant throws it away and recompiles. After 400 recompilations of one method the JVM gives up and leaves it interpreted. The recording of the run has 516 deoptimisation events, and the view by reason sorts them:

Reason                              Count
----------------------------------- -----
unstable_if                           170
bimorphic_or_optimized_type_check     103
class_check                            98
array_check                            58
profile_predicate                      29
speculate_class_check                  24
predicate                               9
null_check                              8

unstable_if is the third bet failing. A branch that was predicted never taken was taken. class_check and the bimorphic reason are the second bet failing. A new receiver class arrived at an inlined call site. array_check is an array store of a type the compiled code did not expect, and null_check is a null where none had been seen. The first event of the recording is a good example of the second bet:

jdk.Deoptimization {
  startTime = 21:30:39.895
  compileId = 1251
  compiler = "c2"
  method = java.util.Collections$UnmodifiableCollection$1.hasNext()
  lineNumber = 1079
  bci = 4
  instruction = "invokeinterface"
  reason = "class_check"
  action = "maybe_recompile"
  eventThread = "main" (javaThreadId = 3)
}

Three seconds into the start, C2 had compiled the hasNext() of an unmodifiable collection wrapper. The method calls hasNext on the iterator it wraps, through an interface, at bytecode index 4. The profile had seen one iterator class, so C2 inlined it. A second iterator class appeared, the check failed, and the method went back to the interpreter with a request to recompile. The stack trace shows that the recording's own start-up code made the call, not the service. Methods that many callers share live this way during a start.

The bean factory method of scene 3 is the extreme case. AbstractBeanFactory::isTypeMatch is 776 bytes of bytecode. The log shows it compiled at tier 4 seven times, with eleven made not entrant lines between. Five of the seven tier 4 compilations took about a second each. Spring calls this method for every type it looks up during startup, and each new type can break the bet of the last compilation. So the seven compilations of one method lasted about 6.6 seconds in all, during the thirty seconds the service took to start. The JVM is not wrong to do it. After startup the method settles, and its final code stays.

The log counts the fallout. There are 6,413 made not entrant lines in it. Most of them, 5,823, say not used. That is tier 3 code replaced by tier 4. Another 299 say uncommon trap, a bet that failed. Another 265 say marked for deoptimization. That is a dependency that a class load broke, such as a second implementor of an interface that had one. The remaining 26 are on-stack replacement and patching cases. And the service's own code appears in none of the 516 events. Most of it never reached C2, so C2 made few bets on it.

What you can see here#

The event jdk.Deoptimization, on in the default recording settings and with stack traces in the profile settings. jfr view deoptimizations-by-reason and deoptimizations-by-site summarise them. In the compilation log, the made not entrant lines with their reason. With -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+LogCompilation, the JVM writes every inlining decision to hotspot.log, for the day you must know whether one call was inlined.

What you can tune here#

Nothing, in the JVM. Compiler directives exist, and jcmd 1 Compiler.directives_add loads them, and a service should not need them. Tune the code instead. Keep one implementation behind each interface on a hot path, and keep the test doubles in the tests. Keep instanceof chains and switch over types out of the hottest loop. Make small objects and let escape analysis remove them. Then measure, because the compiler makes the bets and not the author.

Scene 5: the stop, and the slow requesttrap#

The second mystery. In the timed minute, 1,433 orders were placed. The median took 19 ms, the 99th percentile 56 ms, and the slowest 241 ms. The slowest did nothing different from the others. It waited.

Many things the JVM does need every Java thread to stand still. A collector that moves objects must know that no thread holds a reference it is about to move. A thread dump must read every stack while no stack changes. The JVM does this with a safepoint. A safepoint is a point in the code where the state of the thread is fully known. Every reference on its stack is accounted for, and the heap is consistent. HotSpot does not interrupt threads to get there. It asks them. Compiled code polls a page when a method returns, and some loops poll too. The interpreter switches to a second table of instruction handlers, with the question in each. A thread in native code is stopped on its way back. When the JVM arms the poll, each thread blocks at the next poll it reaches. When the last one has blocked, the JVM is at a safepoint and does its work. Then it releases them all.

The run logged every safepoint with -Xlog:safepoint, and the first line of the log reads so:

[0.652s][info][safepoint] Safepoint "SerialCollectForAllocation", Time since last: 584265372 ns,
  Reaching safepoint: 553092 ns, At safepoint: 1857472 ns, Leaving safepoint: 993898 ns,
  Total: 3404462 ns, Threads: 2 runnable, 9 total

The line is one in the file, and it is wrapped here. The name in quotes is the operation that asked for the stop, and this one is a young collection of the Serial collector. The numbers are the three parts of a stop. Reaching safepoint is the time from arming the poll to the last thread blocking, 0.55 ms here. At safepoint is the work, 1.86 ms. Leaving safepoint is the wake-up. The reaching time is the one that monitoring hides. A collector reports its pause as its work. The time the JVM spent waiting for one thread to reach a poll is not in that number. In the run the longest reaching time was 49 ms, before an ordinary young collection. One thread was somewhere without a poll for 49 ms, and every other thread waited for it.

The log has 196 safepoints in 217 seconds, and they sort by name:

OperationCountWhat asked for the stop
SerialCollectForAllocation176a young collection, because a TLAB could not be refilled
CollectForMetadataAllocation4a collection because metaspace needed room, during and just after startup
SerialGCCollect1a full collection, which the code cache asked for
GC_HeapInspection1the class histogram of scene 2, taken after the timed minute
PrintThreads and FindDeadlocks3 eachthe thread dump that the recording takes once a minute
ClassLoaderStatsOperation3class loader statistics for the recording
JFR operations4the recording's own bookkeeping
SetNotifyJvmtiEventsMode1the tooling interface, at startup

Two lessons are in the table. The first is that the collector is not the only one who stops the world. A thread dump is a safepoint, and the recording took three of them. The class histogram of scene 2 was one, GC_HeapInspection, and it stopped every thread for 772 ms. The memory chapter met the same pause and called it the pause you caused yourself. Since Java 10, some operations that stopped every thread now stop one at a time, through a handshake. The view counts 73 of those as HandshakeAllThreads, with a longest of 3.4 ms. The second lesson is the slow request.

Here are the pauses of the run that lasted longer than 100 ms, with their time since the JVM started. The histogram's pause at 213.7 s is left out, because the script asked for it:

  9.7 s   CollectForMetadataAllocation   104 ms
 16.2 s   CollectForMetadataAllocation   101 ms
 22.2 s   CollectForMetadataAllocation   140 ms
 36.1 s   CollectForMetadataAllocation   238 ms
174.2 s   SerialGCCollect                193 ms

The four CollectForMetadataAllocation pauses are in the first 36 seconds. The service loaded about 22,000 classes then, and metaspace grew in steps. Each step was a collection, and the longest took 238 ms. That is the slow start again, from another side. The SerialGCCollect is the one that matters. At 174 seconds, inside the timed minute, the Serial collector ran a full collection. Every thread stood still for 193 ms. The heap did not ask for it. The recording names the cause of every collection, and the run wrote them to jfr-gc-causes.txt:

startTime = 21:33:31.803 name = "SerialOld" cause = "CodeCache GC Threshold" sumOfPauses = 193 ms

The cause is CodeCache GC Threshold. In the HotSpot source, the code cache asks for a collection when the compilers have filled a set share of it since the last collection. The collection lets the JVM unload compiled code that is no longer used. On Serial, the collection was a full one. So the compilers of scene 3, still compiling in the third minute, caused the stop of scene 5. The two mysteries of the chapter are one story. The script recorded durations and not clock times, so the log cannot name the request that waited. The arithmetic can. A normal request takes 19 ms. Add 193 ms of stop, and a request in flight when the poll was armed took about 212 ms. The script sent one request at a time, so no other request waited behind it. The slowest request took 241 ms. The recording's view of pauses agrees from the other side. Its 172 pauses have a median of 4.2 ms, a 99th percentile of 211 ms and a maximum of 237 ms. One request in a thousand is one full collection in a quiet minute. The CLR stops managed threads for its collector too. Java gives the stop a name, a log line, and three numbers.

The memory chapter said that a container with one CPU gets the Serial collector, and that its pauses are then the service's business. This is what that sentence costs. A young collection of Serial is a few milliseconds, and the service pays 176 of them without anyone noticing. A full collection is the whole old generation, in one thread, with everything stopped. On two CPUs and 2 GB the JVM chooses G1, whose pause target is 200 ms by default and whose young collections are parallel. With a larger heap and more cores, ZGC aims to keep every pause below a millisecond, because it moves objects while the threads run. The choice is the container's size, and the memory chapter's arithmetic sets the size. Fewer late compilations help too, and the AOT cache of scene 1 gives the compilers their profiles earlier.

What you can see here#

-Xlog:safepoint, one line per stop with the three times, written to a file with -Xlog:safepoint:file=/tmp/safepoint.log. In a recording, the view safepoints and the view vm-operations, which names what asked for each stop, with the longest duration of each kind. The event jdk.SafepointBegin is on in the default settings for any safepoint over 10 ms. And the view gc-pauses for the collector's share, with its percentiles.

What you can tune here#

The collector, through the container's size, as the memory chapter showed. Nothing about safepoints themselves. A flag exists that keeps a poll in every counted loop. Its default depends on the collector, and the JVM knows better than the author when to set it. A thread dump or a class histogram in production is a stop of every thread. Take one before a restart, not one every minute.

Scene 6: the threadstwist#

The request that waited 193 ms was running on a thread, and this scene is about which. The run dumped every thread of the service after three minutes of load, with jcmd 1 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json. There were 52 of them. Tomcat owns the largest group, and Spring's task executor the next. The drivers for MongoDB and for the Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) bring their own. Sorted into groups, they are these:

ThreadsCountWho made them
http-nio-8080-exec-1 to 1010Tomcat, ten kept ready even when idle, from a pool of up to 200
http-nio-8080-Acceptor and Poller2Tomcat, to accept connections and to wait for bytes on them
task-1 to 88the application task executor of Spring Boot, for @Async and the event listeners
scheduling-11the task scheduler, for @Scheduled
cluster-* and cluster-rtt-*2the MongoDB driver, to watch the server and to measure its round trip
aws-java-sdk-NettyEventLoop-1-0 and -12the AWS SDK, for its asynchronous HTTP client
sqsListenerEndpointContainer#0 ...3Spring Cloud AWS, to poll the SQS queue and to run the listener
HttpClient-1-*4the JDK HTTP client, for the calls to the other services
JFR Recorder Thread and JFR Periodic Tasks2the recording
Reference Handler, Finalizer, Common-Cleaner, Signal Dispatcher, and others18the JVM, the JDK, Tomcat's utility threads and the tracing exporters

Each of these is a platform thread. A platform thread is an operating-system thread with a Java object in front of it. The JVM creates the native thread when start() is called and gives it back when run() returns. It reserves 1 MB of stack for each on Linux x64, as the memory chapter counted, and the kernel schedules it. The C# reader has exactly this. A Thread in .NET is an operating-system thread, and the thread pool lends them out. Tomcat keeps ten threads ready even when idle, and the pool grows to 200 when more requests arrive at once. When all 200 are inside a call to MongoDB, the next request waits in the acceptor's queue. A thread does nothing while it waits. It keeps its stack, its kernel entry and its place in the pool, and the kernel does not run it.

The .NET answer to that waste is async and await. The method is cut into pieces at each await. The thread goes back to the pool while the I/O is in flight, and a continuation runs the next piece. The code changes shape to get there. Every method on the path returns a Task, and lock around an await is a compile error. Java took the other road in Java 21. A virtual thread is a Thread with its stack on the heap, in chunk objects. The JVM mounts it on a platform thread to run it, and that platform thread is called its carrier. When the virtual thread blocks, on a socket, a lock or a sleep, the JVM copies its frames to the heap and unmounts it. The carrier takes another one. The code keeps its blocking shape. stock.reserve still returns a value, and the method under it still blocks, and the thread under that is swapped out. The carriers are a ForkJoinPool in first-in first-out mode. Its parallelism is the number of CPUs by default, and it may grow to 256 platform threads when carriers are held.

Spring Boot switches the whole service with one setting, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. Tomcat then runs each request on a new virtual thread. The application task executor becomes one that starts a virtual thread per task, and the scheduler does the same. The run started the service a second time with the setting, and dumped its threads under load. There were 39 platform threads and three virtual ones. The ten exec threads were gone, and so were the eight task threads. In their place were two carriers, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 and -3. A thread named VirtualThread-unblocker had appeared beside them. The JSON lists the virtual threads under the executor that made them. Two containers hold virtual threads. One holds the scheduler's thread, scheduling-1. This is the other, with its threads shortened:

{
  "container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@644d4e23",
  "parent": "<root>",
  "threadCount": "2",
  "threads": [
    { "tid": "48", "virtual": true, "name": "SubPoller-0", "state": "WAITING",
      "stack": [ "java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:745)",
                 "java.base/sun.nio.ch.Poller.poll(Poller.java:197)" ] },
    { "tid": "49", "virtual": true, "name": "SubPoller-1", "state": "WAITING" }
  ]
}

These two virtual threads are the SubPoller threads of the JDK itself. They wait on sockets for every virtual thread that is blocked in a read, and they are virtual threads too. No request was in flight at the moment of the dump, so no request thread appears. The log shows a request thread named tomcat-handler-0. The acceptor and the poller of Tomcat were still platform threads, because waiting on a selector is their job.

The latencies did not improve, and the chapter would be dishonest to hide it. On platform threads the timed minute gave a median of 19 ms, a 99th percentile of 56 ms and a maximum of 241 ms. That was 1,433 orders. On virtual threads it gave 22 ms, 74 ms and 307 ms, for 1,250. The script sent one request at a time, so at most one request was in flight, and the container had one CPU. The virtual run also had one minute of warm-up, and the platform run had two. So the two minutes show no gain, but they do not prove a loss. A virtual thread saves a waiting platform thread, and the service was never short of one. The gain appears when ten thousand requests wait on a slow dependency at once. Then Tomcat's pool of 200 is the limit on platform threads, and no limit on virtual threads. The cost appears when the work is CPU. A virtual thread that computes holds its carrier, and there are as many carriers as CPUs.

Pragmatic choice: Tomcat on platform threads

The strict rule. A service whose requests block on a database and on other services runs them on virtual threads. A thread pool is then never the limit on concurrency.

What we do. The service leaves spring.threads.virtual.enabled unset, so Tomcat runs requests on its pool of platform threads.

Why. The run showed no gain in a container with one CPU. The pool of 200 threads is far above the requests a 512 MB instance can have in flight. The MongoDB driver, the SQS listener and the AWS client bring their own threads either way. One setting fewer is one surprise fewer, and the switch is one line when it is needed.

When to stop. When the thread dump under load shows every exec thread waiting on a socket and requests queueing at the acceptor. Set the property, run the recording of scene 7, and look for pinned threads before you ship it.

Pinning is the trap that the C# reader will have read about, and Java 25 has mostly closed it. In Java 21, a virtual thread inside a synchronized block or method could not be unmounted. It was pinned to its carrier, and the carrier waited with it. With few carriers, a few pinned threads stalled the service. Java 24 changed the JVM. A virtual thread that blocks on a monitor, or waits in Object.wait, is now unmounted like any other. What still pins in Java 25 is native code that calls back into Java and then blocks. A block while a class is loaded or initialised pins too. The event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned records every pin over 20 ms, with the reason and the carrier. The recording of the second run has none. The old tracing property jdk.tracePinnedThreads is gone, so the event is the way to look.

One paragraph on what threads see, because the C# reader will ask. The Java memory model is in the language specification, and it is a set of happens-before rules. An unlock happens before the next lock of the same monitor. A write to a volatile field happens before every later read of it. start() happens before anything in the started thread, and everything in a thread happens before join() on it returns. A write that is not ordered by one of these rules may never be seen by another thread. The rules are the same on a virtual thread, because they are rules of the language and not of the carrier. The handbook chapter Locks, atomics and the memory model gives the rules with examples.

What you can see here#

jcmd 1 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json, which includes virtual threads grouped by the executor that owns them. The older Thread.print and a SIGQUIT to the process print only platform threads, and they will not show you a request on a virtual thread. The six thread states, from NEW to TERMINATED, are JVM states and not kernel states, so RUNNABLE may be waiting for a CPU. The view thread-count of a recording shows the platform thread count over time, and pinned-threads lists the pins.

What you can tune here#

spring.threads.virtual.enabled, after a run with the recording on. The carrier pool's parallelism, jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, which defaults to the CPU count, and its maximum, which defaults to 256. The default is right for a service that blocks, and a service that computes should keep platform threads. And server.tomcat.threads.max for the pool on platform threads, whose default of 200 the memory chapter weighed against 1 MB of stack each.

Scene 7: the recording, as the endingnew#

Every number in scenes 3 to 6 that did not come from a log line came from one file, the Flight Recorder recording. Flight Recorder is in the JDK since Java 11 and in the Java Runtime Environment (JRE) image of the service. The run started it with -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=/tmp/recording.jfr,settings=profile. The default settings cost under one percent and are meant to stay on in production. The profile settings cost about two percent and record more. They add stack traces to deoptimisations, and they sample methods every 10 ms instead of 20. The run used them. After 214 seconds the file was 26 MB, and its summary begins so:

 Event Type                          Count   Size (bytes)
=========================================================
 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample          53522         892936
 jdk.ThreadPark                      27344        1079136
 jdk.JavaExceptionThrow              15060         376989
 jdk.SocketRead                      13625         576941
 jdk.NativeMethodSample               9004         115010
 jdk.ExecutionSample                  3851          49100
 jdk.Deoptimization                    516          13348
 jdk.SafepointBegin                    184           2736
 jdk.Compilation                       139           4291

A recording is a list of typed events. Each has a timestamp and a thread, and often a stack trace, and the summary counts them by type. jdk.ExecutionSample is the profiler. Every 10 ms it writes the stack of each thread that is running Java code. The run has 3,851 samples in 214 seconds on one CPU, a sample of where the CPU time went. The view hot-methods sorts them. No method of the service's own code appears in its top. The top methods were a method handle allocation and hash map lookups, at about one percent each. A logging filter had about half a percent. That is the profile of a service that spends its CPU in the framework and its time in the database. jdk.ThreadPark counts threads that waited on a lock or a queue, 27,344 times, mostly pool threads waiting for work. jdk.JavaExceptionThrow counts 15,060 exceptions in three and a half minutes. That is a number to look at on another day. An exception that is thrown and caught inside a library pays for a stack trace every time.

Reading a recording needs memory, and the container did not have it. The jfr tool loads the file into a heap, and the 26 MB file needed more than the 512 MB container could give. So the script copied the file out with docker cp and ran the tool on the laptop's JDK with a 12 GB heap. That is the normal shape. Record in the container, and read anywhere. The tool has four commands that matter. jfr summary is the table above. jfr print --events jdk.Deoptimization prints each event of a type in full, as scene 4 showed. jfr view hot-methods runs one of about seventy named views, and this chapter used ten of them. And jfr print --json gives the events to a script. The desktop tool, JDK Mission Control, opens the same file with graphs, and version 9.1.2 is current.

The ending of the chapter is a runbook, because the recording is only useful if it exists when the question comes. These are the commands the service's team runs on a container that misbehaves, before anyone restarts it:

QuestionCommand, inside the container, where the service is process 1Cost
is a recording running?jcmd 1 JFR.checknothing
start one for the next ten minutesjcmd 1 JFR.start duration=10m filename=/dumps/now.jfr settings=profileabout two percent
write what the running recording has so farjcmd 1 JFR.dump filename=/dumps/sofar.jfra file, and one safepoint
what is every thread doing?jcmd 1 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /dumps/threads.jsonno stop of every thread in the run's safepoint log
is the heap the problem?jcmd 1 GC.heap_info, and the memory chapter's commandsnothing
what did the compilers do?jfr view compiler-statistics now.jfr, on your machinenothing in the container
what stopped the world?jfr view vm-operations now.jfr and jfr view safepoints now.jfrthe same
which bets failed?jfr view deoptimizations-by-site now.jfrthe same
who is pinned?jfr view pinned-threads now.jfrthe same

/dumps is a mounted volume, for the reason the memory chapter gave. A file written inside the container counts against its limit through the page cache. The commands need jcmd, which the JRE image lacks and the JDK image has, and the memory chapter weighed the three ways out. With the JRE image, a recording started at launch is the one that is always there. Start it with -XX:StartFlightRecording and maxage=1h, and dumponexit=true writes it when the JVM exits. It does not write it when the kernel kills the process, because nothing runs after that.

And the two mysteries, closed. The slow minutes after a deploy are three things. The interpreter runs the code. Two compiler threads share the CPU with it. And the compilers compile the hot methods several times as the bets settle. The answer is the AOT cache and a warm-up before traffic, and not a flag on the compiler. The one slow request in a quiet minute waited for a full collection of the Serial collector. It stopped every thread for 193 ms, and the code cache asked for it. The safepoint log and the recording both show it. The answer is the same AOT cache, and a container size that gives the service a collector with short stops. The recording shows no service method among the hot methods or the deoptimisations.

What you can see here#

jcmd 1 JFR.check for the recordings that run. jfr summary for what a file holds, jfr view for the seventy views, and jfr print for one event at a time. java -XX:StartFlightRecording:help for the options of the flag, and jfr --help view for the list of views.

What you can tune here#

The settings file, between default and profile, and jfr configure to write your own. maxage and maxsize on a recording that runs for the life of the process. And the volume the files go to.

Check yourself
1
A Spring Boot service is slow for the first minutes after every deploy, and then fast. The heap is quiet and the database is fast. Name the two causes in the JVM, and the fix that is not a compiler flag.
Every method starts in the interpreter and is compiled only after hundreds of calls, so the code itself is slow at first. And the compiler threads share the CPU with the request threads while they compile thousands of methods, some of them several times. The fix is an AOT cache from a training run, which carries the loaded classes and the method profiles. Add a warm-up of each instance before it takes full traffic.
2
An expert asksWhy does the JVM throw away compiled code and run a method in the interpreter again, when the compiled code was correct?
The code was correct only for the cases the profile had seen. C2 inlines a call behind a check of the receiver's class, and compiles a branch never taken as a jump out. When a new class arrives or the branch is taken, the check fails. The JVM then rebuilds the interpreter frames from the compiled frame and continues there, and usually recompiles with the new profile. This is deoptimisation, and it is how the compiler is allowed to bet.
3
In a timed minute, the median request takes 19 ms and one request takes 241 ms. Which two sources show whether a stop of the whole JVM caused it, and what do they name?
The safepoint log from -Xlog:safepoint, one line per stop. It names the operation and gives the time to reach the safepoint and the time inside it. And a Flight Recorder recording, whose views vm-operations and gc-pauses name what asked for each stop and how long it lasted. In the run, a full collection of the Serial collector stopped every thread for 193 ms inside that minute. Its cause, in the recording, was the code cache.
4
Tomcat is switched to virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. What changes in a thread dump, and which event tells you whether a virtual thread is holding its carrier?
The http-nio-8080-exec pool threads and the task threads disappear. In their place are a few ForkJoinPool carrier threads and an executor that lists one virtual thread per request in flight. Only Thread.dump_to_file shows the virtual threads. The event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned records every pin over 20 ms with its reason and its carrier, and jfr view pinned-threads lists them.
5
TranslateTranslate this C# into Java. It starts ten thousand tasks that each wait on a slow call, without holding ten thousand operating-system threads. 
var tasks = Enumerable.Range(0, 10_000)
    .Select(i => Task.Run(async () => await CheckStockAsync(i)));
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
Java keeps the blocking call and changes the thread under it. Each task runs on a virtual thread, and the executor waits for all of them when it closes. 
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
        int item = i;
        executor.submit(() -> checkStock(item));
    }
}
checkStock blocks on its socket as before. The JVM unmounts the virtual thread while it waits, so ten thousand of them share as many carrier threads as the machine has CPUs.

Changing the service#

Testing, shipping and changing it · Chapter 29· 26 min read· Quick reference

This chapter is for the day you change the service. It gives the checklists for a new service, a new feature and an existing service. It lists the files that each common task touches. It ends with the review checklist for a pull request. Then it gives short answers to "why do we do it this way?", each with a link to the chapter that explains it.
