How to use this partnew#

A developer who joins the team does not need every chapter of the part on the first day. The service has a fixed shape, and once you know the shape, the chapters become a reference. This is the shape of the order service's code:

src/main/java/com/acme/orderservice/
  OrderServiceApplication.java   the class that starts the service
  order/                         the order feature, full style
    domain/                      plain Java: the aggregate, its events and exceptions, the ports
    application/                 the use cases: OrderService and its views
    api/                         the controller, its DTOs and its mapper
    persistence/                 the document, its mapper and the adapter
    client/                      the stock service's client and adapter
    messaging/                   the published events, their mapper and the payment listener
  note/                          the note feature, light style
  reference/                     lookup values, simple style
  migration/                     indexes and seed data
  shared/                        permission annotations and audit names

Each feature, such as order/, owns one aggregate, or a set of lookup data. Each feature has the same layers inside, though a lighter feature has fewer of them. Read the part in this order:

  1. Why, and the shape. Read these three chapters:
    • Why DDD, and the service we build
    • How much DDD: three levels in one service
    • Features, layers and the rules
  2. One request through the layers. Follow POST /orders from the controller to the database, in these chapters:
    • The web layer in depth
    • Use cases: the application service
    • The domain model in plain Java
    • Storing aggregates in DocumentDB
  3. The rules. Read these two chapters:
    • Finding the aggregates
    • Where each rule goes
  4. The rest, as reference. Read the chapter on security, messaging, configuration or testing when you first change that part.
  5. This chapter, for each task. Find the task, and follow its list of files.

The tree above is the map for every task below. A task names the packages it touches, and the tree shows where they are.

Checklist: a new servicenew#

The shop needs a returns service. A team copies the order service and starts deleting. Two weeks later, the new service has the order service's old settings, and a security setup that someone changed for the order service only. A checklist avoids that. A new service takes seven steps:

  1. The structure, the parent and the library. Create the packages as in the tree above. The Project Object Model (POM) names the shop's parent, and depends on shop-platform.
  2. The name and the settings. Set spring.application.name, the MongoDB URI, the token issuer and audience, and the path variables for the log context.
  3. The first migration. One named index for each query, in V001.
  4. The API contract. Write the controllers and the data transfer objects (DTOs) with stub methods first. Generate contracts/openapi.yaml, and agree it with the teams that call the service. Write a JSON schema in contracts/events/ for each event that the service publishes.
  5. The local environment. Add stubs for every service it calls, and its topics and queues to init.sh. Check that the two commands start it.
  6. The tests that protect the shape. The wiring test, the architecture test, the OpenAPI drift test and the event schema test, from the first commit.
  7. The documents. The README holds the rules, the endpoints, the events, the dependencies, the settings and how to run it, as the order service's README does. Add a design note for each feature in docs/design/, a folder docs/adr/ for the decisions, and the pull request template in .github/pull_request_template.md.

The POM of a service is short, because the parent does the rest:

<parent>
    <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-platform-parent</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <relativePath>../shop-platform/shop-platform-parent/pom.xml</relativePath>
</parent>

<groupId>com.acme</groupId>
<artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

<dependencies>
    <!-- Everything cross-cutting. No version: the parent manages it. -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.acme.platform</groupId>
        <artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>
    </dependency>
Reading the code
<relativePath>../shop-platform/shop-platform-parent/pom.xml</relativePath>

In the companion, the three repositories are in one folder, so the parent is found by its path. In a real repository of its own, the comment in the POM says to remove this line. The parent then comes from the company's artifact repository.

<artifactId>shop-platform</artifactId>

One dependency brings the security chain, the error responses, the logging, the MongoDB setup, the outbox and the inbox. For what the library holds, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

Step 2 sets few values, because the platform's defaults apply first. The service's application.yml starts with its name:

spring:
  application:
    name: order-service

The name order-service appears in every log line of the service. The other values come from environment variables, which the deployment sets. For the settings and their order, see the chapter Configuration in depth.

Step 4 is a choice that the contracts chapter explains. The order service writes its controllers first and generates the contract. To agree an API before it is built, the controllers start with stub methods. A team that writes the contract first uses the parent's profile instead. The command mvn verify -Dcontract-first generates Java interfaces from contracts/openapi.yaml, and the controllers implement them. For the choice between code first and contract first, see the chapter API and event contracts.

Some teams make the architecture test of step 6 optional. The book recommends it from the first commit, because a new service breaks none of the rules. For the reasons, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Checklist: a new featurenew#

A feature is a package such as order or note. It owns one aggregate, or a set of lookup data, with its use cases and adapters. A new feature takes these steps:

  1. Check that it is a feature. Does it own data and rules of its own? If it only adds a use case to an aggregate that exists, it belongs in that feature. See the chapter Finding the aggregates.
  2. Choose its level. Simple, light or full, by the rules it holds. The design group writes the level, with the aggregates, states, rules and events, in the feature's design note in docs/design/. See the section Choosing the level for each feature, and the section The feature design note.
  3. Start in the domain, with plain JUnit. Write the aggregate and its tests first. They need no Spring and no database.
  4. Then the application layer, then the adapters. The use cases, with Mockito tests. Then the controller, the storage, any client and any listener, each with its test.
  5. The migration. A new migration with the indexes for the feature's queries.
  6. Tell the others. Update the OpenAPI contract and any event schemas. Add the stubs, topics and queues to the local environment. Tell QA what changed, because their tests use the local environment.

A feature in the full style also gets a line in ArchitectureTest, which lists the full-style features by package. The rule that its application layer uses only ports then applies to it too. See the section A level for each feature.

The order of steps 3 and 4 is the point of the list. A feature written from the controller down tends to put its rules where the code first needed them, in the controller or the service. A feature written from the domain up has its rules in the aggregate before anything calls them.

Each feature has a package-info.java that says what it holds and which level it uses. This is the order feature's:

/**
 * Orders: what a customer bought, the lines that warehouse staff pick, the payment, and shipping.
 *
 * <p>This feature uses the full style. Its {@code domain} package is plain Java with typed IDs.
 * The {@code persistence} package stores the aggregate as a separate document through a mapper,
 * behind the {@code OrderRepository} port. The stock service is called through the
 * {@code StockChecker} port.

The comment says This feature uses the full style, and names the ports. A file named package-info.java holds the documentation of a package, and no class. A reader who opens a feature for the first time reads this comment first. Write it when you create the feature.

Checklist: an existing servicenew#

An older service has a different structure, and a team cannot stop for a month to rebuild it. So the change happens feature by feature, and only where the team changes code anyway:

  1. Add the cheap protection first. The wiring test, and the architecture rules wrapped in FreezingArchRule.freeze, so only new violations fail. See the section Adding the rules to an existing service.
  2. Move a feature when you change it. When a task touches a feature, move that feature to the new packages in the same pull request, or in the pull request before it.
  3. Move its rules into the domain, with tests. Each rule that moves gets its plain JUnit test.
  4. Leave untouched features alone. A feature that nobody changes does not need the new structure yet.

This is slower than a rewrite, and it leaves two structures side by side for a while. But each pull request stays small, and each moved feature is tested before the next. For what to test first, see the section What to test first in an older service.

The architecture test of the order service runs the rules on every build:

@Test
void featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication() {
    ArchitectureRules.featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication(BASE).check(CLASSES);
}

In an existing service, the rule featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication(BASE) is wrapped in FreezingArchRule.freeze. The frozen rule keeps the violations it accepts in a folder of text files, called the store. The file archunit.properties in the test resources names the folder:

freeze.store.default.path=src/test/resources/archunit_store

# Never create a store by accident, for example in CI, where it would accept every violation
# without a review. To create the store, set this to true once, run the test, commit the
# folder, and set it back to false.
freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=false

Commit the folder archunit_store with the code, so each pull request shows whether it grew. The setting allowStoreCreation=false makes a build fail when the store is missing. So a build never accepts every violation without a review. The order service shows a frozen rule in FrozenRuleTest, which the section Adding the rules to an existing service explains.

Task: add an endpointtwist#

The business wants agents to cancel an order. The order service has this endpoint, so it shows every file that such a change touches:

LayerFileWhat changes
domainorder/domain/model/Order.javaa method cancel(Clock) that checks the rule and raises OrderCancelled
domainorder/domain/event/OrderCancelled.javathe new domain event
domainorder/domain/exception/OrderFinishedException.javathe exception for a shipped or cancelled order, if it is new
domain testOrderTest.javaa nested group Cancelling, with the allowed case and each refusal
applicationorder/application/OrderService.javaa method cancel(OrderId) with @Transactional, which saves, publishes and audits
sharedshared/AuditActions.javathe name ORDER_CANCELLED
apiorder/api/OrderController.javaa method with @OrdersWrite and @PostMapping
api testOrderControllerTest.javathe success, each refusal with its status and code, and the 403 without the scope
contractcontracts/openapi.yamlthe drift test fails until you run mvn verify -Dopenapi.update=true and commit the file
event, if publishedOrderCancelledV1, a case in the mapper, its schemaonly if another service needs to know, as the section on publishing an event shows

The controller method is the entry point, so it names the permission:

@OrdersWrite
@PostMapping("/{orderId}/cancel")
@Operation(operationId = "cancelOrder", summary = "Cancel an order that has not shipped")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "204", description = "Cancelled")
// ...
ResponseEntity<Void> cancel(@PathVariable String orderId) {
    orders.cancel(OrderId.of(orderId));
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
Reading the code
@OrdersWrite

The method needs the scope orders.write. The architecture rule fails the build if an endpoint has no permission annotation.

@Operation(operationId = "cancelOrder", summary = "Cancel an order that has not shipped")

springdoc reads this annotation into the OpenAPI document. Each error response gets an @ApiResponse line, which the excerpt leaves out.

orders.cancel(OrderId.of(orderId));

The controller turns the text into a typed ID and calls the use case. It holds no rule and catches no exception.

The use case has no permission annotation. Other features and message listeners call use cases directly, so a check there would need a second, unprotected copy of each method. For the full reasoning, see the section Choosing the place by the shape of the service.

In ASP.NET Core, the action would carry [Authorize(Policy = "orders.write")] and [HttpPost("{orderId}/cancel")]. The two forms put the check in the same place, on the method that receives the request.

Task: add a fieldnew#

The business wants the customer's phone number on an order. A field in the full style goes through every layer, because each layer has its own type:

LayerFileWhat changes
domainCustomerContact.java, or a new value object PhoneNumberthe field and its check, in the compact constructor
domainOrder.javaplace and rehydrate take the value, and the getter returns it
domain testValueObjectTest.java, OrderTest.javathe check of a valid and an invalid value
persistenceOrderDocument.javaa plain field, such as customerPhone
persistenceOrderDocumentMapper.javathe field in both directions, toDocument and toDomain
apiPlaceOrderRequest, OrderResponsethe field in the DTOs, with validation
apiOrderController.java or OrderApiMapper.javathe field in the translation
contractcontracts/openapi.yamlregenerated and committed
old datathe mapper, or a new migrationwhat an order stored before the change means

The value object checks the value once, where it is created:

public record CustomerContact(String name, String email) implements ValueObject {

    public CustomerContact {
        Guard.notBlank(name, "customer.name");
        Guard.maxLength(name, 200, "customer.name");
        Guard.maxLength(email, 254, "customer.email");
        Guard.matches(email, "[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+", "customer.email");
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "CustomerContact[masked]";
    }
}

A phone number is personal data, like the e-mail address. So it stays inside the masked toString, and it stays out of the views and the integration events.

The mapper copies each field in both directions. Forget one direction, and the field is stored but never read, or read but never stored:

@Override
public OrderDocument toDocument(Order order) {
    OrderDocument document = new OrderDocument();
    document.customerName = order.customer().name();
    document.customerEmail = order.customer().email();
    // ...
@Override
public Order toDomain(OrderDocument document) {
    return Order.rehydrate(
            OrderId.of(document.getId()),
            document.getVersion(),
            new CustomerContact(document.customerName, document.customerEmail),

toDocument writes the field, and toDomain reads it back through rehydrate. The persistence test round-trips a whole aggregate, so it catches a missing direction. Add the new field to the values that test compares.

The hard part is the old data. Orders stored before the change have no phone number. Decide what that means. If an order may have no phone, the value object allows an empty value, and the mapper passes it through. If every order needs one, a new migration fills a value into the old documents before the new code reads them. The section Task: add a lookup value shows the shape of such a migration. A migration that changes data is harder to undo than a code change, so prefer an empty value where the business allows it.

The light style needs fewer steps. The note is its own document, so a new field goes into Note and its @PersistenceCreator constructor, with no separate document and no mapper. That is one reason to keep a feature light while its data is simple. See the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

Task: add a querynew#

Agents want to list the orders with one delivery method. A query in the full style touches the port, the adapter and a migration:

LayerFileWhat changes
domainorder/domain/repository/OrderRepository.javaa method in the domain's types, such as findByDeliveryMethod
persistenceOrderMongoRepository.javaa Spring Data method on the document, if a derived query is enough
persistenceOrderPersistenceAdapter.javathe port's method, which calls the Spring Data method and maps the page
migrationa new migration, such as V005a named index for the new filter and sort
applicationOrderService.javaa method that returns a page of views
apiOrderController.javaa GET method with @OrdersRead, or a new filter on the list
teststhe adapter IT, the service test, the controller testthe query, the page and the 400 for a bad filter

The port speaks the domain's language:

PageResult<Order> findAll(PageQuery page);

PageResult<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, PageQuery page);

PageQuery and PageResult are the platform's plain types for a page. The domain knows nothing of Spring Data's Pageable. The adapter translates.

Spring Data writes the query from the method name:

interface OrderMongoRepository extends MongoRepository<OrderDocument, String> {

    Page<OrderDocument> findByStatus(String status, Pageable pageable);
}

findByStatus becomes a query on the field status. For derived queries, see the section Repositories and derived queries.

Every query needs an index. Without one, MongoDB reads the whole collection for each request, and a list that was fast with a hundred orders is slow with a million. The service creates its indexes only in migrations, never at startup. The first migration names an index for the list by status:

// GET /orders?status=PAID, newest first
mongo.indexOps("orders").createIndex(new Index()
        .on("status", Sort.Direction.ASC).on("placedAt", Sort.Direction.DESC)
        .named("orders_status_placedAt"));

The comment names the request that needs the index, and named("orders_status_placedAt") gives the index a name that says what it is for. A new query adds its index in a new migration, such as V005, written the same way. Never add it to V001, because environments where V001 has run would never create it. For named indexes, see the section A named index for each query.

Task: add a lookup valuenew#

The shop starts a new delivery method, collection from a locker. The delivery methods are seed data, in a JSON file:

[
  { "code": "STANDARD", "label": "Standard delivery (3 to 5 days)", "active": true },
  { "code": "EXPRESS", "label": "Express delivery (next day)", "active": true },
  { "code": "COLLECT", "label": "Collect from a store", "active": true },
  { "code": "SECOND_CLASS_POST", "label": "Second-class post (no longer offered)", "active": false }
]

Each value has a code, a label and an active flag. A value that is no longer offered stays in the list with "active": false, so old orders that used it still have a label.

The change has two parts. Add the new value to the file. Then add a new migration that runs the same upserts again. The migration that loaded the file first says why:

/**
 * Loads the lookup values from {@code resources/seed/}. Each value is upserted by its type and
 * code, so the migration is safe to run twice.
 *
 * <p>To change the values, edit the JSON file and add a new migration that runs the same upserts.
 * Never edit this one: environments where it has run would not see the change.
 */

The comment's advice, add a new migration that runs the same upserts, follows from how the runner works. The runner records each migration's ID once it has run. An environment where V002 has run will never run it again, even if its code changes. So the new migration, with a new ID, is what reaches those environments. An upsert updates a value that exists and inserts one that does not, matched by its code. So the new migration can safely load the whole file again. For the rule, see the section Never edit a migration that ran.

Lookup values are cached with no expiry. A new value arrives with a deployment, which restarts every instance and so empties the cache. For the cache, see the chapter Caching and scheduling.

Task: call a new servicetwist#

The order service must ask a new pricing service for prices. A call to another service touches the most files of any task, because the service keeps the other service behind a port:

LayerFileWhat changes
applicationorder/application/port/PriceChecker.javathe port, in the domain's types
clientorder/client/PricingHttpClient.javaan interface with @HttpExchange, one method for each endpoint
clientorder/client/dto/records for the other service's request and response
clientorder/client/PricingAdapter.javaimplements the port, calls the client through ResilientCalls, and translates
clientorder/client/PricingClientConfig.javabinds HttpClientProperties to clients.pricing and creates the client with HttpClientFactory
settingsapplication.yml and application-local.ymlclients.pricing.base-url, from an environment variable and from WireMock
settingsapplication.ymla client registration, such as pricing-service, and clients.pricing.token-registration-id, so each call carries a token
local environmentwiremock/mappings/pricing-service/a default stub, and stubs for the special cases
testPricingAdapterTest.javathe client against a JDK HttpServer, with fast retries

The client is an interface, and Spring creates its implementation:

/**
 * The stock service's HTTP API, declared as an interface. Spring creates the implementation,
 * like Refit does in .NET.
 */
@HttpExchange("/stock")
interface StockHttpClient {

@HttpExchange is like a Refit interface in .NET. For the basics, see the section Declarative clients. The configuration class creates the client with the platform's factory, which adds the timeouts, the token and the error handling:

/** Binds the platform's reusable properties class to this client's prefix. */
@Bean
@ConfigurationProperties("clients.stock")
HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties() {
    return new HttpClientProperties();
}

@Bean
StockHttpClient stockHttpClient(HttpClientFactory clients, HttpClientProperties stockClientProperties) {
    return clients.create(StockHttpClient.class, stockClientProperties);
}

The class binds the settings under clients.stock. A new client copies this class with a new prefix, such as clients.pricing. The settings are then under that prefix in both YAML files. For the timeouts, retries, the circuit breaker and the idempotency key, see the chapter Calling other services.

The stub comes in the same pull request. Without it, the two commands start a service that fails on its first call. See the section The rules of the local environment.

Task: publish a new eventtwist#

The warehouse service wants to know when an order is cancelled. The order service publishes OrderCancelledV1, so it shows every file:

LayerFileWhat changes
domainorder/domain/event/OrderCancelled.javathe domain event, raised by the aggregate
messagingorder/messaging/event/OrderCancelledV1.javathe integration event, a record with @Externalized and plain types
messagingOrderIntegrationEventMapper.javaa case that turns the domain event into the integration event
contractcontracts/events/OrderCancelledV1.jsonthe JSON schema, for the consumers
local environmentaws-init/init.shthe topic, if the event goes to a new one
testOrderIntegrationEventMapperTest.javathe mapping, field by field
testPublishedEventSchemaTest.javathe domain event in publishedDomainEvents, so the JSON is checked against its schema
design notedocs/design/order.mdthe row of the event in the table of events raised

The integration event names its topic:

/** Published when an order ships. The schema is in {@code contracts/events/OrderShippedV1.json}. */
@Externalized(OrderTopics.ORDER_EVENTS)
public record OrderShippedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId) implements IntegrationEvent {
}

@Externalized tells Spring Modulith to send the event to the topic order-events after the transaction commits. The V1 in the name is the version of the contract. A change that breaks consumers is a new record, OrderShippedV2, published beside the old one for a while.

The mapper decides what leaves the service:

case OrderCancelled cancelled -> Optional.of(new OrderCancelledV1(newEventId(), cancelled.occurredAt(),
        cancelled.orderId().value()));
default -> Optional.empty();

A domain event without a case falls to default, and stays inside the service. So adding a domain event publishes nothing by itself. That is safe, because every published event is a contract to maintain. But it is also a trap. A developer who forgets the case wonders why no consumer hears the event. The mapper test is the place to check both. The schema test then writes each published event as JSON, and validates it against its file in contracts/events/. So a renamed field fails the build before a consumer breaks. For the outbox, see the chapter Publishing events: the outbox, and for schemas and versions, see the chapter API and event contracts.

Task: consume a new eventnew#

The order service consumes PaymentReceivedV1 from the payment service. Its files are the template for any consumed event:

LayerFileWhat changes
messagingorder/messaging/PaymentReceivedV1.javathe service's own record of the event, with only the fields it uses
messagingorder/messaging/PaymentReceivedListener.javaextends InboxMessageHandler, with @SqsListener on a method that calls process
applicationOrderService.javathe use case that the listener calls, with no permission check
settingsapplication.ymlmessaging.queues.payment-received, the queue name
local environmentaws-init/init.shthe queue, its dead-letter queue and the subscription with raw delivery
contractcontracts/events/consumed-PaymentReceivedV1.jsonthe part of the producer's schema that this service relies on
testsPaymentReceivedV1Test, PaymentReceivedListenerTestthe JSON, and the translation into the use case
design notedocs/design/order.mdthe producer and the event, in the list of who the feature talks to

The record is the service's own copy, not a shared class:

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
record PaymentReceivedV1(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, String orderId, String paymentReference,
                         BigDecimal amount, String currency, Instant paidAt) implements IntegrationEvent {

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) lets the producer add fields freely. The record's compact constructor refuses a missing field, so a wrong message fails loudly. The listener only translates:

/** The queue name comes from configuration, so each environment can name its own queue. */
@SqsListener("${messaging.queues.payment-received}")
void on(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    process(event);
}

@Override
protected void handle(PaymentReceivedV1 event) {
    Payment payment = new Payment(new PaymentReference(event.paymentReference()),
            new Money(event.amount(), event.currency()), event.paidAt());
    orders.recordPayment(OrderId.of(event.orderId()), payment);
}
Reading the code
@SqsListener("${messaging.queues.payment-received}")

Spring Cloud AWS calls this method for each message on the queue. ${...} reads the queue name from the settings.

process(event);

The base class runs handle once per event, through the inbox, as the system actor.

orders.recordPayment(OrderId.of(event.orderId()), payment);

The listener calls the use case directly. The use case has no permission check, so the listener needs no identity.

The queue, its dead-letter queue and the subscription go into init.sh in the same pull request. That takes one call of queue and one of subscribe. The service fails at startup when its queue does not exist, so a missing line is found at once. For the inbox, raw delivery and the visibility timeout, see the chapter Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

Task: add a featurenew#

The shop starts taking returns. A return has its own rules, such as a time limit and a condition of the goods, so it is a feature. The steps are those of the checklist for a new feature. The files follow the tree of the service:

src/main/java/com/acme/orderservice/returns/
  package-info.java      what the feature holds, and its level
  model/ or domain/      the aggregate and its tests, light or full style
  application/           ReturnService, the only class other features may use
  api/                   ReturnController, its DTOs and mapper
  persistence/           only in the full style

The rule that matters most is the boundary. Other features use the returns feature only through ReturnService, in its application package. They never take its repository, its entity or its ports. The architecture rules featuresUseEachOtherOnlyThroughApplication and servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities fail the build when they do.

Beside the code, the feature's design note goes into docs/design/returns.md, as the order feature's note is in docs/design/order.md.

The rest follows the earlier tasks. The feature's queries get indexes in a new migration. Its endpoints appear in the regenerated contract. Any service it calls gets a stub. A feature that calls another feature, and is called back, is a warning sign. See the section Two features that call each other.

The name of the package is returns, not return, because return is a Java keyword. A package name cannot be a keyword.

Task: upgrade Spring Boot or the platformtrap#

An upgrade changes one version, and it looks like the smallest task of all. The platform's parent names the Spring Boot version:

<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.1.2</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>

The <version> line is the whole change for Spring Boot. A service upgrades by moving to the new platform version. The risk is in what the compiler cannot see.

Gotcha

A setting or a class name in a string is never checked by the compiler. Spring Boot 4 reads the MongoDB URI from spring.mongodb.uri. A service that still sets the old key, spring.data.mongodb.uri, compiles and starts. A run for this book showed that the old key is ignored, with no warning, and the client went to localhost:27017. The platform also names Spring Boot's auto-configurations in beforeName, as strings. If a new Spring Boot version renames one of them, nothing fails at compile time.

So an upgrade has its own checklist:

  1. Read the migration guide of the new Spring Boot version, and search the code for every key and class that it renames.
  2. Run mvn verify. The wiring test starts the whole service, and checks the results that depend on such names. Its test usesTheConfiguredMongoUri fails if the URI key is ignored. Its first test fails if the transaction manager is not the MongoDB one. It also fails if the service has a security chain besides the platform's own chain. A second chain appears when the platform's auto-configuration runs after the auto-configuration of Spring Boot.
  3. Run mvn verify -Pit, against real MongoDB and Floci.
  4. Upgrade the platform first, in its own repository, and release it. Then move each service to the new platform version in its own pull request.

The companion was checked this way. The whole build ran on Spring Boot 4.1.2, and every test passed, including the wiring test and the integration tests. For how a new version reaches every service, see the section Upgrading Spring Boot for every service. For Boot 3 to Boot 4, see the chapter Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4.

The review checklist for a pull requestnew#

A reviewer cannot check every line of a large change. A short list of questions catches the mistakes that cost the most later. The questions come in two parts.

The first part is in the service. Its pull request template, .github/pull_request_template.md, asks the author five domain questions. Can a change of state skip the aggregate? Is each rule in the aggregate, with a test? Does each change of state record its event? Does the change reach into another feature? Are the names business words, at the right level? The author answers them in the description, and the reviewer checks the answers against the code. For the template itself, see the section The pull request checklist.

The second part is the reviewer's own. These ten technical questions cover what the template does not ask, each with the place in the part that explains it:

QuestionWhy it mattersWhere it is explained
Is each class in the right feature and the right layer?a class in the wrong place pulls its dependencies with itthe chapter on features and layers
Does each exception have the right kind, and a message with no personal data?the kind decides the status, and messages reach logs and responsesthe chapter on the domain model
Does each new query have an index, in a new migration? Was no migration edited?a query without an index reads the whole collection, and an edited migration never rerunsthe chapter on migrations
Is each transaction short, with no call to another service inside?a long transaction holds locks and meets the time limit of DocumentDBthe chapter on transactions
Does each new call use the platform's factory and ResilientCalls, with a stub?the factory adds timeouts and the token, and the stub keeps the local environment workingthe chapter on calling other services
Does each new integration event have a case in the mapper, and a schema that PublishedEventSchemaTest checks?a published event is a contract with other teams, and the test finds a field that drifts from its schemathe chapter on contracts
Does each new listener extend InboxMessageHandler?the inbox processes a repeated message oncethe chapter on the inbox
Do the logs leave out personal data?a log line is kept and searched long after the requestthe chapter on logging and health
Does each new endpoint name its permission, with a 403 test and a success test?the architecture rule checks that an annotation exists, not that it is the right onethe chapter on security
Is contracts/openapi.yaml updated, and does its diff match the intent?the diff is the change to the API that other teams seethe chapter on contracts

The question about personal data has a code answer too. A value object that holds personal data hides it in toString, so a careless log line prints nothing personal:

@Override
public String toString() {
    return "CustomerContact[masked]";
}

The test customerContactHidesItsPersonalDataInToString checks that toString() returns "CustomerContact[masked]".

The build answers some questions by itself. The architecture rules check the layers, the setters, the repositories in controllers and the permission annotations. The drift test checks the OpenAPI contract, and the schema test checks the events. So a reviewer spends time on the questions that need judgement. Where does a rule belong? Is this event, or this field, the right one?

Why we do it this waynew#

A new developer asks why the service does something in a way that looks longer than needed. Each answer below is short, and links to the chapter that gives the full reason. The first question shows the pattern. The class comment of OrderService answers it in the code itself:

* <p>The class has no permission annotation. Permissions are checked on the controllers, where
* users enter. Every method here can therefore be called by another feature or by a message
* listener without a second, unprotected copy of the method.

The comment says why there is no permission annotation, and it says so where a developer reads the code. The other questions follow:

QuestionShort answerChapter
Why are permissions checked on the controllers, not the use cases?Users enter through the controllers. A check there lets listeners and other features call the use cases with no second copy.the chapter on security
Why does the domain use no Spring?Its rules are then tested in milliseconds, and no framework change can break them.the chapter on the domain model
Why a separate document and a mapper for an order?The aggregate keeps its rules and its shape, and the stored shape can change on its own.the chapter on storage
Why is the note its own document, with no mapper?Its data is simple, so the light style costs less and loses nothing yet.the chapter on the levels of DDD
Why does save return a new copy of the order?The copy holds the new version. Continuing with the old object would fail the next save.the chapter on storage
Why is the stock service called before the transaction?A slow call inside a transaction holds it open, and DocumentDB limits a transaction's time.the chapter on use cases
Why an idempotency key on the reservation?A retry after a lost response must not hold the stock twice.the chapter on calling other services
Why an outbox, and not a direct send to SNS?The event is stored in the same transaction as the change, so neither is lost without the other.the chapter on the outbox
Why an inbox for the payment event?SQS delivers at least once, so a payment would otherwise be recorded twice.the chapter on the inbox
Why raw message delivery on the subscription?Without it, the queue holds an SNS envelope, and the listener cannot read the event.the chapter on the inbox
Why indexes only in migrations?An index created at startup is invisible and unreviewed, and can block a large collection.the chapter on migrations
Why never edit a migration that has run?An environment where it ran will never run it again, so the change would never reach it.the chapter on migrations
Why a generated OpenAPI file, committed and checked?Every API change then appears as a diff in the pull request, and the file cannot drift.the chapter on contracts
Why one platform library for every service?Security, errors, logs and storage then work the same in every service, and are fixed once.the chapter on the platform library
Why a String ID between features?The feature that owns the ID checks it, and the other feature does not depend on its types.the chapter on aggregates
Why do the architecture tests run in every build?A rule in a document is forgotten, and a rule that fails the build is kept.the chapter on testing
Why two commands to start the service?A new developer, and QA, can run it on the first day with no manual step.the chapter on running locally

A question that has no row here deserves a new row. If the answer is "because we always did", the rule may have lost its reason. Then the team discusses it, and writes the decision down. A short decision is a paragraph in the section "Decisions" of the README. A decision that needs more than a paragraph gets a numbered record in docs/adr/, as the order service does. See the section How each decision is recorded.

Older forms you will still meettwist#

C# 12
[ApiController]
[Route("orders")]
public class OrdersController(IOrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper) : ControllerBase   // a primary constructor
{
}
OrderController.java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
@Tag(name = "orders")
class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final OrderApiMapper mapper;

    OrderController(OrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

C# 12 has primary constructors, so the C# pane declares the dependencies in one line, OrdersController(IOrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper). Java has no primary constructor for a class, so the service writes the constructor and the fields. Many older Java services use Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor, which writes that constructor while the class compiles. The order service uses no Lombok, so every line that runs is in the source. For Lombok, see the section A word on Lombok.

Older guides and services use other forms that this part replaces. Each has a reason:

Older formThe form in this partWhy it changed
Lombok annotations for constructors and accessorsexplicit constructors, and records for valuesthe code shows every line, and records need no Lombok
spring.data.mongodb.urispring.mongodb.uriSpring Boot 4 reads the new key and ignores the old one without a warning
@Retry and @CircuitBreaker annotations, with resilience4j settings in YAMLthe platform's ResilientCalls, with Resilience4j used directlythe platform gives every service the same retry rules, and tests them once
Mongock change unitsthe platform's own migration runnerMongock has no Spring Boot 4 artifact, as of October 2026
ArchUnit tests with @AnalyzeClasses and @ArchTest fieldsplain JUnit tests that call the platform's rulesthe rules ship in a library, take parameters, and need no extra test engine
a container in a static @Container fielda container as a bean in a shared test configurationthe container is declared once for every test class and service
mongo:5.0, wiremock:latest, or Floci with the tag latestan exact version of each image, the same in every placeeveryone runs the same thing, and an upgrade is a reviewed change
a separate query class and command class for each featureone application service for each area of a featurethe service has one entry point for each use case, with no CQRS split it does not need
an exception handler in each featurethe platform's one handlerevery error has the same problem shape, with a traceId
a shared folder in each service, until a library existsthe platform library from the startshared code is fixed once, for every service

When you meet one of these forms in a service, it still works. Replace it when you change that code, as the checklist for an existing service says. Do not replace all of them in one large pull request, because a reviewer cannot check it.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksA developer adds a delivery method by editing the JSON file and the migration V002SeedReferenceData. The change works on their machine. Why does it fail in the test environment?
The runner records each migration's ID once it has run. V002 ran in the test environment long ago, so it never runs again there, even with new code. On the developer's machine, the database was new, so V002 ran. The fix is to edit the file and add a new migration with a new ID that runs the same upserts.
2
Which files does the order service touch to consume a new event from another service?
A record of the event with only the fields it uses, and a listener that extends InboxMessageHandler with @SqsListener. Also the use case it calls, the queue name in application.yml, and the queue, dead-letter queue and subscription in init.sh. Add the consumed schema, and tests of the JSON and of the translation.
3
An expert asksWhy does an upgrade of Spring Boot need the wiring test, when every unit test passes?
Some names are strings that the compiler cannot check, such as property keys and the class names in beforeName. A renamed key or class still compiles, and can then be ignored. Only a test that starts the whole service and checks the result sees it. The wiring test does that in seconds. It checks the MongoDB URI that the service really uses, and the one security chain.
4
TranslateThe order service uses no Lombok. Write the start of this C# 12 controller as the order service's Java controller, with its fields and its constructor: 
[ApiController]
[Route("orders")]
public class OrdersController(IOrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper) : ControllerBase
{
}
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
@Tag(name = "orders")
class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final OrderApiMapper mapper;

    OrderController(OrderService orders, OrderApiMapper mapper) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

A Java class has no primary constructor. So the controller declares each dependency as a final field, and writes the constructor that sets it. Spring passes the two beans to that constructor, because it is the only one.

WordWhat it meansChapter
