DDD for a team: the playbook#

Testing, shipping and changing it · Chapter 30· 19 min read

A Domain-Driven Design (DDD) service stays clean only when the whole team works the same way. This playbook says who decides what, and how each decision is written down. It lists the building blocks a developer may use, and the eight rules every engineer follows. It gives the checks that guard the rules, the wrong decisions to watch for, and a way to roll DDD out to a team.

KindA usual .NET teamThe order service's teamNote
neweach developer designs what they builda small design group decides boundaries, aggregates, rules and workflowsthe decisions that are hardest to change are made by the most experienced people, with business experts Why
newdecisions in chat and in people's headsan ADR for each decision of a servicea decision written beside the code can be found, questioned and replaced later Why
newa ticket, and then the codea one-page feature design noteaggregates, states, rules with examples, events and partners are agreed before the code Why
newone style for every featuresimple, light or full, chosen in the design noteeach feature gets the least DDD that protects its rules Why
newany pattern that a developer likesallowed building blocks, and a short list that needs approvalevent sourcing, full CQRS, generic repositories, shared models and new sagas need the design group Why
newconventions on a wiki pageeight rules for every engineershort rules that each map to a test or a review question Why
twistan ArchUnitNET rule, if the team writes oneArchUnit rules from the platform library, in every servicethe build fails when code breaks a design rule Why
newa general code reviewa five-question pull request checklistthe reviewer asks the questions that the build cannot answer Why
newdotnet new webapi, then folders by kind of classa template feature to copya new feature starts with the right layout, tests and comments Why
trapa design that looks finishednine wrong decisions, each with its sign and its fixmost DDD failures are the same few decisions, and each one shows early Why
newno equivalenta workflow engine or a process manager for long flowsa flow across services and days keeps its state in one place Why
newa framework adopted by every team at oncea pilot service, training from its code, reviews and a weekly slotDDD spreads from one service that works, and the template is fixed when people keep making a mistake Why

Who decides whatnew#

Two developers design the same idea in two ways. One puts the notes inside the order. The other makes them an aggregate of their own. A year later, the service has both designs, and nobody knows which one is right. Some decisions shape everything that comes after them. They must be made once, by the people who can make them well.

So split the decisions in two groups. A small design group makes the first group. It has two or three of the most experienced engineers, and a business expert, such as the product owner. The team makes everything else.

DecisionWho decidesWhy
the boundaries of the servicesthe design group, with business expertsa wrong boundary means moving data between services later
the aggregates and what is inside each onethe design groupa wrong boundary means migrating stored documents
the business rules, and where each one goesthe design group, with business expertsa rule is only right if the business agrees with it
workflows across aggregates and servicesthe design groupa flow decides which data may disagree, and for how long
the level of a featurethe design group, in the feature design notethe level decides how much code the feature needs
everything inside those decisionsthe teamnames, methods, tests, queries, endpoints and the order of the work

The design group does not write all the code. It writes the design note of each feature, and reviews each new aggregate before code is written. The team builds the feature, and asks the group when a decision of the first kind comes up during the work.

The order service shows a decision of the first kind in its code. The note feature is its own aggregate, and the comment of Order says so. That boundary was chosen once, and every later change follows it. For the questions that the group uses to find aggregates, see the chapter Finding the aggregates.

* <p>The aggregate holds what its rules need at every change: the status, the lines and the last
* payment. Notes are a separate aggregate, because no order rule needs every note, and they can
* grow without limit.

The three lines of the comment name what is inside the aggregate. The sentence Notes are a separate aggregate starts the reason why the notes are outside. A developer who wants to add notes to the order finds the reason before writing any code.

How each decision is recordednew#

A decision that nobody wrote down is made again by the next person. So the team writes down two kinds of record.

  • An ADR for each decision of a service. An architecture decision record (ADR) is a short file about one decision. Michael Nygard described the format in a blog post of November 2011. He gave each record five parts. They are a title, the context, the decision, its status and its consequences. The records are kept in the repository and numbered in order. A number is never used twice. A decision that is changed later keeps its record, marked as replaced by the new one.
  • A design note for each feature. One page that the design group writes before the feature is built. The next section shows one.

The order service records its decisions in the section "Decisions" of its README, one paragraph each. Here is one of them:

**One request saves two aggregates.** Placing an order with its first notes stores both in one
transaction, because the agent sees it as one action. Keep such transactions small, and never
let them span services.

The record One request saves two aggregates. names the decision, its reason and its limit. The words "never let them span services" tell a later developer where the decision stops. Keep a test beside each decision that changes behaviour, as the chapter Finding the aggregates shows for the shipping rule.

A paragraph is enough for a short decision. The section "Decisions" of the README starts with the rule for a longer one:

The feature design notes are in `docs/design/`. A decision that needs more than a paragraph gets
a numbered record in `docs/adr/`, such as `0001-order-and-first-notes-in-one-transaction.md`.

The README names both folders, docs/design/ and docs/adr/, so a reader of the README finds the longer records. The decision to save the order and its first notes together needs more than a paragraph. It has a context, a test, and a sign for when to revisit it. So it also has an ADR file, in Nygard's five parts:

# 1. The order and its first notes are saved in one transaction

Status: accepted, 25 October 2026

## Context

An agent places an order and writes its first notes in one form, and sees it as one action. The
order and each note are separate aggregates, in two features. The usual rule is one aggregate for
each transaction. With two transactions, an order could be stored while its notes are lost, and
the agent would not know.

## Decision

`OrderService.place` saves the order and calls `NoteService.addNotes`, which joins the same
transaction. Both are stored, or neither is. The call to the stock service happens before the
transaction begins, so the transaction holds no HTTP call.

## Consequences

- One request writes two collections.
  `OrderJourneyIT.anOrderAndItsNotesAreStoredTogetherOrNotAtAll` checks that a failed note rolls
  back the order too.
- The transaction stays small: one order and a few notes, far below the limits of Amazon
  DocumentDB.
- The two features depend on each other at this point. Only this use case may write both.
- Revisit the decision if notes move to another service, or if a transaction starts to include
  a call to another service. Then the order is saved first, and the notes follow from an event.

The file name starts with the number, 0001, so the records sort in order. The line Status: accepted, 25 October 2026 holds the status and its date. A later record that replaces this one would change the line to "replaced by 0007", and keep the rest. The last item of the consequences says when to look at the decision again.

The feature design notenew#

A feature design note is one page that answers five questions before any code exists. What are the aggregates, and what is inside each one? Which states does each one have, and which changes are allowed? Which rules apply, each with an example? Which events does it raise? Which other features and services does it talk to?

The companion keeps the design note of the order feature in docs/design/order.md. It is a Markdown file, so its tables are plain text with a | between the columns. The note opens with the level, then names the aggregate and its states:

# Feature design note: order

Level: full. Orders, the lines that warehouse staff pick, the last payment, and shipping.
The design group wrote this note before the feature was built. Change it in the same pull
request as the code, so the two never disagree.

## 1. Aggregates and their contents

| Aggregate | Root | Inside | Outside, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order | `Order`, with an `OrderId` | status, delivery method, customer contact, placed and finished times, up to 50 order lines, the last payment | notes, because they have no limit and no order rule needs all of them |

## 2. States and allowed changes

| From | To | Through | Allowed when |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | `NEW` | `place` | every product is held by the stock service, with 1 to 50 lines |
| `NEW` | `PAID` | `recordPayment` | the first payment arrives, and a later one only replaces it |
| `PAID` | `SHIPPED` | `ship` | every line is picked, and no note needs action |
| `NEW` or `PAID` | `CANCELLED` | `cancel` | the order is not shipped or cancelled |
| `SHIPPED` or `CANCELLED` | no change | any method except `recordPayment` | never, because both states are final |

The first line, Level: full, is the decision about the level. The next sentence asks for the note to change in the same pull request as the code. The table of states lists every method that changes the status, and the condition for each one. The last row says that SHIPPED and CANCELLED are final.

Parts 3 and 4 give each rule with an example, and each event with the service that needs it:

## 3. Rules, each with an example

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| an order is placed only if the stock service holds every product | an order for a mug that is out of stock is refused with `PRODUCTS_UNAVAILABLE` |
| an order has 1 to 50 lines | an order with 51 lines is refused with a 400 that names `lines` |
| a line is picked once | picking the same line twice is refused with `LINE_ALREADY_PICKED` |
| an order ships only when it is paid | shipping a new order is refused with `ORDER_NOT_PAID` |
| an order ships only when every line is picked | shipping a paid order with an open line is refused with `UNPICKED_LINES` |
| an order ships only when no note needs action | shipping with one open note is refused with `ORDER_HAS_OPEN_ACTIONS` |
| a repeated or earlier payment changes nothing | the same payment event delivered twice is recorded once |
| a payment for a finished order is still recorded | a payment for a cancelled order is stored, and the status stays `CANCELLED` |

## 4. Events raised

| Domain event | Leaves the service as | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| `OrderPlaced` | `OrderPlacedV1` on `order-events` | the stock service, which keeps the products held |
| `LinePicked` | stays inside | nobody outside the service |
| `PaymentRecorded` | stays inside | nobody, because the payment service already knows |
| `OrderShipped` | `OrderShippedV1` on `order-events` | other services that tell the customer |
| `OrderCancelled` | `OrderCancelledV1` on `order-events` | other services that act on a cancelled order |

Each example in part 3 names the code of the error, such as ORDER_NOT_PAID. So a business expert can read the rule, and a developer can find its test. Part 4 says which events stay inside the service. LinePicked and PaymentRecorded have no integration event, because nobody outside needs them.

Parts 5 and 6 name the partners of the feature and its decisions:

## 5. Who it talks to

- The stock service, over HTTP, to reserve the products before the order is placed.
- The payment service, through the event `PaymentReceivedV1` on an SQS queue.
- The note feature, for the number of notes that need action.
- The reference feature, to check the delivery method.

## 6. Decisions

- The shipping rule holds only at the moment of shipping (option A). See the README.
- The order and its first notes are saved in one transaction. See
  `docs/adr/0001-order-and-first-notes-in-one-transaction.md`.

Part 6 points to the decisions, and does not repeat them. The words See the README. point to a paragraph of the README. The second decision points to the ADR file shown earlier.

Every line of the note can be checked against the code. The state changes are the methods of Order, and the rules are its tests. The comment of the order status already holds the table of states in short:

/**
 * Where an order is in its life. It is stored as its name, so never rename a value.
 *
 * <p>NEW becomes PAID when the payment arrives, and PAID becomes SHIPPED. NEW or PAID may become
 * CANCELLED. SHIPPED and CANCELLED are final.
 */
public enum OrderStatus {
    NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED
}

The comment of OrderStatus lists the same changes as the table of states. When the note and the code disagree, one of them is wrong, and the review finds it. Keep the note in the repository of the service, beside its README, so it changes in the same pull request as the code.

A level for each featurenew#

The design note names the level of the feature, which is simple, light or full. The level decides how many classes the feature has. The design group chooses it with three questions. Does the feature change state under business rules? Are its rules only about its own data, with a stored shape that matches the model? Does it call another service, hold the core rules, or need types that Spring Data cannot store as they are? For the questions and the three levels in code, see the chapter How much DDD: three levels in one service.

The level is also a fact that the build can check. The architecture test of the order service lists its full-style features:

private static final String BASE = "com.acme.orderservice";
/** The features in the full style, whose application layer must use ports only. */
private static final String ORDER = BASE + ".order";

ORDER is the one full-style feature. A feature that moves to the full style is added here in the same pull request.

Pragmatic choice: The light style as the default level

The strict rule. A DDD model is plain code with no framework types, behind repository ports.

What we do. A new feature with rules starts in the light style. The full style needs a reason in the design note.

Why. The light style keeps every part that protects a rule, with far fewer classes. The note feature has 17 source files, and the order feature has 57. Most features have a stored shape that matches their model.

When to stop. Choose the full style when the stored shape bends the model. Choose it too when the feature calls another service, or holds the core rules of the business.

The allowed building blocks, and what needs approvalnew#

A team can use these building blocks without asking. Each one has a home and an example in the order service.

Building blockExample in the order serviceTaught in
aggregate root, entity, value object, typed IDOrder, OrderLine, Money, OrderIdthe chapter on the domain model
domain event, recorded by the aggregateOrderShippedthe outbox chapter
domain service named after a rule across aggregatesShippingPolicythe chapter on rules
repository port for one aggregate, with an adapterOrderRepository and OrderPersistenceAdapterthe chapter on storage
application service with steps only, returning viewsOrderService and OrderViewthe use-case chapter
integration event with one mapper per featureOrderShippedV1 and OrderIntegrationEventMapperthe contracts chapter
port and adapter for another serviceStockChecker and StockAdapterthe chapter on other services
the simple level, with no building blocksthe reference featurethe chapter on levels

These need the approval of the design group, with a written reason:

  • Event sourcing. It changes how every change is stored and read.
  • Full Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS). A second model for reads doubles the code that must stay in step.
  • Generic repositories. A repository that loads any type, or returns a query that callers can extend, lets code reach past the root. The platform's Repository is generic in its types, but each feature has one port for one aggregate, with only the queries it needs.
  • A shared domain library. Domain classes shared by several services tie their releases together.
  • Models shared between features. A feature that uses another feature's entity skips that feature's rules.
  • Sagas outside the chosen workflow approach. A new way to run a long flow means a second way to find, retry and repair it.

The platform library states the rule about a shared domain library in its README:

The parent POM and the library that every shop service uses. It holds no business code and no
domain model: services share contracts (OpenAPI files and event schemas), never domain classes,
because a shared domain library would tie their release cycles together.

The words a shared domain library name the thing to avoid. The platform holds cross-cutting code only. Services share contracts, such as OpenAPI files and event schemas. For what the platform holds, see the chapter Writing the platform library.

Eight rules for every engineernew#

Every engineer on the team follows these eight rules. Each one has a test or a review question that checks it.

  1. Change state only through a method of the aggregate. Never add a public setter to an entity. A test checks it.
  2. Put each business rule in the aggregate. A rule that needs two aggregates goes in a domain service named after the rule. A rule never goes in a controller or an application service.
  3. Record an event for every change that matters to someone. The aggregate records it, and the save step publishes it.
  4. Refer to other aggregates by ID. Never hold another aggregate as a field.
  5. Use another feature only through its application service. Never use its repository, its entities or its domain package. A test checks it.
  6. Change one aggregate in a transaction, and call other services before it starts. An exception is written down as a decision.
  7. Use the business words. A class or method named after a business idea, never Manager, Processor or Helper.
  8. Test each rule with a plain unit test named after the rule. No Spring and no mocks for a rule of an aggregate.

The use case of the order feature states rules 2 and 6 in its own comment, so a developer who opens the class reads them:

/**
 * The use cases of the order feature. This is the one entry point for the controller, the
 * message listener and other features.
 *
 * <p>Every change follows the same steps: load, let the domain apply its rules and change
 * itself, save, publish the events, record the audit. The steps that call other services run
 * before the transaction. This class decides the order of the steps and never contains a
 * business rule: a line that a business expert would recognise as a rule belongs in the domain.
 *
 * <p>Methods take value objects, which are valid already, and return IDs or views, never an
 * aggregate.
 *
 * <p>The class has no permission annotation. Permissions are checked on the controllers, where
 * users enter. Every method here can therefore be called by another feature or by a message
 * listener without a second, unprotected copy of the method.
 *
 * <p>With about ten use cases, split the class by area, such as {@code OrderFulfilmentService},
 * not into a read side and a write side.
 */

The comment gives the steps. It says that the class decides the order of the steps and holds no business rule. It also gives the test for a rule in the wrong place. A line that a business expert would recognise as a rule belongs in the domain.

Guardrails: the architecture rulestwist#

ArchUnitNET 0.13.4
IArchRule domainIsPlain = Types().That().ResideInNamespaceMatching(@"Shop\..*\.Domain")
    .Should().NotDependOnAnyTypesThat().ResideInNamespaceMatching(@"Microsoft\.EntityFrameworkCore.*")
    .Because("a domain namespace is plain C#");
The platform library
/** A {@code domain} package uses no framework, no adapter and no other layer. */
public static ArchRule domainIsPlainJava() {
    return noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage(
                    "org.springframework..", "com.mongodb..", "org.bson..", "jakarta..",
                    "tools.jackson..", "com.fasterxml..", "io.awspring..",
                    "..application..", "..api..", "..persistence..", "..client..", "..messaging..",
                    "com.acme.platform.core..", "com.acme.platform.mongo..")
            .as("A domain package is plain Java");
}

Both panes state that the domain uses no framework. C# writes NotDependOnAnyTypesThat. Java writes dependOnClassesThat after noClasses(). The C# rule uses ArchUnitNET, the C# fork of ArchUnit, and was run against a domain class that held a DbContext. It reported the dependency. The Java rule is in the platform library, so every service runs the same rules. A .NET team rarely has such rules unless someone writes them. The platform makes them part of every build.

A rule that never fails protects nothing. So the companion also tests that the rules fail for code that breaks them:

/** A light-style entity, a document outside persistence, that someone gave a setter. */
@Document("parcels")
static class ParcelWithASetter {
    private String status;

    public void setStatus(String status) {
        this.status = status;
    }
}

@Test
void anEntityWithAPublicSetterFailsTheBuild() {
    JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter().importClasses(ParcelWithASetter.class);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> ArchitectureRules.entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters().check(classes))
            .isInstanceOf(AssertionError.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("setStatus");
}

ParcelWithASetter is a light-style entity with a public setter. The test checks that entitiesHaveNoPublicSetters throws an AssertionError that names setStatus. For every rule of the platform and how the tests run, see the chapter Testing in depth.

The pull request checklistnew#

The build checks dependencies and setters. It cannot check whether a rule is in the right place, or whether a name is a business word. So every pull request that changes a feature answers five questions. The author answers them in the description, and the reviewer checks the answers.

The companion keeps the questions as the template for the description of a pull request. GitHub reads such a template from a file named pull_request_template.md. The file may be in the root of the repository, in docs/, or in .github/. The order service keeps it in .github/pull_request_template.md:

<!--
  Answer each question in a sentence or two, or write "no change". The reviewer checks the
  answers against the code. The build already checks the dependencies between packages and
  the setters, so these questions cover what it cannot see.
-->

## What changes, and why

## Domain questions

1. **Can any new change of state skip a method of the aggregate?**
   Look for a setter, a direct update of a document, or a script.

2. **Is every new rule in the aggregate, or in a domain service named after it, with a test named
   after the rule?**

3. **Does every new change of state record its event?** Is a new public event a versioned
   contract with a schema in `contracts/events`?

4. **Does the change reach into another feature?** Look for another feature's repository, entity
   or domain class. `ArchitectureTest` catches the common cases, not all of them.

5. **Are the names business words, and is the feature still at the right level?**
   If it needs the next level, update its design note in `docs/design/` first.

GitHub shows the contents of the file in the description of each new pull request, once the file is on the default branch. The comment at the top says how to answer. The heading ## What changes, and why asks for a short summary first. The five questions follow the heading ## Domain questions, and the author writes each answer below its question. So a skipped question stays visible to the reviewer. The fifth question links the template to the design note. A feature that needs the next level changes its note in docs/design/ first.

The fourth question has a test of its own. The architecture test fails when a service uses another feature's repository or entity:

@Test
void servicesUseNoRepositoryOrEntityOfAnotherFeature() {
    ArchitectureRules.servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities(BASE).check(CLASSES);
}

servicesDoNotUseOtherFeaturesRepositoriesOrEntities covers the most common way to reach into another feature. The question in the checklist covers the rest, such as a copied query on another feature's collection. For the review checklist of the whole service, see the chapter Changing the service.

Start each feature from a template featurenew#

In a usual .NET team, a new service starts from dotnet new webapi, and each developer adds folders by kind of class. Each service then looks a little different. In this team, a new feature starts as a copy of a template feature. The template has the right packages, the right tests, and a comment in each package that says what goes there.

The companion has no separate template. Its note feature serves as the template of a light-style feature, and its order feature as the template of a full-style one. Here are the files that a light-style feature starts with:

note/
  package-info.java                 what the feature holds, its level, and when to move up
  api/
    NoteController.java             endpoints, each with a permission annotation
    NoteApiMapper.java              DTOs to values, views to DTOs
    dto/                            AddNoteRequest, NoteResponse, NoteAddedResponse
  application/
    NoteService.java                the use cases: load, decide, save, publish, audit
    NewNote.java, NoteView.java     what callers pass in and get back
  model/
    Note.java                       the entity, its rules and its events, stored as a document
    NoteRepository.java             the Spring Data repository
    NoteAdded.java, NoteActionResolved.java
    Note...Exception.java           one exception for each broken rule
test/.../note/
  model/NoteTest.java               the rules, in plain JUnit
  model/NoteMappingTest.java        the stored shape, without a database
  model/NoteRepositoryIT.java       the stored behaviour, against MongoDB
  application/NoteServiceTest.java  the steps of each use case
  api/NoteControllerTest.java       the HTTP layer and the permissions

A developer copies the folder, renames the classes, and replaces the rules. The tests come with it, so no feature starts without tests of its rules. The first file, package-info.java, is the first thing to rewrite, because it states the level and the rules of the new feature.

When the team keeps making the same mistake, fix the template, not the people. If developers keep forgetting the permission annotation, the template's controller shows it on every endpoint, and a test fails without it.

The wrong decisions to watch fortrap#

Most DDD services fail in the same few ways. Each wrong decision shows early, if someone looks for it. The table gives the sign of each one and how to prevent it.

Wrong decisionWhat it looks likeHow to prevent it
aggregates copied from old tablesone aggregate for each table of the old database, with the same columnsfind the aggregates from the rules and the events, in the design group, before looking at the old schema
an aggregate that is too biga list with no limit inside, frequent 409 responses, large documentsask for the maximum of every list, and move a list with no limit to its own aggregate
an aggregate that is too smallevery use case saves the same two aggregates, or a rule needs a lock across themmerge them when a rule must change both every time
rules drifting into servicesan if in an application service that a business expert would recognisethe review question about rules, and a test of each rule on the aggregate
a batch job or loader that bypasses the entitya script or job that writes documents directlyjobs call the use case, and the stored document class is not visible outside its package
forgotten eventsa state change with no event, found when another service misses itthe aggregate records the event in the method, and the save step always publishes
features reaching into each othera service that takes another feature's repository or entitythe architecture test, and calls only through the other feature's application service
jargonnames such as OrderManager, process, handle or updatethe design note names the methods in business words, and the review checks them
gold-platingevent sourcing, CQRS or a full model for a feature with no rulesthe level in the design note, and approval for the building blocks on the list

Two of these need a closer look, because they look harmless.

Gotcha

A batch job that writes documents directly skips every rule of the aggregate. A data fix that sets status to SHIPPED in the database ships an unpaid order without an event. Make every job load the aggregate and call its method through the use case, as the payment listener does.

The order service makes the shortcut hard. Its stored document is package-private, so no code outside the persistence package can build one:

 * <p>Only plain types are stored. Enums and codes are strings, so renaming a Java class never
 * breaks stored data. Money is DECIMAL128, so it is exact. The class and its fields are
 * package-private: nothing outside this package knows the storage shape.
 */
@Document("orders")
class OrderDocument extends BaseDocument {

class OrderDocument has no public, so a job in another package cannot use it. A job can still write raw documents with MongoTemplate. The review question about skipping a method covers that case.

Gold-plating is the other one. A team that learns DDD wants to use all of it. A feature with no rules then gets an aggregate, ports and events. The level in the design note stops it before the code exists.

Each wrong decision breaks a principle. For the principles, and for the questions that teams ask most often, see the part Reasoning from first principles. It starts with the chapter The principles.

Long flows: a workflow engine or a process managernew#

Some flows take many steps across services and days. A return, for example, could need a label, a parcel scan, a check in the warehouse and a refund. Events between services can run such a flow. But then no single place knows where each return is, and a stuck return is hard to find.

Two options keep the state of the flow in one place, as of October 2026.

  • A process manager. The pattern is from the book Enterprise Integration Patterns. A process manager keeps the state of a sequence of steps, and decides the next step from the results so far. It can be an aggregate of its own in one service. The pattern's page warns that the central unit can become a bottleneck.
  • A workflow engine. A product that stores the state of each flow and runs its steps. Temporal is one example. It describes itself as an open-source platform for the durable execution of code, and it has a Java SDK.

The order service has no long flow. Its one step across services, the stock reservation, uses an idempotency key and a timeout:

/**
 * Asks the stock service to confirm that the items are available, and to hold them for the
 * order. The stock service keeps the hold until it sees {@code OrderPlacedV1}, or releases it
 * after a timeout if the order is never placed.
 *
 * <p>Calling it twice for the same order holds nothing twice, because the order ID is the
 * idempotency key.
 */
StockAvailability reserve(OrderId order, List<OrderItem> items);

reserve needs no flow state, because the stock service releases a hold that no OrderPlacedV1 confirms. Choose one approach for the whole team when the first long flow appears, and record it in an ADR. A second approach then needs approval, as the list of building blocks says.

Rolling it outnew#

A team does not learn DDD from a document. It learns from a service that works, and from people who built it. Roll it out in five steps.

  1. A pilot service. The strongest engineers build one service in the new way. Each of them works in a pair with a developer who is new to it. The pilot proves the platform, the template and the rules on real work.
  2. Training from the pilot's code. Teach with the pilot's own classes and tests, not with slides. Each lesson follows one use case, from the controller to the event.
  3. A design review of each new aggregate, before code. The design group reviews the design note. A boundary that is wrong costs an hour here, and weeks after release.
  4. A weekly slot for questions. One hour a week, the design group answers questions about real code. Questions that come back often become changes to the template or to the rules.
  5. Fix the template, not the people. When several people make the same mistake, the template or a guardrail is missing something. Change it, and add a test where one is possible.

An existing service can adopt the architecture rules without fixing every old violation first. The comment of the platform's rules says how:

* <p>To add the rules to an existing service with old violations, wrap a rule in
* {@code FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule)}. ArchUnit then records today's violations, and only new
* ones fail the build.

FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule) records the violations that exist today. After that, only new violations fail the build. So an old service gets the guardrails on its first day, and its old code is fixed feature by feature. For how the freeze store works, see the chapter Testing in depth.

Check yourself
1
Which decisions does the small design group make, and which does the team make?
The design group decides the service boundaries, the aggregates and the business rules, with business experts. It also decides the workflows and the level of each feature. The team decides everything inside those decisions.
2
What does a feature design note contain?
The aggregates and what is inside each one, and the states with the allowed changes. Each rule with an example. The events raised, and the features and services it talks to.
3
An expert asksWhy does the team fix the template when people keep making the same mistake?
A mistake that many people make comes from the way work starts, not from one person. A template that shows the right way stops the mistake for everyone. So does a test that fails for the wrong way, even for people who join later.
4
An expert asksWhy does a batch job that updates documents directly break a DDD service?
It skips the methods of the aggregate, so no rule is checked and no event is recorded. Other services never hear about the change. Every job must load the aggregate and call its method through the use case.
5
TranslateWrite this ArchUnitNET rule as an ArchUnit rule in Java: Types().That().ResideInNamespaceMatching(@"Shop\..*\.Domain").Should().NotDependOnAnyTypesThat().ResideInNamespaceMatching(@"Microsoft\.EntityFrameworkCore.*")
noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("org.springframework.."). noClasses is a static method of ArchUnit's ArchRuleDefinition, and .. matches any number of package levels.
6
Name four building blocks that need the approval of the design group.
Event sourcing, full CQRS, generic repositories, a shared domain library, models shared between features, and sagas outside the chosen workflow approach. Any four of these.

The words#

Reasoning from first principles · Chapter 31· 17 min read

This chapter is a refresher. Read it straight through before a design discussion. It defines the main words of Domain-Driven Design (DDD) and microservices that this book and the Atlas use, in one or two sentences. The words are grouped by topic, in the order in which the ideas build. Each word links to the place that teaches it.

Strategic design#

These words describe the business and its borders. They come before any code.

DDD is a way of building software around a model of the business, in the words of the business. It exists because the business is usually the hardest part of a system.

The domain is the whole area of business that the software serves. For the shop, the domain is selling, paying for and shipping goods.

The problem space is the business as it is, with its needs and its rules. You study it before you decide what to build.

The solution space is the software that you design to answer the problem space. Its parts are models, contexts and services.

A subdomain is one part of the business, such as payments, shipping or the catalogue. It belongs to the problem space, so it exists before any border in the code.

A core subdomain is the part of the business that makes customers choose you. It gets your best people and your richest model, because no vendor can build it for you.

A supporting subdomain is a part that the business needs, but that does not set it apart. You build it simply, because it is specific to you but not a reason to choose you.

A generic subdomain is a part that every business needs in the same way, such as sending email. You buy it or use an open-source product, because building it gives you nothing.

A core domain chart places each subdomain by how complex it is and by how much it sets the business apart. It shows where modelling effort pays.

The ubiquitous language is the set of words that business experts and developers share, used unchanged in the code. It exists so that a conversation and the code mean the same thing.

Event Storming is a workshop in which business people and developers put the events of the business on a wall, in time order. It finds the words, the rules and the borders quickly.

A hotspot is a note on the Event Storming wall that marks a question, a conflict or a pain. Each hotspot needs an owner in the business.

Domain storytelling is a workshop in which a business expert tells one real story, and a moderator draws it as pictures and arrows. It finds the words and the steps of one process.

A bounded context is an area in which one model applies and each word has one meaning. Its border is where a word starts to mean something else.

Strategic design is the part of DDD that finds the subdomains, the bounded contexts and the relations between them. Tactical design is the other part, the building blocks inside one context.

A bounded context canvas is a one-page template that describes one context. It lists the purpose, the language, the inputs and the outputs of the context.

A context map is a picture of the bounded contexts and the relations between them. It shows who depends on whom, and how each border is handled.

Upstream and downstream describe the relation between two contexts. The upstream context decides its own model, and the downstream context depends on it.

A partnership is a relation in which two contexts succeed or fail together. So their two teams plan their changes together.

A shared kernel is a small part of a model that two contexts own together. No team may change it alone, so it must stay small and stable.

A customer-supplier relation is one in which the downstream context is a customer of the upstream context. The upstream team plans its changes with the needs of the downstream team.

A conformist is a downstream context that uses the upstream model as it is, with no translation. It costs little, but every change upstream reaches the downstream model.

An anti-corruption layer is code at a border that translates another model into your own words. It keeps a model that you do not control out of your domain.

An open host service is an interface that a context offers to every consumer, in one documented form. It saves the upstream team from building one integration for each consumer.

A published language is a documented format for the data that crosses a border, such as a JSON Schema for an event. It is separate from the internal model of each side.

Separate ways is a relation in which two contexts do not integrate at all. Each context meets its own need, because integration would cost more than it gives.

A big ball of mud is a system with no clear borders, in which any part may depend on any other part. A change anywhere can then break something anywhere else.

The model#

These words describe the building blocks inside one bounded context. Together they are called tactical design.

An entity is an object with an identity that stays the same while its data changes, such as an order with its ID. Two entities with equal data are still different when their IDs differ.

A value object is an object that is only its values, such as an amount of money. It never changes, so it is safe to share and to compare by value.

An aggregate is a group of objects that one business rule must see at once. The service loads, changes and saves the group as one unit.

The aggregate root is the one object of an aggregate that outside code may hold. Every change to the aggregate goes through a method of the root.

An invariant is a business rule that must be true after every change, such as "an order ships only when every line is picked". The aggregate is drawn around its invariants.

A consistency boundary is the set of data that one transaction keeps consistent. An aggregate is a consistency boundary.

Eventual consistency means that two places agree a little later, not at once. An event carries the change from one place to the other.

A set-based invariant is a rule over many aggregates, such as "each email address is used once". One aggregate cannot check it, so a unique index or a separate process holds it.

A typed ID is a small class that wraps an ID, such as OrderId. The compiler then stops you from passing the wrong kind of ID.

A reference by ID means that one aggregate holds only the ID of another aggregate, never the object. So the two aggregates load, save and change apart.

A factory creates an aggregate in a valid state. A factory for a new aggregate checks the rules, and Order.place is one.

To rehydrate an aggregate is to rebuild it from its stored form. The rules for a new aggregate do not run again.

A repository loads and saves whole aggregates, as if they were in a collection. There is one repository for each aggregate root.

A domain service holds a business rule that needs more than one aggregate, or that belongs to no single object. In this book, it is almost always a rule across aggregates.

A use case is one thing that a user or another system wants to do, such as placing an order.

An application service runs the steps of a use case. It loads aggregates, calls their methods and saves them, but it holds no business rule.

A domain event records that something happened in the domain, such as an order being placed. Its name is in the past tense.

A command asks one named receiver to do something, such as "place this order". A command can be refused, but an event reports something that already happened.

An anaemic domain model has classes with data and setters, but no rules. The rules are in service classes, so they spread and repeat.

A rich domain model keeps each rule in the object that owns the data. So every change goes through a method that checks the rule.

A transaction script is one procedure for each business operation, which reads data, applies the rules and writes the result. It is the simplest choice for a part with few rules.

An active record is an object that holds one row of data and also saves itself. It suits simple data with few rules.

Optimistic locking finds two writers of the same data by comparing a version number on each save. The second save fails, so no change disappears in silence.

A lost update happens when two writers read the same data and the second save overwrites the first. Optimistic locking prevents it.

The business-expert test asks whether a business expert would call a line of code a rule. If the expert would, the line belongs in the domain.

The order service uses three levels of DDD, and the full style is the richest. The order feature uses it, with a rich aggregate, ports and a mapper to a stored document.

The light style keeps the rules in the entity, but the entity is its own document and the service uses Spring Data directly. The note feature uses it.

The simple level has no domain model, because the feature has almost no rules. The reference feature uses it.

A mapper converts one shape of data into another shape, such as an aggregate into its stored document. The order service also uses a mapper to turn domain events into integration events.

A view is a read-only copy of some data of an aggregate, which an application service returns. It keeps the aggregate itself inside the service.

Architecture inside a service#

These words describe how the code of one service is arranged.

A layered architecture stacks the code in layers, such as web, business and data. Each layer calls only the layer below it.

A port is an interface that the domain or the application declares for something that it needs from outside, such as storage.

An adapter implements a port with a real technology, such as a database driver or an HTTP client.

A persistence adapter is the class that implements a repository with a real database. It maps the aggregate to a stored document and back.

Hexagonal architecture puts the domain in the middle and connects everything outside through ports and adapters. It is also called ports and adapters.

Onion architecture draws the code as rings, with the domain model at the centre and the infrastructure at the edge. Every dependency points inward.

Clean architecture is another version of the same idea. Its rings are entities, use cases, adapters and frameworks.

The dependency rule says that code depends only inward, toward the domain. The domain depends on no framework and no adapter.

A feature package holds all the code of one business feature, from the controller to the storage. A change to the feature then stays in one folder.

A vertical slice is the code of one use case, from the request to the database, kept together. It is another way to arrange code than folders by layer.

A modular monolith is one deployable application, divided into modules with enforced borders. It gives clear borders without a network between them.

Spring Modulith is a Spring project that checks the borders between the modules of one application. The order service uses its registry of published events.

The event publication registry is the store in Spring Modulith of the events that transactional listeners must receive. In the order service, it is the outbox.

An architecture rule is a test that fails the build when code breaks a rule of structure. An example is a domain class that imports a framework.

A platform library is a shared library that gives every service the same technical defaults, such as logging, security and the outbox. It holds no business code.

Command query responsibility segregation (CQRS) uses one model to change data and another model to read it. It pays when the screens need a shape that the aggregates do not have.

A read model is data shaped for one screen or one query, built from the data of the write side. It never decides a command.

A projection is the code that builds a read model from a stream of events.

Event sourcing stores every change of an aggregate as an event, and rebuilds the current state by replaying the events. It pays when the history itself matters to the business.

A snapshot is a saved copy of the state of an event-sourced aggregate at one point. A load then replays only the events after it.

An event store is the database of an event-sourced system. It keeps every event in order and never changes one.

Upcasting converts an old stored event into its newer shape when the event is read. The old events stay unchanged in the store.

Integration#

These words describe how services work together, and what happens when a call or a message fails.

A synchronous call waits for the answer before it continues, like an HTTP request. Both services must be up at the same moment.

An asynchronous message is sent without waiting for an answer, through a broker. The receiver reads it when it is ready.

An integration event is an event published to other services, in a stable and versioned form. It is separate from the domain event, so the internal model can still change.

An event notification carries little more than an ID and what happened. A consumer that needs more data asks the producer.

Event-carried state transfer puts the data that consumers need into the event itself. The consumers then need no call back to the producer.

The dual-write problem is the risk of writing to a database and to a broker as two separate steps. One write can succeed while the other fails.

A transactional outbox is a collection in which the service writes its outgoing messages, in the same transaction as its data. A separate process then sends the messages.

Change data capture reads the database's own log of changes and publishes the changes as messages. It is another way to avoid a dual write.

At-least-once delivery means that a message is never lost, but it may arrive more than once.

An operation is idempotent when running it twice has the same effect as running it once. A consumer of messages must be idempotent, because a message can arrive twice.

An idempotency key is a value that the caller chooses once and sends with every attempt of the call. The receiver then recognises a repeat.

An inbox is a list of the IDs of the messages that a consumer has processed, stored in the same transaction as the change. A duplicate then finds its ID and is ignored.

Ordering per key means that a broker keeps the order only among messages with the same key, if it keeps an order at all. An Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) standard queue does not.

A FIFO queue is a queue in SQS that keeps the order of the messages in a message group, and removes duplicates for five minutes. A message group is the set of messages that share one group ID.

The visibility timeout is how long SQS hides a received message from other consumers. If the consumer does not delete the message in that time, it can be received again.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) holds messages that failed too many times. So they stop being delivered again and again, and a person can look at them.

A redrive policy moves a message to the dead-letter queue after a set number of failed receives. A redrive can also move messages back, once the cause is fixed.

A poison message is a message that fails every time it is processed, such as a message with a broken format.

A tolerant reader reads only the fields that it needs and ignores the rest. So a producer can add fields without breaking it.

Expand and contract changes a published contract in three steps. You add the new form, move every consumer to it, and then remove the old form.

An API contract is the shape of an API or an event that other teams build against. It is kept in a file, such as an OpenAPI file.

Contract first means that a team writes the API contract before the code, and generates or checks the code against it.

A consumer-driven contract is a test, written from the needs of a consumer, that the producer runs in its own build. It finds a breaking change before release.

A timeout is the longest time that a caller waits for an answer. Without one, a slow service holds the threads of its callers.

A transient failure is a failure that may pass if you try again, such as a timeout or a 503 answer.

A retry repeats a call that failed with a transient failure. It is safe only for a call that is idempotent.

A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service for a while, and fails them at once. It gives the failing service time to recover.

A cascading failure spreads from one slow or failed service to the services that call it, and then to their callers. Retries without limits make it worse.

A bulkhead gives each dependency its own pool of threads or connections. So one slow dependency cannot use up the resources of the others.

Load shedding refuses some requests when a service is overloaded, so that the other requests still succeed.

Backpressure is a signal from a busy receiver that tells the sender to slow down, such as a full queue that refuses the next item.

A saga is a business process that spans several services as a chain of local transactions. Each step that may need undoing has a compensating action.

A compensating action undoes the effect of an earlier step in business terms, such as a refund for a payment.

The pivot step is the step of a saga after which the saga must finish. Steps before it can be compensated, and steps after it are retried until they succeed.

A semantic lock marks data as pending while a saga runs, such as a reserved item. Other work then treats the pending data with care.

Choreography runs a saga with no central coordinator. Each service reacts to the events of the other services.

Smart endpoints and dumb pipes means that the services hold the logic, and the broker only carries the messages. James Lewis and Martin Fowler wrote it down in 2014.

Orchestration runs a saga from one coordinator, which tells each service what to do next.

A process manager holds the state of a long process and decides the next step. It is one way to orchestrate a saga.

A workflow engine is a product that runs long processes safely, with their state, their timers and their retries.

Two-phase commit is a protocol that joins several databases into one transaction. It holds locks while the network talks, so services rarely use it.

API composition builds one answer by calling several services and joining their results.

A backend for frontend (BFF) is a small service for one kind of client, such as a mobile app. It shapes the data of several services for that client.

A trace ID is an ID that a service sends on with every HTTP call and writes in its log lines. An event carries it only if the service adds it, so a business ID such as the order ID often connects the traces.

A span is one timed step of a trace, such as the part of the work that one service does.

A correlation ID is an ID that ties together the calls and the messages of one piece of work. In the order service, the order ID does this job across events.

Distributed tracing records each step of a request across services, under one trace ID. A tool then shows the whole path and the time of each step.

Organisation and migration#

These words describe services as a whole, the teams that own them, and the way from an old system to a new one.

A microservice is a service that one team can change and deploy alone, with its own data. Its size follows a business border, not a count of lines.

Independent deployability means that a service can go to production while no other service changes. It is the main promise of microservices.

An entity service is a service around one noun, such as a product, with little more than create, read, update and delete. A real operation then needs calls to many of them.

A shared database is one database that several services read and write. It ties the services together, because no service can change a table alone.

Database per service gives each service its own data store, which only that service may touch.

A distributed monolith is a set of services that must change and deploy together. It has the costs of services and the coupling of a monolith.

The fallacies of distributed computing are eight false beliefs about networks, such as "the network is reliable". Peter Deutsch listed seven of them in 1994, and James Gosling added the eighth.

Conway's law says that the structure of a system copies the communication structure of the organisation that builds it. Melvin Conway described it in 1968.

The inverse Conway manoeuvre shapes the teams first, so that the system grows the borders that you want.

A stream-aligned team owns one flow of business change from end to end, such as checkout. Most teams are of this kind.

A platform team builds the shared tools that the other teams use, such as the pipelines and the platform library.

An enabling team helps other teams to learn a skill, and then moves on.

A complicated-subsystem team owns a part that needs rare expert knowledge, such as a pricing engine.

Cognitive load is the amount that a team must hold in mind to do its work. A team that owns too much makes slow and unsafe changes.

The design group is two or three senior engineers and a business expert. It decides the boundaries, the aggregates, where rules go, the workflows and the level of DDD for each feature.

A feature design note is a short document that records how a new feature fits the model, before the code is written.

An architecture decision record (ADR) is a short document that records one decision, its context and its consequences. It tells later readers why the code is as it is.

A template feature is a small, complete feature that a team copies to start a new feature in the agreed shape.

The microservices premium is the extra cost of running many services, such as pipelines, monitoring and contracts. A team pays it before the services give any benefit.

Monolith first is the advice to start with one application and to split it later, when the borders are known. Martin Fowler argued for it in 2015.

The strangler fig pattern replaces an old system piece by piece, by sending more and more requests to new code. Martin Fowler described it in 2004 as the strangler application, and renamed it in 2019.

A seam is a place where you can change behaviour without editing the code around it, such as an interface or a routing point.

Branch by abstraction puts an interface in front of the code that you replace. The old code and the new code then live side by side behind it.

A bubble context is a small new context with a clean model, protected from a legacy system by an anti-corruption layer.

A parallel run sends the same work to the old system and to the new system, and compares the results before the switch.

A feature flag switches a piece of code on or off while the application runs, with no new deployment.

To deploy is to put code into production, and to release is to let users reach it. A feature flag keeps the two steps apart.

A canary release sends a small share of the traffic to a new version first, and watches it before sending the rest.

A service level indicator is a measurement of what users experience, such as the share of requests answered within 300 milliseconds.

A service level objective is a target for a service level indicator, such as 99.9 percent of requests answered within 300 milliseconds.

An error budget is the amount of failure that the service level objective still allows. When it is used up, the team works on reliability before new features.

A data mesh gives each context the job of publishing its own data for analysis, as a product. Zhamak Dehghani described it in 2019.

The principles#

Reasoning from first principles · Chapter 32· 19 min read

Experienced teams do not remember hundreds of answers. They remember a few principles, and they ask which principle decides the case. This chapter gives nineteen principles. Each one says what is true, why it is true, and when it stops being true. The next four chapters answer the common questions with them.

How to use the principles#

Most questions about Domain-Driven Design (DDD) and microservices have a short answer. The answer comes from one or two principles and one fact about your case. A principle tells you what matters. The fact tells you which way it goes.

The principles are in four groups. The first six are about the model, its data, and how much of it to build. The next four are about borders, and the structure of the code inside them. The next six are about calls, messages and callers that cross a border. The last three are about the cost of borders, the teams that build them, and the order of decisions.

Each principle has a short name. Every field question in the next four chapters names the principles that decide it, with a link back here. Review is the mode of this book that asks you one question at a time. In Review, each principle is also a card. The card asks what the principle says and when it stops holding.

A transaction protects one place#

What it says

A transaction makes several changes happen together, or not at all. It can do that only inside one database system, because that system keeps one log of the changes. Anything outside that system is consistent later, or not at all.

In the order service, one transaction usually holds one aggregate, its outbox row and its audit entry. All of them are in one DocumentDB cluster.

Why it holds

A database can undo its own changes, because it keeps a log of them. A second database, a message broker or another service keeps its own log. No single log covers both places, so no single undo covers both.

The rule "one aggregate per transaction" follows from this principle and from the next one. Each aggregate keeps its own rules. So a transaction that spans two aggregates is a border that you can never move to a second database later.

When it stops holding

Two databases can share a transaction through a protocol called two-phase commit. It holds locks while the two sides talk over the network. So one slow or failed partner blocks everyone who waits for those locks. It is rarely worth that cost, and most cloud message services do not support it.

The order service breaks the rule "one aggregate per transaction" once. An order and its first notes are saved together, because the agent sees them as one action. The cost is that the two aggregates now succeed or fail together, and must stay in one database. See the section One aggregate per transaction, and the order with its notes.

Now, or a little later#

What it says

Some rules must be true at every moment. Other rules may be true a little later. A rule of the first kind needs all its data inside one transaction. A rule of the second kind can cover aggregates and services, and an event closes the gap.

Why it holds

A rule that must be true now is checked and saved in one step. Suppose its data is in two places. A second request can then change one place between the check and the save. The rule is broken, and nobody sees it.

A rule that may be true later accepts that window. It is checked again, or repaired, when the event arrives. The line between the two kinds is a business decision. Ask the people who own the rule what happens today when it is broken for a minute. "A refund" or "a phone call" means later. "A fine" or "money that we cannot get back" means now.

When it stops holding

A rule of the first kind makes every writer of its data wait for the others. When many people write at once, as in a flash sale, those writers fail or slow down. Then the cost of the waiting can be higher than the cost of being wrong for a moment.

The business then moves the rule to the second kind on purpose. An airline sells more seats than the plane has, and handles the rare problem with a voucher. For the four ways to handle the gap, see the section Four ways to handle the gap, and how to record the choice.

The root guards the rule#

What it says

An aggregate has one entry point. The entry point is called the aggregate root. Every change to the aggregate goes through a method of the root. The method checks the rules first, and then it changes the data.

Why it holds

A rule that covers several objects can be checked only by code that sees all of them. If any code can change one object directly, that code can skip the check. Then the rule is true only while every caller remembers it.

One entry point gives one place to check the rule, one place to test it and one place to read it. A new use case cannot forget the rule, because it has no other way in. If ordinary features keep wanting to skip the root, the boundary is wrong. The part that they change is probably an aggregate of its own.

When it stops holding

Reads skip the root by design, because a read changes nothing. A data migration and a repair of broken data may also write the stored form directly. They must still leave the data in a state that the root would accept.

A change to a million records is also too slow through the root, one aggregate at a time. A bulk update in the database is then the right tool. The cost is that the rule is now written twice, once in the root and once in the update, and both must agree. For the order aggregate, see the section The root is the only way in.

Every fact has one writer#

What it says

Each piece of data has one owner. Only the owner writes it. Everyone else asks the owner, or keeps a copy that the owner's events update.

Why it holds

Two writers of the same data bring two sets of rules for it. Each writer can break the rules of the other writer. And each writer must agree with the other writer before it can change the shape of the data.

One writer gives one place for the rules, and one team that may change the shape. A copy is safe from conflicting writes, because nobody changes the truth through it. But a copy can be out of date. So a copy may be shown, and the owner decides.

When it stops holding

Two contexts may own a small part of the model together, with its code and sometimes its data. This is called a shared kernel. Every change to it needs both teams, so keep it small and stable.

Some systems need many writers by design. An app that works offline, or a database that accepts writes in two regions at once, lets two copies change at the same time. The cost is a rule that merges the two versions. For the story of a table that had many writers by accident, see the Atlas chapter Nobody owns the product table.

Spend design effort where the business is different#

What it says

Some parts of the business are the reason customers choose you, and their rules are complex. Spend careful modelling there. Other parts are the same in most companies, or their rules are simple. For those parts, write something simple, or buy it.

Why it holds

A rich model costs time to build and time to change. It pays back where the rules are complex and where they set you apart, because mistakes there cost most. A list of delivery methods or a login screen works the same way in most companies. A careful model there gives nothing that a library or a vendor does not already give.

The parts of the business are called subdomains. The three kinds are core, supporting and generic. This is why the order service uses three levels of DDD, and not one level everywhere.

When it stops holding

A supporting part can have complex rules. Customers do not choose you for it, but a simple model would still break its rules. Then it needs a rich model too. The cost is careful work on something that does not set you apart.

The kind of a subdomain also changes over time. A supporting part can become the reason that customers come. So review the kinds when the business changes. See the section Choosing the level for each feature.

Data outlives the code that wrote it#

What it says

Stored documents, messages in a queue and published events stay after the code that wrote them is gone. New code must still read them. And someone must still find them when the data has to be deleted or moved.

Why it holds

During a rolling deployment, old code and new code run at the same time and read the same documents. A message can wait in a queue, or in a dead-letter queue, for days. No compiler sees any of this data. So every change to a stored shape needs a plan for the old shape. First read both forms, then migrate, then remove the old form.

The same is true for personal data. A fact that was copied into ten places must be found in ten places when a customer asks to be forgotten.

When it stops holding

Data that is built again from nothing on every deployment can change its shape freely. A cache is one example. A read model that can be rebuilt from events is another. The cost is the time to rebuild. See the section Changing the shape of stored documents.

A word that changes meaning marks a border#

What it says

A model is a set of words with exact meanings. Where a word starts to mean something different, a new model starts. The area where one model holds is called a bounded context.

Why it holds

One class cannot hold two meanings without fields that only one meaning needs. An order in sales has lines and prices. An order in the warehouse has boxes and a pick list. One class for both changes whenever either team changes its idea of an order.

Two models, with a translation at the border, let each team change its own words. The translation is called an anti-corruption layer when it protects your model from a model you do not control.

When it stops holding

A difference only in the name, with the same rules, is not a border. Two teams that say "client" and "customer" for the same thing need one word, not two models.

A border also costs a translation. In a small system that one team builds, a border may not yet be worth that cost. For how borders are drawn, see the Atlas chapter Drawing the borders.

What changes together stays together#

What it says

Put code that changes for the same reason in the same place. Keep code that changes for different reasons apart. This principle decides folders, modules and services.

Why it holds

A change that touches one place is one review, one test run and one deployment. A change that touches three places needs all three to agree, and to ship in the right order. Between services, that order needs a plan for the releases.

So a boundary that most changes cross is in the wrong place. A good boundary is one that most changes stay inside. David Parnas made this argument in 1972. He said to divide a system by what is likely to change.

When it stops holding

Some code changes together but must still be apart. A part with very different load, security or availability needs may need its own deployment. Then every change that crosses the border costs more. To keep that cost low, keep the contract between the two parts small and stable.

For how the order service groups its code, see the section Features at the top, never technologies.

Depend on your own rules, not on the details#

What it says

Point each dependency from the details toward the business rules. The details are the web framework, the database and the other services. The rules must never have to change because a detail changed.

So the web layer, the database adapter and the clients for other services depend on the domain. The domain depends on none of them.

Why it holds

Suppose the domain imports the database library. An upgrade of the library can then force a change in the business rules. Now suppose the domain only declares an interface for what it needs. That interface is called a port. The adapter behind the port changes, and the rules do not. The rules still change often, but only for business reasons.

The same logic decides which side of a border translates. The side that depends on the other side translates. So a change on the other side stops at the translation.

When it stops holding

In a feature whose rules need no protection from the storage, ports and adapters add files and protect nothing. The order service's reference feature has one simple rule, and it uses a Spring Data repository directly. The ports and adapters are kept for the order feature, where the rules are many.

See the sections The direction of the dependencies and The simple level: the reference feature.

Reads and writes have different shapes#

What it says

A write must protect rules, so it works on one aggregate at a time. A read must show what a person needs, and that often comes from many aggregates. When the two shapes differ, give each one its own model.

Why it holds

An aggregate is shaped by its rules, not by a screen. A list of orders with customer names and stock levels needs data from several owners. To load every aggregate for that list is slow. It also pulls the aggregates toward the shape of the screen.

A model for reading is built for one question, and it never decides anything. So it may be a little late, joined and copied, and nothing breaks.

When it stops holding

When the screen shows one aggregate, the aggregate is already the right shape. A second model then costs code, storage and delay, and it buys nothing.

A model for reading also must not decide a command. It may be out of date at exactly the moment that matters. See the section One model for reads and writes: CQRS or not.

A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order#

What it says

A call or a message to another process can fail, can be slow, or can arrive more than once. Messages can also arrive in a different order from the order they were sent in. Each of these happens in production. So every remote call needs a timeout and a decision about retries. And every receiver must handle a duplicate and a late message.

Why it holds

The caller cannot tell a lost request from a lost answer. In both cases it sees nothing. If it retries, the receiver may process the request twice. If it does not retry, the request may be lost.

A message broker has the same choice, and most brokers deliver a message at least once. So the receiver must make a duplicate harmless, because the network cannot. A receiver that does this is called idempotent. To ignore a late message, compare a version or a sequence from one writer. The clocks of two machines are never exactly the same.

When it stops holding

A direct method call between two modules of one deployment, in the same transaction, does not fail in these ways. It needs no timeout and no idempotency key.

But an event between two modules that goes through an outbox can still arrive twice, because the outbox sends again after a failure. So its listener must still be idempotent. See the chapters Calling other services and Consuming events: SQS and the inbox.

A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability#

What it says

When a request waits for the answer of another service, the request works only while that service works. Each call adds its own chance of failure. So call another service only when you need its answer now.

Why it holds

Suppose each service works 99.9 percent of the time. A request that needs four of them works about 99.6 percent of the time. This is true for a chain of calls, and for four calls made in parallel. The slowest service also sets the speed of the request.

A message does not need the receiver to work at the moment it is sent. The receiver handles it when it can, and the sender is not blocked.

When it stops holding

Some answers are needed now. The order service must know that the stock is held before it accepts an order. Then a call is the right choice, and a timeout, a retry and a circuit breaker limit the damage.

A message has a cost too. The sender does not know when the work is done, or whether it succeeded. See the section Why the order service calls the stock service.

Capacity is finite, so refuse early#

What it says

Every service can do only a limited amount of work at once. When more work arrives, refuse some of it quickly. That is better than accepting everything and failing slowly. Retries are more work, so they must wait longer each time, and then stop.

Why it holds

A request that waits holds a thread, a connection and memory. When requests arrive faster than they finish, the waiting grows until every request times out. Then the callers retry, and the load grows again. This is called a retry storm.

A limit, a timeout and a quick refusal keep the accepted requests fast. A circuit breaker applies the same logic to a dependency that fails. It stops the calls for a while, so the dependency can recover. See the section Retry and circuit breaker: what each one is for.

When it stops holding

Work that can wait, such as a message in a queue, does not need to be refused. The queue holds the peak, and the consumer works at its own speed. The cost is delay. A queue that grows without a limit also hides the problem, so watch how old its oldest message is.

A published contract is hard to take back#

What it says

When another team depends on your API or your event, you cannot change it alone. You can add optional things that a tolerant reader ignores. To remove or rename anything, you run the old form and the new form together, until every consumer has moved.

Why it holds

You do not deploy the consumers, and you often do not know all of them. A change that breaks the contract breaks someone at a time that you do not choose. Even an addition can break a consumer. A new required field is one example. A new value in a list that the consumer does not expect is another.

So keep the published contract small, and keep it apart from your internal model. The internal model can then change every day, and only a mapper changes with it. The safe way to change a contract is called expand and contract. First add the new form, then move every consumer, then remove the old form.

When it stops holding

Between modules that always deploy together, a rename in the code is a refactoring, and the compiler finds every use. But stored documents and messages in a queue are not code. Old and new versions of the service read them during a deployment. So they still need expand and contract. See the principle Data outlives the code that wrote it. See also the sections Domain events and integration events and The mapper decides what leaves.

You can fix only what you can see#

What it says

When work crosses threads or processes, every step must write its log lines with a shared ID. Then a person can follow one request, one message or one order through every service. And the team must measure what the customer feels, such as failed orders, not only how busy the machines are.

Why it holds

A service handles many requests at the same time, so their log lines are mixed together. Across services, each process logs only its own part. Without a shared ID, an incident means matching timestamps across many log files.

So the design includes a trace ID on every request, and an ID on every message. An alert on what the customer feels says that something is wrong before anyone reads a log. These are not extras for later. See the section Keeping event flows traceable.

When it stops holding

A small internal tool, used by a few people who report a problem at once, needs little of this. A phone call costs less than the tracing. See the Atlas chapter Can you see it?.

Check permissions where a user's request enters#

What it says
