A permission belongs to a caller. So check it where the caller's request enters the service, for example in the controller. That place is called an entry point. The code behind it runs for a caller who was already checked, or for the service itself.

Why it holds

Only an entry point knows who the caller is. A message listener, a scheduled job and another feature have no user. A check deep inside the service would refuse work that the service itself decided to do. A developer then writes a helper that pretends to be a user, and the check protects nothing.

A rule about one record, such as "only a note of this order", needs the record. So it is a rule of the domain, and the entry point passes the caller's ID in as a plain value. Between services, each service sends a token of its own. The stock service trusts the order service, not every user.

When it stops holding

A service with several entry points for users, such as REST and GraphQL, may check the permission on the use case instead. Then each new entry point is protected without a new line. The cost is that listeners and jobs need use cases of their own, which carry no check. See the sections Choosing the place by the shape of the service and Why an identity-swapping helper is a warning sign.

Systems copy the teams that build them#

What it says

The borders of a system form where the teams that build it talk least. Melvin Conway described this in 1968, and it is called Conway's law.

Why it holds

Inside a team, a change across two modules is a conversation at one desk. Across two teams, it is a meeting, a ticket and a wait. People avoid the expensive path, so code grows where talking is cheap.

If two teams share one context, the context soon has two models in one place. If one team owns parts of five contexts, the borders between the five contexts blur. So the borders of the teams and the borders of the contexts should match.

When it stops holding

A small company with one team can own several contexts well. The borders then come from the language, not from the teams, and rules in the build hold them.

The law describes a pressure, not a rule. A team can work against it, but it pays for that every day. See the Atlas chapter You ship your org chart.

Every boundary has a price#

What it says

Each boundary has a running cost, which you pay every day, whether it helps or not. A layer costs files. An aggregate costs a rule about transactions. A service costs a network, a pipeline, people who answer alerts at night, and a contract. Draw a boundary only where it gives more than it costs.

Why it holds

The running cost comes in builds, in deployments and in the work to run the system. The return comes only when a part must scale, fail or ship alone, or when a rule needs the protection.

A boundary that no rule needs, and that no part needs alone, is only cost. See the section Three levels in one service.

When it stops holding

Some boundaries cost almost nothing. A package-private class, or an architecture rule in the build, adds no network and no pipeline. Then the test is not needed. Draw the boundary whenever it helps a reader.

Prefer the decision you can undo#

What it says

When you are not sure, choose the option that is cheap to change later. Learn first. Then make the expensive decision with what you learned.

Why it holds

At the start of a project, you know least about the business. A wrong border between modules costs a refactoring. A wrong border between services costs a data migration, two contracts and two pipelines.

So start with the form that you can undo, such as a module. Move to the expensive form, such as a service, when you have evidence that you need it. Feature flags, the strangler pattern and parallel runs follow the same logic.

When it stops holding

Sometimes the cheap form is not cheap to leave. Stefan Tilkov argued in 2015 that a monolith teaches habits, such as shared tables and direct calls, that make a later split harder. When the borders are already known, and the team can run services, it can cost less to start with them.

Some borders are also expensive to add later, whatever you choose first. A border around personal data or payment data is hard to add once code depends on the open form. Draw those borders early, even before they pay. See the Atlas chapter The consultant who said microservices.

A new question in four steps#

Most questions in a design meeting are new in some small way. These four steps turn a new question into an answer that you can explain.

  1. Say the question as a choice between two options.
  2. Find the rule or the data that the question is about. Ask who writes it, and when it must be true.
  3. Find the principle that decides it. Most questions need one principle. A hard question needs two principles that pull in different directions.
  4. Check when that principle stops holding. If your case is one of those cases, the answer changes.

Here is an example. Should the stock level be inside the order aggregate? The stock service writes the stock level. So the principle Every fact has one writer says no. Then ask whether "never sell more than the stock" must be true now. It must, so the stock service checks it now, in its own transaction, and holds the products. The order keeps only the answer.

One part may be true a little later. That part is the link between the hold and the placed order. The stock service keeps the hold until it sees the event OrderPlacedV1, or it releases the hold after a timeout.

Next · Reasoning from first principles33Field questions: the model24 min

Field questions: the model#

Reasoning from first principles · Chapter 33· 24 min read

These are the questions that teams ask about the inside of one service built with Domain-Driven Design (DDD). They are about aggregates, entities, value objects, rules, repositories and events. Each answer starts with what you would say in a meeting. Then it names the principle that decides it, shows where the order service does it, and says when the answer changes.

What an aggregate is#

What qualifies a group of objects as an aggregate?
#
A rule that must be true after every change, and the data that the rule needs. That data, saved in one transaction, is the aggregate.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later and A transaction protects one place.

An aggregate is not a group of things that belong together in a diagram. It is the data that one rule must check and save in one step. "An order ships only when every line is picked" needs the status and every line at the same moment. So the status and the lines are one aggregate.

A rule of that kind is called an invariant. If a rule may be true a little later, it does not pull data into the aggregate. That data can be in another aggregate, and an event or a later check closes the gap.

Where it shows

See the sections What an aggregate is for and Art or science? Questions you can apply. The second section gives seven questions and four tests.

When the answer changes

A table design or a class diagram does not show an aggregate. Two objects joined by a foreign key may be two aggregates. Only the rules decide.

Should every entity be part of an aggregate?
#
Yes. Every entity belongs to exactly one aggregate. Many aggregates hold only one entity, the root, and that is normal.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and The root guards the rule.

Every piece of data needs one owner that writes it and checks its rules. In the model, that owner is an aggregate. An entity outside every aggregate has no root to guard it, so any code may change it.

An aggregate with one entity is common. A note in the order service is one entity, and it is also the root of its own aggregate. The word aggregate does not mean "several objects". It means "the unit that one rule protects".

Where it shows

The note is an aggregate of one entity. See the section Why order and note are separate aggregates.

When the answer changes

A feature with no rules has no aggregates at all. The reference feature of the order service stores lookup values as plain records. See the section The simple level: the reference feature.

Can I update one entity inside an aggregate without going through the root?
#
Not in the domain. Load the root and call its method. The root checks the rules that cover its parts.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule.

A rule such as "a finished order cannot change" covers every line of the order. Only the root sees the status and the lines together. If code changes a line directly, it skips that check. Then the rule holds only while every caller remembers it.

The root also records the event of the change. A direct update changes the data, and no other part of the system hears about it.

Where it shows

The order picks a line through order.pickLine(lineId, clock), and the methods of the line are package-private. See the section The root is the only way in.

When the answer changes

A data migration or a repair of broken data may write the stored form directly. It must still leave data that the root would accept. If ordinary features keep wanting to change the inner entity alone, that entity is probably an aggregate of its own.

Can two aggregates share one entity?
#
No. Each aggregate refers to the other one by its ID, or keeps its own copy of the values that it needs.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and The root guards the rule.

A shared entity has two roots that may change it. Each root guards its own rules, and each can break the rules of the other root. A save of one aggregate would also change the data of the other aggregate, outside its version.

So one aggregate owns the entity. Another aggregate that needs it holds the ID, or a copy of the few values that it uses.

Where it shows

A note holds the order's ID as text, and it never reaches the order. See the section Refer to another aggregate by its ID.

When the answer changes

A copy of a value is not a shared entity. An order keeps the customer's contact as a value object. If the customer later changes an e-mail address, the order keeps the old one. That is usually what the business wants.

Which entity of an aggregate is the root?
#
The one that the business names, and that outside code finds by its ID. Nobody refers to an order line without its order.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule.

The root is the only way in, so it must be the object that callers can reach. Callers reach an object by an ID that they know. A customer knows an order number. Nobody outside the order knows a line ID first.

The root must also see all the data of the rules. So the root is the object at the top of those rules, and the other entities hang below it.

Where it shows

See the section The order aggregate, piece by piece.

When the answer changes

If outside code often needs to find an inner entity by its own ID, that entity may be the root of a separate aggregate. Check whether a rule really needs it inside.

The size of an aggregate#

How big should an aggregate be?
#
As small as its "now" rules allow. Each extra piece slows every change, and adds conflicts between users.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later and Every boundary has a price.

Every change loads and saves the whole aggregate. So each extra piece makes every change slower, and makes conflicts between users more likely. That cost comes on every change.

The cost buys something only for the rules that must be true now. So ask what each change must check, not what belongs to the order in a diagram.

Where it shows

The order holds at most 50 lines and its last payment. Its notes are outside. See the section The order aggregate, piece by piece.

When the answer changes

Too small is also wrong. If every change must update two aggregates together, they are one aggregate. See the section Signs of an aggregate that is too small.

Users often get a 409 conflict when they change one kind of aggregate. What does that tell you?
#
The aggregate is probably too big. Unrelated changes share one version, so they make each other fail.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later and A transaction protects one place.

An aggregate has one version for all its parts. Two saves of the same version conflict, and the second one fails. That is correct when both changes touch the same rule.

It is wrong when the two changes have no rule in common. A note and a picked line need not be consistent with each other now. So they should not share a version.

Where it shows

See the section Signs of an aggregate that is too big. The platform answers every conflict with 409.

When the answer changes

A conflict between a cancel and a ship of the same order is the aggregate doing its job. Do not split it to remove that conflict.

Can I change the boundary of an aggregate after the service is in production?
#
Yes. Move the data with a migration, and keep each rule with a count or an event. It costs a migration, not a rewrite.
Why

Decided by Prefer the decision you can undo and Data outlives the code that wrote it.

A boundary inside one service is a decision that you can undo. The aggregates share one database and one deployment. So a split or a merge changes classes, one migration and some tests.

The stored documents keep their old shape until the migration moves them. So the migration is part of the change, and it runs before the new code takes traffic.

A rule that moves out of the aggregate gets a new home, such as a domain service that takes a count. That rule gets new tests. The rules that stay keep their tests.

Where it shows

See the section How to split or merge an aggregate.

When the answer changes

The cost rises when the boundary is published. If another service stores the aggregate's ID or receives its events, a split changes a contract too.

A small change loads the whole aggregate. Should I load only the part that I change?
#
No. Load the whole aggregate. The root can check its rules only when it sees all the data they need.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule and A transaction protects one place.

A partial load gives the root half of its data. A rule such as "a finished order cannot change" then checks a status that may not be loaded. And a save of half an aggregate may write over the other half.

One load and one save of the whole aggregate keep the check and the save in one step.

Where it shows

Each use case that changes an existing order starts with orders.get(id), which loads the whole order. See the section The steps of a use case.

When the answer changes

If most changes need only a small part of the aggregate, the aggregate is too big. Fix the boundary, not the load.

Between aggregates#

Why does an aggregate refer to another aggregate by its ID, and not by an object reference?
#
An object reference lets code load, change and save two aggregates as one. An ID keeps each aggregate loaded and saved on its own.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and A transaction protects one place.

With an object reference, a note could reach its order and change it. The note would then be a second writer of the order. A save of the note might also save the order, in the same transaction.

An ID gives no such path. To change the order, code must ask the order's own feature. So the order keeps one writer and one version.

Where it shows

See the section Refer to another aggregate by its ID.

When the answer changes

Inside one aggregate, the root holds its entities as objects. The rule applies only between aggregates.

Should a reference to another aggregate's ID have its own type?
#
In the strict full style, yes, such as OrderRef. The order service keeps such IDs as text, and records that choice.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price.

A type of its own gives a check at compile time. The note's order ID can then never be passed where another ID belongs.

Plain text also keeps the note free of the order's classes, so the type adds no independence. It costs a class and a conversion, for a value that the note only stores and compares. So the order service keeps text. The order feature, which owns the ID, checks it when a note is added. A bad ID gets the order feature's own 400, and an unknown one gets its 404.

Where it shows

See the section A type for a foreign ID, or plain text.

When the answer changes

Add a type when the ID takes part in a rule, or when a method takes two IDs that could be swapped.

Where does a rule go that needs data from two aggregates?
#
In a domain service named after the rule. The use case gives it the data, often only a number.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule and Now, or a little later.

Each root guards only its own data. A rule that needs two aggregates cannot be in one root, because that root does not see the other data.

A domain service checks the rule with the values that it receives. It loads nothing itself. So it stays plain code that a test calls with plain values.

Where it shows

ShippingPolicy.assertCanShip(order, notesNeedingAction) checks that no note needs action. See the section Worked example: no shipping while a note needs action.

When the answer changes

When a rule needs only one aggregate's data, it belongs in that aggregate. Prefer the aggregate whenever its own data is enough.

A domain service checks the rule only at one moment. Do not add a separate lock to make it hold longer. If the rule must hold at every moment, make both changes write the same document. That is a lock through the version that already exists, and it costs the conflicts of a bigger aggregate.

May one transaction change two aggregates?
#
Usually not. Vernon (2011) states the rule and names exceptions. The order service uses one, a new order with its first notes.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place and Now, or a little later.

A transaction that changes two aggregates holds both of them at once. It is larger and slower, and it can conflict with every writer of either aggregate. Vaughn Vernon gives the rule in Part I of his essays Effective Aggregate Design (2011). One transaction changes one aggregate, and the other aggregates follow by events.

In Part II, Vernon also names reasons to break the rule. One reason is the convenience of the user interface. It is safe when creating several new aggregates together means the same as creating them one at a time. New aggregates have no other writers, so they cannot conflict.

Where it shows

See the sections One aggregate per transaction, and the order with its notes and One request that saves the order and its first notes.

When the answer changes

Use one transaction when one user action creates new aggregates together. Use an event when the transaction would change an existing aggregate of another feature. That transaction would conflict with the writers of that aggregate.

One aggregate changes, and another aggregate must react. How does the second one learn about it?
#
Through a domain event. The first aggregate commits. Then a listener changes the second aggregate in its own transaction.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later and A transaction protects one place.

The reaction may be true a little later, so it does not need the first transaction. Each aggregate keeps its own transaction, its own version and its own conflicts.

With @ApplicationModuleListener, Spring Modulith stores a row for the event with the first change. So the reaction is not lost if the service stops between the two steps. A plain @EventListener stores nothing, and it runs inside the first transaction.

Where it shows

See the sections One aggregate per transaction, and the order with its notes and Reacting inside the service.

When the answer changes

If the user must see both changes as one action, and both aggregates are new, one transaction may be the better choice.

An aggregate that others refer to is closed or removed. What happens to the aggregates that hold its ID?
#
The owner of each aggregate decides, after an event. Nothing deletes another aggregate in the same transaction.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and Now, or a little later.

Each aggregate has one writer, its own feature. So the order feature must not delete or change notes. The note feature reacts to the order's event with its own rules.

Most such reactions may happen a little later. A note on a cancelled order can stay, or be closed by a handler.

Where it shows

The order service never deletes orders, so a note's order always exists. See the table in the section What holds between two aggregates, and what does not.

When the answer changes

A legal duty to erase personal data is different. Then each owner must erase its own data, and the event must reach every owner.

Entities, value objects and IDs#

How do I decide between an entity and a value object?
#
Ask whether anyone must name it as it changes. A picked line is an entity. A replaced payment is a value object.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule.

An entity changes in place, so the root must find it to change it. That is why an entity has an ID. The root changes a line by its line ID, and checks its rules first.

A value object never changes in place. The root replaces it with a new value, so it needs no ID. A payment is replaced by a later payment.

Where it shows

See the section Inside the aggregate: entities and value objects.

When the answer changes

The same thing can be a value in one place and an entity in another. The order keeps the customer's contact as a value object. A shop that tracks each delivery address over time may make the address an entity.

Can a value object change after it is created?
#
No. A change is a new value that replaces the old one. So no code can change a value behind the root's back.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule.

A value object is often handed to callers, for example in a view. If it could change, a caller could change the aggregate's data without the root. Then the root's rules would not run.

A value that cannot change can be shared freely. The only way to change the aggregate is still a method of the root.

Where it shows

The value objects of the order service are Java records, and their fields cannot be reassigned. See the section Value objects as records.

When the answer changes

A record that holds a list is not fully fixed. The list inside can still change, so copy it in the compact constructor.

Is a separate type for each ID worth the extra classes?
#
For the core feature, yes. The compiler then refuses a line ID where an order ID belongs.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different.

A typed ID costs one small class for each aggregate and entity. In the order, which holds the most important rules, that effort buys a check on every call. An order ID passed where a line ID belongs does not compile.

It also checks the format once, when the ID is created. So every OrderId in the service is valid.

Where it shows

See the sections Typed IDs inside the aggregate and Typed IDs: Identifier and its subclasses.

When the answer changes

In the light style, the note keeps its IDs as text. NoteService.resolveAction takes two IDs, the order ID and the note ID. If a caller swaps them, the note is not found, and 404 is a correct answer. Add a type when a swap could change the wrong note.

Should every string and number in the model be a value object?
#
No. Make a value object when the value has a rule or a format, such as money. Text with no rule stays text.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and The root guards the rule.

A value object puts the rule of a value in one place. Money refuses an amount with too many decimal places, on every path that builds it. That check pays for its class.

A free text, such as the text of a note, has only a length limit. A guard in the entity checks it. A class around it adds a file and protects nothing more.

Where it shows

See the sections Money: a currency, and no silent rounding and Guard: checks that name the field.

When the answer changes

Make a value object when the same check appears in two places. That is the sign that the value has a rule of its own.

The light style keeps some text with a format as text. Note.category must match a pattern. It stays a String, and Note.create checks it with a guard.

The request is already validated. Why does the value object check the same value again?
#
The request check helps the client. The value object's check protects every other path in, such as a message, a migration or another feature.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule and Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

A request check lists every bad field at once, so the client can fix them all. But only one path uses that request. A message, a test, a migration or another feature builds the same value without it.

The value object is the one place that every path passes. So its check is the one that counts. It also needs no web library, so the domain stays plain Java.

Where it shows

See the sections Value objects as records and Guard: checks that name the field.

When the answer changes

A check that needs stored data, such as "the code is an active lookup value", cannot be in the value object. It goes into the service that owns the data.

Where the rules go#

What is the difference between a domain service and an application service?
#
A domain service holds domain logic that fits no single entity or value object. An application service runs a use case's steps.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and The root guards the rule.

Eric Evans (2003) defines a domain service as domain logic that is not the job of one entity or value object. In this book, that is almost always a rule across aggregates, such as ShippingPolicy. A domain service uses only domain types.

An application service loads, calls other services, saves, publishes and audits. It holds no rule. Its steps depend on storage and on other services, so they stay outside the domain, and the domain depends on none of them.

Where it shows

See the sections Three places for a rule and Name a domain service after its rule.

When the answer changes

The simple level has no domain. Its one rule, "a code must be an active lookup value", is in the application service as a recorded choice.

Is an anaemic model always wrong?
#
No. A feature with no rules needs no model. The anaemic model is wrong when entities exist, but their rules are elsewhere.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different and The root guards the rule.

Martin Fowler (2002) describes a transaction script as a fair choice for simple logic. A transaction script is one procedure for each request, with no domain model.

Fowler (2003) calls the anaemic domain model an anti-pattern. It has the classes and the mapping of a domain model, but its rules are in services. So it has the cost of a model, and none of its protection.

The two statements agree. Spend the careful model where the business is different and the rules are many. A feature with a few simple rules gets the light style in the order service, an entity with its own methods.

Where it shows

See the sections What an anaemic model looks like, and what goes wrong and An anaemic model with an outbox, compared fairly.

When the answer changes

When a feature without a model gains a real rule, give it an entity with methods. The same check in two places is the sign.

Can an aggregate call another service, or a repository, inside one of its methods?
#
No. The use case makes the call and passes the answer in. The aggregate decides what the answer means.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

A call from the model would make the domain depend on a client or on storage. It would also hide a slow call that can fail inside a rule, and perhaps inside a transaction.

So the use case asks the stock service first. Order.place receives a StockAvailability value, and it refuses an order when a product is not available.

Where it shows

See the sections A decision from another service, a rule in the domain and Repositories in the domain, other services in the application.

When the answer changes

The domain may declare the repository as a port, because storage is part of the model. But only the use case calls it.

Can domain code read the current time?
#
Not from the system clock. Each method that needs the time receives a Clock, so a test can fix it.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

The system clock is a detail of the machine. A rule that calls Instant.now() gives a different result on every run, so no test can check it at an exact time.

A Clock passed in keeps the rule independent of that detail. Tests pass a fixed clock, and production passes the real one. The rule never changes because the source of the time changed.

Where it shows

See the section The time comes from an injected Clock.

When the answer changes

No common case changes this answer. The platform states a wider rule in the comment on its Clock bean. No code of the service calls Instant.now(), not only the domain.

Should the aggregate check who the user is, and what they may do?
#
No. Permissions are checked where a user's request enters. The aggregate checks only rules about one record, with the actor's ID passed in.
Why

Decided by Check permissions where a user's request enters and The root guards the rule.

Only an entry point knows who the caller is. A message listener, a scheduled job and another feature have no user. If the aggregate checked permissions, it would refuse work that the service itself decided to do.

A rule about one record is different, because it needs the record. "Only a note of this order" is checked by the note itself, and a note of another order gets 404. "The agent who wrote a note may not resolve it" receives the actor's ID as text.

Where it shows

Note.requireBelongsTo(orderId) and Note.resolveAction(actorId, clock) never read the security context. See the section Rules about one record: in the domain, with the actor passed in. For where the check goes, see the section Choosing the place by the shape of the service.

When the answer changes

A service with several entry points for users may check the permission on the use case instead. The aggregate still checks only its rules about one record.

Repositories and storage#

Do I need a repository for each entity?
#
No. One repository for each aggregate, for its root. Inner entities are loaded and saved with their root.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule and Every fact has one writer.

A repository for an inner entity is a way around the root. Code could load a line, change it and save it, and the order would never know.

One repository for each aggregate makes the root the only door. It also makes the aggregate the unit that is stored, with one version.

Where it shows

OrderRepository stores orders, and there is no repository for lines. See the section The repository port.

When the answer changes

Writes that store no aggregate, such as the inbox key or the audit record, need no repository. The order service uses MongoTemplate for them.

Is a generic repository, which loads any type or returns an open query, a good idea?
#
In the full style, no. It lets code reach past the root. Each aggregate gets one port with only the queries it needs.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule.

A query that callers can extend can load an inner entity, or a part of an aggregate. Code can then change data that the root never sees.

A port with named methods states what the feature may do. A reader sees every way in.

Where it shows

The platform's Repository is generic in its types, but each feature has its own port. A generic repository needs the approval of the design group. See the section The allowed building blocks, and what needs approval.

When the answer changes

A base class that implements findById and save for every adapter is fine. It only saves typing, and each port stays specific.

The light-style note uses NoteRepository, a Spring Data repository with generic methods. The note is one entity with few rules, so there is little to reach past.

My repository has a query method for every screen. Is that wrong?
#
A few queries are fine. Many screen-shaped queries show that the reads want a model of their own.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes.

A repository loads whole aggregates for changes. A query that returns orders by status, a page at a time, still returns aggregates. That is normal.

A query that joins data from other aggregates, or returns a few fields for one screen, serves a read. Such queries grow with every screen, and they bend the repository toward the screens.

Where it shows

OrderRepository has two list queries, and both return orders. See the sections The repository port and One model for reads and writes: CQRS or not.

When the answer changes

When a read needs data from several aggregates at once, add a read model. Keep the repository for the writes.

Should an aggregate be one document, or one document for each entity?
#
In a document database, one document for each aggregate. One write then saves the whole aggregate, with one version.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place.

One read returns the whole aggregate, with no join. One version on the document covers all of it. A write of one document is atomic, so the order, its lines and its last payment are never stored half changed.

A document for each entity would need several reads to load one order. It would also need a version check across several documents.

Where it shows

See the sections One aggregate, one document and Embed the lines, keep the notes apart.

When the answer changes

In a relational database, an aggregate is usually several tables, saved in one transaction. The rule is the same. The aggregate is still loaded and saved as one unit.

Does every aggregate need a version?
#
Yes, if it can change. Without one, two edits of the same copy both succeed, and one of them is lost without a word.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later.

Two users load the same order. Each one changes it and saves. The root checked its rules on each copy, but the stored state changed between that check and the second save. Without a version, the second save writes over the first.

A version makes the second save fail. The user then reloads, and the root checks the rules against the real state. This is called optimistic locking.

Where it shows

See the sections Optimistic locking with @Version and One optimistic-lock test for each aggregate.

When the answer changes

Data that the service never changes needs no version. The lookup values of the reference feature are an example. They are not an aggregate, and only a seed migration changes them.

Should the domain class carry the storage annotations, or should a separate document class hold them?
#
In the full style, a separate document class and a mapper. In the light style, the entity is the document.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and Every boundary has a price.

A separate document class keeps the domain free of the storage library. The model can then use types that storage cannot hold as they are, such as typed IDs.

In the light style, the entity itself is stored, with its annotations. That is enough while the stored fields and the model's fields are the same. A separate class would then only copy each field, and protect nothing.

Where it shows

See the sections The full style: a document class and The light style: the note is its own document.

When the answer changes

Give a light feature a document class when storage starts to force changes on the model. A field kept only for the database, or a constructor that only the database needs, is the warning. Remove the document class when every line of the mapper copies a field to a field of the same name.

Domain events#

Who records a domain event, the aggregate or the use case?
#
The aggregate, inside the method that changes the state. The use case only publishes what the aggregate recorded.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule.

If the use case adds the event, each use case that ships must remember it. A new use case can forget it, and no test fails.

In the aggregate, the change and its event are one method. Every path that ships an order also records OrderShipped.

Where it shows

See the section Domain events: collected by the aggregate.

When the answer changes

A record of a step of the use case, and not of a change of the model, comes from the use case. The audit record is an example, and it is not a domain event.

Does every change of state need a domain event?
#
In the order service, yes. Each method that changes an order records one, and an internal event costs one small record class.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and The root guards the rule.

An internal domain event has a small, fixed cost. It is one record class, and it is not a contract, so it may change with the model. Because the method that changes the state records it, no path can forget it.

The gain is possible, not certain. A new listener inside the service can react to the change, and the model does not change. If no listener ever needs the event, it costs a class and nothing more.

Where it shows

LinePicked is recorded, although no other service receives it. See the table in the section Domain events: collected by the aggregate.

When the answer changes

A change with no business meaning, such as an internal counter, needs no event. A feature at the simple level has no events, because it has no business changes.

How much DDD#

Should every feature of a service use the full DDD model?
#
No. Give each feature the least DDD that still protects its rules. That is the full, light or simple level.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different and Every boundary has a price.

The order has the most rules of the service, and they are the hardest to get right. Its stored shape also differs from its model, and it calls another service. So the order service chose the full model there, with an aggregate root, a typed ID, a document class, a mapper and a port.

A lookup list works the same way in every shop. It has no state changes and one rule, that a stored code must be an active lookup value. The same five files would protect nothing, and the time would be missing from the order. See the section The simple level: the reference feature.

Where it shows

See the sections Three levels in one service and Choosing the level for each feature.

When the answer changes

A level is not chosen forever. A feature moves up when storage starts to force changes on its model. It also moves up when it gains a rule across aggregates, or a call to another service. The move is one change, with its tests, so starting low costs little. See the section The sign that a feature needs the next level.

Testing the model#

How should a rule of an aggregate be tested?
#
With a plain unit test. Build the aggregate, call its method, check the state and the events. Use a fixed clock and no mocks.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

The domain depends on nothing. So its test needs nothing either. Each test runs in milliseconds, and it reads like a list of the rules.

A test of a rule that needs mocks of repositories is a warning. The rule is probably in a service, and not in the aggregate.

Where it shows

See the sections Testing the model and Domain tests: plain JUnit, no Spring, no mocks.

When the answer changes

Optimistic locking needs a real database, because the version check happens there. That one test for each aggregate is an integration test.

Next · Reasoning from first principles34Field questions: boundaries28 min

Field questions: boundaries#

Reasoning from first principles · Chapter 34· 28 min read

These questions are about borders. Some borders are in the business, such as subdomains and bounded contexts. Others are in the code, such as layers, features and modules. Each answer starts with what you would say in a meeting. Then it names the principle that decides it, shows where the order service has the case, and says when the answer changes.

Domains and subdomains#

What makes a subdomain core, and not only important?
#
Customers choose you for it. It makes you different from competitors. Payments are critical, but they are rarely core.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different.

In Domain-Driven Design (DDD), the label "core" decides where the best people and the most careful modelling go. That effort pays only where it makes the business different. A part can be critical and still be the same in every shop, such as taking a card payment.

A classification with no generic or supporting entries has stopped working. If everything is core, the extra effort has no target.

Where it shows

The order service treats the order as the core of the shop, and gives it the full level. See the section Choosing the level for each feature. For the three kinds of subdomain, see the Atlas chapter Problem space, solution space. Whether a core subdomain must also be complex is still argued. See the question A rule is simple, but it is the reason customers choose us.

When the answer changes

The answer changes when the market changes. A part that was generic can become the reason customers come, and then it deserves core treatment. The cost of a late change is a rewrite of code that was built cheaply.

Still arguedA rule is simple, but it is the reason customers choose us. Is it core or supporting?
#
Writers disagree. This book treats it as core work, because a small rule that wins customers is easy to lose. That is a choice.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different.

Vlad Khononov, in Learning Domain-Driven Design (2021), defines core strictly. A core subdomain is both complex and different from competitors, so it is hard to copy. A simple rule that differs is then a supporting subdomain that happens to matter. This side uses the principle to spend design effort where the business is different. A simple rule needs little modelling, even there.

Nick Tune draws a softer line. In 2020 he published the Core Domain Chart with the DDD-Crew. The chart places each subdomain by its complexity and by how much it makes the business different. His patterns for the chart count a simple rule that makes you different as core. He calls it a short-term core, because rivals can copy it. He still said, in a talk at DDD Europe in February 2020, that a core domain needs some complexity too.

The chart and its patterns came later than the first books on DDD. Both sides agree on the purpose. The best people work on what wins customers.

Where it shows

The order service does not have such a rule. For the argument in full, see the Atlas chapter Problem space, solution space.

When the answer changes

The strict definition is safer when a team calls everything core. The softer definition is safer when one small rule is the whole business. Choose by the danger that your team faces.

Should we build a generic subdomain ourselves, such as e-mail sending or authentication?
#
No. Buy it, or use an open-source product. Spend your own effort where you differ from competitors.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different.

A generic subdomain works the same in every company. Several good products already solve it. Your own code for it must still be written, tested and kept up to date. And it wins no customer.

The common reason to build is "our needs are special". In a generic subdomain, the needs are rarely special. The cost of building is certain, and the gain is not.

Where it shows

The order service builds none of these parts. It uses a token issuer for identity, and Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) for publishing events. See the Atlas chapter Problem space, solution space.

When the answer changes

Build it when no product fits a rule that makes you different. Then the part was not generic. Build it also when the product's cost or limits are worse than your own code. Write down that reason, because it will be questioned.

Once we classify our subdomains, is the classification fixed?
#
No. Revisit it when the market, a vendor or the strategy changes. A chart from three years ago describes another company.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different and Prefer the decision you can undo.

The classification decides where effort goes. Effort pays only while the classification is true. A supporting subdomain can become the business, and a core one can become a product that anyone can buy.

Reviewing catches a wrong classification before much code is built on it. So make the classification early, and expect to change it.

Where it shows

The order service has no such change yet. For the trap of classifying once, see the Atlas chapter Problem space, solution space.

When the answer changes

A stable market changes rarely, so a yearly review is enough there. The cost of never reviewing is effort spent on yesterday's core.

Is a subdomain the same thing as a bounded context?
#
No. A subdomain is a part of the business problem. A bounded context is a part of the solution, where one model holds.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border.

The business has subdomains whether or not software exists. A bounded context is drawn by the team, where the meaning of the words changes. The two often match one to one, and that is a good sign.

They can also differ. One subdomain may need two contexts, because two groups of users mean different things by the same word. Two small subdomains may share one context, because they share one language.

Where it shows

The order service is one bounded context. It serves the ordering part of the shop. See the Atlas chapter Problem space, solution space.

When the answer changes

When a context serves two subdomains with different importance, check it again. The core part may need more care than the rest of the context allows.

Language and discovery#

Must the code use exactly the words of the business experts?
#
Yes, inside the model. Classes and methods use the experts' words, such as ship and cancel, never update or process.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border.

The words of the business inside one context are called the ubiquitous language. If the code uses other words, every conversation needs a translation. Each translation can lose a meaning, and the error then hides in the code.

A method named ship also tells the reader which rule applies. A method named update could do anything.

Where it shows

An order in the order service is placed, paid, shipped or cancelled, and its lines are picked. See the section What DDD is, in this book's words.

When the answer changes

Adapters and technical code use technical words, such as document and response. The rule is for the model. When the experts use two words for one thing, choose one, and record the choice.

Two teams use the same word with two meanings. Do we need two models?
#
Yes, if the rules differ. Inside one context, agree on one word. Across contexts, each side keeps its word, and an adapter translates.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border.

Two meanings with different rules cannot share one class without fields and checks that only one meaning needs. Each team would then change a class that the other team depends on.

A difference only in the name is not a border. "Client" and "customer" for the same person with the same rules need one word, not two models.

Where it shows

The order service has no case of one word with two meanings. It has the opposite case, two words for one thing. The stock service says sku, the order service says ProductCode, and the adapter translates. See the section The adapter: the anti-corruption layer. For a word with two meanings, see the Atlas chapter Drawing the borders.

When the answer changes

In a small system that one team builds, two meanings can share one model for a while. The cost grows with each rule that one meaning adds and the other meaning must ignore.

Should the company keep one glossary of terms for all teams?
#
No. Keep one glossary for each bounded context. A company-wide glossary forces one meaning and hides real differences.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border.

A word may mean one thing in sales and another thing in the warehouse. A single glossary must choose one meaning. Then one team uses a definition that is wrong for its work, or the glossary becomes vague enough to fit both.

A glossary for each context can be exact. Where two contexts meet, a map shows how their words translate.

Where it shows

The book has no glossary for each context. For the language of a context, see the Atlas chapter Drawing the borders.

When the answer changes

The words of a published contract are shared across contexts by design. Those words belong to the contract, and the contract may keep its own glossary.

Can we design the domain model from the existing database schema?
#
No. A schema shows how data is stored, not what happens in the business. Start from the events and the words.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border and Spend design effort where the business is different.

Tables and foreign keys record the shape of the data. They do not record the rules, the states or the words that change meaning. A model copied from the schema has one class per table, and the rules are placed in services around it.

The borders of contexts are where words change meaning. A schema hides that, because one table often serves several meanings.

Where it shows

The order is an aggregate. Its model differs from its stored document, and a mapper connects the model and the document. See the section The mapper: from the aggregate to the document and back. For the trap, see the Atlas chapter The workshop with the orange stickies.

When the answer changes

For a feature with no rules about changing state, such as a lookup list, the stored shape is the whole model. Then the schema is a fine starting point.

Who must be in the room when we look for the borders of the business?
#
Experts from each business area, not only developers. Without them, the wall shows how the code works, not how the business works.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border.

Borders are where words change meaning. Only the people who use the words know where the meaning changes. Developers know the current code, which may already mix the meanings.

A workshop that maps business events on a wall is called event storming. Its value comes from the disagreements between the people in the room.

Where it shows

The order service starts after this work is done. See the Atlas chapter The workshop with the orange stickies.

When the answer changes

For a small change inside a known context, a developer and one expert are enough. A full workshop costs a day of many people, so keep it for new areas and unclear borders.

Bounded contexts#

How do we find the borders of bounded contexts?
#
Listen for words that change meaning, and look for rules that change together. A border goes where both point.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border and What changes together stays together.

A word that changes meaning shows where one model must stop. Rules that change for the same reason show what must stay inside one model. Each signal alone can mislead. Together they are strong.

The current database is a weak signal of business borders, because it reflects history. The org chart is also a weak signal of business borders. But it is a strong force on the borders of the code, because code grows where teams talk. So check that the two match.

Where it shows

Orders, stock and payments change for different reasons, so each one is a context of its own. See the section Do you need DDD? The conditions that make it worth its cost. For the method, see the Atlas chapter Drawing the borders.

When the answer changes

When the signals disagree, draw the border as a module first. Moving a module costs a refactoring. Moving a service costs a migration.

How big should a bounded context be?
#
As big as one consistent language, and no bigger. Lines of code and numbers of classes are the wrong measure.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border and What changes together stays together.

A context is defined by its model. Inside it, each word has one meaning. When a word starts to mean two things, the context is too big. When one change must cross two contexts that share every word, the contexts are too small. Code that changes together belongs in one context.

Where it shows

The order service is one bounded context. It holds two aggregates, the order and the note, and the note refers to its order by the order's ID. See the section Why order and note are separate aggregates.

When the answer changes

A context that is right in language can still be too big for one team to understand. Then split the work by subdomain inside it, or check whether the language has really stayed one.

Can one bounded context be split into several services?
#
Yes, along a smaller context that is nested inside it. Start with one service for each context. One model never covers two contexts.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border and Systems copy the teams that build them.

Sam Newman, in Building Microservices (2015), aligns services with bounded contexts. He suggests starting with large contexts, one service for each. A large context can hold smaller bounded contexts inside it. Each of those can later become a service of its own.

A nested context has its own language, so the split follows a real border. Whether to split also depends on how the teams are organised. A nested context that one team owns can stay inside the service. A nested context that a second team takes over is a good candidate for its own service.

Adam Gluck described Uber's domain-oriented microservices in 2020. There, a domain is a group of related services, not a bounded context. So that practice does not answer this question.

Where it shows

The order service is one deployable for one context. For the opposite question, several contexts in one deployable, see the question Can one deployable hold several bounded contexts?. For the argument, see the Atlas chapter Drawing the borders.

When the answer changes

A part of a context that must scale, fail or be secured alone may need its own deployable, even with no nested context. The cost is a contract inside one language, which both sides must keep in step.

Can one deployable hold several bounded contexts?
#
Yes, but only as separate modules with enforced borders. This is called a modular monolith. It is the cheapest form to change later.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Prefer the decision you can undo.

A context is a border in the language, not a deployment. Several contexts can share one deployable if each one is its own module, and no code crosses a border except through a published interface. Then a move to a separate service later is a move of one module.

A border between modules is also cheap to redraw. A border between services needs a data migration and a new contract.

Where it shows

The order service is one context. It has the same kind of border, between features inside one context, and the build checks it. See the section The rules as tests that fail the build. For one context split the other way, see the question Can one bounded context be split into several services?. For the argument, see the Atlas chapter The consultant who said microservices.

When the answer changes

A module border that no test checks wears away. Then the modules become one model again, and the later split is a rewrite.

Is a bounded context the same thing as a team?
#
No. A team may own several contexts. But one context should have one owning team, or its model splits in two.
Why

Decided by Systems copy the teams that build them.

Two teams that change one model talk less to each other than to their own members. Their parts of the model grow different. The context then has two languages inside it.

One team can keep several contexts apart, because the borders come from the language. The build rules then hold those borders.

Where it shows

For how teams and contexts match, see the Atlas chapter You ship your org chart.

When the answer changes

A context can be shared for a short, planned period, such as a joint project. The cost is a meeting for each change, so end the period on purpose. Two teams can also share a small part of the model on purpose. This is called a shared kernel. See the question Is a shared kernel, a small model that two contexts own together, ever a good idea?.

Should the company have one shared model of the customer, used by every team?
#
No. Each context models the customer that it needs. One context owns each fact, such as the address, and publishes it.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border and Every fact has one writer.

Sales, billing and support each need different facts about a customer, with different rules. One shared model must hold all of them, so it grows fields that most teams never use. Every team must then agree to every change.

Copies are safe when each fact has one owner. The other contexts keep copies of the facts that they need, in their own words.

Where it shows

The shop in this book has no context that owns customers. The order receives the customer's name and e-mail address with the request that places it, as its own value object. For a shared table with many writers, see the Atlas chapter Nobody owns the product table.

When the answer changes

A published contract for a customer, read by many teams, is fine. It is the owner's public form, not a model that every team must use inside.

Context maps and the borders between contexts#

Why draw a context map at all?
#
It shows, for each border, which side decides and how the other side copes. So you know whom to ask before a change.
Why

Decided by A word that changes meaning marks a border and Systems copy the teams that build them.

A drawing of the borders between contexts, with the relationship at each border, is called a context map. The side whose changes reach the other side is called upstream. The side that receives them is called downstream.

Each border needs a chosen relationship, such as a partnership, customer and supplier, a conformist, an anti-corruption layer or separate ways. Without a map, those choices happen by accident, often when the downstream side imports a class because it was there.

Where it shows

The order service is downstream of the stock service and the payment service, and upstream of every consumer of its events. See the Atlas chapter The map of treaties.

When the answer changes

A map is only useful while it is true. Redraw it when a team, a vendor or a border changes. An old map is worse than none, because people trust it.

Still arguedIs a shared kernel, a small model that two contexts own together, ever a good idea?
#
Writers disagree. This book avoids it, and shares contracts instead. That is a choice. If you use one, keep it tiny.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and What changes together stays together.

Eric Evans, in Domain-Driven Design (2003), lists the shared kernel as a valid pattern. It fits two teams that work closely and share a small, stable core. This side uses the principle that what changes together stays together. The principle that every fact has one writer allows this case, when the shared part is small.

Vaughn Vernon, in Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013), treats it as a last resort. In practice the kernel grows, the teams drift apart, and the kernel becomes the company-wide model that contexts exist to prevent. This side uses the principle that every fact has one writer. It doubts that the shared part stays small enough for that exception.

Both sides agree that it is safe only while it is small and owned together.

Where it shows

The shop's services share no business classes. They share contracts, and only technical base classes come from the platform. See the chapter Writing the platform library, and in it the section What never goes in the platform library.

When the answer changes

Two teams that always plan together and change the kernel rarely can use one. The cost is a meeting for every change, and a kernel that a reorganisation can orphan.

Should we translate the other side's model at the border, or use it as it is?
#
Translate when you do not control their model and its words differ from yours. Use it as it is when it already fits your rules.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and Every boundary has a price.

An anti-corruption layer translates the other model into your words, in one place. Your rules then depend on your model only. When the other side changes, the translation changes, and the rules stay as they are.

A translation also costs code and tests on every change. If the other model already says what you mean, the translation buys nothing. To use the other model as it is, on purpose, is called conformist. The danger is to conform by accident, by importing their classes because they were there.

Where it shows

The order service translates the stock service's answer in one adapter. Without it, a new status from the stock service would reach the order's rules. See the section The adapter: the anti-corruption layer.

When the answer changes

Stop conforming when their model disagrees with your rules, or when their changes keep forcing changes in your rules. Old systems and outside vendors almost always need the layer from the start.

In which package does the anti-corruption layer go?
#
In the adapter that implements your port. The other side's data transfer objects stay in that package, and only your types leave it.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

The port is written in your own types. The adapter behind it is the one class that knows both models. So the translation has one home, and a test can call it with no server.

If a use case reads the other side's records, their model has entered yours. Then the translation is spread over every use case that reads them.

Where it shows

In the order service, StockAdapter implements StockChecker, and the stock service's records stay in order.client.dto. See the section Their DTOs stay in the client package.

When the answer changes

For a light feature that calls nothing, there is no adapter, and no layer is needed. When a light feature starts to call another service, it gains a port and an adapter.

Many teams consume our service. Should we build a special integration for each of them?
#
No. Offer one documented interface for everyone. This is called an open host service. Each consumer adapts to it.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back.

A special integration for each consumer is a contract for each consumer. Each one must be kept, versioned and tested. The cost grows with every new team.

One documented interface is one contract. You change it with care, and every consumer reads the same description.

Where it shows

The order service publishes one API description and one schema for each event. See the section Why the service publishes contracts.

When the answer changes

One important consumer with needs that nobody else has may justify its own interface. That interface is another contract to keep, so add it only for a clear reason.

Should our API and events use the names and shapes of our internal model?
#
No. Publish a separate form made for the outside, and map to it. Then the inside can change every day.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

A form of your model that is documented for other teams is called a published language. It changes slowly, because other teams depend on it. Your internal model must change whenever the rules change.

If the internal model and the published form are the same classes, every internal refactoring becomes a change for every consumer. A mapper between them keeps the two speeds apart.

Where it shows

The order service maps domain events to integration events, and request records to domain values. See the sections The mapper decides what leaves and Publish as few events as needed.

When the answer changes

Between two modules that always deploy together, nothing is published. A shared class there is fine, and a mapper adds only work.

Should a consumer use the producer's classes for its events or its API?
#
No. Share a schema, not code. Keep your own copy of only the fields that you read.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

A producer's class carries every field that the producer has. If you compile against it, you depend on fields that you never read. A new version of the class then becomes your release too. A shared library of classes also ties every consumer to one language and one set of library versions.

A schema in a standard format avoids the shared artifact. Each team writes or generates its own classes from the part that it reads. A copy of the part that you use makes the dependency small and visible. A reader that ignores the rest is called a tolerant reader.

Where it shows

The order service publishes schemas, not classes. It keeps its own schema and record for the payment service's event. See the sections Why the service publishes contracts and Our copy of a consumed contract.

When the answer changes

Generated classes are fine, if each consumer generates them from its own reader schema, or tolerates unknown fields. With Avro, a consumer reads with its own reader schema, and fields that only the writer has are ignored. With Protobuf, unknown fields are skipped, so a consumer can compile a smaller copy of the schema. The coupling comes from sharing the producer's compiled artifact, not from generating code. Inside one team that owns the producer and every consumer, a shared class can be the better choice, because some breaking changes become compile errors.

The upstream team ignores our needs. What can we do?
#
Ask for a customer and supplier relationship, where your needs enter their planning. If that fails, protect yourself with an anti-corruption layer.
Why

Decided by Systems copy the teams that build them.

Code follows how teams talk. If the upstream team never hears your needs, their model will never serve them. A relationship where the downstream team has a say in the upstream plan is called customer and supplier.

When the other team cannot or will not listen, you cannot change their model. You can only protect your own model from it.

Where it shows

The order service treats the stock service as a model that it does not control, behind an adapter. See the section The adapter: the anti-corruption layer. For the patterns, see the Atlas chapter The map of treaties.

When the answer changes

When the upstream is an outside vendor, there is no planning to join. Then the choice is the layer, or conforming on purpose. See the question Should we translate the other side's model at the border, or use it as it is?.

When is a partnership between two contexts the right relationship?
#
When the two contexts must change together for one goal, and both teams can plan together. Review it when the shared goal ends.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Systems copy the teams that build them.

A relationship where two teams plan their changes together is called a partnership. It suits two contexts that change for the same reason during a project. Each change then needs both teams, which is cheap only while they talk every day.

Where it shows

The order service has no partnership. For the patterns, see the Atlas chapter The map of treaties.

When the answer changes

When the shared goal ends, or the teams stop talking daily, change it to customer and supplier. A partnership that nobody reviews turns into a shared model with two owners.

When should two contexts not integrate at all?
#
When integration costs more than doing a little work twice. This is called separate ways, and it is a fair choice.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price.

Each integration costs a contract, a translation and a dependency at run time. If two contexts need only a little from each other, a person or a simple copy can do that part on purpose. The integration would cost more than it saves.

Where it shows

The order service has no such case. For the pattern, see the Atlas chapter The map of treaties.

When the answer changes

When the manual work grows, or its errors start to cost money, integrate. The cost of waiting too long is data that two contexts have already entered differently.

Layers and architecture styles#

Must every feature of a service have the same packages inside it?
#
The same names, but only the packages that the feature needs. A package name then means the same thing in every feature.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price.

Each package is a fixed cost in files and in rules about what it may use. A feature that calls no other service gains nothing from an empty client package. So it leaves it out.

The names must still agree. The build rules match packages by name, so a persistence package that held something else would break a rule.

Where it shows

The order feature has domain, application, api, persistence, client and messaging. The note feature has model, application and api. The reference feature has application, api and persistence. See the section The same sub-packages in every feature.

When the answer changes

Stop when a reader can no longer tell a feature's level from its package names, or when a team invents a fourth shape. Then write the shapes down, and add a rule for each one.

Are hexagonal, onion and clean architecture really different?
#
Mostly in names and drawings. All three keep the domain at the centre, and every dependency points toward it.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

Alistair Cockburn described the hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, in 2005. Jeffrey Palermo described the onion architecture in 2008. Robert C. Martin described the clean architecture in 2012. Each one puts the business code in the middle and the technology outside.

The common rule is that source code depends only inward. The differences are the number of rings and their names.

Where it shows

The order service uses the same ports and adapters, with fewer folders. See the section Why not adapter/in and adapter/out.

When the answer changes

The names matter when a team already knows one style across many services. Then keep the familiar names, because they save reading time.

Still arguedIs the full set of ports and adapters worth it in every feature?
#
Writers disagree. The order service uses it only in its full-style feature. That is a choice made for each feature.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

The advocates follow Alistair Cockburn (2005) and Robert C. Martin (2012). They hold that testability and replaceability pay for themselves quickly. Teams that skip the ports get a domain that depends on a framework. This side uses the principle to depend on your own rules, not on the details. The rules must not change because a detail changed.

Jimmy Bogard (2018) and the vertical-slice camp answer that most features are simple. Uniform layers make simple things as expensive as hard ones. This side uses the principle that every boundary has a price.

Both sides agree that the domain must not depend on the infrastructure.

Where it shows

The order feature has ports and adapters, and the note and reference features do not. See the section Three levels in one service. For the argument, see the Atlas chapter Which way do the arrows point.

When the answer changes

A feature that starts to call another service, or whose rules become the core, needs the ports. The cost of adding them late is one change in one feature.

Should the top-level folders be features or technical layers?
#
Features. Then one business change touches one folder. Layers go inside each feature.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together.

A business change, such as a new rule about notes, belongs to one feature. With folders by technology, it touches the controllers, the services, the repositories and the transfer objects. Each of those folders also holds every other feature.

With folders by feature, the change stays in one place. A feature can also move to its own service later, because its dependencies are few and visible.

Where it shows

The order service has the top-level packages order, note and reference. See the section Features at the top, never technologies.

When the answer changes

A small service with one business area works well with folders by technology. The cost appears when a second area arrives, and every folder starts to mix the two areas.

Should we use a folder for each use case, with no shared domain model?
#
Use slices for features with independent use cases. Keep one shared model when several use cases change the same aggregate.
Why

Decided by The root guards the rule and What changes together stays together.

A folder that holds everything for one use case is called a vertical slice. It keeps one change in one folder. But placing, shipping and cancelling all change an order. Suppose each slice changes the order in its own code. Then a rule such as "a shipped order cannot change" is written twice. A third slice can forget it.

The aggregate guards its rules in one place. So its use cases share it.

Where it shows

The order service keeps one domain model per aggregate, and one application service per feature. See the section Why not one folder per use case.

When the answer changes

Reports and searches have no shared rules. Each one reads differently. For a feature like that, slices are the better choice, even inside a feature-based service.

Should every class, or every use case, have an interface?
#
No. Add an interface at a real border, such as storage or another service, or where a second implementation exists.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and Depend on your own rules, not on the details.

An interface at a border lets the inner code depend on its own types. That protects the domain from a technology. An interface with one implementation, in the same package, protects nothing. It doubles the files and makes the code harder to follow.

A test does not need an interface either. A mocking library can replace a class as easily.

Where it shows

The order service has interfaces for OrderRepository and StockChecker. It has none for OrderService, and a controller test mocks the class. See the section Why not adapter/in and adapter/out.

When the answer changes

A use case needs an interface when it really has several implementations. An example is one use case that each customer of a product implements in its own way.

Where do data transfer objects belong?
#
At the edge that owns them. Request records in the API package, the other service's records in the client package. The domain sees none.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and A published contract is hard to take back.

A data transfer object (DTO) has the shape of a contract outside your model. If the domain uses it, a change to the contract becomes a change to the rules. At the edge, a mapper absorbs the change.

Where it shows

In the order service, request and response records are in api.dto, and the stock service's records are in client.dto. See the section What goes where.

When the answer changes

A simple feature with no domain model can pass its records further in. There is no model to protect there.

Mapping between request records, domain objects and stored documents is a lot of code. Is it worth it?
#
It is the price of letting each shape change alone. Remove a mapping when it only copies fields of the same name.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and A published contract is hard to take back.

The API shape changes with consumers. The stored shape changes with the database. The model changes with the rules. A mapper lets one of them change without the others.

A mapper that copies every field to a field of the same name protects nothing. It is then only cost.

Where it shows

The order feature maps at each edge. The note feature has no document mapper. See the section The sign that a feature needs the next level.

When the answer changes

Keep the mapping at a published contract even when it only copies. The contract will change at a different speed later, and adding the mapper then is harder.

Features and modules inside one service#

What may a shared package inside one service hold?
#
Helpers that every feature uses in the same way and that hold no rule, such as permission annotations. Never business logic.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together.

Code in a shared package changes for every feature at once. A helper with no rule changes rarely, so that is cheap. A business rule changes with one feature. In the shared package, it would tie every feature to that change.

Where it shows

The order service's shared package holds the permission annotations, the audit names and the OpenAPI description. See the section The shared package, and what stays out of it.

When the answer changes

Move a class out of the shared package when it starts to make a business decision. Also move it when one feature needs a change that the other features do not need.

Two features in one service call each other. Is that a problem?
#
Yes, a warning sign. They cannot change, be tested or move apart. Make one call one-way, use an event, or merge them.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together.

A dependency in each direction means a change in either feature can break the other one. The two features then behave as one, but they look like two. A cycle also blocks a later move of either feature to its own service.

If the two features always change together, they are one feature. Then merging them is the honest fix.

Where it shows

The order and note features call each other, and the companion breaks the cycle at startup with @Lazy. Its README lists the ways out. See the section Two features that call each other.

When the answer changes

A cycle that is only a query, such as a count, can also end with a small read class. That class needs no dependency on the other feature.

How do we keep the borders between modules inside one deployable?
#
With a test that fails the build. A border that only code reviews protect is broken sooner or later.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and What changes together stays together.

A border between modules is cheap only while it holds. A reviewer is sometimes tired, or does not see one import at the top of a file. A test that reads the compiled classes sees every dependency, every time.

Without the test, the borders slowly disappear. The modules then change together, and a later split costs a rewrite.

Where it shows

The order service checks its rules with ArchUnit in ArchitectureTest. One rule fails when a feature uses another feature outside its application package. See the section The rules as tests that fail the build.

When the answer changes
