A single small module with one owner may need no rule yet. Add the test before the second team, or the second feature, arrives.

An application service has grown to fifteen use cases. How should we split it?
#
By business area, such as fulfilment or payment. Not into a read class and a write class.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together.

Use cases of one business area change together. A class for each area keeps a change in one class. A read class and a write class split each area in two. Each change to fulfilment would then touch both classes.

Fifteen use cases on one aggregate can also mean that the aggregate holds two things. So check the aggregate too.

Where it shows

The order service plans to split OrderService by area at about ten use cases. See the section Splitting a large application service.

When the answer changes

A real model for reading is a different thing from a read class. If reads need their own shape, add a read model for that query.

Next · Reasoning from first principles35Field questions: integration34 min

Field questions: integration#

Reasoning from first principles · Chapter 35· 34 min read

These are the questions that teams ask about events, messages and calls between services. Each question shows its answer when you open it. The answer starts with what you would say in a meeting. Then it names the principles that decide it, shows where the order service does it, and says when the answer changes.

Events and commands#

What is the difference between an event and a command?
#
An event says what already happened, and anyone may listen. A command asks one named receiver to act, and that receiver may refuse.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer.

An event is a fact that its publisher owns. The publisher wrote the change, so only the publisher can say that it happened. Nobody can refuse a fact.

A command asks for a change that the receiver owns. The receiver checks its own rules first, so it may say no. That is why a command has one receiver, and an event has any number of listeners.

Where it shows

The order service publishes facts such as OrderShippedV1. It sends a command, "hold these products", to the stock service as an HTTP call, because it needs the answer. See the section Why the order service calls the stock service.

When the answer changes

A command can also travel as a message on a queue, when the sender does not need the answer at once. It is still a command. It still has one receiver, and the receiver may still refuse it.

My team publishes an event called SendInvoice. Is that a problem?
#
Yes. It is a command that looks like an event. Publish the fact, such as OrderShipped, and let the invoice service decide.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and A published contract is hard to take back.

The name gives an order to one service. So the publisher now decides work that the invoice service owns. When the invoice rules change, the publisher must change too.

A fact in the past tense gives no orders. The invoice service reads OrderShipped and applies its own rules. A second service can react to the same fact, and the publisher changes nothing.

Where it shows

Every integration event of the order service names a business fact in the past tense, with a version. See the section Domain events and integration events.

When the answer changes

Sometimes the sender really decides that the work must happen. Then send a command to that one receiver, and do not publish it to everyone. The receiver can still refuse, so the sender must handle a refusal.

When may I publish my domain events directly, with no separate integration events?
#
Only while one team owns the publisher and every consumer, and they deploy together.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Systems copy the teams that build them.

A domain event holds the types of your model, such as OrderId. It changes whenever the model changes. Inside one team, that change is one conversation and one release.

When a consumer belongs to another team, every refactoring of your model needs their agreement. From that day, publish a separate integration event, and map to it.

Where it shows

The order service declares OrderShipped in order/domain/event. It declares OrderShippedV1 in order/messaging/event. See the section Domain events and integration events.

When the answer changes

The first consumer from another team ends the exception. Adding the mapper then is cheap, because nobody outside depends on the domain event yet.

Should every domain event become an integration event?
#
No. Publish an event only when another service needs it. Adding an event later is easy, and removing one is hard.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Every boundary has a price.

Every published event is a contract. It needs a schema, a version and care for its consumers. An event that nobody needs is a contract that costs work and gives nothing.

And once some team uses it, you cannot take it back. So start with the events that other services need today.

Where it shows

The order aggregate raises five domain events. Only the placed, shipped and cancelled events leave the service. A test checks that LinePicked stays inside. See the section Publish as few events as needed.

When the answer changes

When a new consumer needs an internal fact, add a new integration event for it, with its own schema. That is cheap, because nobody depends on it yet.

Should I publish a change event for every field, such as OrderStatusChanged?
#
No. Publish business facts, such as OrderShipped. A field change makes every consumer guess what happened in the business.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back.

A consumer cares about a business fact. OrderStatusChanged from "PAID" to "SHIPPED" hides that fact behind a column. Each consumer must then decode the column, and each decodes it in its own way.

The column also becomes the contract. So you cannot rename a status, or split it, without breaking consumers.

Where it shows

The order service publishes OrderPlacedV1, OrderShippedV1 and OrderCancelledV1. Each one names a fact that a business expert would use. See the section Event contracts: a JSON schema for each event.

When the answer changes

A copy of a whole table for a data warehouse may use change events per row. That is data replication, not a business contract, and the warehouse team accepts that the rows change shape.

What an event carries#

Still arguedShould an integration event carry the full state, or only an ID?
#
The order service sends IDs and the facts its consumers need. It is a choice between two costs, and the field has not settled it.
Why

Decided by A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability and Every fact has one writer.

An event with only an ID is called a notification. Every consumer then calls the publisher back for the data. So the consumer fails when the publisher is down. Martin Kleppmann (2017) argues that a consumer holding a slightly old copy is normal. So he prefers events that carry the state.

An event that carries everything copies data into every consumer. The notification style goes back to Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf (2003). Teams that follow it argue that each copy of personal or commercial data must then be protected and deleted.

Martin Fowler (2017) named both styles, and he did not pick one. Both sides agree on one test. If every consumer calls back, you chose notification, so choose it on purpose.

Where it shows

OrderPlacedV1 carries the order ID, the delivery method and the lines, because the stock service needs them. It carries no customer name or email address. See the section Event contracts: a JSON schema for each event.

When the answer changes

When the data is sensitive, and few consumers need it, send only the ID. Those consumers then ask the owner, and they depend on the owner being up.

A consumer calls my API back every time it receives my event. Is that wrong?
#
Then you chose notification events. Choose that on purpose, or put the facts that the consumer needs into the event.
Why

Decided by A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability.

A call back on every event brings back a call chain. If your service is slow or down, the consumer's queue stops too.

The call can also return data that is newer than the event. Then the consumer sees a state that the event did not describe. For the two styles of event, see the question on full state or only an ID.

Where it shows

The Atlas shows the cost of thin events in the chapter Something happened.

When the answer changes

If the data is large, or it changes faster than events arrive, a call back can be right. Then protect the call with a timeout, a retry and a circuit breaker, as for any call.

Can I put personal data, such as an email address, into an integration event?
#
Only what a consumer needs to do its job. Every copy must be protected, and deleted when the customer asks.
Why

Decided by Data outlives the code that wrote it and Every fact has one writer.

The order holds the customer's name and email address, so the order service owns them. An event that carries them creates a copy in every consumer and in every message store. Each copy is one more place to protect. And each copy stays after the event is gone. When the customer asks to be forgotten, every copy must be found and deleted.

A published field is also hard to remove. So a field added "just in case" stays for a long time.

Where it shows

OrderPlacedV1 carries nothing about the customer, because the stock service does not need it. See the section Event contracts: a JSON schema for each event.

When the answer changes

A consumer whose job needs the data, such as a service that emails the customer, may receive it. That consumer then follows the same rules for keeping and deleting it.

Which IDs should every integration event carry?
#
Its own event ID and the business ID, such as the order ID. Add a version from one writer when consumers must order events.
Why

Decided by You can fix only what you can see and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

The event ID lets a consumer detect a duplicate. A duplicate can arrive, because delivery is at least once.

The business ID lets a person follow one order through every service. Search for the order ID, and you find the request, the event and the consumer's log lines.

The time of the fact is useful too, but it is a weak key for order. Two instances of the producer have clocks that differ a little. A version that the aggregate increases, from one writer, orders events safely.

Where it shows

Every integration event of the order service has eventId, occurredAt and the order ID. It has no version, because no consumer needs to order the order's events yet. See the section Keeping event flows traceable.

When the answer changes

A time is safe as a key when one writer's clock sets every value. The payment service alone sets paidAt, so the order service may compare it. A trace ID can also travel, as a message header. The order service does not send one, so the order ID connects the two traces.

Changing a published event#

I publish OrderShippedV2. How long must I keep publishing V1 beside it?
#
Until the last consumer of V1 has moved to V2. Consumers then still read V1 until no V1 message is left in any queue.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Data outlives the code that wrote it.

A consumer of V1 breaks when V1 stops. You do not deploy that consumer, so you cannot move it yourself. So the producer publishes both versions, and each consumer moves in its own time. This order of steps is called expand and contract.

A message can also wait in a queue, or in a dead-letter queue, for days. So a consumer that has moved to V2 keeps reading V1 until the old messages are gone.

Where it shows

The rules for a version are in the comment of the interface that every published event of the order service implements. See the section Versions in names: what may change within V1.

When the answer changes

If you own every consumer, and they deploy with you, you can change the event in one release. Old messages in the queue still need a reader, even then.

How do I find out which services consume my event?
#
Keep a list of the consumers next to each schema. Let their expectations run as tests in your own build.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back.

You cannot change a contract safely if you do not know who depends on it. A wiki page goes out of date.

A list next to the schema is changed in the same pull request as the schema. A consumer test in your build fails when your change breaks that consumer. So you learn about the break before the consumer's on-call engineer does.

Where it shows

The order service keeps consumed-PaymentReceivedV1, its copy of the part of the payment event that it reads. The payment team compares a planned change with that copy. See the section Our copy of a consumed contract.

When the answer changes

A broker can list the queues that subscribe to a topic. That shows who receives the event, but not which fields each consumer reads. So the list alone is not enough to change a field.

Should a consumer fail when an event contains a field that it does not know?
#
No. Ignore fields that you do not know, and require only the fields that you use.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Data outlives the code that wrote it.

The producer may add a field at any time. That change is allowed within a version. During a rolling deployment, new producers and old consumers also run at the same time. A consumer that fails on a new field turns an allowed change into an outage.

A consumer that ignores what it does not know is called a tolerant reader. It still checks the fields it uses, so a missing field fails loudly.

Where it shows

The order service's PaymentReceivedV1 ignores unknown fields, and its compact constructor refuses a missing one. See the section Tolerant readers.

When the answer changes

A strict reader makes sense when an unknown field could change the meaning of the message. That should not happen within one version, so it is rare.

Publishing reliably#

Do I need an outbox if the message broker almost never fails?
#
Yes. The event is lost when your process dies between the save and the send, and no broker can prevent that.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place.

Your database and the broker cannot commit together. So the save and the send are two steps. A deployment or a crash can stop the process between them. Then the change is saved, and the event is never sent.

The transactional outbox writes the event into your own database, in the same transaction as the change. A separate step sends it later. So the change and the event are stored together, or not at all.

Where it shows

See the section The dual-write problem. The order service uses the event publication registry of Spring Modulith as its outbox.

When the answer changes

The transactions of a broker such as Kafka do not include your database. Only a transaction that the broker and the database share, through a protocol called XA, would close the gap. Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) has no transaction that a database can join, so the order service needs the outbox. If losing an event is harmless, such as an event that only feeds a dashboard, you may also accept the loss. Write that decision down.

Should the outbox be read by a polling job, or by change data capture?
#
Both are correct. Change data capture reads the database's log, so nothing polls. But it needs more infrastructure, and it must read only the outbox.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place and A published contract is hard to take back.

Both methods keep the important part. The change and the event are written in one transaction. They differ only in how the stored event reaches the broker.

Change data capture is a tool that reads the database's transaction log. Point it at the outbox, never at your business tables. Otherwise your table shape becomes everyone's contract.

Where it shows

The order service uses a sender that runs after the commit, and a job that resends what failed. See the section Resending what was not sent. For change data capture, see the Atlas chapter The message that never left.

When the answer changes

A team that already runs a change data capture platform may prefer it, because it adds no polling load. A team without one should not build it for one outbox.

Can a scheduled job publish events without a transaction?
#
Not in the order service. The platform refuses, because the event would be stored but not sent.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place.

The outbox sends an event after the transaction commits. Without a transaction, there is no commit, so the sender does not run. The event is stored, but it is not sent when the change is saved. Only a log line at shutdown shows it.

So the platform throws an exception instead. A loud error is better than a silent delay.

Where it shows

See the section Publishing outside a transaction.

When the answer changes

Put the job's work into a use case with @Transactional, or run it in a TransactionTemplate. A job that raises no events needs no transaction.

A reaction inside my own service listens to a domain event. Should it run before or after the commit?
#
After the commit, in most cases. Then it never acts on a change that was rolled back.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place.

A listener that runs at once runs inside the publisher's transaction. If that transaction rolls back later, the listener has already acted. A counter has counted an order that does not exist.

A listener that runs after the commit sees only changes that were stored. In the order service, it also gets an outbox row, so a failed run is repeated.

Where it shows

The order service counts shipped orders with @ApplicationModuleListener, which runs after the commit. See the section Reacting inside the service.

When the answer changes

If the reaction must succeed or fail together with the change, it must run inside the transaction. Then a failure of the reaction also rolls back the change.

Consuming events#

Can I get exactly-once delivery of messages?
#
Not from end to end. You get at-least-once delivery, and an idempotent consumer turns it into exactly-once effect.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

Suppose a consumer handles a message, and then crashes before it deletes the message. No delete arrived before the visibility timeout ended, so Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) delivers the message again.

This is called at-least-once delivery. The consumer must be idempotent. Handling a message twice must have the same effect as handling it once.

Where it shows

A standard queue of SQS delivers at least once. The order service's inbox skips an event whose ID it has seen. See the section Why every consumer needs an inbox.

When the answer changes

A first-in, first-out queue of SQS removes duplicates within five minutes. A resend from an outbox can arrive later than that, so the consumer still needs its own defence. See the section FIFO queues, the other choice.

Can a consumer rely on events arriving in the order they were sent?
#
No. Make the consumer ignore a late event, by comparing a version or a time that one writer set.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order and Now, or a little later.

A standard queue orders messages on a best-effort basis only. An outbox that resends a failed event also delivers it late. So an older event can arrive after a newer one.

A rule such as "the latest payment counts" may be true a little later. The consumer keeps the newest fact that it has seen, and it ignores an older one. "Newer" must come from one writer, because the clocks of two machines are never exactly the same.

Where it shows

The order aggregate ignores a payment whose paidAt is not later than the last one. The payment service alone sets that time. See the section The domain is idempotent too.

When the answer changes

A first-in, first-out queue keeps the order within one message group, such as one order ID. Its throughput is limited, and a resend can still arrive late.

What happens to a message that fails every time?
#
After a fixed number of attempts, the queue moves it to a dead-letter queue. Someone must watch that queue.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order and You can fix only what you can see.

A message that always fails is called a poison message. Without a limit, the consumer receives it again and again, and it uses capacity for ever.

A dead-letter queue takes it out of the way. But a message in that queue is work that was not done. If nobody looks, a customer finds out first.

Where it shows

The order service's local queues move a message to the dead-letter queue after 5 receives. SQS does the move, and the service has no code for it. See the section Failures, redrive and the dead-letter queue.

When the answer changes

A failure that will pass by itself, such as a database that restarts, should not reach the dead-letter queue. Allow enough receives, with enough time between them, to wait it out.

Messages are in the dead-letter queue. What do I do with them?
#
Find the cause, fix the code or the data, then move the messages back. Never delete a message that nobody has read.
Why

Decided by You can fix only what you can see.

Each message is a business fact that your service did not apply. A payment that is not recorded is an order that never ships.

So an alert on the dead-letter queue is part of the design. The message's event ID and order ID let you find its story in the logs.

Where it shows

In the order service, SQS moves a failing message to the dead-letter queue after 5 receives. Each message keeps its event ID. See the section Failures, redrive and the dead-letter queue.

When the answer changes

A message that can never be valid, such as one for an order that does not exist, may be removed. Write down why, so that the decision can be checked later.

My service keeps a copy of another service's data, fed by its events. May my service change the copy?
#
No. The copy is read-only. To change the data, ask the owner, and wait for its event.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer.

The other service owns the data and its rules. A change to your copy is a change that the owner never checked. The next event from the owner also overwrites it.

A copy is safe only because it is never the truth. When the copy and the owner disagree, the owner wins.

Where it shows

The Atlas shows a table with many writers in the chapter Nobody owns the product table.

When the answer changes

Your service may add its own data next to the copy, such as a local note on a product. That data has a different owner, your service, and you may change it.

Where does the logic of a message handler go?
#
In the use case and the domain. The listener only translates the message and calls one use case.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and The root guards the rule.

A message is one more way into the service, like an HTTP request. If the listener holds a rule, the controller needs a copy of the same rule. The two copies will drift apart.

A listener is an adapter. It depends on the application layer, and the rules stay where every caller meets them.

Where it shows

The payment listener turns the event into value objects and calls recordPayment. See the section A thin listener.

When the answer changes

A handler with no business rule, such as one that copies a reference list, may write directly through a repository. A feature with no rules needs no aggregate.

Calls between services#

Should services talk with calls or with messages by default?
#
With events for facts, and with a call only when you need an answer now. The order service calls the stock service for that reason.
Why

Decided by A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability and Now, or a little later.

A call works only while the other service works. An event does not need the receiver to be up when it is sent. So the receiver fails on its own, and the failure does not spread.

Chris Richardson (2018) leans toward messages for anything that is not a real request for an answer. Sam Newman (2015) also prefers event-based collaboration between services. He finds heavily orchestrated designs brittle, and he calls REST a good starting point when a request needs a response.

A call is still simpler to follow and to test. Messages bring duplicates, ordering and delay. So use a call where the answer is needed now, and protect it with a timeout and a circuit breaker.

Where it shows

The order service calls the stock service, because it must not sell products that it does not have. It publishes OrderPlacedV1 as a fact. See the section Why the order service calls the stock service.

When the answer changes

If a rule may be true a little later, a message is enough. Then the order no longer waits for the other service.

One request needs four other services to answer at once. What is wrong with that?
#
The request works only when all four are up and fast. Ask which answers are needed now, and keep a copy of the rest.
Why

Decided by A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability and Now, or a little later.

The chances multiply. Four services at 99.9 percent each give about 99.6 percent together. And the slowest of the four sets the time of the request.

Many of the four answers do not need to be fresh. A product name may be a few minutes old. A copy that events keep up to date removes that call.

Where it shows

The Atlas tells this story in the chapter The night everything deployed together.

When the answer changes

If each answer must be correct at this moment, the calls stay. Then give each call a timeout and a circuit breaker, and decide what the user sees when one fails.

How long should a timeout on a call be?
#
Long enough for a slow but normal answer. All attempts together, with their waits, must end before your own caller gives up.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order and Capacity is finite, so refuse early.

A call without a timeout can wait for ever, and it holds a thread while it waits. A few slow answers then use every thread of your service.

A retry multiplies the timeout. If your caller has already given up, your service keeps waiting for nothing.

Where it shows

The order service waits 3 seconds for the stock service's answer. Three attempts can keep the agent waiting for about 9 seconds, plus the waits between them. See the section How many times a retry calls.

When the answer changes

When a call is not retried, its timeout can be longer. When it is retried, keep each timeout short, so that the total still fits the caller's time.

Which failures should a client retry?
#
Only failures that may pass by themselves, with a longer wait before each retry. Never retry a request that is wrong.
Why

Decided by Capacity is finite, so refuse early and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

A retry helps only when the next attempt may work. A timeout or a 503 Service Unavailable may pass. A 400 Bad Request fails the same way every time, because the request itself is wrong. So does a 501 Not Implemented, or a 500 that comes from a bug.

A failure that may pass by itself is called a transient failure. Every retry is more work for a service that is already in trouble. So each wait is longer than the one before, with a random spread, and the retries stop after a few attempts. Without the random spread, many clients retry at the same moment.

Where it shows

The platform retries timeouts, refused connections and every 5xx answer, up to 3 attempts. It waits 200 ms, then about twice as long, with a random spread. It never retries a 4xx answer. See the sections Which failures are worth a retry and How many times a retry calls.

When the answer changes

Two 4xx answers can pass by themselves. A 408 Request Timeout can, and so can a 429 Too Many Requests. A 429 means that the caller sent too many requests in a given time. It may carry a Retry-After header, and so may a 503. Wait at least that long. Retrying at once only uses more of your quota. The platform does not retry either 4xx answer, so the adapter decides what each one means.

Do I need a circuit breaker if my client already retries?
#
Yes. A retry handles a short failure. A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, so callers fail fast.
Why

Decided by Capacity is finite, so refuse early and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

When the other service is down for ten minutes, every retry waits for a timeout. Your users see slow failures. And your retries add load to a service that is already in trouble, so it takes longer to recover.

A circuit breaker counts the failures. Past a limit, it fails each call at once. After a wait, it lets a few test calls through. So the other service gets time to recover, and your threads are free for other work.

Where it shows

See the section Retry and circuit breaker: what each one is for.

When the answer changes

A call that happens rarely, such as once a night, gains little from a breaker. A retry with a timeout is enough there.

Should I have one circuit breaker per service that I call, or one per endpoint?
#
One per service, in most cases. A service that is down is down for all its endpoints.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

One breaker per service learns faster that the service is down. Every failed endpoint counts toward the same breaker.

A separate breaker per service also keeps failures apart. When the stock service fails, calls to the payment service still go through.

Where it shows

The platform keeps one breaker for each dependency name, such as stock. See the section One circuit breaker for each dependency.

When the answer changes

Use one breaker per endpoint when the endpoints fail on their own, for example when they run on different servers.

A service that my API depends on is down. What should my API return?
#
A 503, which says that a later try may work. Do not name the failed dependency in the response.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

A 500 says that your service has a bug. A 503 says that the service cannot answer now. The caller can then retry later, or tell its user to try again.

The name of the failed dependency belongs in your log, not in the response. A caller does not need it.

Where it shows

The platform turns an open breaker, or a transient failure after the last retry, into a 503. See the section A failed call becomes a 503.

When the answer changes

If your service can answer without the dependency, answer. A product page without its reviews is better than no page. This is called graceful degradation.

Should I send a request over a message queue and wait for the reply on another queue?
#
Usually not. It has the coupling of a call, plus a broker, plus a reply that may never come.
Why

Decided by A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability.

The caller still waits for the other service, so it still fails when that service is down. It also needs a timeout for a reply that may be lost, and it must match each reply to its request.

If you need an answer now, a direct call is simpler. If you do not, do not wait.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The payment taken twice.

When the answer changes

A long job, such as a report that takes an hour, may send its result as a later message. The caller does not wait. It reacts when the result arrives.

Long flows and sagas#

Can I use one distributed transaction across two services?
#
No. Each service commits on its own. Make each step safe to repeat, and handle failure with a timeout or an undo step.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

A transaction protects one database. A protocol that joins two databases holds locks while the network talks. So one slow service blocks the other.

And SNS offers no transaction that a database can join. So each service commits alone, and the services agree after a while.

Where it shows

The order service holds stock with a call before its own transaction. If its transaction fails, the stock service releases the hold after a timeout. See the section Between services: no shared transaction.

When the answer changes

Two services that need a shared transaction often should be one service. Ask whether the border is in the right place before you build the machinery.

When do I need a saga?
#
When one flow changes data in several services, and a failed step must undo the earlier steps. One step with a timeout needs no saga.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later and A transaction protects one place.

No transaction covers the services, so a failure in step three leaves steps one and two done. The business must decide what happens to them.

A saga is a flow of local transactions. Each step has an undo step, which is called a compensation.

Where it shows

The order service has no saga. Its one step across services is a stock hold that ends by itself. See the section Between services: no shared transaction.

When the answer changes

If a failure can be repaired later by a person, a saga may be too much. An alert and a manual fix can cost less than code for every compensation.

Is a compensation the same as a rollback?
#
No. A rollback makes a change disappear. A compensation is a new business action, such as a refund, after others saw the first step.
Why

Decided by A transaction protects one place.

The first step committed in its own transaction, and its events went out. A committed step cannot be undone. Other services may already have acted on it.

So the undo is a step of its own, with its own business meaning. A refund is not a payment that never happened. It is a second fact, and the customer sees both.

Where it shows

The Atlas tells the story of a flow with undo steps in the chapter Who says the order is done?.

When the answer changes

Some steps are not yet seen by anyone outside, such as a hold that no event announced. Such a step can be released with no further action. That is the closest thing to a rollback across services.

Still arguedShould a saga use choreography or orchestration?
#
The order service has no long flow. The team picks one style when the first one appears. The field is still split.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and You can fix only what you can see.

Choreography means that each service reacts to the events of the others. James Lewis and Martin Fowler (2014) argued for "smart endpoints and dumb pipes". People who follow that line see a central coordinator as a bottleneck.

Orchestration means that one coordinator tells each service what to do next. Chris Richardson (2018) argues that a flow with more than a few steps needs it. Otherwise nobody can see, test or run it.

Many teams use choreography for two or three steps, and orchestration beyond that.

Where it shows

See the section Long flows: a workflow engine or a process manager, and the Atlas chapter Who says the order is done?.

When the answer changes

If people often ask "where is this order?", the flow needs one place that knows. That points to orchestration.

A step of a saga never answers. What happens?
#
Every waiting state needs a timeout and a planned outcome. Without one, the flow waits for ever, and nobody is told.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order and You can fix only what you can see.

The other service may be down, or its answer may be lost. A flow that waits only for the answer then holds stock or money for days.

A timeout turns silence into an event that the flow can handle. The flow can retry, compensate or alert a person.

Where it shows

The stock service releases a hold that no OrderPlacedV1 confirms, after a timeout. See the section Between services: no shared transaction.

When the answer changes

Some steps take days by design, such as a parcel that is in transit. Their timeout is then long, and it is a business number, not a technical one.

May the coordinator of a long flow check the business rules of the other services?
#
No. It keeps only the state of the flow. Each service checks its own rules.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and The root guards the rule.

The stock service owns the rules about stock, and the payment service owns the rules about payments. A coordinator that checks them has a second copy of those rules. The copies will disagree.

A coordinator that knows every rule becomes a service that every team must change. It asks, waits and decides the next step. That is all.

Where it shows

A process manager keeps the state of a sequence of steps. See the section Long flows: a workflow engine or a process manager.

When the answer changes

The coordinator may hold rules about the flow itself, such as "refund if the parcel is not delivered in 14 days". Those rules belong to the flow, not to another service.

Should I run long flows with a workflow engine, or with a process manager in my own code?
#
For one or two flows, a process manager in your own code. For many long flows, a workflow engine. Choose once, for the team.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and Prefer the decision you can undo.

A workflow engine stores the state of each flow, and it retries and times out for you. It is also one more product to run and to learn.

A process manager is an aggregate in one of your services. It costs less to start, and you write the retries and timeouts yourself.

Where it shows

The order service has no process manager and no workflow engine, because it has no long flow. The team chooses one approach when the first long flow appears, and records it in an architecture decision record (ADR). See the section Long flows: a workflow engine or a process manager.

When the answer changes

A flow that lasts days, with many steps and many failures, gains most from an engine. Writing durable timers and retries yourself for it is the larger cost.

Should I lock data so that users never see a flow halfway through?
#
No. Give the halfway state a name, such as "payment pending". The business usually has a word for it already.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later.

A lock across services holds data while the network talks. One slow service then blocks everyone.

The business already works with these states. A shop says "awaiting payment" and "out for delivery". A state with a name can be shown, counted and handled.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Who says the order is done?.

When the answer changes

A rule that must be true at every moment cannot have a halfway state. Its data must then be in one aggregate, in one service.

Eventual consistency and what users see#

How do I know that eventual consistency is acceptable for a rule?
#
Ask the business what happens today when the rule is broken for a minute. A phone call or a refund means yes.
Why

Decided by Now, or a little later.

Eventual consistency means that each service is correct on its own, and the services agree after a while. In that while, a rule across them can be false.

The question is not technical. It is about the cost of that short window. Only the people who own the rule know that cost.

Where it shows

The stock service holds products for an order. If the order is not saved, the stock service releases the hold after a timeout. For a while, stock is held for an order that does not exist. See the section Between services: no shared transaction.

When the answer changes

If a broken rule means money that cannot be recovered, or a legal fine, the rule must be true now. Then its data belongs in one aggregate.

A user saves a change, and the list on the next screen still shows the old data. What do I do?
#
Show the result from the answer of the save, or tell the user that the change is coming. Never hide the delay.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes and Now, or a little later.

The list is built from a model for reading, and that model is updated after the write. So for a moment, the list is behind.

The write already returned the new state. The screen can show that state at once, or show the item as "updating".

Where it shows

The Atlas shows this delay in the chapter Two models are cheaper than one.

When the answer changes

The order service reads its lists from the same database as its writes. Its connection string sets readPreference=primary, so every read sees the write before it. A read from a replica can be behind. See the section The connection string and the Boot 4 key.

Read models, reports and queries across services#

Still arguedShould every service separate its read model from its write model?
#
The order service uses one model for both. That is a choice, and the field disagrees about how often a second model pays.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes and Every boundary has a price.

The split is called command query responsibility segregation (CQRS). Greg Young (2010) described it as a small, local pattern. A feature may use it for one screen.

Sam Newman (2021) is more careful. He notes that even a small split adds eventual consistency. And teams often underestimate the work of keeping a read model correct.

Both agree that the split is wrong when reads have the same shape as writes.

Where it shows

The order service reads an aggregate and turns it into a view. See the section One model for reads and writes: CQRS or not.

When the answer changes

A screen that joins many aggregates, or many services, needs a model of its own. Loading every aggregate for it is too slow.

Does CQRS require event sourcing?
#
No. A read model can be fed by ordinary events, or built from the same database. Event sourcing is a separate decision.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes.

A read model needs a way to learn about changes. Integration events give that. So does a query on the write side's own tables.

Greg Young (2010) said that CQRS is not event sourcing. He later argued that bundling the two made CQRS look harder than it is.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Two models are cheaper than one.

When the answer changes

With event sourcing, a read model is the usual way to answer queries. So CQRS and event sourcing often appear together. But each one works without the other.

Can a command check a read model before it decides?
#
No. The read model may be out of date at exactly the moment that matters. Check the rule on the aggregate that owns the data.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes and Now, or a little later.

A read model is updated after the write, so it is a little late. A decision based on it can be wrong in a busy moment, which is when it matters most.

A rule that must be true now needs the data that the transaction protects. That data is in the aggregate.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Two models are cheaper than one.

When the answer changes

A check that may be a little late can use the read model. A warning such as "this customer ordered the same item yesterday" is an example.

What must a read model be able to do that an ordinary table need not?
#
It must be possible to delete it and build it again from its source.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes and Prefer the decision you can undo.

A read model is a copy. Its shape changes when a screen changes, and a bug can corrupt it.

If it can be rebuilt, both problems are a rebuild. If it cannot, the copy has become the truth, and nobody owns it.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Two models are cheaper than one.

When the answer changes

A read model fed by events needs those events again for a rebuild. If the events are gone, build it from the owners' current data instead, through their APIs.

Can a read model call other services to fill in its rows when an event arrives?
#
Avoid it. Put the facts that the read model needs into the events, or keep a copy from other events.
Why

Decided by A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order and Reads and writes have different shapes.

A read model that calls three services fails when any of them is down. It brings the call chain back into the place that should be fast and independent.

The calls also return today's data for yesterday's event. So the row may mix two moments.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Two models are cheaper than one.

When the answer changes

Data that the owner will not put in its events, such as large documents, may be fetched. Then the fetch needs a retry, and the row needs a state for "not complete yet".

A screen shows a list that joins data from three services. How do I build it?
#
Keep a read model that the three services' events fill. Calling three services for each row does not work for a list.
Why

Decided by Reads and writes have different shapes and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

Calling several services and joining their answers is called API composition. It works for one item. For a list, it cannot sort or filter across the services without fetching everything.

A read model shaped for the list answers with one query. It may be a little behind, and a list can usually accept that.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The report nobody could run.

When the answer changes

A screen that shows one order, from three services, can use composition. Give each call a timeout and a fallback.

Should a mobile app call many services, or one backend made for it?
#
One backend made for it, owned by the app's team. It makes the calls near the services and returns one answer shaped for the screen.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

A phone on a slow network pays for every call. One call to a backend near the services costs less than four calls from the phone.

The screen and its backend change together, so one team owns both. This backend is called a backend for frontend. It holds no business rules. The services keep those.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The report nobody could run.

When the answer changes

A single web front end with one team may call the services directly. A separate backend then adds a deployment and buys little.

How does a report get data from every service?
#
Each service publishes its facts, and a reporting store copies them. Never give reporting a user on every service's database.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and A published contract is hard to take back.

A report that reads every database depends on every table. The first migration in any service breaks it, and nobody knew that the report existed.

Published facts are contracts with versions. The reporting store builds its own shape from them, for joining and counting.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The report nobody could run.

When the answer changes

A small system with one database and one team can report from that database directly. The report then breaks only on changes that the same team makes and tests.

Event sourcing#

Still arguedShould my service store its events instead of its current state?
#
The order service stores current state and keeps an audit log. That is a choice. Event sourcing pays where the business asks about history.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different and Data outlives the code that wrote it.

Storing the events as the only truth is called event sourcing. Greg Young (2010) and those who follow him argue that it prevents a whole class of "we did not keep that" failures.

Sam Newman (2021) is more careful. He notes that rebuilds, old event shapes and the deletion of personal data cost more than teams expect. A good audit table answers most questions for less. Stored events also stay for ever, so every old shape of an event must still be read.

Both agree that event sourcing is wrong where nobody asks about the past. So spend it where the history is part of what makes the business different.

Where it shows

The order service writes an audit log in the same transaction as each change. See the section The audit log: a business record, not a log line.

When the answer changes

A ledger, where every change matters and the history is the business, is the strong case. The choice of an event store is also hard to change later, so decide early.

Can other services subscribe to my event store?
#
No. Your stored events are your private history. Publish separate integration events for other services.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and Every fact has one writer.

Stored events follow the shape of your model. If another service reads them, every change to your model breaks that service.

And stored events cannot be edited. So you could never fix their shape for a consumer. A mapper to integration events keeps the history private.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The ledger never lies.

When the answer changes

Modules of one service that deploy together may read the store directly. Nothing is published between them.

Is an audit log the same as event sourcing?
#
No. An audit log records what happened next to the state. In event sourcing, the events are the state.
Why

Decided by Spend design effort where the business is different.

With an audit log, the current state is the truth. The log explains who changed it, and when. With event sourcing, the events are the truth, and the state is computed from them.

An audit log is cheap, and it answers "who did this?". Event sourcing costs much more. So use it only where the business needs every past state, and that need sets it apart.

Where it shows

The order service's audit entry names the action, the resource, the actor and the time. See the section The audit log: a business record, not a log line.

When the answer changes

If you need to rebuild the state as it was on a past date, an audit log is not enough. It keeps actions, not every field. That need points to event sourcing.

Next · Reasoning from first principles36Field questions: services and teams28 min

Field questions: services and teams#

Reasoning from first principles · Chapter 36· 28 min read

These questions are about the system around one service. They ask when to split a service, how big it is and what services may share. They also ask about contracts, tests, tracing and teams. Each answer starts with what you would say in a meeting. Then it names the principle that decides it.

A monolith or services#

Still arguedShould a new system start as one deployable or as several services?
#
Start as one deployable with enforced modules, unless the team already knows the borders and has a platform for many services. That is a choice.
Why

Decided by Prefer the decision you can undo and Every boundary has a price.

At the start, the team knows least about where the borders are. A wrong border between modules costs a refactoring. A wrong border between services costs a data migration, two contracts and two pipelines. So the cheaper mistake comes first.

Martin Fowler argued for this in 2015, in "MonolithFirst". He saw most successful service systems start as a monolith, and most systems that started as services get into trouble. Stefan Tilkov answered the same year, in "Don't start with a monolith". He argued that a team that knows its domain should start with separate services. Then the network enforces the borders from the first day. A monolith teaches habits, such as reading across modules, that make a later split as hard as a rewrite.

The two positions agree on one premise. The borders must be known before they are enforced. They disagree about whether a team can know them on the first day.

Where it shows

The Atlas tells this decision as a story in the chapter The consultant who said microservices. The order service shows the module side inside one service. Its features talk only through their application services. See the section Calls between features.

When the answer changes

Tilkov's answer is right when the team has built this domain before and a platform for many services already runs. Then the borders are known, and the habits of a monolith are the larger risk.

What makes a modular monolith more than a monolith with tidy folders?
#
Each module owns its data. No module reads or writes the data of another module, even inside one database.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and What changes together stays together.

Folders keep code apart, but shared data joins it again. If two modules write the same table, each one can break the rules of the other. Then no folder can change that table alone.

A module that owns its data can change it, and can leave the deployable later. So data ownership is what makes the modules real.

Where it shows

The order and note features of the order service store their own documents. Each feature reaches the other only through its application service, never through its repository. See the section Calls between features. For how the build enforces module borders, see the questions fq-b-module-enforce and fq-b-contexts-one-service.

When the answer changes

Two modules sometimes save together, because the user sees one action. The order service saves an order and its first notes in one transaction for this reason. Write that decision down, because it blocks a later split of the two modules. See the section One request that saves the order and its first notes.

What does one more service cost, apart from its code?
#
Its own pipeline, on-call rota, contract, network failures and tracing. This cost is called the microservices premium.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price.

Each service is a border, and every border has a price. Martin Fowler named this price the microservices premium in 2015. The premium is paid for every service, whether or not that service needed to be separate.

The premium gives independent deployment and team autonomy. It is worth paying only when those two things are worth more to you than the premium.

Where it shows

Inside one deployable, the order service would have no timeouts, retries or remote calls. Its outbox would be smaller, because only in-process listeners would read it, such as the one that counts orders. Logging, tracing and health checks would still exist. See the chapters Calling other services and Publishing events: the outbox.

When the answer changes

A border that a law or a security rule requires, such as one around card data, must be paid for whatever it costs. Then the premium is fixed, and the only question is how to keep it small.

What is a good reason to move a module into a service of its own?
#
A measured need, such as other modules blocking its releases, a different scaling need, or failures that must stay apart.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Every boundary has a price.

A module that moves to a service adds the premium to every change that crosses its border. So the move must give something that the module could not. Independent release, separate scaling and a separate failure are the three things a module cannot give.

Write the triggers down before you need them. Then the decision is made on evidence, not on fashion.

Where it shows

The Atlas writes such triggers down with the decision, in the chapter The consultant who said microservices.

When the answer changes

A border that must exist for legal or security reasons may justify a service before any measurement. Payment data is a common example. Then the premium is the price of that rule.

The code of our monolith is a mess. Will splitting it into services fix that?
#
No. Splitting a mess gives several messes that call each other over a network. Find the business borders first.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and A word that changes meaning marks a border.

A service border helps only where changes do not cross it. In a tangled program, every change crosses everything. A network between the parts keeps the tangle and adds failures.

The fix for the mess is borders that follow the business language. Once they exist inside the program, a split along them is possible. Often it is then no longer needed.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapters Let's do microservices and The night everything deployed together.

When the answer changes

One part of the mess may already have a clear border, a stable contract and its own data. That part can move out first. It is the exception, so check the border before you trust it.

When should two services become one service again?
#
When they always change and ship together, and one team owns both. The border is in the wrong place.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Prefer the decision you can undo.

A border is worth its cost only when changes stay on one side of it. If every change touches both services, the team has the cost of two services and no independence.

A merge is a correction, not a failure. A team that cannot merge services has stopped learning from its own design. In 2018, Alexandra Noonan described how Segment merged its many services back into one deployable.

Where it shows

The Atlas merges two services in the chapter The consultant who said microservices.

When the answer changes

Keep the services apart when one of them has a real need for its own scaling, security or release. Then make the contract between them smaller, so that fewer changes cross it.

How big a service is#

How big should a microservice be?
#
Big enough that most changes stay inside it, and small enough that one team can own it. Lines of code are the wrong measure.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Systems copy the teams that build them.

The size of a service is right when changes rarely cross its border. A service that is too small makes most changes cross into a neighbour. A service that is too large needs two teams, and two teams soon build two models in it.

So the limits come from changes and from people, not from the amount of code.

Where it shows

The order service holds one bounded context with three features. OrderService has seven use cases, and one check, requireExists, for the note feature. See the section One application service per feature.

When the answer changes

A part with a very different load, such as a search index, may need its own service inside the same context. Then size follows the runtime need, and the contract between the two parts must stay small.

Is one service per noun, such as a customer service and a product service, a good split?
#
Usually not. Each real operation then calls several services. Split by what the business does, not by its nouns.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability.

A business operation, such as placing an order, needs a customer, products and prices. If each noun is a service, every operation crosses three borders. Every change to the operation touches three services, and every call can fail.

A split by business capability keeps one operation inside one service. Services named after layers, such as "web", "logic" and "data", fail in the same way.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Let's do microservices. The order service places an order with one call to another service, the stock reservation. See the section Placing an order: the stock call before the transaction.

When the answer changes

A noun can be a capability of its own. A product catalogue that sellers edit, with its own rules and team, is a real context. The test is whether the service does work, not only storage.

How do I keep a feature ready to move into its own service later?
#
Give it its own data, and let other features call it only through its application service. A move then changes a call, not a model.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Every fact has one writer.

A feature that shares nothing but calls can leave without its neighbours noticing much. Each caller changes one call into a remote call.

A feature whose data another feature writes cannot leave alone. The writer would have to move with it, or call it.

Where it shows

The order and note features call each other only through their application services, and pass IDs as text. See the section Calls between features. The shared package holds no business logic, only a few helpers that a moving feature would copy. See the section The shared package, and what stays out of it.

When the answer changes

A call that joins the caller's transaction cannot become a remote call. Placing an order calls the note feature inside the same transaction. If notes move to another service, the order is saved first, and the notes follow from an event. See the section How each decision is recorded.

The distributed monolith#

How do I know that our services are a distributed monolith?
#
They must deploy together, share a database schema, or fail as a chain. You pay for many services and get the coupling of one.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and A synchronous call borrows the other side's availability.

A distributed monolith has borders that changes do not respect. A change crosses them, so the services ship together. A shared schema crosses them, so a migration is a joint release.

Its requests also wait on each other. A chain of synchronous calls works only while every service in it works. So the services fail together, as one program would.

The services still pay for the network, the pipelines and the on-call rotas. So the system has the costs of many services and the coupling of one.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The night everything deployed together.

When the answer changes

A release plan that lists several services is sometimes honest. Two services can ship one feature together without depending on each other's release. The sign is a change that cannot ship unless the other ships too.

Still arguedWe have a distributed monolith. Do we move forward to real borders, or merge the services?
#
Merge where services always change together. Where they change apart, remove the shared schema and the call chains. That is a judgement.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together and Prefer the decision you can undo.

Sam Newman, in 2019, treats a first split along imperfect seams as a stage. The pain gives the evidence for better borders. Alexandra Noonan described in 2018 how Segment merged its services back into one deployable. That view treats the state as a mistake to reverse.

Both views agree that staying in this state is the worst choice. The principle What changes together stays together decides each pair of services on its own. For the pairs that stay apart, the coupling must go.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter The night everything deployed together.

When the answer changes

If the business borders are still unknown, merge first. Borders are cheaper to find inside one deployable. If they are known and the platform runs well, move forward to the real borders.

Data between services#

Does each service need a database of its own?
#
Each service needs private data that others reach only through its API. A private schema is enough until scaling or failure needs a separate server.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer.

The rule that matters is one writer for each fact. Chris Richardson's pattern "Database per service", in his book of 2018, makes each service's data private. Other services reach it only through the service's API.

The pattern accepts private tables, a private schema or a separate database server. It says that private tables and a private schema cost the least. Kirsten Westeinde described in 2019 how Shopify keeps its borders inside one large program, enforced by tools.

What keeps the data private is the access rule, with credentials that enforce it. A separate server alone does not do that.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Nobody owns the product table. The order service never reads the data of another service. It asks the stock service over HTTP, and it receives payments as events. See the section Its events and the services it talks to.

When the answer changes

A separate server becomes necessary when a service needs its own scaling, backup or failure limits. It also helps when credentials cannot keep teams out of each other's schemas. Then pay for the second server, its backups and its failover.

Can two services share one database "for now", to move faster?
#
Only with one owner for each table and a date to end it. A shared schema is a contract that nobody can change alone.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and A published contract is hard to take back.

When two services read the same table, its columns are a published contract between them. A rename needs both teams, a meeting and a joint release.

When two services write the same table, each one can break the other's rules. "For now" has no end date unless someone writes one.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapters Let's do microservices and Nobody owns the product table.

When the answer changes

During a migration from a monolith, a shared table is normal for a while. The plan then names the last reader of the old table, and the date it goes.

Is a service allowed to keep a copy of data that another service owns?
#
Yes, if the other service stays the owner and the copy is never edited. The copy is a cache of someone else's truth.
Why

Decided by Every fact has one writer and Data outlives the code that wrote it.

The rule is one writer for each fact, not one place for each fact. Across services, one service owns the fact and the others may keep copies. When a copy and the owner disagree, the owner wins.

For how a copy stays current, see the question fq-change-copied-data.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Nobody owns the product table.

When the answer changes

Personal data changes the answer. A law may require that a person's data is deleted everywhere on request. Then every copy is a place that must be found and cleaned, so keep fewer copies.

Shared code#

What may a library that every service uses contain?
#
Technical code that means the same in every service, such as error responses, token checks and the outbox. No business concept, with one narrow exception.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and What changes together stays together.

A business concept changes for the reasons of one service. In a shared library, that change forces every other service to take a new version, or to disagree.

Technical code changes for reasons that are the same for every service. Shared, it is written once and fixed once.

Where it shows

The platform library holds base classes, a guard and technical defaults, but no business code. Even Money is written by each service. See the section What never goes in the platform library.

When the answer changes

The exception is a rule that must never differ between services, such as a legal rounding rule. Then put that one rule in a small library of its own, with no other business types, and version it carefully. See the section What never goes in the platform library.

How can a shared library change without forcing every service to ship at once?
#
With semantic versions. A breaking change waits for a major version, and each service upgrades in its own release.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and What changes together stays together.

A shared library is a published contract between its team and every service. A semantic version tells each service what a new version may break. So each service can upgrade when it is ready, and no release plan joins them.

For a library of defaults, "breaking" covers more than a method signature. A renamed property or a changed default value is also breaking.

Where it shows

The platform's rules say which changes wait for a major version. A service stays at most one minor version behind. See the section Versions, and the rules for upgrading.

When the answer changes

A security fix, or the end of support for a major version, can force every service to upgrade before a deadline. Then the services still ship one by one, but the date is no longer theirs to choose. Services that stayed close to the latest version have the least work.

When should a company build its shared platform library?
#
Together with the first two services. Code moves into the library when a second service needs it, and not before.
Why

Decided by Prefer the decision you can undo and Every boundary has a price.

A library written before any service has to guess what services need. A guess is hard to undo, because services start to depend on it.

A library built from the first two services contains what they really used. The border between service code and library code then has a proven reason.

Where it shows

Before the library exists, the first services keep such code in their shared package, under the package names that the library will use. See the section When to build the library, and what to do before it exists.

When the answer changes

A company that already runs many services in another stack knows what it needs. It can build the library first, from the needs it has already measured.

One shared library for everything, or one library for each concern?
#
One library while the company is small. Split it when services skip an area, or an area needs its own release rhythm.
Why

Decided by Every boundary has a price and What changes together stays together.

Each library is a border with its own versions. Several libraries need versions that match. A bug report then names four versions, not one.

When nearly every service uses every area, the extra borders protect nothing.

Where it shows

The shop keeps one library, with each area in its own package, so a later split moves packages and not code. See the section One library, not one per concern.

When the answer changes

Split when several services do not use an area and it slows them. Also split when services in another language need part of the library, because that part is then not a Spring Boot library at all.

Contracts and versions#

When does an HTTP API between services need a new version?
#
Only for a breaking change. To remove, rename or change the meaning of a field, run the new version beside the old one.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back.

Adding a field breaks no consumer that ignores unknown fields. Removing or renaming one breaks every consumer that reads it, at a time that you do not choose.

So the producer adds the new form, waits until every consumer has moved, and then removes the old form. This is called expand and contract. A path such as /v2/ that replaces /v1/ in one deploy is a breaking change with a number on it.

Where it shows

For HTTP interfaces, see the Atlas chapter Can you see it?. For events, see the question fq-v1-v2-how-long.

When the answer changes

If you deploy every consumer yourself, together with the producer, the API is not published. A rename is then a refactoring. Check that this is really true before you rely on it.

Deploying and releasing#

What is the test that a service can be deployed on its own?
#
You can ship a change to it today without deploying, migrating or telling any other service. If you cannot, the border is not real.
Why

Decided by What changes together stays together.

Independent deployment is the main thing that a service gives over a module. Sam Newman made it the test of a service in 2015.

A border that changes respect lets the service ship alone. A border that changes cross makes the service wait for its neighbours.

Where it shows

The order service may add fields to its events within V1, so it ships without its consumers. See the section Versions in names: what may change within V1. The Atlas asks this question in the chapter Let's do microservices.

When the answer changes

A regulator or a large customer may require one release date for all changes. Then the services ship together on that date. Keep each one able to ship alone, so the shared date stays a choice and not a need.

What is the difference between deploying and releasing?
#
Deploying puts new code on the servers. Releasing lets it answer users. A feature flag separates them, so you switch back without a deploy.
Why

Decided by Prefer the decision you can undo and Data outlives the code that wrote it.

A change that is deployed but not released can be undone in seconds. A flag sends one user, then a few, then everyone down the new path.

Each flag doubles the paths that the tests must cover. So delete a flag as soon as the old path is gone.

Where it shows

See the Atlas chapter Strangling the monolith.

When the answer changes

A change of stored data cannot hide behind a flag. During a rolling deploy, old code and new code read the same documents. So change the data in steps that both versions of the code can read.

Testing across services#

Still arguedDo we need a suite of end-to-end tests that runs all the services together?
#
Not a broad suite. The order service tests its own journey alone. Whether a few journeys across services should stay is still argued.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back and What changes together stays together.

A test that needs every service deployed together needs every service at one version. That is a joint release, written as a test. It is slow, it fails for reasons outside the change, and teams learn to ignore it. Both sides of the argument agree on this.

Sam Newman, in 2021, wants as close to zero tests across services as possible, with contract tests at each border instead. Jez Humble and David Farley, in their book Continuous Delivery from 2010, keep a few journeys on the critical path. Such a journey catches wrong settings that no contract can see.

Where it shows

The order service's journey test runs one business story through the order service alone, with real MongoDB and an emulator for messages. The QA team's Playwright tests run across services, in their own repository. See the section The kinds of test, who owns each, and what each costs.

When the answer changes

If you keep journeys across services, keep them few, owned and fast. A journey that fails often and is ignored is worse than none, because it trains people to ship on red.

What does a contract test check, and where does it run?
#
It checks that a producer still gives what its consumers rely on. It runs in the producer's build, before the change ships.
Why

Decided by A published contract is hard to take back.

The change that breaks a consumer starts in the producer. So the check belongs in the producer's build, where the change is made.

When consumers write their expectations, the producer's build can name the consumer that a change breaks. These are called consumer-driven contracts.

Where it shows

The order service checks its published events against committed JSON schemas, and its API against a committed OpenAPI file. A removed field fails its build. See the section The OpenAPI drift test.

When the answer changes

A check of the producer's own schema finds every removed required field. But it cannot tell which change matters to whom. For that, the producer needs the consumers' own expectations.

How do I test my service without running the services that it calls?
#
Replace them at your border. Test your client against a small local HTTP server, and replace the port in the larger tests.
Why

Decided by Depend on your own rules, not on the details and A remote call fails, waits, repeats or arrives out of order.

The service depends on a port, an interface in its own words. So a test can replace the other service at that port, and nothing else changes.

The client still needs its own test against real HTTP. Timeouts, retries and the translation of answers are exactly what fails between services.

Where it shows

The stock client is tested against an HTTP server from the Java Development Kit (JDK). The journey test replaces the stock port. See the section The HTTP client against a real server from the JDK. Also see the section The journey test: real MongoDB and a real SNS and SQS emulator.

When the answer changes

A stub that answers what the real service never answers proves the wrong thing. So copy a real response when you write a stub, and keep its field names.

Seeing across services#

What must every service do so that one request can be followed through all of them?
#
Write a trace ID on every log line, and send it with every call. Put a business ID in every message.
Why

Decided by You can fix only what you can see.

Each service logs only its own part of the work. A shared ID is the only thing that joins those parts into one story. The edge of the system accepts the caller's ID, or creates one.

A message is sent later, on another thread, and often without the trace ID. A business ID in the message, such as the order ID, joins the two traces.

Where it shows

The order service gets the trace ID from Spring Boot's tracing, with no code, and sends it on its HTTP calls. Its events carry no trace ID. A consumer starts a new trace, and the order ID joins the two traces. See the section Keeping event flows traceable.

When the answer changes

A team that needs one trace across a message must add the trace context to the message as a header. That is extra work for each kind of broker, so do it only where support really needs it.

What should wake an engineer at night, a busy processor or failed orders?
#
Failed orders. Alert on what a customer feels. Machine numbers help to explain an incident, but they are not the incident.
Why

Decided by You can fix only what you can see.

A busy machine may serve every customer well. A quiet machine may fail every order. So an alert on the machine wakes people for nothing, and stays silent when it matters.

An alert on a business number, such as the share of failed checkouts, fires when customers are hurt. Google's book on site reliability, from 2016, made this common practice.

Where it shows

The order service counts placed, shipped and cancelled orders in a metric named shop.orders. That metric counts business events, not failures. And nothing is exported until a deployment adds a registry. See the section Business metrics. For the full idea, see the Atlas chapter Can you see it?.

When the answer changes

A cause that always comes before harm, such as a full disk, may deserve a warning. It is a warning for the day, not a call at night.

Trust between services#

Other features, listeners and jobs also call our use cases. Where do we check a user's permission?
#
Where the user's request enters, such as the controller. The use cases behind it then serve internal callers without a second check.
Why

Decided by Check permissions where a user's request enters.

Only the entry point knows who the user is. A listener, a job and another feature have no user, because the service itself decided to do the work.

A check on the use case would refuse that work. A developer then writes a helper that pretends to be a user, and the check protects nothing.

Where it shows
